en: Oṃ. The *Śrī Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya*, composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya;
now begins the first chapter.

(Ascertainment of the Intent of All Scriptures) Oṃ! Salutations, salutations to You, Nārāyaṇa, the ocean of perfect attributes; to the one who bestows the governance over the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe; to the giver of knowledge; to the cause of the happiness, suffering, and honor of the gods and demons; to the all-pervading One. 1.1.
There was Nārāyaṇa, the immeasurable, the supreme beyond the highest, an unfathomable ocean of noble qualities, who alone exists;
he, having placed within his belly the entire peaceful and conscious universe, remains even before the sound of his own voice, nestled between the arms of Lakṣmī.
Of him, whose body is satisfied by the intense bliss of the world residing in his belly—the very delight of Ramā—[the following occurs].
For the sake of the prosperity of those who depend upon him, his glance arose at the end of a moment of the Supreme Name, directed toward the creation of the beings to be created.

(1.3) Having seen within his own belly the multitudes of sentient beings lying there—whose bodies consist of nothing but bliss, who are liberated from the cycle of rebirth, and who have entered into meditative absorption—he likewise beheld Brahmā and the others, as well as humans devoted to the Kali age, who were situated in the state of deep sleep while traversing the path of transmigration. (1.4)
"Indeed, desiring the sport of embodied beings for their attainment of pleasure, pain, or the intermediate state, I shall create the multitudes of conscious entities;
this very play of mine here serves to bring about the manifestation of the nature of those embodied beings, just as prosperity itself brings about further prosperity.
Having reflected thus, he, the Supreme One named Vāsudeva, became the bestower of his own state of liberation.
Then, by his command alone, Ramā also assumed a second form, which they call Māyā. By his permission, he himself became Saṅkarṣaṇa, eternal and possessing a body that is the cause of dissolution.
For the sake of creation, the Goddess became Jayā, and he, having attained the state of Pradyumna, became Kṛti. 1.6–1.7.
Furthermore, for the sake of their maintenance, that Blessed One named Aniruddha and the goddess Śānti remained for a thousand years.

Having remained thus through these forms of his own, he—possessing inconceivable power—in the form of Pradyumna gave these [worlds] to himself as his final state. 1.8. That Blessed One named Aniruddha, having placed within his own belly the bodiless individual souls (jīvas) together with their respective karmas, [reabsorbed them].
Then, he sequentially created all [the worlds] together with their bodies, headed by Svayambhū, Prāṇa, Ātman, Śeṣa, and Garuḍa (1.9).
That Blessed One, who consists of fivefold nature, became sixteenfold; he was five, twice two, a hundred thousand, and immeasurable.
Though he is one, equal, entirely free from defects, and possessed of perfect qualities everywhere, he became manifold in his likenesses (1.10).
His form is perfect in qualities and free from defects; He is self-dependent and devoid of the qualities of a body composed of insentient matter.
His hands, feet, face, belly, and other limbs consist of nothing but bliss, and His nature is everywhere devoid of internal differentiation. 1.11.
Furthermore, for this Supreme Eternal Being, there is no beginning or end, nor any increase or decrease, due to time, space, or qualities.

There has never been anyone like him anywhere, nor will there ever be; there is no one superior to Viṣṇu, the Supreme beyond the supreme. (1.12) He is the omniscient Lord of lords, possessed of all powers, whose essence consists of the full, imperishable self, strength, consciousness, bliss, and valor.
By his command alone—deprived of which this entire universe, from Brahmā and Śiva downwards, would have no master, even if united with Indirā. (1.13)
The illuminator of this [Viṣṇu] is Pavana; of Pavana, Rudra; then Śeṣa, Garuḍa, Indra, and Kāma.
After Viṣṇu and Indra, the others follow, and after these, the sages (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, each possessing fewer qualities in successive order, numbering one hundred and eight.
Furthermore, the illuminators of him (Rudra) are Ramā, who is superior even to Marut; then Gīr, who is more excellent than Śiva.
Of that [Supreme Being], Umā, Vipatinī, and those [goddesses] beginning with Śacī are his wives respectively, just as he is their husband.
And from these, the ones residing in the Śruti are superior by factors of ten, hundred, and five more than ten, respectively.
The word "hundred" is used here in the sense of plurality; therefore, there is no contradiction with the various expressions found in other Śruti texts. 1.15–1.16.

Their true nature is this very one, for even those who are liberated remain eternally of such high and low forms; since a word may mean "hundred" or "ten thousand," it is not therefore a term for the inferior, and thus they are of the highest form. 1.17.
Thus, some are intent on the Supreme Being among men and fit for liberation, while others are intent on worldly existence—such as the *asuras* who dwell in darkness.

Thus, there is always a fixed rule; otherwise, until all those wandering in the cycle of existence have reached completion, there would be no fulfillment. And because fulfillment cannot occur through such a fixed rule, the multitudes of living beings do not reach their end. Since their number is indeed infinite, their activity continues in this manner throughout all time.

Even by these gods and others, endowed with supreme eloquence and the like, who constantly deliberate together, the expansion of the qualities of this Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa—whose greatness is inconceivable and whose fulfillment is infinite—is not found elsewhere; where else could it be? (1.20) Nor can equality with this Supreme One ever be attained even by one who is liberated; therefore, how could there be any identity between Him and another? (1.21)
If this goal were to be attained by hosts of conscious beings who are perpetually dependent, from the Supreme One whose nature is eternally independent;

(1.21) This very meaning is determined with constant affection by all the Vedic statements, along with the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, and the Pañcarātra, as well as by other scriptural words together with the Sūtras on Reality, [all] always [revealed] by Hari. (1.22)

"There is none equal to Nārāyaṇa"; "I am Puruṣottama, for I have transcended both the individual soul (jīva) and the imperishable (akṣara)"; "Whatever else exists is afflicted"; "Having departed as one who is liberated, there is nothing here from anywhere whatsoever."
"Indeed, it is manifold; for by viewing the self as distinct from the phenomena, one falls below. (1.23) "This individual soul is merely an appearance separate from the Lord;
however, for one who is liberated, there is no power regarding the objective world."
"You are devoted to the limited (mātrāpara), yet they do not attain Your greatness";

"the embodiment of the six attributes" (ṣāḍguṇyavigraha); "the singular body of perfectly full qualities" (supūrṇaguṇaikadeha); "the body of majesty" (māhātmyadeha); "the goal for those on the path of transmigration and liberation"; and "Śiva as Brahmā."
And neither the two Lords [Śiva and Viṣṇu] possess even a fraction of its qualities;
how much less, then, others? Even the hosts of liberated souls do not equal even a hundredth part of this bliss. (1.25)
“The forms of the manifestations, counter-manifestations, and supreme manifestations of conscious beings are constant;
yet, due to the perpetual sovereignty of Viṣṇu, the groups beginning with Keśa never depart from liberation. “In that Supreme One, even the other sheaths of the unborn living beings [are contained].”
"Neither Brahmā nor the leaders headed by Marīci, nor even Ramā and the others, know the multitude of His qualities;
who else could there be as a Lord who is eternally independent? (1.27)
"That Puruṣottama is not merely one person;
why? Because that Puruṣa is [one] by birth, and for that very reason, by virtue of Śruti, by his qualities, and by his own essential nature."
"How could there even be [the thought], 'I am that,' if [the two] were eternally distinct? (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.2;
Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.11).
4 Brahma Sūtra 2.3.50.
5 "The illuminator," and so forth, is indeed a scriptural statement (*śrutivacana*),
not one's own word (*svavacana*)— Bhāṣya-pradīpa.

"Haris is the supreme among all; yet it is only by His command that this [universe] can be known. That Hari is the absolutely independent one, an ocean of infinite, imperishable, and countless eternal qualities."
Thus are the Vedic declarations and the statements of others. 1.29.
“The four beginning with the Ṛgveda, the Pañcarātra, the Mahābhārata, the Mūlarāmāyaṇa, and the Brahmasūtra are traditionally held to be authoritative in themselves. 1.30.

That which is not contradicted by this [scripture] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and not otherwise; however, that which is contradicted by it can in no way be considered a valid means of knowledge. (1.31) The *Purāṇas* belonging to Viṣṇu [are authoritative] because they consist of the *Pañcarātra*.
The Smṛtis of Manu and others are indeed authoritative when they are in conformity [with the Vedas].
(1.32) In these, the preeminence of Viṣṇu is declared, and never that of anyone else;
therefore, that alone must be accepted, and not otherwise under any circumstances. (1.33)
Other scriptures were indeed composed for the purpose of delusion by the command of Hari;
therefore, what is stated in them is not to be accepted, because they lead the asuras toward darkness (tamas).
For those [scriptures] were composed here by Viṣṇu through the agency of Śiva and others whom he had commanded.

Whatever among these [scriptural statements] is not contradictory [to our position], that which has been stated therein is not to be rejected. (1.35) Even those Vedic utterances that appear to contradict the preeminence of Viṣṇu are to be interpreted in every way so as to be consistent with the preeminence of Viṣṇu. (1.36)
Whatever Hari may display in his incarnations like an ordinary human being, that is for the delusion of the asuras; Viṣṇu has no defects whatsoever.
Ignorance, dependence on others, or even the piercing of the vital points (vedha) and so forth—these are likewise [for the sake of deluding others]. 1.37.
Likewise, Hari himself displays the state of having an ordinary body, the casting off of the body and so forth,
as well as lack of sovereignty, suffering, equality with others, and inferiority,
in order to delude the Daityas and their like. (1.38–1.39)

He has no defect whatsoever, for he is one whose entire qualities are complete. Since the Lord is present in all forms residing within bodies and in all manifestations, how could there be non-difference from, or equality with, Brahmā and the others for that Great Soul? (1.40)
That scripture which is thus expressive is indeed considered the supreme scripture.

That *Brahmasūtra* which was proclaimed by Viṣṇu in the form of Vyāsa for the sake of definitive determination alone—that is to be accepted, for all definitive determinations are stated therein. (1.41–42)
Indeed, the Blessed One composed the Brahma-sūtra in order to remove doubt regarding statements that are literal and those whose meaning is intended to be delusive.
Therefore, having grasped the meaning of the sūtras, a definitive resolution of all matters must be made. 1.43.
The state of being free from all defects, the preeminence in all virtues, non-difference in all forms, the eternal distinction of individual souls,
and likewise the status of being worshiped by all the Vedas— these have been declared of Viṣṇu in the Sūtras. (1.44–1.45)
And there is a gradation among the liberated ones, as is their liberation through knowledge;
therefore, that which is proclaimed for the sake of delusion is contradictory to this.
Consequently, all those qualities of Viṣṇu whatsoever are indeed to be accepted. 1.46.
Thus it was clearly stated by the Blessed One in the Bhaviṣyat Parvan:
"I shall create this delusion, O Āṇi, which will delude people;
and you, O mighty-armed Rudra, compose treatises of delusion. (1.47–48)
"O mighty-armed one, display as false those things which are true; reveal yourself and conceal me.
Thus is the speech of Vārāha as stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, and likewise another [passage].
“The qualities of Viṣṇu, His form, His having consciousness as His body, His freedom from defects, and even the gradations among the liberated—these are taught for the sake of non-delusion.
Whatever is contrary to this is determined to be for the sake of delusion. (1.50–1.51)
It is also stated in the *Skanda* by Śiva himself with reverence to Ṣaṇmukha:
"In the scripture of Śiva as well, that which is consistent with the scripture of the Lord (Viṣṇu) should be accepted.
Viṣṇu alone is supreme; knowledge of him is the means to liberation. (1.52)
This is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures; anything else is indeed for the sake of delusion.

(1.53) However, that liberation which occurs without knowledge, as well as my equality with Viṣṇu, [are taught] merely by means of sacred fords and the like; whereas my superiority over Viṣṇu is established through knowledge. (1.54)
"O son, statements such as 'there is no difference between those like us and the liberated souls, nor between them and Hari,' are all spoken for the sake of delusion and not otherwise.
And it is stated in the *Pādmapurāṇa* by Śiva himself: "Only a Śaiva [speaks thus]..."
As was previously stated by Hari, Hara said to Umā:
"O Sambhu, having worshipped you, I shall always accept a boon;
appearing with a portion of myself among humans and others at the beginning of the Dvāpara age. (1.56–57)

"By means of fabricated scriptures of your own, you must turn people away from me; and protect me, so that this creation may remain in its proper order of superior and inferior. (1.58) "Indeed, in the Vaiṣṇava scriptures as well as in the Vedas, there is no one higher than Hari."
In some other scriptures, Viṣṇu is declared to be the supreme;
however, because the Vedas are free from defect, that which is stated in the Vedas must indeed be accepted.
And in the Vedas, Viṣṇu is always said to be superior to all.
“At the offering of this god, the impetuous Viṣṇu, with oblations;
for Rudra knows his own Rudrian majesty. O Aśvins, you have gone upon your radiant path.

“Whomever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahman, him a seer, him a man of great wisdom. (1.62) “In the beginning there was only Nārāyaṇa; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara. Vāsudeva alone existed here in the beginning; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara. (1.63)

“When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person whose source is Brahman, then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains the highest equality. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3) “He who knows Him hidden in the cave [of the heart], in the supreme ether... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)
“He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman.
(1.65) “I shall now proclaim the great, true deeds of this Great One, the Truth of truth.
(1.66) “All rejoice after this Truth—the gift of the generous God who is praised. (1.66)
“What he has intended is true; that is not in vain. He is the giver of desirable wealth and of victory.
(1.67) “That true majesty of his is praised at the sacrifices in the realm of the wise.
(1.67) “All the qualities of Viṣṇu are true; true is the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord.”
The distinction between individual souls is real, and this world is likewise real.
(1.68) The internal distinction within Viṣṇu is unreal, and there is nothing else that is unreal.
This flow of the world is real, endowed with the fivefold division. (1.69)

The difference between the individual soul and the Lord, the mutual difference among individual souls, the difference between the insentient and the sentient, and likewise the difference among insentient things and between insentient and sentient beings—
these five differences are eternal in all states and in every respect. (1.70)
9 Ṛgveda 2.33.11;
11 Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3.
16. Ṛgveda 8.3.4:
"And for those who are liberated, their relative gradations never diminish. (1.71)
Kings, human gandharvas, gods, and the long-lived ancestors; the gods born of their station and those born of their karma; Indra, the destroyer of cities;
Rudra, Sarasvatī, and Vāyu—each successive one is a hundred times superior to the one before. 1.72.
Brahmā, Vāyu, Indra, and likewise Rudra are each one;
Rudra is one, and so too is Viṣṇu, yet none is equal to Vāyu.
(1.73) Among those who are liberated, Śrī is thus [equal], yet she possesses qualities a thousandfold greater than those of Vāyu.
"Then Viṣṇu possesses infinite qualities; there is never anyone equal to him"—such Vedic statements loudly proclaim the preeminence of Viṣṇu alone.
"The purport here is great," he himself stated in the verse beginning with "He who [knows] me. (1.75)
For it has been stated in the Sūtras, following the definitive conclusion, that “the greatness [of the Self] is superior” (Bhūmnaḥ jyāyastvam).

And through delight in That alone is liberation to be attained, and not by any other means. (1.76) “This Self is not to be obtained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much learning. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3)
"He who is chosen by Him alone attains Him; to him this Self reveals His own form. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3) "Viṣṇu is indeed the giver of liberation, and Vāyu [acts] by His permission;
liberation and knowledge come in sequence, as do the enjoyment leading to the state of the Liberated. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.7.8)
Through the grace of those who are higher, the state of those who are lower occurs; it cannot be otherwise.
Hari is eternally the controller of all, and others are subject to His will. From this, the gradation [of beings] is to be known, as well as the supreme height of Hari. 1.79.
Without this, liberation cannot belong to anyone in any way whatsoever. (Bhagavad Gītā 15.19; Brahma Sūtra 3.3.59)
The word "iti" denotes a manner;

by this manner [it is meant], as in "from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2) and "the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, because of its own word" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.1).

The sense is that this has been stated in such sūtras as "The Imperishable [is Brahman] because it supports the sky" (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.10) and "And [Brahman] is endowed with all [powers], for that is seen [in scripture]" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.31).
Therefore, the plural form "in the sūtras" is used—[as seen in] Bhā. Pra. 20, Ka. U. 1.2.23, and Mu. U. 3.2.3—[stating]:
"Having understood the fivefold divisions and their non-difference from Viṣṇu..."
Liberation occurs by knowing the state of being free from defects and the abundance of virtues, and not otherwise.
(1.81) Having known the incarnations of Hari, as well as those who are not incarnations of Hari, and having correctly understood those possessed by Him, liberation occurs, and not otherwise. (1.82)
Having understood emanation, protection, withdrawal, knowledge, necessity, ignorance, bondage,
and liberation as proceeding from Viṣṇu alone— there is no liberation otherwise—
one should study the Vedas, the Pañcarātras, along with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. (1.83)
Having known [Viṣṇu] as the supreme alone, one is liberated; never otherwise (1.84).
Devotion is said to be a very firm affection, superior in every respect, preceded by the knowledge of His majesty; through that [devotion] comes liberation, and not otherwise (1.85).
The aggregates of living beings are threefold: gods, humans, and dānavas.
Among them, the gods and likewise the highest among humans are fit for liberation;
those humans who are middling are indeed always fit for the cycle of rebirth.
The lowest beings go indeed to hell, while the Dānavas are absorbed in darkness (tamas).
For these two, there is eternal liberation or eternal darkness, and no returning again.
For the gods, there is neither hell nor darkness in any way whatsoever.
Liberation is never, by anyone, or anywhere, attained by the Asuras;
nor is this pair [of liberation and bondage] ever obtained by those who are intermediate humans.
(1.89) At that time, the attainment of darkness (tamas) occurs for the Asuras as a matter of necessity.
But when, despite the presence of knowledge, they do not grasp that Supreme,
then there is liberation for the gods, since Hari becomes perceptible to them through worship according to their own fitness and likewise through a body suited to that [fitness]. (1.90–1.91)
Hari is always to be worshipped by Brahmā with all his qualities;
indeed, Hari is to be worshipped by human beings as bliss, the knower, and the eternal Self.
This is because, in due order, there is an abundance of these qualities in those others [who follow] up to Viriñca (Brahmā).

The gods named Ṛjus, who are fit for the state of Brahmā, constitute a distinct class; that station is attainable by them alone, and not by any other means whatsoever. In this way, there are distinct classes of beings fit for all the various stations.
Therefore, the gradation among conscious selves is indeed beginningless and endless;
and that can never be altered by anyone, anywhere.
A person who desires what is unattainable surely falls; of this there is no doubt. (1.95)
Therefore, Viṣṇu should indeed always be served according to one's capacity.
(1.96) Because of unbroken service, because of freedom from desire, and because of one's fitness, Hari can be seen by all; but not otherwise, under any circumstances. (1.97)
Since this decree of Hari must not be transgressed by any sentient beings,
Viṣṇu, whose resolve is true, will not act otherwise.
All [deeds] preceded by charity, pilgrimage, austerity, and sacrifice, at all times— 1.98.
“The limbs for the service of Hari are many, but devotion alone leads to liberation”—this statement from the Bhaviṣyat Parva is the supreme [authority] regarding all this.
(1.99) “I hear the Hero, subduing the fierce with the fierce, as he leads one after another across. (RV 2.12.8)

“One who knows this thus becomes immortal here; no other path for reaching [the goal] exists.

“Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8) “He who has supreme devotion for God, and as for God, so for the Guru—for that great-souled one, these truths explained here become fully manifest. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23)
“All things whatsoever are for the sake of devotion; devotion alone leads to liberation.
For even for those who are liberated, devotion is indeed the nature of eternal bliss. Devotion is declared to be that supreme, eternal affection preceded by knowledge. (1.104)
Such Vedic statements as these prescribe the means [of liberation]:
“O Hari, even one who has performed every religious duty remains forever in hell if he is not your devotee; whereas even a killer of a Brahmin is liberated if he is your devotee. (1.105–106)
“O Acyuta, even that which is unrighteous becomes righteous when performed by Your devotees;

"O scorcher of foes, [this is for] the sake of knowing, seeing, and entering [it] in its true essence. (1.108) "The Daityas, who have been hostile from time immemorial, have their hatred toward Viṣṇu increased;
by this certainty, it casts the Daityas into blind darkness at the end. (1.109)

Hatred consists of full-fledged suffering; it remains infinite for those fallen into the blinding darkness that is devoid of every trace of happiness. (1.110) Likewise, there is the non-difference of the individual soul, the absence of qualities, and the state of having incomplete qualities.
When there is equality or superiority, the distinction regarding others resides in that very [state].
The reversal of manifestation and the hatred toward those devoted to it, as well as the censure of its authority—all these are considered forms of hatred. (1.111–1.112)

Devotion devoid of these [impurities] is determined to be true devotion.
This primordial devotion of the gods has indeed increased progressively;
it is the cause of direct perception and, furthermore, the cause of liberation. 1.113.
That very [devotion] exists eternally among the liberated as the nature of bliss.
Just as whiteness and other qualities always belong to a cow, so too do happiness, knowledge, and the like belong to devotion, and not otherwise. (1.114–1.115)
Viṣṇu attains satisfaction through devotion alone, and not by anything else;
he himself is the giver of liberation, and devotion is the sole cause therein.
Furthermore, it is the cause for the gradations among those liberated ones, beginning with Brahmā. (1.116)
Devotion, established in degrees of intensity, is beginningless and eternal, and nothing else is so.
(1.117) Among humans, those who are inferior and always possessed of some degree of hatred toward Hari are destined for suffering; therefore, they too are eternally [bound], without a doubt. (1.118)
Because the middling [devotees] have become mixed, they are remembered as always having mixed results;
the superior ones are always endowed with some degree of devotion, and for that reason they are liberators. (1.119) "Supreme devotion to Brahman is higher than all others."
And such statements as these appear individually throughout the Purāṇas:
“He who is ninety-six finger-breadths in height, whose circumference is that of a banyan tree, who is seven feet tall with four cubits in span, and who is endowed with the thirty-two marks. (1.120)
"Without doubt, the one who cuts away doubt has been called the Guru by the wise.
Therefore, Brahmā is always the primary Guru for all; others also are declared to be Gurus in succession, each being primary for their own respective self. (1.121–122)

Gradually, those devoid of auspicious marks, as well as those equal to both the marked and the unmarked, are merely human; those endowed with middling marks are mediocre, while one possessed of truly inauspicious marks is the Kali age itself.
(1.123) But when one who is perfectly endowed with auspicious marks gives a gift with a very serene mind...
All that becomes true for the disciple; of this there is no doubt.
Because Hari is otherwise unapproachable, when he has entered into him, he becomes the bestower of liberation.
For even such a Guru would not grant [liberation] unless his heart is exceedingly gracious. 1.124.

Therefore, that [teaching] would not be true; hence, the guru must always be honored. (1.125) However, the status of being a guru may occasionally belong to those who are one's own subordinates due to some specific cause.
Even they are to be revered for the sake of maintaining proper boundaries, but not in the same manner as the supreme guru.
This which has been declared in the *Pañcarātra* is approved in the Purāṇas:
"When Hari certainly perceives a form that is suitable for him for the granting of liberation, then all his sins are reduced to ashes. (1.126–127)
"Former [names] pass away and others arise; some do not coalesce.
Therefore, liberation is certain upon seeing Hari according to one's own fitness.
This is the statement from the Bhaviṣyat Parva, and likewise it is contained within the Sūtra. 1.128, 26.
And the Śruti, being intent upon that same point, clearly stated: "Just as... (1.129).
"Released mortals go to the gods; the gods go to Indra, and he to Śaṅkara; he goes to Brahmā in due order, and by that path, all go to Hari" (1.130).
And those who have attained progressively higher states of subjugation, led by the Rudras, are free from defects, eternally blissful, and devoid of rebirth;
they sport here according to their own will, and nothing undesirable occurs for them. (1.131)
The Asuras exist until the end of the Kali age; thus their sufferings become increasingly greater.
Among them, the Kali age is characterized by an excess of suffering, and these groups [of beings] are likewise like Brahmā. 1.132.
Regarding the phrase "contained in this Sūtra," this means that this object of knowledge is contained within the Sūtra.

The meaning is as stated in the *Brahma-sūtra* (4.1.13): "Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because that is so designated. — Bhāṣya-pradīpa.

"Though liberated, he always stands in the position of sovereign over all who are liberated;
the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Master, is eternally his refuge.
Thus [it is stated] according to the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, the Pañcarātra, and the Itihāsas.
Thus, a definitive conclusion has been established from the Purāṇas and other scriptures by the learned sage Ānandatīrtha,
who bears the name Pūrṇaprajña, through the power of Viṣṇu’s grace and by virtue of his exalted state. (1.135–1.136)
I have declared the supreme purport of all the scriptures.
Having obtained the permission of Viṣṇu and having known this very [truth], that Viṣṇu is attained. 1.137.
Thus, in the work composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda...
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Essential Meaning of All Śāstras," is concluded.
Now begins the second chapter.
(Excerpt from the Text) Om! Victorious is Hari, the inconceivable one, the sole object of worship for all gods, the supreme teacher who grants the attainment of desires to the virtuous;
he who is an ocean of the multitude of all virtues, eternally free from defects, the lotus-eyed Lord of Śrī, the bestower of honor upon us. 2.1.

In the preceding chapter, the supreme and divine determination of the scriptures was stated. The statements of the glorious *Mahābhārata* are ascertained by these very [criteria]. (2.2) In some places they insert texts, and in some places they even omit them.
They might occasionally introduce a transposition or, through negligence, alter things elsewhere. (2.3) Even though the texts have not been completely lost, they are everywhere disordered;
for almost all of them have perished, such that not even a ten-millionth part remains. (2.4)
The scripture too has thus become disordered; why then is its meaning difficult for even the gods to grasp?
Since the Kali age is thus so confused, I, being impelled to reach a definitive conclusion, shall speak those conclusions through my understanding by the grace of Hari.
Through his grace, he mastered other treatises and the Vedas;
likewise, having seen various kinds of books in different regions, he became like the blessed Lord Vyāsa himself, the sovereign Nārāyaṇa. (2.6–2.7)
"I shall likewise declare it for the sake of its observation; I shall briefly state the meaning of all the scriptures in accordance with the meaning of the *Bhārata*.
The *Bhārata* is proclaimed to be the definitive conclusion of all scriptures. (2.8)

“In former times, the Bhārata and all the Vedas were placed upon a scale by the gods, led by Brahmā, together with all the ṛṣis; by the command of Vyāsa himself, the Bhārata outweighed them there. (2.9)
“It is called the Mahābhārata because of its greatness and its weightiness;
he who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins. (xv) “Indeed, in the Bhārata lies the definitive conclusion of all scriptures, along with illustrative examples. (2.10)
Indeed, the subordination of Brahmā and the other gods to Viṣṇu has been proclaimed;
for it is stated that Bhīma and all others are perfectly under the control of Kṛṣṇa.
Viṣṇu is declared to be the bestower of knowledge to all and the giver of fame. (2.11–2.12)
Because [Vyāsa], through his own self as Vyāsa, proclaimed their glory in the *Bhārata*,
and because he granted knowledge to Śuka and others who were in the forms of Brahmā, Rudra, and so forth;
and because he was declared to be superior even to the gods, to Śeṣa, and to Rudra— (2.13).
And he is dearer to Viṣṇu than all others, as seen from the example of Bhīma;
for Māruti is indeed the principal limb of Viṣṇu, who removes the burden of the earth, [as evidenced] by the slaying of Māgadha and others, and even by the slaying of Duryodhana. (2.14–2.15)

Whosoever is the strongest among the Kṣatriyas is the most excellent; provided that he is devoted solely to the service of Viṣṇu and not otherwise, and if that strength is innate rather than derived from excellent weapons and the like. (2.16)
If it is argued that the cause of another's possession is a power consisting of another [deity], then devotion and knowledge belong only to those who are powerful among the gods, and not otherwise;
and only such a person is dear to Viṣṇu, and never otherwise in any way. (2.17–2.18)
Therefore, whoever is superior in strength is also superior in virtue;
for strength in a Kṣatriya is perceived by those of coarse vision, whereas qualities such as knowledge are perceived by those of subtle vision. (2.19)
Therefore, wherever there is power, there the supreme qualities are to be recognized;
they reside only in the gods and not in others, because of their opposition to Vāsudeva. (Mahābhārata 1.1.209)
xvi. In cases other than the kṣatriya class, force is the authority wherever Keśava is engaged, whether in the destruction of the wicked or likewise in matters of knowledge;
however, in the case of brahmins, knowledge alone is indeed the authority. 2.21.
The strength of the Kṣatriyas indeed belongs to him, and for all of them, Viṣṇu is the one who effects their tasks.
In forms such as Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, Janārdana performs the work of strength; likewise, in forms such as Datta and Vyāsa, the Lord performs the work of knowledge. (2.22–2.23)
The Fish, the Tortoise, and the Boar; the Lion, Vāmana, and Bhārgava; Rāghava, Kṛṣṇa, and Buddha, as well as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; Kapila, Datta, Ṛṣabha, Śibi, and the son of Ruci, the Porpoise. 2.24.
Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa,
the ascetic Manu, Mahidāsa, as well as I myself in the form of a woman, the horse-headed one,
likewise the mare-mouthed one, Kalki, and the Lord Dhanvantari— 2.25–26.
"Viṣṇu alone is [the source] of these; there is no difference between them in any way.
There is no distinction anywhere by means of any qualities, such as strength, knowledge, and so forth.
[These include] Śrī, Brahmā, Rudra, Śeṣa, Vīndra, Indrā, and Kāma. (2.27)
Kāmaputra, Aniruddha, Sūrya, Candra, and Bṛhaspati;
Dharma was their wife, as were Dakṣa and the others, the Manus, the sons of Manu, the sages, Nārada, and Parvata. (2.28–2.29)
Kaśyapa, Sanaka and the others, the deities such as Agni and the rest, Bharata, Kārtavīrya, and the universal emperors beginning with Vainya;
Gaya, Lakṣmaṇa and the others, and the three sons of Rohiṇī. 2.30.
Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, and his son Aniruddha;
Nara, Phalguna, and others—these are [forms of] Hari characterized by specific *āveśa* (specialized entry).
Vālin, Sāmba, and others are those who possess only a slight *āveśa* of Hari. (2.31–2.32)

xvii. Therefore, Hanumān and Bhīma were the inner instruments (*antaraṅga*) of Hari, who exists as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa when manifesting through power; they were the accomplishers of His task, because Vāyu, whose essence is Brahman, attained the state of Brahman in the past. (2.33)

The state of Brahman does not belong to anything other than Vāyu; therefore, he alone is that [Brahman]. (2.34) Where there is form, there are qualities such as devotion and the like, which are eternally present in women.
For form is the manifest object of perception for those of gross vision; therefore, it is indeed that [manifestation]. (2.35)
Generally, devotion and the like cannot be discerned in women;
therefore, it is certain that their form and qualities are themselves devotion and the like.
And that innate form is endowed with the thirty-two marks. 2.36.

A body that lacks the [auspicious] marks can never, in any way, be a cause for spiritual qualities. (2.37) However, in the case of Asura women, there may be the mere form [of a woman] due to their excellence;
yet because they lack the marks, they can never have devotion in any way. (2.38)

Therefore, Jānakī, Rugmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and others of such form, possessing the excellence of physical beauty, are considered the most supreme among all women. After them, Draupadī is the most excellent in beauty of all.
He was truly a limb of the Lord himself for the removal of the earth's burden, like Bhīma;
yet Bhīma was the slayer and the cause of enmity for the sinful folk, while Draupadī was the cause of enmity immediately following him. (2.40–2.41)
After him came Baladeva, and after him Phalguna;
however, due to the possession by Nara, Drauṇi followed later, and the others after him.
Like Rāma, Jāmbavatī and the other five [wives] followed, and then Revatī likewise.
Lakṣmaṇa followed after Hanumān; then came Bharata and Vālin;
Śatrughna followed after him; and Sugrīva and the others were inferior to him.
(2.43) Those who had not previously properly performed their own appropriate duty for the sake of Rāma’s mission—
That [space] was filled on all sides by Kṛṣṇa, Bībhatsu,
and the others; that which had been done in excess there was made deficient here by them,
while that which had been done in excess by Karṇa and the others in the two manifestations was [made up] here.
For by them, beginning with Vidura, opposition was subsequently shown toward Hari.
Indeed, in these two incarnations, a final judgment has been rendered for all;
there is nothing whatsoever left undone by these two, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
Elsewhere it is fulfilled in some way; therefore, the definitive conclusion lies right here.

Because Kṛṣṇa appeared later and possesses a distinct superiority, the definitive conclusion rests there; for it was by taking this incarnation as his basis that the *Bhārata* was composed. (2.46–2.47)
The story of Rāma has also been told here within the *Mārkaṇḍeya-samāsyā*.
Therefore, whatever is not mentioned in the *Mahābhārata* does not exist anywhere else;
what is stated here has not been properly illustrated in any other scripture. (2.48)
All this and more was spoken by Hari himself in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, and in the *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa* as well, there is praise for the *Mahābhārata*:
"As Vyāsa is among the gods, so is the Brāhmaṇa the best among bipeds. (2.49)
"As the thunderbolt is among weapons and as barley is among herbs, even so the Mahābhārata is the best of all scriptures. (2.50) This praise of the Bhārata is also proclaimed in the Vāyu Purāṇa. (29)
"Know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
for who else but the Lotus-Eyed One could be the author of the Mahābhārata? (2.51).
Thus indeed has it been declared separately in all the scriptures.
This entire subject matter, preceded by the sequence of [the Lord’s] greatness, has been stated.
(2.52/29) Regarding the verse beginning with “Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa,” it should be understood that it exists not only in the *Vāyuprokta* [Purāṇa], but also in the *Mahābhārata*. — Bhā. Pra.

30. As this conclusion has been declared in the *Bhārata* as well, we shall demonstrate it in its proper sequence by citing those very words in their entirety. (2.53) [Padma Purāṇa 1.1.43–44; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4–5; Mahābhārata 12.334.9] / xix.
Just as this determination was proclaimed in the *Bhārata*, so shall we show it in its proper order through those very statements in every respect. (2.53)
“Nārāyaṇa, the preceptor of the gods, the sole lord of the world, beloved by his devotees, and honored by all the worlds;
free from the three qualities, unborn, all-pervading, the primordial Lord.”
I bow to the destroyer of worldly existence, who is worshipped by gods, asuras, and siddhas.
(2.54) That Blessed One is the bestower of knowledge, superior to the entire world beginning with Kamalā, Viriñca, and Śarva;
he is pleased by devotion alone. Devotion to Hari is the sole duty for everyone—this is established in the earlier division [of the scripture]. (2.55)

"Faultless, devoid of rebirth, possessing the quality of noble and perfect consciousness, the first-born, the soul of all power, the sole cause of liberation, and worshipped by gods and asuras alike who have attained release—he alone is such," it is said in the second half [of the verse].
Since the state of being worthy of homage is declared in both cases, his being bowed to by both the liberated and the unliberated multitudes is thus stated. 2.56.
Thus, the fulfillment of all virtues of this Viṣṇu was first introduced by the very one who made the initial declaration:

“Kṛṣṇa is worshipped with sacrifices purified by Soma; Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by heroic men as they display their prowess; Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by forest-dwellers as they gather their provisions; Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by the liberated who have cast off delusion. (2.58)
Salutations to you, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the primordial god of gods, by whom Brahmā and the other deities were created and the Dānavas were slain.
The creatorship of the gods is said to be the creation of liberation, and nothing else.

Since the origin of the Daityas is also measured by this same [principle], this is the distinction. (2.60) Furthermore, the destruction of the Daityas is firmly established in darkness; their fixed state of existence is indeed not otherwise.
This process of the division of bodies among all beings does not create a distinction between those who are Asuras and those who are Daityas. (2.61)
31. Because of the statement "even those that are hidden in some places," some who cannot tolerate this first verse do not write it at the beginning;
however, it is still seen today in ancient manuscripts from the Kerala region.

Otherwise, how could Vyāsa, the teacher of the world, while composing a work of one hundred thousand verses, not have composed a verse of auspiciousness at the beginning of the book for the sake of instructing the world?
For even in shorter works such as the Bhāgavata and the Harivaṃśa, he has written, "We meditate upon the Supreme Truth."

And with the words, “May that Vāsudeva, who is without beginning, pacify the evil accumulated through birth after birth,” he performed an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) for the sake of instructing the world.
Therefore, in this great work, Vyāsa— the teacher of all the learned— must indeed perform an auspicious rite.

In the center of that lotus, which is the very self of the worlds, Viriñca was born again, whose nature consists of the excellent qualities (sadguṇa).
From him, moreover, all the gods were produced; though they already knew [the truth], they sought a definitive conclusion.
Having issued forth from the body of the Lotus-born one, the elements, ending with wind, entered him in succession.
His body fell when the wind ceased its movement, and rose again upon its entry;
therefore, he alone is the foremost of the wise, and the hosts of gods took refuge in him alone.
Because he stands between Hari and Viriñca, that Māruta is the lord of the other gods.

From him, Viriñca created the seven worlds along with their seven [subsidiary] groups from the lotus; and from him, the gods, the sages, and those born of the *vaikārika* [ego], including Śiva, came into being once again. (3.24–3.25)
In the beginning, Śiva was I myself, and Bhava was the intellect; Umā and Manojā were born together with Śakra and Kāma.
Then the Guru, Manu, Dakṣa, and Aniruddha were likewise born subsequently from the mind.
From the eyes, the ears, and the sense of touch, the Sun, the Moon, and Dharma were born together. (3.26)
From his tongue was born Vāripati (Varuṇa), and from his nostrils were born the two Nāsatyas (the Aśvins); these were produced in succession.
From him, Sanaka and the others, as well as Marīci and the other principal sages, and all the gods, were produced in succession.
Then the Asuras and others, the ṛṣis, and human beings—the manifold world—came into being from Viriñca.
According to the sequence described, whichever previous birth is superior remains so, except in the case of the Asuras;
for once born later, that which was previously inferior never attains superiority in any way.
However, virtues may suffer defeat due to time, the faults of the father and mother, or one's own actions. (3.29)

For if they were to occur out of order, there would be dissolution; therefore, at the time of cosmic destruction, Hari, accompanied by Śrī, the infinite one, reclines alone, experiencing his own bliss—a mass of intense and profound joy.
(3.30) He, whose heads, faces, arms, thighs, and feet are infinite, possesses infinite forms and infinite qualities.
Possessing infinite power and full enjoyment, He remains in His own nature, eating eternally. 3.31.
Furthermore, He thus creates all this; for the stream of the world is indeed beginningless and endless.
The individual souls (jīvas) are eternal, and primordial matter (prakṛti) is eternal, and time is eternal—how much more so the God of gods? 3.32.

Just as rivers born from the ocean constantly enter back into that very same ocean, so too does this eternal stream of the world perpetually enter into Him alone. Those who know thus the supreme, infinite power of the Unborn Puruṣottama— 3.33.
Then, through his grace, those whose defects have been burnt attain him, the supreme Lord of the gods.
Having established these gods, now freed from all defects, in his own presence, the Lord again appoints other groups of attendants who are fit for office to their respective positions. (3.34–3.35)
Furthermore, from Mārīca alone the gods were born, and from Aditi the Ādityas and from Diti the Asuras;
likewise, all beings such as cattle, wild animals, birds, and serpents were born from the daughters of Dakṣa.
Then, seeing the earth submerged in the ocean of dissolution, Hari, in the form of a boar, quickly [plunged in].
Having become Viriñca, he lifted this earth, together with its mountains, from the waters and established it firmly above them.
(3.37) Then, by the curse of the lotus-navelled one, two gatekeepers were born upon the surface of the earth three times:
first as Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, sons of Diti; and later as the two Rākṣasas, the nephews of Hari. (3.38)

Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, possessed of noble prowess, who was the younger brother [of Hiraṇyakaśipu], was slain for the sake of the gods by the Creator himself, who had assumed the form of a boar to lift up the earth; he was previously slain by the one born from the lotus (Brahmā).
Then, the lord of the asuras seized the Vedas that had issued from the mouth of the Creator by means of a horse-headed form.

Having slain him, he who had assumed the form of a fish protected Manu and gave those [scriptures] to the sages; 3.40. At the dissolution at the end of a *manvantara*, the God of gods, the Self, in the form of a fish, bestowed knowledge upon Manu Vaivasvata—knowledge which consists of the realization of the true nature of Viṣṇu through the highest wisdom. 3.41.

Then, constantly oppressed by Diti’s eldest son, the lords of the gods, along with Brahmā, approached Hari; they recounted his tyranny to him, even though he was a god himself. (3.42) Praised by them, Hari, of formidable prowess, manifested in the form of the Man-Lion.

Having slain [Hiraṇyakaśipu] and given gold to his son, he gratified the hosts of gods by granting them freedom from fear. While the gods and asuras were churning the ocean, he supported Mount Mandara on his back;
though it could not be held by others due to the granting of boons by Śiva, the Tortoise bore that great mountain with his staff-like shell. 3.43–44.

When Bali, the king of the Daityas, obtained invincibility from the Four-faced One (Brahmā), then the younger brother of Indra was born as a son of Aditi; he was great, unborn, and praised by the Lotus-born One and others.
Assuming the form of a dwarf, he went to the sacrifice of the lord of the Asuras, making the earth sink at every step.
And by means of a stratagem, he took him to heaven in three strides and gave it to his own elder brother.
For long ago, when the Grandfather (Brahmā) had entreated Keśava on behalf of Bali, Keśava spoke these words:
"O fair-faced one, I do not reject that Bali because of a request; rather, I shall subdue him. It was for this reason that [Viṣṇu] then made the request.
In ancient times, by virtue of a boon from Candralalāma, the asuras on the surface of the earth became invincible.

Afflicted by them, the gods led by Vāsava placed the Lotus-born (Brahmā) at their head and praised Hari. Hiraṇyaka and Hiraṇyākṣa, the two sons of Diti, were utterly incapable of being slain even by those created by Viriñca, owing to a boon from the Creator.
Likewise, O Hayagrīva of noble prowess, he was slain by you, the ancient Brahman.

And that [Hayagrīva], O God of gods, having slain all these asuras—who were incapable of being killed even by all the gods due to a boon from Rudra—by means of his boundless power alone, please dwell forever within our heart-lotus. 3.49–3.50.
Thus addressed with reverence by the gods, that descendant of Bhṛgu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow who is invincible, became Rāma;
having slain the fierce host of asuras, he restored the world to its natural state, just as the primordial Nara had done.
Then, two great daityas, the sole enemies of the world, were born in the lineage of Pulastya.
By virtue of a boon from Hari in the past, they were unslayable by others; and by a boon from the Creator, they were unconquerable even by the gods.
And that Kumbhakarṇa was invincible to all by the very boon of the Creator in his former birth.
Then, due to a boon from Nara and the others in that same era, Rāvaṇa [was likewise invincible]; thus those two oppressed the thirty gods.

Then the gods, led by Indra, having approached the Lotus-born and the Wielder of the Trident who was lying upon the coils of the Lord of Serpents in the Ocean of Milk, offered him a fitting hymn of praise:
"O Lord, you alone are the supreme and independent one; you are the beginning and the end of the world, its ordainer. (3.54)

By your command alone, O Lotus-born One, all those others—the foremost and the lowest—have been brought forth. (3.55) They declare that three hundred and sixty human years constitute one year of the celestial dwellers.
Even by those twelve thousand years, the four ages—Tretā and the rest—are diminished by one quarter each.
That constitutes a single day of the Self-born One, and his night is of equal measure; thus, a hundred such autumns pass.
Having enjoyed pleasures according to his own will by your command, he too quickly approaches your presence.
In former times, those two great asuras known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha were fashioned from your ear by your command;

impelled by the entry of the Wind-god and arrogant in their strength, they grew up within the waters. By your command, they were made invulnerable due to a boon from Brahmā, arising from your desire for sport. 3.58. [They grew] from the words issued from your mouth.
Then, as the Lord Hayaśīrṣa, you took away the collections of the Vedas from the Self-born One;
having recovered all the Vedas and restored them to Svayambhū, you slew those two demons.
Having crushed them with the soles of your feet and with your hands, you quickly made the earth out of their very fat.

Thus, both this innate strength of the gods as well as that of the asuras arising from the granting of boons—these two are under your control; therefore, we report everything to you, our father. And slay these two lords of the rākṣasas, who are arrogant due to their boons, by means of your own prowess, for you are preeminent among men.
When all these lords of the gods had thus spoken, Rāma became the sovereign lord of the earth.

He was born in the house of King Daśaratha—named after the ten chariots—who was the son of Vivasvat, himself born from the womb of Aditi and the seed of Kaśyapa; and he was desired by that king for the sake of his two wives named Kausalyā and Kaikeyī.

By his command, the hosts of gods existed both before and after that Infinite One; then, among the monkeys and likewise among men, there arose those born later who were devoted to him of vast virtues.
He was the first among the deities, superior in qualities, known by the name Hanumān, the Son of the Wind.
In the home of Keśarin, Vālī became the lord by his own power, as did Vāsava;
Sugrīva was endowed with the splendor of Parameṣṭhin, as was Ravi; and Jāmbavān arose from his own self.
He who was formerly born from the skin of Parameṣṭhin’s chest became Dharma here on earth. (3.65–66)

He who was formerly Yama, the lord of the southern quarter, known by the name and designation of Sūrya, was created long ago from the mouth of the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) for the sake of the gods’ purpose; he became Jāmbavān.
And Soma, born of Brahmā, became the son of Atri, and he was born as Aṅgada.
Tārā was the wife of Śakra, and Tārā was indeed Śacī as well. (3.68) Bṛhaspati, though the son of Brahmā, was born from the mind together with Śacī;
he became the son of Aṅgiras, who was born of Brahmā, while Śacī was the daughter of Puloman, the son of Marīci. (3.69)
He himself became the monkey Vānara along with Śacī; Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, was born from his own self;
Varuṇa became Suṣeṇa, and the two Aśvins became Vivida and Mainda.
Those two, who were born from Brahmā, were once again born there from the Sun, the younger of the two being the latter.
Through the granting of a boon, Indra’s possession [of power] became even more potent than that of Mainda; for Viduda was indeed stronger than Mainda.
(3.71) Nīla was Agni, born from the Lotus-born [Brahmā]; Kāma, moreover, arose from Śrīramaṇa in Ramā.
He became Pradyumna by name from Īśa; he attained the state of Skanda and also the state of Cakra. (3.72)
Formerly, the discus of Hari was indeed Durgā, whom they call Śrī, abiding in *tamas*;
then the conch was Sattvātmikā; and the earth, named Bhū, who abides in *rajas*, became the lotus of Hari.
The mace was Vāyu, whose nature is the possession of strength; the *sārṅga* bow was Vidya; and the sword was Rama herself.
She herself, whose nature is Durgā, is known by the name Carman; the fivefold wind itself constitutes the arrows.
(3.74) While these ancient [deities] remained thus established, Kāma obtained the state of being a wheel through a boon.
And that Aniruddha, born of Brahmā, whose body is Śaṅkha, attained the status of his son as the Puruṣa-soul. (3.75)
Those two were born as Bharata by name and Satrughna following Rāma;

previously, the son of Sumitrā was Śeṣa, who followed the best of the Raghus under the name Lakṣmaṇa. That one of wide strides was the son of Kausalyā, and likewise, there was one for the mother of Bharata.

These four sons of the king—the two sons of Sumitrā and [the other two]—were indeed like the foremost of the immortals. Viṣṇu was manifested within those three through his three forms beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa.
And Indra was in Aṅgada; thus Aṅgada became exceedingly and perpetually powerful.
xxxix. Furthermore, there are thousands of other kings born of Kṛtavīrya and others who possess great strength;
yet all of them were endowed with the presence of Hari, were preeminent in dharma, and preeminent in virtue. 3.79.
It was from the very essence of Ramā that Sītā herself was born, she who is peerless for the sake of Rāma.
"For she was born on the sacrificial ground of the King of Videha; thus, she became his very own.

(3.80) This creation, arising from the Kalpa, which consists of the definitive conclusion of all the Agamas, has been described by me here along with the secondary creations (anusarga). Whichever [creation] was first is indeed always superior by virtue of its qualities. (3.81)
Even in the Pāñcarātra Kalpas, different accounts of creation are stated, and in the Purāṇas as well, they are described otherwise.
Being first among these is not a cause for superiority; this is understood from specific scriptural statements.
(3.82) Thus ends [the section] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*, the third chapter, titled "The Determination of Creation, Secondary Creation, Dissolution, and Manifestation," [concludes]. (xli.
[Within the Rāmāvatāra: The Entry into Ayodhyā)
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Om! Then the four princes, Puruṣottama and the others, grew up in the king’s palace; yet even as they grew, the growth of that [king]—who was ever-increasing—seemed small by comparison with the [vastness of the] world’s vision. 4.1.
Constantly beholding his four sons, the father attained perpetual and supreme joy;
especially upon gazing at the orb of Rāma’s moon-like face, the king felt his purpose was fulfilled.
Their mothers, the citizens, the ministers, the women of the inner apartments, and all those belonging to the realm likewise rejoiced. (4.2)
Beholding the Supreme Person, they became as if satisfied by their own bliss.
Then, from Suvaṃśa was born Śaśin, and his son was Gādhi; he who, by means of a boon, attained the status of a Brahmin and became a friend to the whole world, arrived here. 4.3–4.4.
Requested by his father for the very purpose of protecting the sacrifice, and released by him with great reluctance out of fear,

Rāma— worthy of the salutations of perfected beings— went forth with Lakṣmaṇa to the hermitage of Siddha. For the sake of favoring the sage, he and Lakṣmaṇa received from that seer only the divine weapons.
The lords of the gods, headed by Brahmā, having assembled, openly worshipped him who had manifested in the form of a weapon.

Then, by means of an arrow, he swiftly struck Tāṭakā—who, due to a boon from the Creator, was otherwise incapable of being slain—thereby destroying Subāhu, who was immune to death even at the word of Īśāna, and thus protected the sage’s sacrifice. (4.6–4.7)
Then, honoring the word of Viriñca, he cast Mārīca into the ocean with an arrow;
for immunity from death had been granted to him by that [god], so he slew the other night-stalkers instead.
At that time, the son of Videha proclaimed his daughter’s svayaṃvara in all directions and intermediate points.
Having taken leave of him, the follower of Gādhi’s son departed for Videha, followed by his younger brother.
Then he reunited Ahalyā—who had been cursed by her husband because of Indra’s assault and turned into stone—with Gautama; she had attained human form through the sight of him. (4.9–4.10)
Displaying a power greater than his own devotion and an incomparable grace toward the gods,
and having created a woman of exclusive devotion whom the Lord of the Gods desired, he departed, honored by her.
[4.11] [He went to] Śyāmāvadātā, the singular essence of the world, lovely with a splendor surpassing that of infinite moons.
When he had entered the city with his younger brother, bow and arrow in hand, the daughters of Videha were filled with joy.
With the bees of their moist eyes, those women of lovely countenances drank in the lotus-face of that Supreme Man;
and the throngs of men and women from Videha gazed upon his feet, just as devotees of the Great Puruṣa gaze upon his feet.

Thus, having obtained Rāma— the younger brother of the thousand-eyed Indra— who had come seeking cattle, along with his younger brothers, Videha honored him and that Ṛṣi who was as radiant as fire itself;
and he considered him a worthy son-in-law for his daughter, a fresh incarnation of beauty.
And the rishi of fierce splendor said to him, "Make him your son-in-law.
He replied to him, "I shall do this supreme word; I have no hesitation in this matter.
But hear from me the vow that was previously made regarding the giving away of my daughter."
In former times, I performed austerities with my mind fixed on obtaining the excellent weapon of Umāpati;
he then granted me this divine bow, which cannot be moved by anyone at all except the wielder of the Pināka.
Neither gods, nor Daityas, nor serpents, nor celestial singers—including Indra himself—are capable of stringing this bow.
Whence could men have servants who, by his boon, drag them here with great difficulty?
Having received this unmanageable bow from Śaṅkara, I am intent on testing the prowess of men;
for the sake of my daughter, I made this vow: "I shall give my daughter to whoever completes this task. (4.18–4.19)

Having heard these words spoken by me, the sons of Diti—the Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas—as well as the kings, gathered together and approached [the pillar]; they seized it, wishing to move it, but were unable to do so. (4.20) With their limbs perspiring and their eyes rolling, Daśānana and the others fell down, unconscious.
Nevertheless, they were unable to violate me for the sake of your daughter, due to the words of the Self-born One.
For long ago, the lotus-born Lord, somehow propitiated by my ascetic penance, granted me this boon:
"No one shall approach your daughter by force, nor shall there be any violation of her by those who desire her. (4.21–4.22)
Then those kings, their pride destroyed, departed from here all together on that very same day.
Thereupon, his heart being completely fulfilled, he said, "Let him choose this maiden for me; this alone is my request.
When the sage had said, "So be it," he then had him led by servants upon a vehicle resembling the coils of Ananta.

Having observed that, Rāghava playfully lifted it with his left hand and, laughing, drew it back; yet as it was being pulled by that other one of boundless strength with ease, it snapped. How could that [other] man's strength possibly have been capable of enduring the unbearable force of him? 4.24–25.

Having playfully split that [sacrificial post] in the middle like a stalk of sugarcane, as Indra’s elephant does, he stood there with Lakṣmaṇa, gazing at the face of the seer, his body complete like the moon with its mark. He, whose eyes were like lotuses, whose chest was broad and high, who was dark yet radiant, and who shone with trembling earrings— 4.26. Him, the lotus-eyed one, with a broad and lofty chest, dark yet fair-complexioned, and brilliant with moving earrings.
The princess beheld him anointed with sandalwood paste that resembled [the blood] from a hare’s wound, and clad in garments of lightning.
Then, taking the garland of unfading lotuses with both hands, she whose eyes were like lotus petals approached slowly with graceful steps; having placed it upon his chest, she stood by his side.
Then, upon seeing the Supreme Lord—the treasure-house of bliss—united with the daughter of the king, an immense joy arose among the people everywhere in the city of Videha.
When the Lord of Ramā was clearly seen accompanied by Lakṣmī, he then quickly sent word to his father. 4.29.
Having heard that from the messenger of the ten directions, the king of Videha, the lord of the earth, was immediately gratified.
Then, accompanied by his two sons and his wife, he set out with his own army consisting of elephants, chariots, and infantry;
placing the son of Dhātṛ, Vasiṣṭha, at the head, the King of Mithilā went to the very place where [the sage] was.

Greatly honored by the King of Mithilā, Vasiṣṭha, the family priest who bore joy, performed the marriage for his son with the approval of Gādhi’s daughter; he offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rites. At that time, the surface of the sky became crowded with rows of celestial chariots belonging to the gods who desired to witness the event.
The kettledrums and drums resounded, and thousands of the finest Gandharvas sang.

(4.33) For previously, the deities, knowing her to be the mother of the worlds, had not come here to request [her hand]; but now, desiring to see the Lord united with Ramā, they filled the expanse of the sky. (4.34)
Just as in the past there was a gathering of the gods at the self-choice marriage of the daughter of the ocean,
so too did it happen then for all the inhabitants of heaven, as well as for the sages together with the kings upon the earth.
And having taken the hand of the king’s daughter, he whose eyes were like lotus petals shone resplendent.

Just as in the past, during the churning of the ocean of nectar by the gods and asuras, the women of the King of Videha moved about there beautifully adorned; and beholding the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu) filled with joy together with Ramā (Lakṣmī), the king bestowed wealth upon Rāma. 4.36–4.37.

Then, with joy, he gave to the younger brothers of Rāma three excellent maidens, as well as beloved garments, chariots with elephants, and the most exquisite jewels belonging to the Lord of all. (4.38) Having experienced that great festival, both the gods and all the men departed as they had come.
Then Rāma’s father, accompanied by his sons, joyfully departed for his own city, Ayodhyā.
In the meantime, he beheld the descendant of Bhṛgu, who possessed the radiance of a thousand million suns;
he was shining within his own circle of rays, bearing a bow and armed with a flaming battle-axe.

Fearing that the king might not recognize the arrival of Rāghava—the primordial Puruṣa—and desiring to inform him through illustrative examples, as if challenging the scion of Raghu to a contest, the terrified monarch prostrated himself and entreated him:
"O Lord, you ought not to slay my son here, for he is advanced in years. Thus addressed, Bhārgava [replied].

"I give you the three Vedas, O Rāghava; I have come here to see you standing in battle. Having spoken thus to the king, the best of the Raghus, the best of the Bhṛgus revealed his own form as Hari, demonstrating his non-difference from the ignorant by saying, "I am the ancient Hari himself."
Listen, O Rāma, to what is being told by me here: formerly there were two most wonderful bows.
One was held by the Lord of Umā, and the other, the most excellent of all, by the Lord of Ramā.
Then, by the gods who desired to provide a demonstration for the world, those two—Hari and Śaṅkara—were challenged.
We, seeking an illustration here, are able to observe you two standing in the midst of battle.

For when those two, Rāma and Śiva, stood ready for combat having grasped their bows, Hari became the restrainer of the space between them; consequently, Hara stood before him like a mountain. 4.45–46.
When Śiva was no longer able even to look at him, much less to move, let alone to fight,
then the entire host of gods loudly praised the strength of Hara, the destroyer of the world, saying:
"If it were not for his mere breath, this Śaṅkara would not have been able even to breathe."
"What more need be said here? Therefore, the power of Hari is superior even to Hara and indeed transcends everything.

(4.48) Then, having quickly prostrated before Janārdana, Hara was gazed upon by Hari with a gracious look and departed for Kailāsa; that very bow of his was indeed broken by you in the presence of the world. (4.49)
"Any other bow suitable for Hari's hand is ten million times superior to this one;
indeed, it is better that this very [bow] be taken in my hand. Therefore, take this Vaiṣṇava bow.
If you can grasp and draw this, then Hari is yours—there is no need for further deliberation. (4.50)
Speaking thus, he presented the excellent bow, demonstrating that it surpassed even Viṣṇu’s strength by the grace of Śiva.
4.51 Taking up that excellent bow, Rāghava made it ready with effortless ease in the blink of an eye;
having fixed an arrow to it, he drew it while all the world looked on, dispelling their doubt. 4.52

When the power of Viṣṇu had been demonstrated as entirely superior to that of Hara by its being incalculable, Bhārgava—the primordial Puruṣa—spoke with a voice as deep as a mass of clouds to Rāghava and his kin:
"Enough! Your strength is superior to all the world; you are indeed Nārāyaṇa himself, and not otherwise."
"Discharge your arrow here at this great Asura composed of ascetic power, who has attained the state of a world-being through the boon of the Lord.
Long ago, there was a great Asura named Atula; by a boon from Brahmā, he indeed attained the status of a world-protector.
Then the Teacher of the World spoke to him again: "When Hari is conquered, only then shall you be slain. (4.54–55)

"Therefore, for the sake of slaying the Ender of the World, I stand as one who has conquered him, though he is unconquered by all. When this was said, Rāghava released his arrow at the asura Jagadantaka. Previously, a boon had been obtained by him from Śiva through the desire for liberation, [granting] entry into the body of Viṣṇu.
Drawn by him into the belly of Rāma, that demon was instantly reduced to ashes by his command alone.
Thus, drawing his arrow against Rāma and having slain the asura, Rāghava rejoiced while proclaiming that demon's ascetic power; for everything belonging to him had indeed become his own. 4.57–4.58.

The primordial Person, whose essence is uninterrupted and infinite awakening, knowing all things, Hari— who is truly one though possessing two bodies— speaks and listens as if in play, and he rejoiced.
He [perceived] the activity of the people who take refuge in him, which serves as the cause for awakening them to the true reality.
Causing confusion to one of them, he played alone among the men as if he were many.

(4.60) Then that treasury of compassion, desiring to manifest the absolute unity inherent within himself toward his own people, became as if divided in two; yet as the best of the Bhṛgus, he attained oneness with the best of the Raghus in their very presence. (4.61)
Having brought about the unity of the world and dispelled all the doubts of the people,
the Lord of Ramā, with the consent of Rāma, gave that excellent bow to Rāma and then departed. Then the king, overflowing with extreme joy, returned to his own city accompanied by all his sons.
Then Rāma also took delight with that very daughter of the king, Sītā, who was the very embodiment of Ramā;
just as in former times the Lover of Śrī dwelt intensely in delight with her in the midst of the ocean of milk,
so too did that best of the Raghus dwell for a very long time in the city of Ayodhyā, rejoicing with her.
"These deeds of Hari, the best of the Raghus, though diverse, are not at all wonderful;
rather, the majesty of him whose power is infinite is here described as his own duty.
(4.65) Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable Ācārya Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the fourth chapter, titled "The Entry into Ayodhyā" in the Rāmāvatāra, ends here.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
In the *Rāmacarita*, the Vision of Hanumān:

Om! Thus, while this Lord of the Universe remained upon the earth accompanied only by Sītā, having established the entire world in its proper state, all people were exceedingly gratified day after day with ever-increasing devotion.
Honoring the words of his subjects during the royal consecration, the king resolved upon his own welfare; yet that [resolve] reached the ears of Mantharā, the earth-dwelling goddess of misfortune.
Formerly born from the Ocean of Milk, she had somehow attained the state of an *apsaras* through her ascetic penance. (5.1)
To lead that [man] into blinding darkness, the Lotus-born (Brahmā) quickly spoke of Rāma’s consecration;
"Become a slave and seize [the kingdom], and through that deed you shall attain your own goal.
Thus addressed, Mantharā immediately committed that evil act. 5.2.
At her word, Kaikeyī indeed secured the kingdom through the power of the boon granted by her husband;
out of respect for her, Rāma entered the forest for the sake of the gods and the sages,
accompanied by his younger brother and joined by Sītā, who was endowed with ever-increasing and profound devotion day by day.
Having settled all living beings upon his shoulders— those who had abandoned all worldly desires out of grief at being separated from him—
and having left behind trees, animals, insects, his father, friends, and his mother and other kin, he then crossed the surging Gaṅgā, honored by Guha as Śiva was by Guha.

Having received worship from the son of the god-worshipper (Bharata) who was accompanied by a host of sages, he departed for Citrakūṭa, the lord of mountains; there he dwelt for several days, rejoicing.
At that very time, King Daśaratha passed away due to the grief of separation.

Then, after the ministers, together with the sons of Viśvāmitra, had brought Rāma’s two sons from the Kekayas and performed for him immediately the funeral rites prescribed by the scriptures, they departed for the path taken by Rāma, grieving and accompanied by the citizens and their mothers. 5.5.

Having arrived there at Rāma’s feet along with the hosts of sages, and having bowed down, Bharata spoke to the lotus-eyed Rāma, who was utterly censuring Kaikeyī and Mantharā— the abode of all evils— saying: "O Lord, may you come here once more for our delight."
"Having quickly reached my own Ayodhyā together with my younger brothers, may I protect this earth"—

when addressed thus, Lord Rāma, who is capable of performing the gratification of the entire host of gods and who desires to make his word true, spoke most emphatically "No" to him who was bowed low with perfect devotion.

"Even if you should entreat me again and again for seven doubled periods of years, once that time has passed, I shall perform this deed for you; these words of mine are most firmly established in truth, there is no doubt in this.
Having heard these words of Rāma and having made his vow regarding the leap into the fire, [he departed].
Having made another vow, saying, "I shall not enter the city as long as Rāma’s word has been rendered otherwise," he then dwelt outside in the village named Nandin;
there, he placed upon his head the supreme golden footstool belonging to the Lord of Śrī himself. 5.8.
When his younger brother had departed for Citrakūṭa followed by all the citizens, the Blessed One remained there.
Then the son of Indra, a crow, arrived, impelled by a great demon who had entered his own body.
When, under the influence of that demonic possession, he thrust his beak into the breast of Ramā, he was then beheld [by the Lord].
When Janārdana quickly employed a blade of grass, he followed it as it blazed;

though he sought refuge with the lords of the gods, headed by Svayambhū, Śiva, and Indra, desiring to live, he was rejected by them because they were unable to withstand the irresistible power of the Supreme One due to their devotion to Hari. (5.10–5.11)
Having gone again for refuge to the best of the Raghus, he was dismissed by him after slaying the asura;
though that [asura] was present before his eyes and even invulnerable, this was through the grace of the one adorned with the moon.
By a boon from the Lord of Umā, that asura had become the "eye-possessor" (cākṣiga) of all the crows.
He was struck down along with those who had crow-like eyes, and by means of a blade of grass, he was reduced to ashes by Rāma.

(5.13) For those crows, seeking strength, had granted him an opening; therefore, that striking down of their eyes was performed by the Lord of Ramā. Yet even the other crows always remained with only one eye. (5.14)

Furthermore, as long as there shall be two eyes for those born of the crow lineage, so long was that eye of the one named Kuraṅga, and the [other] eye of the son of Diti, granted by Śiva to be imperishable. Thus, warding off his future rebirth, he rendered those who were to be born one-eyed.

Then that Rāghava, the primordial being, the son of Śakra, departed at his command along with the crows. Then Rāma, led by the best of sages to the Daṇḍaka forest— having heard that many worlds had been destroyed by those of noble power, Kharas and others, whose bodies were made invulnerable to all by a boon from Hara— set forth accompanied by his wife.
And there dwelt a sage named Śarabhaṅga, aged and of fierce splendor, desiring to go to the world of Hari.
Being gratified by him through the respectful offering of hospitality and worship, the Lord of Ramā granted him his own supreme abode;
for this was the duty of that forest-dweller, since his physical strength had utterly declined, to perform his own prescribed duties such as the offering of oblations into the fire.
Upon the exhaustion of his lifespan, he cast off his body into his own fire in the presence of Rāma and departed for the Supreme Lord.

(5.19) Rāma also beheld there a *yātudhānī* who had been Urvaśī’s lover, a Gandharva named Tumburu, now reduced to this state by the curse of Kubera; though he was known by the name Virādha, he was nonetheless unslayable due to a boon from Śarva. (5.20)
Having severed his pair of arms, he rendered them separate, honoring the word of the Lotus-born One;
and he granted a good rebirth to his own singer, giving him his own body along with his younger brother here as food.
Desiring to show affection, he went to his own abode, that of the Jar-born One, with the utmost reverence.
Having been honored, he took up that bow; however, the Primordial Being (Viṣṇu) then reclaimed his own Śārṅga bow from Indra.
For in former times, Hari had indeed given it to Indra solely for his own sake, and Indra, in turn, gave it to the sage Agastya specifically for the sake of Rāma’s hand.
Having obtained it, Rāma dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forests protecting the sages.
At that very time, the Rākṣasa woman, intent on seeking a husband for herself through the power of Khara and Dūṣaṇa, was devoted to searching for a lord.
When her own husband had been slain by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa through a casual act, she approached Rāma.
By the command of the Lord of the Night-rangers, that fierce woman, accompanied by her two brothers, dwelt in the forest.
Having approached Rāma, she said, "Become my husband," just as darkness approaches the sun when it desires a close union.
Then, while there in the presence of Janaka’s daughter, he spoke words of mockery, saying, "Go, my younger brother; do not stay here with me.
For that very reason, he made her of wicked conduct—with her ears and nose cut off—for the sake of terrifying all the night-stalkers.

To ensure the welfare of all, he—bow in hand—slew fourteen thousand of her kinsmen led by Khara, Triśiras, and Dūṣaṇa, who were dispatched with terrifying strength; for while the best of the Raghus granted safety to the great sages, he instilled fear in the circle of night-stalkers. 5.27.
Having heard from the mouth of his sister and from Avikampana about the power of the Lord of the Raghus, the Lord of the Rākṣasas fell into deep anxiety.
Having quickly deliberated upon his course of action, he went to the field on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams, Śravaṇa, the ear of the earth.
There he beheld Mārīca engaged in ascetic penance, utterly terrified of the arrow of the Lord of the Raghus.
Requested by him for the purpose of deceiving Rāghava, Mārīca, knowing the speed of his arrows, said:
"Indeed, you cannot engage in combat here with the best of the Raghus; for I previously experienced the touch of that arrow.
When he had spoken thus, Rāvaṇa drew his sword and said: "If you do not carry out my command, I shall kill you!"

Having heard that, filled with fear and being wicked by nature, he went toward the presence of the best of the Raghus. Having attained the state of a golden deer, variegated with many jewels, he moved swiftly and at great length near Sītā.
Although the goddess was faultless and possessed of eternal excellence, she spoke thus for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasa and for the purpose of deluding people.
