"Chase this one and capture it; give me that deer for my sport," they said. As soon as he was thus addressed, Rāma, bow and arrow in hand, pursued the illusory deer, knowing its true nature, and struck down the night-stalker. Struck by that excellent arrow, the wicked one cried out to Lakṣmaṇa and died from intense agony.

Upon hearing this, he urged Lakṣmaṇa with harsh words, and he too, equipped with his bow and arrows, followed the path of Rāma. Whatever sport the Supreme Lord performs with ease, the goddess Ramā likewise performs that very same sport after him.
Yet, when one reflects upon it, not even the slightest fault attaches to this Supreme Being or to Ramā, for they are the Great Lords.
Where is ignorance, and where even calamity, for her who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and liberation of the universe through the mere casting of a sidelong glance?
Is this not merely a playful imitation by the Goddess and Hari as they sport together, like gods and men?
Therefore, Rāvaṇa approached the presence of the Goddess; yet, despite his unbearable power, he became invisible.
Having created an image of herself, she departed quickly for Kailāsa and dwelt there with Śiva and Pārvatī, whose feet are worshipped.
But Śakra entered that image of hers—which was present in the presence of the Goddess—for the sake of accomplishing his purpose.
Then the Lord of the Night-rangers took her and departed, having slain Jaṭāyu, though he was obstructed by great exertion.
Then Hanumān, approaching him as he was traveling on the road, was restrained by the son of the Sun (Sugrīva), who knew [the truth];

yet, desiring to accomplish his divine mission and seeking Rāma’s fame, he did not kill him at the word of Hari (Sugrīva). Having reached his own city, that Rākṣasa then stationed a substitute in the form of Sītā and guarded it there.
Rāma, having slain that most wicked Rākṣasa, reached the hermitage but did not see his beloved.
Searching for her, he saw the vulture who had sought to protect Sītā and had been slaughtered by the enemy.

Hearing from that bird—whose movements were now sluggish—the account of what the lord of the demons had done, he cremated the dead creature and likewise bestowed upon him his own celestial destination.

And while wandering elsewhere together with his younger brother, he suddenly encountered Karan, who was named Kabandha; by virtue of a boon from the Creator, the conqueror of all, he had been released from death and remained with arms excessively bent due to the falling of a thunderbolt. Having severed that pair of arms along with his younger brother, and having restored that servant of the Lord of the Gods to his former state, [he departed].
They say that in former times he was born as a Gandharva named Danu by the very name Trijaṭā; honored even by him, he then departed.
(5.43) Having seen him and recognized him as the Supreme Hari, Śabarī entered the fire before his very eyes for her sake.
He granted her his own world, for she had previously waited here in this forest according to the word of Mataṅga. (5.44)

For, having released that excellent *apsaras* from the curse of Śacī—who had acted out of excessive pride before her husband—he went and beheld the Son of the Wind on Ṛśyamūka; for he alone truly understands this Lord. (5.45) It is well known from the Vedic word that where there is wind in the body, there is Hari, and where there is Hari, there is indeed the wind.
Thinking, "In whom indeed shall I take refuge? he likewise descended; therefore, for the sake of Māruti, he protected the son of the Sun (Sugrīva).
In this same way, that one with the dark body (Kṛṣṇa) protected Arjuna as well, having slain that enemy of the Sun's son (Jaya) for the sake of Bhīma alone.
For previously, this son of the Sun (Rāma) obtained Māruti [as an ally], and by him, the descendant of Raghu (Rāma) slew Vālī, who was hostile to him.

Since even the gods are thus under the power of the Wind-god, everyone here and there has taken refuge in Sugrīva and Hanumān—the son of Śakra—for his favor; therefore, the Lord of the Raghus arrived there together with Lakṣmaṇa.
He whose lotus-feet the goddess Śrī, the Lotus-born Brahmā, and Giriśa, along with the world-protectors, bear upon their heads.

For what need has that supreme Lord of all, who possesses every power, for monkeys as allies in the slaying of his enemy? (5.49) But when Rāghava had arrived, the monkeys—including the son of the Sun—leapt away, overcome by fear; yet Māruti restrained them. (5.50)
Having quickly steadied the leaders of the monkeys and knowing the infinite qualities of Viṣṇu, he—thinking, "This one is the manifest father of Brahmā"—fell at his feet. 5.51.
Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
within the narrative of Rāma’s life, the fifth chapter titled "The Vision of Hanumān" (concluding with the determination to cross the ocean).
Then the Sixth Chapter.

Om! Having raised him up with his lotus-hand marked by the wheel and granting boons—his eyes as broad as the petals of a lotus—and having greeted him with this [verse], he, being praised by him, ascended the chariot out of affection along with Lakṣmaṇa, smiling. 6.1.
Having placed the Lord and his younger brother upon the pair of shoulders of the monkey-king Hanumān, he departed;
and in the presence of the Fire-god and others, he quickly established friendship with Rāma, the remover of his own and others' suffering.
Then, having heard of his sorrow, that best of gods, the lord of monkeys, also made a vow for the slaying of Vālin.
Then, for the sake of searching for Sītā, he showed him the carcass of Dundubhi, which had been cast away by Vālin.

Upon seeing it fallen there, Lord Rāma, with great ease and merely by the movement of his thumb, hurled it a hundred yojanas; having split the entire earth with that very body, he slew the sons of Diti dwelling in the subterranean realm.
Having slain all the sons of Diti—who were otherwise invincible—through the power born of Śarva’s grace, he was again addressed by his friend Kuṇapa, who had become terrified of Vālin’s strength.
Pointing out seven very firm *sāla* trees, [Kuṇapa] said that those sons of Diti were even more solid than a thunderbolt.
"He is capable of shaking each one of these," [Vālin replied], "but though he is able to tear off their leaves, he does not dare to do so. (6.5)
If you were to pierce these arrows standing all around with a single shaft, then you would be capable of slaying Vālin.
For a man who possesses four times the strength is able to conquer; one who possesses more than a hundredfold the strength is very powerful and capable of killing the exceedingly strong.
Therefore, having split these arrows—which are as easy to cut as the arm-hair of Indra’s son—dispel my doubt.

Having heard his words and reflecting upon them, Rāma— seeing that those sons of Diti, by virtue of a boon from the Creator, possessed forms impenetrable by any man— immediately pierced them with a single arrow as they were engaged in penance to attain unshakable Brahminhood.
Then, having fixed a sharp arrow upon his excellent bow and drawing it back with his right arm, he released it.

By Rāma, who possesses infinite strength, all those trees were instantly pulverized by his roar (6.9). Having pierced through them along with the mountains, the arrow released by the Blessed One then burned the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*) and all those *asuras* there named Kumudins, who were protected by the word of the Lotus-born Brahmā and were otherwise invincible; that single arrow consumed them all (6.10).
This is not surprising for Viṣṇu, whose power is immeasurable and vast, since through his impulsion the activity of the wind arises;
yet even this [activity] of the world, together with its primordial nature (prakṛti), Rudra, time, karma, and so forth, is unachievable by any other. 6.11.
Then, having witnessed the Lord’s power, that lord of the monkeys placed him in front and went toward the city of his elder brother.

Hearing the roar of the man from the cave, Sugrīva rushed toward him, though forbidden by his beloved; yet, struck by his fists, he fled, rendered powerless. Rāghava, too, observing the dharma, did not kill him, for he understands the conduct of all the world. He said to him: "In battle, you two were not distinguished by me."

If he desires brotherly affection, I shall not kill my innocent elder brother Vālin; for anger directed toward a sibling does not remain long, and even if it persists, it ceases once its cause has passed. Furthermore, anger toward one's own kin generally subsides at the time of death, and it is likewise pacifying.
He thought that one who has instantly cast off his faults through a single failure is not fit to be slain here.

Therefore, he did not kill him, considering that the son of the Sun would not suffer torment in the future, and wishing to demonstrate the principle that when enmity is provoked by kinsmen, no slaughter should be carried out by those connected to them. (6.15–6.16)
"How can there be ignorance in this Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Ruler, who is the impeller of the entire series of sense-faculties?
Then, having been thus addressed, he who had returned discharged a thunderbolt-like arrow with great force at the son of Indra.
When the son of the Sun (Karbura) had been split by the creeper by the command of Rāma, and the arrow had been released by the son of Vāyu (Hanumān) in the form of a Rākṣasa, [the battle continued].
Hearing that incomparable sound, the son of Indra, pierced in his heart by it, fell instantly like a mountain, overcome with grief.
"If he is my devotee and looks upon me here, he will surely fall at my feet without hesitation.
For one who has prostrated himself at one's feet should not be slain; yet the son of the Sun, seeking a kingdom, has requested his death. (6.18–6.19)
"For even a desired task must first be accomplished by one who is prostrate; indeed, the slaying of one who has fallen at one's feet is not praised.

Therefore, I shall slay the son of Śakra while his body remains invisible. Thinking thus, he struck him while remaining unseen. (6.20) He who is the eternal impeller of the power of all the worlds, whose body possesses full, imperishable, supreme strength and heroism, and who is independent—
"What can this monkey do, even with that bow by which [Vālin] formerly shattered the mountain, once he has come within the range of his vision?

Or rather, when Vālin had fallen, he went to his side and spoke to him with tender words: 'If you wish, I shall restore you to life. But he did not desire it, saying: 'Who indeed would not choose death in your presence, O Supreme among Men? (6.21–22)
Having performed his final duties and having first installed his son in the kingdom of the monkeys, the son of the Sun (Sugrīva) remained there;
and Rāma, too, having seen the arrival of the clouds, dwelt for four months on that excellent mountain together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Then, while the king of the monkeys was deeply engrossed and had forgotten the service rendered by Rāma—

Hanumān, the foremost among the wise and devoted to the feet of Rāma, spoke forcefully to him: "You must not, under any circumstances, forget the task for the best of the Raghus, for he is our object of supreme reverence. If you do not wish to perform it yourself today, I shall certainly have it done by force."
Having spoken thus in the presence of the King of Monkeys, the Lord summoned all the monkeys who travel with great speed from across the seven islands and dispatched them.
Those monkeys were sent forth by Hanumān, preceded by his focused devotion to the command of the Lord of the Monkeys.
Then, taking with them all the monkeys dwelling in the groves of mountains and trees, they set out.

At that very moment, the lord Rāma, perceiving the king of monkeys to be intoxicated and addicted to sensual pleasures, spoke these words to the son of Sumitrā: "Go quickly and tell this message of mine to the lord of the monkeys."
“If you are negligent in my task, I shall send you along the path of Indra’s son;

for generally, those arrogant with pride are unable to repay a favor once their own purpose has been accomplished. When the venerable Rāma had spoken thus, Lakṣmaṇa then departed, equipped with his bow and arrows.
Upon seeing him, he went in haste to the presence of Rāma along with him, free from fear because of the heat [of his own power].

(6.30) When the Lord of the Monkeys had become joyful in heart at the excellent words of Hanumān, and when he had arrived together with all the foremost heroes among the monkeys, Rāghava rejoiced upon seeing him. (6.31)
Hurriedly raising up that one who had fallen at his lotus feet, the Lord quickly embraced him;
and once he was seated in the presence of the Lord of the World, by the Lord's command, he dispatched the monkeys with speed.
When they had been sent out in all directions by him, the Lord spoke these words to Hanumān: 6.32.
"There is no one other than you who is capable of accomplishing this task of mine, which is the most excellent of all undertakings.
Therefore, take my signet ring and proceed yourself toward the southern direction.
Thus addressed by the Supreme Person, he set out for that quarter accompanied by the crown prince.

Having received the command of the Lord of Monkeys, those led by Aṅgada and Jāmbavat had been dispatched in all directions; after a month, they returned together with the son of Vāyu, yet they did not arrive. While searching for that most excellent and inaccessible fortress, the Vindhya mountain, those high-souled ones failed to find it.
That time proclaimed by Hari’s king had passed, and then I reached a most wonderful cave. Having beheld that supreme and exceedingly marvelous place constructed by Maya, Tāra said to Aṅgada:
"We shall not go into the presence of the king of monkeys, for his time limit has been exceeded."
"This one is difficult to approach and possesses exceedingly fierce fangs; will he kill even us, Madhuka and the others?
Having reached this inaccessible cave, let us all dwell here in comfort; what could he possibly do here? Furthermore, we who always roam the forest have no need for Rāma along with Lakṣmaṇa."
"He is not capable of afflicting us here; therefore, this is my well-considered resolve.
Having heard these words of his maternal uncle, the son of Vālin also accepted them with respect and spoke these words:
"The Lord of the Monkeys will not be patient with those who have transgressed his command."
"How can he, who out of desire for the kingdom had his elder brother slain and by that most cruel man seized our wives—

how can he, established in power, protect us who have transgressed his commands, who are without refuge and weak? When this was said by the son of Indra's son, those led by Jāmbavān replied, "So be it."
Then, seeing that they were all of one mind, Hanumān spoke these words:
"Indeed, this has been understood by me; for Tārā spoke these words to Aṅgada regarding the kingdom.
And this cannot be accomplished, O son of the Wind, for he would not tolerate speech that is contrary to Rāma."
Nor can I be drawn away by any means whatsoever, even by all of you united together,
from the true path of Rāghava— that cave of his, whose power is boundless and which is inviolable.
If these words of mine are to be accepted with respect, then that would be most pleasing to me.

"If I do not bring those who have set out on the wrong path back to the true way by even using force," having heard this spoken by the son of the Wind-god, they were all struck with great fear; maintaining a state of silence, those of unfathomable wisdom followed him and reached Mount Mahendra, the foremost of mountains.
Beholding that unassailable and boundless ocean, they were suddenly despondent;
with firm resolve and free from hope, they set their minds upon fasting unto death, and so they did.
And as they sat in fasting, they spoke of Rāma, who bestows liberation from the cycle of existence.
They related this account of Jaṭāyu’s fall, which reached the ears of the one named Sampāti.

His elder brother was the son of Aruṇa; while testing his speed, he flew toward the orb of the sun along with him, but having endured that intense heat and protected his plumage, he returned and alighted. (6.48–49)
With his wings burnt by the heat of the sun, Jaṭāyu heard the story of Rāma and immediately regained his wings; then, having asked for further details, he learned precisely of Jaṭāyu’s death.
Thereafter, having reported the course of Rāvaṇa as told by his son and having beheld the form of Janaka’s daughter, [he departed].
Then, while she was seated in the Aśoka grove, he himself spoke to those foremost of monkeys;
thereupon, questioned by the son of Brahmā, they each individually declared their own strength regarding the journey of ten, twenty, and so on, up to one hundred *yojanas* in succession. (6.51–6.52)
When Sanīla, Mainda, and Dvivida, along with all the stars, were unable to go beyond eighty *yojanas*, Jāmbavān then spoke of his own strength;
at that time, Viṣṇu traversed the worlds in three strides while Bali was making a joyful sound. (6.53)
"At that time, this triple world with all its sentient beings seemed to me to be as vast as Mount Meru;
therefore, my speed was not equal to what it once was, for previously I could leap ninety-six [yojanas].
Then Prince Aṅgada said: 'From here I could leap a hundred [yojanas], but beyond that I do not know. (6.54–55)

When all of them had not yet completed a hundred round trips and, having observed the enemy force as well as the extreme difficulty of accessing the city of the Lord of Night-stalkers, the son of the Creator spoke:
"This vulture indeed flew to Mount Trikūṭa, a hundred yojanas away; are there perhaps obstacles here? (6.56)
"Even if there were others, Hanumān alone would be capable; no one else exists who is his equal.
Having spoken thus, he again addressed the son of Pavana, praising his boundless strength:
"You alone are supremely capable here; do this, and protect the monkeys! (6.58)

Thus addressed, Hanumān, having made manifest their incapacity regarding his own desired goal, quickly increased in size after reflecting upon Rāma, whose power is perfectly complete, and having carried out His command. (6.59) Thus ends [the section] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya*,
within the *Śrīrāmacarita*, the sixth chapter, titled "The Decision to Cross the Ocean" (lvii.
Hanumat's Return).
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Om! Having bowed to Rāma—the Lord of all, the great ocean of the essence of bliss, who eternally possesses the six expansive divine attributes—the son of the Wind-god, desiring to leap across the sea, compressed that best of mountains and sprang up. 7.1.
The ocean was agitated and quickly advanced with its hosts of aquatic creatures, drawn by his army;
and the trees that had previously been cast into the sea by the wind along with the mountain were brought back for his sake.
At the time when the wings of the mountains were destroyed, Śiva’s brother-in-law, having cast himself into the ocean, remained there with his wings intact by the power of the wind.
The golden mountain, with its many peaks, rose up from the ocean to provide rest for the son of the Wind;
yet he, being free from fatigue, did not desire rest there—for how could there be fatigue for one whose qualities of prowess are boundless?
Embracing that best of mountains as he proceeded, he beheld the Mother of the Nāgas, who had been sent by the gods as a boon.

"Let whatever you desire be food for those who wish to test their own strength against yours"—to her who had spoken thus to the gods, he entered her mouth and instantly emerged from it; thus protecting his own vows among the gods, he brought them joy.
Seeing his friendship with the gods and his formidable power, the deities praised him with a rain of celestial flowers.
Honored by them, he proceeded once more through the sky and beheld the shadow-grasper named Siṃhika.
The Creator bestowed upon her unimpeded power for the destruction of the entire forest of Laṅkā and for its subjugation.
She cast her shadow upon the son of the Wind; he, having entered her body, quickly tore it asunder. (7.6–7)
Perceiving his own strength to be beyond all bounds, he slew even her, though she was protected by the best of creators;

then, having leaped onto the mountain that served as the rampart of Laṅkā with its towering peaks, he alighted and contracted his form. Having become as small as a cat, he reached that city at night and beheld Laṅkā appearing in its own natural splendor.

Having been obstructed by her, he then conquered her and, with her consent, entered Laṅkā after crushing her with his own fist. Searching both outside and inside, he saw a figure resembling Rāma standing at the foot of a *śiṃśapā* tree in the Aśoka grove.

Knowing the heart's intent of Rāma, who was performing a drama for the world of men, and having observed his actions and understood his thoughts, he then gave him the ring, accompanied by gestures of such a kind. (7.11)

All those ornaments which had belonged to Sītā before her transformation into that form became twofold, and they remained exactly as they were. Then she gave to Rāma the divine crest-jewel from her head.
Although those hosts of night-stalkers do not see this, all the sages who roam the celestial realm do see it;
[I have done this] solely for the purpose of mocking and deceiving those Daityas. (7.13)
"This would be a mockery committed before the foremost of the Kali-demons.
(7.14) Having accomplished all this work, the son of the Wind-god, the best among the wise, became free from doubt and set his mind upon revealing himself. (7.15)
Then, having swiftly ravaged that entire forest while sparing this single tree, the hero—
desiring the destruction of the night-stalker and repeatedly leaping down excessively— ascended the gateway.
Then the Ten-faced one heard the supreme exploits of the Lord of Monkeys.

The monkey commanded many servants, saying, "Let him be seized! 7.17. All those servants, who were deathless by virtue of a boon from Hara, approached the mighty son of Aṅga, whose inner self was a god. 7.18.
The army, led by eighty million troop-commanders and joined by the eight [divine] regiments,
crowded with many weapons, surrounded the lord of monkeys; thus encompassed by those arms, he was struck by them violently.
He crushed them all together,

pulverizing them with his blows; and again, he trampled the seven sons of the ministers, who were sent by Rāvaṇa, who possessed the splendor of mountains, and who were well-protected by excellent guards.
Having slain those who were at the forefront of the army and those who were highly arrogant due to the words of Śarva,
he destroyed one-third of all the Rākṣasas.
Having heard of Hari’s incomparable strength, the lord of the Rākṣasas—
He appointed his own son Akṣa as an equal opponent for the prince.
He rained down arrows upon the son of the witness of all the worlds— arrows sharpened and consecrated with supreme weapons— but he could not shake him.
Beholding that son born from the midst of the *maṇḍala* who resembled Rāvaṇa, he thought:
"This is the third Śakra of our army.
He concluded that this was indeed Rāvaṇa and nothing else for Rāghava.
"If Indrajit has been killed by me, yet his power is not seen;
therefore, this third one, who is equal to those two, shall be slain by me.
Having reflected thus, he seized him by the feet and leapt up.

Having caused the son of Rāvaṇa to whirl about like a wheel, the one whose body was like that of Māruta dashed him against the surface of the earth in an instant. When his own son had been pulverized upon the ground, that Rāvaṇa—
Hearing this, he, tormented by grief, commanded his elder brother.
Then Indrajit, with great arrows discharged using excellent weapons,
mangled the best of monkeys, yet he could not cause him to waver.
Then, in accordance with the ritual injunctions, he discharged that supreme weapon, which was unbearable for all. Struck by it, Hari reflected without agitation:
"Indeed, I have transgressed the boons of the Self-born many times."
"He is indeed worthy of my respect; therefore, I honor him here.
And what would these throngs of delighted Rākṣasas do here?
Thus he is merely being observed by me, and there Rāvaṇa is seen. (7.32–33)
Seeing the lord of monkeys standing there as if bound, they quickly bound him with other nooses; yet that weapon of his departed. Then, seizing the monkey, they brought him near.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the night-stalkers, questioned him:
"O monkey, from where have you come? To whom do you belong? And for what purpose has this been done?
Thus addressed, he bowed to his lord Rāma and spoke.

Know me to have arrived as a messenger from him of irresistible prowess, the best of the Raghus; know me as Māruti, the lord over the destruction of your lineage. (7.37) If you do not quickly restore the beloved of the best of the Raghus, then...
"You shall go to the abode of Yama along with your sons, friends, and kinsmen.
(7.38) Even the lords of the gods, beginning with Viriñci and Śarva, are not capable of withstanding Rāma’s arrows; how much less so you, who are of such little substance? (7.39)
"Who would be able to stand before him when he is provoked,
he whose actions are inconceivable and who rules over the world of gods, asuras, serpents, and others?
When this was said, Vibhīṣaṇa restrained him as he was intent on slaughter.
He directed the night-stalkers to the task of burning his tail;
then, having covered his tail with heaps of rags, they gave it to Agni,
but the consumer of oblations, whose companion is the wind, did not burn it.
That unassailable one, arrogant in his strength, took no heed of all the efforts of the rākṣasas; out of curiosity, he desired nothing less than to burn that city to the ground.
And he set the entire city ablaze with the fire issuing from his own tail.

Even the craftsmanship of Viśvakarman was consumed by his splendor. Having utterly incinerated the city— constructed of gold and jewels— along with the foremost of the Rākṣasas, he roared with great joy.
Having rendered Rāvaṇa along with his sons as insignificant as a blade of grass, he reduced their city to ashes while the two of them looked on;
then, having crossed the ocean once more, he was honored by his own kinsmen. (7.46)
Having consumed the honey, he approached his lord;

having reached Rāma, who is as delightful as the Lord of the Gods and charming with countless virtues, the son of the Wind-god, accompanied by all the foremost heroes among the monkeys, placed the crest-jewel at Rāma’s feet and performed a prostration before him with devotion using all his limbs. (7.47–7.48)
Rāma, perceiving that there was nothing else worthy of being given to him who was so supremely devoted,

and considering the gift of his own self to be the greatest for the son of the Wind-god, embraced him with supreme satisfaction. (7.49) Thus ends [the section] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya*,
within the *Śrīrāmacarita*, the seventh chapter, titled "Hanūmat’s Return," (lxii) [concerning] the bestowal of Śrī Rāma’s compassion upon Hanūmat.
Now begins the eighth chapter. Om! Having heard what was spoken by Hanumān and seeing that everything had been accomplished, Rāma was pleased and resolved upon his departure.
Mounting the son of the Wind (Hanumān), accompanied by Aṅgada, the son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa), Vibhīṣaṇa, and the army, he set forth. 8.1.
Having reached the southern ocean, the Lord, the greatest teacher of the world whose power is inconceivable, lay down there;
for, demonstrating gentleness at the outset, he had set out to seek the path of Dharma with a composed mind.
Thereupon, the younger brother of the lord of the Rākṣasas, named Vibhīṣaṇa, who had been abandoned by Rāvaṇa, arrived at that place.
Thinking, "He is exceedingly devoted to the Lord of the Raghus and is steadfast in righteousness," he abandoned him and sought refuge with that best of the Raghus.

(8.3) By the son of Brahmā, by the son of the Sun, by the leader of the forces Nīla, and by Mainda, Vivida, Aṅgada, Tāra, and the others—all of whom had arrived from the enemy's abode—it was firmly stated: "This brother of his is not fit to be captured. (8.4)
Regarding this, he said: "This very one, who has utterly taken refuge [in me], is another form of the deity Balarāma;
he is a devotee at the feet of Rāma. Knowing the Rākṣasa to be perishable, he has come here to enjoy the kingdom.
When Hanumān had spoken thus, the God of gods, having grasped those words, spoke just as before.
For the sake of Sugrīva, I shall firmly grasp this [ring]; for one who has sought refuge at my feet, this indeed shall always be my vow.

(8.6) Even if all the hosts of gods together with Brahmā, along with the Daityas and mortals, were to assemble and exert themselves to move even a single finger of mine, they would not have the power;
nor do I have any fear of that night-stalker. For I know him to be of pure nature. (8.7)
Having spoken these words, he who possessed an ocean of boundless noble courage installed that kinsman in the kingdom and consecrated him there;

regarding that lord of the Rākṣasas as no more than a blade of grass, he gave Laṅkā to his younger brother. Having granted him a lifespan equal to the end of an eon, beginning from his tenure as the night-stalker's sovereign, he assigned for him at its conclusion the path to his own world.
Seeing that the ocean had not approached even after three nights, he became enraged and cast the corners of his eyes, red with anger, toward the sea.
Struck by the corners of his eyes blazing with wrath, the ocean was instantly dried up by the beings led by the Danujas.
Then the Ocean, assuming a physical form and taking a vessel of honor upon his head, approached the lotus-feet of the Supreme One and spoke as follows. (8.9–8.10)

“O Infinite One, we of dull intellect do not know You—the unchanging, the primordial Person, the sovereign Lord of the worlds. From Your own essence (sattva), You created the hosts of gods; from passion (rajas), human beings; and likewise from the third quality (tamas), the hosts of asuras. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.8.11)
"Go at your pleasure, slay the son of Viśravas, and obtain as your wife this Rāvaṇa of the three worlds who makes the universe cry out, O hero!
Build a bridge here for the expansion of your fame, which kings who have conquered the quarters approach and sing of.
Having spoken thus, he favored Bāṇa and bestowed upon him that weapon [which had been held] against the sons of Diti and the mlecchas.
From Śiva’s boon, he released his arrows at those who were deathless, invincible, and beyond counting; they consumed them all.

Then, having properly provided roots and fruits for the one who had incurred the debt, Bhava’s enemy—whose actions are never in vain—commanded the incarnation of the divine architect to build a bridge there, as well as Nala born of that same lineage and other excellent monkeys.

Having bound a bridge across the ocean with the peaks of various mountains— the trunks of whose trees were shaken by the hands of the monkey-lords— the Lord of the Raghus, together with his armies led by Sugrīva, Nīla, and Hanumān, entered Laṅkā, which had been burnt to ashes, under the guidance of Vibhīṣaṇa.
(8.15) Perceiving that he had reached the supreme essence of the world, one of boundless and limitless prowess, this ten-faced Rāvaṇa—
Out of fear, his heart became utterly despondent, and his mind was bewildered regarding what ought to be done.

(8.16) Having dispatched the son of Vālin to follow the principles of statecraft—even though the words spoken by him were not accepted by Rāma—the Supreme Lord of noble virtues, with his army mobilized, blocked the four gates of the city of the Lord of the Rākṣasas. (8.17)
At the time of the blockade, he assigned his son to the fierce enemy of the Lord of the Gods (Indra) in the direction of the Lord of Rivers (the West);
he dispatched Prahasta to the East, Vajradamṣṭra to the direction of the Lord of the Dead (Yama), and he himself went toward the direction of the Moon (the North).
Having understood that, the Blessed One quickly dispatched Hanumān alone for the victory over the enemy of the Lord of the Gods.
He then commanded Nīla to bring about the death of Prahasta, and Vajradaṃṣṭra to slay the son of the son of the Lord of the Gods (Hanumān).

Having strung his bow and appointed the Lord of the Monkeys (Aṅgada) to the center, that Supreme Person—his body radiant, equipped with arrows and a sword—stood facing the very direction in which the Lord of the Rākṣasas was stationed. 8.19–8.20.
Driven away by Hanumān, Indrajit, knowing his prowess, approached him as if for refuge;
then both Nīla and Vibhīṣaṇa, with a stone and a spear respectively, brought Prahasta—who had been rendered helpless by Yama—to his end. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.8.96)
66. Bhāgavata Purāṇa 9.8.97 lxiv.
Thus, he did not fall under the power of Nīla; rather, Vibhīṣaṇa struck him down with an unfailing weapon.
When he was slain, Aṅgada approached and struck Vajradaṃṣṭra, throwing his head to the ground and trampling it. 8.22.
When all of them had been slain, that lord of the rākṣasas dispatched Dhūmrākṣa;
and he, approaching the son of the Wind from the western gate, was consumed by him despite his protection by the word of Śūlin, for his power was ultimately fickle.
Akampana also, a rākṣasa, was urged on by the lord of the night-stalkers.
Exalted by the boons of Umāpati, he was slain in an instant by Hanūmat.
Then, at the command of the hero of the Raghus, they set fire to the city at night with great torches ignited by their weapons on all sides.

Then Nikumbha and Kumbha, commanded by the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) out of anger because of Kumbha’s report, set forth for battle with great joy; having driven those monkeys entirely outside, they advanced.
That Kumbha conquered the son of Vidhātṛ (Nala), the two sons of Aṃśumat (Nīla and Tāra), and Aṅgada.
Having fought a fierce battle with the son of the Sun, that great sinner was swiftly sent to the realm of Yama.
Then Nikumbha, seizing a massive, formidable iron club capable of shattering the best of mountains, rushed toward the son of the Sun in fear; he leaped back a distance of one hundred bow-lengths.
As that hero whirled him around with his arms, the quarters of the earth and the sky, along with the moon and sun, were made to spin;
and seeing his great strength and excellence born of Śarva, the gods became somewhat dejected.
Then, beholding him as one who could not be overcome by any other, the son of the Wind-god quickly leapt up before him.
With his arms outstretched, he said to him, "What is the use of these? Strike here; this is your weapon.
Thus addressed by him, that best of Rākṣasas hurled his infallible boon-granted weapon at [Rāma’s] chest.
It was shattered against his unbreakable breast, becoming as futile as a thunderbolt striking a mountain.
When his own weapon was shattered, Nikumbha approached the son of Māruta,
seized him, placed him upon his own shoulder, and departed swiftly.
Grasping him by the throat, that preeminent son of the Wind-god—
Then, releasing his own life-breaths, he cast himself down upon the surface of the earth.
At that sacrifice whose nature was battle and whose presiding deity was Viṣṇu, the son of Pavana made him the sacrificial animal; thereupon the deities raised a roar.
Suptaghna, Yajñakopa, Śakuni, Devatāpana, Vidyujjihva, and Pramāthin, joined by Śuka and Sāraṇa—
these, dispatched by Rāvaṇa, began crushing all the elephant-like monkeys.
"By virtue of a boon from Brahmā, they were unslayable; yet they have been struck down by Rāma’s arrows.
Yuddhonmatta, Matta, Devāntaka, Narāntaka, Triśiras, and Atikāya—these have marched forth by the command of Rāvaṇa. (8.36–8.37)
Narāntaka, the son of Rāvaṇa, standing upon an excellent horse,
fearlessly advanced in battle against the monkeys with a spear raised in his hand.
As he was consuming the armies, the powerful prince Aṅgada—
Having observed him, he quickly leapt up and displayed his chest;
that Rākṣasa struck a supreme spear into his breast,
but it was split in two by the splendor of Vāli’s son.
Then the monkey struck him right in the face with his own horse-flesh;
his two eyes fell out, he collapsed, and he died.
Taking up his excellent sword, he rushed toward the monkey in the battle.
Having snatched his sword, he was slain by the son of Vālin.
When the son of Rāvaṇa, born of a Gandharva maiden, had been killed,
his elder brother, Devatāntaka, who was his uterine sibling, arrived.
As he was falling, all the monkeys led by Jāmbavān, scorched by the rain of arrows, fled in fear; meanwhile,
he swiftly seized an arrow resembling the weapon of Ravi’s son.
He struck off Aṅgada’s arm-guard; it fell upon his chest and he swooned. Then Śatananda, seizing a mountain peak with its trembling trees, rushed toward the night-stalker and hurled it at him.
Seeing him rushing from afar, pierced by arrows,
Surāntaka quickly took up another supreme shaft;
drawing that arrow back to his ear, which resembled the staff of Yama— 8.47.
He pierced the heart of the king, and he fell down;
indeed, seeing the incomparable strength of the enemy of the gods, Māruti challenged him to battle,
just as Keśava challenged Kaiṭabha.
Beholding that chariot, along with its horses and charioteer, rushing toward him, he crushed it,
cut his bow asunder, and shattered it.
Then, seizing a sword, [he confronted] the enemy who was charging forward.

Seizing him by the hair in the combat and throwing him down, Hari, the son of Pavamāna, violently crushed his head with his foot. Having slain him— who was indestructible due to a boon— the son of Pavana [triumphed].
Praised by the best of the gods and gazed upon with joy by the monkeys,
he— having routed all the other monkeys by a boon from the Lord— shattered the chariot, broke the bow and sword, and cut off the head of Triśiras. (8.52–8.53)
Yuddhonmatta and Matta, arrogant due to the boon granted by Pārvatī,
were destroying all the monkeys when they were slain by the fist of Māruti.
Then Atikāya, a great chariot-warrior, crushed the monkeys with a chariot given by Svayambhū.
Born of Daśāsya by Gandharvikā, he moved about resembling the fire of cosmic destruction;
because his ears were as large as jars (*kumbha*), his name was Kumbhakarṇa.
Thus, he conquered the monkeys led by the son of the Sun (Sugrīva) and suddenly rushed toward Rāma. (8.55–56)
As he rushed forward like a massive cloud, bearing a downpour of arrows and roaring with the sound of thunder,
the son of Sumitrā, having taken up his bow, warded him off with floods of shafts as the wind disperses a cloud.
Then those two of exceeding prowess rained down arrows with a speed equal to that of Indra’s thunderbolt.
By their own skill with exceedingly swift arrows, they made the sky filled with darkness (8.58).
Having warded off his arrows with his own shafts, the heroic son of Sumitrā neutralized his weapons with a multitude of great missiles;
he then severed [Rāvaṇa’s] arms along with his head, yet he became four-armed and possessed two heads once more (8.59).
When those [arms] were severed, that hero’s face and arms appeared again and again;
then the inner self, the Wind-god of all the world, spoke to the despondent son of Sumitrā:
"O handsome one, he cannot be slain by any means other than the Brahmā-weapon due to the Creator's boon," and thus he vanished from sight.
Having spoken thus to the son of Rākṣasa, "You are not worthy of my arrow," the Wind-god ascended into the sky.
Then the younger brother of that god released the Brahmā-weapon at the son of the Ten-necked one;
by it, Atikāya—the foremost among those skilled in weapons—was consumed along with his chariot, horses, and charioteer.
When his sons were filled with hatred, the Lord of the Rākṣasas himself desired to set out for the sake of battle.
As the Lord of the Night-rangers was preparing, Khara’s son, the best of archers, said:
"O King, employ me for the slaying of my father along with Lakṣmaṇa."
"Having slain all the foremost of the monkeys, I shall today thoroughly satisfy you," he said;
thus addressed by him, that hero named Makarākṣa, having shaken off all the monkey leaders along with Aṅgada, went forth together with the son of the Sun. 8.64–8.65.
Disregarding the multitude of Lakṣmaṇa’s arrows with contempt, he then challenged Rāma to battle.
That night-stalker said to Rāma: "Your father, who was at Janasthāna, has been slain by me.
O best of archers, by some means or other, I shall give you the fruit of that today. (8.66)
Speaking thus, he who was unslayable by virtue of a boon from the Lotus-born [Brahmā] released a multitude of missiles.

Smiling, the immeasurable Rāma warded off those weapons with his own; then, with an arrow resembling a thunderbolt, he struck off the head of Khara’s son, which was radiant with excellent earrings. (8.67–68)
But those who were his followers, remaining after being slain by the foremost of monkeys,
fled just as they had previously when Dhūmrākṣa and the others had been killed by those carrying trees and rocks.
Then the lord of the night-stalkers, having equipped himself and taken up his bow, mounted his chariot.
Surrounded by night-stalkers leading hosts of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions, he advanced swiftly toward the battle.
Then, his army was shattered by the forces of the monkeys with their multitudes of various weapons;
it fled in all directions, while the leaders of the monkeys then swiftly began to crush the night-stalkers.
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Vṛṣaṇa, and Gandhamāda were born from Dhanada;
these five heroic Maruts, beginning with Prāṇa, along with that boastful Lord of Wealth, he [Rāvaṇa] struck down instantly with six arrows of unerring velocity. (8.72)
Then Aṇsu’s two sons, together with Jāmbavat, struck him with three excellent mountain peaks.

Having quickly shattered those mountains with his arrows, the ten-faced one then discharged other arrows at them; as each one was struck down by these, the son of Śakra’s son then rushed toward him. (8.73–8.74)
Taking up a rock as it was falling upon him, the Rākṣasa pierced it in the heart with an arrow;

struck firmly, he too fell to the surface of the earth. Then the son of Ravi (Sugrīva) rushed toward him, and the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), having shattered that very tree held in his hand with arrows into fragments—
He released an arrow at his neck; struck violently, he too fell to the ground.
Then Hanumān, raising his own arm high—resembling the coils of the king of serpents—struck the lord of the Rākṣasas in the chest. Vomiting blood from his mouths, he fell down. (8.76–8.77)
Having regained consciousness, he praised the son of the Wind-god, saying, "Indeed, there is no man equal to you;
who else could have brought me to this state? Thus addressed, the son of the Wind-god spoke to him again.
To the remark, "It is very little that you have merely regained your life," Rāvaṇa replied:

"Receive from me as well this uplifted fist-blow," he said, and struck him down. While Rāvaṇa stood there with his limbs somewhat reeling from the blow, thinking, "This is my opportunity," he rushed toward the son of Agni, even though he had been restrained by Māruti with words.
Beholding him rushing toward him, Nīla moved swiftly over his bow, the tops of his banners, his chariot, and even his head; by him, Rāvaṇa was rendered as insignificant as a mere drop of water. 8.81.
Taking up the Agneya weapon, the lord of the night-rangers quickly released it at Nīla.
He fell to the ground by that [arrow], yet the fire did not consume him, because he was of self-existent nature (*svatanu*).
Then Rāvaṇa went toward Rāghava himself, and Lakṣmaṇa quickly warded him off.
Those two, preeminent among archers, struck each other with arrows capable of rending body armor.

Thoroughly restrained by him, Rāvaṇa, overcome with intense rage, quickly drew back a fierce and unerring arrow given by Svayambhū and released it at the center of Lakṣmaṇa’s forehead. Struck violently by that shaft, Lakṣmaṇa fainted, and Daśānana too leaped down from his chariot.

Rushing forward in an instant and seizing him by force with his own arms, he desired to carry him away. Having regained consciousness, though utterly overwhelmed, Lakṣmaṇa remembered his own true form as a portion of Hari; and Rāvaṇa was not able to move even that which remained joined with the body of Hari.

When Rāvaṇa seized him with all his arms by force and dragged him along with Vīra, the earth, together with Meru, Mandara, and the oceans, trembled; yet Lakṣmaṇa did not move at all. Alas, upon a single head of this thousand-headed one, [the world] including the seven nether regions, the lords of mountains, and the oceans, [remained unmoved]. 8.87.
"Indeed, this entire earth is as small as a mustard seed; who indeed could forcibly carry it away?
(8.88) While the Lord of the Night-rangers was thus dragging the younger brother of Rāma with great haste, Hanumān—the supreme body of the Lord of all living beings—leapt up before him. (8.89)
Wringing his fist, which was like a thunderbolt, he struck Rāvaṇa with it in fury;
stretching out his arms and vomiting warm blood from all his mouths, the demon fell down as if dead.
Having struck down the lord of the Rākṣasas, that son of the Wind-god took the son of Sumitrā by the hand as he lay upon the stage.
That monkey, indeed capable of rescuing the son of Sumitrā, went to the presence of the one named Rāma. 8.91.
With his fatigue dispelled by the touch of Rāma, he rose up when the arrow had been extracted by him;
he shone like the full moon released from the mouth of Rāhu, radiant with its blossoming rays. 8.92.

Then Janārdana, seizing his bow along with an arrow which shone like the remnants of his own enjoyment, spoke again to the lord of the night-rangers who had regained consciousness: "Prepare yourself, Rāvaṇa!
Having mounted his chariot once more, Rāvaṇa, equipped with his bow and arrows, quickly [rushed] toward Rāma.
Having approached from all directions, that master of supreme weapons created a darkness of arrows.
"While this lord of night-stalkers remains stationed on his chariot, my husband will not remain upon the surface of the earth," thinking thus,
the son of the Wind-god placed Rāma upon his shoulder and went toward the Rākṣasa.

Laughing, Rāma struck down his horses and charioteer, cut the banner and chariot into pieces as small as sesame seeds, and having sliced through his bows, sword, all his weapons, and parasol, he severed his head. Seeing him bewildered as to what should be done, Rāma spoke to him again: "Go quickly home! (8.96).
"Having enjoyed all pleasures and quickly gratified your kinsmen, return again to die," he was thus addressed;
with his face cast downward, he went home and deliberated on the matter with his own ministers.
Then, with those who remained after the slaughter, he swiftly resolved to awaken Kumbhakarṇa. (8.97–8.98)

With many tens of thousands of night-stalkers armed with mountain peaks, swords, and axes, who had somehow approached after being struck by the force of his breath, he somehow made himself understood;
and he made me, who resembled a mountain, his food, along with lakes of blood as his drink. 8.99.

Having summoned him with the utmost respect as he was fully satisfied, the lord of the night-rangers called out from the surface of the assembly hall: "I have been defeated today while you still live; for I have been vanquished in battle by a man named Rāma. Grant me satisfaction by slaying him."
Thus addressed, having heard the entire reason, the hero rebuked his elder brother alone:
"Alas! You have today engaged in hostility with Rāghava, whose prowess is unfailing.
Hostility with those who are powerful is praised by us; yet he is considered by me to be exceedingly powerful. (8.102)
Thus addressed, Rāvaṇa said: "Even though I am ill-behaved, I am indeed protected by you; otherwise, how could I be?
Kings sometimes act with transgression when they observe their kinsmen to be superior in strength.
Having been spoken to in this manner by his elder brother, Kumbhakarṇa set out for the battle.
When he, whose weapon was the excellent spear, advanced five *yojanas* beyond the wall to the battlefield,
all the heroic monkeys fled in fear, even leaping over the bridge.
There were Śatabali and Panasa, Vasu and Aṃśumat, the two foremost among the hosts of Maruts, as well as Śveta and Sampāti.

Then that powerful Kumbhakarṇa, the foremost of night-stalkers, cast those excellent ones—Nirṛtitanu, Ugra, Durmukha, and Kesari—into his mouth. Furthermore, he crushed Jayanta along with Kumuda with his hand;
then, with a single blow of his fist, he struck down Nala, Gaja, and the other four, as well as Nīla who was like a great mountain with trees for hands. (8.106–107)
Then Aṅgada, Jāmbavān, and the son of the Wind-god, together with the monkeys,
struck down the night-stalker with trees and mountain peaks;
those Rākṣasas were ground to powder against the body of the night-stalker.
No pain whatsoever arose in that mighty-armed hero.
Then the son of the Sun, seizing another great mountain, hurled it at the Rākṣasa; having seized it, he struck him with it.
Then the son of the Sun fell [upon him] and struck Aṅgada in rage;
he [in turn] struck Jāmbavān. Struck by those palms, both of them fell down. Then that powerful Rākṣasa, seizing the son of the Sun, departed.
And the son of the Wind-god followed him, as minute as a fly, thinking:
"When he oppresses him, then I shall liberate him;
it would indeed be better if he could liberate himself. (8.112–113)
Thus the night-stalker followed after the son of the Wind-god;
and, having been honored by all his kinsmen, he entered the city.
As this best of night-stalkers was showered from all sides with garlands of cool water, the lord of monkeys was likewise sprinkled by him.
Free from all fatigue of battle, he deceived that foremost of night-stalkers and gave him his nose;
then, having severed both his ears with his hands and his nose with his teeth, that Lord of Monkeys quickly leapt up. (8.115–116)
With that very [trident], the Rākṣasa struck him; he crushed him even as he fell to the ground.
Emerging from the space between his fingers, that Rākṣasa struck him again with the trident.
Seeing the infallible trident falling upon the son of the Sun, the son of the Wind-god [intervened].
Quickly seizing his knees and placing them upon [the demon's chest], he broke him and roared loudly.
Then, turning toward him, that Rākṣasa struck the son of Vāyu on the breast with his fist.
Struck by him, Hanumān let out a roar; disregarding that blow, he seized him. (8.118–119)
Struck violently on the chest with that [palm] by Hanumān in his rage, the Rākṣasa fell into a swoon;
then, quickly regaining consciousness, he went to where the hero of the Raghus was.
Then Hanumān reflected: "Indeed, he can be slain by me alone in battle."
Nevertheless, I do not kill him, for I am firmly desiring to proclaim the glory of Rāma. By slaying this one who cannot be killed by others, Rāma himself would acquire fame;
moreover, a boon was previously granted to the two gatekeepers by Janārdana himself. (8.121–122)
"You two shall be slain by me alone during three births once your prowess has fully developed," so it was said by Keśava.
"Even if he were to show me favor by slaying him, that would not be right for me," he reflected;
and having thus considered, he went together with the lord of monkeys to where the heroic monkey leaders were.
Devouring all the monkeys, that Kumbhakarṇa approached Rāma.

(8.124) Those heroic monkey leaders who were devoured by him all emerged from his body through its orifices and even through the pores of his skin; some then climbed upon him as if he were a mountain. (8.125)
Having quickly shaken them off like a great elephant, he went alone toward Rāma for the sake of battle;
devouring his own kin and others on all sides, intoxicated, sniffing about, and drinking blood.
Lakṣmaṇa warded him off with a torrential shower of arrows, yet the latter paid no heed to him.
The mountain-dweller went toward Rāma and quickly challenged him to battle.

Then, taking up his most formidable bow and arrows whose speed was like that of thunderbolts, the Lord Rāghava discharged them into the night-stalker, just as he had done with those previously slain. (8.127–128)

The Rākṣasa did not fall by the mere force with which he struck Khara and the others; rather, laughing and displaying but a fraction of his own power, he discharged excellent arrows. With two of them he cut off his arms, and likewise his two feet with two more.
Then another, having severed his head, cast it into the waters of the ocean. When the body of that night-stalker, which resembled a great mountain, fell, the sea swelled;
and all the gods, praising the foremost of the Raghus with joy, rained flowers upon his head.
Kumbhakarṇa grew to three hundred thousand yojanas; he then contracted his body in order to dwell within Laṅkā himself. But when he returned to his natural state while dying, he grew once more.
When he fell into it, the ocean then swelled even more.

(8.133) Then those other night-stalkers who had been slain on all sides by the heroic monkeys fled swiftly, leaving only those who survived the slaughter; having approached Rāvaṇa, they reported the death of their brother. (8.134)
Tormented by suffering, he fell down unconscious and became despondent regarding his own life.
To him spoke the son of the enemy of the Lord of the Thirty-three: "Employ me without delay for the slaying of the enemy!
Long ago the Lord of the Thirty-three was captured by me; why do you despair because of a prince of men? (8.135)
Having spoken thus, he offered oblations into the fire, worshipped Śiva, and ascended his chariot.
(8.136) Taking up his bow and arrows, he mounted the chariot and rose into the sky, departing beyond sight.
By the power of Śiva’s boon, he bound all the hosts of monkey heroes with the dust raised by his elephants. (8.137)
Formerly, when Viṣṇu commanded all the gods for his incarnation, Garuḍa said to Vṛṣākapi: "At that very time, my service must also be employed by you.
Viṣṇu said to him: "Do not undergo birth upon the earth; otherwise, I shall not accept your service."
In this matter, you must act so that there may be glory and righteousness, and that you yourself may be one who has fulfilled your duty.
(8.139) For when the son of Rāvaṇa binds all the monkeys along with Lakṣmaṇa with the boon of the serpent-king’s dust, you yourself must then go and liberate them all. (8.140)
"Though I am capable, as is Lakṣmaṇa and likewise Hanumān, we do not release him;
for the sake of your pleasure, this very Garuḍa has been made your instrument—do as he says.
For it was previously stated by himself that therefore Rāma would not release anyone.
Neither Lakṣmaṇa nor the son of the Wind knew that secret of the gods.
(8.142) Then, having quickly bound the monkeys along with Lakṣmaṇa, the Rākṣasa went into the presence of his father.
That lord of the flesh-eaters rejoiced and praised his son for having accomplished his task. (8.143)
Then that king of birds, remembering the command of Hari, arrived here with great haste;
by the mere touch of the wind from his wings, their serpent-bond was completely destroyed.
Having bowed to Rāma, the supreme self and deity, he departed, adorned with beautiful garlands, ornaments, and ointments.
And the heroic monkeys, seizing trees and rocks, roared with great strength and joy.

Hearing the clamor of the monkey lords, Rāvaṇa, along with his son, was again struck with fear; thinking, "Has he escaped from that bondage? What must be done here? he remained there reflecting. (8.145–146)
Having offered oblations once more, he mounted that very same chariot and vanished from sight;
and by virtue of the boon of Umā’s Lord as well as the Lotus-born One, he incessantly rained down great weapons.
Furthermore, oppressed by his missiles, the monkeys along with Lakṣmaṇa fell to the earth.
For no weapons ever touch the body of the Wind-god, whose power is boundless.
(8.148) Desiring to learn the news within the city, Vibhīṣaṇa, having gone ahead, then arrived;
he saw all the monkeys fallen, but the son of the Wind alone remained undisturbed. (8.149)
Taking him up, he went to the son of the Creator (Brahmā), who was unconscious; having revived him by sprinkling water, he said, "Are you alive? and he, with a faint voice, replied, "Yes.
He spoke again: "Is Hanumān alive? For we are all indeed alive while he lives."
When it was said, "He being slain, they are all indeed slain," Hanumān, the son of the Wind, replied, "I am here. Having been addressed thus, Jāmbavān immediately spoke to Hanumān:
"That mountain situated near Meru which is named Gandhamādana—"
Therefore, you must bring down from that mountain the four medicinal herbs:
Mṛtasañjīvanī as the foremost, then Sandhānakaraṇī, Savarṇakaraṇī, and Viśalyakaraṇī. (8.152–153)
Thus addressed, he reached Gandhamādana in an instant;
moving through the air, he arrived like an arrow released by Rāma.
Then, the son of the Wind-god, perceiving that the medicinal herbs had vanished, [acted accordingly].
In his wrath, he uprooted a mountain that was a hundred *yojanas* in circumference.
Having torn out that mountain and whirled it around with his hand, the son of Baladeva leapt into the sky with terrible speed, just as Hari, the wielder of the discus, did during his three strides.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, he reached the place where the foremost of monkeys had been struck down;
there, by the touch of the mountain wind, all the leaders of the monkey hosts rose up in an instant.
Then the best of the Raghus, his younger brother, and the others honored Māruti of formidable prowess.
And a shower of flowers, released by the joyful and excellent gods, fell upon his head.

(8.158) Praised by the best of gods, gandharvas, and great seers, and embraced by the hand of Rāma, he brought that mountain, which rose a hundred yojanas high, down once more; yet he remained standing right there. (8.159)
Impelled by the force of the wind as before, he became even more closely joined with it without interruption;
and once again, all those [demons] with trees and mountains in their hands rose up for battle, roaring loudly.
Seeing those monkeys risen once more, a great fear entered the conqueror of Śakra.
Having worshipped the Fire-god as before, he likewise vanished from sight;
then, by means of the boons of Śiva and the Lord of Mountains, he bound those monkeys again with great weapons.
Thereafter, following Rāma’s intent, Lakṣmaṇa pursued his former weapon once more.
"By the command of your father, I shall slay with the Pitāmaha-weapon the evil-minded Śakrajit along with his kinsmen," he said.
When this was spoken by him, Rāghava replied: "You ought not to release [the weapon] against one who is invisible out of fear.
If you are unable to endure this weapon, then I shall [slay him] with a mere arrow."
"Even if he is invisible, I shall slay him whether he be in the subterranean realm (rasātala) or even in the world of truth (satyaloka).
Having thus spoken to demonstrate his own power to the lord of monkeys and Hanumān,
Rāma— whose might is boundless— honored that weapon and then took up the arrow.

Thinking, "I have been seen by him," the wicked one, perceiving the fierce strength of his arms and observing the god-like resolve of the prince, fled swiftly, seeking to save his life. (8.166) While the enemy of Indra was fleeing amidst cries of "Alas! Alas!", the best of the Raghus, because he was terrifying to his foes—
Praised by the gods as "Vibhīṣaṇa," he discharged the weapon of discernment (*vijñāna-astra*) among his own troops.
Indeed, at that moment, the weapon of the night-stalkers vanished through the power of Rāma’s weapon, while the monkeys roared;
seizing lofty, massive mountains, they stood up and loudly extolled the hero of the Raghus.
Praised by the gods who rained down flowers, he of infinite prowess stood with bow in hand;
then the son of Rāvaṇa, having reached Nikumbhilā once more, offered oblations into the fire.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa said to the Lord, the best of the Raghus: "Employ him this very day for the slaying of that evil-minded one."
"Having performed the worship of the fire, he is not to be slain; such is the renowned boon granted him by the Creator.
Indeed, Rāma did not desire his death, for that man had fled and sought refuge with him.
Furthermore, this one who has abandoned his courage and fights with deceit is not worthy of death by me," so said the Lord. (8.170–171)
Janārdana commanded his younger brother; and that high-souled one, together with Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa, and all the leaders of the monkeys, set out for the sake of his destruction.
As he was offering oblations, he created an obstacle through the monkeys; then, with a desire to fight, [Rāvaṇa] mounted his chariot.

Standing firm with bow and arrow in hand, he rushed toward Lakṣmaṇa, roaring aloud. Both of them, the most excellent among those skilled in weapons, struck each other with arrows capable of ending lives;
they rendered all the cardinal and intermediate directions completely obscured by their supreme shafts through the power of their training and mastery of missiles.

Having warded off the enemy’s missiles with his own superior weapons, Lakṣmaṇa swiftly struck off the head of his foe—blazing with its swinging earrings—with an arrow; then he was showered with flowers by the gods. When this one had been felled, the monkeys slaughtered the night-stalkers by the many millions.
Those who remained after the slaughter reported to the Ten-faced One that his son had attained a death worthy of his valor.
Having heard that unpleasant news of such terrible form, he sighed deeply and lamented in his grief;
yet, having resolved upon his purpose, he once again steadied his mind, determined that he too would die.
Facing death, Rāvaṇa quickly prepared for the work of battle; in that very interval, he ordered a formidable army:
thirty-six thousand akṣauhiṇīs, like a great flood. 8.178.
"Quickly prepare Rāma by exerting yourselves," Rāvaṇa commanded.

8.179 Taking up various kinds of missiles and weapons, that army—which was invincible due to a boon from the Self-born Creator and resembled the ocean churned at the time of the end of an eon—marched with the greatest speed toward the monkeys. 8.180

Seeing that immeasurable and most terrible force approaching, like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, the monkey heroes, their minds agitated and dejected with fear, fled in every direction. For a boon had been granted to him long ago by the Self-Existent One: the power to dwell upon even a small portion of the earth’s surface.
And because of his invincibility, even the monkeys born with the sun were unable even to look at him.
Then Rāma, seizing his bow and arrows, slaughtered them on all sides with floods of shafts;
appearing everywhere in all directions and intermediate points, he struck down everyone in every way.
In an instant, having struck down all [the enemies], Rāghava was honored by the leaders of the monkeys;
the Lord was joyfully extolled by the best of all the gods, who showered him with profuse rains of excellent flowers.
Then the lord of all the night-stalkers arrived, surrounded by the remnants of his army that had survived the slaughter.
Mounting the Puṣpaka chariot in haste, Virūpanetra— exalted by his great weapons— set out for the destruction of bodies.
Then Yūpanetra, as well as Mahāpārśva and Mahodara,
along with their ministers, followed him as he went forth to battle, placing death at the forefront.
Then his armies struck back with force from all sides with showers of mountain rocks;
beholding them, the heroic Mahodara rushed forward with speed in a rage.
Seeing him approaching with such a massive body, they cried out, "This is Kumbhakarṇa! 8.187.
The hosts of monkey heroes fled; then the son of Vālin quickly approached them.
Saying, "Stay! that hero leaped forward before Mahodara, shouting, "This is a mere intimidation; do not go away! (8.188–189).

Then, as Mahodara was discharging arrows, Vāli’s son seized his head, brought it down to the ground, and crushed it with his feet; Mahodara became lifeless, pulverized by the son of Vāli. Then Mahāpārśva approached, raining down upon him torrents of arrowy water.
Having violently snatched away the bow from his hand, Aṅgada seized his sword;

8.191 Seizing him by the hair and throwing him to the ground, he cut open the minister of the lord of the night-rangers from the left side right up to the sacred thread, whereupon he was split in two and died. 8.192
Then Virūpanetra and Yūpanetra, with weapons raised, rushed toward him;
just as two clouds in the sky shroud the sun, so did they cover him with showers of arrows.
Bound by them within that cage of arrows, the hero was unable even to stir there.
Harīśvara, having uprooted a mountain of immense size, hurled it at the bodies of the two;
both of them were crushed in battle by that [mountain] driven by the thighs of the son of Ravi.
Then the lord of the night-rangers pierced the son of Surya in the chest with an arrow, and he too fell to the earth. (8.194–195)

Then, having overwhelmed all the monkey heroes with his arrows, the powerful Ten-faced one advanced toward Rāma; at that moment, he obstructed Rāma’s younger brother with a torrent of shafts. Then the Ten-faced one [took up] the bow given by the Lotus-born [Brahmā], which was like the staff of Death.
Having seized it from me at the time of our wedding, he grasped his spear and hurled it at Lakṣmaṇa.
By that weapon, the hero’s chest was deeply torn open, and he fell to the ground, utterly unconscious.
The son of the Wind-god swiftly hurled a mountain of immense size at the breast of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Deeply pained by that [weapon], the Ten-faced one vomited a flood of blood from his mouths;
meanwhile, having seized Lakṣmaṇa, he departed with the spear toward the presence of Rāma.
Then Rāghava extracted that [spear] and restored his life-breath to his son, the best of men.
Then the Lord, in order to bring back the excellent herbs, quickly brought that mountain back once more.
By the mere scent of it, Saumitri rose up as before, endowed with his vast strength as he had been previously.
And that Lord Rāghava, an ocean of countless virtues, smiling, embraced the son of the Wind-god and praised him.
Remaining in Laṅkā, that son of the Wind-god hurled that excellent mountain to a distance of half a hundred thousand yojanas, to where he had previously been stationed;
by the force of his arms, it returned and joined back together exactly as it was before.
Even those monkeys who were dead were restored to life by the scent of that [herb].
By Rāma’s command alone, the monkeys threw the *rakṣasas* into the ocean;
though they were not brought back to life, those monkeys became free from disease.

By the power of the medicinal herbs, all the monkeys became capable of regenerating severed limbs, free from arrows, and restored to their former appearance. Then Rāvaṇa, traveling in his celestial chariot, approached the Lord, the Supreme Person, with a multitude of weapons.

As he was raining down [gifts], Rāma, having taken up his bow, advanced toward that protector of the Raghu lineage. 8.206 Honoring the descendant of Raghu, the primordial being, Purandara presented him with a chariot;
the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa quickly ascended it, along with its weapons, as it was held by Mātali. 8.207

80. Having ascended that excellent chariot, the sole Lord of the world set out for the sake of the world's security against the Lord of the night-rangers; he advanced like the rising sun against the darkness that swallows these entire worlds without exception. Seeing him approaching, the Lord of the world of night-rangers then discharged weapons along with missiles at Rāma.
Rāma, having struck down those [heads] with his own great weapons, simultaneously lopped off his ten excellent arms.
Seeing those severed arms rise up once again, he pierced the heart of Śatadhṛti with an arrow resembling a thunderbolt.
With his heart shattered, vomiting blood, he fell swiftly from his great celestial chariot.
When he, the supreme adversary of the three worlds, had been slain, Brahmā, accompanied by Śiva and the world-protectors,

approached and bowed his head at the pair of feet of Rāma, the sole lord of the universe, filled with devotion. Then the Grandfather of the world, with palms joined in reverence, praised him, the Father who delights in all virtues.
Victory, victory to you, O Unconquered One, Creator of the World! We bow down to you, the protector of those who have sought refuge.

(8.212) You alone are the Lord of this [world], having neither beginning nor end in terms of time or space, O Worthy One. For your qualities are innumerable and infinite, each one individually free from birth and destruction. (8.213)
There is neither the arising nor the suppression of your qualities, whether by another or by yourself.
You alone are the primordial, supreme, and independent one; I and those headed by Śiva are your servants.
Just as the flames belong to fire, the velocities to the wind, the rays to the sun, and the waters to the rivers; 8.214.
They go forth and they return in a continuous stream, as do those beginning with Mada and those headed by Śiva;
and whoever are liberated and whoever are bound, all are forever under your sway, O Lord of Lords.
Though we all constantly speak loftily of the multitude of your qualities, we never reach their end. (8.215–216)

"O Lord, for one such as you, whose qualities are of this nature, the slaying of the Rākṣasa and the protection of all the gods—these two tasks, which are indeed impossible for others to accomplish, have nevertheless been performed by you; homage, homage to you!
When this had been said by the Lotus-born One, the wielder of the trident summoned Rāghava to battle.
"O Rākṣasa, disregarding my boon, you have been slain by me; therefore, come to battle!
When this was said, Rāghava replied, "So be it," and quickly grasping his bow, he fixed an arrow.
As it was being drawn, the earth trembled, and even Rudra fell from the shaking of the ground.
81. Then, rising up and freed from his demonic nature, he bowed at [the Buddha’s] feet, saying, "Forgive me, O Lord!
He further said, "I am forever subject to you; be gracious to me and turn your mind toward my realm. 8.220.
Then the gods, headed by Indra, said to him, "We have been protected today by you from that night-stalker."
"In that very way, may you destroy all calamities; we are all yours.
(8.221) Then, having employed a divine artifice, he placed an image of Sītā there within the fire as she arrived.
When she returned once more from Kailāsa, he accepted her as Sītā, who had been offered by the Fire-god. (8.222)
Knowing that Sītā had gone to the abode of the Lord of Mountains, he accepted her as she was offered by the Fire-god;
and having obtained her, Rāma rejoiced, as did the Goddess herself upon finding the Blessed One. Then, after the bringing [of the mountain], those monkeys who were tormented by the arrows of Rāvaṇa—
Then Suṣeṇa, the best of physicians, restored them to life and freed them from their afflictions.

At that time, Rāghava brought back from the abode of Yama all the hosts of gods who had died, and having obtained his father’s permission there where they had gathered, he then desired to depart. 8.224–225.

Accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa and the monkeys, he ascended that Puṣpaka chariot offered by him and quickly went to his own city, Ayodhyā; there, he first stationed Hanumān at the front. Then he beheld Bharata, who had performed the fire-oblation and was desirous of entering the palace of the Lord of the World.
Having prevented Rāma from leaving because he could not see him, Māruti informed him that [the King] had arrived.
Hearing this, overwhelmed with great joy, he— accompanied by the citizens, his mother, and Śatrughna—
approached Rāghava and bowed down, his face and eyes clouded with tears.

Having raised him up, the Lord of the Raghus embraced Śatrughna with affection; he likewise greeted the others according to their seniority. Having entered the city, he was consecrated by the sages in the sovereignty of the empire.
Having honored them all as was appropriate, the Lord said this:

"By all of you, having performed good deeds with my body, mind, and speech, this much alone is the entire duty of the virtuous: that which consists of the worship of me through body, speech, and mind. (8.230–231)

Because he grants liberation, let there be for me, and likewise for you all, a state of being requited by Hanumān; yet for Hanumān, who is naturally devoted to me, there can be no requital for my disinterested [devotion]. [In those] perfected in knowledge through devotion to me, elevated by unconditioned power, and possessed of stability and fortitude— 8.232 —

In natural disposition, excellence, splendor, wisdom, self-restraint, and tranquility, there is no one equal to him; even Śeṣa, Rudra, and Suparṇa are not equal to a thousandth part of his vast qualities. Therefore, out of joy, I shall enjoy this supreme state together with him alone. 8.233.

Formerly, this Ten-necked one conquered the world by virtue of a boon from the Lotus-born [Brahmā], yet no one ever defeated him; neither did the son of Puruhūta [Indra] because he was in the form of a monkey, nor did Arjuna defeat him because of a boon from Viṣṇu. A boon had not been granted by the Creator against humans or monkeys, and for that reason, he was conquered in battle by Vālin.
Having surpassed the boon-granting power of the Lotus-born One, I conquered the Rākṣasa at the front of the battle as he was challenging me for a wager.
Standing at Bali’s gate, I first granted him a boon;
then, by means of that [boon], I struck down the Rākṣasa with my big toe over ten thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, as Rāvaṇa challenged me again to battle, I struck down that lone foe with a single fist.
I am possessed of great power, appearing in the form known as Kapila, and my son is Pavana, who assumes three crores of forms.
"The two of us shall be victorious by our own strength"—it was thus that Śiva granted me boons, yet he defeated him in this manner.
Knowing this world to be difficult to conquer, Hara chose me, thinking, "I shall conquer that Ten-faced one.
Therefore, by my very nature, both I and Vāyu are victors; that Vāyu is none other than Hanumān.
Indeed, for his sake, even those led by Śiva and Indra were formerly reduced to pieces like wood by Vāyu.

Therefore, by my command, let Hanumān attain the status of the Creator (Brahmā) and proceed, performing the work of creation, protection, and so forth, as well as the liberation of the world at all times; being himself liberated, let him act for the happiness of those who are liberated. (8.240) And whatever enjoyments and whatever multitudes of karmas exist here for me, they are beginningless and endless.

"By my command, all those things exist in the abode of the Creator; that is what is called 'shared enjoyment' (sahabhogana). O Hanumān, such a shared meal as this has been granted to you by me forever.
Having been addressed thus, Hanumān, bowing with steady devotion, spoke these words to him. 8.242.
O Lord, what indeed is difficult for those who partake of Your lotus feet to obtain among the four aims of human life in this world?
Nevertheless, O Infinite One, I choose nothing other than service to Your lotus feet.
You alone are manifest as the supreme independent one; You alone are manifest as the one possessing vast power over all.

You alone are an ocean of countless virtues, which all beings, including Lakṣmī and Brahmā, having gathered together and speaking constantly for infinite time, would never fully exhaust in describing. For you are the embodiment of perfect bliss and knowledge, eternally and utterly pure. (8.244–245)

He who is always a servant of Your stories, whose constant delight is in You, and whose devotion to You is unwavering and singular—he, while living, is none other than Yourself; may his life be for me more precious than all else. O Lord, may my devotion to You increase fully at every moment, forever free from decline.
"Your favor toward me is likewise free from any ulterior motive; that is my every desire.
Thus addressed, he gave him those two [boons] and, in order to establish him in all auspicious states, embraced him with a moistened heart and honored all the people as was appropriate. (8.247–248)

Thus ends [the section] titled "The Bestowal of Śrī Rāma’s Mercy upon Hanumān" within the *Śrī Rāmacarita* from the *Śrī Mahābhārata Tātparya Nirṇaya*, composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The Eighth Chapter:
lxxxiv. (Rāma’s Entry into His Own Abode).
Now begins the Ninth Chapter.
Oṃ! Then the Blessed One, having attained his kingdom, said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Become a king quickly.
Thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa said to his elder brother: "I choose nothing other than your lotus feet;
you ought not to employ me, whose sole longing is for service at your feet, to any other task. (9.1)
"There is no favor like this anywhere; grant that very thing to me forever.

Having been addressed thus, the Lord Rāghava gave him that very boon, embraced him firmly, and having installed Bharata in the position of crown prince, he protected all the worlds together with their righteous duties. 9.2–9.3.
While he ruled as lord, the earth became equal to the world of Viriñca in its excellence of qualities;
all people became devoted to Viṣṇu, and there was no decline in dharma for anyone. All beings rose up with every virtue, each according to their own fitness and status, whether high or low.
All were freed from every disease and the like, possessed of a lifespan of a thousand years, and exalted by wealth.
All were free from old age, endowed with constant strength, and always provided with the accomplishment of their desires.
They were forever devoid of all defects, all were beautiful in form, and always engaged in great festivities. (9.5–9.6)
Everyone always worships Viṣṇu alone with their mind, speech, and body, and never anyone else;
for the earth is filled with all kinds of jewels, possesses grain as desired, and has cows yielding abundant milk.
(9.7) Furthermore, all fragrances there are eternally most heart-pleasing, and the tastes are truly captivating.
All sounds were captivating to the ear, and all touches were pleasing to the sense of touch. (9.8) No one experienced suffering in any way, nor was anyone ever destitute of wealth.
No one was unrighteous in character, nor was anyone childless, nor did anyone have wicked children, nor was anyone an ill-fated husband. (9.9)
There were no widows among the women, nor did any men become bereft of their spouses;
there was no union with the undesired for anyone, nor the loss of what was desired, nor premature death.
(9.10) All [the people] possessed whatever garlands, ornaments, ointments, drinks, seats, and garments they wished for.
