While King Janārdana, the lord of the worlds, ruled with preeminent righteousness, [all things flourished]. 9.11 With the soles of his feet rubbed by the crest-jewels of Brahmā, Rudra, the Maruts, the Aśvins, the Sun, and other gods, the Lord of Ramā (Rameśa) takes his delight; his feet are constantly worshipped by gods, humans, and monkeys alike. 9.12

The Fortune of that Lord of All, whose nature is eternally inseparable and supremely exalted, known by the name Sītā and ever following him from time immemorial—she who is the primordial source of beauty, grace, and auspicious marks—quickened the Lord of the Gods with her voice.
With her, that Supreme One, whose very nature bears the weight of eternal and ever-increasing joy, took delight even more than he did in his own voice. (9.13)

In the deep nights brilliantly illuminated by the full moon, and in the Aśoka groves shining with abundant blossoms, hosts of Gandharvas and Cāraṇas with beautiful voices, together with the Apsarases, sing to him with devoted hearts.
Groups of sages, joined by the lords of the gods, offer praise to him; and kings, ever vigilant, constantly follow after him.

Thus, for thirteen thousand years, he—having conquered his enemies, possessing unfailing valor, like the moon bestowing joy, the lord of Indirā, and an immeasurable ocean of intense bliss—protected the earth.
And upon the queen, he begot two twin sons, Kuśa and Lava, who were powerful, rich in virtues, and honored by Indra and Agni. 9.16.

Having caused Lavaṇa to be consumed by fierce arrows at the hands of Śatrughna, he of formidable valor established the city of Madhurā. He likewise slew thirty million Asuras born as Gandharvas, while Bharata remained devoted to the dharma of the virtuous;
and instructing them in righteousness, he performed his own sacrifices according to the highest rites, wherein Bhava, Aja, and other noble deities served as his officiating priests.
Then the Lord, having slain that Śūdra ascetic, restored to life the son of the Brahmin who had been struck down by the Śūdra’s practice of penance.
Formerly, there was an Asura named Jaṅghana who, by virtue of a boon from the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), [had attained such power].

There was a Śūdra of a thousand-year lifespan who, desiring the destruction of the world, performed austerities with evil intent, seeking the state of Maheśvara. Because he was incapable of being slain by anyone else, Puruṣottama killed him. 9.20.
Likewise, Rāghava obtained from Agastya a garland given by Śveta;
Śveta, the king who performed sacrifices without food, having offered his own flesh to ward off hunger as instructed by Dhātṛ, gave the garland for the sake of Rāma.
This king would not give it directly to Rāma;
[9.22] / "It was not offered directly to the descendant of Raghu as a gift yielding merely the cessation of hunger;
desiring only the cessation of hunger, he asks me about it. [9.23]
"Therefore, O Rāma, you should give it to Śveta through an intermediary," the Lord [Viṣṇu] said;

thinking thus, Brahmā commanded the garland to be given to the jar-born [Agastya]. "This devotee of mine, the jar-born [Agastya], has offered it into the sprout-like hand of Agastya. 9.24. This one is my devotee, born from a jar.
Having understood this, Janārdana accepted [the boon]; praised by him, he returned to the city.

(9.25) Now, in former times, certain Asura-suras known as the Surāṇakas—whose prowess was widely renowned—undertook a very great ascetic practice; and having beheld the Lord born from the lotus, they spoke: (9.26)
"O Lord of noble virtues, even those who have committed many sins shall surely attain liberation.
Having heard this, the unborn Lord, his face beaming with a smile, spoke:
"As long as you do not separate me, the Lord of Ramā, from Ramā, that ocean of excellent qualities..."
"Even a high evil deed might not become an obstacle to the path of liberation," he said.

Having understood what was thus spoken, those asuras, eager to go quickly to liberation and desiring the accumulation of the means for its attainment, came to reside upon the earth while Hari ruled the entire world. (9.28–9.29)

The daughter of the King of Mithilā caused those who were deprived of the fitness for the path to liberation due to the accumulation of faults committed since beginningless time to deviate from their own path by means of her illusory power through her own body.
For it was indeed by the command of Hari that the sons of Diti, deluded by his illusory power, began to revile [the gods].
"Rāghava has been carried off by the night-stalkers; Janakī has been seized again!"—thus [the cry] was heard many times.

Making the word of Brahmā come true as if it were nectar, and casting the Asuras into blinding darkness, he, though always accompanied by Sītā, appeared as if separated from her before the eyes of the ignorant.
Because of him, the Asuras entered into blinding darkness; he, however, summoned the daughter of Mithila to the sacrifice.
There, under the pretext of an oath upon the earth, she remained standing, having removed the path of vision from men.
For Viṣṇu himself created Brahmā as the preceptor of the world.
Therefore, he never makes that speech false among the virtuous (9.34).
He would not make his word false even toward the wicked regarding matters pertaining to the next world;
however, in this world, Janārdana sometimes strikes down even among the asuras (9.35).
By his command, the wind sometimes blows in order to announce his own superiority;
for the Lord truly makes known his own status as Brahmā.
No one else can transgress his boons or even his curses. (9.36)
But toward those who are unworthy, Rudra and the others utter false speech;
yet even toward the worthy, they may occasionally speak the truth only in part.
However, the word of Viṣṇu never becomes false for anyone at any time. (9.37)
For this very purpose, the descent of Viṣṇu occurs at all times.
Having entered the earth, that goddess, in accordance with worldly perception,
took delight with Rāma, never separated from him, just as radiance is never separated from the sun.
Thus, with his tender feet served by Rāmā, he again performed sacrifices for his own sake;
having attained all his desires through the horse-sacrifice and other rites, the charming king took delight in instructing other monarchs.
(9.40) For Rāma, the daughter of Janaka was visible, but for others, she remained unseen.
After entering the [divine] realms, she rejoiced for seven hundred years.

(9.41) Such deeds of Janārdana during his incarnation as Rāma are beyond calculation; they cannot be performed even in thought by other men, nor indeed by the gods headed by Brahmā, Īśa, Śeṣa, and Puruhūta. (9.42)

While he was thus ruling this earth, which was equal to the world of the Lotus-born, the gods, beholding his virtues and longing for the preeminence of their own abode, praised him to the Lotus-born One. Having taken leave of him, the Lord, together with them, desired to depart for his own residence and gave the command.
When the best of the Raghus made his request for Rudra to go to his own world, the powerful Rudra approached him and entreated the Lord.
Having gone into solitude with the leader of the Raghus at the appointed time, Rudra spoke these words to the Creator of the world:
"Indeed, the gods, desiring the excellence of their own abode, together with Brahmā, are petitioning you. (9.44–45)
"O Lord, my son Kamalaprabha has likewise spoken; and though I am but a grandson and unworthy of such honor, those possessed of virtue consider even that worthy.
Therefore, having first bowed to you, I entreat you to go from here to your own abode.
For it was for the sake of accomplishing this task, at the request of the gods, that you manifested your entire true form."

"Since that has indeed been accomplished by you, depart quickly from here to your own abode, bringing joy to the gods. (9.47) Saying "Oṃ," the Blessed One replied. Having heard all of that in secret, another body of Hara then arrived swiftly here, filled with the affliction of evil desires, repeatedly saying, "O Rāma, feed me! I am hungry! (9.48)

Having heard his words, "Neither what is already accomplished nor even what is yet to be achieved shall be given," Rāma then took from his own hand the fourfold food, which was like nectar, produced by the power of his word; and having received it, the sage ate with great satisfaction.
Satisfied, he departed, intending to provoke everyone, thinking, "No one is capable of granting me the boon I have requested."
For that Blessed One alone, and no other, rendered false the promise made by the sage who had vowed thus;
yet, by the boon of that same sage, Kuntī gave birth to him, while Rāma conquered him through his own power in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
When that auspicious manifestation in the form of a sage had departed, the Lord of Ramā said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Go. 9.50–51.
When Rāma was engaged in conversation with Rudra in a secluded place, he then appointed Lakṣmaṇa himself as the gatekeeper, saying the words:
"If anyone should enter here, I shall kill them. (9.52)
Seeing the sage who had arrived in the meantime, Lakṣmaṇa thought:
"Durvāsas’s vow must surely be shattered upon reaching Rāma; otherwise, this muni will certainly bring dishonor upon Rāma. (9.53–9.54)
Thinking, "Even while striking me, Rāghava shows compassion toward me," he then yielded the path to Durvāsas;
for Rāghava himself was desirous of departing for his own world.
Thinking that this vow would serve as the cause [for his departure], he resolved, "I shall kill him.
Reflecting that the death of such a close kinsman was indeed an abandonment [of dharma], he said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Go to your own world without delay. (9.56–57)
Thus addressed, he departed, meditating upon Rāghava, who cuts through the darkness of the fear of worldly existence; endowed with a thousand lotus-like faces, he attained that state.
Śeṣa became the great serpent, Musalabhṛt (the wielder of the mace) became the one of divine form, and Lāṅgalin (the plow-bearer) [became Balarāma].
He who became the couch for Viṣṇu as he lay upon the ocean attained the state of being a mere seat for him [Rāvaṇa].

Then Rāghava, together with all his people, set his mind on returning to his own palace; and he caused a proclamation to be made: "Whoever desires that imperishable station here, let him come at once. 9.58–9.59.
Having heard that, all those who desired the state of liberation here—down to the grass and even the ants—then arrived at his command;
for by Rāma’s order, even the grass and other such beings gained the power of movement, though those long-bound in saṃsāra did not desire it then.
The Lord established Kuśa in his own kingdom, and together with them, he made Lava the crown prince.
Having installed the son of Vālin in the kingdom of the monkeys, the son of the Sun also returned to the presence of the hero of the Raghus.
Then Rāghava, embracing the son of Vāyu, said:
"I shall always remain within the range of your vision; it shall not be otherwise."
"You must always perform great and most excellent penance;
that alone is very dear to me. For a long time you have performed penance, even though you are as powerful as the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa. (9.63)
"You did not kill my beloved; therefore, live for an eon.
And you shall go wherever you desire—even into the midst of the ocean of milk—possessed of your own body, as well as my magnificent palace or any other. 9.64–9.65.
Endowed with all enjoyments as you desire, your fame being celebrated by the lords of the gods, the singers, and others, rejoice forever before me.
Nothing whatsoever that you wish for shall ever be lacking from anywhere or in any way. 9.66.
"Your word would be false, and you shall become dear to me again and again.
Thus addressed, the son of the Wind-god spoke to the Leader of the Universe:
"O Lord, grant me supreme devotion to Your lotus feet. (9.67–9.68)
I rejoice spontaneously with her who is ever-increasing; may she always be greater than the entire collection of living beings. 9.69.
Homage, homage, homage, homage! I am forever bowed before your state.
"I bow again to your feet, which are exalted by all excellent qualities.
When this was said, the lotus-eyed one replied to him, "So be it," and he departed for his own abode along with the grass and other items.
At that time, even birds, wild animals, grasses, and the like, as well as ants and donkeys, were the most excellent of Asuras; how much more so, then, were men and monkeys?
They were always possessed of the realization of Rāma and always knew the true reality.
From where they had come, they then departed for that abode of Hari.
Surrounded by them, the Lord then proceeded toward the northern direction—
he who possesses the radiance of infinite suns and is an ocean of difficult-to-attain, excellent qualities.
His crown and hair blaze like a thousand solar discs;
his face is as beautiful as immeasurable moons, surrounded by deep blue locks of hair;
his eyes are like crimson lotuses, and his earrings have the luster of brilliant lightning. 9.75
His lower lip was like a beautiful coral vine; he was the essence of the speech of all the Vedas.
His broad neck possessed the radiance of the sun, the Kaustubha gem, and the fire.
He bore the weight of the entire world upon his pair of exceedingly thick and elevated thighs. 9.76–9.77.
Marked by his two well-rounded, long, and thick, shimmering arms, an arrow—
forged from the destruction of the universe— is held in his right hand;
by that very weapon, he himself fashioned it, and Madhu and Kaiṭabha were slain.
With that very arrow, Viṣṇu struck Lakṣmaṇa’s younger brother. With the same arrow by which he slew Madhu’s son, the one called Rasa, he also destroyed the city named Mādhura.
In his hand he held that arrow, the source of all essential power;
with his left arm he held the bow known as Śārṅga. Adorned with noble arms, he wore beautiful armlets and bracelets.
Adorned with a great ring, his lotus-like hand beautifully red,
and possessing a broad chest graced by playful movements, the Lord bore a splendor through his forest-like garland of priceless jewels. 9.82–9.83.
Adorned with ornaments like Bhūtivatsa, he had a slender waist marked by three folds; his garment was radiant with the flashing light of magnificent ornaments upon his midriff.
His thighs were like those of a lordly elephant, and his knee-caps were perfectly rounded. (9.84)
With calves tapering in regular proportion and feet like tender, deep-red sprouts,
Rāghava shone with even greater splendor, possessing the luster of shimmering emeralds.
He was an ocean of countless true happiness, his excellent body the embodiment of all powers.

He whose radiant face shines forth, manifesting from his pair of lotus-eyes and his excellent lotus-mouth the essence of the meaning of all the Vedas; he who illuminates both the interior and exterior of the cosmic egg with his surpassing luster; and he who bestows all desired objects and fearlessness upon supplicants with the pair of his excellent hands.
The God of Gods set forth toward his own abode in the northern direction known as Viśokā.
Hanumān held a parasol dripping with nectar, radiant like ten thousand full moons;
and Sītā herself, having come within the range of all eyes, was there as the sole embodiment of Fortune and Modesty.
Dividing herself in two, she held a fan on both sides—one as white as the full moon and radiant with the splendor of the rising sun;
her entire body was the embodiment of all virtues, adorned with her own ornaments.
Likewise, Bharata, whose body was the Discus itself, held the discus in his right hand.
To his left came the destroyer of enemies, bearing the excellent conch and having the nature of the conch itself;
in front went the hosts of gods led by Brahmā and the Vedas accompanied by the syllable Om; and behind followed the entire world as the descendant of Raghu proceeded toward his own abode. 9.89.
Behind him went the monkeys, descendants of the Sun; to his right were the men, while to his left they hurried along, quickly proclaiming with hymns the deeds of Rāma’s birth.
He was being sung of by Gandharvas and throngs of divine sages, headed by the lotus-born Brahmā.

Constantly praised by all beings with words of noble meaning from the Vedas and with flowers offered with devotion, and gazed upon with curiosity by all creatures with unblinking eyes, he departed for his own abode, attended by his own followers such as Śeṣa and Garuḍa. 9.91.
With the vast extent of his excellent qualities being proclaimed by Brahmā, Rudra, Garuḍa, and Śeṣa,
the Lord slowly ascended into the sky, and they too then assumed divine bodies.
Then Brahmā, having praised Hari, spoke these words to the Lord:

By your command, I have indeed granted a place for Daśaratha; and for his mothers as well, that world shall be before me for ten thousand years from now. Furthermore, even for Kaikeyī, who was unworthy of it, you have ordained a state of true felicity.
"Having given birth to Bharata, she would not otherwise have gone to the hells;
nevertheless, because she committed that which was unseemly toward you under the influence of that possession,
I have cast her, known as Nikṛti (Deceit), into eternal darkness."
Kaikayī, however, has reached unstable worlds that are never at rest;
for she was later devoted to you, and thus it is only fitting.
But Mantharā, the woman of wicked conduct, has been cast into blind darkness.
Even those who reviled you for the sake of Sītā have gone to the great darkness;
and when you have become darkened, O Kṛṣṇa, most of the Rākṣasas as well will go there,
along with their remnants, in the twenty-eighth Kali age.
When four thousand three hundred years have passed since [your departure], O Gāminī,
then for those who have come along with you, desiring solely the nectar of your lotus feet, ordain an exalted station. (9.98–99)
"O Lord, I am Bhava, and Sureśa and the others are your servants;
whatever task must be performed by us here, please command us at once.
Having heard these words spoken by Śatānanda, Rāghava—
With his sprout-like lower lip graced by a deep and beautiful smile, he spoke:
"O Lotus-born One, the status of being the Teacher of the World has been assigned to you by me;
and in accordance with the command of my Guru, the True Goal has also been assigned by me."
"Therefore, by my command, these worlds must indeed be granted by you to them;
for you alone always know what resides within my heart.
Thus addressed by Hari, the lotus-born Brahmā, who understands the inner disposition of others, [replied].

The All-pervading Lord granted unsurpassed worlds to all beings, from ants to blades of grass; because they were established in continuity, these Vaiṣṇava realms are known by the name Sāntānika. Devoid of old age and death, they are free from all suffering.
Released from *saṃsāra*, they dwelt there, possessing constant and superior happiness.
But those gods who had arisen here in human or monkey bodies—all of them, with the exception of Mainda and Vivida, regained their own original forms. (9.105–106)
Due to the possession of the Asuras, however, those two did not follow Rāma;
for although they had previously drunk the nectar of immortality, they did not die at that time.
And being pleased by their ascetic penance, [Brahmā] made them both free from old age and death.

Formerly, during the churning for the nectar of immortality, both of them drank [the poison] out of pride; having insulted the gods, they were overlooked by the gods. When the gods had drunk the nectar and were fighting with the Dānavas, (the two of them [continued to consume it]). 9.108.
They drank that [elixir] which had been placed in their own hands by those [gods] for the sake of protection;
yet, due to that fault, the two of them fell into a powerful demonic state.
After some time, Aṅgada cast off his body and regained his own original form.
Ruling the kingdom together with Kuśa by Rāma’s very command,
and the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, honoring the order of the descendant of Raghu,
served as the general of the Lord of Wealth for an eon and protected the Rākṣasas.
By Rāma’s command, Jāmbavān dwelt upon the surface of the earth,
performing severe penance for her sake in order to bring about the birth of Jāmbavatī;
meanwhile, the foremost of the Raghus, worshipped by the gods, himself resided in the abode of the gods in his own body.
By the second [form], he was honored as the presiding lord of the assembly of Brahmā; then, by another [form], in his own abode;
and by the third form, the deities followed closely behind the Lord as he proceeded toward his own station.
Having reached a place beyond the limits of accessibility, they gazed upon him from a great distance and offered praise.

Brahmā, Marut, Mārutasūnu, Īśa, Śeṣa, Garutmān, Harija, Śakra, Kāma, and the others followed the descendant of Raghu in succession; then, having placed their command upon his head, they departed. All the gods, beginning with Purandara and preceded by Viriñca, went each to their own respective abode.
Then the son of Marut, having reached Badarī, attended upon the very abode of Nārāyaṇa.
9.116 There, joyfully filling his ears with the words of Hari, which are overflowing with all the scriptures, he dwelt happily, always speaking the truth to the best of the gods and the sages. 9.117
By the command of Rāma, he ruled the kingdom among the Kimpuruṣas with one form, and likewise with other forms;
and in various other forms, he dwelt eternally as he desired within the entire abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, singing the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata, and the Pañcarātra, which extend to a hundred crores of verses—
Explaining all the Vedas along with the Brahma-sūtras, he became one overflowing with eternal bliss.
(9.119) Rāma also, together with the son of Pavana (Hanumān), Sītā, and those headed by Lakṣmaṇa, as well as being served by his attendants headed by Garuḍa, dwelt upon the ocean of milk. (9.120)
Sometimes the Lord, having manifested all his incarnations as one, lies upon the King of Serpents;
and sometimes, having arranged them separately by his will, the Lord of Ramā, that ocean of immeasurable and true virtues, rejoices.
Thus [it is known] from all the Purāṇas and from the Pañcarātras.
Having determined the truth from the *Bhārata*, the Vedas, and even the great *Rāmāyaṇa*— by resolving their mutual contradictions through reasoning,
the power of the intellect, and solely by the grace of Viṣṇu. (9.122–9.123)
This true narrative has been recounted by me according to the sequence of many eons;
it is not based on a single text, and therefore no contradiction should be suspected here.
In some places, there is an inversion or reversal intended to cause delusion among the asuras.
Therefore, this definitive conclusion has been established by me based on what is stated in the scriptures. (9.125) And thus, regarding what is yet to be said, no contradiction should be suspected;
for this sequence of higher and lower levels is always equal across all ritual manuals. (9.126)
In some Purāṇas and other texts, there may be an expression involving a transposition of genders;
for example, Kṛṣṇa speaks of Kṛṣṇa [the female]: "The Lord will show you those hundred people, Duryodhana and the others, who have been slain by the arrows of Dhanañjaya. (9.127)

For it is known from many statements that they were slain by Bhīmasena; in detail they are said to have been killed by Bhīma, but in summary they are said to have been struck down by Arjuna. Furthermore, many others are mentioned due to the confusion caused by the transposition of names. (9.128)
In the *Vistara*, it is said that they were slain by Kṛṣṇa and killed by Balabhadra;
furthermore, in some places there may even be a transposition of time,
such as when Bhīma laughed at Suyodhana in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, it is known from many such statements through definitive determination;
however, in cases where there is no such determination, the course previously mentioned for Kṛṣṇa applies.
Furthermore, there are likewise reversals of this kind, as well as movements in the opposite direction and so forth. (9.130)
They are seen in the *Bhārata* and other such works through their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), and they are understood through many statements from the books of definitive conclusions (*nirṇaya*).
Therefore, the definition [of a hero] must indeed rely upon the books of definitive conclusions. (9.131)
This decision has been made by me in accordance with many statements. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasāstra* proclaimed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana:
"He who does not know the three languages and the hundred styles... (9.133).

"One who speaks of the seven divisions, such as the transpositions (*vyatyāsa*), for the sake of the Vedas and so forth, goes to a terrible hell arising from false knowledge. Thus, much has been stated in various places within other scriptures.
"Vyatyāsa, prātilomya, gomūtrī, praghasa, as well as ukṣaṇa, sudhura, and sādhu—these seven varieties are proclaimed. (9.135).
The definitions for these and others are not stated here, as they would lead to an extraneous digression. (67)
67. "Vyatyāsa, Prātilomya, Gomūtrī, Praghasa, as well as Ukṣaṇa, Sudhura, and Sādhu—these seven varieties are proclaimed for the faithful disciple who asks me, and for my son. (9.135.1)
"Speak according to the rules, O dear one, regarding the determination of the meaning through its inversion.
Listen, Nārada, and I shall speak as far as the range of your intellect extends. (9.135.2)
The determination of meaning arises from the contraction of the various divisions such as *vyatyāsa* (transposition) and so forth.
Within these, each individual division is further divided separately in a thousand ways;
[this work provides] their definitions, their meanings, and their illustrative examples. (9.135.3–4)
It has been declared in the Mūlarāmāyaṇa and in the Pañcarātra Āgamas by Hari himself, who is of immeasurable soul, in the form of Vyāsa, at great length:
"All those [scriptures] were proclaimed solely for the purpose of determining the meaning of the infinite Vedas. (9.135.5)
Then, due to the power of the Kali age, mortals became short-lived yet possessed of intelligence;
having seen the Vedas, they divided them for the purpose of making their meaning known, and having composed the treatise on grammar (*lakṣaṇa-śāstra*), they were also instructed therein.

By means of inversion and contraction alone, the determination of the meaning of the doctrines stated by myself shall be achieved through the various subdivisions; yet even those [subdivisions] are not exhaustive for us. Now, having thoroughly churned that [subject matter] and reached a firm conclusion, I shall speak.
"Let the determination of the Purāṇas of Bhārata be made by you;
therein, listen with a one-pointed mind to the divisions and their meanings.
*Vyatyāsa* is declared to be *vyatyaya*; the first of these is *puṃ-vyatyāsa*. (9.135.9)
Just as Keśava spoke to the daughter of Pṛṣata in the forest on the day of the full moon—

consoling her while addressing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with the words, "I shall show you the hundred [of them] dead by Arjuna’s arrows"— this is recorded as an instance of the transposition of genders (*puṃvyatyaya*). (9.135.10–11)

In the *Harivaṃśa*, it is recorded that Hari Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses, sported on the bank of the Jāhnavī; this is considered a reversal of the usual instruction. Likewise, in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, it is stated that Rāma killed [the demons] in the previous Kṛta Yuga.

In "daśakaṇṭhaṃ kathā" and so forth, the transposition of syllables is known as *kḷalika*. Because he is devoted to the act of slaying (*hiṃsā-karma-ratatvāt*), the lion (*kesarī*) is called *hiṃsāra*; this transposition of syllables, as in "siṃha," is known as *akṣara-vyatyaya*. (9.135.13–14)
In some cases, such as "Having slain whom did Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, protect Madhurāpurī? and so forth, a transposition of the narrative is said to occur.
Where the sequence is reversed, that is called *pratiloma* (inverted order). (9.135.15)

The state of being that, its reverse, and their various subdivisions may occur in certain cases. Vidhi and Prāṇa were their two wives; Gurutmat, Śeṣaṇa, and Saṅkara were the six chief queens of Hari, as were Sauparṇī, Vāruṇī, and Umā.
"Indra and Kāma are their two wives, each successively a hundred times superior [to the preceding one].
This is the exposition of the gradation as stated in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*.
In such passages, the resolution of the meaning is achieved through the distinction of reverse order (*prātilomya*). (9.135.18)
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali are the meritorious ages of old;
this determination has been stated in direct order for those beginning with Ādi, and in reverse order [for others].
When a calf clearly drinks the milk from the udder of the cow at the very beginning, [it is the Kṛta age].
Then there would be the emergence of cow-urine for the sake of achieving an abundance of milk;
when the cowherd milks her, at that time no urine exists. Later, when the calf drinks, there occurs once again the emergence of urine. (9.135.20–21)
Thus, in some narratives there may be coherence at the beginning and the end,
while in the middle there is a break in coherence due to the introduction of another narrative;
according to these principles, their determination is made by me.
In such cases, it should be understood that there is a sequential distinction based on the "cow's urine" (gomūtrī) arrangement,
just as in the forest the connection of the narrative is established among the Pāṇḍavas;
yet, setting those aside, in their midst [the story] of King Hariścandra [is told].
Nala; and for this Rāghava as well, [the sequence] proceeds by way of the "cow's urine" pattern (*gomūtrī*).

(9.135.24) Thus, among all the Purāṇas, the narratives are recorded as being varied; and the connection between the beginning and the end is recorded as being by way of the "cow's urine" pattern. (9.135.25)
*Praghasa* is the description of meanings that contradict the purpose of all the scriptures;
such things are sometimes stated in the Purāṇas for the sake of deluding the Asuras.
However, from among such statements, the meaning to be accepted is that which is non-contradictory. (9.135.26)
Seeing his son foolish, a father might say, "Eat poison!
Hearing that, one who acts contrary to its meaning would not do so;
in this way, the noble-minded father is the teacher of the entire world.
Vyāsa has elsewhere described things otherwise— for the benefit of his devotees and kinsmen—
stating that the world is both real and illusory,
devoid of a Lord, without foundation, unknowable, and non-different from the individual souls of Hari. (9.135.28)
From the lower gods, there comes degradation; from the [higher] gods, old age and death.

(9.135.29) There is contact with defects such as birth, the absence of qualities, incompleteness, non-omniscience, ignorance, and the lack of distinction between the insentient and the living soul. (9.135.30)

Whether between two insentient objects, or between two living beings, or even between the insentient and the Lord of All, the world is independent [of them]; likewise, Hari Viṣṇu possesses independence. Furthermore, the soul possesses autonomy, omniscience, and freedom from suffering.

"Viṣṇu’s material body and so forth are merely the reversal of his own incarnations"—in such passages, the meaning should be understood according to its non-contradiction through distinctions such as *praghasa* (devouring/dissolution).
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of one part being authoritative while another part is unauthoritative. (9.135.32)
Because of the distinction between sprinkling [the body] here and there, the object of perception is not anything other [than the mind].
(9.135.33) It is stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa* that Gaṅgā and Pārvatī are both daughters of Himavat and beloved wives of Rudra; therefore, he is called Gaṅgādhara and Umāpati. (9.135.34)
In this matter, the wise have declared that the latter is to be accepted and the former abandoned.
O Bhārata, these five are pure: the leavings of food, the remains of offerings made to Śiva, vomit, a shroud from a corpse, and that which has arisen from the dung of a crow.
In such cases, the wise determine the true meaning through the distinction of the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Where understanding arises by abandoning both the sequential order and its inversion, there alone the meaning accepted by the many is to be grasped from the most excellent distinction. (9.135.36–37)
Form, sound, smell, touch, and likewise taste—
these are specifically the qualities of the five elements beginning with space (*vyoman*).
Thus it is stated in the *Pañcarātra*, as well as the distinctions from the *Sudhura*.
In that regard, the object to be grasped is not according to the manner previously stated, but rather in its proper sequence.

(9.135.39) Where a difference in narrative is mentioned among the excellent discourses due to a difference in the eons (*kalpa*), there both [versions] are indeed to be accepted; no fault whatsoever exists therein. (9.135.40)
In that regard, the determination of reality is to be understood through its various classifications;
this has been stated in truth by Vyāsa in the sixth book of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*:
"Indra, having slain Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ and best of the twice-born..."

Afflicted by the sin of killing a Brahmin, he went to Brahmā for refuge. The Great Four-faced One divided that sin into four parts and cast them down upon the earth, into the waters, into trees, and into women during their seasons, respectively.
Salt soil is defiled on the earth; foam is defiled in waters;
sap from trees and the like is indeed defiled; and a woman is defiled during her menses.
Having been released from the slaughter of his kin, the Lord of Śacī protected heaven once again. (9.135.44)
In the Śrī-Bhaviṣyat-Purāṇa, however, this meaning was set forth as prompted by Vyāsa:
"Then the four-faced one, having divided the slaughter of Vṛtra, cast it into the fire, into the first-born flames, and into the rivers. (9.135.45)

"O best of Brahmins, on the mountain peaks, during the woman's fertile seasons, and so forth—thus has it been proclaimed according to the distinctions of the various *sādhus* and the differences between the *kalpas*. In that regard, both [traditions] must indeed be accepted; seven distinct divisions have been proclaimed. (9.135.46–47)
This supreme secret, which is most profound, has been heard from the mouth of Śrī Hari; I have declared it to you in brief. By knowing this, you shall attain liberation.
Without discerning what has been thus spoken, liberation shall not come to anyone. (9.135.48)
Thus ends the compendium of Purāṇic passages establishing the seven divisions, beginning with the transposition [of syllables].
Therefore, because this is a definitive scripture, it should be accepted by those desiring spiritual prosperity (bubhūṣu).
Thus has the supreme narrative of Rāma been recounted by me, which removes worldly existence by following the teachings of all the scriptures.
Whoever should read this or even hear it, being liberated from bondage, shall go to the feet of Hari. 9.137.
Thus ends the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

The ninth chapter, titled "Rāma’s Entry into His Own Abode," exists in my collection (the Śrī Jayatīrtha Sanskrit Manuscript Library) as well as in the collection of the Uttarādimaṭha— Vyāsanakere Prabhañjanācārya.
[Description of the Incarnations of Vyāsa] Now begins the tenth chapter.
Om! Then, when the Dvāpara age had arrived once more, in the twenty-eighth [cycle]...
Svayambhū, Śarva, Śakra, and the others went to the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Having reached the northern shore of the milk-ocean, those bulls among the gods praised the lotus-eyed, imperishable Puruṣottama.
Salutations again and again to the sole abode of innumerable virtues, garlanded with the rays of all-encompassing wisdom;
to the destroyer of the darkness of beginningless ignorance, the bestower of the state of supreme nectar-bliss.
(10.3) Indeed, due to the fault of the garland given by himself, Śrī was quickly deprived of her fortune by the curse of Durvāsas.
In former times, when Śakra was deprived of his power and defeated by the sons of Diti, we went to you for refuge.

(10.4) By your command, while attempting to join Mount Mandara with Bala—who was unshakable by others due to a boon from the Lord of Mountains—the assembled gods arrived at Mandara and were unable to lift it up with their arms. (10.5)

Then, by reason of your eternal strength, you uprooted Mount Mandara with a single hand and placed it upon the shoulder of that Garuḍa named Ananta; he bore it along with you. Furthermore, when the gods and asuras were testing him, they lifted that mountain together. 10.6. Then, while they were testing him, that mountain was raised up by the gods along with the asuras.
You crushed them all, yet by your glance alone, O Lord, they rose up again as before.

10.7 Again, O Lord, placing him upon your left hand and carrying him on your shoulder, you went to the ocean together with the gods and asuras; and with that mountain as a churning-stick, you churned the sea. 10.8
And here Kadrū made her son Vāsuki, that king of serpents born of Kaśyapa, the rope for churning;

together with you, the gods and the asuras churned the ocean, which abounded in divine milk and clarified butter. (10.9) The sons of Diti did not desire the tail, saying it was inauspicious, and so they seized the head, which was fierce with poison.
Then, becoming exhausted from this, those gods, relying upon you and accompanied by you, seized your tail.

(10.10) Thereupon, due to that excessive weight, the mountain of excellent gold sank into the netherworld; then you yourself, assuming the form of a tortoise, supported it upon your own back with great ease, for it could not have been borne by any other. (10.11)

10.12. Having entered into the self, both above and below, and having strengthened the eyes and the mountains by means of your supreme power, the gods and demons, fierce with intoxication, swiftly churned the ocean whose circle of crocodiles was agitated.
When they were exhausted, O Urukrama, you alone, being joyful, churned [the ocean] for the sake of obtaining the essence of nectar.
Then, by your command, Vāyu held in his own hand the world-devouring poison that had arisen.

That very form of Kali, which was exceedingly unbearable and difficult for anyone to touch due to the boon of the Creator, Vāyu crushed in his hand until its strength was destroyed and gave a small portion of it to Giriśa. (10.13–10.14)

Drinking that [poison], Rudra was struck down and fell unconscious as it reached his throat; yet, by the power of Hari’s touch of the hand, he regained consciousness, and at that time his throat became blue. Then, placing your command before him and [placing it] in a vessel of refined gold—

Having churned it himself, he drank that which was endowed with power, and it was digested by him. Because of drinking so little, a piercing pain arose in the head of Śiva, while for Vāyu, who had drunk his fill, there was no adverse effect; indeed, strife arose throughout all the worlds.
From the body of Kāla were born crocodiles, along with scorpions, beasts of prey, and *yātudhānas*.
Then, as you were churning the ocean, the gods obtained the nectar while the *asuras* received [the rest].
Thereafter, the horse named Uccaiḥśravas appeared, as did the elephant known by the name Airāvata. (10.17–10.18)
Furthermore, there were the elephants of the world-protectors, as well as a thousand excellent apsarases;
likewise, the weapons, ornaments, the celestial tree Pārijāta, and Surabhi herself appeared in person, along with that Kaustubha gem, the essence of the worlds. 10.19.
Then, although Indrāṇī possessed an eternal body, she appeared there with another body of her own.
Thereupon, you emerged from that ocean named Dhanvantari, possessing the luster of a green gem, holding a vessel of nectar in your right arm and a water-jar in the other. (10.20–10.21)
Then the sons of Diti seized the jar filled with nectar that had come into your hands,

even though you were intent on it and were causing the Daityas— who had fallen from truth— to be slain. Thereupon, acting with haste, you assumed an incomparable and supreme form consisting of celestial nymphs.
Dark-complexioned, with a jeweled girdle fastened upon her hips, wearing garments of golden luster and possessing a slender waist;

with broad hips, breasts like jars, and eyes as radiant as beautiful lotuses—upon merely seeing her, who was the essence of all things and possessed of perfect virtues, the enemies of the gods were utterly bewildered. (10.23–10.24)
Fighting one another for the sake of the nectar, they all placed it in your hand;
deceived by you, they said, "Divide this vessel of ambrosia equally and let us drink.
At that time, you spoke thus to make known to the sinful folk that there is a deception of righteousness under the guise of righteousness.

"Whatever has been done for you by me, if there is indeed a dispute here, let us divide this nectar; I shall divide it according to your wish. In no way whatsoever should anyone place trust in me at any time.
Hearing these words spoken with a smile, they, bewildered by their feminine nature, replied, "So be it. (10.26–27)

Then, having set aside the gods and asuras separately—having distinguished the gods from the others who were agitated by your supreme form—and seeing that all of them were looking at you, you said, "I am ashamed; close your eyes. When the asuras had closed their eyes, you then caused the divine beings to drink the nectar, O Puruṣa. 10.28.
In an instant, as he was drinking the nectar, you cut off Rāhu’s head with the Sudarśana [discus].

For the sake of the nectar, he had performed austerities for a thousand births and thereby obtained a boon from the Self-Existent One; therefore, having cast a drop of nectar into his hand, you severed his head. (10.29–10.30)

His head, along with his arms, was seized by the gods; his headless trunk (kabandha), cast by you into the ocean of Śubhodaka, remains there even today, still alive. Then the asuras fell upon you with uplifted weapons, but they were all slain by you in battle.
Kali, indeed invincible due to the boon of Brahmā, remained among men except for you;
from half of his body, Alakṣmī was born, and from her, all the multitudes of vices.
Then Indirā took her place upon your chest, and the Creator placed the Kaustubha gem upon your neck.
"Since you have distributed [the nectar] among the gods according to their respective divisions, others too were indeed born there;
thus, the nectar was rightly bestowed by you upon the gods as a demonstration of liberation.
For liberation would certainly belong to the gods, but it could never, under any circumstances, belong to the asuras. (10.34)
For one possessed of enthusiasm, that [adversity] will indeed become as painful as Rāhu;

for now, this Kali age, having entered us and all living beings through the form of ignorance and false intellect—its nature being opposed to true knowledge—afflicts us all by means of the granting of boons from Brahmā and others. (10.35–36)

By your command, a boon was granted to him by the Lotus-born; having entered Śiva, he brought about the subversion of the scriptures of others through fallacious arguments. Indeed, no one other than you is capable of performing such a task.
All the Vedas along with the collections of various treatises have been destroyed by him; they do not exist today. (10.37)
Therefore, it is well that you descend to the earth, recover the Vedas, and properly compose the Śāstras.

Having swiftly slain with the weapon of the true Śāstras Kali— who is invisible, unknowable, of inconceivable form, and who has taken refuge in the hearts of all— grant the Great Man his own rightful place.
"Except for you, there is no slayer of that [demon]; you alone are filled with all powers.
Therefore, we have come to you for refuge—you who are the embodiment of innate awakening—for the destruction of darkness.
Having been addressed thus by them, the Supreme and Immeasurable One granted fearlessness to the lords of the gods.
There appeared in this world the one whose nature is a mass of pure consciousness, the abundant source of nectar.
(10.41) His son was named Vasiṣṭha, born from the lotus; his son was Śakti, and his son was Parāśara.
That Hari also performed supreme austerity, thinking, "May Hari be my son," and Hari granted it to him. (10.42)
And the Blessed One said to him: "Vasu has a beautiful daughter;
while he was wandering in the forest for the sake of deer, his seed fell as his mind was fixed upon his wife.
He placed it in the hand of a hawk to deliver it to her, but as the hawk was fighting with another bird, it fell. (10.43)
The female fish swallowed her; the crocodiles seized her as she lay in the water, the sister of Yama.
From her womb a pair of twins was born, whom they presented to their own king. He, in turn, delivered them to Vasu.
Taking the son, he gave the daughter to him [Vasu]. Thereupon, the son became the King of Matsya.
That girl, endowed with exceeding beauty, grew up in the palace of the King of Daṇḍaka;
she was named Satyavatī, and in her, I, though unborn, shall become your son.
Having been addressed thus by the wielder of the discus, the sage went to that daughter of the Sun who dwells in the ocean.
Then, as she was being rescued there, Viṣṇu, the mass of pure consciousness, suddenly manifested.
Though he is unborn and consists solely of flawless knowledge and bliss, he appears falsely to delude people;
for among women, a man is seen as if born, yet his form, which is not produced by force or other means, is never truly born anywhere. (10.47–10.48)

Just as the form of Nṛsiṃha manifested from a pillar, so too the All-pervading One, possessing an eternal body, manifested within a woman; yet, though not arising from impurity, He appeared in such a way as to cause delusion. (10.49) For after the union of man and woman, this Hari manifests, utterly bewildering the people.
Therefore, people considered this one born of impurity, though he was the embodiment of perfect virtues; 10.50.

In the island of Yama’s sister, that Creator of the Universe, whose orb is a mass of rays of knowledge, shines forth; illuminating both the exterior and the interior of the cosmic egg with the light of a thousand times a hundred thousand suns. 10.51.

The Lord is an immeasurable ocean of vast, divine qualities; he is the sovereign of all sciences, the teacher of the world, possessed of infinite power, the Lord of the universe, whose form is utterly remote from all defects.

(10.52) He has the auspicious color of emerald, with the soles of his lotus-feet, his eyes, lips, hands, nails, and the tips of his tongue being red; he bears the marks of the discus, the conch, and the lotus.
Wearing a deer skin as white as the rays of the sun, bearing a mass of matted locks radiant with tresses as pure as lightning;

broad-chested, with long lotus-eyes, mighty arms, and a neck like a conch shell; emitting all the Vedas from his mouth, his noble face possessed a beauty surpassing that of infinite moons. (10.53–10.54)
Adorned with the *prabodha-mudrā*, the gesture of fearlessness, and two arms, and shining with the sacred thread, deerskin, and girdle,
he shone intensely as he restored to life the world bitten by the great serpent of ignorance with his glance.
Out of a desire to protect worldly conventions for his father's sake, having quickly attained the status of a twice-born, he bestowed his own [status] upon his father.
By the mere act of remembering those two, his knowledge always bestowed the state of direct perception upon the Supreme Self.
Then that Dvaipāyana, followed by the four-faced Brahmā and others, went to Mount Meru;
having recovered all the Vedas from the gods, he gave them to the sages just as at the first creation.
Having likewise reached a definitive conclusion regarding all the scriptures, he composed the *Brahmasūtra*.
The gods, headed by Brahmā and Giriśa, as well as the foremost among the sages, heard it from him.
He then composed the work named the *Mahābhārata*, which consists of the demonstration of the meaning of all the scriptures.
That supreme Veda was heard from his mouth by the gods, headed by Brahmā and Śiva.
Then Kali, who had been tormenting the minds of Giriśa and the others, was swiftly struck down by arrows consisting of the Lord’s speech;
with his head severed by those arrows issued from the Blessed One’s mouth, the gods drank the nectar-essence of true knowledge.
"Furthermore, among humans as well as among the Asuras, Kali alone remains in various forms.
Therefore, while humans still exist, he has remained concealed," thus Hari reflected.
Then Kṛṣṇa, observing that the lifespan, intellect, and actions of men had become very feeble due to the power of Time, [acted accordingly].

That omnipresent Lord divided the Vedas into four and likewise [composed] the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (10.62). Liberating from darkness those various virtuous people who were overcome by it through his excellent words, he wandered through the worlds; while traveling on the road, he saw an insect and Kṛṣṇa spoke to it (10.63).
"Be a king after casting off this wretched body," he said; however, the king did not wish for that.
Therefore, he made that former devotee of his—a low-born man who was excessively greedy—renounce his body, though the king himself had not yet done so.
Having attained the state of an insect due to greed, he quickly became a king again through the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
At that very moment, all the kings bowed down to him and paid him tribute just as Vaiśyas do.
The Blessed One said to him: "I am capable of granting you liberation at this very instant;
nevertheless, having attained the body of a Brahmin for the sake of the boundary [of the Dharma], become liberated through my grace."
He bestowed upon him stainless knowledge and, at the end of that [life], he enjoyed the entire earth;
having cast off his body and attained the status of a preeminent brahmin, he who knew the true reality reached the abode of Hari.
Thus, Janārdana in the form of Vyāsa liberated many people from the bondage of saṃsāra.
Many inconceivable deeds of his were ever proclaimed by the lords of all the gods.

(10.68) Then Rudra, desiring to obtain the status of being his son, performed severe penance for him; and the Blessed One, having himself performed penance, granted him that boon while appearing as if deluded. (10.69)
To delude those born of the asura lineage, the Lord himself performs penance as if it were a mere display;
he falsely manifests defects such as desire, yet for all that, these do not exist in him anywhere.
Then, from the two kindling-sticks (araṇis), a son was born to him; he was Śiva, who became known by the name Śuka.
Having become a female parrot, Ghṛtācī approached Vyāsa as he was churning the fire-sticks.
Desiring him like a lover, she entreated him; having begotten a son from the two fire-sticks, he named him Śuka, thereby deluding those who are unfit for the paths of truth. (10.71–72)
Then the Wind entered that parrot for the sake of serving Vyāsa;

the Blessed One bestowed upon him all knowledge—the entirety of the Vedas along with the Mahābhārata, the Bhāgavata, and the Purāṇas. (10.73) Then Śeṣa entered the sage Paila, and Viṣṇu likewise entered the sage Sumantu, the son of Varuṇa.
Brahmā entered Vaiśampāyana, and the omnipresent Śakra entered Jaimini.
Eager to serve the feet of Kṛṣṇa, the lords of the gods entered those sages with joy.
Having imparted all branches of knowledge to them, Hari again appointed them as the propagators of those teachings.

He then appointed Paila as the propagator of the *Ṛg-veda* verses, Vaiśampāyana alone as the propagator of the *Yajur-veda* formulas, and Jaimini as the second [propagator] of the *Sāman* chants and also of the *Atharvāṅgirasa*. (10.76)
He appointed Sumantu to the Bharata and Vaiśampāyana to the propagation among humans, Gandharvas, and others;
and having instructed Nārada, he sent him forth for its dissemination in the world of the gods.
Then he commanded and created Romaharṣaṇa from the hair on his body (10.78).
He then commanded him for the purpose of setting in motion the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas, the great Rāmāyaṇa, and the entire Pañcarātra (10.79).
Kāmadeva, who was eager for service to Kṛṣṇa, entered into him;
the lord Dvaipāyana bestowed all knowledge upon him. He [Dvaipāyana] made Sanatkumāra and others the initiators of yoga.
Having bestowed the pure and auspicious knowledge of *karmayoga* upon Bhṛgu and the others,
the Lord made Jaimini the author of the *Karmamīmāṃsā*. Then, having appointed Paila as the beginning and end of the *Devamīmāṃsā*, he instructed him.
Furthermore, he composed the remaining Purāṇas as a compendium;
he fashioned the Śaiva scriptures from the Pāśupata for the purpose of creating doubt among the enemies of the gods,
and the Vaiṣṇava Pañcarātra for the attainment of knowledge of reality as it is.
He composed the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the compendiums of the Purāṇa texts.
In this way, the gods, the sages, the yogins headed by Sanatkumāra, and likewise human beings, attained knowledge once again.
Having obtained knowledge from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, those gods rejoiced; the great sun of wisdom, having spread its wheel of rays consisting of all-encompassing insight, dispelled [the darkness] (or:
having drunk it up).
And the world, pervaded by the darkness of ignorance, shone forth as he illuminated it like the sun.

With the sprout-like feet of the Lord always served by the gods, headed by the four-faced Brahmā, Īśāna, and Surendra, he delighted on Mount Meru and likewise at Badarī, constantly revealing his own secret doctrine to them. (10.85–86)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Vyāsa," in the *Śrī Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In ancient manuscripts themselves, both readings— *nirasya* and *nipīya*— are recorded.
In a case where even a person standing nearby is ashamed, how could one who is far removed determine the truth?
— Bannañje Govindācārya. Chapter Eleven (The Promise of the Incarnation of the Blessed One). Now begins the eleventh chapter.

Oṃ! From the son of the Moon (Budha) was born Purūravas; from him, Āyu; from Āyu, Nahuṣa; and from Nahuṣa, Yayāti. He had a pair of wives and five sons who were solely devoted to the station of Viṣṇu:
Yadu and Turvaśu were begotten by Devayānī.
“Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru were born to Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
(69) / 11.2 / In the lineage of Yadu, there arose the universal emperor Kārtavīrya Arjuna,
who possessed the power of yoga through the grace of Viṣṇu, known by the name Dattātreya.
In his lineage arose the Yadavas, who took refuge in Viṣṇu. But in the lineage of Pūru was Bharata, a universal emperor and a beloved of Hari;
in his lineage was born one named Kuru, and in his succession came Pratīpa. (11.3–11.4)
Pratīpa had three sons, possessing the splendor of the three sacred fires:
Devāpi, Bāhlīka, and Śaṃtanu, who was the eldest in virtue.
Devāpi, afflicted with a skin disease, went to the forest for ascetic penance. (11.5)
By the grace of Viṣṇu, that Bāhlīka, the best of kings, having become the son of a daughter, will become a king in the Kṛta Yuga;
he is the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, Prahlāda, who is devoted to the Blessed One. (11.6–11.7)
Pervaded by Vāyu and endowed with great strength,
he was the very one by whose forceful birth the earth was rent asunder;
he indeed attained the state of being an instrument for Viṣṇu in the removal of the earth’s burden.
Having attained the status of a son of Pratīpa, he became the lord among the Bāhlīkas;
among the Rudras was he known as Patratāpa, and his son was Somadatta. Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and Virūpākṣa were the three [others].
Sixty-nine sons of Rudra were born to Somadatta, renowned as his offspring; Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala attained the very nature of Viṣṇu himself. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.10.6–11.10)
Due to the possession by all the Rudras beginning with Śiva, as well as by virtue of a boon,
Bhūriśravas was exceedingly powerful there and a supreme knower of weapons;
for that purpose, Somadatta had performed austerities for Śambhu.
And a boon was granted by him to this [king], saying: "A son named Bhūriśravas, endowed with strength, heroism, and virtue, who shall overcome those who oppose you, will be born;
he shall be possessed by me and devoted to sacrifice. (11.12)

From him was born the mighty Bhūriśravas, the son of Somadatta. When the Lotus-born [Brahmā] had gone to the shore of the eastern ocean on a full-moon day, the ocean, agitated by the presence of Gaṅgā, cast a drop of its own water upon his body; thereupon the Lotus-born cursed him. (11.13–14)
Having become a lord of men named Mahābhiṣaṅ, you will again be born under the name Śantanu;
likewise, this Viṣṇupadī shall also become your wife there.
Because you become peaceful (*śānta*) when spoken of by me, and because you have attained a slender form (*tanutva*), you are therefore called Śantanu.
Thus addressed, that king became known by the name Mahābhiṣaṅ, taking refuge at the feet of Hari.
Having enjoyed the earth there for a long time, he cast off his body and went to the abode of the Creator.
Remaining there in the presence of the hosts of gods, he beheld his own Gaṅgā with her garments loosened.

As the gods looked on with faces turned downward out of passion, the Self-born One spoke again to the king upon the earth: "Become, O King, quickly one who is cursed by me just as you were in the past.
Thus addressed, at that very moment, the king became the opposite [of his former state] and was named Śantanu.
Having obtained Gaṅgā as his own beloved, he rejoiced with her for many groups of years.
Then the eighth Vasu, named Dyu, appeared; his wife was named Varāṅgī.
And that king had a friend, a beloved wife of a king named Suvinda, who bore the same name as his own.

The queen urged her husband to bind that cow of Vasiṣṭha, named Nandini, who was the cause of the destruction of old age and death and who yielded his own nectar, for she removes decrepitude. Thus impelled by her, that Vasu named Dyumat, out of brotherly affection, set out accompanied by seven others.
Then the Lord, the lotus-born Brahmā, who was established in Vasiṣṭha, bound that cow and cursed them:

"O you who follow unrighteous conduct, quickly return to human birth, for because of you all have fallen from dharma. He shall likewise attain a lifespan of eight thousand years; as for the others, you shall be released from this state swiftly thereafter. (11.22–23)

And she who had urged her husband onto the wrong path was born among men as a woman who, being without a husband, would become the cause of her husband's death by resorting to manhood; let him be solely devoted to celibacy, for there would be a great conflict between the two. (11.24)
"May he experience the very suffering of dwelling in the eight stages of the womb while lying upon the bed of arrows;
may he undergo even the agony arising from the eightfold death, being cut into many pieces by weapons.
Having spoken thus, they recognized him as the Lotus-born One, and releasing the earth, they prostrated before him. (11.25–26)
"May we not again enter a human womb; may he be all-knowing and renowned;
may he be a master of great weapons and endowed with your power; and may he attain the strength of us all.
When this was said, they were told "So be it" by the Self-Existent One, and they went to the celestial river at the abode of Vasiṣṭha.
They said to her, "Let us be born from your womb quickly; you must kill us.

Thus addressed, she chose a boon from them: sinlessness and, moreover, being beloved by them, and that they should always consider her as their own self. Then she gave birth to one of them, who was long-lived, for Śāntanu. (11.28–29)
In order to strike them down without obstacle, she formerly resorted to the right thigh of Pratīpa like a woman in love, desiring through her disguise to become the wife of his son.
And by him she was addressed: "Become the wife of my son, since you have taken your place upon my right thigh. (11.30)
For it is well known that Dakṣa was the portion for his daughter and Vāma for his daughter-in-law or wife.
(11.31) She said to him: "Your son did not ask me, 'Who are you? nor did he prevent me;
nor would he ever have asked the reason for my action, even though I was performing what was improper. (11.32)
When he said, "If you choose one from among these three, I shall depart,
leaving him behind," King Pratīpa replied,
"So be it. And in that very manner, by the command of the celestial river, that speech was spoken by the bride to her son.
She said to the youngest, "Your son indeed; no other husband has been chosen by me but Śāntanu.

(11.34) Then, having obtained eight sons from Śāntanu, she killed seven of them and likewise the eighth. Having then resolved to depart, she made a display as if she were about to kill [the last one]. (11.35)

Since dwelling among humans is not for the ultimate happiness of the gods, it was for this very reason that they desired to depart; for her human body had indeed arisen from a man, Śantanu. Śantanu restrained her as she was intent on bringing about the death of her son.

"Who are you, and by what cause do you devour your sons so cruelly? (11.37) Your form is like that of the finest celestial women; therefore, your action cannot be evil. There must be some great reason for this. (11.38)
"Tell me the reason for that, O auspicious one, if it is worthy of my ears.
Thus addressed, she told him everything and departed; for it is not the dharma of the gods to dwell long among men in disguise. (11.39)
For it is solely for a specific purpose that the gods take up residence among men;
when that purpose has ceased, they depart, for their dharma is likewise of such a nature.
They remain invisible, untouchable, and indeed beyond conversation.
Even by the gods and the multitudes of men, the secret dharma of the inhabitants of heaven was not known.
Therefore, she abandoned even that god Varuṇa, her former husband,
as well as Śāntanu who had become a man, and departed for the abode of Varuṇa.
Taking up the eighth vow with her husband’s permission,
she desisted from the effort to kill and gave her son to Bṛhaspati.
That Devavrata was given by his mother to the preceptor of the gods for instruction during the fifty-year period.

For one hundred and thirteen years, with his inner self entirely under their control, he studied all the Vedas. Then, for fifty years, he heard the truth from Rāma, the lord of the Bhṛgus, who was the most venerable in the worlds and an ocean of infinite, perfect virtues.
After practicing weapons for twenty-five more years under the lord of the Bhṛgus, he was brought by his mother to his own bank and stationed there to be presented to his father.
At that very moment, his father, having bound the Gaṅgā within a cage of arrows, sported there. (11.46)
Wandering in search of game, thirsty and looking about, he was greatly astonished to find the Gaṅgā devoid of water.
Then, seeking to discover the cause of this, he saw his own son playing with a weapon; yet, immediately upon seeing his father, the boy vanished from sight. (11.47–48)
While searching for him, Gaṅgā found him and, taking her son with her, said to her husband:
"This son of yours, a master of supreme weapons and endowed with heroism and strength, has been restored;
your elder sons have already gone to the waters purified by the lotus-feet of Hari. (11.49)
"Entrusting your body to my care, do not be distressed by them, and rejoice because of this.
Having spoken thus and bestowed him upon him, Gaṅgā vanished from sight; taking him with her, she went to her own home.
Then the king, having consecrated him as the crown prince, rejoiced greatly, being thoroughly satisfied by his excellent virtues.
Furthermore, with his father’s permission, he acquired the Vedas from Bṛhaspati in half a human lifespan;
likewise, he obtained weapons from Rāma, and in three hundred years, he attained the ultimate truth.
Having thus attained omniscience from Rāma—the lord of all sciences and an ocean of virtues—[he became a great sage].
Having reached his father’s side and serving him, the hero rejoiced. (11.53) At the very moment Gaṅgā gave birth to her eighth son, Śāntanu went out on a hunt;
there in the forest he beheld an excellent pair born of Śaradvat, produced not from a womb. (11.54)
While Śaradvat was performing austerities, he beheld Urvaśī;
his semen then spilled into a clump of reeds, and from that it came into being.
He became known as Viṣkambha among the Rudras, serving as an instrument in the removal of the earth’s burden.

Likewise, Tārā, who was the wife of Bṛhaspati, desired to obtain Hara; Śantanu, seeing them both, took them to his own home out of compassion and gave them names because they were objects of his pity (kṛpā).
Kṛpa and Kṛpī—thus was that Kṛpa; he indeed performed austerities for Viṣṇu.
Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of the lords of all worlds, being pleased with him, granted him the status of one of the future Seven Sages and a lifespan until the end of the kalpa.
While residing in the house of Śāntanu, he became a friend to Devavrata;
he protected Śāntanu’s couple as if they were his own children, and that Kṛpa acquired the divine weapons. (11.58–59)
He studied all the Vedas and all the Śāstras from Kauśika;
likewise, having obtained the knowledge of reality from Vyāsa, he attained omniscience.
(11.60) At the very moment that Kṛpa was born as a twice-born, the son of Bṛhaspati went to the Gaṅgā.
There he beheld the beloved of the foremost of gods, Ghṛtācī, as she was bathing with her silk garment slipping loose.
Upon seeing her, his seed was discharged; he then quickly caught it in a vessel.
From that, Bṛhaspati himself was born, joined by the power of the Lotus-born (Brahmā), in order to perform the task of Hari in lifting the burden of the earth.
His father, the sage Bharadvāja, gave him the name Droṇa and taught him the Vedas along with the entire collection of Śāstras; thus he attained omniscience in no long time.
At that same time, the childless Pṛṣata, the lord of the Pañcālas, was practicing austerities in the forest. (11.63)

Because he had gazed upon that excellent Apsaras, his great ascetic power was shaken and his seed was spilled. Out of shame for that act, he stepped upon it with his foot; from this, a son was born to him named Huhu, who became the singer of Viriñca and the attendant of the Maruts known as Āvaha.

From Drona’s son he acquired the Vedas, as well as all weapons and branches of knowledge; for when he was joined by Drona, he said to the son of his preceptor, "Together with me, [you shall share] the kingdom. (11.66) Because of the swiftness of his step, he was named Drupada; then he obtained his own kingdom and Kṛpī.

Droṇa, too, having obtained a wife, lived happily in the city, renouncing all acceptance of gifts. Sustaining himself by the very practice of gleaning ears of grain, and devoted to the great, stainless Dharma,
he dwelt in the city named Nāga, together with his friends Devavrata and Kṛpa.
Among them, Virāṭa by name was equal to them in age; he was the son of Vidhātṛ and a singer.
He was joined with a portion of him who among the Maruts was named Vivaha, and he followed his own dharma. (11.69) Then, once gone out on a hunt, Śantanu beheld a most excellent maiden.
She who, having been a daughter of the Pitṛs in a previous creation, performed supreme penance for Viṣṇu for a long time;

she to whom Viṣṇu granted a boon in the past, saying, "I shall become your son," she who was the daughter of Vasu, born again in the house of Daṇḍa and raised there, and in whom Viṣṇu became incarnate through the self of Vyāsa. (11.70–71)
Upon seeing him, the king’s heart was filled with longing, and he requested Dāṇsarāja for her hand in marriage;
however, he did not wish to give away his kingdom without that daughter's son, so she then returned to her own home.
Seeing her father with a dejected face due to anxiety over this matter, Devavrata questioned him.
Having heard the entire reason for this from his charioteer, he went to the house of Daṇḍa.

For the sake of gaining his confidence, he made a promise: "I shall not exercise sovereignty, nor shall there be any fear for you from my lineage; likewise, remain forever one whose vital energy is drawn upward (a perpetual celibate). 11.73–74.
Because of his formidable vow, the gods then gave him the name Bhīṣma;
and he, having taken Kālī, whom Daṇḍadhara had bestowed as a gift, presented her to his father.
Having learned that she was a princess, rich in virtues, and by name the mother of Satya Viṣṇu... 11.75.
Bhīṣma married for his father that noble woman known in the world as Satyavatī.

For, knowing that the minds of the virtuous generally do not proceed toward the path of evil, and perceiving that her own mind was likewise fixed [on virtue], Śāntanu—who delighted in the true Dharma—accepted her even though she had been raised in the house of a fisherman. (11.76–77)

Having granted Bhīṣma the boon of death at his own will, as well as invincibility and unassailability in battles, that best of kings rejoiced with her for many groups of years. There he obtained a son, Citrāṅgada, and likewise a second, Vicitravīrya.
And in their youth, he cast off his body, thinking, "What use have I for this worn-out frame? (11.79).
By his own will, he attained the state of Varuṇa; for at that time, the body is not abandoned by the powerful except through death. (11.80)
Those who are excessively attached and devoid of austerity may somehow meet their death even against their will, just as the younger brother of Citrāṅgada did. Then,
having performed the funeral rites for his father, Bhīṣma consecrated [Vicitravīrya].

He installed the hero Citrāṅgada as king and his younger brother in the position of crown prince. Citrāṅgada, however, having not yet performed his marriage, was slain by a Gandharva in a great battle while refusing to abandon his own name. (11.82)
Having made Vicitravīrya the king, Bhīṣma protected him. Then, for his sake, Bhīṣma brought three daughters of the King of Kāśī:
Ambā, Ambikā by name, and likewise the other, Ambālikā. (11.83–84)
At the time of Brahmādatta’s marriage, the heroic king,
having conquered that Sālva monarch as well as all the assembled kṣatriyas,
[returned]. There, the two auspicious daughters, Ambikā and Ambālikā, engaged in a dispute with one another.
In her previous birth, that Ambā was indeed the wife of Bhīṣma, yet she did not desire him.
Due to a curse from Hiraṇyagarbha, she declared, "I am in love with Śālva," and he abandoned her; she then went to Śālva himself. (11.86–87)
She was again rejected by him as well, yet she was touched [by him];
she then approached Bhīṣma, but he did not accept her, and she went to Bhārgava.
He then caused Ambikā and Ambālikā to be married to his brother.
The descendant of Bhṛgu fought with Bhīṣma in order to bestow glory upon him;
yet, although he possessed infinite power, he did not slay Bhīṣma, nor did he cause Ambā to be taken [by force], being restrained by compassion for Bhīṣma. (11.89–90)
He who possesses infinite power, the inner self of all, the omniscient, the controller of all, and the conqueror of all—

for whom there is no other equal anywhere in any way, how indeed could there be a lack of power in that Supreme One? (11.91) Filling his own devotee Bhīṣma with glory, Rāma deluded the Asuras as well.
Having conquered Bhīṣma, the Lord did not slay him, and he made his word true:
"Though Keśava appeared as one pierced, as one bewildered, and as one afflicted by pain, Viṣṇu was not actually so; he displayed this only for the sake of deluding [the enemy]. (11.92)

Thus, from such statements arising in the Purāṇas, Rāma is eternally victorious. Having bestowed his fame upon Bhīṣma, he released Ambā— who had sought refuge with him— from the sin born of her hatred for her husband, and thereby united her with a horse.

Immediately thereafter, because of her status as Śikhaṇḍinī, she then performed a penance that was both auspicious and inauspicious, for the sake of Bhīṣma’s death and for the sake of attaining manhood.
(11.95) It had been said: "I shall act in such a way that Bhīṣma may take you [as his bride]."
When Bhīṣma had passed to another body, Rāma made that promise true.
Then Rudra, pleased by her ascetic penance, granted her a boon:
that she would become the cause of Bhīṣma’s death after a period of time, and that she would be born from his body.
"Whoever takes up this garland shall slay Bhīṣma. Having taken that garland, she went among the kings;
yet no one took it out of fear of Bhīṣma, for such was her power. (11.98)
Having stationed himself at the gate of Drupada’s house, he abandoned his body through yoga. At that very time, Drupada performed austerities for the sake of a son;
Śambhu said to him, "A daughter shall be born to you."
Having been born as a woman, she will become a man; thus Sāmba was born from her.
She was named Śikhaṇḍinī, and she performed the duties of a man.
To her [the King of Pāñcāla] gave the daughter of the Lord of Daśārṇa.
She married her off while she was still disguised in male attire;
indeed, no one except her parents knew of her true identity. Then she informed her nurse, and the nurse informed her father. (11.102)

Enraged, he sent word to the king of the Pañcālas, saying, "I shall slay you along with your kinsmen," and he marched forth with his army. Having heard the words of Viśvāmitra that the son of Pṛṣata was indeed a man, Rudra [reflected]. 11.103.

He sent forth [the message]: "Fie on your intellect, which has been shattered by the words of a child! How can your kingdom belong to one so lacking in discernment? Thus he made sport of him. Then, his father, accompanied by his wife, was distressed with anxiety.
"Having seen her, may she not perish through the sorrows caused by me," thinking thus, she departed for the forest; and there, Tumburu,
known as Sthūṇākarṇa, beheld her from afar with his firm ears.
Having heard her entire account, the high-minded one took pity on her;
he gave her his own body and likewise received hers.
A portion of himself remained in her former body for the sake of maintaining a masculine nature. (11.107)
In some cases, men may attain womanhood, yet in the end they become men again;
however, for women, manhood never occurs even through powerful causes.
Therefore, even in the presence of Śiva’s boon, these [demons] were born as females and not otherwise.
Afterwards, she entered even a male body accompanied by a man;
yet her own body did not attain masculinity, nor did she dwell in a male body unless it was presided over by a man.
Then, she dwelt in a male body presided over by a Gandharva.
Having entered the Gandharva body, he went to his own abode. By the grace of the Gandharva, she attained a resemblance to that body;
subsequently, the Gandharva body itself was presided over by her. (11.110–111)
"Give me your body tomorrow, and enter into my own body.
Having said this, that Gandharva entered the body of the maiden;
he remained in that forest, and there Dhanada arrived. (11.112)
When the son of Tantulī, who did not rise to greet him and was overcome by shame, was thus being spun out,
the god Dhanada cursed him, saying, "May you remain thus for a long time. At that moment, the maiden who had been situated within his body met her death in battle.
"Then you shall return to manhood again because of your fickleness," he was told.
(11.114) Thus that Gandharva lived with the father and mother of the maiden in every respect; he related what he had experienced, and they both attained great joy. (11.115)
Having tested her with various means, the father-in-law departed ashamed;
on the following day, she, having obtained a Gandharva through his word,
returned once more in that very same body, having attained manhood.
He was named Śikhaṇḍin, powerful in the majesty of his missiles and weapons.
Having obtained those two women, Vicitravīrya took his pleasure with them for many years, deeply attached;
then, afflicted by consumption, he abandoned his body, whereupon his mother remembered Kṛṣṇa in her distress.

Janārdana, the progenitor of the universe and the remover of the fear of birth and old age, quickly manifested; he whose body is composed of all knowledge is an ocean of bliss. And his mother worshipped him, who had been previously honored with supreme reverence by Bhīṣma and others, and was being praised by them. His mother then spoke to him.
"My two sons are dead; Bhīṣma did not desire the kingdom, even though he was entreated by me most earnestly.

Then, being requested with supreme devotion, "Therefore, procreate an excellent offspring in the field of your brother," the Teacher of the World, having been thus addressed and having been saluted and praised by Bhīṣma and the others, spoke these words. (11.120–121)
"Except for Ramā, there is no woman in the celestial realm who is ever fit to be united with my body;
nevertheless, I shall carry out your word. Let her perform a vow for one year, and then, her body purified by the Vaiṣṇava vow, let her obtain from me a most excellent son. (11.122)
When this was said, she replied, "The kingdom will not come to ruin. To her, who spoke thus, he spoke these words again:
"Though my nature is gentle, I shall falsely display a most terrifying form to her eyes.
If she can endure that, then her son shall be rich in virtues and endowed with strength and heroism. (11.123–124)
When this was said, Kṛṣṇa replied, "So be it," and went to Ambikā; she, however, closed her eyes out of fear.
Within her was born the king of the Gandharvas named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was possessed by the power of the Wind-god (Pavana).
By the strength of that possession of Māruta, the king named Dhṛtarāṣṭra became superior in power.
And Kṛṣṇa granted him a boon of superior strength; however, he was born blind due to his mother's fault.

(11.126) Knowing him to be blind, the mother spoke again to Kṛṣṇa, saying, "Beget another son, rich in virtues, upon Ambālikā. He did so accordingly; yet out of fear, she became pale and her vision became false. (11.127)
From him was born the wind-god named Parāvaha, who was pale in complexion and so named accordingly.
Through the infusion of Vāyu, he became exceedingly powerful and a knower of all weapons and missiles.
Then Kṛṣṇa himself granted that pale-complexioned one a boon of superior strength and heroism.
Having understood this, the mother spoke to him again: "Beget another son, one who is faultless and supreme.
Having said this to Kṛṣṇa, she then spoke again to her daughter-in-law: "In the past, you closed your eyes;
therefore, your son was born blind. Therefore, once more, serve Kṛṣṇa with devotion."
Although addressed thus, that woman of poor intellect, terrified by his illusory power (*māyā*), appointed him to the service of a slave-girl.
But she, having obtained him whose body was supreme bliss and who was an ocean of virtues, took delight in him with the highest devotion.
