From her was born that god, Dharmarāja, who had assumed the state of a Śūdra due to the curse of Māṇḍavya.
Desiring to attain equality with Vasiṣṭha, he incurred sin by causing him to fall through his own will;
because of the fault of making an effort to obtain what was unattainable, he was indeed impaled upon a stake.
Even though the thief had already taken the object, Yama told him that he would suffer for the killing of the fly out of the mistaken belief that it was a thief. (11.132–11.133)
There was no falsehood in him regarding that matter; having spoken thus, he received a curse and consequently attained the status of a Śūdra.
Then Kṛṣṇa gave him a name and likewise bestowed upon him omniscience.
"Because you delight in knowledge (vidyā-rati), this one shall be named Vidura, endowed with the power of wisdom."
"He possesses a great bow and superior strength of arm, and is endowed with excellent conduct," Kṛṣṇa said.

(11.135) Then, having learned of his Śūdra status, his mother again bowed to Kṛṣṇa and entreated him, saying, "Beget another [son] upon Ambālikā. But Kṛṣṇa did not consent, and he became invisible. (11.136)
Then Bhīṣma duly performed the appropriate rites for them with the sages;
and Kṛṣṇa bestowed all branches of knowledge upon them, while Bhīṣma gave them the weapons and missiles of Pāṇḍu.
They became masters of all sciences, Vidura being especially a knower of everything.
The solitary hero Pāṇḍu, a wielder of the bow skilled in all weapons, conquered the entire earth.
Likewise, from the herd of cattle came the Sūta, and from him was born Tumburu, the sovereign lord of all Gandharvas.
He who is the Marut named Udvaha became his son, the self-controlled one known by the name Sañjaya. (11.138–139)

That son of a Sūta became the friend of Vicitravīrya and was dear to them all; being a disciple of Vyāsa, he possessed complete knowledge and wisdom, and especially followed the will of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. King [Śantanu] married the daughter of Subala, the king of Gāndhāra, named Gāndhārī.

The eldest son of Śakuni, the embodiment of Dvāpara and the cause of evil deeds characterized by atheism, gave his daughter—who was endowed with virtue, character, and beauty—to his friend’s son, Pṛthā, the daughter of Kuntibhoja; for that reason, she was called Kuntī, and she had been the wife of Pāṇḍu even in a previous birth. (11.141–142)
And Kunti, by name Marudeva, was raised properly by Kuntibhoja.
There, the highly irascible Śaṅkara Durvāsas arrived and said to him, "Hospitably entertain me.
"Live happily," he said, and she replied, "Om. Then, for the sake of service, she directed Kuntī toward Āṇsu.
That Pṛthā performed the work for the sage—who was indeed very prone to anger—in such a way that it could not be equaled by others, following him in body, speech, and mind. (11.144–11.145)
Having been duly worshipped by her for thirteen years, he taught her a supreme mantra capable of subduing all the gods. Then,
having bathed at her season, she sought to test the mind of that sage.
He challenged the Maker of Day, and he arrived at that very moment.
Then she was unable to dismiss him without sexual union;
despite her efforts with well-spoken words, Bhāskara nevertheless approached her.
There the all-pervading Lord himself was born in a second form, wearing divine armor and earrings, blazing as if with his own splendor;
this was because of the faults previously produced by the slaying of Vāli. (11.149)
He became surrounded by the asura named Sahasravarman;
for just as the minds of men are corrupted by the planets,
so too did the mind of the Sun’s son become defiled by the Daitya.
Nevertheless, due to his service to Rāma and his proximity to Hari, he became known by the name Karṇa because of his beautiful ear;
thus, placed within a casket filled with jewels, he was cast into the water. (11.152)
Out of fear of public scandal, she had quickly gone by way of the river's current to the sister of Yama; the son of the charioteer saw him there,
seized him along with his jewels, and made him his own son.
His body cherished by his charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā,
he grew up and mastered all the Vedas and all the Śāstras;
from childhood itself, being endowed with great strength and distinguished by his own virtues, he dwelt there.
She was indeed known as Vasuṣeṇā, for that wealth (vasu) was his; 11.155.
Then Kuntī was given to Pāṇḍu, and he too took pleasure with her for a long time.
Vidura married Āruṇī, who was born of a Śūdra woman from a Śūra, and who was rich in virtues. 11.156.

cxxiii. Then the lord of the Madras named Cartāyana, desiring a son equal to Śakra and longing for a jewel of a daughter, performed supreme Brahmanic austerity and obtained a boon. He was Sahlāda by name, the younger brother of Prahlāda, and a devotee of Hari. 11.157.
At the conclusion of the boon from Brahmā, that son of the king became possessed by the power of Vāyu.
By virtue of this infusion of Māruta and by the grace of the Creator, he became superior in strength upon the earth;
he was Śalya by name, a thorn to all his enemies, and he had a daughter named Mādrī. (11.158–159)
She had indeed been the wife of Pāṇḍu in a previous birth, and she was bestowed upon him once again.
And Śalya, a knower of all the scriptures, protected with righteousness the kingdom granted by his father.
Then, having obtained that pair of jewels among women, Pāṇḍu enjoyed pleasures according to his desire.
Relying upon righteousness and honoring his elder brother, he protected the earth according to the path taught by Vidura.

For Bhīṣma, having established Dhṛtarāṣṭra alone in the kingdom, made Pāṇḍu the crown prince; yet, because he was blind, Bhīṣma did not exercise sovereign power himself, nor did Pāṇḍu do so. (11.161–162)
Pāṇḍu, that peerless hero, always devoted to the words of Bhīṣma and Ambikā, ruled the earth;
then Ambikā’s son performed many sacrifices along with Pāṇḍu, using vast floods of wealth.
Vyāsa, whose noble qualities were exalted, spoke thus so that this conflict between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas might not endure.
He led his own mother to his own hermitage, and his two daughters-in-law followed her.

(11.164) Reflecting upon that Hari by means of the path taught by his son, with a mind fixed on his son and through the state of Brahman, he went to the supreme Vaiṣṇava station; and by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, his two daughters-in-law also ascended to heaven. (11.165)
That mother of Vidura, Ambikā, being virtuous, followed after the world of Brahmā;
through the grace of Vyāsa and by virtue of her son’s excellent qualities, she of noble intellect attained liberation in due time.
Ambālikā also, through the gradual application of yoga, reached the supreme goal, though not in quite the same manner as Ambikā. (11.166)

"In whatever manner the conscious self is devoted to Viṣṇu, in that very manner indeed is its course in the hereafter. (11.167) Thereupon, Pāṇḍu, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his elder and younger brothers, went to the forest.
Followed by his two wives, he dwelt at Badarī, which is protected by Nārāyaṇa. (11.168)
Living in the forest with his household in a hermitage, he enjoyed pleasures and performed austerities;
together with the lords of sages, filled with devotion, he worshipped the Lord of the World, the Consort of Ramā.
By fate, he [once] encountered a deer that had attained its state through desire, and a sage who was attached to worldly activities.
Having pierced the target, he attained the water; therefore, Pṛthā said, "You shall die joined with a woman," and he became distressed.
When told by Pṛthā that he should renounce the world, he replied, "No," and likewise remained there after offering his salutations.
Accompanied by those two, he went before the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa situated on Mount Śataśṛṅga.
Taking refuge at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, he practiced most intense austerity accompanied by those two [his parents],
his body perpetually purified by constant immersion in the waters of the celestial river, which were sanctified by contact with them.
At that very time, the gods headed by Brahmā and Śiva, led by Indra—

Unable to endure the assault by the evil-souled Daityas who had made their dwellings upon the earth, the Earth herself sought refuge with the God of gods— the unborn, the vast one whose form is the embodiment of the six perfections, reclining upon the coils of the serpent in the ocean of milk, his body a mass of incomparable bliss. (11.173)
Those led by the lotus-born Brahmā spoke with the *Puruṣasūkta* to this Supreme Person of infinite power:
"O Supreme Lord, the earth is distressed because it has been trampled by the foremost of demons; for those most wicked ones have turned their faces away from You.
O God, even for us who are virtuous, association with the wicked is always like a heavy burden; therefore, O Lord, hear our words. (11.174)
Formerly, the sons of Diti were slain by you in battles for our sake; now they have been born upon this earth.
In ancient times, there was a conflict between the supreme gods and the sons of Diti involving excellent elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
the celestial army consisted of hundreds of *akṣauhiṇīs*, a flood upon a flood, and was equipped with supreme weapons.
Therefore, the army of the great asuras became like a mighty torrent, most terrible, bearing rocks, mountains, and great weapons.
Their chariots were as numerous as many *lakhs*, filled with the excellent bows and arrows of the gods and asuras;
adorned with various garments, ornaments, attire, and superior weapons, those gods and asuras rushed at one another. (11.176–11.177)
They struck the surface of the king of mountains with fists, great missiles, and weapons, and they created rivers carrying floods of blood with their massive torrents.
There, in that battle, hundreds of the hosts of the lords of the asuras were slaughtered by the bulls among the gods with their powerful forces.
Then, seeing his own army being crushed, the asura named Śambara—
The illusory being, having obtained a boon from Umāpati, roamed about deluding the gods, for he was truly free from illusion.
Afflicted in battle by a thousand illusions, the gods, headed by the Moon and the Sun, fell into despair.
Seeing them thus, the wielder of the thunderbolt employed the supreme Vaiṣṇava lore given to him by Svayambhū.

By that very power of the Lord of Lakṣmī—which removes all illusion, which is eternal, and which is truly beyond comprehension—the illusions created by the lord of the Daityas were destroyed; and Varuṇa, Agni, Indra, and the others were liberated.
Then the gods, including Yama, Candra, Sūrya, and the rest, their prowess restored, slew the Asuras. (11.181)

Sureśvara, possessing formidable prowess, struck down Śambara many times with his thunderbolt, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt strikes. (11.182) When that guardian of the world of the Dānavas was slain, the sons of Diti fled, terrified of Indra.
The archer Vipracitti restrained them and pursued the foremost of the gods, headed by Śakra. (11.183)
Seeing that the best of gods had been struck down by the arrows of the invincible Creator himself,
and seeing Śakra rendered unconscious, Pavana quickly warded him off with a torrent of shafts;
having parried his weapons with his own superior missiles, he hurled a golden mace at his chest.
Shattered and driven by the force of the wind, that mighty one fell upon Mount Meru.

Then, by your command, that demon Kālanemi—who had previously received a boon from the Unborn One granting him invincibility against all—quickly approached; he was thousand-headed and possessed two thousand arms. (11.185–186)

Beholding him rushing forward, Māruti—having been granted a boon by you yourself and remembering that he was to be slain by you alone—then called to mind your presence; and so you, of infinite prowess, appeared before his very eyes.
As he rained down many missiles and weapons from his arms, his body filling the world, [Māruti struck him]. 11.187.
Having severed their arms with his discus, he quickly reported their wickedness to Yama.

Then those Asuras were slain without exception; three parts were destroyed by you, and the fourth part was struck down by Vāyu. Having been born again on the surface of the earth, they were endowed with the power of righteousness.
But for those kings born of noble lineage, their minds were free from evil and inclined toward the Dharma;
having received instruction from the best of the twice-born, they possessed at least some devotion to you.
One who performs good deeds, even if joined with only a fraction of devotion to you, shall by no means go to an evil destiny. (11.190) cxxvi.
O you whose desires are ever true, it was indeed by you alone that the realm of the lords of the Daityas was made blind with darkness.

Nevertheless, out of fear that dharma might become false, or from dread of the Daityas attaining auspiciousness, we entreat you to swiftly cause those sons of Diti— who perform good deeds— to fall away from their devotion to you.
He who was Ugrasena, the celestial singer, has been born among the Yadus under that very name;
and for the sake of serving you alone, O Lord, his son Kālanemi, an asura, was born—he who, though a supreme sovereign, was not slain by Vāyu for your pleasure through your grace. (11.193)
He, who was invincible to others by virtue of a boon from Umā’s Lord, was born again among the Bhojas; 11.194.

He was begotten by an Asura through illusion upon a woman of the Augraseni clan who had assumed that form by magic—a Gandharva son named Dramila—by whom Kaṃsa was defeated through a boon from the Lord of Śacī. 11.195.
Having conquered the Lord of Waters, he seized the jewels, and the Yakṣas were defeated by him for Śiva;
they had been dispatched by the Lord of Magadha for the sake of winning the maiden, but they were taken away by force.
That Vipracitti became Jarā’s son through a boon from Vidhātṛ and Giriśa.
Knowing him to be invincible by all and possessed of supreme strength, Kaṃsa joyfully gave him to Suta.

Though he was capable of restraining any arrogant man, there was no one who could withstand his power; he who was peerless on earth or in the subterranean realms brought all kings under his control by force. (11.197–11.198)

O Śivā, those two heroes formerly known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha, whom you yourself slew, have now been born as Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka; by virtue of a boon from Giriśa, they are invincible, yet they are devoted to Jarāsaṃdha.
Furthermore, other asuras who were born on earth and slain by you in the battle between the gods and the daityas have also been reborn. (11.199)

Others likewise fell into blinding darkness; you must likewise bring about their passage through that darkness. Kali, whom you struck down during your incarnation as Vyāsa by means of the very words of the excellent scriptures, has today, upon hearing your speech, fixed his mind slightly upon you, O Lord, while remaining among men.
O Lord, even those most wicked Rākṣasas who were slain by you in the form of Rāma, upon seeing your strength today,
do not consider anyone else to be equal to you;
and likewise, O Keśava, those who are filled with great reverence for you do not fall into the blinding darkness regarding Vāyu [Hanūmat] in the same way.

Therefore, those who are fit to enter that path must first be displaced from it by you; having caused them to be born upon the earth, and having produced extreme opposition to existence through many means, they—those Asuras preceded by Kali—must be cast down into the blinding darkness along with all the gods. 11.203–204.
Those two gatekeepers of yours, Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, whom you have slain, were indeed possessed by great asuras; they must now be liberated by you alone from their curse.
Those two who entered them as your enemies—those two daityas must be cast into blinding darkness. (11.205)
"O Supreme Lord, those two who were yours must be brought back by you to your own abode once more.
(11.206) That asura named Bali, who, having entered your own palace, acted with hostility toward us as well as toward you, O Lord—he has been born on earth as Sālva, the son of Brahmadatta. (11.207)
Therefore, that preeminent and indestructible celestial chariot made of illusion was obtained by him from the Lord of Mountains;
it is that very chariot which you, in the form of Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, have repeatedly put to flight.
He was not slain there even by the powerful one [Śiva]; rather, he is to be killed by me alone during my incarnation as Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, in order to fulfill his own resolve, that most wicked man must be slain by you here.
(11.209) When his father was the lord of Saubha, known by the name of Āruhya-vimāna, and when his father was defeated by Bhīṣma, then that Sālva remained established in ascetic penance. (11.210)
And today he has desisted from that asceticism and stands here by the will of Jarāsandha’s son;

he who was once an invincible great asura, having entered Bāṇa, and who remains there under the name of Bāṇa—though renowned by that name—he is now slayable by you and must be cast into fierce darkness. (11.211)
He was named Kīcaka; by virtue of a boon from Rudra, he was indestructible and could only be entered into by darkness.
Therefore, O Lord, you must descend to earth and perform all the tasks of the gods.
You alone, O Lord of Gods, are the refuge for the deities beginning with Brahmā, Īśa, Śakra, Indra, Candra, and Yama.
"You alone are the eternally risen, perfect power; you alone are the eternally risen, perfect mass of consciousness;
you alone are the eternally risen, perfect reality and bliss. Therefore, there is no one equal to You, much less anyone superior to You.
Thus addressed by the best of gods, he who is an ocean of noble qualities, whose form is the most unshakeable nectar, [remained unmoved].
Rising from there, he departed, accompanied by the gods and possessing a splendor like that of infinite moons, suns, and jewels.
Having reached Mount Meru, the Lord said to the Four-faced One: "Wherever I am told by you to appear, there I shall manifest in every way;
for by your devotion, I am subject to you, even though I am independent and act according to my own will."
Brahmā, having bowed, said to him: "In the past, I gave beautiful cows to Varuṇa as a personal gift.
His father, Kaśyapa, exceedingly arrogant, suddenly and forcibly seized them from him. He was indeed incited by his mother Aditi and likewise by Surabhi; thus were they taken away. (11.217)
Having heard this from the Lord of Waters, I cursed him, saying: "Become a cowherd among the Kṣatriyas.
Born of Śūra, he became exceedingly wealthy in cattle and was called Vasudeva on earth.
His wife was Aditi, who became Devakī, while Surabhi became his other wife, Rohiṇī.

Therefore, become quickly that son of Devakī; for he who is the Vasu named Droṇa has, with noble intent, performed intense penance along with his wife Dhara to obtain you as his father. To him, I have granted this boon, and he shall be known by the name Nanda, and she shall be his wife.
He who is known by the name Yaśodā is indeed the son of the cowherd Nanda, born of a Vaiśya woman.
Both Devakī and Vasudeva are performing penance, desiring a son of yours;
therefore, first manifest your own form there, and from there go to Vraja.
When this was said by the Lotus-born One, Keśava replied, "So be it," and spoke again to the deities:
"All of you, by my command, must quickly descend into the human world in accordance with your respective duties and as is fitting for each.
Then all the deities descended exactly as Hari had commanded them, each according to his own station.
Formerly, Vitteśvara was born from Bhauma, the son of Hari, by the will of that [Lord] even though he was an asura.
Indeed, the elephant named Supratīka, which had been granted by Śiva, was seized by that sinful one.
For that very purpose, his son was born as Dhaneśvara, known by the name Bhagadatta. (11.224–225)

That very son of Mahāsura, endowed with great power and weapons through the possession of Rudra, became the disciple of Mahendra; and when his father was slain, he remained ever devoted to his own duty.
He was the heroic Yadu leader named Śini, and from him was born his son Satyaka.
The dark fortnight was designated as Yuyudhāna, who was joined with a portion of Garuḍa.
That Marut named Saṃvaha became a portion of Viṣṇu’s discus; from him arose Hṛdika among the Yadus, and his son, born of a portion of Bhoja, became Śveta, the white fortnight. (11.227–228)
He was joined with Pāñcajanya among the Maruts, and likewise, that hero was joined with Aṃśa in the wind;
his name became Kṛtavarman. Furthermore, those other Yādavas who were there, along with the Gopas, were all gods and attendants of the gods who had become the allies of the Pāṇḍavas. (11.229)
But all other asuras are indeed middling; those who are non-human have unstable movements of intellect.
(11.230) For the characteristic mark of the gods is supreme devotion to Viṣṇu, while toward others there is opposition to him.
Therefore, among these, whoever are intent on devotion to Hari are gods, being especially filled with that [devotion]. (11.231)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Declaration of the Divine Incarnations," in the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
CXXX. (The Birth of the Pāṇḍavas) Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Oṃ! There was a Gandharva sage named Devaka; he came from Āhuka to serve Hari.
He was the younger brother of Ugrasena, and from him Devakī was born; she received that very name because of him.
Furthermore, among the other wives of Kaṃsa, Devakī—whom Āhuka had made his own daughter—was the eldest. Thus, Devakī became both the paternal aunt and the sister of Kaṃsa.
That very Aditi was given in marriage to Vasudeva; he himself then caused her auspicious chariot to proceed.
For at that time, Vāyu, stationed in the sky, spoke these words to him:
"O Viṣṇu, without fault, neither one greater than him nor his maternal uncle shall meet with death. (12.3)
Because he was conforming to the ways of the world, Vāyu spoke thus for the sake of opposing his parents:
"O fool! Death shall be your eighth son. Having been told this, she seized a sword;
but the son of Śūra, having handed over the other sons and released her, went home together with him.
The son of Śūra took the six younger sisters of those maidens as wives, and he rejoiced with them;

furthermore, the daughter of the Bāhlīka king had previously been taken by him, and Surabhi Rohiṇī was his wife from before. And according to the custom of a "sonless man’s son" (*putrikā-putra*), he married the daughter of King Kāṇsiprabhava.
By that same righteousness, he [the Lord] formerly gave his daughter to Karavīreśvara, and [gave] Diti and Danu [to Kaśyapa].

He who thinks, "I am indeed Viṣṇu," is that wicked Vena, Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva; born again from Śūra’s lineage into the wife of Kaṃsa, he is one who proclaims, "There is no Viṣṇu other than me. (12.7–12.8)

Dhundhu, the son of Madhu, who had been slain by Hari, was born from the daughter of Karavīreśvara; he was named Sṛgāla. Then Vāsudeva, having married Devakī, did not depart with her. Thus, those two became the constant enemies of the Vṛṣṇis as the two eldest sons of Śūra’s daughter.
And from other wives, Vasudeva, the omniscient one, obtained noble sons who were incarnations of the gods.
For all those gods who had come to earth were disciples of the son of Satyavatī;
having attained the knowledge of Viṣṇu, they all became omniscient according to their respective capacities.
cxxxi. Six sages were born from Marīci; they mocked Devaka for the sake of some gain.
Due to his curse, they performed ascetic penance to become incapable of being slain by the offspring of Kālanemi.
Dhātṛ granted them a boon and likewise cursed them: "Be born upon the surface of the earth. 12.12.
There, Hiraṇya, desiring boons from another, said, "Your own father shall be your slayer.
Then Durgā, impelled by the Blessed One, put them to sleep and drew them out from their bodies;
she gradually transferred them into the embryos of Devakī and slew Kaṃsa with them.
Then, accompanied by the lord of sages, he desired to enter the supreme assembly hall of the Creator;
but I restrained him at that time, for a man is born for a specific purpose, and that purpose remains unfulfilled for him. (12.15)
They certainly prevented him from proceeding to a fortunate rebirth;
for they sought to employ his beloved among the ranks of the principal deities.
Without her, that white elephant could find no auspicious destiny for him.
Otherwise, men who speak falsely regarding their sons go to a miserable state, just as Dharmabhūṣaṇa, the son of Sandhyakā, did;
at that time, Kali and the Rākṣasas, headed by Indrajit, came into being. 12.18.

For he was conceived in the womb of the beloved wife of the son of Vicitravīrya. His younger brother heard that he had been defiled by the lord of sages; having reflected upon this, he whose intellect was like that of Vāsudeva spoke thus to his beloved: 12.19–12.20ab. "He was indeed conceived in the womb of the beloved wife of the son of Vicitravīrya. His younger brother heard that he had been defiled by the lord of sages; having reflected upon this, he whose intellect was like that of Vāsudeva spoke thus to his beloved."
"Obtain a son who is superior even to my own virtues;
for without a son, the virtuous say that we have no auspicious path.
To this difficult request, Pṛthā gave her assent and spoke.
I possess this most excellent mantra, which subdues the gods and bestows sons;
there is no one among the gods equal to it, nor indeed anyone superior to you.
Therefore, by your command, whom else but a god could I invoke who is greater than you?
She who, having taken refuge in a husband, should go to one inferior to him, there is no atonement for her whatsoever; she does not reach the world of her husband.
In ancient times, the gods and the celestial nymphs did exactly so. (12.24)
Even in their thoughts, they never once imagined themselves apart from them;
for since time immemorial, those devoted wives had always been accompanied by their husbands in thought, word, and deed. (12.25–26)

Indeed, those women go together with their own husbands to liberation; having reached the end of their time, they became powerful celestial nymphs (apsarases). And likewise, they were unconfined and always had husbands according to their desire.

Therefore, those celestial women did not attain supreme liberation from their husbands; for when they were established otherwise by means of excessive provocations, an unbearable calamity would arise from that difficult consequence. (12.28–29)
"Although you have spoken what is improper, your word is nonetheless inviolable to me; therefore, name a god who can grant me a son.
Being thus addressed, the king replied, "There is no [attainment] of the earth without righteousness."
"The king shall become a protector; therefore, quickly summon that powerful lord. He, born of Dharma, shall indeed be a most righteous and excellent son.
When she had spoken thus, Yama, being summoned, went there swiftly.

And then, immediately thereafter, she gave birth to an excellent son, Yudhiṣṭhira; for Yama himself attained the state of being her own son. As soon as the twins were born from Kuntī, the daughter of Subala [gave birth].

Indeed, out of envy, she long ago destroyed her own embryo. When she had caused the miscarriage of her own fetus, Keśava, the son of Parāśara, went there and placed those [embryos] in jars, dividing them accordingly.
Divided into a hundredfold forms, there were a hundred Suyodhanas and others,
and day by day Duḥśalā became a hundred times greater than before.
Then the Lord protected that embryo for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods.
The lord Parāśarātmaja begot upon Vicitravīrya’s wife the son Suyodhana, who was born as Kali and possessed great strength of arm;
his superior strength was due to the proximity of the Pradhāna Vāyu. 12.37–38.
Long ago, on the summit of Mount Meru, the sons of Diti heard the words of the inhabitants of heaven concerning the emergence [of a being] intent upon the surface of the earth;
thereupon, they gratified the Three-eyed Lord through the power of their ascetic penance.
And that thorn in the side of the gods was indeed invincible from all sides by virtue of a boon from the Lord of Umā; thus Kali, that thorn in the side of the gods,
became Suyodhana, possessed of a body like adamant and endowed with great strength.
While Suyodhana was rising up as one who could not be slain by anyone, Indrajit emerged from a jar filled with ghee;
he then became Duḥkhaśāsana, born from Atikāya. 12.42.
He indeed was called Vikarṇa; from him was born the powerful Khara. He was named Citrasena, and other sons of Vicitravīrya were likewise born as Rākṣasas of fierce prowess.
For those embodied beings were indeed the embodiment of all defects;
she who was known by the name Duḥśalā became the Asurī Mṛṣā, who, joined with Kuhū, was destined for the slaughter of Arjuna. (12.45)
Austerity was performed for the sake of the Trident-bearer; therefore, she was born here. From her, the Saindhava arose as the cause of his slaughter;
that Kālakeya Dānava had been on the earth for that very purpose.
Likewise, that younger brother named Nirṛtha was born of Nirṛti;
he was skilled and named Yuyutsu, begotten by the wind from the nose [of Dhṛtarāṣṭra].
And he was born of the seed of Ambikā, immediately after Suyodhana.
A son born from the womb of a Vaiśya maiden became dear to Hari.

When Yudhiṣṭhira was born, Pāṇḍu said: "By the strength of my arms and by the power of my knowledge, Dharma is to be protected; otherwise, it does not endure. Therefore, quickly procreate a son endowed with these two strengths. (12.49–12.50)
For the horse-sacrifice is the greatest among sacrifices; the sun is indeed the most radiant among all things visible to men;
the Brahmin is the best among the social orders by virtue of all his qualities; and Vāyu is the foremost among the gods—save for the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Moreover, he is especially my father and my lord, Viṣṇu of infinite prowess, in the form of Vyāsa. (12.51)

"Therefore, your father-in-law is not at all fit to give his son; go instead to Vāyu, that lord. When Pṛthā had spoken thus, by the mere touch of the summoned Vāyu, two sons were born who were equal to him—there is no one in the world equal to them—and who were devoted to Viṣṇu and under the control of the Blessed One.
He indeed became the Wind-god himself, who had been sustained here under the name Bhīma, for all the elements were contained within him.
Since he was always joined with Viṣṇu and Īśa, he was therefore named Sena; thus he became Bhīmasena.
At the mere moment of his birth, the earth split apart when he was snatched from his mother’s arms out of fear of the tiger.
That entire mountain named Śataśṛṅga fell down, utterly pulverized by him.
When he was born, the great Asuras, together with their mounts and armies, vomited forth blood;
and all the kings belonging to his faction, as well as the Asuras and Rākṣasas, were then struck with fear.

Vṛkodara grew up right there in the forest, greatly increasing the joy of the gods; at that very time, Śeṣa, urged by Hari, entered the womb of Devaka’s daughter. Having stayed there for three months, he was carried away by Durgā and placed into the womb of Rohiṇī.

Then, having stayed there for seven months with Keśava, who was joined [to her], he was born upon the earth (12.58). He was named Baladeva and became endowed with great strength; after him, the Lord Janārdana appeared here in the daughter of Devaka, perfected by all excellent qualities (12.59).

He who has as his sole body the power of true bliss and knowledge, who is forever untouched by any defect, and whose body is not composed of the unmanifest or its effects—indeed, that Hari is unborn, for his body does not arise from anywhere or consist of anything;
yet it is falsely said that his body was born from Śukla and Raktā, even though he is called their son. 12.60.

That He of stainless nature manifested from her body for the delusion of the world—having first entered Vasudeva alone, He then entered [Devakī] specifically during her fertile period; He dwelt there with the Goddess for seven and a half months, and thereafter, even though He is unborn, He appeared. (12.61–62)
Just as in the past he manifested from a pillar in the form of Nṛsiṃha, though neither white nor red, so too Kṛṣṇa, though unborn, deludes [the world] precisely through the lineage of his parents;
he conforms to the paternal lineage for the sake of delusion, yet not thereby [is he] white or red. 12.63.
He was seen with his body manifest for all to behold, bearing the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace;

adorned with a crown possessing the luster of many suns, wearing earrings with the brilliance of lightning, clad in yellow garments, and garlanded with forest flowers—shining with the great splendor of the rising sun, he appeared as an ocean of bliss. (12.64–65)
Praised by the gods headed by Kañca-yoni, as well as by his father and mother, he spoke to Śūra’s son:
"Take me to the house of Nanda. Thereupon Janārdana became two-armed.
At that very moment, by the command of Hari, the goddess named Durgā was born from the wife of Nanda.
Then, taking that horse, the son of Śūra went from Nanda’s house to Hari at midnight.
Having deposited him there in that very same manner, he took the maiden and returned again to his own home.
Having killed six embryos of his sister in succession, what eighth one did he kill there when he went to her? (12.67–68)
The people indeed considered the child in Devakī’s womb to be the seventh, but he [Kaṃsa] thought that son was the eighth;
thus, seizing him by the feet, he dashed him against the surface of a stone slab.
But that goddess, quickly leaping from his hand, appeared in the sky with all eight of her arms.
Being worshipped by Brahmā and all the other gods, the beloved of Hari, possessing a most wondrous form, spoke:
"O noble one, your death shall occur right here; for you have been born in vain, O sinner!
You wish to slay me, who am innocent; this effort of yours is directed toward an impossible task. (12.70–71)
Having spoken thus to Kaṃsa, Durgā, in her very form as a child, lay down once more upon the bed of Devakī.
No one there recognized her, except for her parents, who were rich in virtue.
Upon hearing what she had said, Kaṃsa immediately felt remorse and [sought out] Vasudeva along with his wife.
Casting aside their anger, the two of them spoke to him again and again, saying:
"O lion among kings, there is no other creator of happiness or sorrow than Vāsudeva.
Then, having summoned his own ministers to his house, he related the entire message of the maiden.
Having heard this, those utterly wicked men said, "The death of children must be carried out by all means. Saying "So be it," that sinful man dismissed them there and entered his own home.
And they, whose nature was always such, remained constantly engaged in the slaughter of children, intent upon their sport.
Then at dawn, Yaśodā and Nanda beheld Kṛṣṇa lying upon his bed, his eyes as broad as lotus petals; he was of immeasurable form, dense with bliss.
From this they recognized him as their own son, the Creator and Lord whose origin is the lotus-born Brahmā. (12.76)
With his heart full from the great festival, Nanda then gave a hundred thousand cows to the Brahmins (12.77).

Furthermore, the lord of the cowherd community gave many gold coins, jewels, garments, and ornaments; then the cowherds approached him with offerings in their hands, and the women joyfully went to see Yaśodā (12.78).
When some days had passed in that very place, Nanda went to the house of Kamsa.
For previously, having departed from the great forest to pay his tax, Nanda had encountered Kṛṣṇa.
Yaśodā, who had come along with him at that time, gave birth to Durgā there, and then Śauri [arrived].
Having entrusted Kṛṣṇa and received the maiden, Nanda went home and dwelt there. Having stayed on that bank of the Yamunā for a month, he departed, desiring to see the king.
Then, seeing that he had paid tribute to the king, the son of Śūra beheld him and spoke these words to him.
When it was announced, "Whatever portents exist there," Nanda went quickly to the Yamunā.
While Nanda was still not yet arrived at night, Kaṃsa’s nurse went to the cow-pen.
Disguising her own true form, that woman named Pūtanā appeared at night with a beautiful appearance.

He entered the house of Nanda, which had been prepared on the road for his journey at the edge of the great forest. There, on the bank of the Yamunā, he took up that Supreme Person who was lying in the cloth-cradle; while his mother Yaśodā slept, she watched him as if she were auspicious sleep itself.

Overpowered by her illusion and by sleep, Nanda’s wife did not prevent him at all; the Lord Janārdana, the Master, quickly drank the breast offered by her along with his own life-breaths. (12.85) Having died, she fell down in her own terrifying form, pervading the entire forest.
Then Nandagopa also arrived there, and upon seeing [the scene], they were all utterly amazed.
(12.86) That Tāṭakā, having been entered by Urvaśī, went to hell because she was incapable of being slain by Kṛṣṇa;
but that Urvaśī, purified by the breast of Kṛṣṇa’s suckling, departed for heaven at that very moment. (12.87)
Having come into contact with Tumburu, she entered the body of a Rākṣasa due to the curse of the Lord of Wealth;

but through the touch of Kṛṣṇa, her form became pure again and she went to heaven. When the Lord of Ramā is pleased, what is unattainable? When four months had passed, the ceremony of taking him out of the house was performed for him.

On that very day, at dawn, his birth-star was in the ascendant, and a great festival took place there. At that time, as he was lying beneath the cart, he kicked the demon with his foot in order to kill him; having entered the cart, that most wicked son of Diti remained there to oppose Hari. (12.89–12.90)

The cart, named Śakaṭākṣa, being thrown by Viṣṇu, fell down together with him; its limbs shattered, it perished instantly, and the cart’s wheels and axle became disarrayed. With apprehension, Yaśodā hurriedly took up Kṛṣṇa and [comforted him] with the well-spoken words of the best of the twice-born.
Then, having arrived from the riverbank and urged by the words of Nanda, she bathed him.
Having slain that Kaṃsa along with his servants, Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of all, lay down again like an infant.
Thus the Lord dwelt there, delighting the cowherds with the diversions of childhood play.
As Kṛṣṇa grew up, seen by all the world, Pāṇḍu spoke these words again to Pṛthā:
"Our eldest son was the most righteous, and another was the eldest of the two in strength.
When he alone becomes endowed with supreme power, then, through him, we shall overcome our enemies. (12.94)
If the city were being set in motion [for war], others might seize those two by theft; therefore, these two are suitable for this purpose.
(12.95) My other son is a hero skilled in weapons and missiles; he would challenge such a god.
As for the remainder, your brother's son is of noble birth, and therefore he is not fit for the giving of a son. (12.96)

A nine-headed *suparṇa* is born among men as one who bestows the pressed soma; yet, because he is thus ignorant, Hari formerly created him as one of mixed nature (*saṅkara*) and wrathful, unfit for the task of protection.
Therefore, the mighty Mahendra, the self-ruling lord who stands immediately after them, deserves to be summoned here. 12.97.
Thus addressed, she quickly summoned Vāsava; then Śakra himself was born.
He was named Arjuna, endowed with human qualities, possessed by Viṣṇu, powerful, and a master of weapons.
When her husband spoke of another son being born, Kuntī said "No" to him on account of dharma.
Formerly, Bṛhaspati, filled with the power of the wind, went to serve the feet of Hari;
he was born as the wise one named Uddhava from the Yadu hero Upagava. [Hari thought:
"May Hari not again make me, who am of the nature of a *droṇa*, his servant. (12.100)
That Uddhava, whose soul was [one with] the Supreme Person, descended among the Yādavas for the sake of serving the Puruṣottama.
As a minister, he was skillful and a knower of all things; from Bṛhaspati himself, he acquired all branches of knowledge.
After three years had passed, Sātyaki was born on that same day, and Cekitāna was born as well. (12.101–102)
Among the Yadus, there was one named Pratīpa, who became known as Cekitāna for the sake of serving Hari.
At that very time, Hṛdika’s son was also born; three years later came Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, after another year, when the burden of the earth had been removed, Giriśa was born to attain the status of being a limb of Hari.
Because that high-souled one, upon being born, made the sound of a horse's neigh, he was named Aśvatthāman by name.
He was all-knowing, powerful, and a master of weapons; he was born to the sister of Kṛpa from the seed of Droṇa.
On the fourth day after his birth, Duryodhana was born, and on the following day, the very resolute Bhīmasena.
When the two pairs were born, then Baladeva was born under Rohiṇī—he who was powerful, rich in virtues, and all-knowing; he who, untiring in service, had previously become Lakṣmaṇa before Hari.
For when these two were bound together by a chain of fetters in order to slay their sons, [they remained steadfast]. (12.106)

Kaṃsa, the evil-minded son of Ugrasena, separated Devakī and the wives of Śūra from their husbands; 12.107 / for the sake of determining which of the sons born of Devakī’s womb were the [true] others, he placed other wives who were pregnant in different locations until their delivery. 12.108 / He, Kaṃsa, was the one.
12.108 / [He] of most wicked intent stationed them in various places until their birth. 12.108 /
For this reason, the goddess Rohiṇī was stationed by him in the house of Nanda for the sake of giving birth;
she obtained a son in Gokula, Balabhadra, who was exceedingly radiant with a face as lovely as the full moon.
When that god had become three months old, the unborn Puruṣottama appeared.
Desiring to obtain Kṛṣṇa and Śeṣa as their two sons, Devakī and the son of Śūra (Vasudeva) performed austerities.
And Rohiṇī [prayed], "May he who is possessed by Viṣṇu, who is powerful and superior in qualities, be my son.
Therefore, Śeṣa, joined with Hari and the white-haired one (Brahmā), was born from Devakī and Rohiṇī.
That son of Rohiṇī, possessed of hair as fair as Hari’s, grew up in Gokula;
Kṛṣṇa too, accompanied by Balarāma, delighted the cowherd settlement while displaying his playful charms. To show himself to his mother, who knew him to be but an ordinary child, he—
Once, as he was yawning, the Lord revealed everything situated within himself.

Yaśodā beheld within his body the cosmic egg, enveloped by the great elements, the mind, ego, and primordial nature (prakṛti), along with Brahmā and the other gods, auspicious beings, and hosts of men and demons. (12.113–114)
Terrified, the Lord of Ramā closed his eyes and then hid himself;

yet, making known his own perfect form—which is of the nature of bliss and consciousness—he revealed it to the virtuous ones. (12.115) Once, while Yaśodā was fondling him, she was unable to carry him, distressed by the excessive weight.

When the Daitya, having placed him upon the surface of the earth, performed his own ritual, a most terrible being named Tṛṇāvarta arrived with his attendants. Having created a fierce whirlwind, he seized that infant and went into the sky; struck by that wind, his breath was obstructed by a grip upon his throat.
Struck by Kṛṣṇa, Tṛṇāvarta, whose body was as lofty as a mountain, fell upon the surface of a rock;
and then those people were filled with great wonder upon seeing Tṛṇāvarta with his limbs completely pulverized.
Keśava did not become angry, but for the sake of showing grace, he struck him down with a blow more auspicious than what he deserved.
The Lord, an ocean of His own true bliss, moved about treading upon butter and other such things while they were being prepared;
in that year, during the month of Bhādrapada, when Jupiter and the Sun were in Leo, the Supreme Lord was born.
Then, in Phālguna, the month of Phalguna appeared, and after that had passed, Mādravatī spoke.

"O you whose sons have been born as the most excellent, I alone among the daughters of Pṛthā am childless; therefore, by your grace, may I too become a mother of sons. Grant this to me, O Kuntī, who gave me the mantra.
Thus addressed, he said to Pṛthā, "Bestow upon Mādrī that most excellent mantra which grants sons."

Having spoken thus, the daughter of Yadu said to her husband, "I would give [the fruit] for your sake, so that it might bear fruit once. He replied to Mādrī, "Take this mantra that grants sons; there will be no further fruit for you.
Having received the mantra, the daughter of Madra reflected, "How might I become the mother of two sons? (12.122–123)
"The two Aśvins among the gods are ever inseparable, for there is never any difference between their names;
they share a single wife, Uṣas, and because she comes to them both at once, they are two. Thinking thus, she summoned those two Aśvins, who arrived swiftly as her sons born of her. (12.124)
Those two very gods became Nakula, born first, and Sahadeva, the younger; they were the twins.
(12.125) Furthermore, for the sake of making her womb fruitful, Mādrī entreated her husband;
thus addressed, Pṛthā said: "This woman is deceitful; without my permission, she has summoned the two Aśvin gods. (12.126)

"Therefore, O King, you ought not to employ me again, fearing that she might cause discord among my sons. Thus addressed, the lord of the earth fell silent. (12.127) It was understood by those two that the gods would grant them daughters when invoked by their specific names, even though no such distinction had been made [in the original command].
He addressed them by their specific names, for it is said that there is a repetition of mantras when the name is changed.
(12.128) Vāyu entered into the four beginning with Yudhiṣṭhira, and especially into Phalguna.
He entered Yudhiṣṭhira in a gentle form, and Dhananjaya in a heroic form. (12.129)
Manifesting only the form of passion (*śṛṅgāra*), Vāyu entered the two sons of Yama as the primary element;
for Pāṇḍu, desiring the exclusive state of passion, lusted after his fourth son.
The form of passion entered Nakula especially, while the form of wise policy (*sunīti*) entered Sahadeva. (12.130)
By all his virtues, Vāyu himself became Bhīma, the inner soul of the world.
(12.131) For one whose body has the form of a well-flowered tree and is tender is generally called "handsome" by people;
therefore, even Bhīma and Arjuna, who possessed bodies like excellent adamant, desired Pāṇḍu’s daughter because she was so well-born. (12.132)

The supreme form of the non-ordinary ones, which is enchanting and endowed with the thirty-two marks, was that very same one; Māruta, Nakula, and Komalābha—thus the Wind-god existed here in five forms. Those past Indras, with Viṣṇu as the sixth, included this former Indra named Yajña, the Lord of Ramā.
Kṛṣṇa was indeed Vāyu, Bhīmasena was the second, and Dharma was the third;
Yudhiṣṭhira was that [Dharma], and then the two Nāsatyas and Dasras were respectively these two sons of Mādravatī.
Purandara was the sixth, and he alone was the seventh here as Phalguna; for these Indras are truly one. 12.134–135.
Having gradually received the sacraments of the Kṣatriyas, they grew strong by their own power and in their greatness;
all were omniscient, endowed with all virtues, devoted to Keśava, and exceedingly disciplined.
(12.136) Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the twelfth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Pāṇḍavas," [ends here].
(cxlii.kaṃ savadhaḥ)
Now begins the thirteenth chapter. Om! Garga, the priest of the Sātvatas, returned to Vraja at the word of Śūra’s son;
he performed the purificatory rites appropriate for Kṣatriyas for the two sons of Rohiṇī and Kṛṣṇa. 13.1.
"He said, 'This son of yours is Viṣṇu; he is not inferior to you in any quality. All these protectors, beginning with you, shall attain exalted happiness.
Having been told this, he rejoiced, and Garga departed; then Keśava, the primordial one, [remained].
Accompanied by his elder brother, he performed meritorious deeds as he traveled toward Vraja.
Once, while his mother was acting out the state of childhood for him, that Supreme Lord, in order to remove her [false] notion, struck the clay in the sight of his companions. (13.3–13.4)
Reproached by his mother, the Lord said, "Mother, I have eaten clay," and opening his mouth,
he showed her within it the entire world, joined with its primary and secondary constituents.
Thus the God displayed his supreme power, which is inconceivable and difficult for others to attain.

Once more, the Blessed One, as if to conceal from those who had already realized the truth of the Self, covered them with his own power. Thus, that Lord Hari, the infinite wealth of bliss and consciousness, wandered through the circle of the cowherd settlement, playfully mimicking the ways of the world.
Once, while drinking milk from Yaśodā’s breast, the Lord was left by her to set down the boiled milk;
he broke a vessel of curd. As that curd was being churned, it produced a mass resembling the moon. 13.7. He [took hold of] that which had arisen from the churning curd, which was like the moon.
For the Lord took up what was brought as fresh and ate it in private.
Indeed, the conduct of those dwelling in heaven at their birth follows the manner of the family, the age, and the time in which they are born. 13.8–13.9.

Thus, demonstrating his own supreme dharma among the denizens of heaven, Janārdana, though he is the fire of unrighteousness, acts as a mere imitation; he assumes the forms of humans, animals, and so forth, as well as the states of childhood, youth, and the rest. (13.10) cxliii.
Although he is eternal, he performs various actions arising from those respective forms;
13.11 / appearing in the forms of a brahmin, a king, and a cowherd, he at each occasion engages in such activities, instructing the gods. 13.12 /
Nevertheless, the unborn Lord, desiring to manifest His own power— which is equal to that of no other deity—
repeatedly displays His qualities. Then, seeing His mother with her staff taken away, the Teacher of the World [spoke].
The woman leaped after him, far beyond the range of the mind; then, perceiving his exhaustion, the Lord of wide strides (Urukrama) went to take her hand,
desiring to manifest his subjection to his devotees.

I quickly attempted to bind the Lord, who is eternally liberated, with a rope; yet the rope provided by the cowherd girl was not sufficient for him. Even the entire collection of ropes, when well-fastened together, remained incomplete. (13.16)
The Lord, who displays his childhood within his infinite form, having again playfully demonstrated his fitness for bondage,
went to another cowherd boy's hut while supporting the entire universe. (13.17–13.18)
Demonstrating that even a son is subject to his mother’s will, the Lord shattered those two sons of the gods, Yama and Arjuna, who reached for the heavens;
likewise in the past, he destroyed Dhuni and Cumu, together with Pūtanā. (13.19)
Anokṣaṇ and Saṃyuta performed austerities directed toward Śivā;
by her, a boon was granted, including invincibility against four [classes of beings]. Immediately thereafter, Tṛṇabindu practiced austerities and obtained that same boon.
Those three were slain by Viṣṇu in his form as a child:
Dhuni and Cumi, who had taken refuge in two trees, were destroyed by him through the breaking of those trees;
for those two trees had originated from a curse. (13.21–22)
Formerly, in the presence of Nārada, he cursed the two sons of the Lord of Wealth, saying: "May you two quickly attain the state of trees!
Thereupon, those two auspicious ones regained their own bodies through the grace of Hari.
Having offered praise to the Lord, they returned home;
having released Nala and Akūbara from the curse, Vāsudeva was then beheld by the astonished cowherds. 13.24–25.
Desirous of going to Vṛndāvana, that son of Nanda created from the pores of his skin wolves equal in strength to tigers within the great forest.
Oppressed by those hosts numbering many millions, the inhabitants of Vraja [were tormented].
Taking the eternally blissful Nandaja [Kṛṣṇa] with him, he went to Vṛndāvana. 13.27.
The Lord of Indirā, the Master who is full of bliss, delighted Nanda and the others in Vṛndāvana with his unrestrained activities. 13.28.
Joined by the son of Rohiṇī, whose face was as radiant as the moon and who possessed the luster of the moon itself, he became a cowherd boy. That immortal one,
seizing the Daitya Kaṃsa— who had assumed the form of a calf and was unslayable by others except through the boon of Hara— together with his followers, [slew him].
Having thrown [the bird] onto the head of the tree, Baka also, accompanied by his followers, struck Kaṃsa; then he approached the Lord Acyuta.
He placed the armor that had been granted by Skanda upon his mouth, but Govinda consumed him intensely like fire.
Seeing him approaching to strike with his very beak, the Lord seized his beak as he was about to vomit it out. (13.30–13.31)

Lord Kṛṣṇa, seizing the two beaks of the bird-demon with his sprout-like hands, swiftly tore them apart while being praised by Brahmā and the other gods who showered flowers; then, accompanied by his elder brother, he returned to the lands of Vraja in the evening.
Thus, with the lotus feet of that Lord worshipped by the best of gods, He spent His sixth year wandering upon the earth among the cowherds.
Although he was the lord of all cows, he became their protector within the dense canopy of creepers in Vṛndāvana.
(13.33) Sometimes, leaving his elder brother behind, that one of inconceivable power, accompanied by the cows, cowherds, and the multitude of calves, took delight in the waters of the Yamunā.
Indeed, foreseeing the future suffering of the cowherds, he placed himself among the foremost of them in order to cause their distress. (13.34)

Recognizing that the serpent was invulnerable to all because of the power of Brahmā’s boon—its potency of venom being irresistible except by Suparṇa—he [the Nāga King] protected even his fellow creatures and his friends who were on the verge of death from drinking water tainted by that poison. Suddenly drenched by the divine nectar of his gaze, they all regained their lives and climbed back up the high branches. (13.35)
“Kṛṣṇa, having climbed the exceedingly high Kadamba tree, then leaped down with his loincloth tightly fastened into the pool of poison.

(13.36) The pool of snake-venom, its waters surging with the rising fumes of the poison from the serpents agitated by the force of the fall of that preeminent man, overflowed—terrifying with waves made bitter by venom—for what is that [distance] to one of infinite strength? It was but a hundred bow-lengths. (13.37)

Having encountered that serpent Kāliya, who was sporting in the pool of the Yamunā, the ignorant snake, along with his own intoxicated followers, bound Vāsudeva with his coils; yet the Lord endured that offense against him, even though he was devoted. (13.38) But then, perceiving that calamity, the entire assembly of cowherds arrived there, even though they had been warned by the wielder of the plow.
Seeing the great suffering of his many dependents, Kṛṣṇa did not crush this serpent, even though he was his devotee.
(13.39) Kṛṣṇa danced upon that serpent’s lofty hoods while being praised by Brahmā and others who showered him with flowers.
Vomiting blood profusely from his mouths in agony, the serpent went in his mind to Nārāyaṇa, his refuge. (13.40)

Seeing the king of serpents—whose parasol-like hoods were shattered by his variegated and violent dance, who was vomiting blood, and whose great pride was utterly crushed—the wives of that serpent approached the Lord of the Earth, the primordial teacher of the entire world, and bowed before him.
(13.41) Praised by them and by him, the Blessed One granted him freedom from fear; then, restrained by Yama’s brother, he [the serpent] led him away.

Having released the Yamunā, whose waters were now free of poison, his deeds were praised by the gods, Siddhas, and Sādhyas. The lotus-eyed Lord, having joined with the cowherds led by Balarāma who were filled with overflowing joy,
stayed that night there on the bank of the Yamunā and drank the ever-present forest fire and its fierce strength for the sake of Vraja.

Thus, while Aja— who possesses inconceivable divine deeds and immeasurable great power— was engaged in Gokula performing these acts for the sake of the inhabitants of Vraja, the demon named Ugra, having assumed the form of a tree, caused them great distress. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.6–7)

46. From the scent of that [tree], O King, all beings, from the chief of men to the beasts, met with death, being afflicted by a severe disease. By the boon of the Creator, that Daitya in the form of a tree had become focused solely on the destruction of the world; he could not be harmed by anyone. When Saṅkarṣaṇa was also overcome by that noble poison, Kṛṣṇa, through his own touch, freed him from the disease.
Having used his strength, he shattered that poison-tree along with all its followers who possessed its very form;
and having struck down the Daityas in the shape of cows—who had received boons from Viriñca and were even immune to death—he burned the trees.
Having sported in the waters of the Yamunā together with Rāma, the lotus-navelled Lord restored Vraja to health.

Having slain the seven extremely powerful and invincible sons of the chief of the Daityas, who had been granted boons by Giriśa, the Lord obtained as his daughter Nīlā, the daughter of Yaśodā’s brother named Kumbhaka.
She, in her previous birth, had performed penance with the sole thought: "May I become his first wife; may there be union with him. 13.48.
It may be that among all excellent women, he first obtained her at the birth of Kṛṣṇa;

for she was the one whom Nīla married first because of her status as a twice-born woman, while even the cowherd women had previously requested this boon, and those who were formerly supreme *apsarases* had prayed that they might be united with him first through the sacrament of marriage. (13.49–13.50)
Then his companions said to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, "Please let us eat the ripe, excellent fruits of the palm trees.
Thus requested, Balarāma went toward that grove of palms which was exceedingly difficult for the cowherds to approach because of Dhenuka.
Having obtained a boon from the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), that wicked demon had become long-lived, possessed of supreme strength, and a lover of slaughter.
That ever-proud one, seeing Rāma dropping fruits from his palm-leaf fan, rushed toward him;
as he sought to strike him, [Rāma] quickly seized his hind legs and severed the head of that "king of grasses" (the palm tree).
When that most cruel demon in the form of a donkey was slain, all the other donkeys residing within the grove of palm trees [fled].
They reached Kṛṣṇa, the enemy of the harsh-natured Rākṣasas, who was accompanied by Balarāma; and by him they were all slain.

Having destroyed all those Daityas who had assumed the forms of donkeys and who were incapable of being killed by other men due to a boon from the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), the Lord of Ramā, overflowing with the quality of irresistible prowess, gave the ripe, excellent fruits of the palm trees to his own people.
While the cowherds were dwelling in two separate groups, the demon named Pralamba, having been dismissed by Kaṃsa, arrived.
As Kṛṣṇa’s side was victorious, that wicked one approached Rāma; being defeated, he of fierce form carried him away.
Praised by the terrified son of Rohiṇī, Hari bestowed upon him his own possession for the sake of fulfilling his strength.
With his strength replenished by that very act, he struck the wicked Pralamba, who moved through the air, with a massive fist until he was slain.
(13.56) When he had been killed, the hosts of gods and Hari, filled with great satisfaction, bestowed the name Baladeva upon Rāma.
Furthermore, the ocean of immeasurable virtues drank the fire as it blazed intensely, and he protected the cowherds and the herd of cattle. (13.57)
Once, when Kṛṣṇa had gone very far away, his companions said to him in a plaintive manner, "We are exceedingly tormented by hunger.
He, whose every desire was already fulfilled, replied, "The hosts of Brahmins are performing a sacrificial session here; go and beg from them.
Having reached them but not obtaining their wish, the cowherds returned once more to Kṛṣṇa; then that divine being spoke to them.

"By my word, provide for your wives," he said; and they did so. Yet even those women attained the Blessed One. (13.59) Having come together with their hands filled with the six kinds of food, and having abandoned their husbands, sons, and all their kinsmen, they arrived.
Among them, one woman—whose sole devotion was to her own worship and who had been cast off by her husband—attained the station of Viṣṇu. (13.60)
Then, having eaten that food together with the cowherds, the Blessed One, the Lord of the universe, rejoiced upon reaching Gokula.
O brahmins, although their minds were deeply tormented by the transgression they had committed in disobeying his command, they remained there.
Then Kṛṣṇa, observing the great effort of Indra, restrained the cowherds so that he might not forget him.
"Let them not perceive me as a mere human"—thinking thus, the Imperishable Lord brought about the destruction of his pride.
By means of the pretext of saying to those cowherds, "The mountain festival is our great duty," he caused them to descend to his own festival;
having assumed an exceedingly vast body, he enjoyed the offerings along with them, together with the qualities of various kinds of food, flavors, and drinks. (13.62–63)
Then Indra, having forgotten his descent as the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), commanded the clouds to pour down a mass of heavy rain.
Urged on, they released torrents like the trunks of great elephants for the destruction of the entire Gokula.
Seeing the whole of Vraja oppressed by them, that lotus-navelled one (Kṛṣṇa) forcibly held up the best of mountains.
With his left hand alone, which was as tender as a lotus petal, he allowed all the cattle to enter there by their own horns.

(13.65) Then, having seen that Vraja had been protected without effort by Hari after seven nights of incessant heavy rain, Śakra—recollecting the descent of the foremost of the gods—sought refuge at the lotus feet of the Lord of the Yadus. (13.66)

And he praised him—who was an ocean of countless, ever-perfect virtues—with words drawn from the Upanishads (the head of the vast Veda), for he was the foremost of the foremost, the teacher of even Hara’s teacher, endowed with a multitude of rays, and possessed of a thousandfold depth.
From you, whose splendor is immeasurable, the entire world has emerged; you alone protect it all, and at the end, [you swallow it].
"Indeed, you alone bring about the bondage and liberation of this world; there is no one equal to you anywhere, O Lord of perfect power.
(13.68) "O Lord, my childishness must surely be forgiven by you, for I am always seeking refuge in you"—thus was the Unborn One (Aja) praised.
"I have always forgiven you for the sake of your instruction; this act of yours was merely a method for testing my devotion," said the Lord of Ramā (Rameśa). (13.69)
Having consecrated this Govinda, he departed with his herds of cows after bowing down to that one who is full of virtues;
and even the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), having approached him along with the cowherds, bowed down to him whose doubts regarding the lifting of Govardhana had been resolved.
From that time forward, the groups of cowherds recognized Kṛṣṇa as Nārāyaṇa, both from the words of Garga and from Nanda.
Having heard it said that he was equal to Nārāyaṇa, the lotus-eyed one performed even greater worship for him.

(13.71) Seeing the mighty Pralamba—who had obtained a boon from Skanda, who was free from death, and who moved about unslain—[the cowherds] reached the conclusion that he surpassed the gods; they then offered him the highest honor. (13.72)

Devoted to the vow of Kātyāyanī for the sake of obtaining a husband, the Blessed One married other young girls; and others, pierced by the arrows of the god whose shafts are odd in number, were brought to him at night under the light of the moon shining upon the sky. From them, he begot there ten lakhs of sons, powerful cowherds known by the name of Nārāyaṇa.
All the hosts of deities descended to the surface of the earth for the sake of attaining the status of being sons of the Blessed One and for the purpose of devotion to Hari.
There, because of his previous granting of boons, the Lord of Ramā caused them all to rejoice even before their attainment of the twice-born state;
for the Blessed One, untainted by inauspiciousness, is indeed a wish-fulfilling gem that grants the accomplishment of every desired goal throughout the nights.

On a beautiful night, resplendent with the rays of the full moon, in Vṛndāvana where the breeze was fragrant with water-lilies and jasmine, the cowherd women fainted upon hearing the essence of the song issuing from the mouth of Mukunda;
there, the Yakṣa Śaṅkhacūḍa arrived—he who had been granted protection by the grace of Rudra, yet was his friend’s powerful and most wicked servant. (13.76)

While Kṛṣṇa was counting those [demons], Ariṣṭa, who was invincible even though he possessed the form of a bull, came to the cow-pen; he acted contrary to the ways of the Wide-strider (Viṣṇu) and followed Kaṃsa constantly due to a boon from Śambhu. As he was terrifying the cows and the people, Kṛṣṇa challenged him with a swift call. By striking him with the sole of his foot, the Blessed One brought about his death and took away Maṇimat’s jewel. (13.77–78)
He too approached Hari; the Lord, placing the tip of his fierce horn against [the demon's] front, seized that horn.

Having thrown the demon Vṛṣāsura of fierce valor to the ground, he of supreme power slew him like an animal at a sacrifice. (13.79) And Keśin, having assumed the form of a horse and having obtained the boon from the Daughter of the Mountain that he should always be free from death, approached Kaṃsa.

That wicked one seized Keśava and thrust his arm into His mouth; then the Blessed One expanded within his body. (13.80) Having made an effort to devour Him, that evil-minded one’s mouth was shattered, and his breath was obstructed by the teeth and gums.
Torn asunder, he fell dead; yet Hari was praised by all, headed by Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and the Sun. (13.81)
And Vyoma, the son of Maya, having obtained a lifespan of ten thousand years through the grace of Brahmā, occupied all the caves.

Śrīpati, having slaughtered him like an animal, caused all those who had been driven from the mouth of the cave to emerge. While the Lord of all worlds, having gone to Gokula, performed deeds of infinite power that had no other object, [the demon was slain]. (13.82)
To whom did Kaṃsa say everything for the sake of the gods' mission—that sage born from the lap of Brahmā had been slain by the father of the Lord?

Having heard this, Kaṃsa, impelled by the onset of extreme fury, bound Śauri along with his wife; then that one of fierce deeds commanded Akrūra to bring Viṣṇu, accompanied by Rāma and the hosts of cowherds, on a chariot.

In order to serve Him, he who had previously been the celestial singer named Kiśora became the wise one associated with the supreme *śaya* (rest) of Svāyambhuva Manu, possessed of the descent (*āveśa*) of the Lotus-born Brahmā. He then became Akrūra among the Vṛṣṇis, a performer of most excellent and worshipful deeds, and indeed the minister of the Lord of the Bhojas.

Having been thus instructed, he became full of joy and serene in mind for the sake of beholding the Lord of the World; his purpose accomplished, he ascended that excellent chariot and proceeded along the road, meditating inwardly upon the lotus feet of the Blessed One which had been saluted by the Lotus-born Brahmā. Seeing from afar the cowherd settlement, he rejoiced at the sight of the ground marked with the footprints of the Supreme Being. (13.86–87)

There he was enveloped by the dust raised from the trampling of the feet of the Lord of the World— a dust capable of shattering all sins, which had acquired its excellence through contact with His limbs, and which fell within the range of the eyes of the crest-jewels of the crowns of Indra and the other gods, shining like brilliant lightning. Then he beheld the sole Teacher of the World, accompanied by the foremost of beings, even as He was milking cows upon the earth.

Beholding him whose body was dense with bliss and imperishable, he fell at the feet of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) filled with joy. Having raised him up, the Lord of the Yadus, together with his followers, led him to his own home; and having performed every hospitable rite for him, though his own eternal, risen, and imperishable consciousness is absolute, he listened to everything from him by way of mimicking the conduct of the world.
Having heard this, the lotus-navelled Lord, with his mind fixed upon Kṛṣṇa, mounted his chariot at dawn accompanied by the cowherds;
joined by the daughters of Rāma and Śvaphalka, he of imperishable soul went by that vehicle to the bank of the Yamunā.
Having halted those two supreme chariots, which are worshipped by the world, the son of Śvaphalka descended from his own and [approached] the sister of Yama.
Having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* expiation, he beheld there the Supreme Person reclining upon Śeṣa.
For while one who has mastered the mantras constantly perceives Śeṣa, that lord of liberality then beheld Hari as well.
Having first seen Kṛṣṇa here in the form of a child, he became intent on his vehicle, wondering, "Is it not here? Where is my vehicle? (13.92–93).
There too, beholding Kṛṣṇa once more, he submerged again and saw the Supreme One reclining on the coils of Śeṣa’s body,
his pair of feet worshipped by hosts of gods and lords of sages headed by Brahmā, Īśa, and Śakra, and accompanied by Indirā.
Having praised the imperishable Lotus-navelled Lord with excellent hymns, he ascended his own chariot when the Blessed One had vanished.
Accompanied by him and his army, the infinite Blessed One proceeded toward the city of Madhurā in the evening.

Then, having sent the lord of the city ahead with his forces, that sovereign of inexhaustible prowess went together with his friends to view the city on the royal road, being honored by the citizens filled with curiosity. (13.95–96)
Having approached a washerman mounted on an elephant, he asked him for the garments of his beloved wife, which had been granted by the supreme Lord of the Mountain.
Pierced by the man's harsh words, he instantly struck that sinner, who was spared from death, with the tip of his hand; [the man] then dispatched him to Yama.
Having slain him, the Blessed One, his strength unimpaired, took the garments and gave them to Bala, choosing those that were suited to himself.
Having given away some [garments] to his friends and cowherd folk, he spread the remaining ones there, placed his foot upon them, and departed.

(13.98) Though his body was filled with the intense bliss of a single consciousness that is free from anything to be grasped or rejected, and though he was devoid of decay or exhaustion, the immeasurable Lord, having imitated the world like a man, appeared as if adorned by a cloth dyed with lac and other colors. (13.99)
Having received the garland from Sudāmā, the Self-dependent Lord granted his grace to his two attendants,
who had previously arrived on earth from the abode of Vikuṇṭha with flowers and unguents in their hands for the service of Hari;
then, on the royal road, Kṛṣṇa bestowed upon them the boon of all desired prosperity here and a form identical to his own there.

As he was walking, he saw a woman named Trivakrā approaching, carrying an abundance of fragrant scent fit for a god among men. Requested by him, she immediately gave the fragrance; with that, the Blessed One, together with his elder brother, anointed himself.
And when requested by her, he made her straight; then, laughing and saying, "I am truly bound by time," he released her.
He whose body bestowed the bliss of a tranquility more radiant than the sun and more beautiful than a multitude of full moons,
who was clad in yellow garments, adorned with fragrant garlands glowing like gold, an ocean of amorous grace and an immeasurable sea of virtues,
arrived. Then, having reached the armory, Kṛṣṇa took up the bow given by Śiva, which was impenetrable by all others.
Having mounted him—who was the very *kaṃsa* (the universe)—and having drawn him in, he whose entire power is eternally complete shattered him in the middle.
When that [universe] which could not be split by all the hosts of gods and demons was broken, there arose a sound as terrifying as the shattering of the cosmic egg;
by that sound, the demon *Kaṃsa*, though possessed of fortitude, fell to the earth with his vital strength shattered at that very moment.
Although he had been commanded, the Blessed One, having destroyed all that great force along with its army, set out once again.
There at night, Hari ate excellent food accompanied by milk with the assembly of cowherds, Nanda and others, and stayed as he pleased.
In the morning, Kaṃsa, his lotus-heart trembling with extreme fear, stood in the midst of the host of kings at a very high place.
He entered the arena together with the country folk and the citizens, who had ascended various platforms along with their young women.
Having stationed the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa— resembling a king of mountains and accompanied by elephant-riders— at the entrance of the vast ring,
and having placed the heroic wrestlers headed by Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika in the arena, he desired, it is said, to subdue Hari.
His army, calculated by the *akṣauhiṇī* standard, consisted of twenty such divisions—vast in power, incapable of being slain by others, and invincible even by the grace of Śambhu.
Furthermore, he had a younger brother named Sunītha, who was formerly an asura known as Vṛka.
Indeed, all seven of his ancient younger brothers, together with their armies, were present at the arena along with Kaṃsa.
Beholding Kṛṣṇa approaching Sāraṇa with uplifted weapons in battle to conquer the Unborn One, those great sinners stood ready for combat.
When the sun had risen, Kṛṣṇa also, accompanied by his companions and his army, went toward the front of the excellent arena along with the lords of the gods.
Being praised as he moved forward, he of vast prowess and immense power set out for the total uprooting of the demons.
Then he beheld the preeminent Teacher of the World approaching the powerful lordly elephant, whose life was protected by the grace of Rudra.
Seeing that beast with its wicked face turned toward him, he cried out the words, "Evil one, depart quickly! (13.112).
He had been cast down by the Supreme Lord, yet, arrogant due to the boon obtained from the Lord of the Mountain, he was invincible to all people in the world.
Then that wicked man, of boundless power, urged the elephant—himself invincible—to attack Vāsudeva from the front.
Having sported with that elephant for a while, the Blessed One seized it by the trunk, dragged it, and threw it to the ground;
planting his foot upon its forehead and pulling back its pair of tusks, he struck down the mahout and fell upon him as well. (13.113–13.114)
Having slain that invincible elephant together with its rider, he hung the tusk upon his shoulder along with his elder brother;
his body adorned by the thick drops of rut-fluid from the lord of elephants, his self-power complete and stainless, he entered the arena.
When the greatest teacher of the world, the embodiment of strength and heroism, had entered the arena, all the people there rejoiced and were filled with joy.
Just as the sun, upon rising, causes the lotus and the night-lily to bloom or wither according to their respective natures, so too does he act toward those who experience him.

13.116 Beholding him who had entered the arena, the wrestler known as Cāṇūra—who was invincible to the worlds by the grace of Śambhu—addressed the Abode of the World (Kṛṣṇa) for the sake of his own interest and spoke thus: "O Mādhava, listen to this! 13.117
"The Brahmins proclaim that the king alone is the deity; indeed, for one who has done what is pleasing to the king, there is supreme success.
Therefore, out of a desire to do what is dear to the monarch, we two shall fight you; let the powerful Rāma engage in combat with Muṣṭika.
When this was said, the Blessed One replied with a smile, "So be it," and he was then approached by him.
Having displayed for a moment his playful ease in combat, the Lord of Devas then seized his enemy by the feet.

Lifting him up as he soared toward the sky—his body unscarred by the thunderbolt—the one of irresistible strength whirled him around hundreds of times and dashed him against the ground; crushed to powder, he fell like a great mountain.
Then the hosts of gods in heaven and mortals on earth praised Kṛṣṇa, the most excellent among supreme persons;
likewise, Muṣṭika, his head crushed by Balarāma’s firm fist, fell down at that very moment.
Also, Kūṭa and Kosala—those two known by deceitful names—were slain there by Kṛṣṇa, while another was killed by Balarāma.
"Kaṃsa, all those heroes who were his younger brothers, headed by Sunītha, have been slain by the club.
Seeing that all his own kinsmen had been killed by these two, the wicked Kaṃsa commanded an inexhaustible army of fierce valor, saying:
'Having removed these two—who are protected by the grace of Rudra and are otherwise unslayable—inflict even greater punishment upon them. (13.122–13.123)
Upon hearing the king’s words, that army of inexhaustible strength— consisting of twenty akṣauhiṇīs and possessing infinite valor—

placed Kṛṣṇa, who wields various weapons, within its own ranks, just as a pack of jackals might surround a lion. Even though Mahendra knew Kṛṣṇa to be the Lord of infinite power, he nevertheless sent his own chariot, laden with weapons, for him.
Just as this man fills the ocean, already full of water, with an offering for the sake of serving the Supreme One,
so the Blessed One, having mounted his own chariot given by Mahendra and held by the excellent charioteer Mātali—
like the sun with its fierce rays of various weapons, he utterly dispelled that army as darkness is destroyed. 13.125–126.
When his own army had been utterly destroyed, he, sword in hand and clad in armor, desired to attack Kṛṣṇa;
at that moment, he beheld the heroic Blessed One advancing toward him upon the top of a lofty palace.
As he moved with the speed of a hawk, the Blessed One forcibly seized him from all sides without leaving any opening.
