Seizing him by the hair with his left hand and lifting him up, he struck him on the head with his right hand.

With his crown shaken, his two ears deprived of their earrings, his chest divested of ornaments, and his hips with their garments slipping down, Kaṃsa—standing before the tip of the lion-man’s (Narasimha’s) claws—assumed a most pitiable appearance. (13.128–13.129)

Having dragged him from that highest couch— one who was invincible by others and endowed with extreme heroism and strength, and protected by the boon of the Lord born from the lotus— the Lord of the Gods, possessed of infinite power, cast him down upon the ground and dealt a blow to his feet.
But the wind within his body, which was the kinsman of the Lord of Ramā, took refuge in the body of Kṛṣṇa and removed the other person's sin.
While the gods, headed by the lotus-born Brahmā, looked on, Ananta, Hari, dragged the Daitya from his body;

13.131 Out of hatred for the sole teacher of the entire world, that evil-minded one, accompanied by all his own former victims—including the Earth and others—departed for the blinding darkness; and others who are not devotees of Hari likewise go there. 13.132
One who is not a devotee of Hara inevitably enters a blind darkness that is eternally and excessively painful, devoid of happiness, and from which there is no cessation.

Even a devotee—though he may be an ocean of all dharmas through his mastery of the conclusions of all the scriptures—if he possesses a mind fixed on Hari as the one who exists at all times throughout the entire universe, beginning with the lotus-born Brahmā and the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), [he alone attains liberation]. 13.133.
One who is endowed with supreme devotion shall be liberated by that Lord of Lakṣmī, who is independent of others and the bestower of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and liberation.

Therefore, having ascertained this Lord of Ramā to be full of infinite qualities and free from defects, and having understood the hosts of deities in their proper order, the wise devotee should always worship them as well, regarding them as belonging to Hari. 13.134–13.135.
Having slain Kaṃsa by his own power, Keśava— who had been praised by Brahmā, Śambhu, and others who showered flowers— rejoiced exceedingly;
for even though he is eternally of the nature of bliss, the expression "joy" applied to him is merely conventional.
Just as the rising of the sun appears to the world despite its being eternally risen,
so too is Hari the ocean of infinite consciousness and bliss, eternally risen in a single form, forever devoid of all defects and consisting of pure qualities. 13.137–13.138.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Killing of Kaṃsa," in the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
CLV. (The Return from Uddhava) Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Om! Having released his parents and paid them homage, Kṛṣṇa—though he is worthy of being worshipped by all—together with Rāma, departed for the sake of protecting [the earth].
Having resolved upon the path of sovereignty for Dharma, he assumed the status of a twice-born among the Ugrasenas and released Nanda.
(14.1) Nanda, too, having been entreated with consoling words by Kṛṣṇa and thus liberated, placed the lotus-feet of that Lord within his own heart;
accompanied by the host of cowherds, he departed with difficulty and dwelt in the forest with his wife, meditating upon Janārdana. (14.2)
Kṛṣṇa, together with Balarāma, approached the Brahmin Sāndīpani, a resident of the city of Avantī, and from him he studied;
for although he possessed complete knowledge of all the Vedas and all branches of learning having been taught but once, he did so for the sake of training the gods.
For even among the gods who know everything, when they take birth among men, their conduct is like that of men, in accordance with the law of dharma.
In order to demonstrate that [the Lord] conceals His knowledge and so forth, as well as His study of the Vedas and other such acts, the Blessed One lived with his teacher.
(14.4) For the sake of his teacher, he returned the son who had been killed; furthermore, the Lord of Ramā went to Mathurā together with Rāma.
Constantly honored by the citizens, the country folk, and his kinsmen, He—who fulfills the desires of His own parents—dwelt there. (14.5)
All of them, having previously obtained Hari as their husband, were indeed tormented intensely by the Lord of the Bhojas;
what more need be said when they obtained Hari as their son, at which there was joy for both his parents and for all virtuous people?
(14.6) Wherever even an ordinary person dwells taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa, there prosperity shall arise; how much more so in the abode of the Lord of Ramā?

By the mere presence of Vṛndāvana, even the city of Indra became its equal; how much more so, then, the city [of Mathurā] itself? For it was there that Viṣṇu, the bull among the worlds, established his residence; therefore, the abode of the Creator is most excellent.
Consequently, by virtue of the Lord’s dwelling there, that city of Mathurā has always been crowded with a multitude of prosperous people.

While this protector of the three worlds was guarding all the Yadus, the two daughters of the King of Magadha, having learned of their father’s death from Kṛṣṇa—their own husband—approached him and, being exceedingly distressed, informed him. Upon hearing that, the King of Magadha—who had been defeated in battle by the strength of his broad, well-developed arms before all the world—[was overcome]. (14.9)
Invincible due to the boons granted by Brahmā, Īśvara, Caṇḍa, and the Munis, and having cast off death, the victorious one grew enraged at the world.
14.10 Overwhelmed by excessive fury, he who is honored by the devotees of Śiva seized his own infallible mace, which had been given by Śiva.
Being thoroughly proficient in all the Śaiva Āgamas, he hurled it for a hundred *yojanas* at his opponent. 14.11
And the mace fell short of Madhurā by one *yojana*, as the celestial sage, when questioned, declared this distance to be "one hundred and one *yojanas*" for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One.
For he thought: "Even though you are capable of shattering the mace, it is fitting for me to serve you. (14.12)
Questioned by the Lord of Magadha, the sage Viṣṇu spoke of the path ahead, measuring one yojana.

Then that wicked mace of the Blessed One, having been hurled, deprived Jarā of her life—the very one who had joined his limbs—and by the command of the Blessed One, it abandoned Magadha and went to the abode of Giriśa, the mountain lord. (14.13–14)

Deprived of his mother and his mace, the king, out of wrath, assembled all the monarchs; accompanied by twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs and exceedingly arrogant with pride, he immediately went to the city of Kṛṣṇa. Having besieged the entire city, that evil-minded one dispatched Vinda and Anuvinda as messengers to the Blessed One.
The two of them spoke these words to the Blessed One, which were filled with extreme arrogance and likewise intended to mock the Blessed One:

"In this world, you alone possess a strength, prowess, and essence that are unknown; yet you have come here to test the strength and valor of my son. Indeed, he was not given to me by me as a son because I knew his nature; for who could have been slain by you, who are devoid of such power? (14.16–17)

"Thus, having come within the range of vision of the most excellent of the powerful, I, the weakest of all, shall depart for the forest of asceticism, my majesty vanished along with my two sons; therefore, from this day forth, be swift to keep me within the scope of your sight. Having heard these words, spoken with reproach, filled with pride in his own strength, and accompanied by self-mockery, the Blessed One [responded].
Having uttered the meaningful words, "That is true," he went forth with a gentle smile accompanied by his army.
At the three gates, the Blessed Lord himself, placing his own troops under the leadership of Sātyaki, emerged to the north;
accompanied by Rāma and joined by the royal host of the Magadha king, the Supreme Lord advanced to do battle.

By his mere will, the weapons of that powerful one descended upon the earth—his own radiant bow Śārṅga, sword, discus, conch, quiver, and mace. Standing upon the chariot held by Dāruka, he took them up;
then, having mounted the earthly chariot yoked with horses whose nature is the Vedas, he strung his bow.

Taking up his Śārṅga bow and sharpened arrows, Rāma rushed with speed toward the fierce King of Magadha and the assembly of monarchs. Grasping his mace and plow, and equipped with a chariot, quivers, and a bow, he—
of immense strength and invincible by enemy forces— charged at the army well-guarded by the son of Jarā, roaring with joy.
Beholding Kṛṣṇa of infinite power approaching, the King of Magadha, accompanied by a multitude of lords of kings,
rushed forward in anger like an overflowing ocean, raining down a shower of various excellent weapons.
Desiring to provoke him to wrath, Kṛṣṇa placed Ugrasena in front and himself followed behind him.
Seeing Ugrasena standing before him, the King of Magadha, his body trembling with rage, spoke these words:
"O wicked one! Begone from my presence, you shameless seeker of a kingdom, you who caused the murder of your own son and have joined the side of the enemy!
You are like a worn-out goat; you are not to be killed by me here, for a lion attacks a lion, never a jackal. (14.25–26)

Thus challenged by him, King Bhoja then drew a sharp arrow from his quiver and, having severed the bow of Jarā’s son with that shaft, roared powerfully and pierced him again with a multitude of fierce arrows. Seeing him approaching with another excellent bow, his eyes bloodshot with rage, Kṛṣṇa—
Desiring to slay the king of the Bhojas, the son of Brihadratha, possessed of fierce speed, advanced against him in his supreme chariot.
Seeing the Blessed One approaching, he of infinite prowess, the lord of the Cedis joined by hosts of kings such as Pauṇḍra and Mukha,
showered him with various excellent missiles and weapons, just as a thundering cloud pours down torrents of water upon Mount Meru.

Having cut down the rain of weapons and missiles on all sides with multitudes of arrows shot from his Śārṅga bow, the Blessed One—possessing inconceivable power—rendered the Lord of Magadha chariotless, deprived of his driver, weaponless, and stripped of his excellent parasol and banner. (14.30) Yet the Blessed One did not kill him; for it was easy to do so in that terrible battle, yet he did not, in order to manifest his own devotion and his lofty dharma.
He rendered the lords of Cedi, Pauṇḍraka, Sakīcaka, the king of Madra, Śālva, Ekalavya, and others leaderless of their chariots.

And those led by Ṣaḍibhaka, Kadru, and Rugmi, as well as the Bāhlīkas, the son of Bhīma, Maida, and the foremost of others—all the kings who were present here on this earth—fled away, pierced by the arrows of Aja. 14.31–14.32.

With their weapons, banners, flags, chariots, horses, drivers, and armor shattered, their limbs mangled by fierce arrows, their garments, ornaments, hair, and garlands hanging loose, wretched and vomiting blood, they fled in terror from the field.
(14.33) While all the kings had reached a pitiable state, their weapons cast aside, they were put to flight in battle by Hari.
Mounting another chariot richly equipped with various weapons, the lord of Magadha, possessed of fierce valor, advanced toward Rāma.

As he charged, Rāma shattered his chariot with a club; he too hurled a mace at Rāma’s broad chest, but Rāma struck it down with his own club. Thus those two foremost among the powerful fought a fierce battle. (14.34–35)
The two of them engaged in a great wrestling match, crushing all the mountains, trees, and heaps of rocks there;
that long wrestling bout between those two, who were exceedingly firm-limbed and powerful, was truly formidable.
Then, hearing the sound of the conch of the lotus-eyed one and seeing even the kings routed, Rāma—
Seeing his enemy fighting, he increased in strength; casting aside his foe, he took up his own infallible mace.
Struck on the head by it, the son of Brihadratha fainted excessively; then the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) seized him.
Thereupon Ekalavya, fleeing from Kṛṣṇa with arrows, quickly discharged his weapons at the head of Rāma.
Terrified by him, the Lord, though unwilling for battle, dispatched his own son Pradyumna, born of his mind.
Pradyumna, having advanced against him with a multitude of great weapons, then brought Rāma, the King of Magadha, to his own chariot.
Having fought for a long time at the front of the fray, that son of the Lord rendered this steadfast Ekalavya weaponless.
He who went to the earth as a portion [of Viṣṇu] is known as Maṇimān, the lord of the hosts of Krodha-tantraka; he was Niṣāda.

(14.40) Having placed Pradyumna within himself and having again destroyed the entire Magadhan army with showers of arrows, that Lord of noble deeds, the unborn one of inexhaustible prowess, then released Bārhadratha in order to lead his host forward. (14.41)
With his face cast down in shame, that wicked son of Bṛhadratha, accompanied by those kings, returned to his own city;
for that dull-witted man had placed his own grandson—who had been consecrated to the sovereignty of the Bhojas—at the very forefront.
Having conquered him of such formidable strength, the Blessed One was praised by Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, who rained down flowers upon him.

Accompanied by Rāma and the others, he entered the city and took delight, his feet being worshipped by multitudes of great men. (14.43) While the sons of Pāṇḍu were growing up, it came to pass that the fourteenth birth-star of the son of the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra) arrived;
then Kuntī, skilled in policy and intent on many duties, served the hosts of sages at the annual festival. (14.44)
At that very moment, the king, together with Mādravatī, beheld a blossoming forest filled with male cuckoos;
there, nourished by the touch of the spring breeze, he suddenly fell under the sway of Kāmadeva’s arrows.
Then, while still sporting with her, he who had once clung to the feet of Hari departed for the abode of Yama.
Previously, even as Śakra desired the lover of Śacī, he created an obstacle for him when [Nahuṣa] approached her sight.
Having attained human status through that very act, while still dwelling in pleasure, he met his death—an obstacle to pleasure—and suffered childlessness.
For this reason, even the slightest fault among those who are superior to oneself, and especially among the gods, attains great magnitude.
Seeing her husband dead, Mādrī wailed from afar; the sons of Pāṇḍu, together with Pṛthā, heard that sound.

When they arrived, at the word of Mādravatī, Pṛthā herself went there, having restrained her sons. Beholding the remains of her husband and hearing the cries of Mādrī, Kuntī’s lotus-like heart was deeply distressed as she looked upon Mādrī.
Having reproached herself, she resolved to follow him in death; the sound of her weeping was heard by the Pārthas.
When they arrived, the lamentation became even more intense; all the foremost sages there heard it.
Then, moved by supreme compassion, they came into the midst of the assembly of sages, and the king’s wife and [the other woman] vied with one another to follow the king in death.

Having restrained Pṛthā, those who had always understood the supreme dharma of the Bhāgavatas refused the repeated entreaties of Mādravatī, who desired to follow her husband; for they perceived that her request was merely a pretext to conceal her own fault.
The two excellent gods, though superior even by their own nature, were made by Mādrī to be no more than her sons in order to fulfill her husband's wishes.

For that very reason, Mādrī—though possessed of excellent virtues—became the cause of her husband’s death and was not highly honored by all the world. (14.52) Then the sons of Pāṇḍu performed the funeral rites for their father here according to tradition, along with hosts of sages; and Mādrī, having offered her own body as an oblation together with him, cleansed away the great sin she had committed and went to the realm of her very husband. (14.53)
Through the virtues of Pāṇḍu’s sons and his own virtues, Kṛṣṇa’s son himself became a constant and sole devotee of his feet;
he attained pure and exalted worlds honored by the great—what wonder is there in this for one whose mind is bowed at the feet of Hari?
(14.54) And the sons of Pāṇḍu, together with Pṛthā, were sent by the lords of sages from the Nārāyaṇa hermitage back to their own city.
In that very manner, the lords of sages went before Dhṛtarāṣṭra and related the entire account, including the death of his younger son.

(14.55) While the king and his son remained silent, the sinful sons of Pāṇḍu, led by Suyodhana and accompanied by the son of Subala, along with the Kṣattṛ and their trusted associates, spoke with exceeding joy: "Pāṇḍu’s death had indeed been foretold long ago; where now are his sons? (14.56)
"Even those born of the field (kṣetraja) are not fit for the state of being [heirs] upon the death of the father, unless they have properly obtained the authorization from their own [relatives].
Having spoken these words to them, Vāyu, remaining in the sky, addressed the assembly of the Kauravas:
"For these [sons], born from Dharma, Marut, Indra, and the best of physicians, possess the essence of vast power while their father is still alive."
14.58–59. Furthermore, they could not possibly be captured by you anywhere, for they were constantly protected by Nārāyaṇa.
While those who suspected the invisible voice of Vāyu were anxious, the Blessed One himself, whose navel is a lotus, manifested in person;
appearing in the form of Vyāsa, his body being the sole repository of all great virtues, he took them and went to the house of the Pāṇḍavas.
When they had been accepted, all the sons of Vicitravīrya, together with Bhīṣma and the others, having honored everyone,
then took them [the weapons] with great longing along with Kuntī, the son of Subala, and the sons of Vicitravīrya;
and from Kṛpa, the sons of Vicitravīrya, together with the sons of Pāṇḍu, acquired the great weapons of all the kings.
There, all the various sons, while performing childish pranks, were defeated by the son of Vāyu.

14.61 Seeing the princes who had climbed trees to gather ripe fruits fit for eating, Bhīma delivered a kick to the base of a massive tree; as they fell down together with the fruit, he ate the fruit. 14.62

In battle, in wrestling, in running, in leaping, and in swimming across the water, he alone—possessing the most noble deeds through the eternal and perfect grace of Viṣṇu—swiftly conquered all the princes together.
Seizing them all, he would dive into the midst of the water; then, releasing them once they were exhausted, he would laugh upon the shore of Viṣṇu’s stride.
Having once drawn together the entire Ganges of vast currents, he, whose manliness is filled with essence, carries his sons across safely.
Indeed, apart from hatred toward Hari, there is no entry into darkness; therefore, those two have taken refuge in the vital breath (Prāṇa).
For that reason, those two supreme ones performed great deeds, their manliness ever extended toward the virtuous, against the enemies of the gods.

Then, having seen the countless arrows constantly discharged by the son of the Wind-god, and having observed his immeasurable strength, all the sons of kings—filled with intense and growing hatred—convened a secret council.
For those princes there who were devoted to the gods felt no love at all for the son of the Wind-god. (14.66)
Leaving those aside, the sons of Diti, born into the lineages of gods and men, deliberated and resolved upon his slaughter:

"If he is slain, all the Pārthas will be destroyed; yet this one cannot be killed by force, for he is exceedingly powerful. Therefore, having slain him through the employment of deception, and having struck down the son of Pṛthā with our prowess, we shall bind the others. (14.67–68)
"If this is done, Duryodhana's kingdom will indeed be free of thorns; otherwise, it would not be so.
Once this son of the Lord of the Gods has been slain and fallen, the rest shall become even the servants of Saubali’s son.
Having thus reflected upon that fierce poison, resembling Death itself, born from the churning of the Ocean of Milk through the power of asceticism from the Lord of Mountains—
Śukra obtained it from that source, and having gratified the Maruts, he gave it to his son Subala.
After consulting with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the king’s sons had all manner of food and drink prepared by their cook and served to him.
Knowing what Yuyutsu had told him, the powerful Bhīma digested it through the strength of Viṣṇu’s grace.
When the poison had been digested, those of wicked intellect, tormented by supreme distress, desired to build a palace in the waters of Hari’s feet.
Having learned from the mouth of Yuyutsu that the son of Māruta (Bhīma) was himself sleeping there at the end, he slept with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Seeing the best of men asleep, they did so only to burn away their own faults among the sons of Vicitravīrya’s offspring.
Having bound him with iron fetters made firm by mantras, they scattered vast quantities of dust over him, the son of Hari’s feet.
14.73 Plunging into that ocean which was ten million yojanas deep, Bhīma tore through the dust merely by his stretching;
having emerged and brought joy to the assembly of virtuous people, he stood there, ever devoted to Viṣṇu of infinite virtues. 14.74

Seeing him, those evil-minded ones, their hearts utterly despondent, consulted together once more and summoned eight great hosts of serpents by the power of the mantras spoken by Śukra; they then placed them in excellent cages and presented them to their own son.
Duryodhana’s charioteer brought those hosts of hooded snakes, summoned by the power of extensive mantras, before the son of the Wind-god.

As he slept with his chest spread out, the serpents bit him on his limbs, yet their teeth shattered as they gnawed upon him. Then, having cast those eight noble offspring of the snake-king lineage a great distance away and destroyed them like ants, the terrible one killed the charioteer with a mere flick of his hand; he fell back to sleep as before, without rising from his bed.
Beholding that immeasurable innate power of his, all the sons of the lords of the earth were greatly distressed;

for even by their mere breath or by the sight of him, the worlds would have been reduced to ashes, and those [worlds] would have become as if non-existent in vain. (14.78) Even the most excellent of serpents, despite their great efforts, were unable to cause him any agitation, even by biting him with their fangs.
Never before had such power been heard of by anyone, much less seen even in the son of Hiraṇyaka.
Having offered excessive praise to Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting himself, that son of the Daitya was saved by Hari;
for his own innate strength was not what drew him, but rather the innate heroic power of his father was forcibly drawn away by the servants.
The Brahmins declare that this natural affection for Viṣṇu is indeed absolute and eternally true;
for such strength does not arise from any other source. Therefore, having destroyed him, let us achieve our purpose together with Hari himself.
(14.81) It is said that this Kṛṣṇa was born among the Yadus as Hari; he is his refuge. Do you therefore act with great hostility toward him! (clxii)
Having thus deliberated, those most wicked sons of the king then committed many hostile acts against Hari.
Urged by them, their fathers—the kings—along with the son of Bṛhadratha, marched against Hari for battle;
yet in eighteen battles, they were utterly shattered in their strength, pride, and arrogance, and were forced to retreat. (14.82–83)
Therefore, having lost their elephants, horses, and chariots, their bodies deeply mangled by weapons, they returned— vomiting blood,
stripped of their armor, banners, horses, and drivers, with their garments falling away and their hair disheveled.
Thus did the son of Bṛhadratha also, appearing most pitiable and afflicted, go back to his own city many times over.

"Released by Kṛṣṇa, who is endowed with perfect strength, heroism, and virtue, he lives, utterly defeated and reduced to mere breath. (14.85) When the kings had thus departed many times with their necks bowed, the Lord of Madhurā, the husband of Ramā, possessed of inconceivable power and the glory of victory, entered his own city along with Rāma and all the Yadus, and rejoiced. (14.86)

Once again, the sons of kings, together with the Dhārtarāṣṭras, made great efforts in their ignorance to slay Bhīma, yet their endeavors were in vain; having rendered all those efforts of theirs utterly futile, the powerful one exerted himself for the conquest of the quarters.
First he conquered the eastern direction, and afterwards the southern, along with the other protected by the Lord of Waters.
He conquered those two, the ancient Daśānana and Kumbhakarṇa, who had become the sons of his maternal aunt.

Of those two, the first was born as the son of Damaghoṣa, whom kings call by the name Śiśupāla; they say the other was King Karūṣa, and likewise the other son of his maternal aunt was Dantavakra. (14.88–14.89)
Having conquered those two as well, he then defeated the son of Śauri named Pauṇḍraka;
thereafter, he vanquished the son of Bhīṣmaka, who had previously been a Daitya named Narahelvala and was known by the name Rukmī, the lord of Kuṇḍina.
(14.90) He was indeed a portion of Agni, while his father was Mitra-bhāga, for he was the very same [deity] of Agni known by the name Sucī.
Rāhu’s son Śayu fought with the two younger brothers of Rāhu known as Kratha and Kaiśika, while Bhāga fought with the two sons of Agni, Pavamāna and Śundhya.
14.91 Śalya, however, though carefully testing the strength of his own kinsman, fought with him and was likewise defeated.
Then Bhīma conquered the heroic Ekalavya in battle; and in this same manner, all the kings were vanquished by him. 14.92
Protected by the prowess of his arms, the powerful son of Indra effortlessly conquered the remaining kings;
and having defeated Śālva, Haṃsa, and Ṣaḍibhaka, Bhīma returned to the city called after the elephant (Hastināpura) accompanied by Arjuna.
Then, beholding that strength of his arms, the son of Dharma rejoiced along with his mother, Kuntī, Vidura, and Bhīṣma.
And other groups of virtuous people, along with the citizens and the inhabitants of the kingdom, rejoiced exceedingly upon hearing this; indeed, all the Yadavas were filled with joy.

(14.94) Knowing that the son of Ambikā, Suyodhana, was about to attack and knowing him to be entirely under the control of his own sons, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, went to the house of Śvāphalki and commanded him to go to the city named Gaja for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s peace. (14.95)
He went there to Hastināpura and was honored by all the Kurus, including Bhīṣma and the sons of Vicitravīrya;
he resided there for several months to ascertain the extent of the Kurus' affection for the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Having learned through the words of Kuntī and Vidura, as well as by his own observation, the disposition of friends, enemies, and neutral parties toward the sons of Pāṇḍu...
Having understood that Dhṛtarāṣṭra was under the influence of his son, the wise Vidura spoke to him with conciliation combined with dissension:
"By maintaining impartial conduct toward your sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu, you shall attain fame, great merit, as well as wealth and pleasure.
Vāsudeva, together with all the Yadavas and accompanied by the gods and others, will bestow supreme affection upon you. (14.97–98)

"Out of affection for him, you seek liberation combined with dharma, artha, and kāma; yet, being of contrary disposition, you will surely attain the opposite of those fruits, O best of kings. Thus were these words of Kṛṣṇa spoken to you today.
Having been addressed in this manner in the midst of all the Kurus, the king, though subject to his son's influence, spoke these words:
"Everything is under the Blessed One's control; we are not independent. He has descended here for the sake of removing the burden of the earth.

Having heard these words, that Yādava, perceiving his mind to be troubled, said, "You have no sons at all," and together with Marutta’s son Arjuna and accompanied by Sahadeva, he departed for his own city.

Having obtained from the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa that supreme, divine knowledge suited to their own nature, Bhīma and Arjuna dwelt there together with the Blessed One, their actions disciplined and honored by the Yadus as the very essence of noble deeds.
(14.102) Even the Blessed One himself would have come forward to meet the mace when its training was being performed by the Blessed One, had it not been for this [rule].

"Let him do so," said Bhīma, having learned from Rāma with the very permission of the Blessed One; 14.103 / And Rāma, for his part, bestowed upon Bhīma the boons he had learned from the son of the Lord of the Daityas (Śukra), as well as the weapons obtained from Hari; Sahadeva, the son of Śakra, likewise acquired the entire noble science of policy from Uddhava. 14.104 /
Then Kṛṣṇa, sending forth Aupagavi, who was endowed with supreme statesmanship, spoke these words to Gokula:
"O friend, quickly go to Nanda and the others and destroy with my words the suffering born of separation from me;
for there is no one here who truly suffers separation from me, since I have destroyed [the ego] within all embodied beings. (14.105)

"Do not let the thought arise in you anywhere that 'I am a human being,' for they declare me to be the most stainless Brahman itself. (14.106) Indeed, in the past, when the great serpent swallowed Nanda, no one was able to effect his release. Then, by the touch of my foot, he became a most divine Vidyadhara; let them all remember everything that occurred then. (14.107)
Formerly, because he did not honor those of beautiful form, he constantly mocked the Brahmins of the Aṅgiras lineage, who were emaciated by their constant asceticism and of unlovely appearance.
Reduced to the state of a python by them, he immediately regained his own body from his intoxication and said to Nanda:
"This is no mere man; this is Hari, the Supreme, the Lord of all beyond the highest, the Sovereign of the Universe, the Cause of all, the Self-sufficient. (14.108)
Having recognized him as the Great Hero, the dispassionate sages, liberated from the cycle of rebirth, go to his pair of feet.
(14.109) And when Varuṇa’s messenger seized Nanda, I too was led to the abode of the Lord of Waters.
There, the Lord of Waters honored me and said, "Releasing Nanda, this is not your son; he is that Supreme Being. (14.110)
"Indeed, the realm of Vaikuṇṭha has been shown by me alone, and even my own way of life as a cowherd is most excellent.
To remove the notion that I am merely human, O Unborn One, they have acted thus toward me; therefore, having attained their station in me, let them proceed to peace.
14.111 Having heard these words spoken by the Supreme Person, Uddhava departed for Vṛndāvana, following his instructions.
Having cast off all the sufferings of animal existence, they shall return once more to the very presence of the feet of Viṣṇu.
(14.112) Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The Fourteenth Chapter, titled "The Return of Uddhava.
(The Pāṇḍavas' Study of the Scriptures).
Now begins the Fifteenth Chapter.

Oṃ! While this Supreme Person was thus governing the world, Bhīma and Arjuna, accompanied by Sahadeva, obtained permission from Kṛṣṇa and returned to their own city after three years, together with the son of Hari named Viśoka.
He, born from the womb of Sairandhrī and a disciple of Nārada, became the charioteer of Vṛkodara’s chariot. 15.1.
Piṅgalā, having recollected that beloved of wide renown who was established within her own self in a previous birth, became Trivakrā.
Having obtained him, the knower of the Pañcarātra, as her excellent charioteer, Bhīma rejoiced and again attained the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
And from Vyāsa he spoke of the Supreme Self; this all-conquering one [Krishna] taught it through Phalguna among the gods for the sake of supreme knowledge.

Having shaken off all paths of non-Vaiṣṇava treatises, he indeed established the auspicious Vaiṣṇava path alone; likewise, for the sake of sport, the one of immeasurable soul defeated Balarāma and Karṇa in a duel of both physical and verbal prowess. Though his own intuition was eternally abundant, most auspicious, and excellent, he attained a supreme intuition from Viṣṇu upon hearing it once again.
Who indeed was there who did not depend upon Viṣṇu, by whose eternal refuge even Ramā is eternally declared to be Śrī?

(15.5) From Vyāsa, the son of Dharma also obtained the knowledge of the true essence of the Supreme Self; those five sons of Pāṇḍu, who were constant devotees of the Blessed One, who practiced the true dharma, and who had learned the meaning [of reality] from the Wide-Strider (Urukrama), rejoiced exceedingly. (15.6)
When the son of Bharadvāja— free from accumulation, rejecting gifts, and abiding in his own duty—
would come to the house to drink water after meeting with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra while playing,
his mother would give him flour mixed with water to drink, and he would always drink that. (15.7)
"Those Dhārtarāṣṭra birds have yellow milk; I have always drunk their milk," he would say.
Sometimes they made him drink milk while he was dancing, and he would know its flavor.
But at other times, when his mother gave him flour-mash, he cried out, "This is not milk! (15.8–15.9).

Seeing his own son crying out, Drona—restrained by his affection for Janardana’s son and impelled by compassion, appearing distressed—then went forth to recover the cow. Having desisted from accepting gifts, he went to Rama; for there can be no acceptance of gifts from Vishnu.
For he was the father, the lord, the teacher, and the supreme deity of all; therefore, his very existence was a source of concern.

(15.11) Upon seeing him, even the son of Jamadagni reflected that Droṇa would be the instrument for removing the earth's burden; he thought, "If this man, along with his son, were to become the slayer of the gods born in human form, it would be a great gain. (15.12)
There would be an increase for them [the gods] if those slain for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas were released, yet there would be no continuity of happiness;
for those born in the Kali age are generally very wicked and unfit for the gods, since those born in the Kali age mostly come into being as such.
(15.13) Indeed, men born of lineage are generally unfit for the sinful deeds of the gods.
It is not possible for even the lineage of the gods—whose seed is ever unfailing—to cease to exist without a cause.
As long as the thread of all the gods remains unbroken, the Kali age shall by no means prevail.
Therefore, O heroes, all these sons of the gods must be exterminated along with this [demon] their son. (15.14–15)
Having reflected thus, that peerless descendant of Bhṛgu spoke with words radiant with a gentle smile:
"Though I am the Lord of all and possess infinite power, I have renounced everything; today I have no wealth remaining.
My self, my knowledge, and my weapons—these alone are what I have. Choose whichever among these you prefer. (15.16)
Having reflected thus, the brahmin spoke: "Who is capable of grasping you?
You alone are the Lord of all, supreme over all, and independent; who else is your equal, O Lord?
For one who desires your sovereignty surely falls downward, unable ever to rise again. (15.17–15.18)
"O Lord, supreme among all, what need have we, who are without strength, for your lofty weapons?
Therefore, O Unborn One, let only that knowledge which is all-pervasive, immovable, and most subtle be granted by you.
Being thus addressed, he bestowed upon them all the sciences, beginning with the knowledge of reality, along with the scriptures and the weapons.
Having completed those [studies] in six years and six months, that high-souled one went to his friend Drupada;
for, remembering his former vow regarding the gift of half the kingdom, he approached his friend.
Although addressed with the words "I am your friend," Drupada spoke these words out of extreme pride: "I am your friend. (15.20–15.21)
"One who is penniless cannot be a friend of the king; go wherever you wish, O Brahmin," he said by the decree of fate.
At these words, anger quickly arose even in that sage who had conquered his senses, through the will of Hari:
"This man has come to me because he was a pupil of my father, though I have since desisted from accepting gifts. (15.22)

15.23–24. Thinking that the disciple’s welfare is indeed his own, [the Guru] considers the disciple to be as much his own self-disciple as he is the son’s. This wicked fool, disregarding me, uttered evil words out of pride; having resolved, "I shall destroy his arrogance," he went to the Kurus to bring them under his discipleship.
Thinking, "If I refrain from accepting gifts, my wealth here shall come from my disciples,
the Kauravas," he observed the sons of Pāṇḍu playing with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra outside the city.
At that very moment, as the son of Dharma was playing, the ball fell along with his ring.
The princes were unable to pull this [elephant] out of the well together; then the son of the Wind-god said:
"I shall leap out and lift it up, even from this very deep well.
Let all the princes behold today the ring together with the ball, by virtue of my prowess. (15.26–15.27)
Then that brahmin said to the princes: "Fie upon your conduct, which is devoid of weapons! Born as you are in the lineage of the Bharatas, you do not know the divine weapons worshipped by the gods.
Thus addressed, the princes recognized the brahmin as a master of weapons and the grandson of one honored by the gods.
Then they prayed for the recovery of the ball together with its principal seal.
And he, having repeatedly struck the ball with blades of *aśvīkā* grass by the power of his divine weapons, lifted it up;
then, addressing those who desired the recovery of the seal, he said again: "Let my enjoyment [of the fruit] be provided."

The son of Dharma quickly promised him whatever wealth, clothing, and drink he desired; likewise, at the word of his son, who was the foremost of those devoted to the three goals of life, he produced the ring.
Then the princes together asked him, "Who are you? and he replied, "I am your grandfather."
"Speak! they cried, and they ran toward Bhīṣma. "This is Droṇa," he said to them then. (15.32) "He never comes to the royal palace; therefore, he was not seen by the princes before.
Bhīṣma, while contemplating the sciences together with him, heard that he had obtained the weapons from Rāma. (15.33)

Having heard that the aged, dark-complexioned brahmin was a master of the great science of weapons, the high-minded [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] recognized him as Droṇa and, having gone there himself, personally offered these princes to him as his pupils. Then Droṇa said to them: "Whoever first makes a vow to do what I desire..."
"I shall master that preeminent archer," thus Arjuna made that vow.
"He knows the *unmādana* and other weapons from Kṛṣṇa; he must not release them except in times of calamity.
By this command of Keśava, he always desired to employ those other weapons that were ready for use. (15.35–36)
"Then we shall have a battle with Bhīṣma and the others; I shall not be constantly fighting my elders.

If Phalguna alone, who is skilled in weapons, should become the one who wards them off for me, that would be a gain of dharma for me. I would not intentionally choose a boon from the Lord of Indirā over Jīṣṇu. (15.37)
Thinking, "Let him do it for the sake of his teacher," Bhīma did not make a vow there.
(15.38) When Arjuna, urged by him, made a vow thereafter, the best of brahmins, having developed intense affection for the son of the king of the gods, bestowed the great weapons upon him. (15.39)
He showed partiality toward him and offered him even greater praise;
he bestowed secret sciences upon him alone, and not upon anyone else in any way whatsoever.
Bhīma, knowing everything through the power of his intuition, felt a love for his youngest brother that was second only to his own.
Having made Droṇa a master of all weapons, he did not make Pārtha [Arjuna] like Arjuna;
he did not have him practice with excessive effort nor observe the target, but placed Pārtha at the forefront for his service.
[Droṇa thought: "By the strength of my own arms and by the grace of the Blessed One, I shall slay the enemies; what need is there for this [Arjuna]? (15.41–42).
Then all the sons of the lords of the earth assembled to obtain all the weapons from Droṇa.

That brahmin bestowed upon them the supreme weapons—those acquired from Rāma that had not been attained by others—as well as various great divine weapons that other kings had not even dreamed of. (15.43)

Having obtained [these weapons], all the sons of kings became no longer capable as they had been before. (15.44) Never before were there such lords of men in the mastery of missiles, in strength, and in all branches of knowledge; nor were there those equal to them—such as the son of Duṣyanta, Māndhātṛ, Marutta, and others—who possessed the prowess of the wives of the gods. (15.45)
Then Karṇa and Ekalavya went to Droṇa to obtain divine weapons;
however, that Brahmin, a disciple of Rāma, did not grant them the weapons because he called them a Sūta and a Niṣāda respectively.
Since Karṇa, having failed to obtain his own desired goal from him, received the multitude of weapons from Puruṣottama.
"This man is also a Brahmin; I shall go to that unborn one born of Bhrigu's lineage"—thinking thus, he went to the hermitage of Bhrigu’s son.
Out of a desire for the excellence of the supreme weapons, that Brahmin said, "I am a Brahmin," out of fear of the all-knowing and omnipresent Lord.
Although Rāma knew [his true nature], the imperishable-souled one bestowed all the divine weapons upon him. 15.47–48.

Knowing that the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra would rely upon this jewel at the crest of his weapon—the knower of missiles—to slay the son of Indra (Arjuna), the Lord of Ramā gave him that missile, thinking, "By relying on this, he shall become firm.
Having obtained from Rāma both the Bhāgavata knowledge and other sciences, as well as victory, the bow, and the preeminent chariot, [he set forth]. 15.49.
Then, after four years had passed, Karṇa was unable to abandon this wide-striding one.

15.50 Once, Rāma, possessed of noble awakening, lay down with his head upon the lap of that child, remaining awake while the other slept like a supreme deity for the sake of the gods' mission and to grant him the fruit of Vālin’s death. 15.51
There, that best of Rākṣasas named Heti, having failed to attend upon Mahendra at the proper time due to a curse from him, became a worm;
and Indra entered into that worm there in order to bring about the curse of Karṇa for the sake of his son (Arjuna).
Karṇa was indeed pierced by that Kirīṭin, who had assumed the body of a worm, from below the thigh up to the skin above it.
Pierced by the arrow, he gushed forth a stream of blood; and Rāma, as if his sleep had been dispelled, said to him:

"Why do you not move, even though this outpouring of blood has occurred which is contrary to purification? Who are you? To him Karṇa replied: "I could not have allowed my sleep to be interrupted here; therefore, O worm, I overlooked you. (15.53–54)

"By birth I am a Sūta, yet I am your son; by that truth I am a Brahmin, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu. O Lord, I spoke thus first: 'There is indeed no one other than you who is a greater mother, father, or guru, even for the world. (15.55) As soon as these words were spoken, that insect assumed a form through the very range of Rāma’s vision.
Having attained heaven by means of a celestial chariot through the grace of that Viṣṇu, who is full of the qualities of his own intellect, [the sage] then said to him:
"O you of untruthful speech, there is no place for you to dwell with me;
nevertheless, let your devotion toward me not be in vain—you shall conquer all your enemies. (15.56–57)

"No one who competes with you can ever defeat you; however, if you compete, you will meet with defeat—there is no doubt about this. Furthermore, you will become negligent regarding the collection of weapons.
Having been told "Go" by that one of noble deeds, Karṇa bowed to his master and departed.
Likewise, Ekalavya, having been rejected by Droṇa, worshipped his image in the forest. (15.59) Then, on one occasion, the sons of Pāṇḍu went out hunting with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
A dog, running ahead in search of deer in that forest, barked at the son of Dharma. (15.60)

Hearing the bark of the dog from afar, Ekalavya, who could pierce a sound with his arrows, filled its mouth with shafts; yet he did not inflict a wound upon it, for the dog fled toward the Pāṇḍavas with its mouth full.
Seeing this marvel, both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas sought out the one who had performed it. (15.61)
They saw him worshipping a clay image in the form of Droṇa, practicing with his very bow.
This Niṣāda had previously learned the multitude of weapons from the Piśācas;
and in order to obtain divine weapons and this training, he constantly worshipped Droṇa with devotion. (15.62–63)
Having observed that distinction, Pārtha said to Droṇa, "The boon you granted me was false.
Thus addressed, the brahmin approached him and requested a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), specifically his right thumb.
To him, the Niṣāda, whose great skill had been increased by the favor of that [brahmin], gave his right thumb.
After that, there was no further instruction for him [Ekalavya] who lacked a proper fist, as he was equal to Arjuna.
Then, on the mountain Raivataka, Kṛpa brought Droṇa to him, and having obtained him, Droṇa bestowed upon him the most excellent weapons.
Being deeply satisfied by his singular devotion, he made him equal to Arjuna, the best of archers. (15.65–66)
Thus ends [the chapter titled] "The Practice of the Pāṇḍava Scripture" in the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya.
Fifteenth Chapter:
(The Slaying of Śṛgāla).
Now begins the Sixteenth Chapter.

At that time, the King of Magadha, desiring to fight, set out against the Yadus accompanied by all the kings; yet Kṛṣṇa, though possessing eternal, inexhaustible, and supreme strength and sovereignty, went there of his own will (16.1),
demonstrating to the powerful that those with small armies and few supplies can prevail over those with vast equipment.
When a conflict arose with those who were powerful, the Lord of Lakṣmī (Rama), together with Sītā, followed the foremost policy;
though he was of infinite prowess, supreme, and fearless, he proceeded according to statecraft and beheld the son of Jamadagni.
Then, hearing that Gomanta was exceedingly difficult to access, he went there with his elder brother, even though he alone could have overcome it for the sake of sport.
Then, in the Ocean of Milk, the gods and others dwelling in the realm of transmigration sought to obtain worship and a place worthy of them;
the unborn Nārāyaṇa came from his abode of liberation, and Bali also arrived there to behold the Lord.
There, Viṣṇu, though eternally sleepless, manifested to him the possession by the Asuras. (16.4)

Having slept soundly, he of noble deeds, immeasurable, looked upon the face of the gods for consciousness. (16.5) Then all the gods, who knew his state of being, lay down upon their couches with eyes closed;
at that time, Bali took Viṣṇu’s crown and departed, and all the gods laughed. (16.6)
While Nārāyaṇa was surrounded by all the gods, including Brahmā and others who were laughing [at him],
Suparṇa went to Pātāla, defeated Bali in battle, took his crown, and returned to where Kṛṣṇa was. Having placed that crown upon his head, the bird bowed and praised the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā.
"Come," he was thus addressed; remembered by him, he departed for the Ocean of Milk where Nārāyaṇa resides.
(16.8) That crown entered the head of Kṛṣṇa and became indistinguishable from it, due to the lack of difference between their forms.
And by his will, it simultaneously appeared upon the head of Nārāyaṇa as well, in the midst of the Milky Ocean. (16.9)
The divine weapons that had previously been obtained returned once more to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha;
at that time, the wife of Rauhiṇeya likewise descended, she who was formerly named Vāruṇī.
Assuming another form, she arrived as the foremost one known as Śrī, accompanied by Indirā’s presence. (16.10)

Another wife of that Soma, named Kānti, who was more beautiful than the former two, arrived. 16.11. While staying there, Rāma, whose splendor was as intense as the moon and who was radiant as nectar, rejoiced with her.
He drank that Vāruṇī wine, which was the very image of that goddess Vāruṇī, appearing in the form of a drink known as Kādambarī. 16.12.
While the two were thus sporting at their ease, Jarāsandha, followed by a host of kṣatriyas, surrounded Mount Gomanta; seeing this, the two gods leaped into the ocean of strength.
Being pressed down by them, the mountain sank eleven yojanas into the earth beneath their feet.
The stream of water squeezed from [their bodies] extinguished all the fire that had spread from him.
Having entered the army, those two best of gods agitated the entire host of kṣatriyas with their own weapons.
There were Haṃsa, Ḍibhaka, Ekalavya, Kīcaka, Śiśupāla, and Pauṇḍraka. (16.14–16.15)

Bhaumātmaja, Dantavakra, Rukmī, the lord of Saubha, Mainda and Maindānuja, and all the other kings, surrounding Kṛṣṇa in their wrath, rained down upon him weapons, missiles, clusters of trees, and stones; as did Śalya, Bāhlīka, and the other chiefs who were devoted to him. 16.16.

Saumadatti, along with Somadatta, Virāṭa, and the Pāñcāla king, rained down showers of weapons upon Kṛṣṇa out of fear of Jarāsandha’s son; they had been imprisoned in a dungeon by the King of Magadha.
With a rain of arrows, Kṛṣṇa deprived them all of their horses, banners, weapons, and armor.
Having rendered them pale with blood from their left sides and appearing as if they were no longer in pain, he put them to flight like Hari does deer.
(16.18) Having destroyed that army of twenty akṣauhiṇīs, Kṛṣṇa did not afflict Rukmin for the sake of Rukmiṇī;
rather, having severed his weapons and deprived him of his chariot, he drove him away. (16.19)
Jarāsandha’s son, having fought for a long time with the son of Rohiṇī, was crushed by his club;
he was rendered unconscious, but after a long while regained consciousness and, filled with rage, struck him on the chest with a mace.
Struck violently by that blow, the son of Rohiṇī fell down, overcome by a swoon, in an instant.
Indeed, his invincibility had been granted by the Creator in the past, but it was revoked when he was seized by Viṣṇu in the form of Rāma.
When Balabhadra had thus been rendered powerless, Kṛṣṇa took up his own club and went toward the Lord of Magadha;
he struck him on the collarbone, and being struck by it, he fell to the earth, his limbs overwhelmed by a swoon.
CLXXIII. Then Rauhiṇeya rose up, and the King of Magadha, possessed of preeminent valor, rose up along with him.
Seizing his crown in his rage, the mighty-armed Rāma quickly prepared his club for slaughter.
Then Vāyu said to him: "O Rāma, this King of Magadha cannot be slain by you."
"The strength of your arms should not be exerted in vain; let that power of yours which is unfailing be employed as a weapon.
Having heard that another powerful man was his slayer, Balabhadra released him and departed.
But when Jarāsandha attempted to lift him up again, Kṛṣṇa himself struck him down with his own mace.
Struck by him, his entire body collapsing, the king fell down overcome by fainting.
Regaining consciousness after a long time, he vanished from sight and fled in great terror and shame.
Accompanied by the remaining kings, he went to his city, released by Kṛṣṇa with the words, "Live! (16.26).
Having fought many times with Keśava, he was defeated along with the hosts of kings.
Having conquered the King of Magadha, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the son of Rohiṇī, went together with Damaghoṣa;
for he had previously been addressed as a kinsman by that husband of his father’s sister, even though he had been defeated in battle.
"Let us go to the city named Karivīra to behold the sacred field of Mahālakṣmī.
Having heard these words from him—who was filled with fear after being defeated in battle—the king went along with him.
That Gandharva named Danu had become a human; therefore, the king became devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Knowing that they had reached the city, the wicked one named Sṛgāla, who was a Vāsudeva, came forth in a rage.

Mounted upon a divine chariot given by the Sun, he—being invulnerable due to a boon from the Hot-rayed One—went to fight Kṛṣṇa and discharged a multitude of weapons; then Kṛṣṇa swiftly struck off his head. (16.30–31)
Having divided his body in two with a sword and consecrated his devoted son upon the throne,

he— Māṇibhadra, who in former times had gone to his own city together with his elder brother Śakradeva— abandoned the army of the powerful king from afar, displaying battle after battle merely for the sake of protection. (16.32) [clxxiv] He abandoned the policy of the stronger one for the sake of safety.
Having regained his city with the full power of his own army, he dwelt there, honored by all. 16.33.
Thus ends the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The sixteenth chapter, named "The Slaying of the Jackal.
(Ha: The Slaying of Śaḍibhaka).
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Oṃ! Then, while he was in his own city of Cedi, Janārdana heard that Rama, whose name was Rugmiṇī, had prepared herself for a *svayaṃvara*.
Her elder brother, named Rugmin, was an enemy of the Lord of Ramā (Kṛṣṇa).
He prevented the beloved of Hari from being given away by Hari.
Then, when the *svayaṃvara* had been proclaimed by him, the kings of Magadha and other lands—possessing fierce prowess, including the rulers of Śālva, Pauṇḍra, and Cedi—assembled there. (17.2–17.3)
Then Keśava went with speed to the city of Kuṇḍina;
then, being remembered by him, the king of birds arrived at Keśava’s side. By the wind from his wings, those lords of men were cast down. (17.4)
"When the power of Hari’s bird is such as this, what more need be said?
What could we do here that would lead to our happiness? they asked.
Then the victorious son of Jarā spoke, he whose abode is the ocean of milk:
"Surely he is one whose vehicle is a bird, for it cannot be otherwise;
we have been conquered by this single man in battle on every front, yet he has never before been conquered even by many joined together. (17.6–17.7)

In the past, his elder brother was indeed intent on killing me; yet, through his invisible speech, he spared me from being struck down, even though I was severely tormented. What can be said of his power? We have been rendered as insignificant as blades of grass.
"For in every single battle, alas, by whom has it been done unhurt? What happiness could there be for those acting here in the midst of such a surging calamity?
Speaking thus, the king, his face cast down and his complexion faded, became despondent.
Then the King of Cedi, together with Dantavakra, spoke these words:
"O best of kings, listen! Formerly, a certain attendant of Hari, possessed of serene intellect, [spoke] concerning the Lord who is both Śiva and Svayambhū."
Some say that Hari is this very thing, and this cannot indeed be false.
Likewise, upon seeing us two, his powerful devotion might sometimes arise; otherwise, however, it may instead be born as anger. (17.12–17.13)
We know of no other cause; there is no doubt that Hari is supreme.
Seeking happiness, we shall go to him, abandoning our enmity.
For this alone bestows auspiciousness upon us, and nowhere else is there any other source of well-being.
Thus addressed, the son of Jarā looked upon them as if burning them with his gaze.
Then the lord of the Saubhas, laughing, spoke these words to the king of Magadha,
while glaring in anger at the trembling man and censuring those two.
"It is not false that Janārdana Hari himself has been born for our destruction;
he is born as a Yādava, while we are lords of the Dānavas. It is always our own duty to maintain firm hostility toward Hari. (17.17)
"Even if those who follow their own dharma are slain, they surely attain a good state.
And Śiva is our supreme goal; you are our guru, though an enemy of Hari.
Thus addressed, that Magadhan said, "Excellent! Excellent! (17.18–17.19).
In the same way, those evil-minded ones— Rukmī and the others, as well as Karūṣa and the two lords of Cedi— made a firm resolve for battle,
saying, "O Kṛṣṇa, let us always act as his adversaries. (17.20)
The King of Karūṣa and the Lord of Cedi obtained the favor of their preceptor.
Furthermore, those evil-minded men consulted together once more:
"If Hari should certainly arrive here, he might obtain this Rukmiṇī."
This Trilokasundara has Rugmiṇī as his worthy consort;
he is the conqueror of all worlds and a master of self-control through both his face and his arms.
He is the best among all who possess complete knowledge, the vanquisher of enemies, and endowed with the most excellent form.
"Rukmiṇī, the most excellent among all women, will surely depart;
and we too shall then experience the utter destruction of our pride.
We are not able to ward him off by any means whatsoever with our arrows. (17.24–25)

Therefore, our firm and powerful policy is certainly this: to ensure that no union with Hari occurs at the *svayaṃvara*, we must not give her away in the assembly of these excellent kings. (17.26) Thus, she must not be given to him in the gathering of us, the noble monarchs.
Sometimes, at some time, there was no seat provided, nor the ritual preceded by the offering of water (arghya).
Nor did he ever sit upon the ground, for he has never been slighted before us; indeed, he is honored by the gods themselves when seated upon an excellent throne among kings.

"Filled with pride and arrogance, he will surely depart in anger for his own city; thereafter, we shall perform the *svayaṃvara*. Thus did all the kings, together with Kaiśika, reach this firm conclusion.
Kratha, the younger brother of Bhīṣmaka, having understood [the situation], quickly approached Hari;
having prostrated at his lotus feet and led him into his own home,
he offered them a great seat and performed an excellent worship.
Then, having received the message of Śatakratu,
the man spoke meaningful words to the king, Jarāsandha, and the others:
"I am always dear to the Lord of Śacī, and I am ever within his sight."
By the command of Surendra, he said to the kings: "For He alone is the Lord;
Hari is the true master of all kings, and no other. Therefore, perform the excellent consecration of the Lord without any doubt. (17.33-34)
"Otherwise, I shall hurl my thunderbolt upon your heads," thus he went forth with this command of Indra: "Carry this out!
Hearing what he had said, their hearts were once again deeply tormented.
They spoke these words with great arrogance:
"In the past, Vāsava was always afraid of us; he would tremble at every one of us. But today, relying on Kṛṣṇa, he causes us intense terror. (17.36–37)
If the King of the Gods were to hurl his thunderbolt while remaining invisible,
we would be afflicted, for even though we are immortal,
O Giver of Boons, we were previously capable only of crushing those who remained in heaven. (17.38)
"Or rather, if we go to him today, Kṛṣṇa will come;
therefore, if the Lord of Śacī does not hurl his thunderbolt here at the moment of the consecration of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, then we shall consecrate him. (17.39–17.40)
Otherwise, just as Danu— though he was immortal by virtue of a boon—
became one whose mouth entered his belly when struck by the thunderbolt of the Lord of the Gods,
even so might the Lord of Śacī lead him away through his reliance upon Kṛṣṇa.
Thus having resolved, the kings sent word to Śauri;
for when the consecration had been performed by the son of Jarā and the others,
they were utterly humiliated in their pride, and no one followed him.
"If even the Asuras were to take refuge in Keśava at that very moment out of a desire for life, the purpose of the gods would be frustrated.
Having perceived this, Indra spoke to the son of Jarā and the others.
Neither the King of Cedi, nor the Śālva, nor the Magadhan could restrain Hari.
Then, with the exception of those [three], the other kings, acting as the supreme king of kings,
prepared at that time to consecrate him according to the command of the Lord of the Gods.
Therefore, the Lord of Śacī gave his own excellent throne to Hari.
When it had been brought down from the sky, Keśava entered there;
taking [Indra] by the hand, Keśava seated him upon the throne together with himself.
Then that lord, along with the two younger brothers of Bhīṣmaka, honored the preeminent among birds;
thereafter, all the sovereigns of men, joined by the lords of sages, performed the consecration of Hari with vessels of refined gold.

Keśava was praised by the gods and others, headed by Viriñca and Śarva, and he was celebrated in song by all the celestial musicians. Then the Lord said to Bhīṣmaka: "It is said that you [have chosen] the Svayaṃvara."
That which you desire for the sake of a son will not lead to your welfare;
this Ramā has become your daughter, and she belongs to Hari.
If her father were to give her away, he would fall into misfortune.
"This has been spoken for your benefit; do not think otherwise.
I do not speak according to my own desire as a woman; see what kind [of being] I am. Having spoken thus, the Lord manifested his own form.
He possessed a supreme universal form with countless heads and arms; he was endowed with infinite splendor, pervasive and joined with innumerable manifestations,
adorned with a variegated crown, earrings, armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and anklets.

"Behold such women as mine! he said, and showed Śrī, who was radiant with the light of the blazing Kaustubha gem, clad in auspicious garments, possessing infinite forms, supreme, and surpassing human vision. (17.56)
And he revealed the deities even within the body of Svarugmiṇī.
Having witnessed that marvel, Bhīṣmaka was struck with fear; he fell at the feet of the Lord and said, "I shall do exactly as you say."
And again, having concealed his universal form, the lotus-eyed one,
whose vehicle is a bird, departed for the city protected by his own arm;
and the Lord of Waters and the King of Mithilā likewise performed their own self-choice ceremonies.
They both resolved that she would go to Hari, thinking,
"A self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) is the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of the kings of the earth";
therefore, Bhīṣmaka committed no fault, nor did he desire her for the sake of Keśava.
Then, after that most compassionate and excellent being had awakened Hari and departed,
and after Bhīṣmaka had been brought under control, the kings consulted once more with Vṛkodara, who desired to achieve both fame and the highest dharma. (17.62)
For Jarāsandha does not believe he has been slain by Keśava;
"Because of a supreme boon from Śiva, he is unable to kill me.
Therefore, though already conquered by the grace of Śiva, I shall yet conquer him in the future. (17.63–64)

"Though defeated in battle after battle, he repeatedly strives for combat with firm resolve; he seeks Śiva's favor and never disregards anyone anywhere. (17.65) Therefore, Bārhadratha spoke again to the kings:
"Fie on our manliness indeed, since he has always defeated us!
O kings, it was declared that 'no seat should be offered to one who is not a sovereign,' yet for him, our intention turned out otherwise. (17.66–67)

This man has ascended the throne of Mahendra in the courtyard of the best of kings and has attained the sovereignty over all kings, even against our will. Therefore, let us consider how we might once again defeat Hari. 17.68.
"And how the King of Cedi might obtain the daughter of Bhīṣmaka—
since this adopted son is indeed superior to my own biological son,
let him be established in marriage with the beautiful Rugmiṇī."
"In the Śiva-āgamas, the Niṣādas, the Rugmiṇas, the Sālvas, and the Pauṇḍrakas—all these kings are mine; therefore, do exactly this for me. When this was said, the king of Saubha spoke to Rugmiṇa.
"The self-choice ceremony has been canceled; he will give his sister to him.
His father is not able to overrule this, for he is advanced in age and weak, and he desires to give his daughter to the King of Cedi. (17.72–73)
But let Kṛṣṇa himself come and, having defeated us, carry off the maiden; thus, even before that, our safety will be secured. O Lord of Magadha, this is the stratagem I have devised for this matter.
For a *sāla* tree once insulted the sage named Garga by discharging its excrement before him when he was declared impotent;
because of that, the Vṛṣṇis laughed at him, and Garga grew enraged toward them. (17.75–76)
For he made this vow: "I shall quickly cleanse the earth of the stain of the Vṛṣṇis, whoever shall bring about its freedom from blackness.
Alas, because of our reliance on Kṛṣṇa, we have been mocked! (17.77)
Speaking thus, he went to the forest and practiced the ascetic discipline of Śiva.
After a year, he saw Śiva [as] iron powder;
from him, he obtained a boon that would grant him a son who would bring about the destruction of Hari.
Although he was devoted to Viṣṇu, having been entered by fierce Asuras,
he performed rites hostile to Hari and abandoned his lifelong vow. Then the Apsaras Ārā approached him, desiring a son as powerful as Bali.

Having entered into the midst of the assembly of cowherd women, that king was honored by the gopīs; for the childless monarch, knowing the intention of the sage’s mind, had brought him there. (17.81–82)
Having discharged his seed upon the breasts of the Apsaras and into a vessel for the sake of a son, he was deluded by anger; "What is this, O Lord, that my enemy has done?
Thus reviled, he became a detractor from the lifelong vow of a forest-dweller. 17.83.
Having experienced suffering on account of Hari, he censured his own intellect;
then, saying "O Hari, the Wandering One, protect me, a great sinner," he performed Vaiṣṇava penance with the permission of Viṣṇu.
For how could such good fortune ever fall to the sage who is always devoted to the worship of Śiva?
Indeed, demons like you are always steadfast in the worship of Śiva.
He had a son named Kāla, who set out to crush Kṛṣṇa.
Because he was always longing for the time [of his death], he had not yet been consecrated;
moreover, this man is your very own disciple, possessed of extreme devotion to Śaṅkara, and is ever accompanied by a vast army and arrogant in his strength. (17.87–88)
"Therefore, at your command, I shall go quickly to bring him here;
having made the surface of the earth free of darkness, let us rejoice!
And then we shall cause Rukmiṇī to be given to the King of Cedi."
"May we always remain as we please, free from the divine birds," thus addressed, the son of Jarā became deeply dejected;
he repeatedly struck his head, which was adorned with a diadem, with his hand. 17.90–91.
Pressing hand against hand and gazing at his own arms, he said:
"For the sake of accomplishing my task, how could I beg another?
Indeed, it was by relying on my own arms that they have overcome a succession of most difficult undertakings. (17.92) clxxxiii.
All the kings of the entire earth, as well as I, this Magadhan—
how can I alone today accomplish that which has never been performed before?
For the Lord who takes refuge at the feet of the Lord of Mountains is the sovereign of all mountain-like kings.
Thus addressed, the king of the Saubharas spoke this reply:
"O Lord, even you were once deluded; how much more so those like us? For what could have been accomplished by others that has not already been done by our own disciples? (17.95)
Kings are supported by their own disciples and groups of servants;
even we and others like us proceed by relying on force. For is a man ever called "incapable" merely because he has taken up an axe? (17.96–97)
For this lord of the Yavanas is indeed like an axe to you;
he is not capable of acting anywhere without your strength.
Indeed, he chose a boon from Śiva solely for the purpose of crushing Kṛṣṇa. (17.98)
Because you alone protect him from the affliction of other enemies, you are his guardian.
Indeed, through the grace of Śiva, you possess invincibility against all;
this boon is especially sought for the sake of victory over Hari. 17.99–17.100.
Even when this had been said, while the son of Bṛhadratha remained as if unsatisfied,
the king of Saubha, mounted upon his Saubha chariot, departed for the land of Yavana.
Then Kālayavana approached Jarāsandha, who was present near him.
Having heard this, he bowed down with devotion and quickly offered worship.
For the son of Jarā regarded Kṛṣṇa as a deity for all those who hate him;
thus, having bowed toward that direction, he honored his presence.
Having heard what was said by him, he quickly set forth with his own army, accompanied by an *akṣauhiṇī* consisting of thirty million troops.
At that time, it became known as *Śakṛt* (Excrement) because of the horses' urine and dung.
In the Kali age, rivers flow with great speed and rush swiftly;
observing again and again the destruction of regions resulting from the formation of new rivers, the wind indeed dried up the urine of other lands. (17.105–17.106)
Hari, together with Vainateya, having deliberated and being joined by Rāma, though he is the unborn one whose consciousness is eternally and perfectly full, then remembered [his form] out of sport.
"This Yavana has come near us today, desiring to fight. (17.107)
Desiring to fight with us, the son of Jarā will attack; provoked by our defeat, he will slay the Yādavas. For previously, out of a desire for victory, he did not kill the Yadus.
"Today, even the Yādavas will be tormented by one who is free from desire;
therefore, the establishment of a city in the midst of the ocean pleases me today, as it would serve as a refuge for all the Sātvatas. (17.110)
Having spoken thus, the Lord remembered the architect of the Lord of the Gods;
that son of Bhuvana arrived and constructed Kuśasthalī once the ocean had been rendered free of water by the command of Janārdana. (17.111)
In the midst of the great waters, he built that auspicious city,
twelve yojanas in extent, resembling a dwelling in the middle of the ocean;
Janārdana made its waters salty, yet comparable to nectar.
Vāyu gave him the assembly hall named Sudharma;
and having given that assembly hall to Keśava, the performer of a hundred sacrifices,
and having offered all his treasures, he departed after bowing down to that Lord.
The entire hosts of deities offered themselves to Hari;
having released the foremost of birds, that Acyuta desired to fight.
The Lord [then] [subdued] all the inhabitants of Māthura residing in Kuśasthalī in an instant.
Having arranged for the Yavana to engage in hand-to-hand combat, he advanced against him;
though unborn and possessed of infinite power, he merely settled his own people through sport alone, so that men might behold the vision of sound policy.
The entire circle of worlds, which has existed for time without beginning or end, is protected by his mere glance; what need then is there for him to protect the Vṛṣṇis?
Moreover, because of a boon from Śiva, he is not capable of harming me, even though I am unarmed.
Though accompanied by his entire army, he displayed his intent to fight thus:
Keśava placed a black serpent in a jar and offered it [to Śiva], saying, "Even though I am unarmed, I am capable of slaying my enemies. (17.119–120)

"Having filled a jar with swarms of ants, [the king] showed him a dead snake, saying, 'I shall conquer as many [ants] as there are in this [jar] because of their great number. Then Aja said, 'I shall show you what is true in this matter. (17.121)
Having dispatched a messenger, he went forth to harass the Yavana;
that lord Keśava, having conquered the Yavana with his bare arms and slaughtered all his soldiers, sent him back to his own city.
Keśava, the slayer of enemies, struck down Yavana from his excellent chariot with his palm as he was discharging a multitude of missiles and weapons;
in an instant, he deprived him of his vehicle and rendered him weaponless with his arm.
Remembering that she had been requested by the gods, Hari did not kill her even though she was unconscious.
For in the past, when she was in her youth, the lords of the gods, who grant boons, had approached Janārdana—the supreme granter of boons—and made their request for a boon. (17.125–17.126)
"Even though this boon was chosen by him as useless, it shall become meaningful:
'O Lord, let this [fire] burn your future enemy, Aṅgana.
Keśava spoke these very words of his own: 'So be it.'"
He approached the vicinity of the son of Yuvanāśva to establish the *ṛta*.
Then the Yavana, named Sasañjñaka, rose up from the surface of the earth; having struck down the Lord as he was departing, he pursued him from behind in a rage. (17.128–129)
Hari, having entered the king’s cave, remained there;
that Yavana struck the king with his foot, but the king beheld him.
At the mere sight of him, he was reduced to ashes in an instant.

That very Viṣṇu, the imperishable, consumed him like fire. 17.131 In ancient times, the Dānavas were unslayable by the gods due to a boon from Śiva; having slain them by virtue of a boon from Hari, he obtained this supreme boon. 17.132
Then, by the mere sight of himself, that Yavana was destroyed, bringing an end to his own very long sleep and shattering his slumber;
consequently, through the grace of the gods, he attained imperishable merit.
That king, having cast off his youth, did not perform the propitiation of the gods in vain.
Then, having beheld Hari and offered him supreme praise,
he practiced austerities with the permission of Hari and attained liberation.
Then Hari, the Lord, having emerged from the mouth of the cave, conquered the son of Jarā, who was surrounded by all the kings, with his arms alone;
they were crushed by him with kicks, fists, and likewise with trees. 17.136.
His soldiers fell down, and he himself fell unconscious.
Having struck down all those kings, including the rulers of Sālva, Pauṇḍra, and Cedi,
Janārdana leaped in an instant to that city of Kuśasthalī.

Then the kings known as the Sāsakas arose and set out once more, desiring to conquer Hari; having placed the King of Cedi in charge of Rukmiṇī, they arrived at the entire circle of kings with a firm resolve. (17.139)
When Rukmiṇī was joyfully prepared to give her away in the presence of Śiśupāla,
the daughter of Vidarbha— the most excellent of all women in the world—
bound that best of the twice-born to the foot of Hari.
Having heard those words, Hari went to Vidarbha in an instant;
Halāyudha followed him along with all the Yādavas.
Seeing Keśava departing, the entire circle of kings [followed].
In the grove of maidens, his bow was drawn to its full extent.
Long ago, under the pretext of divine vision, Hari placed her— who had gone outside for her marriage—
upon his chariot, even as the kings looked on.
Jarāsutā and the others rushed at him in fury with their finest arrows;
having rendered them weaponless, Keśava proceeded slowly toward Hari as they again took up their bows and prepared to attack. 17.145.

Then Halāyudha, the foremost of those endowed with strength, forcibly restrained him. At that time, Bala’s white hair, remaining upon Halāyudha, entered the army of Māgadha in order to conquer it there.

Crushed by the descent of his mace in battle, that Māgadha king fell to the earth; having conquered him, Balarāma proceeded to the city. Then the King of Cedi, arrayed in excellent garments and ornaments, advanced against him.
Sātyaki rushed toward him, roaring like a lord of beasts.
Having fought for a long time, both of them, showering excellent missiles and weapons,
stood glaring at one another in fury with their bodies quivering.
Unable to endure that act of equality, the son of Śini’s son instantly uprooted an arrow and forcibly released it at his chest.
Struck by that, the prince fell down unconscious.
Having conquered him, Sātyaki departed with a joyful heart.
Then other Yādavas, having defeated that army, also proceeded;
led by Rukmi, they went ahead toward Acyuta.

Having joined together with Ekalavya and the others, the son of Bhīṣmaka rained arrows upon Hari; he, however, turned back like a lion. Then Hari, having slain three akṣauhiṇīs with his arrows, [proceeded].
In an instant, he deprived the Niṣāda chief of his mount and weapons with his arrows.
As the lord [Arjuna] was taking up an arrow capable of destroying the body,
Ekalavya quickly abandoned him and fled in fear.

When that best of archers had abandoned the battle and departed, the kings, led by Karṇa and the king of the Kārūṣas, fled in an instant out of fear. Then that son of Bhīṣmaka approached Keśava in a rage.
Hari discharged a stream of arrows and brought that chariot to a halt.
Then he, bearing sword and shield, cut the bow of Hari;
the Lord mounted his own chariot and cut down the sword with his arrows.
Having rendered him weaponless with arrows only a span long, Acyuta did not strike him down, honoring the words of his beloved;
instead, having bound him with five locks of hair, he released him. (17.160)
This was a mere imitation of the two Lords of the world, Rāma and Keśava, who, though always of one mind, were the instructors of men in their respective duties.
There, Rukmiṇī and Hari indeed sported together. (17.161–162)
Then the king of the Saubharas assailed Hari with a rain of arrows;
Hari released a shaft like Yama at his chest.
Afflicted by that arrow, he fell down with his movements weakened. (17.163)
Desiring to please the Three-eyed Lord, he who was known as Cirātasañjñaka went forth.
Having declared, "I shall make this earth devoid of Yādavas in the presence of all the kings," he performed an exceedingly difficult penance. (17.164–17.165)
Then the powerful Keśava entered the city of Kuśasthalī,
accompanied by his beloved and praised by the lotus-born Brahmā and other lords of the gods;
even before that, Halāyudha had previously [entered] his own beloved city.
The powerful lord obtained Raivatī, who was called Vāruṇī,
as a wife suited to him, just like his own predecessor.
His father desired to learn of this from the Lotus-born Brahmā.
Having gone to that assembly by virtue of his boon, he did not perceive the passage of vast ages upon hearing their song;
for a song beyond human capacity might thus delude even a king. (17.169)

With his intellect utterly deluded, he thought that only a short time had passed; 17.170 / having fainted and been revived by the Lotus-born One, he questioned him, and he (Brahmā) spoke of the great destruction at the end of the Yuga, as well as of the daughter's husband and Bala. 17.171 /
