Having given her to Bala, Raivata went to Gandhamādana; there, having performed severe austerities, he reached the presence of Keśava.
Bala, the powerful one, [received] her, who was equal in stature to his former self.
By his power and by his command, Satyavān made her equal to himself;
delighted by her, he begot two sons named Śaṭha and Ulmuka.
In former times, Bala, whose deeds were noble, produced the two gods Aryaman and Śakra.
And on an auspicious day, Janārdana took the hand of Rukmiṇī;
then there was a great festival for the inhabitants of Kuśasthalī. The gods, headed by the four-faced Lord Śiva, stood stationed in the sky.
They praised Janārdana, the imperishable one who is united with Ramā.
Even the lords of sages, celestial singers, and others, together with the Yādavas,
moved about during that supreme festival of the union of Ramā and the Lord of Ramā.
The kings of the Suras and Śakas who had been invited to the great festival arrived together with the Pāṇḍavas to see Hari, who was joined by Ramā;
there were Ramā and the Lord of Ramā, united, both of whom were the most beautiful in all the worlds. 17.178.
Having observed this, all the virtuous people of the world rejoiced.
17.179 / While sporting with her—who was forever free from separation—Janārdana conceived an excellent son, the ancient Manobhava. 17.180 /
Endowed with the third form of the Lord Hari who possesses four bodies,
that powerful son of Rukmiṇī then became known by that same name;
for he had previously spoken of that very [form] as the death of Śambara.
"Even though he was born from the lap of the lotus-born [Brahmā], this one is your destroyer," [he thought].
17.182 By the illusory power (*māyā*) of Hari, he seized the son from the lying-in chamber and hurled him into the great ocean, while being overlooked by the hand of his enemy. 17.183

A water-dwelling crocodile seized him; having come with its mouth wide open, they placed the prince within its belly and gave him to Śambara. Having ripped open the belly of the fish, that Śambara [found] the young boy.
They reported that he was handsome, a bringer of joy to the mind-born god (Kāmadeva).
Previously, when the son of Hari (Kāmadeva) had become bodiless after being struck by Hara,
she fell under the power of Śambara due to the curse of Viriñca.
Long ago, having heard the words spoken by the Lotus-born regarding the daughter of Pṛṣata who had five husbands, Aja laughed;
he then cursed her, saying, "For you have been defiled by an Asura through illusion. (17.187)

Having concealed her own body, she approached the asura with another form. (17.188) Even while staying in the asura’s house, she did not approach her husband in her true form, for she was filled with joy upon seeing him. (17.189)

Rati nourished her young husband with elixirs, and he attained full youth within just four years. Seeing her husband in the full bloom of youth and observing her deep attachment to him, [the gods... 17.190.
The son of Kṛṣṇa said, "O Mother, how indeed was this evil deed of yours committed? (17.191) She told her husband everything regarding his birth and arrival;
then the son of the Lord of Ramā took that beloved woman as his wife. (17.192)
And Rati gave that supreme mantra, which destroys all deceivers, dedicated to Rāma born of Bhṛgu, to the son of Hari. Then the son of Aṅga summoned the violator of his wife to battle.

The powerful one fought Śambara and that Caitya to the best of his ability. When he could not prevail in battle against the son of Hari, who bore shield and sword and possessed excellent missiles, weapons, and trees, he was no longer seen.

Approaching him as he was creating mountains from the sky by means of a thousandfold, formidable, and invisible magic, the son of Kṛṣṇa struck him down with his own supernatural power. Deprived of his magic, Śambara quickly fell lifeless.
With that excellent sword, his neck was severed in an instant, and he fell. Having slain him, Hari’s son ascended into the sky by means of that very same science and,
together with his wife, went to Kuśasthalī.
To that son of Ramā and the Lord of Ramā—who were both omniscient sages yet mimicking human beings—Nārada spoke;
he [the boy] was [surrounded] by Rugmiṇī, Janārdana, and others, along with Rāma and the Yādavas. (17.199)
And with the affection of his grandfather, he lived happily, well-nourished.
Then, in former times, Satrājit—who was always a worshiper of Keśava—obtained the Syamantaka jewel from Hari while He was situated within the solar orb. (17.200–201)

Although he was always devoted to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Ramā, desiring to provoke excessive internal greed in him, begged for the jewel; he, however, did not give it, and so his younger brother bound that jewel [to his neck]. (17.202)

Prasenaka, having gone to the forest, was struck down by a lord of beasts. Then Satrājit informed Hari that his brother had been killed; subsequently, Hari went along a secret path together with the Yādavas.
In the forest, having pointed out with footprints that the lion had been slain by the Vṛṣṇis,
he then showed them that the lion itself had been struck down by a bear.
Then, leaving those men at the cave under the protection of Jāmbavat, he entered.
He entered there, and a battle took place between him and the Lord.
The Unborn One fought only mildly with that lord, thinking, "He is my devotee";
yet in the end, he acted fiercely, for he wished to burn away his [the demon's] impurity.
With his body crushed by the fist, having fallen into extreme distress,
he went in his mind to the best of the Raghus, his own lord and refuge. (17.208) But when Rāghava came to mind, the best of the Yadus assumed his form.
Having perceived her as devoid of all distinctions, he realized, "This is indeed she.
Then, seeking forgiveness and having offered his auspicious daughter Rohiṇī and that jewel, he fell at his feet and praised him.
Having restored his well-worn body to youth by tearing it apart with his discus, Keśava quickly made him free from pain;
having fulfilled the desire of his devotee, the Lord remained in the company of his beloved.
Taking up that great jewel, he emerged from the mouth of the cave.
(17.212) The Yādavas, who had previously gone home while waiting for the Lord—who had entered the cave and remained there for many days—to return, were then filled with joy. (17.213)
In the presence of all the Vṛṣṇis, that best of the Yadus gave the Syamantaka jewel into the hand of Satrājit, and he indeed became lusterless.
Having falsely attributed ill repute to the Lord of Ramā, he tormented himself with remorse.
Desiring the destruction of his own sins, he gave his daughter to Janārdana;
having presented that jewel and bowing down while seeking forgiveness,
Hari returned the jewel, and he rejoiced with Satyabhāmā.
For she was indeed that very Rāmā, the supreme second manifestation who became Bhūḥ;
she was the daughter of Satrājit, the most beautiful woman in all the world.
Therefore, among your beloveds, O dear one, she, Rugmiṇī, was the most dear to you. (17.217)
Since she was never separated from that Hari Janārdana,
Rohiṇī then gave birth to a son named Sāmba for Hari, as well as to the four-faced Kumāra and the six-faced one. 17.218–219.

While Lord Janārdana, that ocean of innumerable excellent qualities, was thus governing the entire world, once a twice-born man arrived. By name he was Janārdana, and he was a refuge at the feet of the Lord of Ramā. (17.220) xciv.
Honored by Viṣṇu, he bowed and spoke these words:
"Forgive my speech, O Lord; I have spoken exceedingly sinful words. For since I am a messenger of great evil, my speech is indeed of such a nature. (17.221–222)
"There is nothing whatsoever that is beyond your range; nevertheless, speak at my command.
Thus urged by him, the twice-born spoke to Mādhava:
"The two sons of King Śālva were indeed devotees of Śiva."
Born from the grace of Śiva, those two, through the power of their father’s asceticism, obtained from Śiva a boon of invincibility and immunity from death;
they were disciples of Jarāsandha solely by virtue of the power of their penance. (17.224–225)
Śaṅkara commanded both Bhūtas, Mahodara and Kuṇḍadhārin— who were unconquerable and unslayable—
to be the companions of those two; by the boon of Śiva, those two Bhūtas became their very helpers.
Even though they were immortals, they did not attain invincibility; nor was it otherwise for them.
Having obtained both invincibility and immunity from death from Śiva, the two of them became arrogant with pride because their father desired to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice. (17.227–228)
Out of respect for his elder brother, the son of Jarā does not wish to oppose him here; however,
he desires to conquer those kings who side with the gods and perform the Rājasūya sacrifice himself, for the son of Jarā does not consider himself fit to be consecrated for that very rite.
"For the Vedic scholars, O Lord, call that sacrifice a Vaiṣṇava rite.
Desiring your father's fame and likewise seeking your defeat, those two have now approached you and spoken to you regarding that sacrifice. (17.230–231)
"Taking many salt-laden vessels, go to the ships that rely upon the ocean; forgive my words.
Having spoken thus, he bowed to him, and the Yādavas laughed aloud.
Then Hari, with a voice like the roar of a thundercloud, spoke these words to Sātyaki:
"Go, O Sātyaki, and speak my words to those two lowest of kings:
'When you have encountered me with your excellent weapons, I shall grant you my hand [in combat] without a doubt.'"
"Let us both go together toward Puṣkara, seeking our goal"—
thus addressed, the son of Śini departed accompanied by the brāhmaṇas.
Having approached them, the mighty Sātyaki spoke the words of Hari.
Having treated those two as if they were blades of grass with his words, he went to Keśava.
Then, even before that, those two had already treated the brahmin named Suduḥkhavāsana— who was in the form of Hara— as if he were a blade of grass.
Surrounded by ten hundred masters of asceticism,
that omniscient one tore apart his loincloth and all his other belongings;
yet, due to a boon originating from himself, he did not possess the power of a curse.
Then Keśava obtained the power to shatter all [enemies] with his thighs;
having honored them and given them excellent clubs, Mādhava departed together with them for the sake of slaying the two sons of Śālva.
Since the Magadha king knew that Atri’s son was of the nature of Hara,
he abandoned his two disciples upon learning that they were opponents of him;
for when Hari had gone to Puṣkara, where he was worshipped by the lords of sages.
Then those two, Haṃsa and Ḍībhaka, met there;
and his father, named Brahmadatta, also arrived at that place.
And the two bhūtas who were the precursors of Śiva came together.

In ancient times, an asura named Vicakra obtained from Viriñca a boon of being unslayable and invincible, and he began to harass the gods. Desiring to assist them, he became their friend and came to their aid.
The Rākṣasa Hiḍimba also, who had previously obtained a boon from Śaṅkara—
who was pleased with him— saying, "You shall neither be conquered nor slain by anyone," became a friend to these two and arrived there. (17.245–246)
The army of those two kings consisted of ten *akṣauhiṇīs*;
it was divided into six parts, with one part being that of the Rākṣasa alone.
Those two kings were joined by an army of twice eight [akṣauhiṇīs] plus one more.
They both encountered Hari in battle, and Hari rushed toward them.
Then a great and terrifying combat took place between the two pairs;
Hari strode forth, and Bala likewise advanced with uplifted strength.
Then the hero of the Śinis, Āyudhī, followed his younger brother;
and Gada by name was the younger brother of Hari, the son of Rohiṇī. Formerly, that group known as Caṇḍakas was devoted to the service of Hari.
He indeed challenged their father alone to battle.
Then all the Yādavas, accompanied by three akṣauhiṇīs, as well as those two who were followers of Trilocana, together with the Rākṣasas, held him back. (17.251–252)
With his arrows, Hari instantly deprived of his chariot and his weapons the one who was raining down great missiles and weapons by his might;
and furthermore, the slayer of enemies [neutralized] the enemy who was discharging trees and mountains with his shafts.
The deity severed his head, and there the gods, filled with joy, let out a roar.
Praised by the four-faced Brahmā and others who rained down flowers,
the Lord advanced toward those two devourers of the Sātvatas who were following Hara.
Having shaken off all the Yādavas in battle, those two approached Janārdana;
and having reached the presence of Hari, those two, with beautiful ears, [were struck] by the hundred [blows].
Shaking them both with the force of his arms, he [cast them] into the abode of Śaṅkara.
What need is there to speak of that ocean of strength as he struck down the immeasurable one?
Indeed, as Hiḍimba was devouring the arrogant army with his might, Hari’s father, accompanied by Ugrasena, advanced while discharging arrows. (17.257–258)
Having devoured two chariots along with their weapons, the powerful Rākṣasa seized those two and spoke: "Come quickly into my mouth!
Then, together with me and the mountain, he [the Rākṣasa] was armed with his excellent mace.
Halāyudha, while engaged in combat, left him and advanced.
Seeing that he had arrived, the lord of the Rākṣasas abandoned those two and,
approaching Bala in a rage, struck him on the chest with his fist.
For both were mighty-armed, and they fought with their fists;
after fighting for a long time, the powerful Lord Bala seized him by the thighs.
Then Bala violently lifted him up and hurled him a great distance away.
He fell at his feet, yet he did not go back to him again. Leaving behind those two kings and their soldiers, he departed for the forest.
Having slain the Rākṣasas of that place, Halāyudha let out a roar.

But Gada, fighting the king of the Sālvas despite his advanced age, deprived him of his chariot and left him weaponless; he, too, fled. Then the car-warrior Sātyaki fought with the younger son of that king.
Both of them, fighting with excellent missiles and weapons, continued their combat for a long time; then the mighty Sātyaki, along with his younger brother,
cut down one hundred and five of his bows in battle.
Bearing sword and shield, he advanced in battle against the son of Śini’s son;
and he too, bearing an excellent sword and shield, fearlessly advanced against him.
Tireless, they engaged in a duel with excellent swords that split the armor and bodies of their enemies.
Having displayed themselves, both remained for a long time in their undifferentiated state;
seeking each other's weak points, they did not perceive any weakness.
Then, abandoning the contest, they departed, thinking it to have been in vain.
Then he, together with Saṃsaṃyu, went to fight the Infallible One.
In an instant, Keśava rendered them both weaponless with his arrows.
And their army was slaughtered, leaving only a quarter remaining.
In an instant, out of fear of Keśava, those two departed.
Then that lotus-eyed Lord, of immeasurable splendor, praised by the gods at Puṣkara, dwelt there for that night together with the Yādavas.
On the following day, the Lord Janārdana overtook from behind the two princes as they were fleeing on the bank of Yamunā’s sister;
he was accompanied by the son of Rohiṇī and joined by his army.

Surrounded by his own disciplined army, he checked those two who were fleeing. Turning back, they, together with their own troops and the best of warriors, being utterly enraged and possessing irresistible prowess, showered arrows upon all the Yadus.
Then Śakra approached Halāyudha with his great bow;
Anantara [approached] Satyaki, Gada, and all the soldiers.
He [then encountered] Satyaki, who was deprived of weapons, stripped of his chariot, and divested of armor.
They struck him with disease and, abandoning the battle, fled in distress.
Shaking off his soldiers and grasping his drawn bow,
he advanced toward Hari, roaring and raining down a shower of great missiles and weapons.
Keśava, the slayer of enemies, deprived him of all his weapons in an instant; he too, having released Halāyudha, departed.
Having rendered Halāyudha weaponless by means of his own power, [Balarāma] struck him.
With his bow drawn, he beheld his younger brother approaching. Grasping his bow once more, Keśava, when that powerful one came near, warded him off with his splendor.
This son of Śini’s grandson, having abandoned his younger brother Haṃsa, mounted another chariot and went to his father;
meanwhile, their aged father fought with that Vṛṣṇi. (17.283)
And he discharged an arrow at Sātyaki’s neck-joint. Struck hard by that, Sātyaki fell into a swoon; but having quickly regained consciousness, he rose and took up a crescent-headed shaft.
With that [sword], the powerful one cut off his head with its white hair;
that head, which had long been desired by Ambā, fell upon the earth.
Then Sātyaki, exultant, went to the side of Hari, the slayer of Naraka.
Even though he was but a child, Haṃ fought against his younger brother along with his army.
But Hari, overwhelming Haṃ with fierce arrows, struck down his entire force; not a single person remained there.
He alone discharged the great weapon at Keśava;
but Hari, having warded it off in every way, took up his own weapon.
Beholding that Vaiṣṇava weapon raised, [the enemy] descended from his vehicle to the earth.
Fleeing in fear, he ran away and fell into the waters of the Yamunā.
With his excellent weapon in hand, the Lord struck him on the head with his foot;
he fell unconscious into the mouth of a great serpent.
Just as he had entered the blinding darkness within the belly of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, so too, dwelling there joined with extreme suffering, he might die after a Manvantara;
for it is certain that for the hater of Hari, that darkness remains truly blind. (17.292)
Then his younger brother, searching for his elder brother, fell into the water;
having left the son of Rohiṇī and plunged into the water to search,
not seeing him, he tore open his own throat.
Having cast off his formidable body and brought his elder brother down into darkness,
he awaited that terrible [destruction] and devoured it with ease.
Then Hari, joined by his forces and accompanied by the lords of sages, was endowed with power.
Praised by Kaśyapa, Śaṅkara, and others, he went to Kuśasthalī;
gladdening the people who took refuge at the sprouts of his own feet, the Lord of Ramā dwelt in their homes as an eternal ocean of true bliss. (17.296–297)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Haṃsa and Ḍibhaka," in the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
cci. (The Conquest of the Quarters by Bhīma and Arjuna) Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Oṃ! When they had obtained the divine weapons from Rāma, they acquired them.
Among all those princes, Arjuna was superior even to Droṇa;
(18.1) knowing through his own genius that he surpassed him in all weapons, Bhīma did not straightforwardly consider a battle of missiles to be righteous at any time. (18.2)
For the dharma of a devotee of the Lord does not consist in supplicating deities;
indeed, there is no satisfaction for even Viṣṇu anywhere except through knowledge and devotion to Hari.
(18.3) Since nothing is to be desired from others, how much less so a weapon that yields only fruits born of desire?

Since Vṛkodara was devoted to the pure dharma of the Bhāgavatas, he performed no actions for the sake of personal desire; therefore, he did not beg from gods or men, nor did he ever petition Hari out of a wish for gain. (18.4–18.5)
While wandering for alms, he received a blow from a Vaiśya because of his utterance of "huṃ";
yet he did not bow to other gods, nor was Vāsudeva worshipped by him. He never, under any circumstances, acted in opposition to Hari.

In battle, one who possesses equipment does not attack one who is without equipment; he never retreats from combat, nor does he ever employ deceit. (18.7) He did not grant permission for funeral rites for anyone who was not a Vaiṣṇava.

He does not do these things himself, nor would he ever practice even that which is pleasing to them. He forms no friendship with those who are not Vaiṣṇavas, nor does he act in opposition to a Vaiṣṇava.
Even behind one's back, he cuts out the tongue of anyone who reviles Hari. (18.8–18.9)

He slew those who acted as his adversaries, yet he never struck down his own kin; he never harbored any doubt regarding either dharma or knowledge. He never made a living from his learning, even in times of distress.
18.11–12. Therefore, he did not answer Dharma or Nahuṣa in any way at all.
By the command of Hari alone, he destroyed the weapons of the son of Droṇa with his own weapons;
for Alambuṣa was invincible elsewhere, and could not be defeated by any other means.
Indeed, there is no one equal to the son of Droṇa in battle with weapons except for Arjuna;
therefore, the Lord, wishing to demonstrate Bhīma’s omniscience, gave him permission to engage in a duel of weapons against Alambuṣa. (18.13)
When his kinsmen and elders had become visible to him as gods,
the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, commanded them to bow down for the sake of maintaining proper decorum;
even then, he would bow only to Viṣṇu and never to anyone else.
By his command alone, he impelled the deities of the weapons, not by means of a request.
(18.15) She remained ever devoted solely to him in that dharma;
therefore, she did not accept even from Dhṛtarāṣṭra anything for her own sake. (18.16)

Even in times of great adversity, she never acted with hostility toward Keśava, either in word or in thought, even toward the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Others, despite being devotees of the Lord, were occasionally distressed in their adherence to dharma.
On account of the Syamantaka jewel, even Rāma became despondent toward Kṛṣṇa;
Arjuna held Kṛṣṇa in contempt for his protection of the brāhmaṇa’s child;
and Pradyumna, Uddhava, Sāmba, Aniruddha, and all the others likewise [felt resentment]. (18.18–19)
Knowing that Hari’s desired gift to Subhadrā was indeed for Phalguna, Sātyaki, who was equal to Kṛṣṇa, properly restrained him;
for even Dharmaja sometimes considered Pārtha to be a man and Hari to be a god. 18.20.
Fearing that Jarāsaṃdha might kill him, Vidura was apprehensive of speaking to Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, suspecting Kṛṣṇa’s imprisonment, he did not favor his descent into the midst of the Kuru assembly. (18.21–22)
Nakula sent word to Keśava to pay tribute;
Sahadeva, however, disregarded Hari’s wisdom because of the destruction of his own kin.
Devakī, Vasudeva, and the others regarded Hari as a mere human being.
Bhīṣma, however, disregarded Rāma Bhārgava and fought him; Droṇa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), and Kṛpa set their minds upon Kṛṣṇa’s absence;
even the gods, Śiva and others, at times engaged in opposition.
The sages, humans, and gandharvas should be told: what more can be said than this, that they always disregard [the truth] out of ignorance throughout various births?
Therefore, Vāyu alone is steadfast in the Bhāgavata dharma.
"Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī—thus the supreme triad of Śuklas is heard.
All of this has been narrated here and there by Vyāsa himself, whose soul is immeasurable, in the Purāṇas and in the Mahābhārata through his own direct knowledge. (18.27–18.28)

When those princes, who were masters of all weapons and missiles, had become proficient in the midst of the arena, Bhāradvāja also demonstrated them with red sandalwood, fine flowers, garments, weapons, and balls of rice. 18.29.
Having honored Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, he gave leave to his young sons.
They, having bowed down to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Vidura, Gāndhārī, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the circles of kings, as well as Kuntī, showed him their exhaustion.

When all [the weapons] had been displayed by everyone, the son of Droṇa— who had received the knowledge of great weapons from Droṇa— demonstrated immeasurable missiles even more excellently than they.
Then Pārtha, in turn, displayed divine weapons that surpassed even those.
He pierced the flesh of his foot and even the eyelashes of the bird;
he displayed many such diverse wonders. At that very moment, Karṇa approached, having acquired the wealth of weapons from Rāma.
Displaying his superiority over Pārtha in that assembly of kings, [Karna] was present.
(18.34) Recognizing him as her own son, Kuntī did not speak to him out of shame; however, Pārtha, unable to endure it, challenged him to battle right there in the assembly. (18.35)

Knowing that challenging a non-Kṣatriya to battle is contrary to dharma, Bhīma restrained Bībhatsu and handed him the whip for Karṇa. Though born in a Kṣatriya lineage, he was devoid of the marks of a Kṣatriya. (18.36)
For a Kṣatriya does not become like a Vrātya, O best of the twice-born. (18.37) When Karṇa had been rendered speechless by Bhīma, Suyodhana,
with the permission of his father, consecrated Aṅga as king.
Out of partiality, Dhṛtarāṣṭra became subject to the will of his son. When Karṇa had been consecrated, his father Adhiratha then went forth and,
in the midst of the assembly of all the kings, Vṛṣa then paid him homage.
All the virtuous men who had assembled there were delighted by his feat.
Then Bhīma and Duryodhana, under the pretext of displaying their training, took up their heavy maces and rose up in rivalry. (18.39–18.40)
Then this entire world of gods, asuras, humans, and so forth—both moving and unmoving—became divided into two factions due to their reliance on Bhīma and Duryodhana.
The gods and those favorable to the gods likewise took refuge in Bhīma alone. (18.41)
The Asuras and those who were like Asuras, relying upon Duryodhana, and the humans, divided into two factions according to the distinction between gods and Asuras, cried out:
"Victory to you, O Bhima of mighty arms! Victory to Duryodhana! (18.42)
Even the gods and the asuras let out cries of "huṃ" and "bhit.
Then, seeing the world so intensely agitated, Droṇa, the best of the twice-born, thought:
"This world shall not perish because of its reliance on Bhīma and Duryodhana."
Thus, by his son, those two heroes, the subduers of enemies, were restrained;
in each case according to their respective fitness, and never otherwise.
Having said, "The son of Droṇa is equal to you both," he restrained these two.
Restrained by Droṇa’s command, those two departed for their respective abodes.
And Brahmā, having forbidden the gods and asuras who were fiercely engaged in combat, saying, "You shall see them [slain] by Time," departed with the gods and Īśa for his own abode. (18.45–46)
Taking Karna by the hand, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra went home;
taking Pārtha by the hand, Bhīma departed for his own abode.
It was Bhīma’s firm resolve that Karna must be slain by Pārtha. (18.47)
By contrast, Duryodhana’s resolve was the opposite;
for that purpose, both of them employed incomparable stratagems (18.48),
even as Phalguna’s excellence in fame and victory increased.
The exertion of Bhīma was one way, while that of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was otherwise.
For the sake of Bhīma, Keśava and the other gods took the side of Phalguna, just as Rāma and the others were on the side of Hanūmat in his gathering [of allies]. 18.49.
Indeed, the gods who were formerly on the side of Sugrīva remained exactly as they were.
For that very reason, the Lord of the Gods attained the status of being Bhīma’s younger brother out of remorse for his former conduct; it was because of that that Bhīma acted in such a manner.

For the sake of Duryodhana, all the birds, Daityas, and Dānavas were on Karna’s side; these two, Karna and Phalguna, became the stakes. Then, asked for the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), Droṇa spoke to the princes.

"Having bound the King of the Pañcālas, give him [to us]," they said; "So be it," they replied. Then those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with Karṇa, and the Pāṇḍavas also, accompanied by Droṇa, set out toward the city of the Pañcālas.

CCVI. Then Bhīma said to his preceptor, desiring to discern his capability: "O best of the twice-born, this pride of the princes is irresistible. Let them go on ahead; Drupada shall not fall under their control. (18.55)
"When our purpose is not yet accomplished and they have turned back, we shall bind your enemy and bring him here;
of this there is no doubt. Thus he stood with his brothers.
While the sons of Pṛthā remained with Droṇa, the others stood together with the son of the charioteer.

Taking up their weapons, they went swiftly to the inner apartments of the Pāñcālas. Seeing those princes approaching with the desire to seize them, Drupada, accompanied by three akṣauhiṇīs, emerged from his palace.
Raining down arrows, they surrounded the princes and began to strike down the women and children on all sides;
even the women and children staying within the palaces [attacked] with stones and pestles. (18.59)
They tormented the princes, who had been raised in great luxury.
For Drupada possessed a boon granted by the Sun through the power of his asceticism:
"No one shall conquer you within a league of your city. (18.60–61)
Thus, by that very boon, those princes were made to prosper in happiness;
yet when they were broken, they turned back and fled toward where the Pāṇḍavas were, pursued even by the Pāñcālas along with their women, children, and the elderly. 18.62.
Crying out "Bhīma! Arjuna!", they went to where the Pāṇḍavas were;
seeing them broken, Bhīma, the best of strikers and a hero who had already taken up his bow, mounted his chariot and advanced.
Following him were the sons of Indra (Arjuna) and the twins (Nakula and Sahadeva), positioned at his very two wheels;
Yudhiṣṭhira, however, stood with Droṇa as a spectator.
Seeing Bhīma approaching ahead of them with his bow drawn, [he watched].
All the Pāñcālas fled and entered the city itself.
Drupada, however, advanced against Bhīma along with his sons and the Sārasena army;
Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas were his two wheel-protectors.
Viśvāvasu and Parāvasu were his two sons of great prowess, born together with Dhātṛ and Aryaman; Satyajit followed behind them.
That hero Citrasena, a great chariot-warrior, was joined by Mitrāṃśa. (18.68)
At the front, however, the noble car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin advanced, discharging arrows;
Janamejaya followed right after him—he who was formerly Citraratha, endowed with a portion of Tvaṣṭṛ—and he rained down shafts. (18.69)
Having deprived both of them of their chariots, their bows, and their armor,
Bhīma slaughtered that army, along with its horses, chariots, and elephants.
Then Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas assailed him with a shower of arrows.
Those two, deprived of their chariots, rushed at him; Bhīma rendered them weaponless.
Yet Vṛkodara did not seize the Pāñcāla prince who was within his grasp, for he wished to fulfill Arjuna’s solemn vow regarding the earth as a debt to his elder brother.
He directed Pārtha specifically toward Karṇa to break his pride (18.72).
As that Pāñcāla prince was discharging arrows, Arjuna swiftly leaped onto his chariot,
severed his bow, and seized him in an instant.
Having seized Siṃha like a deer, he mounted his own chariot.
Then the enraged army surrounded Phalguna;
Bhīma swiftly struck that army with showers of arrows.
Then Satyajit approached Pārtha, discharging many arrows;
Arjuna, in a mere moment, deprived him of his chariot and bow.
As he was again striking at Bhīma’s army, Arjuna said to him, "Do not [do this]. (18.75)
"O hero, he is worthy of destroying this king’s army entirely.
This most virtuous friend of our father is a fit kinsman for him;
therefore, out of respect for our elder’s word, we shall lead him away. (18.76–77)
Then Drupada showed even greater affection for Bībhatsu;
thereupon Bhīma, leaving the army behind, followed Bībhatsu. Having somehow escaped from Bhīma’s presence, that army fled in fear.
Then Arjuna established Drupada in the presence of Droṇa.
At that time, Droṇa asked him, "Is there still friendship between us?
Drupada replied to the best of the Aṅgirasas, "It exists now. (18.79–18.80)
Then Droṇa said to Drupada: "I desire an everlasting friendship with you.
For friendship cannot exist between one who is not a king and you; it was for this reason that I acted thus.
Since fighting is not the duty of a brahmin, you were not restrained by me. (18.81)
This was caused to be done for me by my disciples, who desired friendship with you.
Therefore, for the sake of that very friendship, half of your kingdom was taken by me today;
you shall be king on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā, while I shall be king on the northern.
"O friend, as long as one of us is not a king, there can be no friendship between the two of us.
Having said this, Droṇa untied him, took half the kingdom from him,
and went with his disciples to Nāgapura, where he lived happily.
Though he was fearful of abandoning his Brahminhood and did not even take up a bow,
he fought with the enemies along with his sons because the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had prostrated at Bhīma’s feet and entreated him for protection out of fear.
Thus, by the will of Hari alone, he (Drupada) came to adopt the duty of a Kshatriya;
meanwhile, Drupada, tormented day and night by his defeat,
and seeing the strength of Bhima and Arjuna, desired to seek refuge with the Pandavas.
Desiring to act upon Arjuna’s words regarding their kinship and wishing to speak the truth, and seeing gentleness in Arjuna, he sought his daughter for that purpose;
and desiring a son who would be the slayer of Droṇa, he went to the two best of Brahmins. (18.87)
Then, O King, having summoned Yāja and Upayāja, the monarch performed a sacrifice with a hundred thousand cows;
however, his wife was not invited there by the two brahmins.
For the sake of obtaining a son from Drupada, she became resentful out of pride. (18.88)

Disregarding them with the thought, "What is this woman?", those two best of brahmins then offered that oblation of their wife's life-breaths for the sake of their son. As soon as the oblation had been offered with two Vaiṣṇava mantras, 18.89.
A fire, resembling glowing embers, rose up from the middle of the sacrificial pit.
Wearing a diadem and earrings, radiant, adorned with a golden garland and bearing an excellent sword,
he rushed toward Drupada on a chariot bright as the sun, uttering a roar.
Because of his boldness and his brilliance, he was called Dhṛṣṭadyumna by the sages and by Drupada as well, who knew the true essence of the meaning of all the Vedas.
Following him, Bhāratī herself rose up from the center of the sacrificial altar.
For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is known by the name Bharata because it sustains (*bharaṇa*) everything.
His wife is Sarasvatī, named Bhāratī, who is the embodiment of the Vedas; she has resorted to the form of *śam* (peace) and is celebrated as Śrī when associated with Vāyu. 18.93–94.
Possessed of divine influence, endowed with grace, dark-complexioned, and radiant like the dawn, she was declared to be the very embodiment of Śrī, taking refuge in Indra, Dharma, and the Aśvins.
Because of her excellence among women, she was known by the name Kṛṣṇā. (18.95)

She was dark in complexion, yet she was excellent and full of joy; by her very birth she was all-knowing and adorned with every ornament; she possessed the bloom of youth, was free from old age, and was the most beautiful woman in the world. (18.96)
Umā was exceedingly endowed with beauty and possessed of all auspicious marks.
(18.97) For previously, those goddesses, Umā and the others, once displayed their amorous charms together with their husbands even more intensely while Brahmā looked on. (18.98)
Then Brahmā cursed them: "You shall enter a human womb;
there you shall become the wives of others. Thus were the celestial women cursed.
Having reflected upon these words and approached her, they reported everything to her.
Having served her for a thousand years, they said:
"O Queen, among humans there is nothing further to be attained by us, nor is there any other state whatsoever;
nevertheless, we would never, under any circumstances, touch anyone other than Māruta. (18.100–18.101)
We were previously cursed by Brahmā himself for our playful behavior on another occasion:
"When you go to deceive him after attaining a single body, you three arrogant ones shall attain human birth with a single body. (18.102)
"Three times he said to us, 'Come to my rescue!';
therefore, O Goddess, we desire to share one body with you throughout four births, since for us there are two curses as the cause. (18.103)
There shall be four births for you on earth; no one other than Māruti can surpass you.
(18.104) This is the decree of Hari, for it is beginningless and eternal;
therefore, among us, no one other than Māruti shall attain a body equal to yours. (18.105)
When this was said, she replied, "So be it," and together with Pārvatī and the others, that brahmin girl became fourfold;
all remaining within a single body, they performed great penance for the Lord of the Mountains. (18.106)
Bhāratī, residing within that body and having undertaken a vow for the sake of the unification of action, gratified Hari who was stationed within the body of Rudra through her ascetic penance.
To her, the Lord Hari, dwelling within the body of Rudra, granted a boon.

Śaṅkara himself granted a boon to all the others as well: that they should have endless satisfaction with their husbands throughout all their births, even during births among human beings. (18.108–109)
Then, at that very moment, having cast off their bodies, those women who delighted in Nala became perfectly united with him as one body under the name Indrasenā.
At that time, there was a sage named Mudgala, firmly established in ascetic penance.
In the course of their conversation, he heard that Brahmā had desired a daughter;
he mocked the lotus-born one, and the four-faced god cursed him:
"O conceited man, go for your misfortune to the five goddesses, Bhāratī and the others! (18.111–112)
Thus addressed, Mudgala gratified him with his ascetic penance;
then the lotus-born Brahmā granted him a favor regarding the curse:
"You shall not go to those goddesses, for the Wind-god remains within your body."
"You shall fall into a perpetual swoon and never regain consciousness;
moreover, no sin shall accrue to you from that," he said, and as soon as this was spoken, a wind entered him, and having seized Indrasena, he became possessed. 18.114–115.
The Lord of the World sported with her for a long time;
then, having awakened Mudgala, he departed for his own abode.
Thereafter, having gone to another land, that Mudgala performed austerities.

Then Indrasenā, separated from her husband, performed great ascetic penance. Meanwhile, the goddess Sarasvatī, residing within her body, gratified Keśava— who was present with Śaṅkara— through that penance, just as before, for the sake of the unification of their actions.

Just as in former times Umā and the others performed fierce ascetic penance, so too did these five, though residing in a single body, perform it individually in order to obtain their respective husbands once Śiva had become manifest and Keśava was present within his body. (18.118)
They made their request five times, for those were his words.
Viṣṇu, residing within Śiva’s body, gave Bhāratī a husband;
then Śiva himself gave four husbands to the other women.
Then, as soon as that boon had been granted by him, the four goddesses—
thinking "we five are goddesses"— did not realize they were actually one body due to their union with consciousness, like milk and water. (18.121)
Having heard those words— "O Goddess, you shall regain your husband before long"—
and that which was spoken by Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, namely, "you shall have four husbands separately," the women then concluded that one woman would have five husbands. (18.122)
Remaining in one body, they wept, each thinking, "I am the only one.
Then Mahendra arrived there and said to that excellent woman, "For what reason do you weep? She replied to him who was in the form of a young brahmin. (18.123–18.124)

"Having shown Śaṅkara to me, he granted this state of having five husbands as a boon requested for my sake"; then Śakra, not knowing that he was Śiva, said loudly: "What is this in the three worlds? (18.125)
"O evil-minded one, you are vainly lusting after a woman protected by me," he said.
When this was spoken, Śiva replied: "Fall [from heaven] and attain human birth;
you shall become her husband, for she herself will choose you. (18.126–127)
"Behold here, due to your contemptuous ignorance, gods such as yourselves fallen beneath this very mountain! Thus addressed,
Pākaśāsana uprooted that mountain and saw those gods there.
[He saw] the four former Indras— the Marutvat, Vṛṣan, and Nāsatyas— standing there,
performing a secret mantra for the sake of descending among human beings. Then, having approached Viṣṇu, the most excellent giver of boons, that Vāsava...

Through his grace, he was born upon the earth endowed with a portion of human nature. (18.130) At that time, Brahmā spoke falsely to Śiva regarding those gods, Māruta and the others, saying, "They have fallen because of their contempt for me. (18.131)

"I curse you that you shall quickly suffer defeat among mortals at the hands of Śakra, because you spoke falsely to him who is the embodiment of a man. Furthermore, since I have acted without hesitation toward the goddesses cursed by me," (18.132)
He granted him an excellent boon: "Thereafter, you shall obtain your beloved among humans;
subsequently, she will emerge from her body in the land of Bhārata, and you shall find her in your own world. This boon granted for your sake shall not be in vain. (18.133–134)
This is she named Draupadī, who shall become the body of the five gods;
those to whom you spoke false words—Māruti and all the others—they shall attain the status of husbands to these [five] through Bhāratī alone, for Pārvatī herself. (18.135)
She should engage in worldly affairs with due propriety and not otherwise.
For these Maruts and others were born for the sake of the weighty purpose of the gods;
such is the sacred tradition (śruti) regarding this matter, and you should have no disregard for it.
"Then you shall obtain a long-lasting residence among human beings.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed; that Aśvatthāman became Śiva, while this body of the five goddesses became known as Draupadī.
This entire matter, as well as those points previously mentioned, is understood from the Vedas along with the Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata.
All the Pāñcālas rejoiced at the birth of those two sons. 18.139.
Through the enjoyment of human food and through association with humans,
the nature of these two as sons of a man and their human state did not become excessive, because of the cause of their non-uterine birth. (18.140–141)
Yāja and Upayāja were those very two; she was the beloved wife of Drupada.
Out of maternal affection for these two, he made his request, and they both granted it.
Having learned that the son born would be the slayer of himself, Bhāradvāja—
Yayāti gave him the supreme weapons, and he accepted them out of greed; for even among the gods, those weapons of Rāma were difficult to obtain.
Having heard that the King of Pañcāla had been bound by Bhīma and Arjuna, [the powerful one... (18.143).

Janārdana, the Lord, dispatched Kṛtavarman against the Pāṇḍavas in order to proclaim his incomparable affection for them throughout the world. He too, the son of the younger brother of Śūra, honored the heroic Pāṇḍavas.

Honored by them due to his devotion to Kṛṣṇa and their brotherhood, he went to Hari. From that time forward, having recognized the strength of Bhīma and Arjuna, the kings abandoned the side of the gods and took refuge with the Pāṇḍavas. 18.145–146.
For they had specifically perceived Kṛṣṇa’s affection for them, and they had been defeated many times by Kṛṣṇa of inconceivable deeds;
indeed, it was solely through his prowess that they had previously fallen under the power of Jarāsaṃdha. (18.147)
Knowing that strength to belong to the Pārthas and to Keśava,
and because they were affectionate toward Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍus due to the influence of practice in previous births,
[the people] cast aside their fear of Jarāsaṃdha and took refuge with them alone. (18.148–149)

Even though he had been repeatedly defeated by Kṛṣṇa, the Asuras did not abandon him at all, because of their former impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*); for an impression is powerful. Indeed, even when the gods relied on others for some reason, they did not do so for long.
Others clearly abandon their affection for the gods, and likewise for one another. Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having repeatedly recognized the strength of Bhīma and Pārtha,
[remained neutral] because of their divinity, his own nature, and the fact that the son of Dharma was the eldest.

He, being well-pleased, indeed performed his consecration as the crown prince (yauvarājya). Then Bhīma and Arjuna, invincible, having conquered the lords of the earth in all directions, made them all payers of tribute to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
He too was pleased with those two, as were the citizens and the people of the countryside, and all those headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, because of their superhuman deeds. 18.154.
Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable Ācārya Bhagavatpāda Ānandatīrtha.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the eighteenth chapter, titled "The World-Conquest of Bhīma and Arjuna" (ccxvi),
[concludes with] "The Acquisition of the Kingdom by the Pāṇḍavas."
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.

Om! While the Pāṇḍavas—endowed with auspiciousness, exalted virtues, and joined by Janārdana—were performing exceedingly meritorious deeds, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra naturally adopted the entire doctrine of atheism toward their elders, deities, and other holy beings. 19.1.
There was a twice-born man named Kaṇiṅka Asuraka, who was a disciple of Śakuni, the preceptor of the asuras;
he, at the secret bidding of Śakuni, instilled that most contemptible policy among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
In that policy, deceit was paramount, wherein neither the gods were to be honored nor the entire world was to be deceived for one's own sake. (19.2)
"Even the effects of Dharma and the like are but a great attribute for him; he alone is the best among the entire host of Asuras and Daityas.
(19.3) Thus, and so forth, they all, led by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, accepted that most contemptible knowledge while remaining ignorant.
By the power of their own nature, that very [knowledge] was pleasing to them and was propagated through the strength of their own intellects. (19.4)
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, whose mind was entirely filled with evil intent, his heart burning with grief throughout all those days,
approached his father along with the son of Subala and, seeing the supreme prosperity and victory belonging to the sons of Pṛthā,
said this: "Though we were born from your own heart, O eldest brother, we have been rendered unworthy of the kingdom by you yourself."
Indeed, even the younger brother of our father, as well as those born of his wife and others, were led to the path of sovereignty by you alone.

(19.6) The son of Dharma shall obtain a great kingdom either from you or through the strength of his younger brothers; as for us, we shall become slaves along with our very own offspring, first to the son of Kuntī and thereafter to his lineage. (19.7)
"My suffering is not for my own sake, O you whose fame is like a sword and whose renown is established by the exceedingly pure world;
rather, it is because of us that this suffering exists. Therefore, we all wish to die; so grant us also your permission.
Having heard these words of his son, the king spoke: "Alas, this mind of yours is not appropriate!"
Who indeed would not feel affection for the sons of Pāṇḍu, who are supreme in virtue and have accumulated a mass of their own heroic prowess?
(19.9) For they, by the strength of their own arms, draw all the glory of every king toward me, and they offer no resistance to you.
Therefore, my dear, attain peace for the welfare of your lineage; a powerful conflict with us will bring no security to you. (19.10)
Even as the king spoke thus, the wicked man, relying on the counsel of Saubala, spoke again:

"If you do not drive the sons of Pṛthā elsewhere from the City of Elephants, then, having seen all of us as departed spirits, you will surely find joy with the sons of Pṛthā. Having heard these words, the king was quickly dragged away by the tears of his son's heart, solely through the desire of the enemy-slayer.
"O son, even though the Pārthas are powerful, they cannot by any means be sent away from the city," he said.

(19.12) Thus addressed, [Yudhiṣṭhira] looked at his father Śakuni and said: "Listen now to the plan devised by me here today. While these men have been staying in the city for thirteen years, this very plan has been desired by me. (19.13)

For there is no one equal to the son of Droṇa in strength and prowess; yet he has been brought under my control by me through various supreme means, along with his maternal uncle, and his father followed him—this son of the River as well.
Indeed, even the hosts of soldiers have for the most part come under my influence through gifts and honors, as has this Karṇa.
The weapon of the son of the Lord of the Gods is indeed superior even in its power; yet, by the strength of my mantra, I alone shall conquer Bhīma.
(19.15) Indeed, three hundred supreme mantras, difficult even for the gods to obtain, were acquired by me today from Durvāsas.
They have been deposited elsewhere; they would not be effective against Bhīma, therefore I do not employ them. (19.16)
These [mantras] bestow vigor and victory; they grant the power to paralyze fire, water, and so forth, and can obstruct all the hosts of gods.
They fulfill every desire, such as bringing rain; with these, which are singular and undecaying, I shall conquer this Bhīma.
Or, if you feel excessive affection for them, even in that case, no opposition will be shown by me.
"Let them dwell in Vāraṇavata; let that very kingdom be theirs, while Nāgapura shall remain mine for your sake.

(19.18) In this way, through the protection of your own sons, your fame shall increase; it would perish if you were to over-nourish the offspring of others. Once your own strength is born, they will become your adversaries, for they follow you only so long as it serves their own interests. (19.19)
"O Kṣattṛ, he alone is constantly sufficient as their nourisher; yet by the power of his counsel, he is my enemy.

Furthermore, the citizens and the country-folk constantly hate me, while their hearts are exceedingly firm in friendship toward him. When they have been sent far away, being left without support, they will, out of weakness, seek refuge all around with me alone. (19.20)
Moreover, Bhīṣma and the others would certainly not create opposition in his presence; for when they have departed, that friendship will perish.
(19.21) A division of the family will arise, which is the cause of the family's destruction, while these [enemies] remain united and dwelling in the city.
Therefore, by the power of strategic means, they must be driven away from here to Vāraṇāvata; this is the method that has been devised. (19.22)
Viṣṇu, known as Jayanta, shall remain there as an associate of Śambhu, and a truly magnificent festival of the gods will take place here.
For those devotees of yours, urged by you, will quickly approach that festival with the enemy-slaying conch in hand.
Having commanded my attendants to assume the status of my own men, they shall be stationed there like mediators, endowed with many virtues.

"A desire has arisen in them to go there, surely to see the city of the Pāṇḍavas which possesses many virtues. When his daughter had spoken thus, he replied, "So be it. And when the sons of Pāṇḍu arrived, he spoke to them in the same manner. Having understood the king's entire intention, they too went with Pṛthā and their father for the sake of following proper conduct.
"Bhīma will surely become a wanderer for alms here," having thus correctly understood his own duty, he declared to his elder brother, "One's own work must not be abandoned;
let us go, for staying at home is our natural duty. (19.26) If they drive us out while we are established in our own duty, we shall fight here; for even the killing of bandits is not unrighteous."
Having spoken thus, the son of Dharma said to Umā: "Indeed, our fame perishes through conflict with our elders.
To him, who had spoken these words, his elder brother Bhīma replied, demonstrating his own duty for the sake of compliance:
"Since a fault would arise from either side, one's own duty must be declared; however, no persistence should be maintained in this matter. (19.27–28)
When his own duty required him to abandon [the kingdom] for the sake of fame alone,
Hari, capable of warding off both faults of Bhīma, made his eldest son the protector of righteousness here;
for when Suyodhana and others have become liable to be slain, one's own duty cannot be fulfilled through any other pretext.
"Previously, in the act of killing, no faults at all accrued to them; for that very reason, they have now come forth.
Then Vidura, understanding the situation and fearing the danger of poison and fire, spoke these kind words to the Son of Dharma in the dialect of the outcastes: "Please stay!
He replied, "So be it," and departed for Vāraṇāvata along with Pṛthā and his younger brothers.
Then, in order to kill them, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra immediately had a house made of lac, concealed with gold and jewels;
he sent his own minister named Purocana there, who was formerly the very wicked one known as Prahasta, and having approached, he became the counselor of the sons of Pāṇḍu. (19.32)

"Having left Duryodhana, I have come into your presence," he said with these deceitful words. "Indeed, a celestial palace has been brought by me for you; I am not able to follow that evil man out of mere affection. I shall always dwell among you who are steadfast in righteousness. To him who spoke thus, they replied, "Ah, how auspicious! (19.33–34).

Upon seeing that house made of lac mixed with fat—its scent being known by the son of Vṛṣa (Nakula) to have been produced from fire—the son of Pavana (Bhīma) spoke to that most wicked man: "This villain wishes to kill us with a pleasant face; always remain alert! (19.35).
Then the Steward (Vidura), knowing the conduct of all the world through the power of political science and from the reports of his own spies, spoke to the digger:

Having spoken my previous words to the son of Dharma, he quickly made a very distant tunnel there. And so, under the pretext of constructing a wall, he made a path and blocked its entrance; then Bhīma and Purocana went to their own homes. Both of them, seeking each other's flaws for the sake of killing one another, lived together for half a year.

His elder sister arrived there accompanied by her five sons; following that, this son of the Wind (Hanumān) reflected thus: "Now is the time. Having considered this and observing that they were fast asleep, he first quickly placed his brothers and mother into the cave.
Then the son of the Wind set fire to the wicked sister along with her house and her nephew.
She too had indeed come to destroy these [serpents] with her poison, yet she was unable to do so because of Bhīma’s prior consumption [of it].
(19.39) She, along with her sons, performed most intense austerities, thinking, "May I become Aditi together with my sons by force within a year.
And Giriśa granted her this boon: "If you do not depart with your sons, you shall not meet death; this is your boon. (19.40)

Knowing all this—that Bhīmasena had killed that evil-minded one along with his sons, and having dragged out his brothers and mother from the cave—he departed; for they, having emerged, had fallen into a state of weakness due to the power of fear.
(19.41) Having learned of the slaughter of Purocana, if the sons of Vicitravīrya, led by Bhīṣma, were to attack [us],...

"What might happen to us?"—this terrible fear entered them all, with the exception of Pṛthā’s sons. Although Bhīma was fearless and personally disliked fighting with his elders, for the sake of Yudhiṣṭhira’s words, he set out after them; and having crossed the celestial river (Gaṅgā) by boat, he boarded a water-vehicle provided by a Kṣatriya.
Convinced by the words of Vidura, which were consistent with what had occurred before, and having mounted the back of Bhīma, they all departed for the forest;
yet when the sun had risen, the citizens saw the seven dead bodies and wept aloud:
"Alas! This evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra has indeed caused the Pāṇḍavas, who stood firm in righteousness, to be consumed by fire through Purocana! (19.44)
"Even he, that most wicked man, has been consumed here by the power of fate; for what person, however malicious, could prevail against the virtuous for their happiness?
(19.45) Having heard this entirely from the citizens, Bhīṣma and the others, together with the son of Vicitravīrya, spoke.
Then Suyodhana and the rest, their minds deeply distressed, wept falsely and performed their duties under the direction of Kṣattṛ (Vidura). (19.46)

Bhīma, too, having carried away the forest, reached the brothers of Hiḍimba and Pṛthā; and being entreated by those who were thirsty, he saw her sleeping after having carried water from afar in his upper garment, which was tied with lotus leaves. While Bhīmasena remained awake for the sake of guarding them, the Rākṣasa sent his sister Hiḍimbī toward her.

Having assumed a beautiful form, she beheld Bhīma, who was visibly the very essence of all auspicious marks. (19.48) She took on the body of a rākṣasī, appearing like the splendor of the world of the lord of gods, yet another Śacī distinct from the beloved wife of Śakra.
Having obtained her husband Māruta through a curse born of rivalry, she requested Bhīmasena that she might regain her own original form. (19.49)
Bhīma said to her of lovely form: "I do not approach a woman before my elder brother; this is not the dharma.
She, however, being under the sway of desire, replied: "O you who are joined with your own entrance, [this is the case] for one who has been wedded by the foremost of the Maruts.
Sarasvatī granted this boon to her: her own entrance and union with her beloved.
Because she was pleased by her exceedingly intense penance, she granted him liberation from the curse and bestowed her own body upon the son of the Wind-god (Hanumān).
Furthermore, the Lord, the teacher of the entire world and master of Indirā, spoke again:
"In this world, I shall appear in the form of Vyāsa after two days; at that time, He will grant me to you, and then you may fulfill my request. (19.51–52)
At that very moment, Hiḍimba became enraged and set out to kill Bhīma, as well as his own sister;
for previously he had employed her solely for the purpose of devouring them, and now he approached Bhīma swiftly to seize them.
She fled to Bhīma alone for refuge, and he then advanced to protect her, her brother, and their mother.
Fearing that he might disturb his brothers' sleep, Bhīma drew him a great distance away and fought with him.

Having fought with fists, trees, stones, and rocks, and having awakened those who were deeply asleep, they then gathered around in agitation upon seeing their brother; at that very sight, the son of the Wind struck the Rākṣasa in the chest.
Struck by the strength of Bhīma’s arms in accordance with the Lord’s word, he fell to the surface of the earth despite being invincible to all;
with copious blood flowing from his mouth, he met death and then gradually entered the eternal, blinding darkness.
Having slain that Rākṣasa Śarvara—who was protected by the gods and unslayable by anyone—Bhīma, together with his brother and mother, [returned].
Bhīma followed him, and Hiḍimbī likewise followed; she then entreated Kuntī on his behalf for Yudhiṣṭhira.

Although Bhīma did not act upon what those two had urged, Hari—the soul of Vyāsa, filled with all supreme qualities, an ocean of infinite bliss, spread with the rays of knowledge, and the most excellent of all—manifested himself. 19.57–58.

Upon seeing him, the sons of Pṛthā, together with their mother, were filled with supreme joy; having honored the Guru of Viriñci, they sat down as Hari, whose lotus-eyes blossomed with the deepest affection, looked upon them.
Beholding them with their heads bowed in devotion, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Bhīma, who was likewise bowing along with Hiḍimbā.
"Accept this young woman, who is the very ornament of the celestial abode; once a son is born, let her return with that son.
When Rameśa spoke thus, Bhīma—whose great virtues were beyond counting—uttered "Oṃ" and did exactly as requested.
Carrying her on his shoulder through regions frequented by the gods, Hiḍimbī set out at the very moment the sun rose.
Having sported in the Nandana and other groves, she would return in the evening with the Pārthas and Pṛthā;
thus they passed half a year, during which a son was born to them, endowed with exceeding heroism and strength.
He was the god Nirṛti in the form of a Rākṣasa, who had formerly been possessed by Giriśa, known by the name Ghaṭotkaca.
Previously, his head was like a jar, and from it hair emerged in an instant; thus indeed was he named.
When the son was born according to the agreement made by the Blessed One, Bhīma spoke to her regarding the departure of both mother and son.
Remembering their mutual agreement and having fulfilled their promise to them, she departed for the world of the gods.

Vyāsa, too, accompanied by the sons of Pāṇḍu, went to Ekacakrā for the sake of Bakas’ slaughter— Baka who had become invincible through a fierce boon— and he, of immeasurable glory, arrived there with his full and inexhaustible joy unimpeded. Then Kṛṣṇa, having placed those boys, who were in the form of Brahmin youths, in the house of a Brahmin, saying, "These are my disciples," [departed].
Having instructed them, saying, "I am departing," he went away; then they made their dwelling there after having recited the Vedas.
(19.66) While they were constantly wandering for alms, a terrifying man in the very midst of the village would give a loud grunt at the size of a house.
Taking a vessel made by a potter, he would depart out of fear that he might be recognized; Dharmarāja spoke to him. (19.67)

For you have lifted up with one hand this massive dwelling together with the earth from the mouth of the fire, while a great potter gave you a vessel for that purpose; and you wander for alms, receiving it with a mere grunt of "hum.
May there arise through the power of your well-established Dharma an awakening in Suyodhana and his people, and from that, may my fear cease.

“Dwell together with your mother and enjoy what has been brought for you by the eldest of the Phalguna brothers; do not go out. (19.69) Having been told this, Bhīma did exactly so. They too remained silent for the sake of preserving their own duty.
Then, when those four had gone out to wander for alms, he would sometimes remain alone with his mother. (19.70)

At that very moment, hearing the weeping of a Brahmin and his wife for the sake of their own dwelling, Bhīma—fearing he might be ashamed in a house filled with women, children, and the play of infants—said to his mother, "Go and find out why the Brahmin is weeping; I shall do what is appropriate. She then departed quickly. (19.71)
Remaining concealed within the house, she overheard his entire speech. Then that best of brahmins said to his beloved:
"Indeed, tribute must be paid today to this Rākṣasa Baka, who consumes food and drink as vast as a mountain.
We must provide a man with a cart and a bull; for there is no man among us who would not suffer total ruin by failing to give. (19.72–73)
"I am going elsewhere," I said previously; this was not what was in your heart, my dear, and therefore you spoke thus.
"I shall go to the mouth of the Rākṣasa myself to die. To him, his wife said: "O Lord, I will not go here.
By abandoning my body today for your sake, I shall become one whose conduct is praised among virtuous women in this world; otherwise, I would fall into sin. (19.74)
The maiden said to him, "I am indeed [the one]; the purpose is not for a maiden. Thus addressed, that best of brahmins exclaimed, "Fie! (19.75).
"The maiden has declared herself the deliverer of both families; she is my wife, my companion, and my son—these words have reached my ears.
She is my very self, and not merely for the sake of livelihood, do I deliberately offer her up to this cruel man" (19.76).

While they were thus weeping together, the boy, pointing to a blade of grass held in his own hand, said to them, "With this, I shall surely slay the Rākṣasa. When he had spoken these excellent words, Kuntī entered after him.
Questioned by her, that best of Brahmins described Baka’s prowess and strength as being unbearable even for the enemies of the sons of Diti.

Having heard that his maternal uncle, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, possessed formidable strength and immense heroism, and was terrified by the arrows of the noble descendant of Raghu as described in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, he paid tribute for a decade of thirty years;
and having brought the kings under his control, they subsequently offered tribute out of sheer fear, whereupon he rejoiced. (19.78–79)
"By slaying this man who is so rich in strength, Bhīma will attain fame and even greater righteousness here;
and we all, having embraced dharma, shall follow him"—thus he spoke to that bull among the earth-dwellers.
"O best of brahmins, I have five sons today; let one of them go to face the enemy of men."
Thus addressed, he said: "I am not to be slain by your son; alas, your mind is exceedingly firm!
Though thus spoken to, Pṛthā replied: 'My son possesses a knowledge whose form is unassailable even by the lords of the quarters.
Although he has been commanded by his teachers, he will not employ this [knowledge] against one who is not to be slain, even by the guardians of the gods and asuras. (19.81–82)
Having spoken thus, Bhīma returned and related everything; hearing that great account of his own dharma, he was filled with joy.

Seeing him arrive with eyes rolling wildly, the son of Yama approached along with the others and said, "Mother, why is he so exceedingly delighted? She told him everything, and he spoke to her in return.
Alas, a grievous deed has been done by you! Oh, how terrible it is that you would slay this very Bhīma, upon whose strength alone we all rely!
For it is by depending on the supreme power of his arms that we desire sovereignty and the slaughter of all our enemies as our own duty.
O Mother, tell me quickly, with what intention is he today being dispatched by you to the mouth of the enemy at night?
To him who had spoken thus, the wise Kuntī said: "O son, he cannot be slain by anyone—not even by all the gods, asuras, or yogis; for at his birth, Mount Śataśṛṅga was pulverized by him.
Indeed, this Marut himself has become a human being; what person in the worlds, however great his strength, could possibly kill him? (19.86)
"So be it," he said to her. On the following day, Bhīma set out in a cart, having made ample provision.

Having arrived in haste at the vicinity of Baka’s forest, Bhīma desired to eat that foremost of mountains, which resembled a hill and was terrifying to the touch, even before the man-eater had a chance to do so, bringing with him jars of milk-rice, fine foods, and vessels of water. (19.87–88)
While he was eating at that very meal, a fierce *rākṣasa* uprooted a tree and rushed at him;
then the son of the Wind, warding off those blows with his left hand, took up all the food along with the side-dishes.
Having drunk water and quickly not looking at him, and having sipped it, he fought with him using heavy trees and rocks.

Struck by him, he then [fled] with many mountains; but Bhīma seized him by force and crushed him upon the surface of the earth. Having stepped on his head with the sole of his foot and grasped him firmly by both arms, Bhīma tore him apart.
Having died, that wicked one went to the most terrible and fierce Avīci hell, which is difficult to escape, just like a hater of Viṣṇu.
Having slain that destroyer of the world, who was invincible even to the Rākṣasa Jārāsaṃdha and previously to King Bhārata, son of the Earth, Bhīma had his body placed at the front;
having set it down right at the gate, Bhīma then went back to the side of his own brothers after bathing. 19.92.

Having heard of his supreme deed, they were all filled with joy; together with their mother, they followed him as he stood before them. Upon seeing the massive body of the Rākṣasa, they were terrified, but then, having understood through various reasons that he was dead, and having heard from the words of that Brahmin how Bhīmasena had destroyed him, they rejoiced exceedingly in him.

They performed the *annaprāśana* rite for him; he too, impelled by the words of Viṣṇu—the son of Satyavatī and Hari who had assumed the form of Narasiṃha—then set out. Having related the account of the birth of Drupada’s daughter, Vyāsa, the teacher of the worlds and Lord of lords, spoke thus.
Then other foremost of the twice-born urged, "Let them go," and those brahmins said, "The meal shall be theirs.
For previously, having heard that these sons of Pṛṣata had been burned in the house of lac, the king’s mind was filled with extreme sorrow;
yet, upon hearing the counsel emerging from the mouths of Yāja and Upayāja, he concluded that they were not guilty of falsehood and deemed their lives to be spared.

Thinking that the sons of Pṛthā were dwelling somewhere in disguise, he proclaimed the *svayaṃvara* for the sake of Phalguna; and among the kings, he made it impossible for anyone other than the Lord Śiva to bend the bow. At that very time, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, [learned] everything through his own complete awakening.
Although he already knew [the truth], having heard that the sons of Pṛthā were dead, he went together with Halin for the sake of the funeral water-offerings (kulyā).
Having reached Hastināpura, he deceived the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by telling stories consistent with their own views;
then, surrounded by Bhīṣma and the others, he returned to Dvāravatī like something unpleasant, yet possessing eternal happiness filled with joy.
In his absence, Hṛdika’s son, relying on the power of Śvaphalka’s intellect, spoke thus:
"For in the past, this Satrājit promised us his own daughter along with the jewel;
yet he has now disregarded all of us and given the daughter to Kṛṣṇa. Slay that man of evil intent in the night! (19.101)
"Take this jewel and come to us; in our conflict with Kṛṣṇa, I shall seek assistance from the Lord of Gifts (Kubera).

When he had spoken thus, that evil-minded one—who was indeed a Daitya in a former body—did so. Then Satyabhāmā, though filled with joy, approached her husband in that body for the sake of deceiving the world. (19.102–19.103)

Having heard those words of his, and having learned from the report of the Pāñcāla king’s men that a great festival was taking place in his own city, the Blessed One went to that city together with the best of the Vṛṣṇis and the wielder of the mace (Balarāma).
Bhīma as well— worshipped by the devotees of Hari— having slain that Rākṣasa who had been protected by a boon from Rudra, treated him as if he were a mere blade of grass.

Having stayed there for some days, they departed with their own people at the command of Acyuta, who was Vyāsa in person. Hearing these words uttered here and there by the Brahmins—“Go quickly; this is an incomparable auspicious omen! Upon reaching the Pāñcālas, supreme food shall be prepared here”—they wandered through the northern regions.

"Upon seeing him—standing in the midst of the six, with uplifted arms, a broad chest, and the marks of abundant manliness—the Brahmins declared: 'In this place, Māruti shall surely find Kṛṣṇā. (19.107) Then, traveling constantly by day and night along the road, they eventually reached the Viṣṇupadī at nightfall.
In order to protect everyone here, Bhīma was stationed at the rear, while the son of Śatamanyu (Arjuna) was at the front, and others were in between.
(19.108) Then, when Arjuna—who carried a firebrand—reached the Gaṅgā at midnight, Citraratha, the king of the Gandharvas, arrived there.
Seeing them standing within the water without their brahmin (Dhaumya), he approached with the intent to assault them, thinking, "These are merely sons of the Kṣatriya class. (19.109)
"I shall indeed slay you all when you have approached the water's edge of this river at a time forbidden for the movement of mortals.
To him who spoke thus, the son of the Lord of the Gods said: "O Gandharva, there is no fear for you today from those who know the divine weapons (astras).
For this vast army of yours is like foam; even when employed by one skilled in weapons, it does not achieve its purpose. (19.110)
When he had spoken thus, the servant of the Lord of the Gods, standing upon his excellent vehicle and discharging arrows, rushed toward him.
At that moment, the son of Śakra, having consecrated a fire-weapon (*āgneya-astra*) over a firebrand, hurled it; and his chariot was consumed by the flames.
Seizing him by the hair as he was enveloped by the fire, the son of the Lord of the Gods quickly dragged him along.
Provoked by Pārtha, he sought refuge with that son of Dharma; then, having withdrawn his own fierce weapon, he became known by the name Aṅgāravarṇa due to the change in his complexion.
Having previously formed a friendship, he now became a Gandharva with a body intensely red, yet formerly fair as gold.
Although Pārtha knew it, he did not know such a great weapon as this which was difficult to obtain, yet he requested it.

For that knowledge was most perfectly mastered by the son of the Lord of the Gods; he [Indra] imparted it to him, and later, at the word of the son of Puruhūta, he also taught him the Gandharva-gāminī, the invisible-knowledge, in due course of time. (19.114–115)

Out of his own superior self-knowledge, Dhanañjaya did not desire an exchange with him even in a state of equality; rather, having entrusted her to him solely for the sake of dharma, he later returned her to him according to dharma. (19.116) Having conversed at length with Pārtha, he also spoke of Dhaumya’s appointment as the domestic priest.
Having spoken these words to Arjuna, "I shall give you divine horses," he ascended to heaven and vanished.
Having obtained Dhaumya as their preceptor, who was supremely wise and like unto the son of a Brahmin, they entered the city.
There they beheld the entire assembly of consecrated kings (mūrdhāvasikta) of the Pāñcāla king, all beautifully adorned. (19.117–118)
Beholding the circle of kings fully assembled there, his brother took Kṛṣṇā by the hand, her natural garland still held fast, and led her into the midst of them.
Then, he spoke to all those kings regarding the splendor endowed with noble lineage and heroic prowess;
having displayed all those [kings] who had offered oblations to the fire, he set down that bow along with its five arrows.
Then, having addressed all the kings with a loud voice, his body radiant like a blazing fire and his roar like a thundercloud, he said:

"O heroes among kings, today this fish will follow that man by whom it was seen reflected in the water upon the tree as a mere image, using this excellent bow and these arrows, by which the fish was struck down here. (19.120–19.121)
At these words, all the sons of the lords of men rose up, their faces adorned with earrings swaying from their haughty pride;
beholding their own great skill in weapons and strength, and competing with one another, they stood with their bodies fully ornamented.
Some, having approached the bow and looked at it, said, "It is not possible for me," and turned away; others, however, shook it. (19.122)
There, Śiśupāla of vast prowess approached it; having seized it, he exerted himself to mount it.
(19.123) Just as he pulled it toward him with ten million [units of force], it rose up and instantly struck him back.
Realizing that this was impossible for anyone other than Phalguna, he went away broken, his hopes shattered by the boon of the Lord of Mountains. (19.124)
The lord of Madre, though aged, approached and by his prowess drew [the bow] even more than the lord of Cedi had done on a target the size of a mung bean;
having been thwarted by him when only that much remained, he departed, realizing his own inability, and thereafter the kings became despondent.
When the kings had withdrawn, the king of Magadha approached, arrogant with the pride of his own strength and heroism, treating them with utter contempt.

He drew his bow with the strength of one whose soles were steady; he struck that [arrow] which was the size of a mustard seed right back at him. At that very moment, his two knees sank into the earth, and out of pride, he stood on unsteady feet merely for the sake of maintaining his position.
Then, by a fierce boon, the king was rendered waterless; failing to look upon the faces of other kings, he departed for his own kingdom.
Most of the kings followed him [into the fire]; then Karṇa, having taken up the bow for the sake of Duryodhana, drew it.
Having received only the auspicious training from Rāma, he reduced the end of the bow to nothing but its feathers as it snapped.
When that [bow] was thus destroyed by him and he had returned, Bhīma and Arjuna sat down among the assembly of brahmins.
They rose up, their forms resembling the sun and the moon, even as the brahmins there tried to restrain them out of fear.
Some of the brahmins then spoke these words: "These two heroes are indeed exceedingly powerful, for they are like gods.
Upon seeing the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa, those two, the essence of supreme valor, quickly withdrew from the vicinity of the bow.

There, Arjuna, having obtained permission from Vāyu—who is dearer to him than even his own life—and having mentally bowed to Keśava, the Unborn, effortlessly strung that bow endowed with excellent qualities using a mechanical device; then, with arrows, he struck the target.
At that time, Kṛṣṇā placed a garland of fresh lotuses around his neck, and having positioned herself between the two princes, she [bestowed it]. (19.131)
Bhīma and Arjuna went forth after bowing to Acyuta; then this ocean of the best of kings became agitated as they rushed forward.

"For [Arjuna] alone has the right to go, but not for the sake of the maiden; let the best of the Vṛṣṇis not even touch the bow here"—by this command of the wielder of the excellent discus, the heroes of the Yadu clan did not entertain even the desire to take part in this matter. (19.132–133)

But Bhīma, seeing the royal assembly approaching, uprooted a tree ten *yojanas* high and stood over all the kings; seeing them intent on flight, they became [terrified]. "This is Bhīma, this is the son of Puruhūta, and these others are the Pārthas"—thus did Hari speak to Halin. 19.134.
Upon seeing him, the grandson of Śini also attained joy and, seizing his sword, leaped up there in exultation.

(19.135) While all the Yadus were delighted and all the kings, beginning with Duryodhana, had fled from Bhīma, Karṇa rushed toward the son of Hari’s charioteer, and the heroic King of Madra went toward the son of the Wind-god himself. (19.136)
