When the brahmins were angrily throwing sticks, cloths, *darbha* grass, and great skins at him, there was no destruction for him; for it was said that such hostility from a kshatriya brings no harm. Then the son of the Wind-god (Bhima) asked Drupada for Krishna (Draupadi) and the brahmins as well. Taking the King of Madra as a substitute tree, he seized him with his two arms and swiftly lifted him into the sky.
Having recognized his prowess on the earth, he [Kṛṣṇa] gradually established him in kinship; then, having understood his valor, he returned to his own capital.
Pārtha also fought with that bow against Karṇa, and Karṇa displayed his mastery of weapons and the strength of his arms there.
"Are you Phalguna, or Indra, the slayer of the demon Paka, or perhaps the best of the twice-born in bodily form? No one else is capable of standing before me.
Whether you are who you are, or whoever you may be—if it pleases you, release your arrows today; otherwise, come to me in battle! Thus spoke Partha.
Having said, "I have no need for combat with the best of the twice-born," the son of the Sun departed along with Suyodhana and his followers.

Then Bhīma, accompanied by Arjuna, set out for the city called Nāga, taking the daughter of Drupada with him. Meanwhile, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) traveled ahead together with the two Aśvin sons, while Bhīma and Pārtha followed behind to the potter’s house.
When they announced, "Alms! Kuntī said, "Eat all together," and she presented the maiden [to them].
And the speech uttered by her was not false, for she had previously reflected on how this could be so; thus, a great anxiety arose among them.
Then the son of Vasudeva, Hari, arrived there with supreme affection.
Having conversed with them, the Blessed One, whose power is immeasurable, departed for his own city accompanied by all the Yadus.

In order to identify them during the night, Drupada sent his own son; and he beheld them there eating alms-food, as well as his own sister, her heart filled with contentment upon hearing the news of the battle. Hearing their deep voices, resonant like the sound of clouds, that hero concluded that they were of the highest warrior caste.

In the morning, however, at the word of his father, the family priest approached them; having been honored by the highly learned son of Marut according to the ritual of mantras, he accepted them and, together with the mother, ushered them into the king’s palace. Having welcomed those who had arrived and his own daughter with various articles of offering specified separately as befitting Brahmins and others, [he honored them].

The king assigned them four houses that were fully furnished; they went there, and those houses were filled with weapons and other necessities. (19.147) Having recognized the sons of the lord of the earth by their gestures, voices, appearances, intended prowess, valor, confidence, and other such qualities, Drupada approached the son of Dharma and asked: "Who are you, O best of men? Tell me the truth. (19.148)
Smiling gently, he said: "O King, why is this being asked today? For previously, no distinction was stated regarding the castes.

But now that you have made him your son, the 'piercing of the target with a hundred thousand arrows' has been mentioned; and though it was performed by him in the assembly of kings—" To him who was speaking thus, the king, together with Pṛthā, again entreated him, saying, "Speak."

Pṛthā told him everything, and he, pleased by that, spoke these words: "I have accomplished my purpose today; indeed, this effort was made by me solely for the sake of Pārtha. Whether you be Phalguna or someone else, take whatever portion of my daughter’s dowry you wish. When thus addressed, the son of Dharma replied: "Everything—this is what has taken root in my mind. (19.150–151)
"Though no authoritative proof appears here in my heart, nevertheless my mind, firm in dharma, considers that very thing as authority.
Even after he had spoken thus, the king did not wish to go along with his son; however, the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa arrived there.
Seeing that Blessed Vyāsa, whose nature consists of immeasurable, perfect, eternal, and imperishable qualities, everyone was filled with longing.
Having bowed and offered worship, and having received the command of him who was seated upon the excellent throne, they sat down together at his side.
Then Kṛṣṇa said to the king: "Give the maiden to all of us;
for these—the bull, Vāyu, Purandara, along with the two Nāsatyas and the Dasras—are indeed the Indras, both those of former times and those of the present, following after Hari."
"All their splendors and even their bodies as one are but your own daughter; therefore, there is no contradiction here.
Even when this was said, Drupada did not direct his mind toward such a conclusion. Then Kṛṣṇa said to him:
"Indeed, this divine vision has been granted to you today; behold quickly the sons of Pāṇḍu stationed in the sky!"
"And this daughter of yours, along with those [beings], standing apart with their respective characteristics—then do with them as you wish.
After these words were spoken, the king beheld them in the sky, such as they were, by the power of Kṛṣṇa’s grace.
Having observed these, and having seen the feet of the Lord of the World, he went for refuge out of fear, disregarding his own [former] contempt.
Having granted his protection, the Blessed One, when Drupada had replied "So be it" regarding the matter, personally arranged the entire marriage ceremony;
then, accompanied by Dhaumya, he performed the rites in due order, and all the [brides] took the hands of the [grooms].
A great festival took place among the Pāñcālas, and the king became joyful along with his sons and all his kinsmen.
Just as Janaka had attained joy after giving his daughter to Rāma in the presence of the citizens and countryfolk, so too,
having heard that the Pāṇḍavas were dwelling there after their marriage ceremony, Kṛṣṇa— accompanied by Rāma and the Yādavas—
took abundant wedding gifts and came with great joy to meet the sons of Pṛthā along with Pṛthā herself.
Upon seeing him, the heroes of the Kurus rejoiced; having embraced Kṛṣṇa, they then bowed, and he [in turn] bowed to Draupadī.
Seeing them, Acyuta gave them all the vessels suitable for household use and bestowed upon them abundant golden ornaments.
He gave them magnificent jewels along with earrings, necklaces, crowns, armlets, garments, and other fine trinkets worthy of celestial beings.
He gave to each of the six separately what was appropriate for them, and then he gave to his father’s sister what was suitable for her:
jewels, cows, elephants, horses, chariots, and even many loads of gold; and then he bestowed the highest blessings.
Vyāsa also gave here and in the hereafter, as did the son of Pṛṣata, ornaments, chariots, horses, excellent elephants, and fine gold.
There, Hari and the king gave thousands of female slaves along with male servants, all of auspicious form and attire;

they also gave each of them garments of various colors, long necklaces of great jewels, and abundant ornaments. (19.164) Having spent many months together with the sons of Pṛthā, Kṛṣṇa departed for the city of the Yadus, accompanied by his elder brother.
When the Blessed One had vanished and Vyāsa, whose power was vast, had departed, these sons of Pṛthā dwelt here for a year.

Then those sons of Vicitravīrya, together with the son of Subala, Karṇa, the Lord of Sindhu, and hosts of chariots and elephants, along with Bhūriśravas and others, arrived at the city once more, intent on slaying the King of the Pañcālas. (19.165–166)
Afflicted by them in his own city, that king of the Somakas emerged together with his sons and his army.
A great conflict ensued between them and him; his two sons were slain and his forces were scattered.
When Citra had been killed in battle along with Citraketu, the elite soldiers of Pārṣata’s side fled.
The sons of Pṛthā, holding their bows and arrows, advanced on chariots against the sons of Vicitravīrya who were yoked with the son of the Sun.
While those five fought back equally against them, Bhūriśravas deprived the son of the Sun of his chariot.
Thereafter, the son of the Wind-god, with his two arms, uprooted a massive tree resembling a mountain and hurled it at the son of Śakra.

Seeing this son of the Wind-god approaching with a tree in his hand, Suyodhana and all the others, including Karṇa, Bhūriśravas, Śakuni, and Jayadratha, fled; indeed, they all retreated and entered their own city. (19.170) Having learned all of that, Vidura said: "O King, your sons are surely prospering."
Thus he spoke, and he too was delighted that Kṛṣṇā had been recovered by his son; he gave him excellent ornaments and garments.
Vidura said, "The Pārthas," and he [Dhṛtarāṣṭra], intent on concealing his true feelings, replied very loudly:
"Blessings! Are the Pārthas alive along with Pṛthā? Tell me everything regarding their news. (19.171-172)

Thus addressed, Vidura related the entire account beginning with the slaying of Hiḍimba, including the feat of piercing the target at a distance of a hundred *lakṣas*, the marriage, and the sons born of the river-born Kuntī; and all were satisfied, even as they dwelt there for a year.
Then, having heard that Kṛṣṇa had arrived and bestowed great wealth and jewels upon the sons of Pāṇḍu, and that he had departed once more, [they rejoiced].
With hearts burning with grief, Suyodhana and the others then held a consultation; led by Karṇa, they set out for battle once more.
When they had departed again on their chariots, Vidura spoke to the elder brother [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] regarding the chief sons of the River [the Kauravas]:
"These men, whose minds are most sinful, will surely meet their death upon encountering the sons of Pṛthā in battle; there is no doubt in this. (19.174–175)
There is no one, even among the foremost of the gods, who possesses the strength to withstand Bhīma and Arjuna, for they have been nurtured by you.
Knowing this, you have committed a great unrighteousness by neglecting them for so many years; therefore, enough!
Employ them. Having first conciliated them with gentle words, bring them back and establish them among the kings with half the kingdom.
"By doing this, it will lead to the prosperity of your lineage and to righteousness; otherwise, you would be the destroyer of both.
When she had spoken thus, Droṇa, the son of the River (Bhīṣma), and Kṛpa said, "So be it," and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra also spoke to Vidura:
"Go and bring him here. He arrived there in a swift chariot, and was thereafter honored by them all.
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, and Vyāsa—both possessed of boundless power—approached them;
accompanied by Vidura, they took the people together with Kuntī and their wife and went to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
When they had arrived, there arose a great and intense joy among the people of the city and the countryside alike.

Bhīṣma and the others, being delighted, honored them and, together with the king, escorted them into their homes with great celebration. There, the daughter of Subala (Gāndhārī) and her beloved Duryodhana paid Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) the highest honor; they all remained there, yet due to the misconduct of their own sons and the great fear caused by Bhīma on account of Kṛṣṇā, [they lived in anxiety]. 19.180–181.

"Kunti, go home together with your daughter-in-law; I am terrified of Bhima due to the wickedness of my own son," she said, "for Krishna possesses a beauty and excellence that surpasses all women in the three worlds. Thus, accompanied by her sons, she departed for her home.
In this manner, they lived for five years in the house of Pāṇḍu, very happy and endowed with every enjoyment.
And Kṛṣṇā, though possessing a single body, sported with them individually in four forms due to the distinction of their respective desires.
She remained a maiden; thus, for each day, her birth occurred separately according to their individual inclinations, not because of a difference in the Supreme Being.
For Vāṇī generally does not undergo birth through the agency of desire; therefore, Marut was present within all of them. (19.183–184)
The Wind-god (Marut), having entered into Dharmaputra and the others, constantly sports by deluding their intellect;
for that intellect remains pure precisely because of that [divine presence], yet through its daily delusion, the maiden here experiences as if death.
This is not like sleep, however, because it is due to being under the control of another; for there is no such delusion in Hari, who possesses perfect mindfulness. 19.185.
And because she is not like one possessed, her very nature is such that she dies; for this maiden is born anew every day.
(19.186) Thus, that wind, having entered Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, rejoices constantly and alone with her as his own self.
For the enjoyment of the gods is of one kind, while the enjoyment of humans is of another form; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (19.187)
Vasiṣṭha’s son and Vṛṣa, those two Keśavas, also dwelt there out of supreme affection for them;
and with those two, who were full of infinite virtues and whose nature was bliss, the sons of Pṛthā rejoiced in excellent conversations.
For previously, while they were living in the forest, King Kaṃsa had arranged the marriage of his daughter to the great king Ugrasena.
There, at her *svayaṃvara*, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, excessively arrogant because of his own strength, seized the maiden by force.

For previously, during the counting of kings, that sovereign of Magadha had been counted [among the ranks]; thus, in great rage, the kings fought with Duryodhana when he had seized the maiden, but they were defeated by him together with Karṇa and his younger brother. 19.189–190.

When they had broken and taken up their bows again, Karṇa said to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra: "Go forth, joined by your brothers! For you who are accompanied by Bhīṣma, your preceptor, and the other leaders, there is no cause for fear upon entering the city.
Bārhadratha does not follow you unless he perceives certain victory; there is no certainty of success for one remaining within the city. (19.191)
Knowing that the son of Droṇa is always an incarnation of Rudra, this devotee of Rudra does not desire to fight with him.
(19.192) "I alone shall fight against the kings; even if they defeat me, you will have no infamy.
And if they should capture your one younger brother here by means of their prowess, your fame will reach its full extent. (19.193)

"Indeed, even Bhīṣma and the others were not capable of fighting this king; for that very reason, Bāhlika became his servant, yet he did not go to war against Bhīṣma, nor was there any enmity with him. (19.194) Having been told this, Aṇsu reflected and went to his own city; Karṇa also fought against them and conquered them.
Disregarding the prowess of Karṇa, the son of Jarā commanded each king individually to fight him.
When all of them had been defeated, the son of Bṛhadratha also approached to fight with him on that very chariot.
By virtue of Rāma’s boon, he rendered him chariotless and weaponless; then the two of them closed in upon each other, attacking with their fists.
When Karṇa struck at the joint of his body while it was being joined together by the surgeon, the King did not find satisfaction in that other matter;
nor was this even known by the Plough-bearer (Balarāma), but this has been known by you—therefore, from now on, be my servant.
(19.197) I shall not kill you, who are so skilled and experienced in many battles, but rather [I shall kill] your father first.
"Indeed, the kingdom of Aṅga was seized by me through the strength of my arms; therefore, take it and become my servant in battle.

When thus addressed, Karṇa did exactly so. For previously, after Karṇa had conquered the King of Magadha, that portion of his own ancestral kingdom which had been taken away by Vṛkodara was restored to him by Duryodhana.
Having obtained the sovereignty over the Aṅgas and out of affection for the son of Jarā, the son of Sūrya went to the Kurus.
Upon seeing him, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra rejoiced; they found nothing equal to him, nor even to Hari.
Having married the daughter of Kaṃsa, who was presided over by Girijā and was the first pure Lakṣmī manifested directly among men—
In her, he begot a son who was formerly Akṣa, and a daughter who was the beloved of the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya).

That son became known by the name Lakṣaṇa, and that daughter, possessing superior beauty and virtues, was named Lakṣaṇā. Furthermore, his younger brothers, endowed with qualities suited to themselves, obtained wives; and Suyodhana also obtained wives. (19.201–202)

Formerly, there was a son of Duḥśāsana known as Surāntaka; subsequently, tormented upon seeing the strength, heroism, virtues, and prosperity of the Pārtha, they departed for the Kaliṅga country. There, a *svayaṃvara* was held for the daughter of the King of Kaliṅga, whom kings call Suvajra.
The arrogant son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra forcibly seized the daughter of that [king] who had been unconquered due to a boon from Rudra.
Thereupon, joined by the son of Jarā, he defeated Suyodhana and bound him in battle by virtue of that boon from Rudra.
Karṇa fled from there because he had come out of rivalry with the sons of Pāṇḍu; thus was he defeated.

When Duryodhana, along with his younger brothers, was captured by them, Bhīma—urged by the words of Bhīṣma, Ambikā’s son (Dhṛtarāṣṭra), and Vidura’s elder brother (Kṣattṛ)—conquered those kings together with the sons of Jarā, and having struck down the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he released Suvarcas. They too, accompanied by Karṇa, their appearance like that of the dead, then returned to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura). 19.206. Even though they had come to these [cities].
Seeing the conflict, the king said to the son of Dharma, "Go quickly to the place established by Purandara.

There, enjoy half the kingdom together with your younger brothers, and take half of the treasury; for formerly Śakra was consecrated there by the gods, beginning with the one born from the lotus (Brahmā).
Having been consecrated there, he indeed ruled the kingdom for a long time while remaining in that very place. (19.207–208)
"O hero, you are indeed equal to Śakra; therefore, this city is worthy of you alone, so come, I shall consecrate you.
In the *Prācīnakośa*, the reading "mṛtakapratīpāḥ" is found, but the meaning is not clear.
Since the word *pratīpa* is not commonly known to denote "similarity," as stated by Govindācārya [in his commentary on the Mahābhārata],
Yudhiṣṭhira said "Oṃ" and that son of Ambikā (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) performed his consecration as well. (19.209)

Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the Vasiṣṭhas, first performed his consecration, saying: "Become great, a universal monarch, a performer of the horse sacrifice and all other royal rites such as the Rājasūya, and one who is ever constant in righteousness. (19.210) Thus, when the son of Pārṣata had been consecrated along with his daughter, Kṛṣṇa, that bull among the Vṛṣṇis, likewise consecrated him.
And so, these two performed the consecration upon the head of Māruti for the position of crown prince along with his wife;

and when Bhīma was consecrated together with the son of Pṛṣata by those two—who consist of infinite bliss, power, and consciousness—and by other bulls among brahmins, all virtuous people rejoiced as the righteous son of Dharma completed the consecration. (19.211–212)

When that most excellent festival had lasted for seven days, those Pārthas— accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, by Kṛṣṇa the leader of the Vṛṣṇis, by Pṛthā, and by that daughter of the Pāñcāla king— went to the abode of Indra. And as soon as the sons of Pṛthā set out with half of the treasury, all the citizens followed them.
And they said: "Alas! O Suyodhana, this wicked man has indeed cast far away the sons of Pāṇḍu, who are rich in virtue.
Relying on Bhīma’s prowess, he was released from captivity by the Kaliṅgas and even led his daughter to that city.
Even so, he always hates the exceedingly powerful sons of Pṛthā; let us now go together with the virtuous sons of Pṛthā. (19.214–215)
"By the sound of his drum he commands the sons of Pṛthā: 'If you do not follow me, I shall seize all your wealth here today! Let that wicked man do so; we shall not abandon the sons of Pṛthā.
For association with the virtuous is the cause of happiness in this very world, and the sole cause of liberation, whereas the opposite is otherwise. (19.216)

"Therefore, let us indeed go together with the sons of Pāṇḍu to Śakraprastha," said Dharmarāja, his mind firm. "If you have affection for me and my younger brothers, then remain here under the very command of our father;
for your fame would perish by following [him] after his passing—do not follow the son of Ambikā here. (19.217–218)
Thus forbidden by all the city-dwellers, they stood with difficulty, yet followed after them in their minds;
having reached the city of Indra, the two Kṛṣṇas remembered the architect of the Lord of Gods, who then arrived there.
[19.219] He was told by Vasudeva and the Yadu prince to bring from the city of Puruhūta a heap of jewels for the city of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having been thus instructed by the words "on account of their resemblance," he bowed to both lords of all and established the city exactly as before.
(19.220) And the region, not overly crowded with people, was filled with inhabitants from other lands; the sons of Pṛthā caused it to be so.
On account of their virtues and because they were the cause of bowing at the feet of Hari, people from other kingdoms made their auspicious dwellings here. (19.221)
Having sent his sons far away, that king performed the consecration of Suyodhana there;
and having appointed Duḥśāsana as the crown prince, he whose desires were not yet stilled considered himself as one who had achieved his purpose.
And the sons of Pṛthā rejoiced there at those discourses on the determination of all truths uttered by Vasiṣṭha and the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis.
"For they were always hearing [the truth], and they enjoyed the earth according to dharma, with their feet placed upon the heads of their enemies.
(19.223) Thus ends the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Acquisition of the Pāṇḍava Kingdom," [ends].
(The Burning of the Khāṇḍava Forest) Now begins the twentieth chapter.

Oṃ! Yudhiṣṭhira was preeminent in sacrifices, the proclamation of royal power, being honored by gods and men, receiving the salutations of sages, and in matters of dharma-instruction, the praise of the essence of the *Harivaṃśa*, and the protection of the kingdom.
Bhīma was present in the governance of the army, the treasury, expenditures, and the deliberation upon virtues and faults.
(20.1) [Arjuna was preeminent] in instructing women in their duties, the protection of servants and the treasury, expenditures, and the consideration of merits and defects.
For the people residing in the inner apartments, Kṛṣṇā was the manifestation of Dharma for Hari;

Bībhatsu was for the crushing of enemy kingdoms; and Bhīma was for the subduing of Jarāsandha’s sons and others who were unrestrained, as well as Kīcaka and his ilk—who were perpetually terrified of his very strength. (20.2–3)
When the kingdoms had been crushed by Bhīma and were rendered inactive after being defeated in battle, the people generally became devoted to the dharma of Hari due to his command.
At that time, the son of Mādrī was the first, and then the second, among those who provided wages to the livelihood-seekers. 20.4.
After Dharmarāja, he became a sword-wielder protecting against the breaking of alliances and other such threats.
There, Dhṛṣṭadyumna was the leader of the army; out of great affection, he always resided at Indraprastha.
He was especially a friend of Bhīma, and their kingdom was fully provided with all objects of desire.

While Bhīmasena ruled their kingdom, there was no one who was not a Vaiṣṇava, none who was poor, and no loss of dharma for anyone. There were no diseased persons, nor was there death through unnatural calamities.
Indeed, people would come to Yudhiṣṭhira, eager for his audience, seeking gifts as well as for him to officiate at sacrifices.
Since all tasks have been accomplished by Vṛkodara for the sake of his purpose,
all the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas constantly serve them;
and just as all the sages and even the gods come to worship the Lord of the Gods, so too do they come to honor Kṛṣṇa.

In their kingdom, the duties of the Kṛta Age were indeed established, and even more so than that; and their prosperity was greater than that, consisting not only of gold, jewels, and garments, but also of the abundance of crops. 20.10.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira first married the daughter of Śiśupāla, named Devakī.
His own wife was Dhṛṣṭaketu, the sister of Anuhlāda, who was endowed with the splendor of the Sun. From her was born a son named Suhotra, who was formerly Citragupta, the one of excellent writing.
She herself, Kṛṣṇā, was born again in another form as the daughter of the King of Kaṃsa, whom they call Kālī.

That was the goddess Bhāratī alone, and no other goddesses were present there; for her sake, King Kāṇsiraṇa summoned all the monarchs for the svayaṃvara, and they too assembled there with great joy. From among them, she placed the garland upon Bhīmasena, while Jarāsandha and the others stood by.
Enraged, they reviled those who had taken refuge in Viṣṇu and approached Śiva, praising him loudly.
First, Bhīma defeated them with Vedic utterances and with well-employed, sound arguments;
for he had already established that the Vedas are indeed faultless by means of the authoritative scriptures. (20.14–20.15)

The Śaiva scriptures state the superiority of the Vedas and express extensive condemnation of those who have abandoned the Vedas; likewise, they declare the Vaiṣṇava nature of the Ṛg, Sāman, Yajus, Skanda, Saura, and other Vedic hymns.
However, those same scriptures state the superiority of Viṣṇu over Śiva and others, yet this is nowhere found in the Veda itself.

Some declare Viṣṇu to be superior to [Brahmā], while others say that Viṣṇu is the supreme being even above the Buddhists. 20.17 In some places, the Lokāyatas call Viṣṇu the foremost, the teacher, and the most excellent even of Bṛhaspati.
Therefore, Viṣṇu is renowned in all the scriptures as being indeed superior to all and the bestower of liberation. 20.18
"O kings, there is indeed mutual contradiction among those very scriptures regarding other doctrines.
Behold here with your own eyes the power of my arms, which take refuge in the foot of Viṣṇu!
For formerly, when Gaṅgā came to obstruct my worship of Viṣṇu, she was seized by me with my left hand."
Driven away, she went many yojanas beyond to the city of the Kurus; then Śiva arrived there.
Assuming the form of a tiger, he rushed swiftly as if to kill me, testing Umā who was in the form of Kapilā.
He was defeated by me in battle and rendered unconscious by a blow from my mace; then he entered within the *liṅga*. (20.20–21)
The *liṅga* named Vyāghreśvara is famous on earth; likewise, it exists elsewhere in battle.

Indeed, on the Himalayan mountain on the banks of the Gomatī, he was even there conquered by the *liṅga* of Śārdūla. When such is the case regarding the superiority of power belonging to one who takes refuge in Viṣṇupada, what more need be said here?
20.23. Regarding the superiority of Viṣṇu, they say that the authority of Kṣatriyas is strength, while for a Brāhmaṇa it is knowledge alone.
20.24. At Kedāra, I defeated Rudra in the form of a Brāhmaṇa; terrified, he immediately entered his own linga.
Thereafter, Śaṅkara, overcome with shame, bestowed upon me here the state of being inaccessible even to those who know the Vedas.
"Since his mind is thus hostile toward Viṣṇu's manifest power, let him speak his reply;

if his anger is excessive, let him come quickly to fight. Having been addressed thus, they advanced with weapons in hand. Having routed them all with volleys of arrows, he engaged the son of Jarā in combat with his mace.
Seizing him by both arms, he quickly cast him into the celestial river that rises from the foot of Viṣṇu.
20.26 Ashamed, Bhīmasena departed for the Magadha country; accompanied by the kings and honored by the lord of Kāṃsī, he mounted his own chariot and went to the city named after Indra, Kālindī. 20.27

Delighting in her, who was highly esteemed for her beauty and excellent virtues that surpassed those of the three worlds, he begot a son named Śarvatrāta, who was endowed with strength and valor equal to Vāyu; this was he who, in former times, was possessed of equal wind, strength, and heroism.
Kṛṣṇa also, together with Rāma, went to Dvāravatī to find the very one who had carried out the slaying of Satyā’s father.
He desired to kill Śatadhanvan, who in turn entreated Akrūra, who was being pursued by Kṛtavarman.
Those two replied, "We do not harbor even the slightest thought of hostility toward the creator of all the worlds.
Having been thus addressed regarding Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of All, Śatadhanvan mounted his horse and fled in fear.
Kṛṣṇa and Rāma followed him on their chariot for a hundred *yojanas* in a single day.
Having reached the Mare’s Mouth (*baḍabāmukha*), he fled on foot; Kṛṣṇa pursued him on foot and struck him down.
Knowing that Akrūra had given him the jewel, Kṛṣṇa severed his head with his discus. 20.31.
Thinking that even an ignorant person might mock him, he examined the garment and told Rāma, "Not here.

(20.32) Out of distrust, he departed in anger and dwelt in Videha for five years. Knowing that Keshava could not be led away by the sons of Pṛthā, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son went with an army to bring him under his control. (20.33)
Thus he became his disciple, awaiting Keśava’s absence from the mace;
then he requested his sister, and he (Keśava) made a promise regarding her giving.
For the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra thought that Keśava would not bypass this eldest brother. (20.34) ccxxxix.
For the sake of truth, he took his right hand, and Rāma gave him his hand marked with the plow. 20.35.

Deluded by her beauty, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra especially thought, "Kṛṣṇa and Rāma will come under my control out of affection for their sister," and so he took the hand of the enemy-slayer, the wielder of the plow, which was marked with the plow. 20.36.
She who was born of Devakī was named Subhadrā; she was auspicious in form. Having made her his daughter, Ānakadundubhi protected Rohiṇī, who had previously been known by the name Trijaṭā.
Because of her constant service from the beginning, she became the beloved sister of Viṣṇu.
Through the possession by Umā, she became endowed with beauty and virtue, lotus-eyed and fair as a garland of campaka flowers.
(20.38) Having performed this, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra departed for the Kurus, where Rāma dwells.
Kṛṣṇa, having summoned Akrūra—who was staying elsewhere out of fear—and Ārddikya, spoke to them. (20.39)
When Keśava brought Rāma into the presence of all the Sātvatas and said, "The jewel is with you; show it," Akrūra, being afraid, then showed him the gem.
Having displayed his own sincerity toward Halāyudha, Keśava, knowing [the truth] of him—
He spoke again to Ratnākāṅkṣā, to Ugrasena, and to the mother of Sāmba:
"Let the jewel remain with Akrūra; it is not to be worn by others. It should always be worn by the Lord of Sacrifices [Ugrasena].
Even though Satyabhāmā would desire nothing that Kṛṣṇa does not wish for her, Kṛṣṇa said that it was nevertheless suitable for her. (20.41–42)
Having obtained the jewel, the lord of liberality always remained consecrated and unwearied in his sacrificial rites;
having displayed this jewel to Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa went to Śakraprastha out of affection for the Pāṇḍavas.
(20.43) Dwelling there for many months, Arjuna once went out on a hunt accompanied by Phalguna.
Having killed deer while staying on the banks of the Yamunā, he saw another woman, Kālindī, his sister.
She was the daughter of the Sun, born after Yamunā, who was performing austerities desiring to become the wife of Kṛṣṇa.
When questioned by Arjuna, she told him all of this, and Vāsudeva took her as his wife.

Then, having gone to the house of Nagnajit, he took the seven bulls at the *svayaṃvara*—those bulls which could not be seized by anyone else and by which the kings had been defeated through the boon of Śiva.
Then he obtained his daughter Nīlā, who had previously been the cowherd girl Nīlā. (20.46) ccxl.
Since she had previously entered her body, she was born as one person divided into two.
Mitravindā, the daughter of her father’s sister, placed a garland upon Kṛṣṇa in the midst of the kings;
however, her two fierce brothers, Vinda and Anuvinda, forbade it for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Having conquered those two kings of Avanti and all the others, Vāsudeva took them and set out for her;
he, along with his brothers, accepted Bhadrā, the second daughter of his father’s sister who had been given to him.
For those five Kaikeya brothers were indeed incarnations of the Viśvedevas and of Hari.
My father was also constantly devoted to the Pāṇḍavas and remained under their influence; he was the foremost of the Śibis. 20.50.
His svayaṃvara for Lakṣaṇā was likewise like that of Draupadī, consisting of the piercing of a target.
In the Madra country, his father obtained the Pināka bow from the Lord of the Mountains for the sake of her svayaṃvara. 20.51.
That target was covered on all sides by arrows even above the opening;
it was to be brought down with a single shaft from that distance, for which purpose it was impossible to do otherwise.
Then the Magadhas and others all arrived there, and the sons of Pṛthā also came to witness the event.
Duryodhana and the others, along with the son of the Sūta, were even unable to string the bow.
(20.53) Some fell down as if struck by the bow itself; indeed, none were able to move it.
Duryodhana, the Māgadha, and the son of the Sūta, having strung it, were unable to aim at the target. (20.54)
Dhanañjaya, displaying his own prowess, strung his bow and looked toward the target;

yet he did not take up an arrow, knowing that she was to be obtained by Keśava alone and having no desire for her. Bhīma likewise neither desired to string his bow nor even to look at this target, which was held by the enemy of the lord of mountains (Arjuna). 20.55.

Seeing that even one who was diligent in a worthy task might commit an offense, the unborn and great-souled Kṛṣṇa then strung his bow and, being inconceivable, struck down the target with a single arrow.
Celestial drums resounded and the gods rained down flowers. (20.56–57)

While Kṛṣṇa was being praised by Brahmā and the other gods, the princess placed the garland upon Keśava and stood there in worship; then all the kings, having taken up their own weapons, came for battle.
Having routed those [kings] headed by the Magadha king, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Bhīma and Arjuna, returned to his own city.
By her [the primordial Prakṛti], these eight great queens of Kṛṣṇa were brought forth—divine, the most beautiful in the world, and beloved.
Bhaiṣmī and Satyā are her very body manifested as two; she is the fundamental nature (prakṛti) existing on earth.
By her alone are the others always pervaded, and among them, Jāmbavatī is the foremost. 20.59–20.60.
Jāmbavatī is equal to Rāmā in her love for Kṛṣṇa, while the others are slightly less than she;
when the descent (āveśa) of Ramā is abundant, Keśava takes great delight in them.
When that descent diminishes, they become twenty times superior to Pradyumnā. (20.61)
From time immemorial, those women had belonged to no one other than Keśava; with them, Keśava took his pleasure in Dvāravatī.

(20.62) While Kṛṣṇa was thus residing in the midst of Dvārakā, all the kings—including Duryodhana and the others, as well as the Pāṇḍavas and hosts of monarchs from various lands—gathered at Mount Raivataka. (20.63)
On Mount Raivataka, Kṛṣṇa beheld his own people who had come to see him;

while Kṛṣṇa sat upon a divine throne together with the princess of Vidarbha, saluted by all the foremost of kings, Nārada approached and spoke to Kṛṣṇa out of desire: "You are the supreme among all; there is no one like you."
When these two words, "wonderful" and "fortunate," had been spoken, Vāsudeva said to him. (20.65) The kings asked Kṛṣṇa, "What is this [gift] along with the sacrificial fees?
Nārāyaṇa told the sage, "Speak! and Nārada also said, "Listen! (20.66)

"The tortoise was seen by me in the Viṣṇupadī, and I said, 'You are the best; there is no one equal to you. She [the tortoise] spoke of Gaṅgā as the most excellent; he [Gaṅgā] spoke of the Mistress of Waters (Varuṇa); and she spoke of the Earth by name. That [Earth] is called *pṛthivī* because she supports all those deities like me in every way, owing to her vastness. (20.67)

She also spoke of Śiva, Śeṣa, and Garuḍa, as well as those named Parvata, because she was dependent on another. Then they replied, "By them alone am I, as well as the goddesses equal to me, sustained.
She then spoke of Brahmā as the supreme; he too [spoke of] Prakṛti, whose essence is the Vedas and who is the consort of Viṣṇu.

CCXLII. When I, the goddess Bahurūpā, was united with the wise Nārāyaṇa, I was named Yajñā because I took pride in the performance of sacrifice; through that entry [into him], I received that name. 20.70. Possessed by Viṣṇu and seated upon his lap, she who was named Yajñā said: "Keśava is indeed supreme and sufficient."

"There is none equal to him, much less superior; O Sage, this is the truth and not otherwise," he said repeatedly. (20.71) Thus addressed by her, I said to that hero of the Yadus, "There is no distinction among your incarnations;
you are the supreme of all. He replied, "It is not only from Śrī, who rests upon my lap, that I [derive this]. (20.72)

But when she, my most excellent beloved, who is the form of my left half, is designated as the "Right" (dakṣiṇā)— because I stand to her right— therefore she shall be known by the name Dakṣiṇā alone. She is the deity who considers herself the "Right," and she stands as my own half, possessing many forms.
"Since she has entered my left half, I shall therefore be known as Ardhanārāyaṇa.

Even then, remembering the supreme excellence of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he spoke thus with sacrificial fees, saying: "I am the most excellent and perfectly complete; there is no one like me who is superior. (20.74–75)

"O Nārada, by virtue of these sacrificial gifts combined with these [other merits], I am always the most excellent in the entire world; and by my power, there exists not even an infinite fraction of the sacrificial gifts [that can equal mine]," so it was said by the incomparable Kṛṣṇa, O King, regarding the eternal superiority of the sacrificial gifts over all others.
This is the daughter of Bhīṣma, the sacrificial fee; this Keśava is her most excellent [husband]. Behold, O hosts of kings!

Your very eyes have witnessed the prowess of Kuntī, and when she requested Keśava for the sake of battle, he displayed his valor against the Pāṇḍavas, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with Bhīṣma, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Karṇa.
In an instant, the Discus alone [slew] those foremost of men who were weaponless and unconquerable even by the gods.
By the command of Viṣṇu, Bībhatsu had a vow that he would never approach Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, having bowed to Kṛṣṇa, he took the Discus from the front of the chariot, and Keśava drew it away from him.
Thus, even as they were playing and exerting themselves to the full extent of their own power, they were defeated by Keśava.
Thereupon, they all bowed down to him, and Pṛthā, filled with wonder, prostrated herself before Vāsudeva.
(20.80) Such marvelous deeds as these have been seen by you here in Kṛṣṇa by the hundreds of thousands.
"Therefore, he is indeed wonderful and most supreme"; having spoken thus, they all bowed to Vāsudeva.

By the command of Vāyu, Nārada, the disciple of Vāyu, said "It is true" and so forth, and after praising both [Kṛṣṇa and] Rukmiṇī and giving her a flower from the Pārijāta tree, he quickly departed for the world of the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
Satyā is the personification of truth itself; though she is one, she has become twofold, and there is no difference whatsoever between them.
Nevertheless, for the sake of manifesting the natural disposition of women, Satyā acted as if she were angry.
(20.83) This was because of her entry into the midst of the kings together with Rukmiṇī, and because of the sage’s praise and the offering of flowers to the Goddess.
Showing her face with a frown, Kṛṣṇa spoke to mock the people filled with desire:

"I shall give you that Pārijāta tree. Then Vāsava also arrived there; though he had conquered Bhauma along with all the gods, he was nevertheless deprived of those two earrings belonging to Aditi by him (Kṛṣṇa). 20.84–85.
At that very moment, all those sages of Badarī, pierced by him, quickly bowed down to Kṛṣṇa and,
having praised him with Vedic and Tantric hymns, requested the slaying of Bhauma.
Requested thus by Indra together with the gods and by the brahmins, he remembered the King of Birds.
Having approached and bowed down, Hari, together with Satyā, mounted him as he stood before them and departed.

(20.87) That very nature which is eternal, for the sake of instructing the world by her own will, observed the fast known as Bhīmadvādaśī and bore [the weight of] ten million streams of water; indeed, she is Satyabhāmā herself, acting for the pleasure of Viṣṇu. (20.88)
Accompanied by her and seated upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, the wielder of the thunderbolt followed from afar;
yet, having granted him permission, Kṛṣṇa—whose soul was resolved on the slaying of Bhauma—proceeded to the city of Māṇṣā, which is frequented by the wind.
For Bhauma had become invulnerable due to a boon from Brahmā, who had declared that he could not be slain by any bearer of weapons, no matter how superior. Thus [Kṛṣṇa] went to him.
A boon was likewise granted by Brahmā to his ministers, including their own immunity from death;

20.90 / for even invincibility against Bhauma was granted to them by Brahmā when he had assumed the form of a boar, and the city named Prāgjyotiṣa was given as a fortress to him who was born from Viṣṇu by all [the gods]. 20.91 /

Outside was a mountain fortress; within that was a water fortress, and inside that was a sand fortress. Within that as well was one like the edge of a razor. Those sands and those six thousand fierce [beings] were granted by Brahmā, who had been propitiated, for the sake of the fortresses' impenetrability to enemies and their unassailability. (20.92)
In that city, his ministers were the heroic Pīṭha, Muru, Nisumbha, Hayagrīva, and Pañcajana.
Regarding them as the world-protectors and himself as Brahmā, he remained there speaking the truth.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having gone there to slay Naraka, shattered the mountain fortress with his mace.
Having dried up the water with the Vāyavya weapon, he cut off the hands of Mura with his sword.
Then the Daityas Nisumbha, Hayagrīva, and Pañcajana rushed forward;
raining down mountains, weapons, missiles, and stones, Viṣṇu rendered them lifeless, their necks severed by his discus.
Their sons, seven in number and of immense prowess, were invulnerable by virtue of a boon from Giriśa;
yet the infallible [Arjuna], discharging missiles and weapons, dispatched them to death with his supreme arrows.
Having slain thirty-five of the ministers' sons, he proceeded toward the presence of Bhauma.
Hearing that Kṛṣṇa had arrived nearby, Bhauma advanced against him with thirty *akṣauhiṇīs*.

Garuḍa struck the army with the flapping of his wings, while Keśava destroyed the remainder with floods of arrows—one-third of the host. Then Bhauma quickly approached Acyuta, swiftly discharging arrows consecrated with mantras.
Keśava pierced him with a flood of arrows, while Bhauma discharged the *śataghnī* weapon granted by Brahmā.

That Kṛṣṇa—the one who cannot be cut, cannot be pierced, whose nature is eternal consciousness and bliss, who is eternally immutable and possessed of full power—swallowed that *śataghnī*, the best of divine weapons; though eternally unwearied, he appeared as if exhausted. (20.98–99)

Seeing that the many boons granted by Brahmā to others—which are never in vain—had been rendered futile, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord beyond the highest, thought, "How might he be filled with great respect? and thus He showed Himself as if fatigued.
Then, seeing Naraka arrogant, Queen Satyā took up the bow named Śārṅga.

In an instant, Kṛṣṇa rendered that striving Bhauma weaponless and chariotless; then, having embraced Satyabhāmā, he quickly delivered the fierce Bhauma— who had been stationed within the chariot and was discharging weapons— with his neck severed by the enemy, into the hands of Death.

Accompanied by his ministers and the sons of his ministers, he went into the blinding darkness due to his contempt for Kṛṣṇa; then Vāyu, possessed by Him, entered the inner apartments as the Lord of Truth. At that time, there was the earth, the lowest of the five elements, in which Naraka was born from the illustrious Varāha.
She, who was intensely possessed by the earth through its very primal nature, approached the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Placing the two earrings of Aditi at his feet, she presented her grandson named Bhagadatta;
and Kṛṣṇa caused his consecration to be performed in Prāgjyotiṣa.

Having established that most noble elephant Supratīka— which had been seized by Bhauma from Vaiśravaṇa by force— within the entire kingdom of the Kirātas, he entrusted him to Bhagadatta, who was given [the beast] safely by the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
Having thus bestowed that lordly elephant upon him and having shown favor toward the Earth, [he departed].
He dispatched six thousand lordly elephants with four tusks each, born from the ocean, to Dvāravatī;
and having conquered kings, gods, gandharvas, and nāgas, he sent back to his own city two hundred yojanas in extent, filled on all sides with heaps of gold and jewels brought as tribute.
Having caused Nirṛti to fight against the Nairṛtas, the lords of the Rākṣasas of great prowess who had been brought from the earth,

that primordial god Nārāyaṇa dispatched all the excellent jewels, chariots, and elephants. There, having conquered those kings of the earth who had been brought from the earth in battle, he beheld the daughters of the rulers.
There were sixteen thousand one hundred maidens, noble in form and character, unblemished, and established in their virtuous vows.
Among them were certain daughters of the gods and Gandharvas; the most distinguished of them was Kaśeru, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ.
These were formerly the sons of Agni, and they performed severe austerities in order to attain womanhood.

To those who desired to assume female bodies for the sake of becoming the wives of Vāsudeva, the Wind-god, being propitiated by their ascetic penance, granted the boon; having become women, they went to Badarī. There, serving Nārāyaṇa, they attained the state of Apsarases and were born into royal families.
Some, having heard of Kṛṣṇa in heaven, chose him as their husband— he who is delightful with all virtues.
Since they were equal to the gods by birth in all virtues, whether by nature or through the infusion of Lakṣmī,
Kṛṣṇa placed those women, who were superior in virtue, upon palanquins and sent them to Dvāravatī.

Hari placed that mountain of jewels belonging to Indra, which extended for two hundred yojanas on all sides and constantly dripped with nectar, as well as the umbrella of Varuṇa, upon Garuḍa’s shoulders with his two arms.
Then, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, he himself ascended and went to heaven with effortless ease.
Having set out accompanied by all the world-protectors, Janārdana entered the palace of Śakra (20.116).
Honored with great respect by Śakra together with Sacyā, and accompanied by Satyabhāmā, he—
worshipped by all the gods and sages— gave the two auspicious earrings even to Aditi (20.117).
Unaware of the truth due to the influence of the Asuras' possession, Aditi— though she was the mother of all and the source of the universe,

whose bodies were composed solely of faultless bliss— bestowed blessings upon them as if they were her own sons. Then, the Unborn One, whose body is the essence of eternal bliss and consciousness, did not find even the Nandana garden to be a worthy match for his consort.
The Lord of All, possessed of infinite power, entered [the palace] with his beloved Satyabhāmā in order to sport.

With her—who was as radiant as gold, clad in saffron-colored garments smeared with excellent saffron, and whose lotus-face surpassed the splendor of millions of full moons—the infallible Acyuta, the immeasurable soul and the singular beauty of the world, took his delight. (20.119–20.120)

In that forest of excellent trees made of jewels and refined gold, where all splendors were eternally manifest and which was always graced by the full moon, Hari wandered with the Goddess along a path frequented by the breeze.
There, his body free from the three defects, he beheld a noble tree born from the churning of truth and the nectar of immortality.

Upon seeing that Pārijāta tree— which was composed of jewels and gold, granted all desires, and dispelled all distress— the virtuous lady, her lotus-face shimmering with the moonlight of a gentle smile, her dark, tremulous eyes, and her fine earrings swaying against her cheeks, spoke to her husband, the lord of the gods: 20.122–20.123.
"O you of inconceivable prowess, let this tree that gives life to the world be planted in the courtyard of my house.
Thus addressed, the Lord embraced her whose breasts were like water-jars and uprooted the tree;
together with that tree and with the goddess, Keśava ascended to his supreme prowess.
Having heard that [the demon] Khageśvara, Indra, urged on by Śacī, arrived with the gods.

Hari’s beloved [Subhadrā] then warded off all those gods—who were possessed by the influence of the Asuras and intent on provoking the power of Hari—with excellent arrows discharged from her bow, the Śārṅga. 20.125–20.126.

Garuḍa rendered Vaiśravaṇa weaponless and cast Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, into the ocean. Then Hari, having awakened Vāyu— the son of the primary wind— as well as Agni, the lord of the intermediate quarter, Yama, and the others who had been possessed by the Asuras through the sounds produced from his Śārṅga bow, entered their own bodies.
Awakened by him, they abandoned the battle and departed, recognizing him as the Primeval Person.
And Śiva, who had arrived for the sake of Śakra, Hari put to flight with arrows discharged from the Śārṅga bow;
struck down at a great distance along with his vehicle by the son of Garuḍa, Śambhu fled, wounded by the arrows.
When Hari had been put to flight by Śauri with his volleys of arrows, Indra swiftly hurled his thunderbolt at him;
Janārdana caught it with his left hand while laughing, and he snatched away the bow.
Then the beloved of Hari, the world’s peerless beauty, pushed aside that mother of the world.
Śakra said to the progenitor of the worlds, "We shall show our own childhood.
Then the lord of the gods, surrounded by the deities, went for refuge to Janārdana, seeking his forgiveness;
and having offered the peak of the Jewel Mountain, he bowed down before the Teacher of the World together with the Goddess.
The Lord of Śacī requested Keśava for the protection of Arjuna;

Kṛṣṇa also replied, "As long as I remain upon the surface of the earth, no one shall defeat him. Having obtained that boon for Arjuna's sake, Vāsava bowed again and again to the wielder of the discus.
Beheld by Hari with a gracious glance, the great devotee departed for his own abode.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having taken leave of Purandara and proceeding toward his own city, shone with exceeding splendor;
he wore a diadem, his lotus-face was radiant with excellent earrings, and he was clad in yellow garments and adorned with the beautiful Kaustubha gem.
For the Lord of the universe, who is ever-effulgent and infallible, there is never any change whatsoever;
nevertheless, such words may be spoken to remind Him, having regard for the intellect of those of little knowledge as found in the Purāṇas.
(20.136) And having entered His own city, the Lord, being well-honored by the Yādavas, went to the inner apartments from the courtyard.
He placed the tree of his beloved upon the peak of the mountain of jewels together with its summit.

Having bestowed all the jewels upon the Sāttvatas according to their desire, the Lord, possessing infinite forms, married those maidens as well and took his pleasure with them individually, each seated within a jeweled palace.
In each of them, the Lord begot ten sons and one daughter in every case.
Among them, Pradyumna, Sāmba, Bhānu, and Cārudeṣṇa were preeminent in their virtues.
He who was the younger brother of Vivasvat and the son of Aditi, known by the name Savitṛ, [was born] from Kṛṣṇa.
He who was born here from Satyabhāmā’s womb was named Bhānu, and from Bhaiṣmī came Cārudeṣṇa.
Indeed, that Cārudeṣṇa was Vighnarāja (Gaṇeśa), and all the other sons of Kṛṣṇa were likewise hosts of deities; all those who dwell in Dvārakā are such [divine beings]. 20.140–141.
While that infinite god was dwelling in his own city, being worshipped by all,
that son of Rukmiṇī once went to the world of the lord of serpents together with Sāmba.
There, though provoked to battle by them out of ignorance, he conquered them all, including Vāsuki.
Having routed him with his arrows, he then seized the heaps of jewels; they then bowed down before him.

Honored by them, accompanied by Sāmba, he quickly conquered the deceitful Maya—who was obstructing him—with showers of weapons; honored by him in turn, he departed for heaven in a chariot that travels through the sky.
In that very battle, when the *pārijāta* tree had been seized by Kṛṣṇa, Sāmba defeated Jayanta;
and out of rivalry, he also conquered with his weapons Jayanta’s younger brother, named Vṛṣabha, who had come to challenge him.
Having neutralized their missiles with his own superior weapons, he rendered those two brothers powerless against him.
Having paralyzed those two who were honored by the lord of the gods with his excellent arrows, they departed through the sky by means of their supernatural power (vidyā).
Then, having carried away Sāmba by means of the *vidyā* bestowed by Rati, the son of Rugmiṇī went to his city;
thereafter, Nārada arrived swiftly to learn of the conduct of Hari among his many wives.
Seeing him dwelling alone within the eighteen thousand houses in as many forms, he was greatly amazed; having bowed to him, he departed for Śakraprastha, where he was honored by the sons of Pṛthā.
By the command of Brahmā, he told Kṛṣṇā that Bhīma alone should, in due order, take his place at each house.
Having put all other goddesses to sleep within her body, it was solely for the sake of providing full enjoyment to that Bhāratī.
(20.149) The two brothers, Sunda and Upasunda, were not to be slain by anyone other than each other, according to the word of Brahmā;
however, for the sake of Tilottamā, those two Daityas were killed by one another, having been created by him for the purpose of their mutual destruction. (20.150)

20.151. "Therefore, from this year onwards, whoever among you should see Kṛṣṇā staying with another in succession, he shall perform a pilgrimage for one year. Thus they were instructed, and they acted accordingly. Then, on one occasion, she was joined by Dharmarāja in the armory for the purpose of protecting the brahmins and the cattle.

Desiring to take up weapons, Phalguna saw the bandits with their arms; having slain them, he set out for a pilgrimage to sacred sites. (20.152) Though restrained out of friendship by Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, he once went to the river Dyunadī for the sake of truth.
While performing his ablutions, he was carried away in an instant to the world of serpents by the illusory power of a Naga maiden. (20.153)

Her father, whose husband had been carried off by Garuḍa, urged Pārtha, desiring a son; for a year Pārtha had observed a vow of celibacy for the sake of Kṛṣṇā, according to the agreement. Being entreated again and again by the serpent for the sake of a son for her, that Pārtha [consented].
He begot a son named Airāvata from Kujā; he was endowed with the splendor of Varuṇa.

(20.155) Since the virtues of sons generally belong to their fathers and their lineage to their mothers, that elephant was powerful because he was the first-born of Pṛthu, a master of illusion, skilled in weapons, and most righteous. (20.156)

Then Arjuna departed on his pilgrimage circuit; meanwhile, his mother, along with the Pāṇḍyas, was abandoned by the serpents and dwelt in the world of the gods, honored by the deities. Therefore, one should not consider it in any way as a fault of the exceedingly powerful Arjuna, due to the transgression of truth. 20.157.
"In the case of the powerful, there is no trace of fault in another for a transgression against a superior; for this is the established rule in the scriptures.
Out of great affection for his two elder brothers, he forgave him, and his daughter was given by the King of Pāṇḍya.
At the end of that year, the beautiful Citrāṅgadā was given by Vīrasena out of satisfaction. (20.158–159)
That Vīrasena was possessed by the spirit of Tvaṣṭṛ, and that maiden was possessed by the spirit of Yama; for she was Śacī.

From the contact of her body with the body of the Sun’s son, she descended from heaven and the intermediate space to this world. For that very reason, there was no excessive intimacy between them, as she maintained the conduct of a daughter-in-law toward her husband.

Born of her was Babhruvāhana, previously begotten by Arjuna, who was endowed with the splendor of Kāmadeva. Having fathered that heroic son, Arjuna then departed for Prabhāsa; there, due to a curse, he was released from the body of a crocodile.
He then liberated five Apsarases, and having been seized by them, he was dragged to the shore.

"Thus was their release from the curse granted: 'When one of you shall draw them all out simultaneously, then alone shall he regain his own form. Enough with this Brahmin who was satisfied with those who were bowed down before him! (20.163) Having liberated them at Kanyātīrtha from that base womb resulting from the Brahmin's derision, the Pāṇḍava..."

Having reached Prabhāsa, he heard that Suyodhana had been challenged by Rāma, the younger brother of Vāsudeva. Reflecting upon his duty, he assumed the guise of an ascetic and went to him at Kuśasthalī. When Kṛṣṇa learned that he had arrived, he laughed while reclining on his bed, accompanied only by Satyā.
She, who possesses all knowledge, playfully asked him the cause of his laughter; he too spoke it to her.
Then, desiring to see Līlā and Ābhāja, the two went again to Raivata, the king of mountains.
That was the pleasure garden of the Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, and Andhakas; there Keśava saw that Phalguna.
Then Kṛṣṇa made a secret promise to him regarding the gift of his sister; thereafter, he sat with all the Vṛṣṇis.
Seeing on the mountain the son of Rohiṇī (Balarāma) dressed as an ascetic, Pārtha, accompanied by his kinsmen, bowed down;
Phalguna (Arjuna) also performed worship, and Baladeva, in turn, paid homage to him, saying, "You are the eldest by virtue of your qualities. (20.167–168)

Seeing that eloquent man who was all-knowing, Rāma said, "Let him dwell in the maiden's quarters during the rainy season," and he had Kṛṣṇa treated with due honor; however, Keśava spoke thus, declaring it a fault:
"He is young, strong, handsome, and exceedingly eloquent; he is not fit to dwell in the maiden's quarters. (20.169)

To him who had spoken thus, Rāma said to the Lord of the World, "I have no doubt regarding this man of perfected knowledge. "Your opinion does not please us; however, let it be honored by all of us," Keśava said to that virtuous lord of ascetics, and told his sister, "Serve him. 20.170–171.

"O virtuous one, remain ever vigilant and satisfy her. Thus instructed, he did so there; and he, placing his faith in the words of Hari, spent the months of the rainy season engaged in sacred discourses.
When requested by Phalguna, he spoke these words: "That which Vāsudeva knows, no one else knows. (20.172)

"Except for Vipṛthu or Sātyaki, I shall give Subhadrā to you; this is the truth. (20.173) In the knowledge of missiles, weapons, and the sciences of reality, the descendant of Śini was a disciple of both Vāsudeva and the son of Indra.
Therefore, because he was his own disciple and also that of Vipṛthu, Kṛṣṇa explained everything to him. (20.174)
Although all others knew that the Pārthas were always dear to Vāsudeva,
when commanded by Rāma, Uddhava, Āhuka, and others— including the Hārdikyas— did not wish to give [the earrings] to Jiṣṇu.
All of them desired to give them to Duryodhana, knowing that this was for the sake of pleasing Rāma and out of devotion to Hari.
Even though they were possessed by Rākṣasas and thus acted unpleasantly toward him, Kṛṣṇa deceived them all.
Deceived, Pradyumna, Sāmba, and the others, together with Rāma, all went for the sake of visiting sacred fords (tīrthas).
While the great festivals were recurring there, Subhadrā spoke at one point regarding the *piṇḍoddhāra* (the offering of funeral cakes).

"O ascetic, while wandering among the sacred fords, did you perhaps see our beloved kinsmen, the sons of Pṛthā, as well as Kuntī and Kṛṣṇā? Thus questioned, he said "Om," and he reported their well-being to them. She spoke again: "O Blessed One, I have heard from the brahmins that the son of Indra has gone to the sacred fords."

"Have you seen him? "Yes," Pārtha replied. "Where? she asked him. "Right here," said Pārtha with a smile. Again and again the fair-limbed woman questioned him; he too said, "Am I mad? Indeed, it is I. With eyes wide open in wonder, she looked at him with great joy. (20.179–180)
Then, out of both joy and shame, the lotus-eyed woman said nothing; Pārtha spoke to her:
"Overcome by desire, this is indeed the prime time for us; it was not mentioned for the sake of marriage. She replied to him:
"An overstepping of Vāsudeva’s [command] is not fitting; therefore, [accept me] as I have been given by my own parents. (20.181)
Then he thought of Kṛṣṇa, saying, "Come, O Kṛṣṇa, and marry me at this festival, joined by your own kinsmen.

(20.182) Then Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his parents, arrived right there; and Vāsava, being remembered along with Śacī and the lords of sages, as well as Phalguna, arrived there at night, full of joy. (20.183)
Then Kṛṣṇa, together with Puruhūta, properly performed the marriage of those two,
accompanied by their parents and Satyaki during a great festival unknown to others and witnessed by the lords of sages.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having left his own chariot for the sake of Phalguna, departed that very night.

When Śakra had departed, Pārtha mounted his chariot at dawn together with his wife alone. (20.185) When Phalguna, having taken up his bow, stood upon the chariot equipped with all weapons in Dvāravatī, there arose a clamor: "What is this? Is this ascetic with a triple staff carrying off a maiden, wielding a bow in hand? (20.186)
Then, seeing him wearing his armor, the divine earrings given by Mahendra, the two garments,
and the celestial jewels and ornaments, the guards tried to stop him. Then, with his palms, finger-guards, and quiver fastened, he drew his bow and [prepared] with arrows.
By means of his training and knowledge, he made the atmosphere, the intermediate directions, and the cardinal directions continuous [with his arrows].
(20.188) For this purpose, Keśava acted as his charioteer; well-trained by him, Subhadrā was perfectly attentive.
Guided by her, Pārtha, while playing, never once pierced the skin of anyone. (20.189)
Through his wondrous training, having terrified them all and put them to flight with showers of arrows,
he emerged from the city and beheld Vipṛthu, who had been appointed by Rāma to guard the city.
As if doing a favor for Rāma, he too, under a pretext, surrounded that son of Pṛthā with his own army.
At Kṛṣṇa’s command, he did not properly obstruct Pārtha, but fought him through deception.
For that one among the Maruts, named Saumya, was born for the sake of serving Vāsudeva;
he rained showers of arrows upon that Yādava so that Savyasācin would not be wounded. 20.191–20.192.
Pārtha rendered him weaponless and chariotless, yet he did not strike down his army.
Seeing that his arrows were sharp, though they did not even cut through skin, Vipṛthu was highly gratified.
Honoring Pārtha’s superior skill, he approached Pārtha and praised him for everything.
Having first been struck down by Phalguna with his weapons already severed— as if he were merely carrying out the command of Viṣṇu—
he quickly returned like one defeated and reported everything to Halin (Balarāma).
Then he too, accompanied by Pradyumna, Sāmba, and others, set out in anger from the city, desiring to slay Arjuna.
Kṛṣṇa, having heard everything from Vipṛthu, arrived at the Sudharmā hall appearing dejected;
there the heroes of the Yadu clan, headed by Pradyumna, spoke aloud with loud voices:
"Having quickly destroyed that practitioner of illusion, we shall bring Subhadrā back in an instant. (20.196)
20.197–198. Having spoken these words, Balarāma said to them: "By Kṛṣṇa’s command they shall go, not by their own will.
The intention of Hari must first be ascertained; in opposition to him, you will not achieve victory.
When the wielder of the plow had spoken thus, they all bowed to Janārdana and questioned him.
Then Vāsudeva of immeasurable prowess said: "Let everyone hear my words.
Long ago I spoke thus: 'A man observing the Māyā-vow is not fit to remain in the presence of a maiden.
Yet this elder brother of mine did not heed those words of mine, even though I pointed out many faults. (20.199)
Because it was impossible to violate, the elder brother followed [the plan] while residing in the maiden’s chamber with a deceitful mind.
This undertaking has now passed out of sight; since the maiden was taken away without our presence, what loss of honor is there for us?
On the contrary, that prideful man would suffer greater humiliation, and your own distinct status as sons of Pṛthu would become known. (20.200–201)

"A maiden must be given away, yet there is no bridegroom equal to Pārtha; and this Pārtha is a Kaurava, the grandson of Kṛṣṇa who possesses perfect power, the son of his paternal aunt, the most heroic and rich in virtues.
Since he, the son of Śakra, has come here seeking us of his own accord, there shall be no loss for us in this matter. (20.202)

"If you pursue him and there should be defeat, it would result in a severe loss of your reputation; 20.203 / but if you conquer him and bring back the maiden, no one else will ever desire her once she has been touched by you.
Therefore, your pursuit does not please me," so spoke the Supreme Lord, and they remained silent. 20.204 /
Having heard the words of Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) spoke: "Do not go; my mind is aware of this.
Following him will lead to our victory, to our welfare, to peace, and ultimately to liberation.
Then Arjuna stood where, by Kṛṣṇa’s command alone, no one could suffer defeat.

By that very chariot, he went with his wife and entered Śakraprastha, which was protected by his brothers. (20.206) Honored by his brothers, who were exceedingly joyful, Kṛṣṇa then related everything regarding his own conduct to them; and when the Yādavas had become quiet through his words, he, joined by the Plow-bearer, went to the sons of Pṛthā. (20.207)
Accompanied by carts filled with jewels, he went to Śakraprastha, where he was honored by the sons of Pṛthā;
there, joined by Rāma, he gave those ornaments to them, as well as to Kṛṣṇā and his sister. Having stayed for some months, the son of Rohiṇī departed for his own city, while Keśava remained there.

Honored by the Pāṇḍavas for many years and bestowing upon them ever-increasing affection, [he dwelt there]. (20.209) Kṛṣṇā had five sons, rich in virtues, who were the Viśvedevas themselves. They were successively possessed by the five chief Gandharvas: Citraratha, Abhitāmra, Kiśora, Gopāla, and Bala. (20.210)
Prativindhya, Sutasoma, Śrutakarman, Kīrtivardhana, Śatānīka, and Śrutakīrti were born in order from Yudhiṣṭhira and the others; and Abhimanyu was the youngest of two born to them.
That wise one, joined with the splendor of the moon, was born in the womb of Subhadrā by Arjuna. (20.211)
Accompanied by Dharmarāja, Śakra, and the Aśvins, as well as Kṛṣṇa himself,
who was present there, all those sons were heroic, handsome, devoted to Viṣṇu, and learned in all the scriptures; the Pāṇḍavas found great joy with them, especially with the delight of the Sāttvatas.
Then once, Satyabhāmā and Subhadrā, desiring to sport in the Khāṇḍava forest, took Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha and departed by chariot with their attendants, while being sung to by the Gandharva kings.
As they sported there at their own pleasure with those two jewels among women, a gentle breeze began to blow.

In the forest, which was magnificent with clusters of blossoms, and upon the waters of the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā), the Brahmin approached those two and begged for food. Then, in accordance with the will of the Lord of Lakṣmī, Kuśa spoke:
"O son of Pṛthā, tell me, what kind of food is desired by you? He replied, "I am Agni, seeking wood. (20.215–20.216)
"In former times, when I was giving the sacrificial oblation to the deities, I requested the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings as my fee;

yet, having cursed me, saying, 'May there be a loss of strength for you,' they gave them to me. Now, having bowed before the Lotus-born One, I asked him: 'By what means may my strength be restored? (20.217)
"When you consume the Khandava forest, then your strength shall be restored," he said.
"This Khandava belongs to Śakra; therefore, he creates obstacles for you. For this reason, I entreat you both.
When this was said, Pārtha replied to him: "If there were a chariot and a bow, then I would hold back Śakra."
Due to the possession by a spirit and his promise to give food, Pārtha even desired opposition with Śakra himself;

and at the instigation of Kṛṣṇa, Agni likewise requested Pārtha for the sake of pacifying the enmity with Śakra. (20.220) For Śakra would not personally harbor enmity toward that which was given by himself, since Pārtha is indeed Indra himself.
Thinking that Pārtha would not have obstructed him unless urged by Viṣṇu, he entreated Kṛṣṇa; and since he was not unattached to Keśava, he obtained further permission from Kṛṣṇa.
He went to the presence of Hari at Badarī, and taking the discus from there, he gave it back to Keśava. (20.221–222)
In former times, even while at Gomanta, Kṛṣṇa obtained the discus; out of devotion, Agni gave it back to Keśava.
That discus of Viṣṇu exists in many forms, yet that which was previously given by Agni remains as one. And there is the bow Gāṇḍīva, with which the Son of the Lotus performs the destruction of all.
That [weapon] was given by a portion of Umāpati, and by Śakra, Soma, and the Lord of Waters.
By that very [weapon], they conquered the three worlds through the grace of the Lotus-born One (Brahmā) in due order;
it was impossible for others to bear, it brought victory, and it was auspicious despite its weight equal to a hundred thousand [loads].
Varuṇa gave to Arjuna a chariot yoked with ten thousand white horses that brings victory, as well as two beautiful quivers containing inexhaustible arrows;
and taking the banner of Rāma, which bore the image of Hanumān, he gave it all to Arjuna.
(20.226) Specifically, the banner was placed upon Hanumān so that his invincibility would take the form of victory.
All that was divine and indeed impenetrable; the bowstring of the Gāṇḍīva possessed the brilliance of lightning.
Even the Gāṇḍīva, which was otherwise impossible for the Pāṇḍava to hold, became capable of being wielded through the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
It had been held by those gods due to a boon from Brahmā; Brahmā himself was the direct lord over its wielding.
A boon had been granted to Indra by the Self-born One, and it was for that reason that he had to be supported by Pārtha;
for this very Indra was born as Phalguna, and thus he constructed a hall of arrows with his celestial weapons. The son of Purandara quickly built a city twelve *yojanas* in extent.

Even though he was one whose fuel had been offered [into the fire], he seized the forest and began to devour it with his uplifted flames. Seeing his own dry wood being consumed, the one with many eyes (Agni), his mind undisturbed, quickly fanned the fire with streams of water resembling axle-holes for its destruction. (20.230–231)
Having warded off the shower of missiles with their own weapons, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha fought against Śakra, who was accompanied by hosts of gods.
He too was defeated, yet he was pleased upon seeing that power of his own;
for he observed both Kṛṣṇa’s affection held for Arjuna and such great strength as Pārtha possessed.
Having turned back the clouds with a heart full of great joy, he bowed to Kṛṣṇa and embraced his son.
Viṣṇu, having approached Keśava along with Śakra, embraced him without distinction, as did Ananta;
for previously, while merely playing, he had stood together with Śakra and had not fought at all.

Brahmā and Śarva, having come together and bowed to Kṛṣṇa and the name of Kṛṣṇa belonging to Pārtha, and because of their excellence in training, they both made a promise regarding the bestowal of their respective weapons. Having been permitted by Keśava, they departed; for there, Indra fought for the sake of sport.
Then, being pleased along with the gods, he granted fame to Arjuna out of affection for the two of them.
All the Daityas, Nāgas, Piśācas, and Yakṣas dwelling in that forest had been slain by those two well-wishers;
nothing remained there except four birds, Aśvasena, Maya, and nothing else. (20.236–20.237)
Having praised the Fire-god with the mantras beginning with "O Agni, this singer," the birds were not consumed by him.
Aṇṣvasena, the son of Takṣaka, was swallowed head-first by his mother in her throat;
when she was cut asunder by Arjuna while falling through the air, he was rescued by Śakra, though his tail was severed.
Out of anger at the killing of his mother and the breaking of his tail, Maya, who was situated in Karna’s quiver, sought to kill Pārtha;
but when he was seen by Kṛṣṇa, whose discus had been taken away, he went to Pārtha for refuge, seeking to save his life.
For the sake of Pārtha, Kṛṣṇa did not slay him, thinking, "He is my devotee"—thus the Supreme Lord displayed His supreme illusory power.

"Kṛṣṇa’s anger toward me is solely because of [my enmity] toward Devāri; therefore, I seek refuge in this Purandara, who is identical with Pārtha, thinking, 'By this means I shall become dear to Kṛṣṇa. (20.241) Desiring to repay the assistance rendered to his life, he said to Pārtha, "What may I do for you?"
"Indeed, you have been liberated by the grace of Kṛṣṇa; therefore, perform [this sacrifice] for him," said that son of Pṛthā.
(20.242) Kṛṣṇa, who had created a hall of most wonderful form for the king, commanded him, and he carried it out.
Then, having ensured that no living being could escape and having fulfilled the requests of those two, Hutāśana departed. (20.243)
And having seen those two, all the Pāṇḍavas attained great joy upon hearing this;
Kṛṣṇa also rejoiced with the sons of Pṛthā, he who possesses infinite power, bliss, knowledge, majesty, generosity, and valor. 20.244.
Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the twentieth chapter, titled "The Burning of Khāṇḍava" (258), [concludes].
(The Entry of the Pāṇḍavas into the Forest)
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Oṃ! By the command of Janārdana, Maya constructed a hall surpassing all wonders and presented it to the king; he also gave the mace to Vṛkodara. 21.1.

Having obtained the mace (*gadā*) sustained by Vāyu, which he had received through the grace of this king who was like a youthful mountain, Keśava indeed rejoiced. And after staying there for another two years, Keśava departed.
And he was honored by the Pāṇḍavas, who were unable to prevent his departure.
Then Hari, dwelling in his own city, went at a certain solar eclipse to Samantapañcaka along with his wife, sons, and kinsmen.
And all the sons of Pṛthā, together with their wives, sons, and mothers;
all the lords of the earth, both those dear to Hari and those who were not;
likewise Nanda the cowherd, along with his wife, the cowherds, and the cowherdesses. 21.5.
The lords of sages and the subjects gathered there from all sides;
and those who were dear to Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, having assumed his threefold form,
worshipped Vasiṣṭha, the delighter of the Vṛṣṇis, as well as the best of the Bhṛgus.
And they attained their purpose by beholding the feet of the Lord of Rama;
they bathed during a solar eclipse in the sacred ford (tīrtha) produced by the descendant of Bhrigu.
Having bestowed his grace upon his own people, Keśava, who is threefold, [departed]. 21.8.

And he caused Śūrajit to perform sacrifices accompanied by complete sacrificial fees (21.9). Hari bestowed his supreme favor upon that man who was devoted to him and whose soul was established in all the worlds, by appearing to him at an auspicious time (21.10).
Then Acyuta went to his own city together with the sons of Pṛthā;
there he performed his daily rites and the great Aśvamedha sacrifice. Mounted upon Hari’s chariot along with Bhīma and Phalguna, they followed the horse.
Within a mere quarter of a day, the sons of Hari deliberated;
in an instant, all the kings, including the son of Jarā,
were defeated by Vṛkodara and his companions, and the divine horse arrived.
That horse created by Kṛṣṇa was capable of traveling a hundred thousand *yojanas* in a single day with ease, for the sake of accomplishing the horse sacrifice;
this was when Hari, the son of Parāśara, showed it to Hari.
Then the Brahmin Tṛṇāvaha approached and cried out:
"My sons always go after birth and yet remain invisible.
When he had spoken thus, Arjuna said, "I shall indeed protect your sons."
"Have my sons Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Kārṣṇi not been protected here?
Where is your power in this matter? Thus that twice-born man spoke to Arjuna.
Then Phalguna, whose soul was distressed by the Asuras, replied.

"O Brahmin, I am not like Keśava and the others. For I have already conquered the gods and the asuras in the Khāṇḍava forest; furthermore, I shall later defeat those known as the Nivātakavacas. (21.18–21.19)
Having addressed Keśava in this way, he said, "I am departing.
When he had spoken thus, Hari replied, "What indeed can be done in this matter? Seeing him feeling ashamed, Keśava, the slayer of enemies, spoke to him.
He made this promise: "Alas, if I am unable to protect [them], I shall enter the fire. Having said this, Keśava departed with all the Yādavas, but he did not take Rāma, Pradyumna, or Aniruddha.
He appointed him along with his companions to protect their fame;
for Rāma was exceedingly dear to Kṛṣṇa,
and after him came his son Aniruddha, who was born from Pradyumna, the son of Kṛṣṇa.
