When Rugmavatī, the daughter of Rugmi, had been brought there by force at her svayaṃvara, he was born from her as Rati herself; he was the delighter of Kāma,
and even previously he was known by the name Aniruddha, after that very name of Viṣṇu.
Endowed with possession, powerful, handsome, and a knower of all scriptures,
Kṛṣṇa therefore employed that [power] for the sake of assisting Pārtha at the time of the birth of the Brāhmaṇa’s daughter, and Phalguna did likewise. 21.24–21.25.
Then, in an instant, Kumāra performed a binding of the directions with missiles;
Pārtha, becoming despondent along with the Yādavas, vanished from sight.
Rebuked by the Brāhmaṇa, he went to where the Lord of Śrī was. (21.26)

Having turned back that [Arjuna] who was about to enter the fire, Hari, together with the Brahmin and Phalguna, set out toward the northern direction on his great chariot; and in a mere moment, having crossed the seven oceans, he proceeded.
The mountains and the seas likewise gave way, and the Lord, having pierced the blinding darkness with his discus, cleared the path.
Having crossed even the Ghanodaka ocean, he of infinite prowess beheld his own abode there.

Having stationed the chariot and the Brahmin Pārtha at a distance, the Lord entered his own form— which possesses two, four, or eight arms, is adorned with divine ornaments blazing with every kind of jewel, and is an eternal ocean of vast qualities.
Seated upon the thousand-headed, vast body of Śeṣa— which was formless yet possessed the radiance of immeasurable suns—
accompanied by Ramā, with a garment as bright as lightning, and eternally worshipped by liberated beings such as Viriñca and others;
the Lord, remaining in that single form for a moment, went forth taking the sons of the Brahmins with him.
Those very attendants, Sunanda, Nanda, and the others, were born on the surface of the earth as Vaiṣṇavas.
(21.31) To quell the pride of Arjuna, Hari, the Supreme Lord, brought together the sons of Brahmins;
for since Hari’s affection for Arjuna was exceedingly great, he therefore instructed him. (21.32)

From his extraordinary abode, Vāsudeva, having dispatched [his chariot] with a brilliance exceeding a hundred thousand suns, mounted the chariot along with Arjuna and the Brahmin; he arrived and gave his daughter to the twice-born. (21.33) Indeed, he performed this atonement for the act of moving [the chariot] solely for the purpose of instructing the world.
Having returned within half a muhūrta, he performed the sacrifice once more.
Having honored Brahmā and the others who had arrived, along with their respective attendants,
and having given them leave to depart, he also honored the Brahmins.
Having performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) along with his wives and friends,
Kṛṣṇa was returning to Dvārakā when Dantavakra obstructed him.
In an instant, Kṛṣṇa struck him down with his mace, together with his chariot and its horses.
Viḍūratha, who was the asura Dantavakra, quickly went to Hari; that attendant of Hari took refuge in Hari alone. When Kṛṣṇa had reached his own world, he departed from this place in his true form.
He will attain oneness with his own essential nature through the gateway. Then Kṛṣṇa, having returned to the city, awakened Phalguna;
when asked by him, "What is this that has been seen?", the Lord of Ramā replied.
This continent and the ocean are each one hundred thousand yojanas in extent;
the others, however, increase successively by double each time. Beyond the last is a region of one and a half [parts], golden and externally as hard as adamantine cement.
All this is indeed called the world; beyond it is darkness twice as great, where the fierce ones, devoted to false knowledge, fall into blindness.
(21.41) Beyond that is the Ghanodaka ocean, twice as large, at the end of which is my own abode.
O Pārtha, that Supreme Person whom you saw there, eternally stationed and served by all beings beginning with Brahmā who have been liberated—
beyond that lies the region of Lokāloka, extending for five hundred thousand *yojanas*. 21.42.

And its measurement is likewise five hundred and sixty thousand [yojanas]. From Mount Meru, the cosmic egg is proclaimed to extend twenty-five crores of yojanas in all four directions, as well as upwards and downwards. (21.43–44)
Beyond that, this [universe] is successively enveloped by water, fire, air, ether, the *ahaṃkāra*, the *mahat-tattva*, and the three *guṇas*, each increasing by tenfold.
I am all-pervading, omnipresent, infinite, of infinite forms, and without interval.
With infinite heads, infinite eyes, and infinite feet, hands, and thighs;
possessing infinite virtues and majesty, with a body of consciousness and bliss—O Dhanañjaya, you and all others are entirely under my control. (21.46)
“By my grace alone come strength, victory, and all virtues;
therefore, O sinless one, you should feel neither astonishment nor pride. (21.47) ‘Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me.’”
"You shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me.
Having been addressed thus, Phalguna prostrated before Him and said, "Forgive me.
After dwelling there for several months, all the Pāṇḍavas departed.
Permitted by Keśava, their minds bowed in devotion toward Acyuta,
they were honored by Keśava with great affection and friendship.
Then, on one occasion, in an excellent assembly hall, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) was present together with kings and his brothers.
Having heard about the assemblies of the gods, Vṛtra questioned Nārada as to how they were situated:
"The intermediate space was described by you as being one hundred thousand *yojanas* in height; heaven is half a million *yojanas* high and crowded with rows of celestial chariots. (21.50–51)
Bhuvaḥ and Svarga are each ten million yojanas in extent;
Mahas, Jana, and Tapa are respectively one and a half times that in extent;
and collectively, they all have a total extent of fifty million yojanas. (21.52)
The extent of these worlds that have been described is said to be equal to the world of Brahmā known as Satya, where Brahmā shines forth. (Bhagavad Gītā 18.65)
And thereafter, the eternal realm of Viṣṇu is said to be double [in size].
Each successive one is a hundred times greater in happiness than the preceding.
Although they are filled with infinite beings, they are indeed [capacious] by the will of Hari. (21.54)
Possessing celestial ponds, they are never filled [with water] due to their divine nature;
they are full of all the pleasures of the senses, radiant with divine women and men, and likewise the seven netherworlds (pātāla) are strewn with divine jewels. 21.55.
Below, it is presided over by the remaining powerful deity.
Men and women in the seven continents are said to be endowed with the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, possessing great beauty, and living for many thousands of years. (21.56–21.57)
And Nārāyaṇa is the supreme sustainer of all these worlds;
residing in the world of Viṣṇu, he is eternally worshipped by all those who are liberated. Even the attendants of Brahmā, the gods, and the Vedas in their entirety [worship him].
Śakra, all the sages, and King Hariścandra—
indeed, all kings, O sage, as well as our father Pāṇḍu—
are declared to be followers of Yama by those kings and by Yama himself. (21.59–21.60)
While the Blessed Lord Rāma was being worshipped on the surface of Yama’s assembly hall,
Janārdana in his Vāmana form was addressed by Indra as one worthy of worship;
and all the incarnations were constantly worshipped by Brahmā.
The Nāgas are followers of Varuṇa; there Hari takes the form of a fish.
The Gandharvas belong to Dhanada as well; there the Lord Hari appears as Kalki.
The fierce beings belong to Rudra; and by Śiva, [Hari appears] as Nṛsiṃha.

"O sinless one, you have spoken of how Viṣṇu is always worshipped while describing the divine worlds of the gods, the abodes of all jewels. Regarding that, I have a great doubt: how was King Hariścandra [born there]? (21.63)
"O Sage, our father Pāṇḍu has not reached the surface of Indra’s assembly hall.
When addressed thus, Nārada spoke of the exaltation of Hariścandra, who had performed the Rājasūya sacrifice,
seeing that [Pāṇḍu] was at the surface of Yama’s assembly hall.
Standing there, Pāṇḍu spoke to you, O Rāma, whose divine power is double that of others:
"Let my son, honored by his invincible younger brothers and protected by Vāsudeva, perform the Rājasūya sacrifice; for what indeed is impossible for him here? (21.65–66).
Having heard this, the self-controlled Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma and knower of righteousness, deliberated with his brothers on the attainment of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having fully considered what his brothers had said, he concluded, "This is a noble undertaking."
The king urged his charioteer toward Keśava;
at that very moment, the excellent messenger, dispatched by Keśava’s wives and his own uterine brothers, reached Mādhava.
Having bowed to Keśava, he spoke these words:
"By the King of Magadha, your kinsmen from the wedding have been defeated in battle and confined upon a mountain by twenty thousand and two hundred and eighty kings. (21.70)
While you stand by, O Lord, release those who desire to sacrifice to the one of fierce form and three eyes;
slay the lord of Magadha and tear away that non-Vedic mouth for the protection of Dharma.
Having heard this spoken by the son of Dharma,
and having listened to those words, the charioteer then departed for the abode of the Pāṇḍavas.
He was honored by the Pāṇḍavas and by the son of Dharma for the sake of the sacrifice.
Being thus questioned, Mādhava spoke words that bring happiness to the world:
"For when a sacrifice is performed according to the prescribed rules, it may lead one to the supreme station of Brahmā;
he is truly fit for that state, and not otherwise. (21.74–75)
21.76. Indeed, this sacrifice of the Creator bestows upon those who are unfit for great states a boon that leads to liberation by means of a collection of equal fitness;
furthermore, it elevates them above their own former state even prior to final liberation.
Therefore, the son of Triśaṅku stands surpassing all other kings. Even your father Śakra, though a god, was unable to obtain the status of "King" without performing the Rājasūya sacrifice;
but today, he shall not be able to attain superiority over the son of Triśaṅku.
Long ago, while you were performing austerities, your father—the foremost of the Maruts—did not rise when Indra arrived; he therefore cursed him:
"Go to a human body, and from there, after dying, return again to heaven. (21.79)
"Even though you have gone, you are not able to enter your own body here.
Therefore, let the son of Triśaṅku become superior to you.
Then Vāsava, having been propitiated, spoke regarding the Rājasūya sacrifice.
"You shall regain your own body, becoming even superior to Triśaṅku.
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, this most excellent sacrifice is indeed a good undertaking for you;
by means of it, all that is appropriate for you shall also be attained."
Having thus proclaimed the Lord’s suitability for this sacrifice—
since all the fitness for the state of the Four-faced One resides within Vṛkodara—
he then proceeded to swiftly bestow upon him that perfectly complete fruit.
The one whose vehicle is the wind spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Where is your Rājasūya now, while the son of Jarā lives?
Who indeed could conquer him in battle—he who was not even slain by Balarāma when he was already dead?"
"O mother of all the worlds, as long as that son of Jarā remains, despite the words of Viriñca and Śarva, this supreme sacrifice will not succeed.
When this was said by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) replied:
"O Lord, my mind has been turned away from sacrifice; enough with this for me.
(21.87) Even the kings themselves did not seek overlordship;
for when one is a universal monarch, such as these are not his enemies. (21.88)
When this was said by him, the son of the Wind-god replied:
"The station of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is indeed easily attainable through effort;
yet those who are devoid of their own inherent power and abandoned by the grace of Hari [cannot reach it]. 21.89.
People who are devoid of great effort do not attain eminence. (21.90) This very greatness of mine is a firm manifestation of Hari’s great favor;
by placing singular effort at the forefront, one attains prosperity. (21.91)
When this was said by him, Hari spoke from his preeminent resolve regarding Vṛkodara, who stood there as the primary cause for the sacrifice:
"That one Puruṣa alone, the son of Jarā, exists today. (21.92)
The power of all those who oppose the virtuous belongs to Kali; yet there is one who follows immediately after him, the refuge of the good, from whose birth the virtues of the virtuous arise.
You should reflect upon that very person and strive to reach him.
Know this to be certain and not otherwise: if the Magadhan were slain by him, victory would belong to the virtuous; and in the opposite case, to the wicked.
He who goes forth to battle shall undoubtedly attain the supreme and eternal state.
He alone who slays the King of Magadha is the protector of the Vedic dharma;
for he who destroys the Lord of Magadha makes this world Vaiṣṇava,
since that Bārhadratha is protected by Śarva.

"He who is the leader of the Vaiṣṇavas shall indeed slay the leader of the Śaivas"—when the Unborn One spoke thus, filled with such intent, the King was not afraid. (21.98) When Yudhiṣṭhira said to the Unborn One, "Enough for me of sacrifice," [the Lord replied: "I am yours. (cclxvii)
The son of the Wind-god said to him, "I shall slay the King of Magadha in battle. When this was said, Hari replied, "Let us three go—
the three of us, Bhīma and Phalguna and I— to slay the King of Magadha."
"If the lord of Magadha were slain by Vṛkodara,
the sacrifice would certainly be accomplished and the world would come under your control.
When Śauri had spoken thus, the son of Dharma replied:
He caused terror to the circle of the Śūrasenas; indeed, out of fear of him, you yourselves abandoned the region of Mādhura and fled to the ocean. Therefore, I am afraid of that enemy.
For these two, Bhīma and Phalguna, are my eyes, O Lord;
and you are always like my mind. Therefore, I am no man without you.
Thus, I do not value life more than [the thought of being] separated from you, even from a powerful enemy.
"O Lord, I offer myself along with my own kinsmen for your sake.
When this was said, Vṛkodara, the consumer of his enemies' armpits, spoke again:
"If they have you as their leader, then even those preceded by Ramā, Viriñca, and Śarva [would follow]."
He under whose control stands that army of gods, asuras, serpents, and others—that very Keśava is the Lord; where, then, is this son of Bṛhadratha?
"My army is invincible," he says, yet Hari is its leader.
For indeed, all power resides in the Lord who is the leader of the entire world;
likewise, Arjuna possesses invincibility arising from the boons granted by Hari.
Therefore, let us three go today to that enemy, the King of Magadha.
"I shall surely slay the King of Magadha before Hari; of this there is no doubt.
When this was said by him, Hari spoke to the son of Dharma:
"The three of us, having united, shall send him to his death."
Vṛkodara will clearly slay the son of Jarā in battle.
You must not feel any fear, thinking, "He has been killed by me. For it is not the case that the enemy is slain by me personally for the sake of his destruction. (21.111–112)
When he, the foremost of those who take refuge in Śarva, is struck down by my supreme reliance on Mada, then indeed will my power be made manifest.
Therefore, O King, do not let your mind be apprehensive in any way. 21.113.
"I shall show you your two younger brothers after slaying the Lord of Magadha.
Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, he reflected upon their supreme virtues and said, "So be it. Those three then set out swiftly toward the Magadhas.
Having gathered together, they went to the mountain in Magadha known as Śivarauliṅga, which was richly adorned with excellent garlands, garments, and ornaments;
yet even that mountain was held in contempt by the son of Jarā. 21.116.
With their arms they struck him as if it were his head;
having entered the city by a non-gate, those who had crushed the lord of Magadha—like unto the treatises on fame that bestow prosperity—broke open Māṣa’s nostrils with their arrows. (21.117–118)
Likewise, having forcibly seized many garlands and perfumes from the market stalls, they took beautiful garments;
they rushed into his house through a non-doorway, and at their cry of "Alas!", the king rushed toward them.
Seeing those long-armed men in the guise of Brahmins, though dressed as *snātakas*, the king [perceived them].
Having closely observed the second class of men and seen their arms hardened by the bowstring, he spoke to them:
"Who are you? From what cause have you come here? And why was this breaking of my mountain-linga performed?
What has been done by you, you ill-behaved ones? Furthermore, why were these other acts committed by those in the guise of the best of the twice-born? (21.120–121)
21.122. To him who was speaking thus, the Blessed One said: "Indeed, every action against an enemy must be hostile.
Being addressed in this way, he replied: "I am no enemy to the brahmins; how could there be enmity between you and me?
To the king who had spoken these words, Janārdana said: "For such brahmins as those do not exist at all."
"O Vāsudeva, we are indeed your enemies; so too are these two named Bhīma and Arjuna.

Since you desire to offer our kinsmen as flesh-eating victims in a fierce sacrifice according to the dharma, abandoning the path of the Vedas—O enemy, we have come here to restrain you by force. (21.123–124)
"If you do not release our kinsmen today after having seized you, we shall liberate ourselves;
or else, release them and come against us for battle, for I am resolved here to die.
Thus addressed, the Lord of Magadha replied in anger: "I will not [slay] those engaged in an auspicious sacrifice."

I shall release the animals all at once, or I shall fight you in succession; or else, with you as my allies, I shall fight even if I am without weapons, or with weapons, or with whatever weapon you desire. Even alone, I shall fight against all of you, or with my army, against you and your soldiers. (21.126–127)
To him who had spoken thus, Hari, whose strength was unconquered, replied: "Come, O King! Either come alone against us, or with your entire army in battle.
Whomever among us you desire to fight, quickly encounter him."
"Whether unarmed or armed, or with whatever weapon you desire," thus spoke the Blessed One to his enemy, increasing Bhīma’s fame;
and having caused his own enemy to be slain, he bestowed supreme favor upon Bhīmasena. (21.129)

Desiring to increase Bhīma’s devotion, knowledge, and other virtues, and wishing to treat his enemy as if he were a blade of grass, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Arjuna went forth without weapons; therefore, they assumed the disguises of brahmins. (21.130–131)
"One clad in the garb of a kṣatriya but unarmed is by no means suitable for this task in any way.
Thereupon, they departed in the guise of brahmins to humiliate the Magadhan king while he was staying in his own palace together with his army. (21.132)
When Bhīma, unarmed, issued a challenge of immeasurable scope,
Keśava increased both the righteousness and the fame of Bhīma;
then, taking Arjuna as his third companion, he marched against the enemy.
Then Hari, wishing to demonstrate his own great superiority over Bhīma, said with the mouth of the Māgadha himself, "I choose one from among these.
Thus addressed, the son of Jarā replied: "I choose one from among us. (21.134)
I shall certainly not engage in combat with Arjuna, for he is indeed weak. For today he is only fifty-five years old, and thus he is like a child;
because of his lack of strength, though he is a youth, in my estimation he is merely a child.
Though addressed thus, Arjuna did not speak, suspecting defeat, thinking, "Then let the test be by means of arms or by the bow.
Consequently, Bhīma's great superiority in strength became well-established.
For this very purpose was Phalguna brought here by Kṛṣṇa.
Knowing that Kṛṣṇa possessed terrible and unbearable power, that king of Magadha insulted him as a mere cowherd and, out of fear, did not challenge the Lord.
He challenged Bhīma, thinking, "Perhaps I might still live.
The king was afraid that Kṛṣṇa would surely kill him;
therefore, that King of Magadha did not challenge Vāsudeva. (21.140)
"If Arjuna is defeated, Kṛṣṇa and Bhīma will slay me;
from the defeat of these three, my fame would surely perish.
Thinking thus, that King of Magadha challenged Bhīmasena.
"Perhaps I may somehow survive, but my fame shall not perish.
Thinking thus, the powerful king, the son of Jarā, seized Bhīma to fight him back;
he then consecrated his own son, formerly known as Rudra and called Patratāpa, upon the throne.
Considering his own strength to be superior in the mace-encounter, yet perceiving Bhīma’s skill with the mace to be greater than his own, the king was afraid;
he gave his mace to Bhīma and, being powerful himself, took up another.
For that very purpose, quickly seizing a mace, Bhīma went forth accompanied by the Māgadha.
In that place, before Keśava and Pārtha, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna themselves did not yet fight;
first Vṛkodara, desiring to manifest the qualities of Viṣṇu, defeated with his speech that [elephant] which had taken refuge in Śiva.
Then the two of them rushed forward with their maces, displaying various wonderful maneuvers.

Those two maces, which sounded like thunderbolts, were pulverized by the great firmness of their bodies and fell with fury upon each other’s chests, like two well-aimed lumps of clay hurled against rocks.
With their maces shattered, the two heroes struck one another with their fists.
With the terrifying sounds of the shattering of the cosmic egg, Keśava and Kaiṭabha caused the earth to tremble;
the mountains were pulverized, the principal mountain ranges shook violently, and all the oceans were utterly agitated.
The gods and asuras, including Viriñca, Śarva, and the others, reached for the sky.

The gods, desiring victory for Bhīma, and likewise the asuras and others for the lord of Magadha, all watched their respective strengths; then the son of Māruta also summoned his own power. Having honored the boon of the Creator for fifteen days, he prepared himself. (21.150)
By the command of Vāsudeva, Bhīma resolved to slay the enemy.
Having bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa and joyfully embraced Phalguna,
he seized the foe by the crown of his head, as a lion seizes an elephant.
Placing his knee upon the enemy's back, he broke the region of his shell;
yet at the time of death, he did not tear the body apart as he had done before, for the son of the Wind thought, "I must not kill him in a vital organ. (21.153)
He shattered him at a non-vital spot in order to manifest his own prowess.
As his body was being broken, there arose a roar resembling the bursting of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), by which these three worlds were terrified.
Having slain the enemy of Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma offered that worship to Hari.
For the Unborn One (Aja) had indeed come here to receive that very worship performed by Bhīma in his presence.
And having accepted the worship of Vṛkodara and firmly embraced him, Janārdana—
Deeply delighted once again, Bhīma bowed down to Kṛṣṇa, while Arjuna remained prostrate.

21.157 The gods, led by Brahmā, departed exceedingly joyful, whereas the Daityas were most dejected, now that the boon of Umā’s lord had been forcibly shattered by Vṛkodara through his reliance on Acyuta. 21.158
The son [of Arjuna], along with the wise Sahadeva, went for refuge to those lords of Rama, Bhima, and Arjuna;
he gave his chariot and his sister to the son of the Wind-god (Bhima), and bowed with supreme devotion to Krishna.
For that chariot had been obtained from Vasudeva through Vasu, who had received it from Indra, because of its power to grant wealth.
Vṛkodara seized Jarāsandha’s son and drove him onto the chariot of Hari.
Kṛṣṇa called to mind Garuḍa, who appeared upon the banner; then Kṛṣṇa ascended the chariot with the two Pāṇḍavas.
Bhīma took the maiden for the sake of Sahadeva, while he himself took the daughter of the Anu descendant.
For previously the King of Madra gave his own daughter to Nakula, and she was indeed this very Uṣā;
she alone was formerly the wife of the two Aśvins, with whom the twins took their delight—Uṣā, the wife of the Aśvins.
Therefore, those two sons of Mādrī behaved toward Kṛṣṇā exactly as one behaves toward the wife of an elder brother. 21.162.
The son of Jarāsandha, having honored Keśava and the others with jewels, departed with their permission;
by their command he performed the ancestral rites, and by their command alone he dismissed those kings.
Praised by them, Keśava, accompanied by Bhīma and Pārtha, departed as was fitting, while they remained bowed in devotion. (21.163)

Having been duly honored and praised by Sahadeva, they all—Kṛṣṇa and Bhīmasena—went to their own homes. Jarāsandha’s son fell, step by step, into blind darkness along with Keśava. Then Kṛṣṇa and the two Pārthas, mounted upon a single vehicle, approached the son of Dharma.
Their king, his soul awakened by the sound of the conch shells, became exceedingly joyful.
Then the blessed Dvaipāyana approached the sons of Pṛthā and commanded them to prepare all the necessary materials;
he enjoined upon them that supreme Aśvamedha sacrifice, accompanied by the Rājasūya, which had not been performed by anyone else since the time of Viriñca.
Indeed, the performer of that [sacrifice] attains the station of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), provided he is equal to the Supreme Lord through his own preeminent virtues;
Vyāsa, the teacher of the Lotus-born Brahmā, ordained that sacrifice in order to bestow an exceedingly great fruit upon Bhīma.
For the conscious agent is the unique cause of whatever action it performs.
It is the established rule that he alone enjoys the full fruit of that [action], while another enjoys only a small portion;
this is the conclusion reached apart from Viṣṇu, for he is indeed liberated from the fruits of karma.
Even the causes of sin generally do not partake in its fruit.

The gods are the sharers of merit, and the Daityas and humans are likewise its sharers. Bhīma alone is proclaimed to be the uncommon cause of this sacrifice, both through the slaying of Jarāsaṃdha and the victory over Karṇa.
Because Kīcaka and the others could not be conquered by anyone else,
Phalguna was the second [to succeed], and Yudhiṣṭhira was the third.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the state of Brahman, Vyāsa [described] that sacrifice of Bhīma.

Having commanded that the conquest of the quarters be accomplished by no one else, he gave his orders. Then Dhanañjaya said: "O Lord, I possess the bow, the banner, and the excellent chariot; therefore, the victory over the quarters is mine alone, as it is my own desire."
Thus addressed, the Lord of All replied: "It is true that you possess every means of success and you have great valor;
nevertheless, Kīcaka and the others cannot be brought under control except by Vṛkodara. (21.174)
They do not go [to him], nor does Karna come under their control.
Although you are superior in strength to Karna, nevertheless he did not give up his hand [in submission] while you were still alive;
for out of excessive rivalry, he thought, "He is not to be slain by you today."
"Since he is not to be slain by you because he wears armor and earrings,
let Vṛkodara go instead toward the direction dear to your father.
Out of fear of being captured alive, Karṇa will readily pay tribute."

There is no doubt that Bhīma has conquered him in battle; 21.178 / by the word of Śarva, Kīcaka and Pauṇḍraka were invincible in combat, yet they both fell under the power of Bhīma, as did the King of Cedi, even though he was otherwise unslayable. 21.179 /
For they live in constant fear of being seized alive from the terrifying fall of Māgadha;

therefore, they either pay tribute once they are conquered, or even before that. Go forth toward the quarter protected by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), across the seven islands in the directions of the intermediate points.
"Having quickly conquered the Nāgas and Daityas who dwell below, return here once more.
For you possess a divine chariot that travels through the sky, as well as divine weapons and a divine bow;
let Bhīma also come, O Śarva, bringing those other invincible [beings] headed by Bāṇa, who rely upon you. 21.181–21.182.
Likewise, all the gods, other than those who know me, offer him tribute;
and Yama and his brother go respectively to the western and southern quarters for the sake of the sacrifice.
"May fame and righteousness belong to them as well"—thus did Kṛṣṇa, the son of Kālī, say.
Having been thus addressed, those of most noble and virtuous qualities bowed to him and departed toward the directions as instructed.
Vṛkodara, having conquered the kings, reached Virāṭa;
and once Kīcaka had been defeated in battle there, he then exacted tribute from him.

Then, having conquered the kings in succession, he went to the territory of the Cedis; there, out of his mother’s words and out of fear, he was honored by Śiśupāla. Having stayed happily for some days in the house of his maternal aunt, [he departed]. 21.186.
Taking a vast tribute, he then proceeded toward the eastern direction;
having conquered all in due order, including the mighty Pauṇḍraka, and having deprived Karṇa of his chariot, he took tribute from every side.
Having defeated the gods led by Śakra on the peak of the Himavat,
he received from them— a multitude of jewels— from those who were pleased as they fought for the sake of sport;
and [he also subdued] Śeṣa and the mighty Garuḍa through wrestling with the arms.
Having defeated them while they were playing, he took their ornaments out of affection;
and being firmly embraced by them with hearts melting with love,
that powerful one, floating upon the ocean, went to the city of Bāṇa and to Hara.

In battle, he defeated one who had assumed the form of an elephant while playing; and Hara was pleased by this. Then, questioned by the Lord of the Mountain, he [Arjuna] related in detail his conquest of the quarters and how he had himself conquered those in the forms of lions, tigers, and other creatures.
Garuda, Śeṣa, Indra, and all the other gods said that to him. Having heard everything regarding the completion of the sacrifice, Śaṅkara then gave Hari the collection of jewels from the son of Bali.
Having taken that great and supreme collection of jewels bestowed by Śiva from the Daitya Bāṇa, he returned to his own city.
He [then] approached Janārdana, the Lord of the Vipras and Yadus, who was present in two forms.
Having placed that abundant wealth before him, he then bowed down;
having saluted his elder brother, he joyfully reported everything concerning himself and the two Kṛṣṇas to Dharmarāja, exactly as it had occurred. (21.195–196)
Just as Kīcaka and others were conquered by him who had Ekalavya as his ally;
and just as Pauṇḍraka, Karṇa, and others were likewise defeated;
and just as Śeṣa, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the rest, whose bodies were struck like lions—21.197.
Śarva, who possesses the body of an elephant, described all of that;
and being honored by the two Kṛṣṇas and by the king, that one of great strength gathered the materials for the sacrifice at the command of the venerable Vyāsa.
The Blessed Vyāsa said to him: "O slayer of enemies, all has been conquered by you!
In the victory over all, this sacrifice becomes complete, and not otherwise.
Viriñca was the first universal conqueror; now you have become the second here."
Having spoken thus and embraced him, he assigned him the sacrificial implements.
At that very time, his other younger brothers, having conquered the various quarters, returned to him;
Sahadeva, having conquered the southern regions, brought back treasures.
There, the heroic Rukmī did not fight with Sahadeva;
for he had previously been defeated by Kṛṣṇa, and having propitiated Śarva through ascetic penance, he had obtained from Kṛṣṇa a supreme bow and all other weapons from him alone. (21.203)
"When you defeat Kṛṣṇa, then this bow shall return to me"— having been told this by him, he did not oppose Keśava,
out of affection for his sister and because Kṛṣṇa was the one who caused the sacrifice to be performed. (21.204)
And by means of Bhīma and Arjuna’s strength, he gave tribute to the son of Mādrī;
the powerful Sahadeva conquered other kings by his might.
Likewise, Ghaṭotkaca was remembered as having arrived at Vibhīṣaṇa.
He gave instructions and departed; he too paid a great tribute.
Having reflected upon everything previously mentioned by Hiraṇyagarbha, as well as Keśava and the strength of Bhīma and Pārtha, he then [acted].
And having learned of the Pāṇḍavas, that lord of the gods (Indra) paid tribute;
21.207 / Having obtained a great flood of accumulated jewels, the son of Bhīmasena went to the son of Mādrī, and he (the son of Mādrī) returned to his own city. 21.208 /
Nakula conquered all the kings in the western region;
that hero received tribute from his maternal uncle out of sheer affection, and returned to his own city with a great collection of jewels. (21.209)

When Arjuna, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, having mounted his chariot whose banner was raised high with the foremost of apes, had already set out toward the northern direction, the mountain kings arrived; the Traigartas and the mountaineers together approached the son of Pāṇḍu. (21.210) cclxxvii.traigartāḥ pārvateyāṇsca sahitāḥ pāṇḍunandanam /
Knowing his intention, they approached and fought him;
having defeated them all at once, that son of Pāṇḍu proceeded toward that direction by stages,
reaching the powerful Bhagadatta, with whom he engaged in a great battle.
Having fought for eight days with his elephant, he became exhausted and said to the son of Indra, "Tell me the reason for your war. Then Arjuna said, "Give me tribute.
Vāsava also respectfully gave him tribute, saying, "Madgu is your father; he is your elder."
"You shall certainly not be able to conquer me here," said [Kṛṣṇa] through the power of his supreme weapons;
yet, when Arjuna placed his hand upon him out of affection, he gave no reply, for Arjuna, constrained by love, did not wish for a futile quarrel. (21.214–215)
Having conquered the eight regions for eight years, Pārtha also subdued the other six continents;
he further defeated [the enemies] in all four directions by the fiery power of his weapons. Having gone to the seven netherworlds (pātāla), he conquered the Daityas and Dānavas.
At the word of Viṣṇu, Bala took the hand [of Rukmiṇī] according to the Sāma-veda rites.
Having conquered Vāsuki and quickly taken abundant jewels,
the hero returned to his own city within the span of a single year.
The mountains of gold and jewels were acquired by those four [kings];
they were respectively four hundred, thirty-four,
one hundred, and four hundred yojanas in height, earned through their conquests of the quarters.
Gathered from the directions in sequence by moving clockwise starting from the west,
those mountains— though the site of the city was small— were contained within it because they were fashioned by Viśvakarman; it was as if a marvel.
Then the sacrifice commenced, impelled by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
the sages, who were masters of all branches of knowledge, served as the officiating priests (ṛtvijas).
Following the ritual procedure declared by Dvaipāyana, they initiated the king. 21.222.
Having entrusted the duties of the sacrificer to Yudhiṣṭhira because of his seniority,
Bhīma, Arjuna, and all the others remained together with him.
Since she alone was worthy of the status of Brahmāṇī, Kṛṣṇā alone became the wife of the sacrifice.
Because they were unfit for that station, no other wives accompanied them,
solely by the command of Vyāsa, the sustainer of the world and possessor of infinite splendor;
for even the entire ground there became composed of jewels and gold.
What need is there to mention all the vessels and so forth, and the camps in every direction?
When the sons of Pṛthā were summoned for the conquest of the quarters, then the entire world, numbering fourteen realms,
arrived here, preceded by Brahmā, Śarva, Śakra, and the others.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Vidura, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra with his sons,
along with their wives, arrived there, as did Bāhlīka with his son;
likewise, all the Yādavas came, led by Balabhadra.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and the other queens of Keśava were present there;
at that gathering of the entire world, discourses on the determination of ultimate truth took place.
The venerable Vyāsa himself was the presiding authority there, the very embodiment of perfect consciousness.
In those discourses for the determination of truth, the conclusion was the expansion of the qualities of Vāsudeva:

"There is nothing superior equal to him; how could there be another? This is the limit, and there is nothing beyond this. (21.230) Thus, when the supreme determination was made while Bādarāyaṇa and Rāma, the son of Bhṛgu, were listening.
In that assembly where the people were rejoicing, the king questioned Yati-vrata (Bhīṣma).
Although the king knew Hari to be the most worthy of worship by all,
that ruler of the earth, seeking to dispel the doubts of kings, questioned Bhīṣma, who was himself a knower of dharma.
When the conclusion was reached through the declaration that "there is none equal to Nārāyaṇa," even Brahmā and the others considered Kṛṣṇa to be merely mortal.
Therefore, the kings [thought], "This Kṛṣṇa is indeed Nārāyaṇa. (21.233)
To provide correct instruction, the Son of Dharma questioned Bhīṣma:
"Since the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are seen by men as if they were mortals, and yet men do not possess even the slightest degree of habitual familiarity with the sages," 21.234–235.
Even these kings did not know Bhīṣma, who was learned in all the śāstras;
therefore, because of his seniority in the lineage, he questioned Bhīṣma:
"In this assembly of worlds, who is worthy of the foremost worship due to a grandfather? (21.236)
"Brahmā, Śarva, and others are here, as are kings.
Thus questioned, Bhīṣma spoke to Kṛṣṇa, the most worshipful Lord:
"Even though Viṣṇu is one, he is threefold among Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and the Vṛṣṇis. (21.237)
Nevertheless, even though these kings appeared as incarnations of Viṣṇu and Rāma,
they did not conflict with their status as Brahmins; for that very reason, they considered themselves appropriate,
and there was no contradiction among them, for such was the nature of their state.
"If there were no dispute, its establishment would never occur anywhere;
therefore, Bhīṣma thought, 'It must be given to Kṛṣṇa.
For if it were given to Kṛṣṇa, the kings would immediately raise a dispute."
Through this dispute, the fame of Vāsudeva would spread far and wide;
consequently, the Pārthas offered the first worship to Kṛṣṇa before the world.
Immediately thereafter, because of the manifest identity between Vyāsa and Bhārgava, [the same honor was accorded to him]. 21.241.
They offered the foremost worship and honored the others as was appropriate.
(21.242) As soon as Kṛṣṇa had presented the supreme offering, the King of Cedi, out of anger, reviled him;
and upon hearing that, the son of the Wind-god, filled with intense wrath, set out to slay that king who reviled the Teacher of the World. (21.243)

"Even from afar, he shall sever the tongue that reviles Keśava"—this was Bhīma’s ever-greater vow. Then the son of the River (Bhīṣma) accepted that [vow], having been told by Keśava that those two had previously been declared by him as fit to be slain only by himself. (21.244) ccclxxx. "By me alone are they to be killed," so Keśava had said long ago.
Having heard that, Bhīmasena also remained there because he had been seized by Bhīṣma’s hand;
though he knew it was pleasing to Hari, he rose up as his own duty required,
and then stood once more, considering that this much was appropriate.
Great was the joy of those belonging to the host of gods upon seeing Keśava receive such excessive worship here;
that human being who performed this worship remained established in the very midst [of the assembly].
(21.247) Here, Suyodhana and the others, who were of demonic nature, became dejected in spirit.

The King of Cedi assailed Kṛṣṇa, that ocean of vast and noble virtues, with exceedingly harsh words. He challenged Keśava to battle, but Keśava quickly warded off his arrows and struck him down with a blade.
With his neck being severed, that devoted one became fixed upon Hari;
and the asura who had taken refuge in him attained the Great Darkness.
Jaya, having entered Keśava, once again became an attendant.
And that sacrifice of the Pāṇḍava was carried out exactly as prescribed.
(21.251) The kings brought many loads of gold and jewels; and the king appointed Suyodhana to receive these offerings during the sacrifice. (21.252)
Likewise, they fed the twice-born with whatever foods and drinks they desired, and they gave them many loads of gold and jewels as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*);
whatever was desired by each person was indeed bestowed by the Pāṇḍavas. (21.253)
Then, having emerged, they all bathed there with great joy;
while the divine singers sang and the great drums resounded,
the gods plunged into the celestial river as the divine women danced.
Having plunged into the waters of the Jāhnavī together with all the kings,
those gods returned again to their city and reached their own abodes; thus,
when all the kings had departed for their own cities and their respective homes.

In that assembly hall, which was constructed entirely of various jewels and possessed the brilliance of the sun, the son of Dharma, accompanied by Keśava, entered upon an excellent throne along with the Ambikeya princes and those led by Abhiṣmaka.
In the same way, the wives of the Lord of Rama, headed by Rukmiṇī, sat down;
likewise Bhīma and Phalguna sat near Hari, together with the son of Vāyu and the daughter of Pṛṣata. 21.259.
The beautiful Rugmiṇī likewise approached Satyabhāmā; the twins and the sons of Pṛṣata and others entered into the presence of Dhanañjaya; and Rāma and Sātyaki likewise remained close to the king.
In its entirety, that assembly then shone even more brilliantly,
just like the assembly of Svayambhū when it is presided over by Viṣṇu;
those [gods], wearing variegated golden garlands and auspicious garments, appeared exceedingly resplendent.
There those kings shone with their glittering crowns and earrings;
Janārdana, the Lord of the World, together with his wife, shone especially so,
like an ocean of infinite and true virtues in the assembly of the gods.
And all those kings and their circles of friends waited upon them;
at that time, Suyodhana, bearing his sword, arrived with his younger brothers.
Not knowing that the door of the assembly hall was formed by the radiance of sapphires, he passed through it, thinking it a wall. (21.265)
He firmly kissed the crystal-like, pure eyes of his inner circle, which did not obstruct his vision;
and when the twins were led by the king’s command into that hall, he took them by the arms and entered.
Having sat there for a moment, he departed elsewhere, unable to endure their divine splendor.
There, upon the sapphire ground, seeing lotuses made of jewels, he took up his own garment with the thought that it was water.
Thinking the dry land to be water because it was hidden by the intense radiance of the gems, he fell along with his younger brothers into a flood of water.
The Lord laughed at him; for Bhīma had here clearly indicated, by his loud cry, that he was capable of bearing the burden of the earth.

The queens of the Lord laughed together with the daughter of the Pāñcāla king and with their own other attendants. But Nārāyaṇa, beholding the face of the son of the Wind-god with its moon-like orb radiant with a gentle smile, said nothing; instead, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) restrained him and sent away the garments, garlands, and unguents.
Having cast his intense wrath upon Kṛṣṇa and Vṛkodara, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son departed with Śakuni;
then, filled with shame after having insulted the king who had bestowed garments and other gifts, he spoke to his maternal uncle as they traveled along the road:
"Kṛṣṇa and Bhīma, who laughed at me in the presence of Kṛṣṇa..."
Without causing them distress, I have no desire to live.
(21.272) If I possessed the power here, I would have Vṛkodara slain; and I would undoubtedly have subverted Kṛṣṇa’s preeminent honor. (21.273)

"Seeing such sovereignty as this belonging to the Pāṇḍavas, who indeed would wish to live, when all the lords of the earth pay them tribute like commoners? Having been addressed thus, Śakuni spoke these words in order to strengthen the enmity.
"O Indra among kings, what use have you for enmity toward your powerful brothers?
Live under them—those heroes who are superior in virtue and preeminent in strength.
Thus addressed, Suyodhana, his anger having increased even further, replied: [21.275–276]

"If that sovereignty of theirs does not come to me in its entirety, I shall certainly not live at all; this I tell you in truth. Nor would it ever be possible to seize that glory by the strength of my arms. (21.277)
"Even Indra is not capable of conquering them in battle, much less mere mortals.
Thus addressed, the most wicked King of Gāndhāra spoke to the Cakravartin, the foremost of all evildoers. (21.278–21.279)
"That prosperity which you see blazing among the Pāṇḍavas, I shall seize from them without any effort,
playing with dice in your presence.
When addressed thus, Suyodhana became cheerful in mind.
And those two went together to the king born of Vicitravīrya,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra; then Śakuni, that perpetrator of great evil, who was atheistic in nature, spoke to the pale, deer-like, and emaciated Dvāpara.

Having heard that from Duryodhana, the dejected king asked, "Why? They both immediately told the monarch what had been deliberated by the two of them on the road. Upon hearing that, the king said, "No," for it was opposed to righteousness and a cause of destruction.
"This ill-advised speech is not pleasing to me; for you have attained great sovereignty through the prowess of your own arms.

You too, having conquered the quarters, must perform the foremost sacrifices; do not be envious of those who are most virtuous, especially your brothers of preeminent manliness. Thus addressed, Suyodhana quickly replied to him: [21.284–285]
If you do not wish to seize the fortune of the Pāṇḍavas by means of dice, know me to be as good as dead today; be happy with the Pāṇḍavas.
If you desire my life, bring the Pāṇḍavas here yourself.
It is for the sake of the gods alone that one may take [wealth] together with his wife, and there is no unrighteousness in this at all.
(21.287) Brahmins subsist on the Vedas, and Kṣatriyas subsist on weapons; that weapon by which the enemy is destroyed, and not any other, is their means of livelihood. (21.288)
"Therefore, this very duty of yours shall also yield great fruit for you.
When he was thus addressed, he replied, "Let there be no fruit for me; let it be yours alone.
Even while speaking thus, O King, he himself was possessed by Kali.
Out of affection for his son, he dispatched Vidura to the Pāṇḍavas. For Kali had entered him so that he might achieve the status of a son;
from that moment on, Kali did not depart from him even for a moment.
Just as he was about to abandon the city and enter the forest,
in the interval between those two moments, his mind became possessed by sin.
Vidura restrained him, saying, "This great sin of yours will bring about the destruction of the entire lineage."
"There is no need for deliberation here; do not exert yourself, lest you incur infamy.
To him who spoke thus [Duryodhana replied]: "There shall be no quarrel here, for we ourselves shall prevent it.
I wish to see my sons playing together in one place, along with the sons of Pṛthā, Suyodhana, and the others. (21.293–294)
"Therefore, the sons of Pṛthā must be brought here quickly," said Baladeva;
and so Vidura set out for Dvārakā to find the sons of Pṛthā once Keśava had departed.
Indeed, after Suyodhana had left the presence of the sons of Pṛthā, Nārada—
Urged by the son of Dharma, Śaśa spoke of his approaching enemy.
When asked, "Who among kings is truly enterprising?", Nārada replied:
"That king of Saubha obtained from Śiva the boon of invincibility against the Vṛṣṇis. (21.296–21.297)
Having performed penance for many years while eating only a single handful of dust at a time,
he returned from Hara after obtaining a boon regarding the victory over Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard of the slaughter of the Magadhas and the conquest of the quarters, [he set out].
Having heard that he was performing the Rājasūya sacrifice, the slaying of Śiśupāla, and his preparations against the Yadus, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) gazed upon the cool orb of Kṛṣṇa’s face.
Having said, "So be it," Govinda dispatched Pradyumna and the other Yādavas; after some days, he himself arrived along with his elder brother.
Then Vidura went and summoned Dharmarāja.
Although being restrained by his brothers and by Kṛṣṇā, that King of Dharma departed swiftly together with his mother, his brothers, and Kṛṣṇā.
At the command of his eldest brother, Vidura also summoned the son of Dharma.
"He said, 'You must not come,' after enumerating many defects born of the senses.
Thus, having considered both this accumulation of faults and the words of your father, perform for yourself what you deem right."

Though addressed in this manner, the son of Pāṇḍu went forth, entered by Kali; accompanied by his army, he approached that son of Vicitravīrya. Even before, the righteous king had already made a vow due to the possession by Kali.
"I would return from the field of battle even if challenged, but never if forbidden.
Thus, although restrained by his own friends, he went toward Nāgapura;
for gambling is not a righteous act, especially for a Kṣatriya who is a teacher to the world.
The sons of Pāṇḍu were honored by the son of Vicitravīrya and took up residence with him for that night.
And at dawn, all the kings, led by Bhīṣma, arrived together with the sons of Pāṇḍu at the assembly hall.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Vicitravīrya, accompanied by Vidura, his sons along with Karṇa, and the King of Gāndhāra, [also arrived].
Having reached the assembly hall, the son of Subala challenged the King of Dharma there to a game of dice.

Kali himself entered into all those present—Bhīma and the others, with the exception of the four [Pāṇḍavas], as well as Pṛthā and Kṛṣṇā, and even Vidura; they were not restrained by Bhīṣma and the other elders, for their conduct was such that it would bring about the destruction of the lineage.
Though restrained by Bhīma and the others, as well as by Vidura, he staked his entire wealth in the gambling match;
then, swiftly defeated by the son of Gāndhārī, who was well-acquainted with the secrets of the dice, the son of Pāṇḍu next staked Nakula as a wager.
When he too was lost, he then staked Sahadeva, Arjuna, Bhīma, the daughter of the Somakas (Draupadī), and finally himself, in succession.

Then King Suyodhana, having been defeated, commanded his charioteer regarding the daughter of the son of Pṛṣata: "Go to her presence and say, 'You have been won at dice; come quickly to the great assembly of kings. Thereupon, she replied: 21.312. "The king, having been defeated, then gave instructions to his own charioteer concerning the daughter of the son of Pṛṣata.
The charioteer went to her side and said, 'You have been won at dice; come quickly to the grand assembly of kings. Then she spoke."
"I will not go to the assembly of the elders," he said; yet, knowing him to be terrified of Bhīma, Duḥśāsana went [to him], and then King Dhṛtarāṣṭra commanded his own younger brother.
That most wicked of men, seizing him by the hair, [dragged him away].
She brought her mother, who was dressed in an uneven number of garments, before the assembly. Having been brought there while in her menses, she spoke to those headed by Bhīṣma:
"This is unrighteousness; it is not being prevented by virtuous men such as yourselves. (21.314–315)
How could there be a victory through righteousness in a game of dice whose very nature is deceit?
For they say that gambling is not righteous, especially for kings. Those who do not speak of righteousness here are said not to be elders.
The wise say that an assembly is not truly adorned unless it includes elders.
(21.317) How could I have been defeated at dice while my husband remains undefeated?
For the learned declare that a wife shares the same status as her husband. (21.318)
"A wife must perform her duties together with her husband;
for even when the husband is conquered, the state of servitude does not belong to her separately.
Although they were told this, Bhīṣma and the others remained deluded by the possession of Kali.
"Ask the son of Dharma," they said, and then they became silent. For at that time, no one was able to speak against Duryodhana;
only Vidura spoke there clearly, saying, "This is not dharma."
Neither Dhṛtarāṣṭra nor his sons accepted his words;
with arms upraised, he then cried out to the gods, making himself known:
"I have won my own Śakuni and Draupadī, yet you have not been won according to dharma. (21.322)
"For this great unrighteousness stands here, having entered and occupied this assembly.
When Vidura had spoken thus, Vikarṇa, though being a wicked man,
spoke there merely for the sake of hypocrisy, seeking to display his own knowledge of dharma.
"This is indeed unrighteousness," Karṇa then rebuked him.

Seeing Kṛṣṇā being tormented, and seeing Dharmarāja departing from righteousness, King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words because he was wavering from dharma due to his status as a crown prince. (21.324–325)
"Indeed, these two arms of yours should have been burned for staking them in this game.
Arjuna replied, "It was not so intended. Then Vṛkodara said to him:
"One must speak, but one must not act; therefore, I did not do it."
"For the highest offense, there is instruction with words; for a middling one, the seizure of wealth; and for the lowest, corporal punishment. Therefore, Yudhiṣṭhira must be spoken to.
Then Karṇa said to Kṛṣṇā, "O beautiful lady, you are indeed without a protector."
Then Duryodhana said, "Go to the house of Dhṛtarāṣṭra," speaking these words for the sake of mutual discord among the Pāṇḍavas:
"If Yudhiṣṭhira alone is the cause of your grief, then if you consider him neither a teacher nor a superior, [then let us go]. (21.328)
"Or they might say: 'Either Bhīma and Pārtha, or even Bhīma alone, shall abandon you here.
(21.329) Thus addressed, the son of Pavamāna replied: "The son of Dharma is beyond comparison and is worthy of our worship;
moreover, I am the elder of you all, for the great declare that the Kṣatriya is preeminent in strength. (21.330)
"If you have any doubt regarding seniority by strength, all you heroes, rise up this very day!
I shall trample you all with the soles of my feet, along with your followers, whoever among you desires to fight me.
When Vṛkodara spoke thus, he rose up, roaring.
The entire assembly was reeling with fear, yet no one said anything.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Vidura, and the others took him by the hands and restrained him, saying, "Forgive everything he has said; it is the truth.
While he remained thus, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra sought peace.
At that time, though forbidden by Dharmaja and by his other elders,
Bhīma did not slay them out of respect for his superiors;
nor did he overstep the eldest, the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira.

To increase their wickedness and to demonstrate the conduct of an elder brother, the sinful Duryodhana then, while Bhīmasena was looking on, showed his thigh to Kṛṣṇā; Bhīma said to him: (21.335–336).
"O Suyodhana, with this mace of mine, swift as a thunderbolt, I shall shatter this [arm] of yours"—so he spoke again.
"You have no other wealth; stake Kṛṣṇa in the game!
Thus Vṛkodara spoke when the insult to Hari had been committed.
"Having cast him down upon the surface of the earth, I shall crush his head with my feet; enough!
He who would revile Hari, even behind my back, must always be put to death by me—this was indeed the firm vow made by the Son of the Wind. (21.338–339)
Furthermore, at that very moment, in order to increase his own sin, the son of Vikartana did not kill him;
instead, he spoke again to the daughter of Somaka:
"Go to our home, for the Pāṇḍavas are no longer there. (21.340)
When this was said, Vṛkodara rose up, followed by Arjuna;
both of them Yudhiṣṭhira restrained, as did the others. Then, as those two were despondent, Suyodhana spoke these words: (21.341–342).
"Remove these garments of ours, these slaves who are difficult to govern!
Thus addressed, he went to the sons of Pṛthā, and they gave him their clothes.
Having become clad in skins and having cast off the remaining garments, [they departed]. 21.343.
And they sat down upon the broad earth, taking refuge in patience.
Then, while the sons of Pṛthā were looking on, Duryodhana again pulled at Draupadī’s garment; at that moment, Vṛkodara spoke.

Tearing open the chest of this Duḥśāsana— the foremost among the wicked and the lowest of the Kurus who are otherwise great in their practice of dharma— I shall drink his blood before the eyes of the world. (21.346) But as her garment was being dragged away, Kṛṣṇā remembered Kṛṣṇa with particular intensity.
At that time, she had another garment, divine, very fine, and bright as gold. (21.347) As he repeatedly pulled at her, other such garments appeared;
yet the wicked man reached no end, and exhausted, with his limbs perspiring, he sat down in the assembly hall. (21.348)
When she had emerged from the mountain-like heap of garments, Duryodhana, filled with rage, spoke:
"Bring her into the house immediately; why do you delay us?"—thus did that one of very dull intellect speak.
Having heard those words, Kṛṣṇā then made a vow.
"Bhīma shall slay Duryodhana; Dhanañjaya shall slay Karṇa;
and Sahadeva shall kill Śakuni, that gambler with dice.
When this was said, Bhīmasena replied from the floor of the assembly hall, "So be it."
Pārtha took up that vow, and likewise the son of Mādrī;
then Nakula pledged himself to the slaughter of the son of Śakuni. Thereafter, Suyodhana’s younger brother dragged away the daughter of Pṛṣata.
Having heard that, the son of the Wind-god spoke in anger:
"Arjuna, Arjuna! My dear, patience does not appeal to me at all in this matter;
for this fallen body is no different from wood or excrement."
"Three fruits remain: knowledge, action, and offspring"—this is the statement proclaimed in the Veda. A son is not [the cause] for the corruption of a wife;
nor does one with a corrupt wife fail to attain the worlds, for he who is himself corrupted is indeed ruined.
"Because they were not protected, their prosperity has been defiled; nor will any merit arise from abandoning them.
Saying, "Therefore, today I shall slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their followers," he looked at his enemies as if burning them with his splendor.
And he saw him, in a rage, about to seize a massive iron club with the intent to utterly exterminate all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; at that moment,
cries were heard from the house of fire within Suyodhana’s palace.

In the same way, many terrifying omens occurred in the house of his father as well. When the son of Māruta had become enraged, the son of Ambikā, seeing those most dreadful portents, quickly questioned Vidura regarding their outcome.
Vidura said to that eldest brother: "In this very moment, O son, your sons along with their followers shall perish, struck down by the power of Vṛkodara.
For you are playing like a child, asking, 'What has been won? What has been won? (21.359)
"O Pāṇḍavas, you see yourselves here as conquered by one who has acted unrighteously.
The wise declare that what is given by a man blinded by intoxication—whether in matters of women or at gambling—is not truly given, nor is it accepted by his kinsmen. (21.360–361)
"Moreover, they say that [the victory] was brought about by chance; yet even so, it was not achieved by the Pāṇḍavas, but rather by your sons who displayed their lack of discipline.
When this was said, the son of Ambikā asked: "How can there be a fruit for mere omens?"
"It must not be so," he said; "let Kṛṣṇā be released at once.
Satisfy her with boons, otherwise know that your sons will be crushed by Bhīma and killed—let there be no doubt in this matter. (21.363–364)

"Kṛṣṇā and the Pāṇḍavas themselves desire an increase in their ascetic merit; they will not be harmed by that asceticism, and thus your sons shall live. Nevertheless, if you do not release Kṛṣṇā, [your sons will perish]. 21.365.
"Vṛkodara will slay him without a doubt by his strength alone," [said the king]. Having thus spoken and rebuked his son Duḥśāsana,
the king released her and offered boons to gratify the daughter of Pṛṣata.
Having been honored with boons by him, she remained steadfast in the Bhagavata dharma;
she did not choose boons for herself, but chose their liberation—the liberation of Yudhiṣṭhira along with his brothers, his kingdom, and his realm. (21.368)

The king offered her [to another], but she did not choose him even though she was being enticed. (21.369) It is held that the acceptance of a bridegroom other than Viṣṇu, the Lord, is not desired for one’s husband; for such is the dharma of the Blessed One. Therefore, she did not choose anyone else. (21.370)
"Since it was taken away through unrighteousness, that gift would not be valid";
thinking thus, Kṛṣṇā chose the liberation of the Pāṇḍavas, because for a Kṣatriya woman there are three husbands from her father-in-law [and his lineage] in this world. (21.371)
Then, having spoken a hundred verses on the dharma of the Bhāgavata to the brahmin,
she chose nothing further than this for her reason.
Thereupon, liberated from their grief, the Pārthas, together with Kṛṣṇā, paid homage to their elders and departed for their own city.
The evil-doer who was born immediately after Duryodhana spoke to his father, the chief one: "Alas!
You have once again released the entire fortune of the Pāṇḍavas that had come into our possession;
and our own destruction would surely be certain. (21.373–374)
"Therefore, call the Pāṇḍavas back once more for our sake;
let there be another game of dice, and let the one who is defeated go to the forest.
Thus addressed by him, the king then challenged the Pāṇḍavas once again.
Summoned again by his father for the gambling match, Yudhiṣṭhira entered the assembly hall despite being restrained by his brothers and by Kṛṣṇā;
[he was to undergo] twelve years of dwelling in the forest and one year in concealment.
Let us take up residence in the city of the famous king, not very far from where we might see either Kṛṣṇā or the Pāṇḍavas while living in concealment;
otherwise, for all of us together, there will be another twelve years in the forest. (21.377–378)
And regarding the secret dwelling of the King of Vatsa, as well as the manner of renunciation prescribed by the rules,

Duryodhana made a wager through the intelligence suggested by Duḥśāsana; furthermore, the son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira] was challenged again by the son of Gāndhārī, who was skilled in the secret of the dice.
When he who was defeated desired to go to the forest with his brothers,
then the evil-doer, the younger brother of Suyodhana,
danced while laughing and repeatedly calling out "O cow! to the son of the Wind-god.
And while still dancing upon the floor of the assembly hall, he spoke again to Kṛṣṇā:
"O auspicious lady, you are indeed husbandless; go now to the abode of Duryodhana!
All these [Pāṇḍavas] are like sterile sesame seeds who have fallen into the blinding darkness; there shall be no rising up for them again."
Speaking thus, Bhīma then mocked them, and all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra laughed.
Then Bhīmasena made this vow: "I shall slay you all in battle.
When he had spoken these words, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra went for refuge to Droṇa alone.

"Where Droṇa is, there is his son, and there are Bhīṣma and Kṛpa; and since Bhīma does not surpass his elders, they went to him for refuge. (21.385) And Droṇa, though a brahmin, spoke to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as he prepared for battle:
"Out of compassion for you all, I shall take up arms along with my son;
21.386 / and indeed, I will make an effort according to my own power for your protection.
Yet, I tell you the truth: I am not able to protect you from Bhīma. 21.387 /
Then those heroic Pāṇḍavas, accompanied by Kṛṣṇā, departed from the assembly hall for the forest.
As they went, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son mocked Bhīma, whose playful gait imitated that of a young lion.
Seeing him with half his body still outside the hall, Bhīma turned back and spoke to him with blood-red eyes.
"I shall split your other thigh in battle," having said this, he departed from that assembly of the wicked.
Following those who had set out, Kuntī, longing for her son, went forth;
Vidura restrained her as she was weeping bitterly and settled her in her home.
Having paid homage to her, the sons of Pṛthā, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, departed with swift strides.
King Yudhiṣṭhira went with his face cast downward, not looking at them with eyes of wrath;
for that compassionate monarch thought, "May I consume all the Kauravas. (21.390–391)
Raising his arms, Vṛkodara (Bhīma) set forth like Bāhuśālī,
thinking, "By these two arms alone, I am capable of slaying all my enemies.
Draupadī, with her hair unbound, departed from the surface of the assembly hall.

"The women of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s lineage shall have their hair disheveled," so saying, Pārtha, the best among those skilled in supreme weapons, advanced while raining down dust upon his enemies; his intention was to rain down arrows. (21.393–394)
"May our enemies not see our faces while we are in this state,"—with their minds fixed solely on this, the twins went with their heads cast downward;
Dhaumya walked in front, reciting the hymns for the consecration of the deceased. (21.395)
"I must perform my duties toward the hateful sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra"— thinking thus,
the charioteers followed them with fourteen chariots,
as did the cooks, the stewards, and those servants who were proven trustworthy.
Then, having approached a banyan tree in the forest on the bank of the Jāhnavī, they all sat down upon seeing that all the city-dwellers had arrived.
Then they [beheld] Nārāyaṇa, the abode of the entire world, who is eternally endowed with all excellent qualities.
They constantly remembered with devotion the Lord, the remover of the suffering of his devotees, who is eternally worshipped by Svayambhū, Śarva, and others.
(21.399) Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The twenty-first chapter, named "The Entry into the Pāṇḍava Forest," (the acquisition of the fire-drills).
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Oṃ! Having established those city-dwellers who desired to come with great difficulty, the heroes of the Kurus entered the forest at night and then reached the dense Kirmīra grove.
That younger brother of Baka, who was invincible by all due to a boon from the Lord of the Mountains, was intent on slaying them.
Accompanied by his wife and brother, he advanced toward Bhīma, discharging great trees and mountains.
Having engaged in combat with him, Bhīma swiftly struck him down to the surface of the earth;
in that sacrifice named Saṅgara, which had Nārāyaṇa as its presiding deity, he made him the sacrificial victim.
Having slain the Rākṣasa while staying in the middle of the forest,
they then deliberated together with ten thousand ascetics and eighty thousand preeminent sages.
Having reflected, the son of Dharma, for their support, worshipped the Lord Acyuta who was stationed within the sun.
Then he obtained from that vessel inexhaustible food, as well as jewels and this [vessel] which grants all desired boons.
With that very [vessel], Yudhiṣṭhira provided thirty servants and slave-girls to each of them.
Indeed, in his house, which possessed many millions of slaves, they ate from golden plates.
Desiring the company of the virtuous, those other hosts of great sages lived together with the sons of Pṛthā,
listening from them to stories of the essence of the supreme truth and likewise recounting ancient tales themselves.
(22.7) Thus there were many tens of millions of herds of elephants, as well as multitudes of chariots and horses.
Having bestowed jewels and crowds of men, they sported happily in the forest like gods in heaven. 22.8 / Yudhiṣṭhira constantly gave away a hundred thousand cows and a hundred loads of gold;
having reached the forest with his brothers, he rejoiced at ease together with the brahmins, like Śakra. 22.9 /
When the Pārthas had departed, Vidura was asked by his elder brother, "What is to be done here?
Ambikēya then summoned him and said to him with anger:
"I know you are hostile toward my sons; I have no further need for you here. (22.10)
"Stay or go as you please," Vidura was told, and he departed for the sons of Pāṇḍu.

(22.11) When he had gone, the king, emaciated by the separation from his brother, suddenly fell to the ground. Regaining consciousness, he quickly commanded Sañjaya: "If I am to live, bring my younger brother to me at once. (22.12)
Thus addressed, Sañjaya reached the sons of Pāṇḍu and quickly brought Vidura.
He too arrived swiftly, his faults cast aside, and saluted the eldest brother; then he embraced him.
Placing him on his lap and smelling his head, he then experienced supreme joy. 22.13.
Seeing the steward approaching, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with Saubala, out of indignation, consulted among themselves;
and desiring to kill one of the Pāṇḍavas by means of a concealed stratagem, they set out along with the son of the Sūta.
Having perceived their departure, the Supreme Lord of the lords of all, the inner self of the entire world, [acted].
Vyāsa approached Ambikā’s son and said, "Restrain your son as if with a horse.

"Having encountered the Pārthas today, he will undoubtedly be brought to death along with his followers"—when this was said by him, [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] replied, "Restrain them! To which Hari (Kṛṣṇa) said, "I do not speak with them."
"Maitreya will come here as well, and he too will speak these words for the sake of instruction.
If your son performs them, it will be well for him; otherwise, he will curse him.
Having spoken thus to the king, Vyāsa of infinite power departed once they had all gone. 22.17.
"If Suyodhana and the others were slain by the sons of Pṛthā, the burden of the earth would not be removed"—thus the Lord [thought].

(22.18) All activities are always directed by the Blessed One for the sake of the entire world, both sentient and insentient; nevertheless, Viṣṇu sometimes restrains [them] with his word and ordains [others], mimicking human beings. (22.19)

Then Maitreya arrived, and the king, having summoned his sons along with Karṇa and the son of Subala, honored the sage; and he, praising the Pāṇḍavas, said that the kingdom should be given to them. The lord of sages specifically praised the strength of Bhīma, speaking of how he had torn apart Kirmīra and others.
Hearing that, the fierce son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra slapped his own thigh.
Then the sage of fierce splendor cursed him, saying: "May there be a great battle for the breaking of your thigh.
Having spoken thus, he departed from the presence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, adding, "If you do not give up the kingdom, so shall it be."
Having heard of the slaughter of Kirmīra as told by his father Pṛṣata, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was struck with fear. Then those sons of Pṛthā, dwelling in the forest, sent word of their own situation;
and Kṛṣṇa, along with Satyabhāmā and the leading chiefs of the Pañcālas who were their kinsmen, quickly arrived.
The sons of Pṛthā, loudly praising his immeasurable virtues, sought forgiveness from the enraged Kṛṣṇa regarding the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Then Draupadī, weeping and bowing down, touched his feet;
having fallen at his feet, she praised Vāsudeva, the sovereign Lord of all, who is self-dependent. 22.24.
O inconceivable one, eternally imperishable, the singular embodiment of an ocean of perfect qualities, far removed from all defects;
O you who are constantly worshipped by the hosts of gods beginning with Lakṣmī, Brahmā, and Śiva, as well as the lords of the asuras;
O bestower of all activities, Lord of all living beings, refuge of the liberated, the essence of all! 22.25.
Speaking thus, she related everything she had experienced concerning Acyuta, the Lord of All—
He who is indeed the recipient of her supreme grace even over Śeṣa and the other gods.
Having heard all of it, the Blessed One made a promise to them and to all those women.
"Embracing their husbands, who have been struck down by Bhīma and whose hair is disheveled, I shall show them [the field] and not otherwise.
Having consoled her with sweet and gentle words, Nārāyaṇa spoke these words:
"If I had remained here, I would not have let this happen; I would have fought you."
That evil-minded king of the Śālvas, a doer of great wickedness, has been slain—
whether he was nearby or far away, whether separated by time,
or even separated by his own nature or by the intervening object.
Viṣṇu possesses no attachment, because he is eternally unimpeded; nevertheless, the Lord imitates the ways of the world of men,
for the sake of increasing the faults of the wicked and for the exaltation of the virtues of those such as Bhīma.
In order to transfer the merit arising from the Rājasūya and other sacrifices— which had become excessive in Yudhiṣṭhira—
to Kṛṣṇā and his younger brothers,
Viṣṇu willed it thus according to their respective capacities.
"Edhamānadvil"—this indeed is the Vedic name of Viṣṇu.

(22.32) [ccxcvii] The fruit arising from knowledge of dharma and other qualities superior to one's own fitness was intended to be bestowed solely upon the sons of Pṛthā, rather than upon Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Ambikā’s son (Duryodhana), and the others. (22.33)
Furthermore, for the sake of increasing the wickedness of Duryodhana and the others, Vyāsa said to the son of Ambikā: "The sons of Pṛthā are exceedingly dear to me;
their exile is by no means pleasing to me. (22.34)
Thus, because he spoke of the Pāṇḍavas as "dear" solely for the sake of increasing the wickedness of Duryodhana and the others,
and because of Bhīmasena’s gravity, there was forgiveness toward Arjuna and the rest during the gambling match. 22.35.
In this situation, there was no dharma that did not involve excessive cruelty toward Bhīma;
yet, due to the extreme suffering of Draupadī, forbearance became the great dharma. For she knew Bhīma’s mind well enough to realize that he must not utter a curse. (22.36–37)
Therefore, Keśava explained the reason for his absence there, saying that Hari had performed the increase of dharma according to what was appropriate;
meanwhile, having heard that Śālva had arrived, the son of Rukmiṇī and the others were with me.
For they had been dispatched by you from your presence and went to the city;
at that time, Śālva also tormented Dvārakā severely with his Saubha.
Then Pradyumna went forth quickly, accompanied by all the other armies and the hosts of Yādavas, as well as his younger brothers.

Realizing that he was my son, the wicked Sālva descended from that celestial chariot and mounted his own chariot to fight here. Having engaged in a fierce battle with him, my son warded off his weapons with a multitude of great missiles (*mahāstra*). Then, as he was intent on killing the king, he took up an unerring arrow given by me; at that moment, he heard a voice in the sky: 22.40–41. "This is my son. Realizing this, the wicked Sālva descended from that celestial chariot and mounted his own chariot to fight here. Having engaged in a fierce battle with him, my son warded off his weapons with a multitude of great missiles. Then, as he was intent on killing the king, he took up an unerring arrow given by me; at that moment, he heard a voice in the sky.
"For in the past, Nārāyaṇa resolved in his mind, 'Having taken the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, I shall slay Śālva.
Yet even by that Hari, he was merely put to flight by Bhārgava and not slain, according to his own mental resolve.
Therefore, he is not to be killed by you; moreover, this Bāṇa is the most beloved and truly unerring [weapon] of the wielder of the discus."

"Do not release it; I shall turn him back," said Vāyu, who dwells within the heart. Having heard these words of the Wind-god, he withdrew his unerring arrow. And that lord of the Sālvas, having mounted his own Saubha, departed for his own country, thinking, "What is the use here of a quarrel with a child? What business have I with Kṛṣṇa in battle? (22.43–44)

Having destroyed that army along with its ministers, Pradyumna, Sāmba, Gada, Sāraṇa, and Cārudeṣṇa—rejoicing—returned to their own city; and I too went there immediately and heard everything from them.
That arrow, by the power of my splendor, would ensure certain victory for my sons if it were grasped by them. 22.45.
Having heard that my enemy had departed and seeing my own city destroyed, he pursued me;

yet, upon seeing me stationed above the ocean on the Saubha and observing the rain of weapons and great missiles discharged by him, I warded off that host of arrows and pierced that most wicked Śālva with a multitude of shafts, whereupon he employed his illusory powers against me. (22.46–47)
Having observed them for a moment in play during the battle, I warded off many demons with my weapon of knowledge (*jñānāstra*);
then, having swiftly slain him who was raining down mountains, I cast the city of Saubha—its moorings shattered by the enemy of the gods—into the ocean.
Furthermore, having rendered him armless while he stood upon his chariot, I pierced that excellent chariot with my mace using an arrow.
Having severed his head with the discus, I returned to my own city, praised by Dhātṛ, Śarva, and the other gods.

"Therefore, this calamity befell me indeed due to my distance from him, though it was for the sake of duty," having said this to the sons of Pṛthā, he dwelt there for some days to console Kṛṣṇā; and Satyā remained there, consoling the daughter of the Somakas.
The wives of the Pāṇḍavas and their sons as well have all followed the Pāṇḍavas to the forest and remain right there;
then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having consoled Kṛṣṇā, [approached] Keśava.
Having prostrated and received permission, he went to his city with his nephews.
Dhṛṣṭaketu and the King of Kāṃsi also took their sister and their daughter,
and together with Kuntī and the others who remained with her, they both departed for their cities.

Formerly, Tilottamā was the wife of Nakula, while Pārvatī was the wife of the two previously mentioned twins; they were all prevented by Kuntī. Then Keśava, having placed Subhadrā and Abhimanyu upon the chariot, [departed].

Having taken leave of the Pāṇḍavas, he went to his own city together with his wife. After the sons of Draupadī had stayed for some time in the city of the Pañcālas, they went to Dvāravatī and dwelt there, cherished by Kṛṣṇa.
Thereafter, Dharmarāja, despondent with what he had done,
