always placed Kṛṣṇā in the position of his brother’s wife. And those sons of Pṛthā dwelt in the forest, subsisting on food left over by sages.
King Yudhiṣṭhira eats only after his younger brothers have finished eating. (22.58) Because his command is not to be transgressed, the younger brothers eat first;
immediately after them, that daughter of Pṛṣata eats alone. (22.59)

Thus, as a year passed for those who were ever devoted to Viṣṇu and who ate but once a day in order to attain him, Kṛṣṇā, being well-informed, spoke there to Dharmarāja by the command of Bhīma. Because of his extreme gentleness, Dharmarāja [remained] in the fourteenth [year].
"Even if he were to rule for a year, out of fear of his elders he would not desire the kingdom"—
thinking thus, the Lord Hanumān sent Kṛṣṇā as a pretext.
(22.61) Forgiveness is virtue in all circumstances, yet it is not a cause for sin even when directed toward a wicked person.
Having established, according to the scriptures, that this applies to kings endowed with power, he was addressed by his elder brother:
"After fourteen years have passed, having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who have seized the kingdom, you shall go before me to establish the sovereignty. (22.62–63)
Wishing to proceed with the trial by ordeal, Bhīma caused a solemn oath to be administered; he first directed Kṛṣṇā [to take it], and she said to the king:
"It is not at all fitting for a king to show leniency toward wicked people; you have held her for you at all times quite in vain. (22.64)
Thus addressed, the king said: "Forbearance alone is supreme in all things; by it the entire world is sustained.

Indeed, Nārāyaṇa is the creator of the whole world and of its joys and sorrows; everything here has been granted to him by Him. Therefore, there is no one whatsoever who is an object of anger for me. Consequently, forbearance alone is his highest duty toward all. (22.65–66)

To the king who had spoken thus, the daughter of Pṛṣata replied: "If forbearance toward all men were considered righteousness, there would be no royal duty nor the maintenance of worldly order; the world would perish through such cowards.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu is the instigator of everything, as are Ramā, Viriñci, Īśa, and the others. (22.67)

All things are subject to it, like pieces of wood and so forth; nevertheless, human effort is not rendered futile. (22.68) By its command, a person exerts effort, and according to that effort, one experiences the pleasant or unpleasant results. That exertion would not come to pass otherwise; therefore, the person too is subject to it as its agent. (22.69)
If human effort were in vain, for what purpose would there be injunctions and prohibitions found in all the Vedas?
If the person were not within the scope of injunction and prohibition, then indeed those two would belong to Hari alone.
By that very fact, he (the person) would be affected by merit and sin, yet he would not be affected at all [by them]. (22.70)
"If the agent were absolutely independent, he would be stained by those two; therefore, even Puruṣa must be subject to him.
Thus addressed, Dharmaja (Yudhiṣṭhira), rendered speechless by Kṛṣṇā herself, rebuked him, saying: "Relying on fallacious reasoning, you seek to prove even Hari's lack of independence. (22.71–72)
Threatened by that trickery, she sought to appease the king, for a woman does not look well when she is excessively talkative; therefore Vṛkodara said to him:
"O King, Viṣṇu is the creator of all and there is no other; everything else is dependent on him, while he is independent."
Nevertheless, a man’s own prescribed duty must be performed, while other [duties] should be abandoned with great effort.

(22.74) This is evident from a person’s own action; by that, the instigation of Keśava is to be inferred. For having performed his prescribed duty, a wise person concludes that it was indeed Viṣṇu who instigated him. (22.75)
Therefore, thinking that fate alone is the cause, a person of impure nature follows this path of Viṣṇu toward a right destination;

yet, having abandoned his own duty, he goes to a state of darkness. Therefore, one's own duty must indeed be performed. Furthermore, one must recognize the sovereignty of this Viṣṇu, and one's own duty as an agent must be carried out.
This agency resides in the individual soul; thus, everything is known through direct perception, scripture, and inference.
Knowing that both [the soul and its agency] are under the control of Viṣṇu, the wise man performs his duties without attachment.
Recognizing Viṣṇu alone as the impeller, he should follow the three means of valid knowledge.
The three are complete as valid means of knowledge when they abide together without contradiction, and these three are non-contradictory.
Separately, the middle one would be invalid and contradictory; therefore, all three must be applied together.
An ignorant person, however, having abandoned direct perception and considering fate alone to be the agent, would abandon his own actions.

The wise man, knowing that the living being is under the control of Viṣṇu, performs his duty incessantly. (22.80) That which is called "nature" (*svabhāva*), known as "capacity," and known as "force" (*haṭha*), which is established from time immemorial and eternal in all living beings—that is the first cause; the second is beginningless action (*karma*) itself; and likewise the third.

The life-force (*jīva*), effort (*prayatna*), and that which is called human exertion (*pauruṣa*)—this triad is always subject to the control of Viṣṇu. Vāsudeva, who is higher than the highest and supreme, is not under the control of anyone; he is the ultimate independent one.
Indeed, this [power of] *haṭha* exists in a hierarchy, beginning from Brahmā down to Kali.
Through force (*haṭha*), actions arise; from action comes effort, and effort is the employer of forceful action.

Without effort, there is neither force nor action that yields fruit. Vāsudeva is the director of the independent power of all things; nevertheless, even he employs these [factors] only by depending upon them. (22.82–83)
His sovereignty consists in the resolve: "I grant the fruit only by depending upon these [beings].
This sovereignty of His does not depart, for He is omnipotent; there is no lack of power in Him anywhere due to His lordship.
Therefore, whatever action is ordained by Him is His own work, performed for the sake of His worship; through that, there is indeed the attainment of Him. 22.84.
Otherwise, hell would surely await the Brahmin in every way; yet for him, there are his own rites, recitation, and instruction.
The Brahmin caste originated from the mouth of Viṣṇu; since action arose from the mouth, he assigned that [duty] to him.
Born from the arms is the Kṣatriya; therefore, his duty is with the arms, for it is indeed the warding off of evil.

Viṣṇu established for the Kṣatriya as well the duties of promoting the true dharma, the recitation of prayers, and instruction; and for the Brāhmaṇa, he established the duties of sacrifice and ritual acts. Since the Vaiśya was born from the thighs, his increase of progeny and his specific labor constitute his duty.

Due to that similarity, the growth of stationary beings [occurs] because of the proximity of the knees; Viṣṇu performed the duty consisting of livelihood (vārtā), and from his very feet the Śūdra is said to have arisen. Service, which consists primarily of movement, was likewise [assigned] to the hands and feet due to their similarity.
Action arises from the hands, and for him, Dharma and the increase of progeny result from their proximity.

(22.88) The arms, the chest, and the heart are the seats of strength and wisdom for kings; therefore, both strength and wisdom are said to be Dharma. For the skillful, however, Dharma resides solely in the hand. (22.89)
Therefore, because of their skill in the actions of hands, thighs, feet, and the private parts, these two—the Vaiśya and the Śūdra—are so named.
Primarily, this is a distinction of dharma; generally, however, it applies to all without exception.
For we are gods, and thus almost all our actions eternally conform to the nature of dharma. (22.89–22.90)
By all these qualities previously ordained by Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu alone is to be worshipped by all castes;
devotion to Him alone is the dharma for everyone, and knowledge of Him is His worship according to one's capacity.
(22.91) Viṣṇu is the father, the teacher, and the supreme deity of all; therefore, He alone is to be worshipped.
Because they are devoted to Him, the deities are especially to be honored, particularly those among them who are intensely devoted.
22.92. Vāsudeva, when fully honored, bestows liberation; when not honored, He bestows only suffering.
Because He is independent, He is the giver of pleasure and pain; no other is so, for all others are under His control. 22.93.

Because of His sovereignty, He is filled with all qualities preceded by the powers of bliss, existence, and knowledge; and because of His sovereignty, He is free from all defects, for He who is sovereign possesses limitless power. Since His power exists due to its boundlessness, He remains untouched by defects and perfected in qualities. 22.94–95.

Thus Nārāyaṇa, filled with all virtues and his own duties, is most worthy of worship; for it is not at all improper for us that he should perform the duty of warding off the wicked. A Kṣatriya who slays the wicked—and especially those who have come to battle while remembering Hari—is performing his duty.
By his own strength of arm, his two arms—though consisting of mere consciousness—become possessed of bodies.
Having slain those who are preeminent in sin and preeminent in power, there arises an increase in liberation and supreme bliss;
and Viṣṇu’s joy therein is indeed supreme. Therefore, sinners must be killed by all means.
But those wicked men who are rogues or have been captured should be slain by others with their own arms;

or one should kill a king, a prince, or likewise a younger brother of the king who has come against him. (22.98) Even a king’s son who has not yet been married should be slain, but he must not be killed by one's own hand.
Even another cruel act, if it is joined with righteousness, should be accomplished by others—the Kṣatriyas—and not as one's own private business.
Thus, dharma is ordained in the Veda itself; such is the word of Viṣṇu in the Pañcarātras.
Gambling with dice is a deceitful and sinful act, yet it was committed by you, who are censured even by Saubala.
Nowhere is there a scriptural injunction for this; therefore, they say that it is not "given" [and thus not recoverable], as it is like what is won at gambling.
What is given out of fear is likewise considered "given at gambling," and what is given to a woman out of lust must be recovered.
Such is the eternal Vedic law; for regarding gambling and women, they say that nothing given is irrecoverable. (22.100–101)
If their wealth to be enjoyed is indeed small, it should be taken by their kinsmen through enjoyment;
for if they are unable to prevent a man from taking it, that kingdom cannot be recovered again.
O King, because you are ever devoted to dharma and the elder brother, I did not do that without your permission.
"If you grant me permission, having slain them, I shall today properly establish the kingdom in you alone.
Even if you desire to act with truthfulness toward these sinners, nevertheless twelve months have passed for us;
for according to the authority of the Vedas, those years for men are said to be a thousand-year sacrificial session measured by months."
"Having spent one month in concealment, we shall then slay our enemies and protect the kingdom.
O King, do not become a bringer of grief to your friends, nor a source of joy to your enemies.
Blaze upon the heads of your foes while constantly gladdening your friends; devote yourself to Vāsudeva. (22.104–105)
O King, the sovereign independence of Vāsudeva is indeed clearly perceived through direct observation today;
for Kṛṣṇa has conquered Śaṅkara and others, as well as the son of Jarā and others who were unconquerable by the boons of Brahmā and the rest.
Furthermore, the subordination of Brahmā and the other gods to Prakṛti was seen by us many times in the body of Vyāsa.
Pārāśarya, having bestowed divine vision upon us, has shown us our sovereignty throughout all the worlds.
Therefore, O King, go forth to slay all your enemies and enjoy supreme sovereignty;
in this way, O King, you shall attain great fame and merit through the grace of Vāsudeva.
Thus addressed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, spoke to Bhīma:
"At the end of the thirteenth year, I shall certainly do as you have said.
This is the truth, there is no doubt; I swear it by my own soul."
"You should not say anything other than this to me, who am afraid of public reproach.
(22.110) And if you thus strike me with excessive words, O Bhīma, you must act against me immediately; indeed, enemies are to be slain."
You ought not now to oppose [me] with such words as these:

"How were Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others—experts in weapons and those who were to be restrained—restrained in battle? They are venerable; they should by no means be restrained by hand-to-hand combat. (22.111–112)
"Even though you know the celestial weapons, you do not employ them at any time;
therefore, we must depart this very moment once Dhananjaya has mastered the weapons.
Having been addressed thus, Bhimasena, fearing that his affection [for Arjuna] might be broken, then—
Having attained his own desired object, he spoke not a single word;
for Bhīma’s intention was certainly that Yudhiṣṭhira should make a promise regarding the journey for the sake of the kingdom in the thirteenth year.
Otherwise, because of his extreme gentleness, he would not advance against the enemies with his divided mind.
(22.115) For while Bhīma stood there having accomplished his task, the son of Dharma reflected: "How can victory over Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others be achieved? (22.116)
"Bhīma never desires to oppose his elders;
therefore, he must be restrained by Arjuna himself," he thought.
For Bhīma would indeed restrain them only in times of distress, and not otherwise. 22.117.
Perceiving Yudhiṣṭhira thus possessed by anxiety,
Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana— omniscient and omnipotent—
approached the king and enlightened him whose mind was agitated by worry.
"I shall speak this mantra by which Phalguna will conquer Bhishma, Drona, and all others; recite it for Dhananjaya. Having said this, he spoke the mantra that grants the vision of all the deities.
For he did not himself say to the son of Pṛthā that there would be an excess of fruit;
indeed, the victory over Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others was achieved by this much prowess alone.
There is no need for more than this, and this much is sufficient for him.
"Regarding Phalguna," the Blessed One did not speak of it himself to Manu.
(22.122) When the Blessed Vyāsa—the omniscient creator of all—had departed, Dharmarāja imparted this secret mantra to Phalguna. (22.123)
Having received that mantra, Phalguna bowed to his elder brothers and embraced the twin-born ones;
then, having reached Mount Indrakīla, he performed austerities there while remembering Hari, who dwells within Śaṅkara. 22.124.
When six months had passed, he saw on the mountain an asura named Mūka,
who had assumed the form of a boar for the purpose of slaying Phalguna. Recognizing him, the heroic Phalguna strung his bow Gāṇḍīva.
He discharged many arrows, sharpened with adamant, at his body;
Triambaka, in the form of a Kirāta, followed him along with his wife.
That evil-minded Dānava died, slain by those two.
He was told by him: "Indeed, this boar has been pursued by me alone today; since you have pierced him, therefore fight with me! (22.128).
Thus addressed, Phalguna said: "Stay! Stay! You shall not escape!"
Having spoken thus, those two bulls among men engaged in battle.
There, Śiva neutralized all the weapons of Phalguna;
then Arjuna, taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow, struck him.
Then the Lord of the Mountain, laughing, spoke to that foremost of gods;
thereafter, a wrestling match ensued between those two lions among men.
Then Rudra, having gathered him up into a ball, hurled Dhanañjaya away.
Afflicted by Rudra, Phalguna fell into a deep swoon.
Previously, Śaṅkara had requested the one whose banner is Garuḍa:
"Grant from me a boon to those who are inferior, whom you yourself bestow."
"By your grace, they shall be invincible, yet they may also be conquered by me.
Having been addressed thus, Viṣṇu granted that boon to the Lord of Umā;
with that [boon], Giriśa conquered Śvetavāha who was in the midst of the battle.
Vyāsa did not give the *Pārtha* (Arjuna) exclusively Vaiṣṇava mantras, [thinking],
"This alone is sufficient for the victory of Bhīṣma and the others," he who is the embodiment of consciousness.
By means of the exclusively Vaiṣṇava mantras given by him, which bring about victory— 22.135.
He thought, "Pārtha, being excessively old, might become arrogant.
Then Pārtha, having regained consciousness and desiring victory, worshipped Śiva with those flowers upon his head using the mantra spoken by Vyāsa.
But Phalguna, having recognized him as Rudra, ascended [the chariot] and paid homage;
then Śiva bestowed upon him the *pāṃsupata* weapon—that weapon which has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity and was mastered by Śaṅkara. (22.138)
Therefore, at that very moment, all the other gods appeared before his eyes and bestowed upon Pārtha their own weapons, including the one named Pāśupata.
Then Indra, having approached Arjuna, said, "O sinless one, I am pleased with you."
"Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, who resides within the body of Rudra, has been gratified by you;
therefore, come to my world—I send this chariot for you.
Having spoken thus, Indra departed, as did Mātali with that chariot.
Having arrived there, Pārtha indeed went to his father’s abode.
Honored by all the gods and established there by Indra himself,
he sat together with him upon that excellent seat belonging to Indra.

Embracing the hero of the Kurus with affection, Śakra, his own second body, rejoiced at beholding his face; he too dwelt there in that world for five years. Then Vāsava bestowed upon him great divine weapons, and Urvaśī [bestowed them] upon him.

Having been rejected by his mother with the thought that he was merely human, Pārtha was cursed by her, saying, "Become a eunuch! Śakra then granted him a favor, saying, "Dhṛṣṇu, live for one year in the form of a eunuch; thereafter, you shall no longer be a eunuch. 22.144–145.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu dwelt there, practicing the Gāndharva Veda and likewise acquiring weapons from the Gandharva Citrasena, who was like the Lord of the Gods; thereafter,
he returned to his own city together with Subhadrā and Abhimanyu.
While Janārdana was dwelling there, he once observed thus:
"Indeed, a boon was previously granted by me to Śambhu; I shall surely accept a boon from him, deluding him according to my desire. (22.147–148)
“O Lord of the Gods, having worshipped you, I shall always accept a boon by becoming present in human beings and others through a portion of myself at the beginning of the Dvāpara age.
Knowing his intention to make this speech true, she [spoke].
For the sake of pleasing Vāsudeva, Rugmiṇī spoke these words:
"Even though a son has been born, she [the Earth] still desires a son, for she knows the thought within his mind:
'O Lord, may I have a son who is powerful and the most excellent among those skilled in all weapons. (22.150–151)
Thus addressed by the goddess for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods, the Blessed One mounted his own vehicle, Suparṇa, and went to his hermitage at Badarikā.
"I shall now create a delusion which will bewilder living beings. 22.152.
And you, O Rudra of mighty arms, compose treatises that cause delusion; O mighty-armed one, display as truths those things which are untruths.
(Padma Purāṇa 6.71.106)
"Make yourself manifest and make me unmanifest;
I shall worship you, eager as I am to delude the world.
For it is my conviction that the Tāmasa Asuras will not depart otherwise. (22.154–155)
All the omniscient sages honored the Lord Kṛṣṇa, who had come to Badarikāśrama to make true those words which Keśava had previously spoken for the sake of Śiva. 22.156.
At night, while Kṛṣṇa was seated among the sages, two Piśācas named Ghaṇṭākarṇa and Karṇa arrived;
they had been dispatched by Giriśa and were desirous of going to Dvārakā to see Kṛṣṇa. Seeing Keśava situated in the midst of the sages, they did not recognize him. (22.157)
Having performed the customary rites of their own kind, they beheld him through meditation.
Seeing him situated within the heart, those two auspicious ones, filled with wonder,
praised him with devotion and prostrated themselves before him many times.

The Blessed One, pleased with the two of them, touched those best of Gandharvas and in a mere moment made them endowed with divine forms and voices. Then the Lord was worshipped by them once more with dances, songs, and hymns of praise.
Viṣṇu went to Kailāsa, the lord of mountains, and as it were performed penance there,
enjoying his own qualities with his eternal radiance.
He performed penance for Śarva and utterly deluded the wicked. (22.162) Previously, he had spoken that which immediately deludes the worlds:
"But as for you, O Śarva, I shall perform [penance] for twelve years. (22.163)
"May the gods be free from anxiety, for the asceticism of the asuras is intended to delude them.
(74) "Constantly uniting with the qualities of Viṣṇu"— here, "uniting" means meditating with a mind that is joined with the eternal light, which is the witness and whose form is all-pervading.

Regarding the reading *bhuñjan*, it is derived from the verbal root *bhuj* in the sense of "protecting" (*pālana*) and "eating" (*abhyavahāra*); thus, it means protecting with the mind, that is, contemplating and making [the object] firm.
Such is the intended meaning (*bhāva*).
Therefore, at that time, Kṛṣṇa, by his command, caused Bṛhaspati to wander swiftly through the twelve signs of the zodiac in a single day. (22.164)

By his will, that single day became twelve years for Keśava. On that one day, the Blessed One, having mentally fashioned twelve years consisting of nights and days, as well as fasts and other observances, [performed them]. (22.165–166)
He ordained the month-long vow (*māsavrata*)— to be performed with intervals of one hundred and fifty breaths—
for the sake of his devotees attaining the fruit of a twelve-year vow through the mind alone.
Therein, Garuḍa and his other personal attendants performed service for him.
Janārdana performed the rites beginning with the fire-oblation (*homa*),
desiring to purify himself from his sins for the sake of Śiva.
While he of the long eyes like lotus petals was thus situated, Brahmā, Indra, and the foremost gods, along with the excellent yogins and lords of progeny, [approached him].
The hosts of Gandharvas, Siddhas, excellent Yakṣas, birds, and others, together with the multitudes of Pitṛs and great sages,

approached. Śarva too, perceiving that his own deity— the source of all the gods— had arrived in the vicinity of his own home, came forth accompanied by his attendants and his wife, having received the finest offerings with devotion and great haste.
Approaching the pair of feet of Kṛṣṇa, the sole Lord of the universe, he, filled with devotion, bowed his head;

and he offered supreme praise to the Supreme One, whose form consists of the six perfections and who possesses great, faultless majesty. (22.171) Kṛṣṇa also, desiring only to delude unworthy people, praised his own form residing within the heart of Rudra.
Having heard that, Rudra spoke to all the gods: "I speak the truth; listen today to my words.
Viṣṇu is indeed the supreme refuge for all virtuous beings; for the sake of attaining Him, I am the means, as are the Wind-god and Lakṣmī.
For this [conclusion] arises from the definitive determination of the meaning of all the Vedas: that Viṣṇu alone is supreme, even to me, O Lotus-born One."
"From the unmanifest and from the entire multitude of living beings, He is indeed eternal; this is the certain conclusion—remember this!
When the Lord of the Mountain had spoken thus, all the hosts of gods bowed to Kṛṣṇa with exceedingly increased devotion to the Lord of Ramā.
[22.173] By these and other words of the Lord of the Mountain, which determined the true nature of reality, they were instructed.

Through the narrations of Kṛṣṇa’s very qualities, Indra and the other deities attained an increase in knowledge; even previously, they were already more knowledgeable. (22.174) For the gods always know him to be the supreme among all the deities.
Nevertheless, because those means of knowledge were so numerous,
whatever doubts existed there were also dispelled at that time by the mere word of Rudra.
Then the Unborn One said, "Kṛṣṇa shall take from you an excellent son."
In order to make true what he had previously said to Śiva, he spoke:
"Give me a son. He [Śiva] replied: "That son of yours who was born long ago under the name Pradyumna was given by me; it was merely a matter of common report. (22.176–177)
Long ago, when Kāma was consumed by me, Rati entreated me, saying, "Give me my beloved. Then I said to her:
"When he is born from Vāsudeva, you shall regain that husband. (22.178)
"Therefore, O Lord, by your command, he has been given to me as if by me;
I am your slave, O Lord of Gods, protect me who have come to you for refuge. Having spoken thus and bowed down to him, Hara spoke again to the gods: (22.179–180).

O immortals, hear the purpose for which this Keśava has come: there was an asura named Vakra who was indestructible due to a boon from Brahmā; he [has been slain] by that son of Vāsudeva born at that time, except for Kāma, against whom he could not prevail anywhere. (22.181)
Having placed his own son Pradyumna within her womb, she came here specifically to kill him;
yet, having extracted that son from her womb, she burned him, while the gods watched as the dry wood was consumed by the fire. (22.182)

Having burnt that Daitya along with the forest by means of Pradyumna— who was formidable with garlands of flames and augmented by his own splendor— Keśava then placed his son back within his own belly. 22.183.
Furthermore, he will cause that very same [son] to be born from Rukmiṇī along with his innate yoga;
and just as before, he shall become a youth in a mere moment.
All of this was indeed seen by Nārada and the other sages.
"This god sports thus with complete sovereignty alone"—
when this was said, the gods, led by Śakra, bowed to Keśava. Then Hari, being praised by the gods headed by Brahmā and the lords of the asuras, stood upon the shoulders of Garuḍa.

Having bowed down again and again and being praised by Śaṅkara, he returned to his own city on the third day. (22.186) When Kṛṣṇa had departed for the abode of the enemy of Pura, Vāsudeva of Pauṇḍra arrived at night together with his maternal uncle Ekalavya and three akṣauhiṇīs. (22.187)

Perceiving that he was shattering the city, the heroes of the Yadus, together with Rāma, Śaineya, and the other leaders, engaged him in battle; then Ekalavya, the lord of the Niṣādas, rained down arrows upon them.
At that moment, the Yadu heroes were suddenly despondent from his missiles and weapons, like those whose lamps have been extinguished.
Together with Rāma and the grandson of Niṣadha, they all entered their own city.
Then, taking up their great torches and placing Rauhiṇeya at their head,
they emerged from their city with weapons grasped, like lions emerging from their own caves.

“Then Rāma Śaineya approached Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva with his chariot and Ekalavya; Satyaki and Pauṇḍraka fought one another and likewise deprived each other of their chariots. (75/22.191) Thereupon, a mace-duel took place between those two heroes, Rāma and Ekalavya.
Having deprived each other of their chariots, those two foremost of powerful men, filled with pride, fought with maces.
At that time, Keśava, having mounted Vainateya, arrived at the place where those two were engaged in battle.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, his soul overflowing with joy, desired to slay Ekalavya.
Raising his mace with both arms, the son of Rohiṇī rushed impetuously toward the Niṣāda;
seeing his strength and wrath, Ekalavya, desiring to live, fled a great distance away.
Pursuing him while putting him to flight, the son of Rohiṇī gave chase, and the terrified Ekalavya fell into the ocean.
Having put that [army] to flight as far as the shore of the ocean, Rāma, undaunted in spirit and mace in hand, remained there. (Harivaṃśa, Bhaviṣyatparvan,
Adhyāya 102) That most wicked Ekalavya, being greatly terrified and thinking that Rāma had indeed followed him once again, [fled].
Having crossed eighty *yojanas* across the ocean, Rāma beheld the island of Adhi-rūhya behind him;
having utterly defeated his exceedingly powerful enemy in battle, he approached Dāmodara with joy.
Pauṇḍra, however, disregarding the hero of the Śini clan, proceeded toward Janārdana even though he was being restrained.
Keśava rendered him chariotless and weaponless in an instant, and he departed for his own city.
He then dispatched a messenger again to Kṛṣṇa, saying: "I alone am Vāsudeva.
Casting off my emblems immediately, you should come to me, the Infinite, for refuge. (22.198)
Having heard these words spoken by his messenger, the heroes of the Yadu clan laughed aloud. Laughing, Kṛṣṇa said, "I shall give you weapons that serve as my own emblems in battle.
Thus addressed, the messenger went and told him; and Hari, desiring to fight, approached him.

Seeing him seated upon a golden Garuḍa chariot, wielding artificial discuses and other weapons, and his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, Kṛṣṇa laughed at Pāpabuddhi. Then Vāsudeva, having conquered him who was raining down missiles and weapons as if with a mere blade of grass, [subdued him].
He cut off his neck, and immediately thereafter, with an arrow, he severed the head of his maternal grandfather;
that Lord of Vārāṇasī quickly felled it by means of that [arrow].
And he, through the realization that "I am Brahman, I am eternally Vāsudeva," attained that state beyond the blinding darkness.
Just as Kamsa the king, as well as Kirmira, Hidimba, Salva,
and other Daityas who had aided him, fell into the blinding darkness, even so did that evil-minded one fall.
Having slain those two, Kesava immediately begot a son upon the princess of Vidarbha through the son of Rukmini.
And that Ekalavya, having been defeated by Rāma, performed austerities for the sake of Śiva and attained invincibility from him.
Arrogant due to the boon granted by Śarva, he approached Kṛṣṇa once more to fight.
Having warded off his missiles and weapons, Keśava struck off his head with the discus.

And that most wicked one indeed became terrible and eternally miserable due to his hatred for Kṛṣṇa. (22.206) When Pauṇḍra had been thus slain by the bull among the Yadus, as well as the sinful King Kāṃsī, the son of the lord of Kāṃsī, named Sudakṣiṇa, performed penance with intense devotion to Śaṅkara. (22.207)
The evil-minded and wicked-hearted Pāpabuddhi begged Śiva—who was present before his very eyes and whose nature is darkness—for a *kṛtyā*.

Out of possession by a demon, Śiva himself, though his own self was veiled, bestowed it upon him in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. That *dakṣiṇāgni*, possessed by the influence of an asura, was then worshipped by the son of King Kāṃsi.
Kṛṣṇa, whose power had increased through the boon of Umā’s lord, went to where his own power was fully perfected.
To counter that [fire], Kṛṣṇa, who possesses infinite valor, commanded his fierce discus;
blazing with unerring power, it drove this fire far away.
This fire, whose nature is to perform its task, was the son of the primary fire; then, driven by the discus, it quickly reduced Sudakṣiṇa to ashes along with his followers, his sons, and his wife.
Having burnt the city of Vāraṇasī, Sudarśana returned once more to the side of Vāsudeva.
That most wicked Sudakṣiṇa, out of hatred for Kṛṣṇa, went to him accompanied by his followers.

(22.212) While sporting in Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa—who is ever full of bliss—once said to the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, imitating the very behavior of householders, even though he was eternally free from conflict with her who was herself faultless. (22.213)

"O blessed lady, you must not do anything for me; I have brought you here solely for the purpose of breaking the pride of my enemies. And she, knowing herself to be forever inseparable from Kṛṣṇa, remained there like one in sorrow, making known the duty that "a woman must fear her husband."
Even the God of gods consoled her, explaining the duties of a householder so that she would no longer suffer.
(22.215) While the lotus-navelled Lord was thus sporting with Ramā, the son of Rohiṇī, commanded by Kṛṣṇa, set out for Gokula;
there he saw Nanda and Yaśodā, was honored by them, and asked for news of Kṛṣṇa. (22.216)

He dwelt there for two months and sported with the cowherd girls, intoxicated by wine; and calling out to the Yamunā, Rāma, of foremost valor, thinking "she has become drunk," dragged with his plow the river who had not come.
Then, having been bowed to and praised by her, he released her and [sent] Nandagopa back.
Having taken his leave, he departed for Dvārakā and reported to Keśava the devotion of Nanda Gopa and the others.

(22.218) At that very time, Mainda and Vivida—two companions who were possessed by Dānavas—having slain Bhauma, marched against the kingdom of Ānarta with hostility toward Vāsudeva; then Vāsudeva spoke. (22.219)
The lotus-navelled Lord granted him this boon: "These two shall be slayable by you, yet they themselves shall be unslayable;
furthermore, because of the boon of Viriñca and from the drinking of the nectar, both Mainda and Vivida are invincible.
Having gone there, he first slew Mainda—who had come to the peak of Mount Raivata for battle—in his wrath. (22.220)
On the following day, the one of preeminent deeds struck Vivida, who was raining down stones, with his mace;
those two Asuras who had possessed him entered the blinding darkness, while the Aśvins returned to their own world.
Duryodhana’s daughter, who had previously been named Lakṣaṇā and was lovely in form, became Rati.
While she was standing at her *svayaṃvara*, Samba seized her by force; she, in turn, became enamored of him.
(22.222) Seeing her taken by force, Duryodhana and the other leaders, headed by Karṇa, fought in a blaze of anger.
Having with great difficulty deprived that lone warrior of his chariot, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together captured him.
Upon hearing that Duryodhana had, by the sheer strength of his arms, [slain] both Karṇa and Bhūriśravas,
all the Vṛṣṇis prepared for war against the Kauravas.
Balabhadra, having restrained them, went himself with Uddhava to the Kauravas seeking peace.
Staying in a grove outside the city, he dispatched Uddhava on behalf of the Kauravas;
all the Kurus came and paid him honor, and he delivered the command of Ugrasena:
"The king commands you that which our young prince was seized by you."
"Though he was alone against many gathered together for the sake of their kinsmen, he endured it; therefore, do not release him, just as Aśvina released Sāmba.
Having heard these words spoken by Ugrasena, "I command you," the heroes of the Kurus, after hearing those wicked words, entered their own city and army out of anger; thereupon Rāma became enraged.
Dragging that city with his plow and casting it into the waters of the Ganges, he was restrained by all the Kauravas who bowed down before him; then,
along with his wife and son, he was honored by Suyodhana.
Having obtained his full equipment, he departed for his own city.
(22.229) Such were the great deeds of Rāma, who was entirely absorbed in Acyuta;
indeed, even Bhīma would not rise against him in battle once he recognized the specific moment of Acyuta’s descent into him. (22.230)
During their many playful battles, Bhīmasena recognized the manifestation of Viṣṇu within the son of Rohiṇī;

thus, even while playing with him at that time, he made no effort against him out of devotion to Viṣṇu. At such times, this Rāma was victorious, because Janārdana was not yet fully manifest there. (22.231)

"Then Bhīma would always be victorious, for that Rāma possesses the hair and the power of Viṣṇu. (22.232) While Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-navelled one, was dwelling in Dvārakā joined with such a Rāma, Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, once took pleasure in Aniruddha in a dream and spoke to Citralekhā: (22.233)
"Bring him here," she said; then, pointing out the worlds in a variegated cloth, she showed them to him.
Recognizing her grandson through her words, Kṛṣṇa had him brought there that night—Aniruddha, noble in his virtues, who had been brought by Citralekhā. 22.234.

Having obtained him, the daughter of Bāṇa took her pleasure for many days. But when the guardians of the maidens discovered that he was hidden within the maiden’s quarters, they informed Bāṇa, and he commanded his servants to seize him.

When they arrived, the exceedingly powerful Aniruddha struck them down with his iron club and put them to flight; then the asura himself came forward. Having fought with great difficulty, he bound him with the Naga-missile. (22.237)
Then Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Rāma and Pradyumna, mounted Garuḍa and arrived there first;
having fought with the son of Aṅgiras (Bṛhaspati), Hari dispersed those fires in an instant.

Having routed all the Pramathas, he then approached Jvara. With that blow of ashes, Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, embraced the son of Rohiṇī who was afflicted by fever and rendered him free from fever.
Then Janārdana, the infallible Lord, having sported with him for some time himself,
and having crushed another with his fists, unleashed a fever.
Although the Lord had personally conquered the servant of Giriśa, he considered it not enough.
Thinking that he must be conquered by his own servant alone, [Viṣṇu] then created another;
at that time, he was severely afflicted by the fever of Viṣṇu and,
having been brought before him as food, he went for refuge to Hari.
Praised by him, the Lord, the all-pervading Master, liberated him. (22.243) "For the sake of sport, even among very few people, the Lord somehow manifested [this] without suffering.
Thus and so forth, the Unborn One displays this for the purpose of deluding [the ignorant]; for how could there be suffering and the like for the eternally independent? (22.244)
When all [the afflictions] such as fever had fled, then Giriśa himself approached Hari.
Then a battle took place between the two, and Acyuta caused him to yawn by means of the yawning-weapon (*jṛmbhaṇāstra*).
When Śaṅkara was thus made to yawn and stood motionless like a pillar, the lotus-born [Brahmā]—*22.245*—intervened.
Due to the possession by a Daitya, [Vāsudeva] was unaware of Vāsudeva; the Lord (Viṣṇu) awakened him with well-spoken words.

Having taken hold of Śarva, he entered the belly of Viṣṇu and showed him there the form of Śiva that had been paralyzed in the forest named Bilva while the Lord of the Mountains (Śiva) was performing penance. 22.246–247.
In order to attain the state of Śiva, the Lotus-born (Brahmā) spoke to Acyuta (Viṣṇu) regarding that [state] of Śaṅkara;
then, his delusion dispelled, the Bull-bannered One (Śiva) praised Hari, while Bāṇa rushed toward Keśava.
Acyuta cut off his thousand arms, yet the enemy seized it again for the sake of that head. 22.248.
Then, having been saluted by Śiva with the desire to protect Bāṇa, he made his devotee Bāṇa two-armed and protected him;
and having liberated Aniruddha, he departed, honored by Bāṇa. 22.249.
Thus, having effortlessly conquered Agni, Aṅgiras, Jvara, Skanda, Umāpati, and Bāṇa, he returned once more to Dvāravatī—
he by whom Hara, the destroyer of all worlds, was conquered without effort. (22.250)
Is it said that Viṣṇu, that Ananta, has conquered fever and other ailments?
(22.251) Even for Śivas and Brahmas of such infinite number, as well as for Ramā herself, there is no power to move without his glance. (22.252)
There are no such entities as knowledge and the like, nor even existence anywhere;
yet the victory of the trident-bearing Kṛṣṇa, who possesses infinite power, is not a marvel.
[He is] accompanied by Citralekhā, Uṣā, and his grandson.

Accompanied by his son and the monkeys, Kṛṣṇa ascended Mount Vṛndāvana and went to Dvārakā; there, the eternally blissful one sported for a long time according to his own will. (22.254) Such are the countless deeds of the best of the Yadus, whose greatness is immeasurable and who is a source of great festivity.
These [names] are eternally praised by Ramā, Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, Sūrya, and others, and they bestow liberation. Thus, while Nārāyaṇa— who is the essence of immeasurable prowess and heroism—
dwells in his own city, Lomaśa Muni, having been addressed by Indra and Dhanañjaya, became a companion to the sons of Pāṇḍu so that they might visit all the sacred fords (tīrthas).

Having circumambulated the earth and performed ablutions at all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in their proper order, the sons of Pṛthā worshipped Hari with great devotion at each and every one of them; then they reached Prabhāsa in order to offer [their worship] unto Kṛṣṇa.
Accompanied by all the Yadus, Hari, together with Rāma, arrived there to receive them. (22.257)
There, Kṛṣṇa, together with the hosts of Yadus, was honored by the sons of Pṛthā;
and by the command of Hari, the Vṛṣṇis in turn honored the sons of Pṛthā.
There, seeing Bhīma dressed in the garb of an ascetic, [they were moved] by the cause of their great affection.
Satyaki spoke thus to Rāma while censuring Duryodhana:
"Today, having slain all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with Karṇa,
we shall establish Abhimanyu upon the throne for as long as thirteen years."
"Having completed the year, the Pāṇḍavas shall indeed go to their city;
then let King Yudhiṣṭhira rule the kingdom as before.
Even as the hero of the Śinis was speaking thus, Janārdana looked toward the faces of the sons of Pṛthā.

Śaineya said, "The sons of Pāṇḍu do not desire the kingdom by means of another; having slain their enemies with the strength of their own arms, they shall obtain the kingdom. When this was said by him, the sons of Pṛthā replied, "So be it," and those Daśārhas set out, placing Kṛṣṇa at their head.
In due course, the sons of Pṛthā also reached the snowy mountain; there, seeing Kṛṣṇā stuck in that difficult terrain, they remembered the son of Hiḍimbā, who arrived accompanied by night-stalkers.
He carried Kṛṣṇā, while his servants carried the sons of Pṛthā, and they reached the hermitage of Badarī.
Having reached this place and performed their own rites through the worship of Nārāyaṇa, they departed for the northern direction.

(22.265) Having passed beyond the mountain Śarvaśvaśura, the mountain Suvarṇakūṭa, and the Niṣadha mountain, they reached on the eastern side of Meru, upon Mount Gandhamādana, the supreme hermitage of Badarī on earth. (22.266)

There, being honored by the lords of sages and always worshipping Nārāyaṇa, they performed austerities joined with knowledge and meditative absorption, expounding the science of the true nature of reality. While they were thus dwelling in Badarī, on one occasion in a secluded place, [the conversation turned] toward Kṛṣṇa and the son of the Wind.
While [the mountain] stood still, Garuḍa, the foremost of the serpents that serve as the seat of Vāsudeva, seized the serpent from the great lake.
By the wind from his wings, that mountain was shaken, and a supreme golden lotus—
possessing the luster of the rising sun’s orb and fragrant— fell into the presence of Kṛṣṇa and Bhīma.

Seeing that lotus of excellent gold with its exquisite fragrance, Draupadī, out of curiosity, requested many more such flowers from Bhīmasena; for she knew his power to be insurmountable even by gods and demons.
(22.270) Thus entreated by her, the son of Vāyu, though holding his mace, ascended that lofty mountain with speed.
Praised by the hosts of gods and *siddhas*, and slaying the Daityas who had taken the forms of lions and tigers,
he assumed there his own form known as Hanumān, which shone like the rising sun; yet Bhīma, though knowing him to be his own self, played with him as if with another.
Dharma is supreme among the gods; in human form, their conduct is just like that of others.
Due to the excellence of their divine power, they never engage in the taking of food, yet they always abide in the nature of *nara*.
Therefore, Bhīma and Hanumān, though being one and the same, have here assumed the conduct of the younger and the elder respectively. 22.273.
All qualities are veiled in the human state according to the age (yuga) and according to the fundamental form;
sequentially, through the portions of the gods, they attain manifestation from their unmanifest forms for those of great stature.
There is no such thing as non-manifestation here for Viṣṇu, whose power is exceedingly manifest even during his incarnations.
The manifestation of desire generally belongs to the wind; for other [elements], it is manifest due to a specific cause.
Therefore, Bhīma, for the sake of increasing righteousness alone, displayed a conduct like that of others even in his own form;
likewise, he appeared as one whose power was unattached, solely for the purpose of deluding the Asuras.

Then Bhīmasena, having seen that increase of his [Rāma's] form and having heard from the mouth of Hanumān the stories of Rāma’s fourfold nature, his divine character, and even the foremost Dharma of the four ages;
and having heard of the roar from the banner of Bībhatsu (Arjuna) which signified the defeat of the enemy granted by him (Rāma). 22.277.
Having bowed to him, Bhīma departed on his own feet toward the Saugandhika forest of unsurpassed beauty.
Reaching that place inaccessible to men, he saw there lotuses of wondrous form—
golden, divine, and exceedingly fragrant— and approached them despite being forbidden by the guards.

Those hundred thousand invincible Krodhavaśas, having gathered together, warded off Bhīma—who was fierce in appearance, possessed of great strength, had taken up his weapons, and had assumed a new form—in that battle.
By the very boon of Śiva, they were unconquerable by others; they unleashed a most terrifying rain of missiles and weapons.
While they were proclaiming the Śaiva scriptures before Bhīma— the knower of all things, the treasury of ascetic powers, and an ocean of strength—
that Bhīma first defeated them in the battle of words by means of Vaiṣṇava scriptures alone;
then, repelling their rain of scriptural weapons, he slew all those heroes with his mace.
Born of Kuntī by the Wind-god, he was powerful, heroic, ascetic, and a slayer of his enemies;
ever devoted to truth and righteousness, he was invincible to his foes in prowess.
Therein [he taught] many other things as well, such as untruth, the absence of a Lord, and that the world has no foundation.
Proclaiming the virtues of Viṣṇu by saying, "I am perfected, I am the Lord," he was invincible in debate;
speaking of Viṣṇu as distinct and superior to all, he slew a hundred thousand of those great heroes.
They, having seen his heroism and strength, as well as the power of his knowledge and the strength of his arms—
Unable to withstand him, all together and with their foremost heroes slain, they suddenly retreated.

Having displayed his prowess, that hero of the Kurus struck them with his mace, defeated and routed them all, and entered the Nalinī lake. There, having drunk the water of immortality, the Kuru hero gathered the divine lotuses.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing ill omens on the battlefield, asked Draupadī with a dejected mind, "Where is Bhīma?
Having heard from the mouth of Kṛṣṇā that he had gone for the sake of the *saugandhika* lotuses, the king [inquired further].
Having mounted upon the foremost of the Rākṣasas, Vṛkodara went with Kṛṣṇā and his brothers;
and having seen him standing there,
he spoke to him, saying "Do not do this," being afraid of Giriśa’s wrath.

Fearing death at the hands of the gods, those Rākṣasas protect Nalini by the command of Kubera; for Hara is her refuge. Knowing the greatness of Bhīma, the Lord of Wealth did not become angry. (22.290)
While the Pārthas were dwelling there, after some more days had passed,
Kṛṣṇā, having seen flowers of five colors that had been brought [there], spoke for the sake of increasing Bhīmasena’s fame, dharma, and other virtues. (22.291)
"By the power of Māruta, this mountain—unapproachable for men and protected by Kubera—is inaccessible to all;
yet today you alone must go there, having dispelled all the Rākṣasas. (22.292–293)
Thus addressed, Bhima—whose vast strength was unconquered—entered the king of mountains with tears in his eyes, bearing his mace, bow, and arrows.

Perceiving that the son of the god of strength had arrived there, he blocked the path of the fiercely raging Rākṣasas by placing before him the invincible and formidable Maṇimān, who, by the boon of Śambhu, rained down a great shower of various weapons. (22.294)

Bhīma instantly struck all those hosts of Rākṣasas, together with Maṇimat, with showers of excellent arrows. Having slain in a mere moment those who were otherwise unslayable, the mighty Bhīma stood upon the mountain peak in battle, having overcome all the Krodhavaśas.
CCCXXI. All those slain by Bhīmasena entered into blinding darkness;

and Maṇimān, who had been killed in the Saugandhika grove, was born again in the Kali age with a false intellect, having thoroughly spread out [his delusion], and entered even greater darkness. (22.297)
Then, when the three great lotuses had been destroyed, King Vaiśravaṇa— along with his friend Maṇimatī, who was herself invulnerable to the Rākṣasas—
ascended a divine chariot, desiring to fight Vṛkodara. (22.298)
Due to the possession by an asura, a great and terrible rage arose within him;
the Lord of Wealth himself came to fight with Bhīma.
At that time, hearing the roar of Bhīmasena, the king quickly questioned Kṛṣṇā.
Having heard her cry out, "Where is Bhīma?", the Rākṣasa quickly departed with his chariot.

(22.300) When the King had gone to where Bhīma was, accompanied by his brothers, the sage Kṛṣṇā, and the others, Kubera saw Dharmaja; freed somewhat from the possession of the Asura, he became filled with affection for him. (22.301)
Even upon seeing Bhīma with his weapons raised, he did not consider him to be much of a threat due to the influence of the Daitya;
moreover, the King of Kings explained that the curse of Agastya was the reason for his former friendship [with Bhīma].
(22.302) Having cast off his peaceful disposition through the possession of the Daitya, he, being well-pleased, restored his own place to them.
The sons of Pṛthā, as well as those others, dwelt there for the sake of residence in the houses of various deities.
While those high-souled ones were living there, after four years had passed,
Indra was requested by Phalguna for the sake of his preceptor’s fee, having taught him five great weapons during that fifth year.
Indra chose the slaughter of his enemies from Pārtha in their own forms—
those known as the Nivātakavacas, to whom Brahmā had granted the boon of being unslayable by gods, daityas, gandharvas, birds, or rākṣasas. (22.305)
When requested again by Indra, [Śiva] said, "Kill these who possess human bodies.
Thus Śakra spoke to Arjuna, identifying himself as one dwelling in a human body, saying, "Kill them indeed," and having bound his own diadem. (22.306)
Having mounted Indra’s chariot accompanied by Mātali, and taking up the bow Gāṇḍīva, Pārtha went forth to slay the great asuras.
The gods gave him a conch; that king of conchs was Devadatta.
Making the air resound with the blast of his conch and twanging his great bow,
wearing the two radiant divine earrings given by Śakra,
the son of Indra approached the celestial city of the Daityas.
Hearing the blast of his conch and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
the immensely powerful Asuras known as the Nivātakavacas rushed forward—
three crores of Dānavas who were proud of their own self-born prowess.

Well-prepared for battle, they rained down various weapons upon Pārtha. But the hero adorned with a diadem, having warded off their missiles with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow— arrows endowed with the power of great mastery in weaponry— cut off their heads.
All those Dānavas were slain by that great chariot-warrior, and he likewise advanced against others—
the sixty thousand great chariot-warriors known as the hosts of Paulomas and Kāleyas—
who were raining down missiles and weapons; Dhananjaya suddenly struck them with the dust-cloud weapon (*pāṃsupātāstra*).
Having burned [the city], he went once again to the abode of Indra; and Śakra, filled with affection, embraced him. Even the darkness of the blind and all the Asuras, enemies of the gods, fled.
Then, having taken leave of his father, [he departed] on the radiant chariot of Indra.
The son of the wielder of the thunderbolt went to the presence of his brothers.
(22.315) Seeing Bībhatsu approaching, the brothers rejoiced exceedingly; they lived there on Mount Meru for four years, full of joy. (22.316)

Time passed in perfect happiness for those whose souls were devoted to Viṣṇu, through stories of Vāsudeva, through meditation, and through worship; yet they did not feel satisfied until they had utterly destroyed their enemies and acquired great fame. (22.317)

Without following the command of Vāsudeva, one cannot become the foremost leader among kings. (22.318) But for the other castes, forbearance toward external enemies is generally declared to be the duty of all, in accordance with the command of Hari. (22.319)
Having heard these words of Bhīma, Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers and Kṛṣṇā, mounted the shoulder of the Rākṣasa and returned once more.
(22.320) While they were dwelling at the southern slopes of the Himālaya mountains, the son of the Wind-god once upon a time—

While pursuing deer, the archer suddenly encountered Nahusha, the son of Āyu, who had assumed the massive form of a serpent. For previously, having reflected upon the fact that Shachi’s lover was as thin as the fiber of a lotus stalk due to the slaughter of Vṛtra, the gods made the son of Āyu the lord of the three worlds, granting him a boon and all the power of his asceticism so long as it remained within the range of his vision.
Having obtained the inexhaustible power of all the gods and the foremost of the brahmin-sages through his asceticism,
he grew ever more arrogant and even desired Śacī.
At Indra’s command, [he was placed] upon the vehicle of the great rishis for Śacī’s sake.
Appointed solely for the purpose of deception, he drove those sages [away].
When questioned by the high-souled Agastya regarding the authority of the Vedas— specifically for the sake of obstructing Śacī— that fool-minded man replied, "No."
When he was told, "You are my authority," he struck him on the head with his foot.

At that time, Bhrigu had been hidden within his matted locks, never having come within the range of his vision; entering [the body] of the lotus-born Brahmā, he cursed him: "Go quickly and become a sinful python! (22.325–326).
Whoever has been seized by you at the sixth watch shall come under your power, even if he is superior in strength.
If, when you have seized a man, you are unable to kill him, and if he—though capable—does not free himself while held by you, then his foremost power shall be your ascetic merit. (22.327)

Whatever austerity has been undertaken by all the gods and sages, all of that returns to you alone; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (22.328) When someone shall answer your questions, [you will know him].
"Then, having cast off this body of a python, you shall go to heaven;
and by my grace, you will always possess the power of recollection.
Thus was he cursed by the lotus-born Brahmā while he was still within the body of Bhṛgu.
In an instant, Nahuṣa fell, having become a serpent;
Indra, too, being cleansed of sin, regained his own station after worshipping Viṣṇu.
This sin of the Lord of Śacī occurred solely for the sake of increasing righteousness.
Indeed, there is no sin in the destruction of worlds for the wielder of the thunderbolt, the Lord of the three worlds;
and as for that Vedic passage beginning with "Having slain Vṛtra, he became great-nosed," it is clear that in some cases even sin leads to the increase of merits.
Just as the slaying of Vṛtra occurred for Indra for the sake of increasing Dharma—
whether among the gods or the sages— it is not so for ordinary men;
that which is sin for them is indeed merit for the Asuras, because their nature is contrary.
Thus, indeed, there is a statement in the Skanda Purāṇa: "There is no sin for that lord of Śacī;
they shall not attain the station of another. That is the supreme vow of the gods.
Therefore, those lords placed Nahuṣa in the position of Śakra. (22.334–335)
When he had thus fallen due to the cause of Brahmā’s curse,
Bhīma reached that terrible twenty-eighth *yuga*,
even while knowing it, out of a desire to acquire his ascetic power.

That ascetic power which resides in all the gods and sages, Māruti desired to seize it as if by his mere will, like one who has gained control over a cow. For the strength of gods who have taken human form is clearly seen to be slight.
It becomes manifest through will, but that is not the case for air and other elements. The conclusion of the scripture is that the qualities of Viṣṇu are eternally manifest.
Likewise, indeed, his other qualities [become manifest] during births such as those of human beings.
22.340. Even though it is possible for gods to appear among humans and other beings, because they remain unmanifest in form, their merit increases; Keśava becomes pleased with them.
Thus, his human strength remains restrained by his own boon.
Though capable, the son of the Wind-god did not manifest his divine power;
nor did that conqueror offer answers for the sake of his own liberation,
because even for Brahmins, living by means of specialized knowledge is not considered their true duty.

Although Vṛkodara knew that this was especially true for a Kṣatriya, he did not seek his own liberation by avoiding that question; for even though he made no effort, he could not move it even slightly. 22.343.
At that time, Nahuṣa, though possessed of strength equal to all the worlds, stood encircling that formidable being; yet he was not able to kill him.
Out of affection for his brother, mother, and others, [the being] quickly sought his own liberation.
Although he desired it, Vṛkodara made no effort toward liberation;
he came here to take upon himself the ascetic power of all the gods and the lords of sages.
Even though he thought, "I must not remain here due to the influence of affection for my brothers and others," [he stayed]. 22.345.

Thinking, "In time this snake will fall away by itself," and considering the firmness of my body through the command of Vāsudeva, he reflected: "When the snake has fallen with its limbs slackened, I shall go. (22.346)
Bhīma remained there meditating on Hari, not by his own will but according to his nature;
at that very moment, by the previously mentioned word of Brahmā and the command of Keśava,
the strength and ascetic power of everyone resided within Vṛkodara.
When Bhīma had been filled with the ascetic power and strength residing in Nahuṣa,
that Nahuṣa then gradually became slackened in his coils.
When Bhīma had departed, King Yudhiṣṭhira, having observed certain omens, [reflected].
With a restless mind, he asked Kṛṣṇā, "Where has Bhīma gone? (22.350).

Having heard her reply that he had gone for the sake of deer, and seeing the lords of mountains fallen by the force of her thighs along that path, he went there; and seeing it covered with snakes, he questioned her. (22.351)
He heard from Nahuṣa the entire reason for that and the answer to his question in its entirety;
out of brotherly affection, the son of Dharma explained it at that very moment, and he too ascended to the heavenly world.
When his two ancestors, adorned with celestial garments and earrings, had departed in a celestial chariot, that King of Dharma—
Then Bhīma arrived, and Yudhiṣṭhira related everything there to his own people.
Having heard it, Kṛṣṇā, all his brothers, and all the lords of sages—who were exceedingly devoted to Bhīmasena—were overcome with shame at Bhīmasena’s boldness;
thus they spoke to Bhīmasena out of affection. (22.353–354)

"Such a rash act was not worthy of you, that even though you were capable of liberating yourself, you did not exert effort for that purpose; instead, you have cast great suffering into the hearts of your own kin.
Saying, "Do not do this again," they all approached Bhīma and embraced him.
Then, after some days, the sons of Pṛthā, accompanied by the foremost of sages, reached the kingdom of the Kurus.
Thereupon the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa of immeasurable splendor arrived, accompanied by Satyabhāmā.
Honored by those Pāṇḍavas, he then engaged in friendly conversations for the sake of mutual affection.
Kṛṣṇā and Satyā, the foremost of women, conversed with one another with joy.
Urged by Satyā—who was all-knowing, faultless, and intent on testing her—Kṛṣṇā spoke there concerning all the duties of women to Satyā, who was recognized as being without blemish. (22.358)

Although she already knew the truth, Kṛṣṇā spoke only for the sake of instructing the world; 22.359 / knowing that the words uttered by Satyabhāmā were spoken merely in jest, she replied with corresponding words solely out of affection for her. 22.360 /
Then, after staying there for several days, Janārdana, having taken leave of the Pāṇḍavas, departed for his own city together with his wife.
Then, on one occasion, while the sons of Pṛthā had gone out hunting, King Saindhava fell upon them.
Accompanied by Sakoṭika and Bala, he saw Kṛṣṇā there in their excellent hermitage.
While proceeding for the sake of the marriage, having heard of Kṛṣṇā, he sent Kaṇva away and said, "Come to me! Being utterly wicked, he was repulsed by her and seized her by the hand. (22.362–363)
Struck by her, he fell quickly to the ground; then, ashamed, he rose up again and rushed forward.

Then, because she was without a companion, Kṛṣṇā said to Dhaumya, "Follow me with the fire," and having urged him, saying, "Go quickly so that you do not suffer," she mounted the chariot of the King of Sindhu. (22.364)
Then, observing the omens, the sons of Pṛthā hastened toward the hermitage;
having heard everything from the words of the maidservant, they quickly set out in pursuit of the ruler of the Sindhus.
Seeing Dhaumya crying out "Bhīmasena! and the exceedingly wicked ruler of the Sindhus before him, [they rushed forward]. 22.365.

The sons of Pāṇḍu let out lion-like roars upon seeing Kṛṣṇā; she then descended from the chariot and went toward the hermitage together with Dhaumya, while the Pārthas struck down the army there with their might. [22.366] First, they slew the most wicked Koṭikaṇṣya, who had said to the King of Sindhu, "Go! regarding Kṛṣṇā.
Having severed his head, Bhīmasena presented it to Death, and he arrived.

(22.367) Having slain the entire army of the ruler of the Sindhus, Bhīma and Arjuna, after releasing Dharmarāja—who was proceeding with self-restraint—followed after Jayadratha as he fled on foot, now deprived of his chariot; Phalguna struck him down. (22.368)
Bhīmasena seized him as he was running on foot, struck him violently until he was distressed, and taking him up, the son of Dharma placed him at the feet of Draupadī and released him;
when he himself had uttered the words, "I am the slave of Draupadī," Bhīmasena also let him go. 22.369.
Ashamed, he departed for the forest with his face cast down; meanwhile, the sons of Pṛthā remained there, exceedingly joyful.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya arrived and told them many wonderful tales, composed in three different languages.
Relying on worldly convention, gods and sages may speak certain stories;
in those cases, the instruction is to be grasped, but never the literal meaning.
In the discourses spoken from meditative concentration, however, the entire meaning should be grasped without any doubt.
In the languages of other philosophical systems, that system should be understood accordingly;
however, the [literal] meaning is not to be accepted, but rather the Vedic system alone is to be accepted.
In the secret languages (*guhyabhāṣā*), the other meaning is indeed to be accepted—such is the definitive conclusion.
Jayadratha, however, having been made to wear five topknots by Bhīma, propitiated Śiva through ascetic penance and chose as his boon the capture of the Pāṇḍavas, with the exception of Arjuna;
for Śiva was pleased by the penance of Arjuna. (22.375)

While the Pāṇḍavas were still dwelling in the forest, King Duryodhana, out of rivalry with the Rājasūya sacrifice, performed the sacrifice known as the Pauṇḍarīka; yet he was not even a fraction worthy of it. By the command of Duryodhana, Duḥśāsana sent messengers there to the Pāṇḍavas.
"Come! Bhīma said to him thus, intending to humiliate him at his own sacrifice of battle.

(22.377) Then, after some days, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with Karṇa and the king of Gāndhāra, acting out of evil counsel, brought the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī, together with their wife, into the assembly hall to show them great opulence for the sake of humiliating them. (22.378)
Adorned with various garlands and garments, they set out swiftly for the Dvaitavana forest on chariots variegated with gold and jewels, as well as upon great elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers.
Knowing that they had departed under the pretext of visiting the cows, Indra, desiring to shatter their splendor, [prepared his stratagem].
Having granted him that supreme power, he commanded Citrasena to bind him.
Surrounded by sixty thousand crores of the chief Gandharvas, he went to that lake at the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, who desired to bathe there; then, at his order, the men spoke to them.

"The lord of kings, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, will come here to bathe; therefore, depart from this sacred ford while still obeying his command. When they were thus addressed, the Gandharvas laughed aloud at them and said: "We honor that command which belongs to Śakra-deva, the lord of the three worlds."
"Not even for human *cakravartins*, much less for Suyodhana, who is weak in essence.
When this was said, the enraged son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra struck down the foremost Gandharvas with showers of arrows.
Even Karṇa and his brothers struck them, and they in turn struck the army of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
For a moment, the battle between them and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was equal;
then, by virtue of his boons and through illusion, the Gandharva heroes gained the upper hand.
This was so that they might effect a break in Suyodhana’s splendor for the sake of the sons of Pṛthā.
The Lotus-born and Keśava bestowed strength [upon them], and those Gandharvas went over to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
That Citrasena first fought with Karṇa alone, vying with Pārtha;
yet, while fighting him, Karṇa was unable [to overcome him] because of the word of Bhārgava Rāma, who is eternally immeasurable and possesses the six qualities.
His own chariot having been shattered, he mounted Vikarṇa’s chariot and, having restrained its horses, fled swiftly with him; meanwhile, Duryodhana fought Citrasena.
Having fought with him for a moment, he then engaged in combat through illusion with many other Gandharvas.

When his chariot was shattered, he stood upon the surface of the earth and was seized by Citrasena in the conflict. Although the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had grown through the boon of Śakra and the command of Viṣṇu,
he was then held by Citrasena and bound with lightning-like cords bestowed by Indra.
Her younger brothers, the wives of the king, and all [the attendants] were bound and led away by the servants of Śakra.
When they had departed taking those garments, the ministers of this [king] spoke to the Pāṇḍavas:
"Having approached the sons of Pṛthā, they said, 'Your family has been humiliated by the servants of Śakra. (22.391)
"O foremost of the Bharatas, rescue that brother of yours, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who has been seized along with his wife and younger brothers.
Having been addressed thus, Bhīmasena said to his elder brother: "I know, O King, what kind of conflict this is;
showing off his own power, Duryodhana did not come here wishing for a blow to his pride."
Having understood their counsel, Vajrabāhu said, "In this matter, there shall be no failure in our purpose.
Having spoken thus, the formidable Bhīma ceased, demonstrating his own divine knowledge.
Bhīmasena and Arjuna were dispatched by the king, who was himself consecrated for the sacrifice to be performed on the very next day.
The two Samādreyas, having defeated Citrasena in battle, released Duryodhana from his bonds.
Citrasena then related everything that Vāsava had said regarding the evil counsel of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Upon hearing this concerning Pārtha and Bhīma, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was overcome with great shame.

When the sacrifice was completed, everyone approached the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), who in turn quickly honored and dismissed Citrasena, saying: "O son of Gāndhārī, such a deed must never be done again.
Having been released by the Pāṇḍavas along with his younger brothers and his wife, he departed from there after traveling a short distance.
Seated there among those who had gathered without invitation, he, filled with shame, beheld the son of the Sūta (Karna).
And he said to Suyodhana, "By good fortune you are victorious, O King! But Suyodhana, having been overcome by shame, replied to him, "No," and related exactly what had occurred.
Having spoken thus, Suyodhana, deeply distressed, undertook a fast unto death there.
Even though he was entreated by Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, the gambler Saubala, and others, he did not rise at all.
Then, when night had fallen and his own side was despondent,
Śukra consulted with the asuras and, through the performance of a fire-offering (homakarma), conjured up a magical being (kṛtyā).
While the ministers were fast asleep, that kṛtyā was produced by Śukra.
Taking Dhārtarāṣṭra with them, they went to Pātāla. Then the Daityas addressed King Duryodhana:
"O hero, you are a divine being created by us when we were well-pleased."
"By virtue of his asceticism, he possesses a vajra-body and is forever invincible against the Āsaṅkara weapon.
O Pāṇḍavas, you have been on our side as well as that of the gods;
yet now, by the boon of all the gods, you have been defeated in battle. (22.403)
"We shall act in such a way that you will defeat the Pāṇḍavas. Karṇa, Naraka was indeed slain by Kṛṣṇa;
relying on him, he will undoubtedly bring about the absence of both Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna."
"We shall all enter into Bhīṣma and the others for your victory;
we will strengthen you and Karna and all the rest through our ascetic power.
Therefore, O King, go and protect the kingdom, free from fear. (22.406)
"This must not be told to anyone; it is well-guarded and increases prosperity.
Having spoken thus, the Kṛtyā once again established the king in his own place. Umā fashioned for herself a northern half, created from Hara.
Having realized his own invincibility, Suyodhana set his mind upon the kingdom;
yet he did not speak of what he had experienced to anyone among them.
When the night had turned to dawn, Karṇa spoke these words once more.

"O scorcher of enemies, because you were liberated by your very servants, the Pārthas, you are therefore held in even greater honor in the world; for such are servants indeed. How much more so are you, O tiger among kings? Therefore, arise and be steadfast. (22.410)
"And let that doubt of yours regarding the greatness of Arjuna depart; listen to me:
'I shall not slay Arjuna until I have myself washed his feet.
Thus was he addressed by all his younger brothers as well as by Śakuni.

Having been entreated, he mounted his chariot and went swiftly to Nāgapura. Knowing that the son of the Sun was equipped with earrings and armor and was therefore invincible, Indra desired to take both of those supreme items from him.
Having learned of this, Ravi spoke to Karṇa in a dream and restrained him; when Karṇa replied, "I shall give [my body] in every way," he said, "The excellent weapon must not be given.
And so, having cut off the armor and the two earrings of the Lord of Śacī, he gave them [to Karṇa].
"Taking this infallible spear and recognizing him indeed as one in the form of a brahmin, you shall slay him alone by this improper means—except for Arjuna.
Having thus given the spear along with the armor and earrings, Śakra departed. (22.415–416)
Having left that Suyodhana behind, the sons of Pṛthā lived in the forest always with joy;

then, hearing that the fire-drill and vessel belonging to a twice-born man had been carried off by a deer, they quickly pursued it. (22.417) When the deer was no longer in sight, each of them, being thirsty, went separately in search of water.
Except for Yudhiṣṭhira, they went to sleep by the power of dharma; those drinkers of water were restrained by invisible dharma itself,
so that the best of the wise did not answer his questions for the sake of protecting the duty of a kṣatriya.
Though they were capable, those subduers of enemies refrained from speaking for the sake of water.
"This is not the dharma of Brahmins to subsist upon their learning;
how much less so for Kṣatriyas?"—thinking thus, they drank by force.

For even the gods, though born among men and possessed of great strength, would be endowed with merely human nature, with the exception of Keśava; for their excellent qualities manifest themselves in their tasks only gradually. (22.421)

Therefore, although Bhīma and Arjuna possessed superior strength through righteousness (*dharma*), they were instantly laid to sleep by means of that very righteousness, relying upon the illusion (*māyā*) of the god.
That illusion was capable of obscuring them for only a moment. (22.422)
Therefore, once they have awakened, dharma possesses no power over them at all. This entire matter has been clearly stated in the *Pādmapurāṇa*.
Consequently, it is impossible for attachment to arise between these two, Bhīma and Pārtha.
Then Dharmātmaja went to the edge of the water; seeing his brothers there, he was tormented by grief.

Desiring to drink the water, he was restrained by his father, who had assumed the form of a crane, and so he did not drink. Out of compassion for his brothers, that merciful one desired to answer their questions regarding the matter.
Then Dharma, having assumed the body of a Yakṣa, posed questions, and Pārtha answered them.
Thereupon, being pleased, he offered him a boon; he chose the restoration of one brother from among his brothers.
Then [Dharma] said, "If there is to be only one, let it be Nakula. Then the pleased Dharma asked, "How was this done by you?"
"You have great affection for Bhīmasena, and he is powerful; he might even become the cause of your kingdom.
When addressed thus, the son of Kuntī replied, "I must not raise him up, setting aside the son of Mādrī.
Having been told this, he was exceedingly pleased and raised them all up.

He granted them the attainment of forms at will, and furthermore, by his own desire, he bestowed upon them the recovery of their original forms; during their period of living incognito, he always ensured they remained unrecognized, as if out of affection and compassion. Thus sporting with them like a son, he increased his own fame and merit. (22.429)
For the sake of increasing the fame and merit of Yudhiṣṭhira himself,
Dharma took away the forest and other items, and having personally returned them, went back to heaven once more to give them into the hand of a Brahmin. 22.430.
Then the king, Bhīmasena, and Arjuna, together with the twins, having offered the kindling wood, were filled with joy; along with Kṛṣṇā, they praised the infinite and infallible Kṛṣṇa. 22.431.
Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Acquisition of the Araṇī," [concluding with] the completion of the period of living in the forest (ajñātavāsa).
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.

Oṃ! Having duly spent those twelve years in the forest through the grace of Nārāyaṇa, and having dismissed the Brāhmaṇas and others along with Dhaumya, they then set their minds upon living incognito. 23.1.
Having gone to the city of Virāṭa and laid aside their weapons, they remained in disguised forms:
he became an ascetic, another a cook, one a eunuch, one a charioteer of horses, one a cowherd, and another a perfumer.
23.2. All of them, endowed with auspicious and noble marks, went to Virāṭa and were honored by him like gods.
In their hearts, they performed service for Yudhiṣṭhira alone, and for Vāsudeva, and nothing else.
(23.3) Thinking that the food prepared by others was unfit for a householder, and especially for a Kṣatriya, Vṛkodara assumed the guise of a cook. (23.4)
Because of his renown for superior knowledge in Vedic practices, they would simply recognize him as Bhīma; therefore, he assumed the guise of a Śūdra.
(23.5) [He concealed] all that was his own among the knowers of the Vedas, and how much more so among the lords of the gods?
Therefore, they did not seek refuge with others, relying instead on their own strength.
(23.6) It was solely due to a curse that Arjuna became disguised as a eunuch, and Nakula likewise;
however, this occurred because of his birth from a *sūta* caste, which follows immediately after the *kṣatriya*. (23.7)
Because he was born immediately after a Sūta, he likewise became of the Vaiśya caste;
Sahadeva was thus of the Vaiśya caste, and among them, Gopāla was the most excellent.
Consequently, he attained the status of a cowherd, for as an ascetic, he was worthy of worship by all. (23.8)

Yati was born from Dharmaja; he was constantly devoted to practice, yet later he became addicted to dice in order to demonstrate his own disciplined nature. Sairandhrī, a Śūdra woman, became the wife of Bhīmasena for the sake of dharma and wealth.

Since the duty of women is always to conform to the character of their husbands, Draupadī [spoke thus]. Then there arrived Mallaka, who was undefeated by any boon throughout the entire circle of the earth; that victor of Śiva roared aloud.
Seeing him, all the wrestlers who had taken refuge with King Virāṭa fled, afflicted by fear; then Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"That cook who was among us—having slain that wrestler with his might," 23.12.
"O King, challenge him today so that his fame may increase!
When this was said, the son of the Wind-god, being thus challenged, spoke these words:
"By the grace of Hari, I shall slay this wrestler this very day."
Keśava alone is greater than the entire host of gods;
by devotion to him, one gains strength equal to all the gods.
Indeed, the Śruti has declared that he alone bears the names of all the gods.
"And this great god shall grant me victory—he who is named Yudhiṣṭhira, yet who always abides in Yudhiṣṭhira;
he who is Hari, and who is always addressed as 'You' when you are present. (23.16–17)
Speaking thus, Vṛkodara rushed at that wrestler and sent him,
