who was difficult to conquer even for those endowed with great strength, to the realm of death. (23.18) While the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were dwelling there in this manner...

Having conquered the quarters, Kīcaka—the best among the powerful and the brother-in-law of the King of Matsya—returned after a year less two months. Upon seeing Draupadī, he was afflicted by the god of love; though he made his request, he was rejected by her.

When a month had passed, he entreated his own sister Sudeṣṇā for that very purpose. Although he was repeatedly forbidden by her, when he continued to beg her again and again, she then said to Kṛṣṇā, "Bring wine for my sake as soon as you can. Being thus addressed, she, fearing [the consequences], said, "No. (23.20–23.21)
When she was sent by force by her [mother] to his house and was seized by him by the hand,
she shook him off and ran toward the assembly hall, remembering Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord, who dwells within the sun.
Pursuing her and throwing her down, he then struck her with his foot while standing in the orb of the sun.
Nārāyaṇa dispatched a Rākṣasa named Heti, who arrived there invisibly.
Vāyu entered that Kīcaka and felled him as soon as Bhīma beheld him.
Becoming enraged at the tree [about to be hurled], Yudhiṣṭhira, his elder brother, restrained him as he looked upon it.
At night, Kṛṣṇā approached Bhīma and incited him to slay the wicked Kīcaka. Following Bhīma’s plan, she told Kīcaka that she wished to go to an empty house; he went there.
Having found him there, Bhīmasena defeated him in a wrestling match and struck him down.
The hero crushed him and thrust his head, anus, hands, and feet into his own body.
Seeing that he, who was otherwise unslayable, had been killed, his one hundred and five younger brothers—
rendered invulnerable by a boon from Śaṅkara— bound Kṛṣṇā along with him in order to burn them all together.
As she was being carried away by the Kīcakas, she cried out; hearing that great sound, Bhīmasena uprooted a tree and struck them all with it. Taking Kṛṣṇā with him, he returned again to the city.
Thus, through effort and austerity, they obtained a boon from Śiva: invincibility in battles.
And those one hundred and six who were considered invincible were slain by Bhīmasena in battle.
Having killed them all, thinking they were merely Gandharvas, Bhīma rejoiced, as did Draupadī Kṛṣṇā.
Out of fear, Sudeṣṇā told her, "Go," but she said to her, "Protect me for thirteen days."

Out of fear, Sudeṣṇā said to her, "So be it," and they lived there for a full year. Then, having searched throughout the entire earth for the sons of Pṛthā but failing to find them hidden, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s messengers returned to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and reported that Kīcaka had been killed on account of a woman.
Because of Draupadī, he spoke thus regarding Kīcaka, who had been slain by Bhīma. Then Duryodhana and the others, along with Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and the rest, arrived there.
Suśarman went at the head to fight; he brought together the cattle of Virāṭa. (23.32)

Upon hearing this, Virāṭa followed him with his army, and the Pāṇḍavas also followed, except for Arjuna. Having defeated him in battle, Suśarman seized Virāṭa; then Vṛkodara rescued him and captured King Suśarman after destroying his army.
Yudhiṣṭhira caused him to be released, and they then dwelt outside for that night.
Then, on the following day, all of them, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, went forth,
believing the King of Matsya to be free from the Kīcakas.
Indeed, even Bhīṣma and the others were in no way able to cause harm to Kīcaka, Hiḍimba, Baka, Kirmīra, nor to King Jarāsaṃdha and all the horse-riders. (23.36)

Therefore, having heard that Kīcaka was slain, those followers of the Matsya king went forth to battle. Drona, along with his son, set out in order to make his own promise true— that he would strive to protect the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra from Bhīma.
"If the Pāṇḍavas go out to battle, they will be recognized;
otherwise, we shall humble Virāṭa.
Thinking thus, they seized Virāṭa’s cattle from all sides. (23.39)
Then Uttara, having appointed Pārtha as his charioteer, fled upon merely seeing them;

but Arjuna, having made him his charioteer and steadied him with great difficulty, proceeded toward the Kurus. Then, taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow and the banner marked with Hanumān, he went forward in haste.
Having turned them back from battle, he went toward those Kurus and conquered all of them who were engaged in single combat.

Then, having once again bewildered those who had united and pursued him with the *sammohana* weapon, he seized their upper garments—except for Bhīṣma’s alone—following the injunction of the Vedas regarding the discharge of weapons. (23.41–42)

Having deprived Bhīṣma of his chariot, he then departed. Upon hearing that the Kurus had been defeated, the Lord of Matsya rejoiced, saying, "They were conquered by my son. Yudhiṣṭhira then said, "They were conquered by a eunuch.
Enraged at this, Virāṭa struck him with a die, which was [actually] Bhīma and Dhanañjaya.
Then, hearing that the two were enraged, the Son of Dharma restrained them as well.

"If he does not first prostrate himself and ask for our forgiveness while we remain in our own true forms, he shall deserve death. Thinking thus, they remained in their own forms on the following day. (23.44–45)
Then, seeing King Yudhiṣṭhira seated upon the throne of Virāṭa, Virāṭa asked, "What is this? Uttara told him about those Pāṇḍavas and what had occurred during the cattle-raid.
Thereupon, Virāṭa, his limbs trembling with fear, bowed down and sought refuge with the sons of Pṛthā.
And he gave his daughter Uttarā to Phalguna, and he too accepted her for the sake of a son.
Thus, having liberated Virāṭa and having cast the Kīcakas into blind darkness,
a very great merit was attained by the son of Vāyu and subsequently by Pārtha through the release of the cattle.
Then Keśava dispatched messengers, and Abhimanyu also went together with Rāma.
Vāsudeva, whose consciousness is infinite bliss, arrived; then they married Abhimanyu. (23.49) A great festival took place there among those Pāṇḍavas together with the heroes of the Daśārhas.
May he, having completed his period of living incognito together with Vāsudeva among the Pañcālas, rejoice!

(23.50) Duryodhana and the others, along with the Sūta’s son and the son of Subala, being oppressed by the sons of Pṛthā in battle, approached Hastināpura together with Bhīṣma and the rest, and there they held counsel. (23.51)
"Phalguna has been seen by us today while he was living in concealment; therefore, let the sons of Pṛthā go back to the forest again.
To those speaking thus, Bhīṣma said, "The period of living in concealment has already passed," and Droṇa said the very same thing.
Disregarding the words of those two, the wicked ones said, "Let the sons of Pṛthā go back to the forest once more."
"Thus they dispatched a messenger, thinking that the Brahmins here would know [the truth]," said Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma.
(23.53) "The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra declared the period to be incomplete according to the solar month, yet they said that this entire time was complete according to the lunar month. (23.54)
The Sun is the lord of the days, while the Moon is the lord of the fortnights, months, and years;
therefore, the wise declare that only the lunar year is primary here.
Consequently, they take the lunar time for sacrifice, and not that which is born of the Sun. 23.55.

Without having reflected upon this, and out of greed, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not give the kingdom to the sons of Pṛthā; instead, the sons of Pṛthā, proclaiming the fullness of time, approached Upaplāvya with the best of Brahmins. 23.56.

Accompanied by Suvāsudeva and all the Yādavas, as well as the Pāñcālas and Matsyas, together with their wives, they—having been instructed in their duties by Kṛṣṇa—dwelt for some days at Upaplāvya. 23.57.
Thus ends [the section] composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Incognito Dwelling" (ajñātavāsasamāpti), [ends here].
(440) (Yuddhodyoga).
Then, the twenty-fourth chapter.
Om! Thereupon, having consulted and obtained the consent of Kṛṣṇa, Drupada dispatched his own priest to Dhṛtarāṣṭra for the sake of peace. 24.1.

Having gone there, he spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was accompanied by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others: "No hostility should be provoked by you against the Son of Dharma, whose warriors are Bhīma and Arjuna, and whose leader is Janārdana. (24.2)
You have heard how Jarāsaṃdha and all the others were slain by Bhīma;
and how, by the word of Rudra, the lords of the Rākṣasas became invincible, obstructing the holy fords and remaining there having covered all the sacred bathing places. 24.3.
Three crores of those of great prowess were slain by Bhīma alone—
those brothers, the brahmins, and [the enemies of] the worlds— by him who desired the welfare of the worlds.
Consequently, all sacred fords (tīrthas) on earth became accessible to men.
Just as the wicked Jaṭāsura, relying on the boon of Śarvāṇī, became incapable of being slain while deceiving the Pāṇḍavas in the guise of a brahmin;
even though Bhīmasena recognized him, he did not kill him because of his brahminical form. (24.6)

When Bhīma had gone somewhere for the sake of hunting, Aśvatthāman, deeming himself capable, fled away taking the twins, Yudhiṣṭhira, and Kṛṣṇā with him. He was spotted by Bhīma; leaving them behind, he engaged in combat with him.
Having struck him down to the ground with his foot, he crushed his head and entered the darkness; for were his sons not capable of being slain?
Indeed, you have heard that those Nivātakavacas were also killed by Pārtha.
And you know the prowess of Hari, under whose control this entire universe—
consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, including Brahmā, Rudra, Śakra, and the others—
is held. Therefore, [give] your own wealth to the son of Dharma, who is protected by these [gods].
When he was told by him, "Let it be given," Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not do so.
Then, while Kṛṣṇa had gone to Dvāravatī together with the Yadus,
both the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Dhanañjaya desired his assistance in war.
Then Duryodhana and Arjuna rushed there simultaneously with great speed;
at that moment, Duryodhana sat upon the head of Hari, thinking out of pride, "I am the king of kings, I will not worship at his feet. (24.13)
Having already anticipated their arrival, the Lord Hari lay there as if asleep though he was not; meanwhile, Dhanañjaya remained standing,
bowing low at his feet with palms joined in reverence due to the intensity of his devotion.
The god, though knowing Suyodhana, first looked at Tama;
when Phalguna said, "Welcome," Duryodhana replied, "I have come first," and he honored him with a welcome. (24.16)
Having heard the reason for their arrival, Janārdana said:
"Since one has arrived here first and the other was previously seen by me, I shall make it equal for you both; I will fight with neither weapon in hand."
"Except for ten lakhs of my sons, who are brave foot-soldiers.
When this was said, Phalguna, being devoted to him, chose Kṛṣṇa;
the other, because of his lack of devotion, chose the cowherds who were ready to fight.
Although Keśava intended to provide assistance to the sons of Pṛthā alone, the Lord acted in such a way as to demonstrate his lack of partiality toward them.
Then, accompanied by Arjuna, Keśava went to the Pāṇḍavas.

Duryodhana went to Rāma out of fear of Keśava; though he was well-disposed toward him, Rāma said, "I will not provide assistance," for at Upaplāvya, while speaking in the assembly, he had uttered words siding with that party. 24.21. ccxlii.
Having been repulsed by Sātyaki in the very presence of Keśava,
Duryodhana did not return; accompanied by the son of Hṛdika,
he went to Hastināpura, where ten akṣauhiṇīs remained.
The army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son consisted of one [division] joined by kings from various lands;
and that of the sons of Pāṇḍu consisted of seven [divisions] joined by the Mātsyas, Drupada, the Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, the son of Jarāsaṃdha, and the kings of Kaṃsa.
Purujit, Kuntibhoja, Cekitāna, and Sātyaki—
these partisans of the gods, joined by their armies, encountered the Pāṇḍavas. Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Jayatsena, and other Kekayas [did likewise].
Kṣemadhūrti, Daṇḍadhāra, Kaliṅga, and Ambaṣṭha;
Śrutāyus and Acyutāyus, Bṛhadbala and Sudakṣiṇa; Śrutāyudha, the ruler of the Sindhus, and likewise the Rākṣasa Alambusa. (24.26–24.27)
Alāyudha and Alambala, the Daityas, went to Duryodhana;
having been summoned by Duryodhana, Bhagadatta also went there. Along with his sons and grandsons, Bāhlīka, as well as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa, [went too]. 24.28.

For the sake of pleasing Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his sons and followers became [their allies]. Pāṇḍya, known as Vīrasena, sought refuge with the Pāṇḍavas alone. And Suyodhana, perceiving that Śalya was likewise going over to the Pāṇḍavas, [acted accordingly].
He had assembly halls constructed, provided with every luxury;
considering these to have been planned by Yudhiṣṭhira, Śalya said this:
"I shall do that which is desired by him who caused these to be built. (24.30–31)
Having heard this, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, being despondent, said, "Do what is right.
Seeking glory, he also said, "Give me assistance in battle.
In order to protect his own word, he replied, "So be it. (24.32)

Then, having gone there to the Pāṇḍavas and being permitted by them, he was requested for the sake of Dhananjaya to diminish the splendor of Karṇa; saying "So be it," he went toward the Kauravas to see the son of Dharma. 24.33.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra dispatched Sañjaya for the sake of peace;
he [Sañjaya] explained to the Pāṇḍavas that the war was unrighteous, yet Bhīma and Draupadī spoke of that which they considered righteousness amidst their stubborn resolve. (24.34)
Having spoken thus, the son of Dharma rendered him speechless;
Kṛṣṇa also established the authority of that dharma. Then, rendered speechless, he bowed down to Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍavas.

He went to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and, having reproached him, departed for his own home. (24.36) Having been censured by Sañjaya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra summoned Vidura in the night and questioned him; he spoke of the righteousness that would result in the restoration of the kingdom to the sons of Pṛthā. (24.37)
Even for the sake of worldly happiness, that blameless [dharma] is the cause;
otherwise, there would be no destruction of sin for all sons through the transgression of dharma.
Having failed to cultivate devotion toward it, he merely desires the destruction of evil through knowledge and other means.
He inquired about the true nature of Viṣṇu and remembered the Eternal One.
He arrived and spoke the truth: "O auspicious lady, there is no access to the illusory power of Viṣṇu. Then, in the morning, Sañjaya reported what had been said by the Pāṇḍava.
He spoke thus to Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly hall in the presence of the Kurus.
Having heard that, although the king was terrified, he followed his affection for his son and did not grant the kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas; therefore, O King, the son of Dharma [remained].

When he had said to Sañjaya, "If our father intends to give us the kingdom, then you or Vidura must come; otherwise, neither," and having learned that the two had not arrived, he consulted with Śauri. (24.42)

He also said: "I too shall go into the assembly in the presence of the sages; I will speak words that are beneficial and appropriate, provided he does not accept them. He who destroys all dharma should be put to death by the whole world. (24.43)
When this was said, Bhīmasena spoke these words for the sake of winning over the world, causing the enmity arising from himself to be cast aside in the midst of the people:
"Let there be no sin on our account; we are the family of the Kuru lineage. (24.44)
"Let us become the subordinates of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son in order to protect him.
(24.45) Although he was capable of slaying all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the firm-souled Bhīma spoke thus to Vāsudeva out of a desire to maintain the welfare of the world. (24.46)
In order to make known the very law of their destruction in this world,
Hari strongly urged Bhīma toward battle, as if casting him down;
knowing Keśava’s intention, Bhīma [displayed] his own strength.
In the midst of the kings, Kṛṣṇa spoke even more emphatically;
proclaiming it among the kings with truthful and virtuous words, he extolled the slaughter of the Kurus, the true dharma, and the immeasurable virtues of Bhīma. 24.48–49.

Those two, Keśava and Māruti, were always of one mind; thus, for the sake of the world's report, they made a public agreement. Then Kṛṣṇa [spoke] to Arjuna, who was compassionate and desirous of peace.
Having conciliated him with reasoned and auspicious words, the Lord of the World was addressed by Nakula, who possessed human intelligence and excellent policy:
"May you engage in battle solely for the purpose of displaying your heroism. (24.51)
Thus addressed by Sahadeva and Yuyudhāna, Acyuta said:
"Since the suppression of bandits is the supreme duty of Kṣatriyas,
there can be no peace for us with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra," so spoke the daughter of Pṛṣata.
He spoke to Kṛṣṇa, and he too, having said "Oṃ," departed.

(24.53) Accompanied by Sātyaki and stationed upon his excellent chariot, he was followed from afar by all the sons of Pṛthā and the kings; having halted them with his voice, he went toward the Kurus along with the foremost of the Brahmins. (24.54)

Though Viṣṇu is one, he exists as Bhārgava; that Vyāsa, together with his disciples, was seen by none other than him, for he went there to understand the qualities described by him, since no one else is capable of it except that Lord.
(24.55) Being saluted by all the inhabitants of the kingdom, he was showered with rains of flowers by the gods.
Being praised by Brahmā and the other gods as he bowed down, that supreme and immeasurable one reached the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Accompanied by Bhīṣma and the other leaders, he proceeded along the royal highway;
all the people there went forth, desiring to behold him, the sole beauty of the world and an ocean of virtues.
Honored by them with the utmost respect, Ananta entered the palace of the king;

placing Bhīṣma and the other chiefs at his front, the Unborn Lord, worshipped by the son of Vicitravīrya, sat upon a supreme golden throne and shone with his own radiance, illuminating the quarters of the sky. (24.58)
Having performed the appropriate rites for them, Keśava went to the house of Duryodhana and was honored there;
yet, perceiving that his worship was offered by one who hates the virtuous, he accepted it but did not go to Vidura.
Although entreated by Bhīṣma and the others, that primordial deity did not go to their homes.
Upeksita, the immeasurable son of Draupadi, went quickly to the house of Vidura.

Having approached him with devotion, the Lord, the Unborn One, was pleased; and having entered the inner chamber, he was worshipped with full devotion, haste, and the offering of everything. 24.60–24.61.
On the following day, he was ushered into the assembly of the Kauravas by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
together with the lords of sages who knew the supreme truth, he entered the divine throne of jewels and gold.
Honored by all the leaders headed by Bhīṣma, he whose eyes were like lotus petals shone with splendor.
Having engaged in appropriate conversation there, he who removes the defilement of the Kali age spoke at the proper time:
"O son of Vicitravīrya, for the prosperity of your own lineage, bestow the kingdom upon your virtuous son;
O King, you shall then obtain fame, supreme righteousness, and my favor."
"Therefore, being deficient in both fame and righteousness, you are here to act as my adversary.
(24.64) Thus addressed, he replied, "Please enlighten me yourself regarding my son who has transgressed.
Although thus enlightened by Vāsudeva, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remained intent on evil.

Rising up from that [assembly], the evil-minded one resolved to restrain the Lord by means of his younger brothers and ministers. Those who at that time invited Keśava to the sacrifice for Yama— those enemies of the gods,
including Vikarṇa and others— met their destruction and went to an inauspicious state.
Although Karṇa was the foremost among the gods, he invited [Viṣṇu] for the sake of Suyodhana; yet he was not at all wicked in his disposition.
Therefore, his destiny became most auspicious; those who are favorable toward the Supreme are blessed.
(24.67) [He was honored] by the sages, by the son of Jamadagni, and also by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor.
And by Viṣṇu himself, who exists as Vāsudeva and possesses three forms,
[he was protected]; yet the evil-minded Duryodhana, though instructed by his parents and by Bhīṣma and others, plotted the swift imprisonment of Mukunda.
Satyaki and Kritavarman heard that at once;
having stationed Kritavarman aside in private,
Satyaki approached Keshava there and spoke of Duryodhana’s resolve.
Although Kṛṣṇa already knew everything, upon hearing it from the mouth of Sātyaki,
he said to the son of Vicitravīrya, "Behold me, who am all-pervading. Then, when that son along with his ministers was summoned by him, Puruṣottama [spoke].
He revealed his own form, which is all-pervading and endowed with perfect, auspicious qualities.

24.72 Upon seeing that eternal and immeasurable one, who possesses the boundless radiance of a thousand suns at the end of time and who sustains the entire universe, Suyodhana and the others closed their eyes, as they were overwhelmed by its brilliance. 24.73
Having covered his form once more, Hari, being entreated by the son of Vicitravīrya, again made Suyodhana blind and departed with his followers, intending to destroy that most wicked man;
for that Supreme Person of infinite power was capable of restraining even the mind of Duryodhana. 24.74.

Then Ananta, casting that doer of his bidding into the blinding darkness, did not strike him down. Again, Kṛṣṇa, having returned to the house of Kuntī and heard from her the remaining efforts of the son of Dharma, went to the son of the Sun on his own vehicle and told him of his own birth.
"Come to the Pāṇḍus"—this word he did not accept at all, having been honored by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having established him [in his position], the Blessed One spoke in private to the son of Droṇa regarding a friendly alliance with the sons of Pṛthā.
He too chose friendship with the Pārthas until his father’s death; and Kṛṣṇa, having dismissed him, departed.
That lord had already departed for the Kurus, leaving behind the sons of Pṛthā;

yet he was entreated by Pṛthā herself: "O Karṇa, go to the sons of Pṛthā; you are my son. He, however, replied to her through Vāsavi: "Without him, I shall not slay your sons under any circumstances. (24.78–79)
Then the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, went to Kurukṣetra desiring to fight;
and there, in a beautiful location, all the Pāṇḍavas established their camps according to the counsel of Kṛṣṇa.
(24.80) Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*, the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Preparation for War" (Bhīṣmapāta), ends here.
448. (Bhīṣmapāta)
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Oṃ! When those two armies, resembling the ocean, had met at the commencement of battle with Bhīma and Bhīṣma at their heads, the son of Vāsava (Arjuna) beheld them and spoke to Acyuta (Kṛṣṇa). 25.1.
“O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies,” so was he addressed;
and Pārtha did accordingly, while observing his kinsmen.
He cast aside his bow, filled with remorse; then Mādhava said to him:
"The subduing of the wicked and the protection of the knowledge of dharma are the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of a Kṣatriya. Having abandoned that, one surely goes downward, censured. (25.2–25.3)

“From whom the activity of beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded— by worshipping Him through one’s own duty, a human being attains perfection. (78) “And you should not feel grief at the loss and death of your kinsmen.”

The creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world], the knowledge, bondage, and liberation, as well as the activity and the power of regulation, belong to the imperishable Brahman, the Īśvara, and so forth; for the body is in every way subject to destruction, whereas the conscious principle is not. (25.5)
O virtuous ones, those whose nature is imperishable come from me alone and not from any other.

25.6 Because of my sovereignty and the perfection of my qualities, there are no creations or other such acts for me from any source; therefore, due to the absence of anything equal or superior, everything is indeed under my control. 25.7

"Knowing their beginning with death and the lack of independence of living beings and the rest, and because of this lack of independence regarding cessation [of rebirth], remember Me and fight. (25.8) "But those who, having surrendered all actions unto Me, are intent on Me..."
Meditating on me with undivided yoga, they worship me;
for them, I become the deliverer from the ocean of the mortal cycle of birth and death. (Bhagavad Gītā 12.6–7)
78. Bhagavad Gītā 18.46:
"I become [the goal] without delay, O Pārtha, for those whose minds are absorbed in Me. 79 / 25.10:
"By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded."

"All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them. (80) 25.11 "I am the Lord whose body is eternally perfected with all true qualities; I am the imperishable one whose singular, eternal, and truly existent form is untouched by any defect whatsoever."
Thus addressed, the son of Vasava said, "O Lord, show me your pervasiveness. Then,
having granted him divine vision, [the Lord] revealed his own body as pervasive—
complete in space and time, and always endowed with all qualities.
The Blessed One revealed [his form] to as great an extent as Arjuna was capable of bearing;
then, being entreated by him, Kṛṣṇa again showed that world-surpassing form as it was before, and instructed him once more.
Making known the nature of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, the Supreme Person instructed him;
thus instructed, Pārtha took up his bow along with an arrow. Then, as the armies were drawn up in battle array, the son of Vāyu advanced, roaring aloud.
All those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded him in the assembly and released a shower of arrows upon Bhīmasena’s head.
"One must not strike quickly even at kinsmen who are striking back. 25.16.
While he was thus failing to strike back, though pierced by the arrows of his enemies,
all the heroic sons of the Pāṇḍavas, led by the son of Subhadrā, unleashed an unassailable shower of weapons upon the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra sought to afflict them from all sides with floods of weapons; however, the son of Vāyu protected them by discharging volleys of arrows. There, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were driven back on every side by Bhīma’s shafts.
79 Bhagavadgītā 12.6–7; 80 Bhagavadgītā 9.4;
25.20: Then the son of Gaṅgā, skilled in divine weapons, held back those broken [forces].
Then, as they sought victory, there occurred dual combats:
between Droṇa and the son of Pṛṣata, and between the descendant of Śini and Kṛtavarman, as well as between the heroic younger son of Mādrī and Duḥśāsana. (25.21)

When the great duel between Nakula and Vikarṇa, along with those of the sons of Kṛṣṇa such as Durmukha and others, had taken place, those on the side of the son of Dharma were defeated even without the aid of Śaineya; he alone then conquered the son of Hṛdika.
Then, as his own army was being routed by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and their leaders, as well as Bhagadatta and others, Māruti steadied it;
he [confronted] Droṇa, Bhagadatta, Kṛpa, and likewise Duryodhana.
Relying solely on the strength of his arms, he of terrible prowess conquered;
having slain Uttara, the King of Madra put the army to flight.
Then Bhīṣma, with uplifted weapons, began to scatter the host.
Accompanied by the son of Subhadrā, Arjuna approached the son of Somadatta;
there, the son of the celestial river, having bypassed the valiant son of Subhadrā,
put the Pāñcālas to flight even as Savyasācin looked on.
Observing that prowess of Pārtha and following out of respect for him,
King Yudhiṣṭhira became enraged and withdrew his army.
At night, Yudhiṣṭhira fell into reflection and censured Pārtha.
Consoled by Kṛṣṇa and others, he went forth once more for battle.
Thus Bhīṣma held the command of the army for ten days,
having engaged in a battle with the Pāṇḍavas that was beyond comparison.
Having declared that Karṇa was but a half-charioteer (*ardharatha*), he was made to withdraw from the battle with the condition:
"As long as you fight, I shall not fight. When he had departed, Karṇa [promised] the constant slaughter of ten thousand chariot-warriors (*ayuta-ratha*) in combat.
The best among those skilled in weapons made that vow and fulfilled it;
yet Bhīma and Dhanañjaya, though both fully capable of slaying him,
submitted to his will, restrained by affection and out of respect for him.
Many wonderful battles took place there;
all the gods led by Brahmā and Rudra, along with the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras, watched them from their celestial chariots in the sky. (25.34)
The great archer Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
invincible by his enemies in battle, having arrayed himself against the son of the River (Bhīṣma), engaged in many combats; there, Kṛṣṇa also protected Phalguna, who fought with gentleness.
Having seen [the discus] and likewise raising his arm, he went toward Bhīṣma;
praised by him and grasped by Phalguna after bowing down, he was entreated [to stay], mounted the chariot, and once again blew his conch shell. (25.36–37)
Then Bhīṣma and Arjuna both rained down a shower of weapons and missiles;
yet the son of the River was defeated by Phalguna without effort, and he [Arjuna] slew many tens of thousands of chariots in the battle. 25.38.
Then Bhīṣma and the others, being defeated, carried off the army.
At one time, Bhīma, moving to the front, deprived Bhīṣma and Droṇa of their charioteers;
having put them to flight and scattered their horses, he broke through the array and entered it.
Having effortlessly defeated those two who had steadied their chariots,
the mighty hero slaughtered the striving sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, those great archers; twenty-five of those powerful sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were slain there.

Bhagadatta, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, Duryodhana, and the others—all were conquered and put to flight, and their vast army was slaughtered. Though deprived of his chariot and weapons and rendered unconscious by the force of the firm impact, [he remained]. 25.42. ccclii.
While all the kings looked on, Bhīma brought Duryodhana under his power;
then the Kauravas, having been defeated, withdrew their troops,
and Duryodhana went at night to where the son of the River (Bhīṣma) was.
Afflicted by Bhīma’s arrows and with his limbs streaming with blood, he bowed down before him.
"For what reason," he said, "are we always wasting away, while the Pāṇḍavas, having constantly achieved victory, obtain joy? (25.44–45)
Bhīṣma said to him: "Those gods are invincible; they have come to the earth, and especially so because they are always protected by Keśava, who is dear to them.
For in ancient times, on Mount Mānasottara, they were led by Brahmā. (25.46)
Then the gods saw Brahmā alone in the sky, beholding Hari.
Having praised and worshipped him, he requested him for the sake of relieving the earth's burden. The Lord, having been addressed by him, spoke to the gods. (25.47–48)
This god Nārāyaṇa, an ocean of infinite and perfect qualities, commands you all to manifest upon the surface of the earth;
and he himself shall become the Lord of the World as the son of Devakī. 25.49.
Thus commanded by him, Dharmavāyu and all the others became the Pāṇḍavas and their followers, together with Indra and the hosts of Maruts;
and that god Nārāyaṇa became the son of Devakī.
"Therefore, these sons of Pṛthā, protected by him and born of the divine race, are invincible.
For that reason, seek peace with them if you desire to avoid defeat.
Having been addressed thus, he bowed to Viṣṇu with a mind full of deceit and then departed.
At dawn, the evil-minded one dispatched his army for battle.
Having been freed from disease by means of a divine herb,
Bhīṣma then placed himself at the head and marched forth for the fray with a fierce spirit.
There occurred an incomparable battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas— those heroic warriors who never retreated, following Bhīma and Bhīṣma.
There, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, following Bhīma, fought with the younger brothers of Duryodhana.
Having bewildered them with the *sammohana* weapon, he struck the army led by Vikarṇa. Then Droṇa, having raised them all up with the *vijñāna* weapon, assailed the son of Pṛṣata as well.
Bhīmasena, having deprived him of his charioteer, put the hosts of enemies to flight with showers of arrows.
Then Kṛtavarman, seated upon his chariot, rushed toward Dhṛṣṭadyumna;

both of them rained down fierce showers of arrows, but there Draupadi’s son deprived him of his chariot. When that hero among charioteers was defeated, Duryodhana himself approached the son of Pṛṣata.
Bhimasena, having deprived him of his chariot and weapons, struck him in the region of the collarbone with an arrow.
Having placed him—who was unconscious and vomiting a great torrent of blood—upon his own chariot, Kṛpa departed;
meanwhile, the son of Māruta (Bhīma) put the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons to flight with multitudes of arrows.
Then the son of Indra, scattering his enemies with floods of arrows from the chariot urged on by Keśava,
sent twenty-five thousand chariots in battle to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Yuyudhāna, the skilled archer, followed him, putting the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son to flight.
The son of Somadatta advanced against him, and between those two there occurred a most terrifying battle involving fierce weapons.
Having swiftly slain ten of the sons of Daśāsya, that hero, the son of Somadatta, along with Sātyaki,
struck them both with body-piercing arrows and deprived them both of their chariots.

Then, seeing Yuyudhāna sword in hand and approached by the son of Somadatta who held a great sword, the son of Anila (Bhīma) caused him to mount his own chariot. Suyodhana, having stationed the son of Somadatta upon his own chariot, [fought] against Bhīmasena.

The son of Vasava fled from Bhishma in battle, but that one who was equal to the great Indra quickly returned to confront him. Both of them, the foremost among those skilled in weapons, possessed of great strength and filled with pride, mangled each other with arrows resembling venomous serpents in the very presence of the dwellers of heaven.
By the prowess of his own arms, that Bhīṣma was defeated by Kirīṭin, the great chariot-warrior of the world;
having withdrawn his army, he departed at nightfall, and then the Pāṇḍavas [remained].
On the following day, they once again approached, placing Bhīma and Bhīṣma at their head.
Then, having deprived Bhīṣma of his charioteer, the son of the Wind-god (Bhīmasena) advanced against the enemies;
by him, the chariot-horses were struck down, and all the survivors fled.
When Duryodhana and the others had been defeated, with Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the son of Droṇa at their head, [the rest followed suit].
Seated upon a great elephant, Bhagadatta advanced and released an arrow at Bhīmasena.

When Bhīmasena was deeply pierced by it, his son, the hero Ghaṭotkaca, restrained his father as he was about to strike back; mounting four elephants through his own illusory power, he rushed swiftly toward him. (25.68–69)

Recognizing that the Vaiṣṇava weapon was stationed with Bhagadatta due specifically to a boon from Viṣṇu— and knowing it to be infallible except against Hari— the son of the Maruts did not personally attack it when his own son had departed,
even though he knew himself to be eternally incapable of being slain by Vāsudeva because of that supreme grace.
Precisely because of his exceptional devotion to him, Aṛiṇa could not make his word true;
for he would only realize it when he had been defeated by his own son, or perhaps even by himself. When Bhīṣma becomes oblivious to his weapons, then Bhīma advances against Bhagadatta.
"Bhīma knew this well: 'He will not discharge his weapon except against Bhīma or Arjuna.

(25.72) Then Ghaṭotkaca, who was composed of four elephants and the soul of the upper regions, along with Supratīka, began to strike him with various blows, leaving both of them with their lives in doubt before the eyes of the world. (25.73)

Hearing the elephants’ cries of distress and seeing that massive and terrifying being, the warriors led by Bhīṣma were struck with great fear; even the son of Vāyu, who was protecting his rear, trembled violently.
Terrified beyond measure, they abandoned the battlefield and fled quickly toward their camp. (25.74)
On the following day, the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas met once again with one another. There, the son of Pṛthā, born of the daughter of the Naga, alone encountered the six sons of Śakuni.
With his body mangled by those who wielded spears, he, overcome with intense rage, cut them down with his sword.

Seeing that hero, the powerful and tireless one who struck terror into the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the fierce son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra commanded the Rākṣasa named Alambuṣa: "Slay the son of Arjuna quickly! And he approached the son born from the daughter of the Naga. (25.76–77)
Between those two, both skilled in illusion and possessed of great prowess, there occurred an exceedingly fierce, wondrous, and mighty battle.
That Rākṣasa then conjured up horses with their riders, and they slew the riders of Pārtha’s son.
Then the Rākṣasa, assuming the form of Garuḍa, swiftly struck down the son of Arjuna, who had assumed an infinite form. (25.78)
Hearing that the son of Arjuna had been slain, the son of Vṛkodara, possessed of fierce prowess, roared in anger;
at the sound of him shouting, the earth, along with its oceans, great mountains, and peaks, then trembled violently.
Beholding that mighty son of Māruta, Alambuṣa fled away in fear.

The entire army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son fled; then King Suyodhana, having approached him, slew four ministers of Bhīma’s son as well as four other mighty warriors. When those who remained after being slain were fleeing, Ghaṭotkaca struck that king with arrows.
Being thus afflicted in battle by that Rākṣasa, he discharged an arrow at Ghaṭotkaca.

Struck firmly by that more powerful one, Ghaṭotkaca’s senses were then violently distressed; though falling to the ground, he remained there with great difficulty and continued to discharge arrows at Suyodhana. (25.82)

Seeing the long-fighting king and the lord of the Rākṣasas, both most difficult for each other to defeat on the field of battle, Droṇa and the others— enduring their foes and desiring to protect Suyodhana—
arrived; namely Droṇa, Śalya, the son of the preceptor (Aśvatthāman), Gautama (Kṛpa), Bhūriśravas, Kṛtavarman, and the rest.
Ghaṭotkaca, stationed in the sky, rained down arrows of immense thickness and great velocity.
Beholding him surrounded by those one-pointed chariot-warriors, Bhīma advanced against them all.
There, Droṇa, severely afflicted by the excellent arrows discharged by Bhīma, fell down having reached a state of unconsciousness.
In an instant, Bhīma deprived the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa and the others, along with Suyodhana, of their chariots;

yet, though being restrained by Vṛkodara, Ghaṭotkaca showered them with arrows. (25.86) Oppressed by those floods of arrows from him as he stood in the sky, the size of trees, the Kurus were struck down.

Afflicted by the torrent of Bhīma’s arrows, they fell to the ground, wailed, and fled in extreme terror. Having driven all those Kauravas, with the exception of Bhīṣma, back to their camp, Bhīmasena and Ghaṭotkaca roared with a great sound, filling the worlds with their clamor.
Then Duryodhana, together with his kinsmen, went once more to the battlefield to Bhīṣma;
he asked for a means to defeat the son of Bhīmasena, but Bhīṣma told him, "Do not go against him.
Then the son of the Ganges dispatched the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa against Ghaṭotkaca.
Having reached him, the mighty one fought with the son of Hiḍimbā and assailed him along with his elephant.
Afflicted by him, Ghaṭotkaca then leaped into the air and hurled a spear at him;
seizing the spear and pressing it against his knee, he broke it, and the gods rejoiced upon seeing that.
Then the king struck those very followers of his, and the son of the Wind-god (Māruti) rushed at him in battle.
That hero hurled an elephant at Bhīmasena, but he paralyzed that elephant instantly with his arrows.
When the elephant was thus paralyzed by those excellent shafts, he struck Bhīma’s own arrows with his own arrows.

His bow shattered, he then seized a mace and approached that king, together with his elephant, in order to slay him. Attacked in fury by Bhīma, who desired to kill him, the king fled in great terror from both front and rear, along with Arjuna, to seize the Vaiṣṇava weapon held by Kṛṣṇa.
When he had departed, and the entire host of kings had been put to flight by Bhīmasena and Arjuna, Bhīṣma withdrew his army and retreated; Duryodhana then approached him at night.
Having been made to hear those cruel words by him, he cast aside the fear of death and made them come true.
"I shall slay the enemies with my power"—thinking thus, he performed that deed on the following day.

The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra resisted him to the best of their ability, while the Cedis, Pañcālas, and Matsyas, afflicted by him, fled in all directions, terrified by Bhīṣma’s arrows like distressed small animals harassed by a lion. (25.96–97)
Having halted them, Alambusa obstructed the son of Pṛthā as he was advancing toward Bhīṣma;
having defeated him, the nephew of Keśava proceeded against Bhīṣma, while the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra slew that other [Alambusa].
That battle between the king and the son of Pṛthā was wonderful, most marvelous, and fierce in appearance.
There, the king suddenly cut down Abhimanyu’s bow and his standard equally and at once.
Then that hero showered him with fierce arrows and quickly slew his charioteer.
Thereupon Bhīmasena approached that king and struck down the arrows of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Droṇa, the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman), Bhagadatta, and Kṛpa, along with Citrasena, rushed toward Bhīmasena.
Having turned them all back, Bhīma took up his mace against Citrasena.
Seeing it raised, they fled; Citrasena, for his part, leaped down from his chariot.

His chariot was crushed by the mace, and the Kauravas were emboldened by his life remaining. But the fierce Bhīṣma, possessed of exceeding sharp energy, slew fourteen thousand Pāñcālas, Karūṣas, and Cedis;
that foremost of car-warriors put the enemy to flight like a lion [driving away] deer.

Having routed the entire Pandava army and proclaimed his own fame throughout the worlds, Drona withdrew his troops and departed at nightfall, being honored by the sons of Dhritarashtra; he had previously struck down Shankha, the son of Virata, and conquered that king as well. 25.104.

Having routed even the army of the Pāṇḍavas, he went forth joyfully together with the son of the River (Aśvatthāman). Bhīma and Arjuna also, having slain their enemies and routed all the great warriors in battle,
returned to their camp when their own army had been carried off by Yudhiṣṭhira out of fear of Bhīṣma.
Terrified by Bhīṣma’s prowess, Yudhiṣṭhira went at night to ask Bhīṣma himself for the means of his own death; Kṛṣṇa and his younger brothers followed him, as did his grandfather.
Although Bhīma and Arjuna were capable of slaying him, they did not wish to kill him without his permission. (25.107)

Since Bhīṣma, whose deeds were noble, was worthy of worship, Kṛṣṇa also went for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas. (25.108) Having obtained permission from Bhīṣma, they set out for battle on the following day, placing Śikhaṇḍin—who had been urged by his word—to the forefront for the purpose of slaying him; likewise, the others also marched forth, placing Bhīṣma at their head. (25.109)
Phalguna became the protector of Śikhaṇḍin, and Duḥśāsana stood at the front of Bhīṣma;
all the others protected Bhīṣma alone, while Bhīmasena and the others held them back. Then, as Yuyudhāna was advancing toward Bhīṣma in battle, the Rākṣasa Alambuṣa checked him.
The Vṛṣṇi hero pierced him with arrows like thunderbolts; he then unleashed a fierce illusion.
Dispelling that illusion with a divine weapon, the heroic Sātyaki put that Rākṣasa to flight.
Once he had gone, Yuyudhāna, the bowman, followed after Pārtha on his chariot toward Bhīṣma.
Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, Bhūriśravas, Bhagadatta, Kṛpa, Śalya, Bāhlīka, Kṛtavarman, Suśarman, and all the armies were held back by the son of Vāyu.
Having repeatedly deprived them of their chariots, that hero put to flight the king of Prāgjyotiṣa along with his elephant.
He warded off Phalguna, who was intent on obstructing him; and Pārtha approached Devavrata.
Śakuni, accompanied by ten thousand excellent horsemen, checked Yudhiṣṭhira—that hero among men—as he advanced together with the two sons of Mādrī. (25.114–115)
Having slain all those horsemen and horses and having defeated Śakuni, those Pāṇḍavas,
all the sons of Draupadī, as well as Virāṭa, Drupada, and Kuntibhoja, reached Bhīṣma.
Then the ruler of the Sindhus restrained Dhṛṣṭadyumna with his arrows as he was advancing toward Bhīṣma.
Having routed his own army along with its charioteers and followers, the hero quickly approached Bhīṣma himself.
Then, protected by Pārtha in battle, Śikhaṇḍin reached Bhīṣma and struck him with arrows;
Bhīṣma, knowing his femininity, did not discharge arrows at him, yet he tormented him. (25.117–118)
Durmarṣaṇa, his eyes agitated with rage, warded off Śikhaṇḍin with arrows;
yet Śikhaṇḍin was unable to pass him by, for Duḥśāsana then held back Pārtha.
Though he was a hero of the world, being thus obstructed by that evil-minded man, he was unable to advance past him.

Pārtha’s arrows became entangled in Bhīṣma, even though they would have passed unimpeded through mountains. 25.120 Filled with indignation, the two heroes, Arjuna and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, fought for a long time.
That great battle was equal and marvelous to behold for the dwellers of heaven and the lords of the earth. 25.121
Then Virāṭa, Drupada, Kuntibhoja, the sons of Kṛṣṇā, the Kekayas, Cekitāna, Bhūri, Śala, Somadatta, and Vikarṇa, along with the Kekayas, fiercely opposed him.
Having defeated them, they advanced toward Bhīṣma; then Arjuna, bypassing Duḥśāsana, [proceeded].

Having freed Śikhaṇḍin from the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he struck Bhīṣma with enemy-crushing arrows. Tormented in his vital organs by all those multitudes of various weapons released from the bow, he deprived the entire host— Śaineya, the Pāñcālya, Yudhiṣṭhira, and the others— of their chariots in battle.
Like a blazing fire at the end of an eon, he dispatched twenty-five thousand of the finest chariot-warriors— the leaders of the Cedis, Pañcālas, and Karūṣas— to the realm of Yama with his arrows;
seeing him scorching like the sun, Pārtha was urged on by Vāsudeva.
That hero of the world cut his bow in battle with a crescent-shaped arrow, and he took up another;
[the opponent] cut that one as well, and likewise eight bows, a spear, an excellent shield, and other weapons.
All the bows given to the king by men were cut down by that son of Indra.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira and all the others pierced him with arrows as radiant as the rays of the sun.
Afflicted by them, he fell to the earth; yet, though his life-force was departing, he sustained it through the power of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
When he had been struck down, Bhīmasena, having routed the leaders headed by Droṇa, quickly arrived there, and they too [fled].
Having laid down their weapons, the heroic sons of Pṛthā and their enemies sat down before him. At his command, they all approached him on that day and paid their respects;
on the following day, they all presented themselves before Bhīṣma together with the lord of the Yadus.
On the previous day, having used the arrows given by Pārtha as his pillow,
he was then again overcome by thirst and asked for a suitable drink.
Knowing this while it remained unnoticed by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Vāsava [intervened].
Having pierced the earth with the Vāruṇa weapon, he released fragrant water in an upward stream into his mouth; being satisfied by this, he spoke:
"O descendants of Kuru, such mastery of weapons as has been seen here in Pārtha [is remarkable]. (25.132) ccclx.
Whatever strength Bhīma possesses in his arms, demonstrated again and again in battles,
and whatever infinite and undecaying majesty Hari possesses, has been recognized by all the world and witnessed directly in the assembly hall. (25.133–134)
"Cease this war; let the lords of the earth be happy, and may you, O kings, always enjoy the land divided according to what is fitting.
Having been addressed thus, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra departed silently for his own home. 25.135.

Having heard everything from Sañjaya, who possessed the profound wisdom bestowed by Vyāsa, his father then was consumed with grief; meanwhile, all the Pāṇḍavas, whose deity is Kṛṣṇa, rejoiced upon reaching their camp, being cheered by Kṛṣṇa himself. 25.136.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Fall of Bhīṣma," in the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda.
391. (The Pacification of the Nārāyaṇa Weapon) Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Oṃ! Then [he addressed] the preeminent teacher of all the lords of the earth, who was highly skilled in chariot warfare.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra made Karna, the archer who was previously slighted by Rāma, the lord of the universe, his general-in-chief, even though he had been a good pupil;
and with Bhīṣma’s approval, that archer prepared for battle. While Karna stood there having not yet taken up his bow, Duryodhana mounted his chariot and followed his preceptor.

When Drona was chosen by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra on the promise of capturing the son of Dharma, the Pāṇḍavas, having learned of it, prepared themselves and advanced there for battle; a fierce combat took place.
There, Drona agitated his enemies with winged arrows released from the circle of his bow and the power of his mantras.
Vṛkodara quickly assailed Nada, while the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the King of Madra also attacked him.
Shaking them off, that leader fell upon Droṇa in battle; Arjuna’s son followed after him toward the enemies.
The Lord of Madra intercepted him, and between those two there was a great battle, in which he took up his mace.
Then Śalya and Bhīma, both wielding maces, advanced against one another, and there a battle took place between them.
Both were invincible, the most excellent among mace-wielders, possessed of incomparable prowess, and the foremost of the mighty;
roaring aloud, they moved in a most wonderful manner, enchanting those who watched them.
In that battle, the entire world beheld those two, whose vajra-like limbs were marked by the falling blows of their maces.
By the impact of Vṛkodara’s mace, the King of Madra fell there unconscious;
Bhīma too, his feet trembling with rage, placed a knee upon the ground and rose up again in an instant.
Seeing the King of Madra fallen unconscious and Bhīma calling out to him,
Kṛpa placed him upon his chariot and departed while the people looked on and before Bhīma’s very eyes.
Having conquered the lord of Madra by his prowess, that slayer of enemies, the son of the Wind-god, reached his own chariot and let out a roar.

He put to flight the enemy host with multitudes of arrows even in the very presence of Droṇa. (26.9) While Vṛkodara was thus putting the Kurus to flight—having shaken off the sons of Subhadrā led by Abhimanyu along with the followers of Sātyaki—Droṇa advanced to seize the king; then the car-warrior Dhanañjaya quickly approached him. (26.10)

Mounted upon the chariot driven by Vāsudeva, he stood firm; having struck down elephants and men on all sides with body-ending arrows, he caused rivers of blood to flow even as he moved through the horses.
While the armies were being slaughtered by the Diademed One (Arjuna) and the Son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) was thus left in a state of peril, [Kṛṣṇa spoke].
And Drona, having withdrawn the army shattered by the arrows of Bhima and Arjuna, retreated at the onset of night.
(26.12) Having been made to hear these cruel words by the son of Dhritarashtra through Yudhishthira’s insistence during the night, he said:
"Let Partha be led far away from the battle; then I shall seize the son of Dharma. (26.13)

Then Suśarman, accompanied by great chariot-warriors among the Śapathakas, was urged by Duryodhana to lead them to a much greater distance for battle against the younger brother of Bhīma; he replied, "So be it. Then they challenged Arjuna to combat in the morning, toward the direction where the sun rises.

Having gone there, Bhīma fought them and then slaughtered that elephant division. While the elephants were being struck down on all sides and all the kings were being put to flight, the archer from Prāgjyotiṣa, acting on behalf of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, approached him with his elephant Supratīka.
Terrified by Supratīka’s fearsome neighing, they could not stand their ground;
then Sātyaki and the foremost warriors led by Subhadrā’s son rushed toward that elephant. He [the elephant] hurled their chariots into the air.
When those led by Śaineya had been deprived of their chariots, they somehow leaped down to the ground.
While Bhīma remained among those who were terrifying and causing terror, Kṛṣṇa observed that he was fighting with his senses fully restrained.
"Afflicted indeed, the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa might discharge the Vaiṣṇava weapon at Bhīmasena;
therefore, I shall take that weapon of mine back by means of Arjuna alone, for it cannot be held by another due to a boon. (26.18–19)
Having reflected thus, he then arrived there with Arjuna; meanwhile, the Trigartas obstructed Pārtha, but the hero quickly discharged the Tvaṣṭra weapon at them for the purpose of bewildering them.
Bewildered by the power of that weapon, they mistook Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha for one another.
Then, having abandoned those [demons] whom Vāsavi (Arjuna) was slaying, he went swiftly here to kill the King of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Having left Bhīma, he went toward Pārtha (Arjuna) alone; mounted upon the shoulder of that elephant, he urged the beast toward his chariot, and Hari quickly made it wheel to the right of him.
As the chariot was being whirled around by that supreme speed of thought, the elephant was unable to catch up with it;
then that son of Vāsava afflicted the king with exceedingly sharp arrows.
And for a long time, those two heroes among men, the foremost of the mighty, fought each other with missiles and weapons.
Then Pārtha cut his bow, and he directed that Vaiṣṇava weapon toward Aṅkuśa. When that weapon was released by him, Vāsudeva of immeasurable power held it;
it became the Vaijayantī garland upon the neck of the Lord of all the worlds.
Upon seeing that [universe] held by Acyuta, Pārtha asked, "For what purpose is this being held by you?

He replied to him quickly: "The Abode of the World maintains everything at all times. There is no one else like me; how could there be anyone superior to me? It is I who, for the welfare of the world, manifest in four forms. (26.26)
I abide as the creator of liberation, dissolution, maintenance, and creation, sequentially through my own forms;
that Aniruddha, whose nature consists of the fourfold form beginning with Vāsudeva, dwells in the heart of all.
He alone is the one who assumed the body of the Boar (Varāha) for the sake of the beloved of the Earth and for the destruction of Naraka.
"I gave him my supreme weapon and granted him invincibility for as long as that weapon remained with him and his son.
Furthermore, there is no one else other than me who can slay this weapon; thus, I myself have withheld that weapon, so now slay him when he is deprived of it. (26.28–29)
Having heard what was thus spoken, Keśava consulted and released an arrow at Bāṇa’s heart;
he then plunged another excellent shaft into the frontal globes of the lordly elephant of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Both of them, resembling mountains, quickly fell like two peaks struck by the thunderbolt of Mahendra.

Having slain those two, the son of Vasava, possessed of fierce prowess, rejoiced, being duly honored by his own people. (26.31) Then, having struck down Acala and Vṛṣaka—the younger brothers of Śakuni—he pierced him with arrows;
he created an illusion, but the prince quickly destroyed it with the weapon of higher knowledge (*vijñāna-astra*). (26.32)
Having his illusions destroyed, that evildoer fled; then Pārtha, with volleys of arrows, put that army to flight.
Then the preceptor’s son slew the lord of Māhiṣmatī in battle.
Then Bhīma, having slain his horses, routed the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons.
Seeing that army being slaughtered by Bhīma and Arjuna, Droṇa quickly withdrew it.

(26.34) When the ruler of Prāgjyotiṣa had been slain, Duryodhana, appearing deeply dejected, spoke these piteous words to Yudhiṣṭhira; thereupon, he made them heard to Droṇa, who then addressed the king. (26.35)
"When Pārtha has departed, tomorrow I shall seize the king, or I shall slay one of his equals"— having thus made this vow, he went forth again at dawn, longing for battle;
having formed the lotus-array (*padmavyūha*), which was impenetrable by enemies due to a boon from Viṣṇu, for he had indeed not recited its secret mantra.
The sons of Pṛthā reached him, with the exception of Arjuna; that hero, too, fought with the Śapathakas.
Having reached that formation, the sons of Pṛthā were intent on breaking it, but through the power of their intuition, they did not even mutter the desired mantra.
There Bhīma said to the son of Subhadrā, who was skilled in such matters:
"O dear one, break this formation; we shall follow after you.
Thus addressed, that foremost of chariot-warriors entered, having pierced through that army of his enemies.

Vāyusuta and the others, desiring to enter after him, were likewise held back by Jayadratha alone, as if by a barrier of salt-earth. But Vṛkodara, though capable and though Jayadratha was obstructing him there by virtue of a boon from Rudra, did not bypass him, having recognized that this was the will of Viṣṇu for Arjuna’s slaughter.
While Vṛkodara and the others were engaged in combat with the bull-bannered Kṛṣṇa stationed at Jayadratha’s side,
that hero, the son of Dhanañjaya, having entered, agitated the vast army of the enemy. He [fought] against Droṇa, Duryodhana, Karṇa, Śalya, and those led by Droṇa’s son, together with Kṛtavarman.
He moved fearlessly through the enemy forces, severing the heads of those who followed him.

By force, he brought the prince Lakṣaṇa before his father for execution; and that hero of supreme valor and deeds swiftly slew Bṛhadbala and ten thousand choice chariot-warriors with his feathered shafts.
Droṇa and the others, fearing the wrath of Hari and unable to slay him before their very eyes,
consulted together and, placing Karṇa at the front, in an instant rendered his chariot wheel-less.
Karṇa destroyed his bow, Kṛpa his charioteer, and Droṇa, with his arrows, struck down his horses.
Having pushed away his chariot wheel along with his shield and sword, they stood with those weapons still held in their hands.

Then, while they were terrified of Kṛṣṇa, the mace-wielding son of Duḥśāsana quickly approached them for the sake of slaying them. Those two, both possessed of great prowess, died simultaneously by the blow of each other’s maces.
When that [elephant] was slain, hearing the roar of the enemy born of joy, Māruti of fierce prowess,
having conquered all those led by Saindhava, sat down with the consent of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then Vyāsa, whose self-majesty is immeasurable, enlightened Yudhiṣṭhira and the others who were despondent.
Having conquered that host of Śaptakas, the fierce son of Vasava, accompanied by Achyuta, returned at the onset of night.
Hearing of his son’s slaughter, the hero was deeply afflicted, yet he made a solemn vow for the slaying of Jayadratha during the night. Hari then led him to the presence of Giriśa in a dream.

Although he himself possesses immeasurable power for the protection of the entire world, Acyuta [Kṛṣṇa] immediately informed Giriśa (Śiva), the preceptor of Phalguna’s weapons, saying: "I am the one who bestows grace through the medium of the Guru. 26.51.
Having brought him [the weapon] here by his grace, he made that formidable weapon manifest;
for that very purpose, he then performed a protection consisting of that [weapon].
Having consoled Subhadrā and gone to Upaplāvya, Acyuta—
Having prepared his chariot in the morning, Arjuna advanced toward the battle.
Having heard the vow of the son of Puruhūta, Duryodhana requested the King of Sindhu;
meanwhile, Droṇa, having made the vow, "I shall protect him by all means," drew up an impenetrable military formation.

Having himself formed that foremost divine array in the shape of a chariot-wheel, he stationed himself at its head; while Jayadratha was protected from the enemy by Karṇa, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Śalya, and others in the rear. Then Arjuna, standing upon his divine chariot, was well-guarded by the imperishable Keśava.
Having defeated Durmarṣaṇa, Sudhanvan, of fierce prowess and excellent bow, advanced toward his preceptor Droṇa.
Having circumambulated him, he then departed quickly, fearing a delay;
he drove the chariot with the speed of thought, and his arrows fell behind him like Hari [leaving] his tracks.
Having conquered the son of Hṛdika without effort, that son of Indra entered that army;
and like a lordly elephant, arrogant in its strength, he agitated the *nalini* lotus-pond with his excellent arrows.
That great chariot-warrior, together with Vāsudeva, shone resplendent upon his supreme chariot, just as Indra does with Hari.
With body-ending arrows, he fiercely severed the heads of his enemies on all sides.
Having slain Dṛḍhāyu and Acyutāyu, as well as Vinda and Anuvinda,
Vijaya dispatched them to Yama with two arrows in battle.
Having slain Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja and Ambaṣṭha as well,
he reached Śrutāyudha, the son of Nadīja,
from whom Varuṇa had given him a great, divine, and unerring mace. (26.61)
Pierced by those sharp arrows, he was deprived of his chariot in an instant;
mounting Pārtha’s chariot, he hurled that mace at the enemy-slaying Vāruṇi. It struck Vāruṇi right upon the head.

His skull shattered, he fell to the ground in a hundred pieces. "If you yourself strike with your own mace one who does not fight back, you will die with your brain crushed by it; of this there is no doubt. (26.63)
"Otherwise, this mace of yours will become unfailing," Varuṇa said to him in the past; therefore, when Keśava did not fight, he was shattered by the hurling of that mace. 26.64–65.

When his own heroic warriors had been routed in great numbers and the army thrown into confusion, Duryodhana approached Droṇa and spoke dejectedly: "Alas! Pārtha has been let slip by you. When this was said, that Brahmin bound his impenetrable armor with the power of a great mantra.
"Go against Phalguna with that very same strength with which you oppose the sons of Pritha!
(26.67) Thus addressed, the son of Dhritarashtra, standing upon his golden chariot and taking up his bow, went toward Partha and obstructed him with many arrows that blazed like fire. (26.68)
Pārtha also pierced him with arrows of fierce velocity, yet they did not pierce his armor;
thereupon, the son of Vāsava, in a rage, took up a divine weapon to break through that armor. But as it was being aimed, the son of the Preceptor cut down those arrows of Pārtha, O Suyodhana.
Having struck that [shield], the son of Droṇa then warded off Pārtha in battle with fierce arrows.
Dhananjaya fought against those led by the son of Droṇa and Karṇa, and they in turn warded him off with their shafts.
That battle, for the sake of Jayadratha, between those of wondrous heroism and marvelous deeds, was incomparable and miraculous.
When Pārtha had entered the midst of the Kuru army, Droṇa quickly entered the Pāṇḍava host. Shaking that array of chariots with arrows of fierce velocity, he struck down the heroes.
Though he was an aged man, that best of warriors moved among the young archers like a youth himself.
Felling the heads of heroes with his arrows, the one of fierce valor approached Yudhiṣṭhira;
perceiving that he desired to seize the king, the powerful Satyajit, the son of Draupadī, warded him off with arrows.
Being thus restrained by him, the Brahmin cut off the head of the Pāñcāla prince with a shaft.
Having slain that most heroic Yudhiṣṭhira, who was fierce in battle, he struck him with a multitude of arrows.
Having engaged him in combat with a spear, he was in an instant rendered weaponless, deprived of his horses and chariot.
Though he stood upon the ground with arms raised, he was overcome by the Guru in the fray as he attempted to seize him.
Then, having mounted their chariots, the younger son of Mādrī departed with speed.
Thereupon, the son of Śiśupāla along with his sons, Jārāsaṃdhi, the king of Kāṃsi, and Śaivya, as well as the five Kekayas, approached Droṇa and assailed him from all sides with multitudes of arrows.
Having there successively severed their necks with his excellent arrows, that brahmin led them to the supreme world, which the *ūrdhvaretas* sages enter by piercing through the solar orb.
While the heavy army of the sons of Pṛthā was being shaken, the forces of the enemies [were likewise overwhelmed].
For the most part, their foremost heroes having been slain and crushed by the Son of the Wind in battle, they fled away.
At that very moment, a *rākṣasa* named Alambusa encountered the Son of the Wind, who was possessed of fierce prowess.
Afflicted by him with well-sharpened arrows, he vanished in an instant through his illusory power (*māyā*).
Seeing that he was afflicting even Bhīma’s followers while remaining invisible, Māruti grew enraged;
though he had encountered a crisis of righteousness, he displayed his own mastery of weapons by the command of Keśava.
Although Bhīma was devoid of ritual action (*kāmyakarman*), he took up the Tvaṣṭra-weapon, and from it arrows arose. (26.81)
Those excellent arrows, which struck their targets invisibly, tore through the Rakshasa and entered the surface of the earth. Being thus struck, he fled far away in great terror, abandoning Bhima.
Then Bhima put the army of his enemies to flight with well-aimed arrows.
At that very moment, the sons of Kṛṣṇa united and slew Śala, the son of Somadatta, in the encounter.
Then Ghaṭotkaca encountered Alambuṣa; those two chariot-warriors fought with one another.
Having deprived him of his chariot, Ghaṭotkaca, remaining stationed in the sky, fought him while he was still in the air.
Then the son of Bhīma, having seized him and thrown him to the ground, delivered a blow with his foot directly upon his head;
with his skull crushed, he died in the midst of the lords of the earth.
When he was slain, the son of Bhīmasena put the host of Kuru chariots to flight in every direction.
Then Kṛtavarman advanced against the army of the Pāṇḍavas on his chariot, discharging a rain of arrows;
for Acyuta, being pleased by his hymn of praise, had previously granted him a boon of universal victory for a moment.
With that [boon], he conquered the hosts of the Pañcālas, the twins, Bhīma, and then him as well.
Knowing him to be the preeminent Vāsudeva, he pierced him with an arrow but did not then advance against him.

Because that hero had achieved victory even without the Vṛṣṇis, Satyaki slew his horses with arrows; having struck them down, he pierced his chariot and, mounting another vehicle, then departed. 26.88–89.
Then Hari, intent on destroying the strength of his enemies led by Karṇa and headed by the son of Droṇa, blew his resonant conch Pāñcajanya as he strove for victory over his foes.
That Pāñcajanya, its interior completely filled by the breath from Acyuta’s mouth, emitted a sound that issued forth intensely.
It made the world, including Viriñci, the Lord of the Gods, and Indra, tremble as if at the end of an eon.
And when the roar of the Gāṇḍīva had been thus overwhelmed, Yudhiṣṭhira, overcome with fear, approached the grandson of Śini and said:
"O son of Śinī, while Pārtha is fighting the enemy army himself, Keśava is [also] fighting."
"The sound of the Gāṇḍīva is not heard today; instead, the sound of the Pāñcajanya is heard.
Therefore, go and find out whether that Pārtha still lives, for he must be here alone.
Thus addressed, O brahmins, Sātyaki honored the priests with wealth and desired their supreme blessing.
Having accepted the vanguard of their army for victory, he advanced followed by Bhīmasena. But Bhīma, having pierced the front of the army with his arrows, caused Yuyudhāna to enter that host.
While fighting, disregarded by his preceptor, he slew the charioteer and put the enemy ranks to flight.
Then the strength of that Sātyaki increased through the blessings of the brahmins and also by the grace of Kṛṣṇa;
for on that very day, his strength had been granted to increase by the pleased Kṛṣṇa in the past.
Then, with his great strength thus augmented, Sātyaki halted Bhīma and proceeded on his chariot.
As he was striking down that army on all sides in battle with showers of arrows, the son of Hṛdika advanced against him.
An exceedingly fierce combat took place between the two; there, Sātyaki deprived him of his chariot.
Having conquered him, the fierce bowman Sātyaki proceeded onward, passing over the heads of the youths.

While Satyaki was cutting him down with arrows, Jalasandha, mounted upon the neck of an elephant, came forward in battle to fight him. Having struck down that Asaṅga— who was indeed irresistible and of great prowess— with his shafts in the encounter, Satyaki agitated the army of the Kurus, slaughtering their elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry.
Having struck down the mountain-dwellers who rained down boulders and having routed all the soldiers,
that mighty one whose banner bears the sacrificial post quickly approached Keśava and Phalguna;
between those two there occurred a battle that was exceedingly terrible, long-lasting, wonderful, great, and fearsome.
Having struck down each other’s horses, felled their charioteers, and cut away their bows, the two of them,
wielding large shields and great swords, encountered one another as they moved through marvelous maneuvers in the battle.
That son of Somadatta, having thrown Sātyaki to the ground in the fight and seized him by the hair—
377. With his foot he stepped upon the man’s chest and seized his sword, intending swiftly to sever his head.
But Vāsudeva, whose eyes behold all things, seeing this in the battle, quickly said to Dhanañjaya, “Protect Śaineya! And he too severed the other’s arm with a broad-headed arrow. 26.103.
With his arm and sword severed by him, he censured Pārtha and sat down upon the earth;
having sat down to fast unto death upon a bed of arrows, he meditated on Hari while censuring [Arjuna] for the entry of the asura.
When the asura-possession had departed, and as he continued to meditate on that Garuḍa-bannered Lord out of extreme devotion, 26.104.
Though being restrained by Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, and the others, Śaineya rose up and struck off his head (26.105).

Then Kṛṣṇa gave his own chariot, prepared for this very purpose, along with its driver, to Sātyaki. At that time, the horses of Pārtha were afflicted by thirst; therefore, Pārtha discharged the Vāruṇa weapon (26.106).
He created a supreme bathing place with that very [blood], as well as a horse-stable in the form of an arrow.

Then, having released the horses there, Hari caused them to drink; meanwhile, the son of Vasava struck down his enemies. The Lord Kṛṣṇa again yoked the horses to the chariot—horses whose fatigue had vanished and from whom the arrows had been removed.
Standing upon that chariot urged on by him, Bībhatsu once again fought the enemies in that very same manner.
But when the hero of the Śinis had departed, Yudhiṣṭhira became once more overwhelmed with anxiety;
he said to Bhīma, "The sound of the Gāṇḍīva is not heard, nor is the roar of the Pāñcajanya."
"Commanded by me, Sātyaki has gone; I consider his burden to be even greater.
Therefore, O Bhīma, go and protect both Pārtha and Yuyudhāna, if they still live.
Thus addressed, Vṛkodara said to him: "Pārtha cannot be protected by Vāsudeva alone."
Even Brahmā and Īśāna would be capable of conquering him; what need then mention the archers such as the son of Droṇa and Karṇa?
Therefore, by the grace of Hari, there is no fear for Dhanañjaya nor for Sātyaki.
However, you alone must be protected by me here today, for this Droṇa is striving to capture you.
Thus addressed, Yudhiṣṭhira said to him: "As long as Ghaṭotkaca lives and Dhṛṣṭadyumna—the foremost among those skilled in weapons—is alive, Droṇa will never be able to bring me under his power here.
If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, go quickly against the son of Pṛthā and Sātyaki. (26.113)
"Protect my consciousness even from the lion's roar; O Bhīma, ensure that I remain conscious when the son of Pṛthā and the grandson of Śini behold me.

Furthermore, once Jayadratha has been slain, restore my consciousness"—having been thus addressed by him, Bhīma duly appointed the son of Hiḍimbā as the protector of his life and the commander of the army.
And that general said: "O Bhīma, proceed to where Keśava and Arjuna are.
As long as I am alive, Droṇa is not capable of overpowering the king; for I am his death.
While he was speaking thus, Bhīma, the wielder of the mace, repeatedly took leave of the king.
With his bow strung, he advanced against the enemy's army, raining down continuous volleys of arrows. Drona, who showered a rain of shafts, checked him and spoke these words to Bhima:
"Out of affection for my pupil, the son of Vasava [Arjuna] and Satyaki have been released by me; they both hold me in high regard."
"Indeed, my own promise was made by me for the sake of Pārtha regarding the protection of Saindhava:
'I shall by no means grant you passage; behold the divine and wonderful power of my weapons!
Having spoken these words, Bhīma took up his mace and hurled it at Droṇa’s chariot.
And he said: "I have always honored you like a father; I have been gentle toward you and never otherwise.

But behold what kind of power I possess when I am not mild! At that, Vṛkodara’s chariot—along with its driver, horses, banner, machinery, and pole—was instantly pulverized by the blow of his mace. (26.120–121)
Seeing the mace rushing toward him, Droṇa leaped lightly onto the surface of the earth;
at that very moment, mounting another chariot sent by Duryodhana, he showered arrows.
Being rained upon by his arrows, which were consecrated with supreme mantras, the son of the Earth-shaker (Bhīma) [was overwhelmed].
Placing his head forward like a bull, Bhīma quickly leaped down from the chariot;
having reached him with the speed of thought, he seized the chariot and in an instant hurled it into the sky.
This was done solely to make it clearly known to him: "Though I am capable, I do not slay you out of respect. (26.123–124)
That chariot, drawn by excellent horses, fell shattered upon the earth; though heavy, Droṇa leaped down from it.
Then Viśoka brought him another chariot, and Bhīma, of noble prowess, mounted it.
Droṇa also, having ascended another chariot provided by Duryodhana, proceeded against Yudhiṣṭhira.

The commander of the army restrained the king as he was advancing with the intent to seize him. Having rallied his own army, which had been torn apart by Droṇa’s arrows, the son of Drupada once more checked Droṇa with his shafts and put to flight the enemy host while the latter looked on.
Between those two, the son of Pāṇḍu and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, both desiring victory, there occurred an exceedingly fierce battle—

most wonderful, with a continuous rain of arrows, incessant, for a very long time, and without distinction. Then Bhīmasena, of immeasurable prowess, advanced, crushing the army of the Kuru king with his shafts.
Twelve preeminent heroes among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, headed by Vinda and Anuvinda, assailed him;
though pierced by their many arrows, Vṛkodara simultaneously severed their heads. When those foremost archers had been slain, Satyavrata, Purumitra, and Jaya [remained].
Vṛndāraka and Paurava—these ministers approached Bhīma on behalf of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

26.130 Being overwhelmed by their arrows, he simultaneously took up sharp *vipāṭha* shafts; with those very same weapons, he struck off their heads. When they were slain, the others fled in all directions. 26.131
Like a lion, having routed the small deer on all sides, he approached his enemies in battle;
but having been warded off by him with arrows, he was in an instant deprived of his chariot, horses, and charioteer.
Deeply pierced by Vṛkodara, he abandoned the fight and retreated in a moment. (26.132)
Having quickly defeated the son of Hṛdika, Bhīma then put that army to flight;
sending all the men, horses, and elephants toward Yama, he went to the side of Hari and Pārtha.
Upon merely seeing Kṛṣṇa and Vijaya (Arjuna), he was exceedingly delighted, and he was both gazed upon and addressed by them.
Hearing the lion-roars, that king of foremost intelligence felt supreme joy, yet he gave the king [Duryodhana] the impression of fear.
Even as Bhīma roared with a great sound, some met their death, discharging excrement, urine, and blood;
while all the kings were terrified, Karṇa and the Dhārtarāṣṭras led by Vikarṇa quickly fled.
Having slain Vikarṇa and Citrasena there, he shattered the chariot of the Sun’s son (Karṇa).
Again assailed by terrible arrows, Karṇa fled swiftly from Bhīma.
Having rested for a very long time, he once more advanced toward Bhīma to fight, along with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others.
Having likewise struck them down there, Karṇa was deprived of his horses and weapons; yet in an instant, he advanced again.
Even the most heroic sons, such as Vikarṇa and Citrasena, had their necks severed by Bhīma’s arrows while Karṇa looked on.
Twenty-three warriors fell from their chariots onto the surface of the earth, desiring to assist Karṇa;
and twenty-one times he was deprived of his horses, charioteer, chariot, and standard.
Severely afflicted by Bhīma’s sharp arrows in that battle,
and having reached a state where his very life was in peril while all the world looked on,
he fled from the field, weeping again and again out of distress. (26.140–141)

In the twenty-second battle, however, having mounted the radiant and impenetrable chariot given by Rāma, and having taken up the bow Vijaya as well as the two quivers of inexhaustible arrows— all of which had been bestowed by him— 26.142.
The bull-like Karṇa, son of Vaikartana, encountered Bhīma in battle.
That encounter between Bhīma and Karṇa was most terrible and lasted for a long time;
they both covered the very sky with showers of arrows, their eyes blood-red as they struck one another.
"Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, joined by his two brothers,
