would be able to slay you easily with your earrings and armor.
To inform him of this, [he gave] those earrings and the armor.
Having torn him apart with arrows in battle, he felled him to the ground.
(26.146) Thus making it known, "I shall strike you down after drawing you away," he again afflicted him with many sharp arrows. (26.147)

Then the thought occurred to Bhīma, who was no longer competing: "Indeed, victory over all was granted to him by Rāma; yet this Karṇa does not fight with me out of rivalry, for he is in a state of distress.
Nevertheless, through his extreme favor toward me, the Blessed One grants me victory, setting aside his own word. (26.148)
"Since I have always held the words of Hari as worthy of honor, I shall today grant an opening to my enemy.

Having remembered this, Karna cut through the bow at that vulnerable point with the power of his weapon, while displaying his own strength, he then severed the reins and the horses of the chariot. 26.149–26.150.
"I have no need for chariots or even my bow," Vṛkodara proclaimed;
then, with his supreme heroism and splendor, he leapt into the sky and in an instant mounted Karṇa’s chariot.
Terrified, Karṇa then hid behind the pole of his chariot, and from there Vṛkodara descended upon him from the vehicle.
Having leaped down to demonstrate his own power in subduing enemies even while unarmed,
he did not wish to seize, nor even to slay him in battle, nor to carry off his chariot or bow;
for although he was exceedingly capable, out of devotion to him he disregarded Rāma’s words, just as Droṇa had previously done.
In order to fulfill his promise to Indra, out of respect for Karna’s devotion to Viṣṇu,

and desiring to provide an opening for the son of the Sun, he went forth and stood at a distance to discharge his arrow. Then Karna, recognizing that Vṛkodara had gone far away and understanding the words of Rāma, [acted accordingly].
He pierced them with arrows, and Karṇa warded them off with dead elephants and cut them down.

Approaching Bhīma as he was casting aside the lifeless elephants and touching him with his bow, Karṇa addressed him with harsh words, making him hear the insults of Suyodhana for the sake of pleasing him, even though he was well aware of Bhīma’s prowess. (26.155–156)
Then Arjuna struck down Bhīma, who was uttering harsh words, with his excellent arrows;
deprived of his armor and scorched by the shafts of Pārtha, Bhīma fled toward his own chariot.
Karna did not wish to release the Vāsavi weapon at Bhīma, nor did he wish to use it against anyone other than Bībhatsu.
"I shall kill him," he said to Kuntī; for although Bhīma was unslayable by her, she nevertheless spoke thus.
Even the Nārāyaṇa weapon, when brought down upon his head, did not burn so much as a single hair of his, despite having remained there for a long time.
What power, then, could the Vāsavi weapon or any other great missile or weapon exert against him? (26.158–159)

Bhīma, having reached Karṇa’s chariot, did not wish to discharge his spear, knowing Keśava’s intention [that it should be used] for the death of the son of Hiḍimbā (Ghaṭotkaca). Thereupon, Karṇa, mounting another chariot, advanced against Arjuna. 26.160.

"Arjuna, with his mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, might seize the divine chariot and the bow. Fearing this, Śalya took up that spear for the sake of Arjuna's death; yet he did not place the chariot, the bow, and the spear together in one place. (26.161)
Thinking that "if one is taken away, the other might be," he was overwhelmed by fear;
he was constantly afraid of Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor due to his policy.
At the time of death, he was indeed certain of dying [in] that chariot. (26.162)
Having mounted [the chariot], he indeed went forth previously, for he did not reckon the time of death.
But Kṛṣṇa, having observed that power residing in his chariot, stationed Pārtha and Satyaki as well to fight;
having given his own chariot to the son of Virocana and having bestowed upon him strength, he commanded him.

Thinking, "This disciple of mine is incapable of challenging Pārtha here," he looked toward Sātyaki and fought him out of sheer rivalry; yet Sātyaki deprived him of his chariot with that very same [weapon], while he himself remained on his chariot drawn by bay horses. No one standing in Keshava’s chariot ever suffers defeat.
And for this reason, Sātyaki did not suffer defeat here at the hands of Karṇa.
"At the time of taking up weapons, however, there should be a vow for princes"—
this was said by the son of Jamadagni, who was formerly accomplished in the science of archery.
This act of slaying his enemy was previously unaccomplished and kept secret;
it was not contrary to righteousness, it brought satisfaction to Rāma, and it caused no harm to the world. Therefore, Bhīma undertook this vow.
When Tūbara said, "I shall kill him," the Lord replied in private, "No;
for the sake of the world's lack of distress, let my circle of beard be well-manifested.
For no one would speak thus of me if I were clearly bearded. (26.169)
Arjuna understands from affection that which Bhīma spoke to him in private;
and when told by Arjuna, "Give me the Gāṇḍīva bow," he replies, "I shall slay [the foe]"—
this too Bhīma alone understands, and no one else.
For Duryodhana already knew from Nārada about the previous arrival of the Gāṇḍīva; moreover, he overheard Bhīmasena’s vow as he spoke it in private to Phalguna, and he told that very thing to Karṇa.
Because of that, he was called "Tūbara" (the Bald One); yet, this name was uttered merely to provoke his anger. Therefore, he spoke to Arjuna:
"Do you know my vow? Likewise, I know yours. (26.173)
In this matter, Vaikartana has become one who must be slain by me;
furthermore, his slaughter was promised by you as well, with my approval.
Therefore, this son of a Sūta must be killed either by you or by me.
Thus addressed, the son of Vāsava said: "He must indeed be slain by me alone;
since I am yours, what is done by me shall be as if done by you. What is done by you would not be as if done by me, because you are my guru. (26.176)
"Therefore, he must be slain by me alone," saying this, he spoke to Karṇa:
"While Kṛṣṇa was listening, Bhīma was made to hear harsh words;
and Abhimanyu, though alone, was struck down by you all acting together. (26.177–178)
"Therefore, I shall slay you and your son right before your eyes.
Having been addressed thus, Karṇa mounted another chariot and protected Jayadratha;
yet Arjuna was unable to kill him, as he was shielded by both the son of Droṇa and Karṇa.
Thereupon, the son of Droṇa exerted his utmost speed in warding off Pārtha;
yet, despite his efforts, Phalguna was unable to overcome him.
A battle ensued between the two that was long-lasting, wonderful, swift, and skillful.
Having seen that, while the sun was turning red, when Drona’s son had not yet been conquered and Jayadratha had not been slain, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa,
desiring victory for Arjuna, unleashed a powerful darkness. (26.182)
When the sky was shrouded in darkness, they all, led by the son of Droṇa, thought the sun had set and took their rest;
meanwhile, Jayadratha gazed upon the face of Arjuna, whose vow had been fulfilled.
Then, at the command of Hari, the son of Indra severed Jayadratha’s head with an arrow.

Then Janārdana, appearing like one about to enter the fire, spoke these words to him: "Do not let this head fall upon the earth. Thus addressed, and struck by the power of the dust-throwing weapon, he held it back with arrows whose feathers met feather to feather; then the one whose banner is Garuḍa spoke these words to him again.
"Let this [head] be placed in the hand of his father, for this boon was granted to him by him long ago:
'May he whose head you cut off fall to the ground, and may his head be split into a thousand pieces.
When these words were spoken by him as he performed his evening rites, even his father became an object of execution.
The son of Vasava placed that head on his lap and, out of agitation, cast it down upon the earth.
Then his head shattered into a thousand pieces, and Hari once again brought about the dissolution of darkness.
At that very moment, as the sun was seen by all, there arose a great cry of "Alas! Alas! (26.187–188).
Then Bhīma, having conquered the sons of Śalya and Suyodhana as well as Kṛpa, let out a most terrifying roar;
and the descendant of Śini (Sātyaki), being satisfied, rendered assistance to Phalguna once his enemy was slain.
Then Kṛṣṇa joyfully blew the Pāñcajanya conch, and Pārtha blew the Devadatta.
Hearing Bhīma’s roar along with the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, and knowing that the King of the Sindhus had been slain,
the King, the son of Dharma, rejoiced, while Duryodhana then became deeply distressed. Then Bhīma advanced against the entire army led by the son of Droṇa.
Then that army, with Karṇa as its leader, was shattered by Pārtha;
26.191 / led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, they entered the broken ranks and reached that place where Bhīma and Dhanañjaya were. 26.192 /
Then all the Pāṇḍavas, united with the Somakas, put the enemies to flight; terrified, they fled in all directions.
Seeing that army being routed, King Duryodhana—

Enraged by the slaughter of Jayadratha, he rushed toward his enemies. Alone, he rained showers of arrows upon Bhīmasena, Dhanañjaya, Yudhiṣṭhira, the two sons of Mādravatī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Sātyaki, and all the sons of Draupadī.

They pierced him with many stone-tipped arrows, but disregarding them, he cut down their bows with his shafts; in that battle, he deprived the great car-warriors of their chariots and rendered the two Yamas (the twins) carless.
Taking up other bows, they too rained down floods of arrows upon Duryodhana.

Without even thinking, he alone warded off all those arrows with his own shafts. Seeing him penetrating the midst of many enemies, with Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, and Kṛpa as their leaders, they all guarded him, incessantly discharging volleys of arrows from their bows.
Suyodhana said to Karṇa, "Slay this Bhīma in battle!
He replied, "Indeed, he cannot be conquered even by the gods led by Vāsava.
O King, I survive by chance, having fought while being excessively tormented by him."
Therefore, we shall strive according to our power; for victory is ordained by destiny.
(26.200) Duryodhana said to Droṇa: "O Preceptor, through your neglect, Jayadratha has been slain by Pārtha, and my army has been destroyed by Bhīma and Sātyaki. (26.201)
"And your vow has been abandoned by you out of affection for the Pāṇḍavas.
Thus addressed, Droṇa became enraged and then made a vow:
"From now on, neither by night nor by day, nor at any time, shall I ever [withdraw] from the battle. (26.202)

"I shall go, and I will not be released from my armor by any means. "And you must tell my son: 'Do not leave any of the Pāñcālas remaining, including their daughter's sons. Having said this at the onset of night, he plunged into the fray.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna advanced against the army of the enemy, and the son of Māruta (Bhīma) swiftly rendered both the son of Droṇa and Duryodhana carless there;
while all the kings looked on, he put that host to flight. 26.205.
There were seven akṣauhiṇīs in each of the two armies;
of these, three were slain by Bhīma and two by Phalguna. In their midst, Śakra was struck down by the sixteen [heroes] headed by Saubhadra and Sātyaki.
Then Śakra struck off the tenth part with the leaders headed by Haiḍimba and Pārṣata;
and when Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the son of Droṇa were slain together, he struck off two parts; and when all the others joined together, he struck off yet another fourth part. (26.207–208)
Then at night, having arrayed their forces in battle formation with five *akṣauhiṇīs* each, the sons of Pṛthā and the Kauravas engaged in a most terrible combat.
As Bhīma was putting the army to flight, Karṇa once again approached him. (26.209)
In the presence of Karṇa, Bhīma instantly crushed Duṣkarṇa and Karṇa—the two younger brothers of Duryodhana—with his foot;
along with their chariots, poles, banners, and drivers, they both vanished from sight. (26.210)
"You spoke these words to me, a man, saying 'I am unarmed';
at that time, being unarmed, I was unable to strike you with my feet.
Thus did Bhīma signal to Karṇa on the ground by means of signs.
He crushed the Kalinga with his foot and struck him with his fist alone.
What need is there for me to say, "I am capable of slaying you with my fist"?
Rather, the Lord did this to make it known that you have been protected by me.
The Kalinga king, whose chariot was destroyed along with its horses, driver, and banner, was crushed by Bhīma’s fist;
and his father Ketumān, as well as Śakradeva and Śrutāyudha,
were struck down by Bhīma together with an akṣauhiṇī of troops.
Formerly, during a sword-fight while Bhīṣma was acting as commander-in-chief,
he slew many of Karṇa’s younger brothers, beginning with Dhruva, in the night; then,
recognizing that Bhīma had regained consciousness, he hurled another *sakti* spear at him.
"Karna, it was because that divine spear was not released by me that you live.
Having realized this, Bhima then instantly leapt into the air, seized the spear, and quickly hurled it back at Karna.

"If that *śakti* was released by you then, it will destroy you"—wishing to make this known and desiring to protect his ear, he then released it upon his right arm; thereupon, having split through the earth, it [pierced] him. (26.217)

Having pierced through [the enemy], he entered, displaying an example for all to see. Then Bhīma, once again mounting his own chariot and wielding his bow, put the enemies to flight from all sides in front of Karṇa.
Karna warded him off with straight-knotted arrows;
Bhima, for his part, hurled a mace with great force at Karna’s chariot.
To counter that blow from the mace, he [Karna] discharged the Sthūṇākarṇa weapon.
Repelled by that weapon, the mace returned toward Bhīma.
Taking up his mace, Bhīma ascended Karna’s chariot and crushed the pole of Karna’s chariot with it.
"Thus you are capable of crushing me, yet you live only because of my desire for you.
Having thus demonstrated this, he returned once more to his own chariot;
then, with Karṇa at the forefront, he struck down the army many times in battle.
Karna, however, leaving him aside, rushed toward Sahadeva. Having deprived him of his chariot and hung his bow around his neck, Karna reviled him many times; he, for his part, fell into despondency.
Remembering his own words to Pṛthā, Karṇa did not wish to kill him;
having defeated him in battle, Karṇa struck the army of the sons of Pṛthā.
Then the son of Droṇa, with various multitudes of arrows, struck Pārtha’s host from all sides.
Being struck by him who was skilled in battle, she found no peace, like a people afflicted by death.
(26.227) Seeing his army overwhelmed by the power of the son of Droṇa, Ghaṭotkaca challenged him to combat.
The son of Droṇa said to him: "Enough, enough! My child, you must not fight your father today. (26.228)
Thus addressed, he said: "You are not my father; even if you were to take refuge with my enemy, you are still my foe.
To him he replied: "If you consider me an enemy, then I shall do as you wish.
Having spoken thus, he drew his bow, which shone like Indra’s rainbow, and loosed a torrent of arrows.
The Rākṣasa of fierce impetuosity approached, and he too advanced against him with his own army.
Surrounded by a hundred thousand Rākṣasas and by many well-trained heroic men, that powerful Rākṣasa,
with a force equal to an Akṣauhiṇī, agitated the preceptor’s son with his arrows.
Afflicted by those many arrows, his limbs pierced and his body drenched in blood,
he turned his eyes in anger, drew his great bow, and made the night dark with his shafts.
In a mere moment, discharging great torrents of arrows, he brought that akṣauhiṇī army and those rākṣasas as well to destruction.
And he led away the son of Ghaṭotkaca, who had previously been the enemy named Añjanavarmā.

(26.233) Beholding his army and his own son struck down, Ghaṭotkaca pierced the son of Droṇa deeply with an arrow. He, however, being overwhelmed, took refuge behind his banner; but quickly regaining consciousness, he stood firm. (26.234)
Rising up, he fixed upon his bow an arrow resembling the staff of Yama, drew it back, and released it at the Rākṣasa.
Struck by that shaft, Ghaṭotkaca fell senseless upon his own chariot.
As the world looked on, his charioteer carried him far away from the battle while he lay unconscious.
And the son of Droṇa put to flight the army of the Pāṇḍavas and Somakas at night with those excellent arrows.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, having regained consciousness, entered the Kaurava host in a rage;
he scattered them with showers of arrows and made the great car-warriors tremble.
At that very moment, seeing Vaikartana arrive to fight against Pārtha, Hari, the Lord of the World,
dispatched Ghaṭotkaca to hurl a fierce *śakti* at him for the sole purpose of protecting Pārtha.
He challenged Karṇa and fought with him, and thereafter he fought those who were led by Duryodhana.
Droṇa alone held them back in battle and crushed them even more severely (26.239).

Though they were repeatedly oppressed by that stronger warrior, they fought against him placing Karṇa at their head. Karṇa, the knower of great weapons, did not waver there in battle, relying upon his own prowess (26.240).
Then Bhīma, the son of Śatamanyu, warded off the son of his preceptor from the Trigartas.
At that very moment, a Rākṣasa named Alambala arrived to slay the son of Bhīma. Having fought and seized him, Ghaṭotkaca then struck him down upon the surface of the earth with his sword.
Having cut off the head of Suyodhana, he threw it down; thereupon all the protectors of the earth were filled with grief.
Then Alāyudha, of fierce prowess, arrived; Ghaṭotkaca rushed against that slayer of men.
Having fought with him for a moment, he struck him down to the ground and made him a sacrificial victim.
Then, having severed his head, he hurled it in anger at Duryodhana’s chest;
by that act, all those led by Duryodhana were thrown into confusion—
[he who], though capable in battle, acted for the sake of Ghaṭotkaca’s renown.
"He was not slain by Bhīmasena; he has been slain by the son of Bhīmasena. 26.245 They all urged Karṇa to release his spear:
"If he is slain, everyone is slain; what can Pārtha do to us? 26.246
Thus being repeatedly urged by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
while being struck by the son of Hiḍimbā and himself severely afflicted, he seized a massive spear esteemed by Indra, the subduer of Pāka. (26.247)
He hurled at Ghaṭotkaca— who stood in the sky like a mountain, possessed of incomparable prowess—
that weapon resembling the tongue of Death, which utterly scorched the intermediate and cardinal directions.
With his chest pierced by it, he fell, crushing the enemy's army even as he was being slain.
When he was slain, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra rejoiced, they shouted aloud, and they shook their garments.
Then Keśava danced and embraced Phalguna;
he blew his conch shell, laughed, and let out a roar like that of a lion.
Guḍākeśa, dejected in mind, asked him: "What is this?
O Lord, now that our heroic son and eldest brother has been slain, why do you rejoice?
The Blessed Kṛṣṇa said to him: "By good fortune you live, O Phalguna!"
"For your sake, my attachment was set aside and indeed released upon this Rākṣasa.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, overcome by grief and indignation, turned toward Karṇa; thereupon the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke to him.
"The very weapon by which Arjuna was to have been slain has instead killed this Rākṣasa. Therefore, O Indra among kings, do not grieve; by good fortune, Phalguna lives.
Having said this, Vyāsa departed, and then the battle resumed. 26.254.
While the army of the Kurus was being slaughtered here by Bhīma and Arjuna, and the Pāṇḍava forces by others, all the warriors, though holding lamps in their hands, fell under the power of sleep.
Seeing them thus, Dhanañjaya then said: "Let them sleep as long as the light of the moon remains."
Having thus been addressed, they all offered their blessings to Phalguna and fell asleep as they had been positioned.
When the moon rose again, they returned to the battle, raining down weapons and great missiles.
Somadatta and Bhuri arrived there and that single warrior fought against both of them, including Satyaki.
Slain by him, those two fell to the ground; meanwhile, Bāhlīka fought him in battle.
Having deprived Sātyaki of his chariot, that hero quickly released an arrow for his slaughter.
Bhīmasena cut that arrow into three pieces, and Bāhlīka hurled a *śataghnī* at him.
Struck by her and rendered unconscious, Vṛkodara slew him with his mace, and he fell down.
(26.259) Previously, Bāhlīka had requested Bhīma with affection: "If you desire my welfare, you alone must slay me in battle. (ccclxxxiv)
"Then I shall obtain fame, righteousness, and the world," [Yudhiṣṭhira said].
To him who had spoken thus, Bhīma, being deeply distressed at that time, replied:
"I would not slay him otherwise; only in battle would that be service to you."
Thus was Bāhlīka slain there by Bhīmasena. (26.261) When Bāhlīka had been killed, the Kauravas—led by Karṇa and Duryodhana—rushed toward Bhīmasena.
Placing the son of Droṇa and their preceptor at their head, the son of Pṛṣata, together with his brothers, advanced against them along with Sātyaki. (26.262)
Pārtha fought against the Śaptakas alone; that battle was fierce and wonderful.
There, in that night-battle, an entire *akṣauhiṇī* was slaughtered by Bhīma and Arjuna.
Then, as the sun rose, Droṇa performed a most terrible deed in the fight.
Having entered the multitude of Pāñcāla chariots, he slew elephants, horses, chariots, and men.
Great car-warriors, put to flight by him in the darkness of arrows, found no refuge at all.
Though aged, he moved in battle like a youth; he was a fierce archer and a master of supreme weapons.
By him, who was fierce in battle, a hundred million chariots were destroyed there, and then a thousand times that many men;
furthermore, ten times that number of horses and a hundred million elephants were slain. Likewise, in the midst of the great conflict, he sent Virāṭa and Drupada to the other world with two arrows.

Then, having conquered the son of the preceptor and the others, Bhīmasena protected Dhṛṣṭadyumna. Protected by Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna made a great effort to slay Droṇa; the preceptor warded him off with a shower of arrows, and he [Dhṛṣṭadyumna] likewise [warded him off] with a shaft.
Struck by that [arrow], the brahmin fell into a swoon and quickly collapsed;
Dhrishtadyumna, swiftly seizing sword and shield, mounted his excellent chariot.
Then, having regained consciousness, the preceptor tormented him with showers of arrows the size of a span.
Greatly pained by them, he turned away from that chariot and mounted his own.
Those two, firmly grasping their weapons, once again engaged in battle, raining down showers of arrows like clouds pouring rain.
Having warded off the enemy with his shafts, the twice-born one discharged the Brahmā weapon.
With that [weapon], he consumed many Pāñcālas in battle;
Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and others were then slain by it.
Bhīma, Arjuna, and Sātyaki took turns attacking the son of the Preceptor.
Accompanied by a vast army, they held them back from afar;
Karna, Duryodhana, and the others, as well as Śalya, Bhoja, and Kṛpa, were likewise turned back.
Then Bhīma and Arjuna, with a torrent of arrows, held them at bay in the battle.

There, Bhīma slew the elephant division and Jayatsena, the king of Magadha, as well as a great many hosts of Magadhan charioteers. Then [he slew] the elephant named Aśvatthāman belonging to the king of Mālava.
Seeing that Aśvatthāman had been slain, King Yudhiṣṭhira, urged on by Vāsudeva, proclaimed, "Aśvatthāman is killed!
Having heard of the slaughter of Aśvatthāman, he himself said, "I will not fight. (26.275)
Droṇa said to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, as previously mentioned:
"Tell the truth. He replied, "The truth. But he spoke in a whisper, "And the elephant. Thereupon, Droṇa became distressed.
Seizing his chariot pole, Bhīma said, "Such a thing is not worthy of you, who are always virtuous; living off the wealth of others is never appropriate.
Then the sages, stationed in the sky, said to him, "Enough! Desist! (26.278).

Having understood all that, Droṇa spoke it; he then laid aside his weapons. Having renounced all activities and ascended to yoga, meditating upon Vāsudeva—the Supreme Lord of all, eternally free from defect—he cast off his body and went to his own abode.
Keśava, the Pāṇḍavas, and Gautama beheld him traveling through the sky toward his own world.
Though Dṛṣṭadyumna was being restrained by the Pāṇḍavas, he went there taking up his sword and shield;
having severed his [the opponent’s] head with the blade, he quickly mounted his own chariot once again.
Seeing this, Kṛpa, deeply afflicted by fear, fled away mounted upon a single horse.
When Droṇa’s head had been severed,
the son of Vāsava (Arjuna) censured Yudhiṣṭhira and the Pāñcālya prince, and Sātyaki was likewise filled with wrath.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, however, asked, "How was Bhūriśravas slain?
At this, the enraged Sātyaki, mace in hand, rushed toward him; the Pāñcālya prince, sword girded and undaunted, challenged him. (26.283)
Then Bhīma, urged by Kṛṣṇa, seized Śaineya;
and Pārtha, constrained by his affection for the Pāñcāla king, was pacified. 26.284.
Instructed then by Vāsudeva, they once again attained their former supreme affection.
Then, as they were prepared for battle, the son of Droṇa also arrived, bow in hand.
Having heard that his father had been slain, he made a vow to annihilate all his enemies without exception;
then, out of anger, he discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon, and everyone became terrified except for Bhīma.

Yudhiṣṭhira, his mind despondent, said, "Let all of them, led by the descendant of Śini, return; I shall remain here with my brothers, submerged as I am in the supreme weapon of Droṇa’s son. To this Keśava replied: "Bow down to the weapon, and then you shall be released from it. Thereupon, Dhananjaya and the others prostrated themselves.
None of them fell upon his head; rather, like fire remaining within fire, he stood firm.
Even as Bhīma was not being consumed by the fire that stood there like a flame, Pārtha, for the sake of seeking refuge for himself, enveloped him with a *vāruṇa* weapon.
There was no benefit from wrapping the weapon outside the body of one whose weapon had already fallen;
nevertheless, Phalguna, overcome by affection, wrapped it [around Bhīma]. (26.290) [He did so] to ensure the infallibility of his own weapon and the invincibility of Bhīma.

Accomplishing his purpose, Kṛṣṇa, together with Arjuna, ascended Bhīma’s chariot, which had been encircled by the Vāruṇa weapon and was now situated on the outside; for Keśava, due to his association with him, and Phalguna, due to his human nature, [were both protected]. 26.291–292.
Then that weapon did not strike them once they had been made to descend from their chariot by him,
and when Bhīma’s weapons were cut away, that weapon attained pacification;
for Vṛkodara was devoted to the pure duties of a Kṣatriya.
Having dismounted from his vehicle, though others bowed down weaponless before him,
he— armed and still mounted on his chariot— fought against those who were unbearable even for the lords of gods,
for it is the duty to restrain friends when they are about to abandon their own dharma. (26.294)
Therefore, he himself said to the others as well, "Do not go.
(26.295) For even a weapon that is worthy of homage must not be saluted by one who desires to live when it is discharged by an enemy in battle; therefore, he did not do so. (26.296)
For Vāyu, the presiding deity of the weapon, is Hari himself;
therefore, because of his formidable nature, he did not burn Agni, who was like fire itself.
At that time, Bhīma showed great respect toward both the weapon and Hari by means of his mind alone.

In accordance with the duty of a warrior (*kṣatradharma*), he did not bow down outwardly. Vāsudeva, possessing infinite power, having successfully employed his own formidable and unfailing weapon, again urged on the horses.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra urged him again to employ that weapon;
but the son of Droṇa, saying "it cannot be done," rushed toward Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Seeing the preceptor’s son approaching, Sātyaki followed Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle.
Both of them pierced [the other] with two arrows and fell down in the battle, unconscious.
As Bhīma approached, the son of Droṇa put his own troops to flight;
Arjuna saw the son of Droṇa rallying them against Bhīma.
Then Arjuna, appearing enraged, advanced to fight him back while uttering harsh words.
Thereupon, the son of Droṇa released the Agneya weapon, by which the army of the Pāṇḍavas was overwhelmed.
An akṣauhiṇī of that host was destroyed there, and Hari bore Pārtha away on his chariot.
Seeing the son of the Lord of the Gods still alive, the son of Droṇa cast aside his bow in anger and rushed toward him;
then Kṛṣṇa, the author of the Vedānta, whose body is the embodiment of the six perfections, approached and said:
"Do not go! You are Śiva himself, born on earth as a powerful being for the sake of the gods. (26.304)
"Furthermore, there is a great task that has been observed; accomplish it quickly for me.
Thus addressed, he said, "So be it," and having prostrated before the source of all Vedas, he departed at dawn.
Suyodhana and the others, bowed down with grief and filled with fear, followed him immediately to the camp.
And all the sons of Pṛthā, filled with joy and praising Janārdana supremely, went to their camp;
there too, during the night, they rejoiced together, recollecting the immeasurable virtues of Hari. 26.307.
Thus ends [the section] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Nārāyaṇa’s Weapon," [ending with] the slaying of Karṇa (ccclxxxix).
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Oṃ! Then, having obtained the permission of the son of Droṇa, King Duryodhana appointed Karṇa as the commander-in-chief; he went forth for battle, baring his teeth in a grimace. 27.1.
There, an exceedingly terrible battle took place between the sons of Pāṇḍu and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra over that elephant.
There, Bhīma appeared like the exceedingly pure sun rising upon the Mountain of Sunrise;
as he was driving back the kings, Kṣemadhūrti approached him and struck his elephant.
Having obtained that intoxication of valor, Bhima swiftly led him to the abode of Death.
Having slain him, the son of the Wind-god cut off the heads of the youths who had sided with the enemy faction;
he threw the hostile army into turmoil, just as a lion agitates a pack of jackals.
Seeing that army being agitated, the son of Droṇa advanced against it on his chariot;
that battle was exceedingly terrible and wonderful, such as had never occurred for anyone anywhere before.
Upon seeing it, the gods, Gandharvas, and Brahmins said, "Never before has such a great battle been seen."
Nor will there ever be another such as this; all others do not equal even a sixteenth part of him.
Such an excellence of knowledge or strength—how could both exist together except for the auspicious Vāyu?
Here, it is the combination of these two: the splendor of both wisdom and physical power. (27.6–27.7)

Thus, as those two best of men were being assailed by the gods with feathered shafts in all directions and across the sky, they rendered it entirely without interval; seeing this, the great car-warriors were struck with fear.
Repelled by the son of the Wind-god at his bow, the son of Droṇa discharged great weapons upon him.
The powerful son of Anila, free from pride, quelled those [missiles] with his own excellent arrows.
Once more, those two fought each other with arrows in a manner that was wonderful, intense, and skillful.
Then, severely afflicted by Bhīmasena’s arrows, the son of Droṇa fell down quickly, unconscious and deeply shaken.

And Bhīma, his body reeling slightly as the son of the Preceptor had already advanced a short distance, quickly shook off the fatigue of battle; taking up his bow and filling the air with his roars, he set out to fight the host of elephants. While he was crushing those elephants, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son [Duryodhana] [attacked] Yudhiṣṭhira.
The two kings went forth for battle and fought for a long time.
There, Yudhiṣṭhira suddenly deprived him of his chariot in the fight;
he took up a heavy mace, and Bhīma, armed with a mace, rushed toward him.
Seeing him, Kṛpa placed him upon his own chariot and departed from there;
at that very moment, Karṇa and Nakula fought fiercely with arrows.
Having deprived Nakula of his chariot, Karṇa then pursued the one who was fleeing.
Having pursued him with speed, he placed his bow around [Nakula's] neck;
but having spoken words to the men out of respect for Kuntī’s command,
he did not strike Nakula at all, and releasing him, he went against the enemies.
Then Satyaki of fierce prowess encountered Vinda and Anuvinda, the two Kaikayas, in battle.
As they both rained down many excellent arrows, a terrible slaughter ensued between them.
Blocked by those two, he suddenly struck off the head of Anuvinda; then Vinda [was also slain].
Then, in that supreme combat, both chariot-warriors fought against one another, O descendant of Śini.
Thereafter, wielding shields and swords, they moved about like two hawks in the sky, having practiced their skills.
Having sliced each other's shields, both, with excellent swords in hand, simultaneously closed in upon one another.
There in the battle, Satyaki struck off Vinda’s head, adorned with earrings, with his hand;
having slain him, he was highly honored by his kinsmen and proceeded against the other enemies, making them tremble.
(27.20) Seeing Kṛpa approaching, [Satyaki thought], "He might afflict me, who am devoted to asceticism."
Thinking thus, the son of Pṛṣata sought refuge with Bhīma. As Karṇa was driving the army back from all sides, the son of Indra (Arjuna) advanced against him;
in an instant, he deprived him of his chariot in battle and then carried away the host.
Having been defeated in battle by the son of Śakra, that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the descendant of the Sun, approached Pārtha;
grasping his arm, he said: "Pārtha has conquered me while I was distracted in the fray. Granted, the chariot and the unbreakable divine bow were given to me by the lord of the Bhr̥gus. (27.23)
"If Śalya were my charioteer, such as Hari is for me, I would slay your enemy," said Sūta’s son when thus addressed. Then, as if enraged, he spoke to Śalya;
Duryodhana, however, by extolling the excellence of the chariot-warrior's charioteer, pacified him.
He who excels in intellect, strength, knowledge, fortitude, and other virtues—
he shall be the charioteer of the warrior, just as Hari was for Arjuna,
or as Brahmā was for Śiva when he formerly consumed Tripura. (27.26)
With these and other words, his charioteer Śalya became as if pacified;
accompanied by him, the son of Ravi (Karṇa) drew up his army in battle array.
As he proceeded toward the fight with pride, he said: "Whatever man shall give Arjuna to me... (27.27).
"If you show him to me, I shall gladly give you wealth without restraint. To him who was saying this repeatedly, Śalya laughed and said:
"He by whom the Nivātakavacas were slain and the Khāṇḍava forest was consumed—"

"What mortal indeed could conquer him, even as you have seen him during the seizure of the cattle? You possess the nature of a crow or a jackal; do not go against him who is like a swan or a lion in battle!
Do not go against Pārtha! Do not go! He has been slain by him and sent to the abode of Yama. (27.29–27.30)
When this was said, the son of the Sun (Karna) severely reviled the Madras;
yet Shalya, declaring that among all peoples there are men who are base, mediocre, and excellent, took up the charioteership for him out of a desire for the welfare of Partha. 27.31.
Then Karṇa, having reached the army of Pārtha on a chariot guided by Śalya, scattered it on all sides with his arrows;
he was protected in battle by Suyodhana, Gautama, and others, as well as by the son of the Preceptor, the best among those skilled in great weapons.
The Pandava host, guarded by Bhīma, the son of Pṛṣata, and the foremost of the Śini clan, showered him with arrows.
Then the son of Sūrya, having pierced the son of Dharma with showers of arrows, further tormented him with sharp shafts.
Having deprived him of his chariot and placed his strung bow around his neck, he spoke harsh words aloud.
Having seen him thus, the son of Māruta, having rendered Duryodhana chariotless and weaponless, struck him violently.
Beholding the king fallen into a state where his life was at stake, the Lord of Madra pointed him out to Karṇa and said:

"He for whose sake you have waged this battle and for whom this army exists—him, who today desires to depart for the abode of Yama, protect quickly from the oppression of Bhīma! Why indeed do you oppress this Yudhiṣṭhira in vain? (27.35)
Having heard his words and disregarding Yudhiṣṭhira, Karṇa, fully intent on protecting the king, advanced.

Upon seeing him, the son of the Wind-god, of immeasurable splendor, rushed toward him in wrath as if wishing to consume Karṇa. Having instructed the bull of the Śinis and the two Pārṣatas to protect the king, he assumed the appearance of one approaching Karṇa.
Just as when Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of Narasiṃha at the end of the eon, was about to swallow Hara while holding the entire universe,
the whole earth trembled from that force and the entire opposing army was put to flight;
so too, struck by the mass of Vaikartana’s arrows, he discharged a shaft resembling a thunderbolt at him.

Struck by him, Karṇa fell like a corpse; Bhīma seized a razor-sharp arrow and advanced on foot. "Even though he is out of my sight, I shall seize and slay that one who utters insults against Hari"—with such a great vow, the son of Vāyu rushed toward the wing of the son of Ravi to cut it off. (27.38–39)
Seeing him approaching nearby, Śalya said, "No," for he was not one whose vow could be proven false by mere reasons:
"O son of Indra, you must yourself slay the son of the charioteer; do not cause him to fall by his own hand, O son of the Maruts.
Having spoken thus in the presence of that [Arjuna], the King of Madra departed on his very chariot.
While all the world looked on, he carried away the son of Vaikartana;
having conquered the son of Surya, Bhima put to flight the entire army of the Kauravas, which was crowded with the son of Drona and Duryodhana.
At that moment, three akṣauhiṇīs were instantly thrown into turmoil by him;
at that very instant, the preceptor’s son arrived at the army of the Pāṇḍavas,
having crushed the entire host and deprived the king of his chariot.
Having deprived Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the twins, Sātyaki, and the sons of Draupadī of their chariots in an instant, he rendered them all weaponless.
Their pride shattered, they fled from the battle; indeed, the sky was filled with arrows following right after them.

As he proceeded performing [his duties], Dharmarāja said to him, "Why do you strike us, who are devoted to our own dharma? Do not harm these kṣatriyas who abide in another's dharma. Thus addressed, he laughed and, leaving them behind, went to where Acyuta and Arjuna were.
While he was fighting there with the Saṃśaptakas, he challenged the son of the Lord of the Gods;
that very heroic one raised his arm, which was equipped with arrows and resembled the king of serpents, for the sake of battle.
Pārtha, having been joined by the hosts of Saṃśaptakas who were seeking combat, [advanced].
Challenged by the son of Droṇa, he indeed asked Kṛṣṇa about his duty;
and Kṛṣṇa urged the horses toward the chariot of the son of Droṇa.
Both of them were the foremost among those skilled in weapons, possessed of great strength, and filled with pride as they encountered one another.
With their arrows, Droṇa and the son of Indra made all the intermediate and cardinal directions shrouded in darkness.

Then the son of Droṇa, continuously discharging unerring arrows from the horses of his chariot, from the hair on their bodies, from the pores of their skin, and from his banner and bow, bound Pārtha within a cage of arrows.
When that [bow] was fixed, the immeasurable Hari awakened the son of the Lord of the Gods;
by embracing him, he bestowed strength upon him, and having risen, he discharged great weapons.
Having warded off those weapons with his own missiles, the son of the Preceptor severed the string of the Gāṇḍīva in battle.
Then he rained arrows upon Pārtha, and another bowstring was attached; he too fixed the Gāṇḍīva to it.
Thereupon, the enraged son of Kuntī, with a sharp arrow, struck off the head of the charioteer of Droṇa’s son, who then took up the charioteering himself.
While he was discharging arrows and even acting as a charioteer,
that son of Pṛthā was bound again by the twice-born one with a mass of arrows;
then Kṛṣṇa embraced him once more, the destroyer of enemies.
Then, O Pārtha, the subduer of enemies rose up from that spot, bearing his bow and arrows;
and he rained down arrows once more upon the son of Droṇa.
The son of Droṇa, having fixed it, again struck his string.
Pārtha cut the reins of Droṇa’s son with his arrows.
Struck again by Pārtha’s shafts, the horses of the son of Droṇa, now devoid of reins, carried him far away from that spot; yet he, having steadied them once more, remained there.

He reflected: "Nothing more than this can be achieved by Arjuna, because of Keshava’s role as his charioteer, because of Hanuman’s presence upon the banner, because of the Gandiva bow, and because of the inexhaustibility of the two quivers. (27.57–58)
"Because the horses are invulnerable and the chariot is likewise impenetrable, even though I am capable of fighting, I will not go against Dhananjaya today.
Having reflected thus, he entered the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu; then [Arjuna] advanced against him.
Between those two, as they rained down fierce volleys of arrows, there occurred a wonderful and great battle.
When eight carts carried their weapons, the son of Droṇa discharged them there in a single eighth part of a day. (27.60–61)
Then, having deprived him of his chariot and severed his bow in the combat,
the son of Droṇa struck off his head, which was adorned with earrings and radiant with a crown. Thereafter, he put the Pāṇḍava army to flight with his arrows.
Then Pārtha also slew the Magadhan named Daṇḍadhāra.

Beholding the army being put to flight by the preceptor’s son, Dhṛṣṭadyumna approached him in haste; he said to that most wicked man, "I shall slay you today in battle, you murderer of your preceptor."
Thus addressed, the son of Pṛṣata displayed his excellent sword, saying:
"This shall be the slayer of your father; he will give you an answer. Having said this, he took up his bow and rained down many arrows.
Between the two of them there occurred a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end.
There, the son of Droṇa, having in an instant deprived the son of Pṛṣata of his chariot and weapons, discharged sharp arrows for the sake of his destruction; yet they did not strike him.
The son of Droṇa, sword in hand, approached and cut through his skin;
then, having felled him to the ground with a bowstring, he pierced that skin—which could not be penetrated even by swords or other weapons—with the blade of his bow. (27.67–68)
Seeing the son of Pṛṣata being drawn away, Pārtha and Bhīma, urged by Kṛṣṇa, struck him from both sides with arrows.
He was severely struck by those two with arrows resembling thunderbolts.
Having abandoned the son of Pṛṣata, he mounted his own chariot again;
and the prince of the Pañcālas also went elsewhere from there. Having mounted another chariot of his own, Dhanvin advanced against Kṛtavarman.
Between those two there occurred a most tumultuous battle, wonderful to behold;
there, without much effort, the Pāñcālya deprived Kṛtavarman of his chariot and weapons, and Gautama carried him away. 27.72.
Then King Duryodhana, a chariot-warrior, advanced against the two sons of Mādrī.
A fierce battle, wonderful to behold, took place between them; there, with little effort, he deprived those two of their chariots. (27.73)
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira himself restrained him;
and in that battle, Duryodhana deprived him of his horses, charioteer, and standard.
Then the impetuous Bhīma went forth again on his chariot toward the son of the Sun who had approached.
And before his very eyes, the hero deprived Duryodhana of his chariot in an instant;
having warded off Karṇa with arrows, he severed the head of Suṣeṇa, the son of that man,
which fell upon the ground near his father, just as Satyasena had been slain by him.
Just as the two younger brothers of Karṇa had previously been struck down before Karṇa himself in the night battle,
so too, upon seeing him slain, the son of Vikartana was overcome with rage; abandoning Bhīmasena,
he advanced, crushing the army, toward Yudhiṣṭhira who was stationed on another chariot yoked with his own horses.
The sons of Kṛṣṇā, joined by the hosts of the Somakas, held back the grandson of Śini and Pārṣata;

having deprived all of them of their chariots in battle, he reached Yudhiṣṭhira, who was accompanied by the twins. Having slain the horses of the son of Dharma in combat, he rendered those two twins weaponless.
He crushed those who had approached in various vehicles again with arrows and fierce words.
At that very moment, for the sake of the king's liberation, Bhīma, having deprived Duryodhana of his chariot,
pierced him in his vital organs with exceedingly sharp shafts and showed him to the son of the Sun.

Then Śalya, leaving the son of Dharma, went to where Karṇa was; Yudhiṣṭhira also, having gone slowly to his camp, lay down there when Karṇa had departed, greedy for the kingdom. At that very moment, the son of Droṇa and Kṛpa also went there; then Bhīma set out against the son of Droṇa and Karṇa.
When Bhīma had gone against the son of Droṇa and Karṇa, Kṛpa placed the king upon his chariot.
When Kṛpa had departed taking the king with him, the son of Droṇa and Karṇa, afflicted by Bhīma,
left him and went toward the army of the Somakas, striking them down with showers of arrows.
Then, disregarding the king there, Dhanañjaya, urged on by Vāsudeva, advanced;
while the son of Pṛṣata, seeing his own army struck down by Karṇa, harassed the Kurus and checked the approaching one whose banner bore the foremost of monkeys. 27.84.
The son of Droṇa and Duḥśāsana both opposed Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Those two great car-warriors rained down showers of weapons and missiles;
Duḥśāsana and the son of Pṛṣata created a darkness born of arrows.
There, Drupada’s son was held back in battle by Duḥśāsana;
though he strove, he was rendered effortless and disarmed in the fight. Then there occurred an exceedingly terrible battle between the son of Droṇa and the wielder of the thunderbolt.
There too, Pārtha was bound by a cage of arrows, for even the string of his Gāṇḍīva bow had been removed.
Then Pārtha, his arm-strength invigorated by Kṛṣṇa, having slain the charioteer of the preceptor’s son,
cut his reins and, with his arrows, drove his horses far away.
But when Pārtha had passed beyond his preceptor’s son and arrived, Karṇa put the army to flight;
Duryodhana, pouring forth a rain of arrows against the sons of Pāṇḍu, followed right after him. Beholding Karṇa approaching and putting his own host to flight—
Taking up another bow, Dhṛṣṭadyumna held him back;
between the two there was a great battle for a long time, equal and unceasing.
At that very moment, the hero Sātyaki held back Duryodhana.
King Duryodhana was checked in battle by Sātyaki;
having slain Sātyaki’s horses, he cut asunder the bow of Draupadi’s son. In that very interval, Karṇa also struck down the horses of the son of Pṛṣata.
While those two were still without their chariots, that Pāṇḍava army was broken.
Seeing his own forces shattered in many ways, Bhīma, whose banner bears the king of beasts,
let out a fierce roar that made the earth tremble and rushed against the army of the Kuru king in battle.
Then, shattered by the roar and the arrows of Vṛkodara, the Kaurava army fled swiftly in all directions; even Suyodhana was deprived of his chariot and weapons in that battle.
Upon seeing this, the army of the Pāṇḍavas turned back, its irresistible momentum swift.
Furthermore, that army of the Kauravas, shattered by her, fled far, even further away (27.97).
Seeing Suyodhana’s force being slaughtered and fleeing in all directions, having sought refuge with Bhīma and the Pāñcālas, the son of Adhiratha blazed up in rage (27.98).
He took up that divine, peerless weapon known as Bhārgava, which was dedicated to Rāma, unfailing, and the destroyer of all other weapons;
and he discharged it with a roar against the armies led by Bhīma.
By the grace of Rāma, that weapon avoided Bhīma;
however, some others fled, while those remaining reached the abode of Yama.
For that weapon does not slay those who are fleeing; thus, along with the son of Pṛṣata, they escaped.

The Pāñcālas, the sons of Draupadī, the Śaineyas, and all the others were left behind in flight; Arjuna, too, seeing that his raised weapon was devoid of a counter-weapon and failing to reach the son of the Sun, [withdrew]. (27.101–102)
"O Vāsudeva, speak this to the son of the Sūta [Karna], excluding him:
'I shall go nowhere else; there is no life for me other than through this weapon.
Having spoken thus to Pārtha, Kṛṣṇa did not reach the son of the Sūta.
The Creator of All led Bhīma along a different path.
There, Arjuna said to Bhīma: "Go to see Yudhiṣṭhira;
learn the news of the king, for the Saṃśaptakas have challenged me to battle."
"Those who remain after being slain will challenge them; I shall go to that battle," so he spoke.
To him, Bhīma, knowing the immeasurable strength of his own arms, replied:
"I alone shall fight the Śaptakas, the son of the Sūta, and the Kauravas; you, however, approach the king."
"I shall not abandon the battlefield and depart from here, nor shall anyone say of me that I am afraid of battle"—
to him who spoke thus, Kṛṣṇa, possessed of infinite power, being pleased, praised his excellent resolve; then Hari, accompanied by Arjuna, went to the camp to see Yudhiṣṭhira.
Seeing them, the king, thinking that Karṇa had been slain, was filled with joy.
Having saluted him, he was told by Pārtha with anger, "I shall kill [you].
Having severely censured Bībhatsu, he said to Kṛṣṇa, "Give me the Gāṇḍīva."
"Give him a son; he shall slay [the enemy], of this there is no doubt.
Or else, Bhīma himself shall strike him down once you have returned.
As for you, O Sūta, you were begotten in vain by Kuntī—a eunuch who has made a false promise. (27.109–110)
"Indeed, I have been tormented by the son of the Sūta, who possesses the energy of the Wind-god.
When addressed thus by the elder brother, saying "I shall live," Vāsudeva, the all-knowing one, then said this: "What is this? (27.111)

Hari said to him: "I have vowed that whoever speaks of giving the Gāṇḍīva shall be slain by me; therefore, I will kill that king. "The speaking of truth is excellent, but the knowledge of truth is difficult to attain. (27.112)
"That which is of ultimate benefit to the virtuous is truth; this is the certainty.
The practice of Dharma is excellent, yet the knowledge of Dharma is difficult to attain.
He who constantly upholds the virtuous—that is Dharma; this is the certainty. (27.113–114)
A brahmin named Kauśika, having falsely accused some villagers of being thieves, fell into hell;
likewise, a certain hunter, having killed a deer for the sake of his parents, [fell into hell]. (27.115)

"Since that evil-minded asura, having come to heaven for the sake of food, now performs penance for the affliction of the world; therefore, having reached the firm conclusion that 'Dharma is the bearer of the good'— " 27.116.
"Do not slay the king; make your word true, and then act accordingly.
Thus addressed in many ways, Arjuna, out of sheer anger, reviled him severely:
"You are cruel, ungrateful, devoid of prowess, and you speak harshly! (27.117)
There is no happiness whatsoever apart from you; you ought not to reproach me.
Bhīma is the one worthy of reproaching me, for he is always our refuge;
he fights against all heroes even now, yet you are a reviler.
Having spoken thus and unsheathed his sword for the sake of killing himself, he was again questioned by Kṛṣṇa and stated his intention.
Having heard that and having censured him, Janārdana spoke once more. (27.120)
By intentionally destroying the body, one incurs great sin;
for it is through the body that the means to achieve dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa exist.
Therefore, do not abandon the body, but rather practice self-praise.

"Killing one's elders, addressing them with 'thou', and praising oneself—these are said to be [the marks of] egoism. Thus addressed, he, out of pride, praised his own numerous virtues. "Censuring one's elders and self-adulation can never lead to dharma."
Nevertheless, Janārdana, desiring to reveal that which was in Arjuna’s heart, and having produced shame in him and caused him to abandon his pride, said:
"I do not know the supreme dharma; Kṛṣṇa alone is my refuge. (27.123–124)
Having thus resolved to destroy his faults,
Hari, the Lord of the World, caused Arjuna to perform all of that.
Then, because of this lack of understanding, the king became exceedingly angry.
"Let King Bhīma be the one to eat; you, being young, kill me yourself, or else I shall go to the forest fruitless. Having said this, he rose from his bed.
Vāsudeva, the leader, having received him and explained everything with reason, pacified him.
And Pārtha fell at the feet of the king, seeking his forgiveness; he too attained great joy.
Those two brothers, having obtained liberation from great danger through the grace of Vāsudeva, were exceedingly delighted.
With devotion, they praised the Lord of All: "O Hari, who indeed is as well-disposed toward us as you? (27.127–128)
Then, having bowed down, Bībhatsu was embraced by his elder brother;
greeted with affection by him with blessings, he set out for battle.
At that time, Hari [spoke to] him, who was anxious about Karṇa’s victory and whose limbs were perspiring.
Having recounted his former deeds, he manifested a special possession by Narasimha;
through that, his fortitude became exceedingly firm.
Then Bhima put the entire enemy force to flight and slaughtered them in battle.

While he himself was making the heroes face the battle with his own machines and remaining engaged in the sport of conversation, Śakuni then approached him accompanied by his army and joined by Duryodhana’s younger brothers.
Then Bhīmasena, having deprived him of his chariot and weapons with his arrows, struck him down upon the earth. 27.131–132.
Duryodhana did not kill Sahadeva’s share, which had been staked by him at that time in the gambling hall;
instead, Duryodhana carried him away on his own chariot while he lay unconscious, with only his breath remaining.
Thereupon, ten of Duryodhana’s younger brothers fled, abandoning Bhīmasena.

Then, having seen Arjuna and Vāsudeva and having heard news of Dharmarāja, Duḥśāsana was filled with joy; taking up his bow, he rushed forward as he saw him again slaying the foremost of the enemy's heroes and putting his own army to flight, while Bhīma also charged at him like a lion. (27.134–135)
As he repeatedly uttered harsh words, Bhīma, having deprived him of his chariot in an instant, seized him and threw him to the ground;
then, tearing open his chest with a blow from his mace, he stood upon his neck with the sole of his foot and, filled with rage, gazed into his face. 27.136.
Drawing his great sword from its scabbard until it resembled the sky, he struck the chest of the fisherman.
Having made a vast lake of blood upon his breast, the thirsty [hero] drank his fill of that nectar-like gore;
as he whirled his eyes about that sea of blood, it reminded him of deeds done in the past.
He repeatedly and intensely reminded him of the word-arrows previously discharged;
yet the blood did not enter between his teeth, for he knew it was the blood of a man who should not be drunk. Nevertheless, as if to terrify the enemy, he drank it again and again, as if tasting it.

Remembering the Lord Nṛsiṃha, the Sovereign, he recited with devotion the *Manyu-sūkta* beginning with "O Manyu, that which is yours" (*yaste manyo*). In this battle, which was like a sacrifice, he offered the blood known as *soma* to Him, perceiving the enemy's chest as the *soma-vessel*, while piercing it with his mace according to the *Sāman* chant. (27.140–141)
The hero among men spoke these words, having established a true vow in the midst of the world:
"Those who were co-wives have indeed become wifeless, and she who had no husband has become one with a co-wife.
Let those who were formerly sterile sesame seeds behold the wonderful, supreme power of the Highest. (27.142)
"81. Ṛgveda 10.83.1cd:
'If any man here can release him who has been seized by me through his own prowess'—speaking thus, he drank the blood once more, just as the best of gods drinks nectar in heaven. (27.143)
Again, having cast aside that living being and being unarmed, he danced while roaring amidst the enemy host:
"Those who danced against us, crying 'Cow! Cow!', we now dance back against them, crying 'Cow! Cow! (27.144–145).
Speaking thus, dancing in the midst of his enemies, and slapping his arms, he challenged the hosts of foes;
yet none among Vaikartana, the son of Droṇa, Suyodhana, and the others were able to look upon him. Out of fear of Karṇa, his bow fell from his hand and his eyes were then closed.
Having been restrained by the King of Madra, that portion of Pārtha stood somehow in the battle;
but the son of Droṇa, leaving him behind, departed far away, whereupon Bhīmasena said:
"The Soma has been drunk by me today in this sacrifice of war; Suyodhana is my sacrificial animal to be slain for Hari. (27.147–148)
Speaking thus, he abandoned the dead enemy and swiftly rushed in fury toward Duryodhana.
Upon seeing him approaching with such fierce prowess, Suyodhana fled in great fear;
abandoning both his armies out of terror, he left Bhīma behind, as well as Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha. 27.149.

For a moment the battlefield became empty; then Bhīma, having imagined his enemies in the midst of the fray like cattle, danced with joy in the tiger’s stride (vyāghrapada). Having observed that deed of his, Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya laughed; greatly delighted, they praised and applauded him. 27.150–151.
When the son of Pavana had rendered Sāraṅga empty in a mere moment,
Duryodhana’s younger brothers showered volleys of arrows upon the noble-minded Bhīma. The heroic son of Māruta swiftly dispatched them to Yama, their heads severed by his excellent arrows.

On that day, twenty of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were slain, and the others fled from the battle. While Bhīma was thus performing deeds impossible for any other as the host of enemies became utterly terrified, Karṇa closed his eyes out of fear; then the son of Karṇa rushed toward Nakula.
The son of Mādrī [Nakula] warded off Vṛṣasena with showers of arrows and deprived him of his chariot.
That son of Karṇa, sword and shield in hand, then slew three thousand of his followers.
Having cut through his shield, the son of Karṇa [then struck] Bhīma, Arjuna, and the others with multitudes of arrows.
Pārtha showered him with arrows and simultaneously severed his neck, arms, and thighs with a single shaft.
(27.156) When his own son had been slain by that one arrow, Vaikartana rushed toward Vāsavi.
A wondrous and fierce duel took place between those two foremost masters of all weapons. (27.157)
There, the gods, the asuras, and other living beings who had taken sides took their places in the sky;
a great dispute then arose between the two of them, and Girīśa spoke to the Lotus-born One:
"Among the gods and asuras, there are two—Bhīma and Duryodhana—who are the primary supporters, and their favorites are Karṇa and Pārtha. (27.158)
"Since these two are like his very life-breath, the gods and asuras desire to wage war on his account;
then there would be a great destruction of the worlds. Therefore, let the battle between these two be equal.
When this was said, Vāsava spoke to the Lotus-born One: "Where Kṛṣṇa is, there victory is."
"Kāma shall not be false to Kṛṣṇa; for his desire is to grant victory to this son of Pṛthā. Having spoken thus, Vāsava said, "Let there be victory for Phalguna and likewise the slaying of Karṇa.
Brahmā, born from the lotus, replied, "So be it," and having spoken, he addressed both the Asuras and the deities.

"Do not engage in conflict anywhere for the sake of Karṇa and Arjuna, nor for the sake of Bhīma and Duryodhana; rather, simply witness their battle. When this was said, they attained peace and beheld the encounter between those two. 27.162.
And those two rained down great missiles and weapons; Bhīma, standing upon his chariot, protected his younger brother.
The son of Śini, the Pāñcālas, and others stood at the head of the host, roaring fiercely as they shielded the son of Pṛthā.
Duryodhana and those led by the son of Droṇa protected Karṇa, and thus that battle commenced.
There, Karṇa overwhelmed Arjuna with excellent arrows, excelling him in battle.
Then Bhīmasena, roaring and filled with rage, took up his mace and said:
"Either I shall crush him with my mace, or you, having summoned your prowess, must slay him."
Kṛṣṇa also fully awakened him, further manifesting his human incarnation.
Then Dhananjaya, whose prowess was perfected by the gods, deprived Suyodhana, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the Bhojas of their chariots with his arrows;
that slayer of foes pierced them as well with well-feathered shafts.
Standing at some distance, they watched that supreme battle;
having seen that superhuman feat of Pārtha, the son of the Preceptor, taking Duryodhana by the hand with his own, spoke to him: 27.167.
For you have seen today the strength of Bhīma, and likewise that of Pārtha, by which we were defeated.
Enough with hostility; come together with the Pāṇḍavas and rule the kingdom along with me.
Dhanañjaya remains restrained by me, and Janārdana does not desire conflict at all.
Vṛkodara always abides by those words, as does Yudhiṣṭhira of tranquil mind, and likewise the twins.
(27.169) These words have been spoken for your benefit; accept them from me, for they were not uttered out of fear.
For I am incapable of being slain, and my maternal uncle is as well; you ought not to doubt my word. (27.170)
Thus addressed, Suyodhana said to him: "Today Bhīma has indeed drunk the blood of Duḥśāsana;
he has acted with the prowess of a tiger. There can be no peace for me with him under any circumstances.
Having been told this, the son of Droṇa remained silent, as did Karṇa and Dhanañjaya.
With a rain of great missiles and weapons, they made the sky continuous;
these [missiles], such as the Āgneya, Vāruṇa, Aindra, and others, were for each other's destruction.
There, both having employed even the Brahmāstra, they roared in the battle.
Having struck one another's missiles, both shone forth brilliantly.
Gradually, as his great strength increased, the son of Virocana was repelled there by the son of the Lord of the Gods;
he then discharged an excellent serpent-arrow joined with the Brahmā-missile at Vāsava.
Vāsudeva, having caused that chariot to bend down, rendered Arjuna’s kirīṭa crown useless;
by him, the divine elephant of the son of the Lord of the Gods was crushed to powder, and the arrow returned to its source.
When the chariot had been bent down by Vāsudeva, it sank five finger-breadths into the earth.
When the serpent released by the Diademed One was aimed at the region of the corner of his eye,
it shattered the crown and sped into the sky;
then the son of Vāsava, urged by his Lord, struck that former enemy, the son of Takṣaka, with arrows.
Having struck it down, he caused it to fall to the ground while Karna looked on;
for the extreme velocity of the Brahmā weapon had been acquired by Karna from Bhārgava.
Furthermore, as the son of the Sun engaged once more in a battle of great weapons with Pārtha, his chariot wheel—
The earth swallowed the chariot, and by the curse, his divine weapons were forgotten. (27.179) Desiring to lift [the chariot], he begged Pārtha for the opportunity to do so.
Kṛṣṇa said "No," and Pārtha seized the most terrible *añjalika* weapon granted by the Three-eyed One. (27.180)
Having bound him with truth and righteousness, he released an arrow for the sake of slaying Karṇa;
and with that very [arrow], he severed his head as he was about to fit another most terrible, excellent shaft. Thus, in the afternoon, the son of the Sūta was struck down by the son of Indra.
With his hands severed, his head fell high upon the battlefield. When he was slain, Suyodhana, with a dejected face and pierced by arrows, retreated after gathering his forces.
Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard of Karna’s death, then arrived and beheld that body.
He praised Śaśin, Kṛṣṇa, Dhanañjaya, Bhīma, and those others who were heroes in battle; having gone to the enemy camp, they dwelt there joyfully with Kṛṣṇa, always devoted to him.
(27.184) Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Karṇa" (followed by "The Acquisition of the Kingdom for the Pāṇḍavas").
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Om! When the night had turned to dawn, Duryodhana, having obtained the approval of his preceptor’s son and having appointed Śalya as the commander-in-chief, advanced to do battle. 28.1.
The Pāṇḍavas, joyful and eager for battle, advanced against him;
there occurred a very great battle between the Pāṇḍavas and their enemies. Bhīma was at the forefront of the Pāṇḍavas, and King Yudhiṣṭhira was in their midst.
On the rear was the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, protected by Vāsudeva;
the two Yamas and Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Sātyaki were the wheel-protectors of the king.
On both sides of the monarch stood others, while the son of the Preceptor was at the front.
In the center was Śalya, with Suyodhana and his brothers at the rear;
Śakuni and his son were the protectors of the wheels for Śalya, while Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman stood stationed on the two flanks. (28.5)
There, a great battle took place between Bhīma and the son of Droṇa,
as well as a terrible and fearsome one between the King and Śalya;
there, with no great effort, the son of Droṇa [was struck] by Bhīma with his arrows.
Thus deprived of his chariot by Śalya at that very moment, the son of Dharma, whose banner bears the foremost of monkeys, then encountered the son of Śalya.
A great, wonderful, and hair-raising battle took place between the two of them. (28.7–28.8)
Mounting another chariot, the son of Droṇa rushed toward Bhīma;
and Duryodhana, for his part, blocked all directions with arrows against Bhīma.
Then the son of the Wind-god (Bhīma) warded off both of them with a shower of arrows.
With those two, there occurred a most terrible and superhuman battle.
The sons of Draupadī, together with Duryodhana’s younger brothers,
Yuyutsu, Śikhaṇḍin, and their maternal uncles, held them all in check.
Then Sahadeva [attacked] Śakuni, Nakula Ulūka, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Hṛdika, and Sātyaki Kṛpa;
their battle was wonderful, swift, and excellent. 28.12.
Śalya, however, blocked all directions for Pārtha with volleys of arrows;
he too pierced Śalya, who graced the battlefield, with his own shafts.
For a long time, their combat was perfectly equal, resembling the battle between the gods and the asuras. (28.13)
Then the King of Madra took up an arrow resembling a thunderbolt;
with it he pierced Bībhatsu in the heart, and he fainted. Having regained consciousness once more, the son of Vāsava, the scorcher of his enemies, [prepared for battle].
In that battle, he cut through the bow of the wise King of Madra.
Taking up another bow, the latter discharged celestial weapons— the solar, the infernal, and the rain-cloud weapon— but Phalguna destroyed them all with an Aindra weapon.
The son of Indra, filled with indignation, cut that bow asunder once more;
Śalya, having whirled his mace, hurled it at Arjuna’s chest. Then Bībhatsu fainted, and the enemies raised a loud shout. 28.17.
Having regained consciousness, Pārtha once again pierced Śalya in the chest;
with all his limbs reeling, Śalya leaned against his excellent standard. Having recovered his breath, he again took up an arrow in battle that resembled the staff of Yama.
And that [arrow] released by him pierced the center of Pārtha’s chest.
Distraught by it, Pārtha leaned against his flagpole;
once supported by it, he cut through the bow of the King of Madra.
He swiftly struck down the umbrella, the banner, and the charioteer.
Then, mounting another chariot, Dharmarāja slew Śalya’s four horses with four excellent arrows.
28.22. Mounting another chariot, Śalya covered all those kings with showers of arrows and deprived them of their vehicles;
that conqueror struck down the arrows of Sātyaki and Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

Having severed the bows of the twins, he blew his loud-sounding conch shell. Then, seeing Śalya being raised up in battle, the impetuous Bhīmasena checked him with numerous showers of arrows and deprived him of his chariot in an instant.

Mounting another chariot that was rushing toward him, Bhīma once again pierced Śalya deeply in his vital organs with arrows and deprived him of his vehicle; he then shattered a third chariot as well. All the various weapons taken up by Śalya, Bhīma cut to pieces and shattered them all.
Having pierced his vital organs even more deeply with arrows, he again raised his fist and rushed at the son of Dharma.
With his vital organs shattered by Bhīma, deprived of armor and weapons,
and reduced to nothing but breath, he was destined solely for death.

Seeing his opponent approaching him while mounted upon another chariot, the son of Dharma, desiring to slay that hero in battle, took up an unerring spear; he then charged it with divine weapons. 28.28.

Hurrying, he struck him in the heart with the fruits of truth and dharma. With his heart pierced, Śalya, who was devoted to truth and dharma, fell upon the earth facing the king and became a guest of Indra.
When the heroic king of Madra had been slain, Suśarman advanced against Arjuna;
Arjuna then sent him, along with the remnants of the Śaptakas, to his death.
Vṛkodara [then slew] the remaining younger brothers of Duryodhana.
He slew them all and left the army entirely destroyed in battle (28.32).
Then Sahadeva killed Ulūka, and Bhīma and Arjuna killed the exceedingly sinful Śakuni, as well as the son of Droṇa, the son of Hṛdika, and Kṛpa (28.33).
Having repeatedly deprived him of his chariot and afflicted him again and again, those two put him to flight; terrified, he entered the forest.
Then Sañjaya was captured by the descendant of Śini, who possesses infinite power.
Then, released by Vyāsa, Duryodhana advanced against the sons of Pṛthā.

A battle of terrible form took place between them and him; with many arrows, he caused Arjuna to fall into a swoon in battle, and effortlessly deprived Yudhiṣṭhira and the twins of their chariots. (28.35–36)
Bhimasena deprived him of his chariot; mounting an elephant, he charged forward again.
Once more, he rendered the grandson of Śini, Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Pṛṣata, the twins, and the king weaponless.
When the elephant had been struck down by Bhima’s arrows, he fearlessly mounted an excellent horse.
With that spear, the enemy-slayer, skilled with the lance, moved through the battle and struck the son of Śini.
Struck by it, Sātyaki fainted; both he and Yama, oppressed by the spear, sat down upon their chariot.
Seeing the son of Dharma proceeding on, Bhīma slew his horse.
When his lance was cut off by Vṛkodara, Suyodhana fled on his vehicle;
taking up his heavy mace, he set out and entered the lake that was the thigh of Dvaipāyana.
Thus, six akṣauhiṇīs were slain by Bhīma in battle.

Five [akṣauhiṇīs] were slain by Pārtha, excluding half of the Kāliṅgas; the remainder from the eleven akṣauhiṇīs was destroyed by others. And four akṣauhiṇīs of the Pārthas were killed by the son of Droṇa.
Others were slain by others, and Droṇa, Karṇa, and the Great Vow-keeper (Kṛpa) by all combined; Duryodhana, the son of Bhīma, and the slayer of the army (Aśvatthāman) followed in succession.
Having thus achieved victory over those high-souled Pāṇḍavas, he exulted greatly.
Duryodhana, having created a solidification of the waters, chanted the mantras.
These mantras, bestowed by Durvāsas, grant the power to restore the dead to life;
by chanting them while standing in water for seven days, one can revive even all those who have died.
"Let this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra rescue them, for they are again unslayable by you.
Having learned of his power through such knowledge, the sons of Pāṇḍu,
while searching, heard from hunters that he was staying in the water.
Then, placing Janārdana at our head, we went there;
having emerged from the water along with the three led by the son of Droṇa, they saw us consulting together, and upon seeing us, they fled. 28.45–46.
Seeing him, Duryodhana entered the water at the command of Keśava;
then Yudhiṣṭhira challenged him with words worthy of a noble man. Enraged, that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra then hissed like a snake struck by a staff.
Out of deceit, he said, "I shall go to the forest for asceticism; may you rule the entire earth.
To him, the king born of Dharma replied: "When Kṛṣṇa arrived, how is it that you did not wish to give even a piece of land pricked by the point of a needle? (28.48–49)

Having caused the entire earth, including even Bhīṣma and Droṇa, to be slain, you now wish to give away the whole world; we will not accept it today. Come, stand firm in battle and do not receive [the earth] without having killed [us].
"You were not born in the lineage of the Kurus, you who, out of fear, entered the waters!
Having heard such harsh words, Duryodhana rose from the pillar of water in rage, hissing like a venomous serpent. (28.51–28.52)
And he said: "I am but one, without crown and without armor;
you are many, though equipped with armor and helmets. Even so, if you consider my battle with you to be equal," (28.53)
"I shall fight with all of them or with one alone, and I have no fear," he said.
To this, the righteous-souled one replied: "I grant you armor today;
choose as your opponent whichever one among the five you desire."

"Having slain one, you may enjoy the kingdom; we others shall go to the forest. Or, if you are slain by him, we shall enjoy the entire earth. Take up the weapon with which you wish to conquer your enemies. (28.56)
Thus addressed, he said: "I will not fight with these four weaklings—yourself, Arjuna, and the others.
I shall fight with Bhīma; for my mace is always dear to me, and I would never touch any other weapon.
Having heard his words, the impetuous Vṛkodara then joyfully took up a mace weighing more than a full bhāra.
Having seized King Gadā’s mace, the hero rose up, roaring with a mind intent on battle.
Then the primordial god Nārāyaṇa said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "This is a grievous thing you have done!
For this king, while moving about in combat with his mace, cannot be conquered even by all the gods and asuras combined. (28.58–59)
"By some means, Bhīmasena might defeat the four [Kauravas] along with Arjuna through his resolve;

however, let him slay this man [Duryodhana] in battle, for among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, none is equal to Bhīma in strength, yet he is skilled. To protect his vow against the enemy, Bhīma must break the thighs [of Duryodhana]. 28.60.
"People say that striking below the navel with a mace in battle is unrighteousness (adharma). To avoid public censure, Kṛṣṇa,
being joined by a certain pretext, demonstrated that it was an act of necessity (āpad-dharma)."
Although Bhīma clearly stated, "I shall slay the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra," he spoke of his own boundless strength even without any pretext;
he declared that his training was no less than Duryodhana’s, yet his effort toward Duryodhana was superior. 28.63.
"It is not that Bhīma would fail to exert great effort; indeed, this is a virtue. To fulfill one's promise is dharma, especially toward the wicked.
Thus did Kṛṣṇa and Vṛkodara understand the secret of dharma. 28.64–65.

"I shall indeed break your thighs according to my vow; there is no need for hesitation here.
Having spoken thus, he advanced in battle, and there a fight ensued.
Then Bhīma, desiring to carry out his foremost resolve, moved about in the fray for the sake of the people—that dull-witted man.
Displaying various maneuvers with their maces, the two of them moved about;
then Balabhadra also arrived to restrain them. Though restrained by him, both of them did not at all desist from the fight.
Then, honored by Kṛṣṇa and the others, he witnessed that battle;
those two, endowed with skill and strength, moved through various circular maneuvers.
Then, in order to deceive Bhīma, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra lowered his head toward the ground.
Then, by Kṛṣṇa’s permission, Bhīma raised his thighs and struck him on the base of the back; with his thighs shattered, he fell down.
For the sake of fulfilling his vow, he did not strike from the front, nor from above, nor from below.
To preserve the rules of mace-fighting and his own reputation,
Vṛkodara struck him neither below nor above, but precisely in the middle;
thus, in accordance with his vow, he broke both of his thighs in battle.
In accordance with the vow that Suyodhana had made when he said, "Place Kṛṣṇa at the game of dice," Bhīma kicked his head, saying,
"O bull among equals! (82)
He beheld the hymn (Ṛgveda 10.166.1), and having fully gathered their merits and their sciences, he made them goers into darkness; he stepped upon their heads with his foot. (28.74–75)
He reminded him of the deeds he had committed, saying, "A conspiracy was made against Kṛṣṇa's kinsmen," and struck him on the head with his foot;
seeing this again and again, the wielder of the club (Baladeva) grew enraged. (28.76)
Thus, with his arms raised, he cried out, "This is not dharma! (28.77).
Then, his eyes copper-red with rage, he seized his mace and plow.
He rushed at Bhīma, but Vṛkodara did not waver. While Bhīma remained standing fearlessly, Keśava seized Rāma and said, "This Suyodhana has been slain by Bhīma in accordance with dharma."
One should not strike from the side, nor from the front, nor from above while [the opponent] is retreating or advancing;
but one may strike below one who is deceiving, and having struck below, one does not incur sin. Vṛkodara had made a solemn vow according to the proper method: "I shall split your thighs. 28.80.
Having caused that to be proclaimed, he of preeminent deeds struck down Duryodhana in accordance with the law.
Having heard the words of Vāsudeva and declaring it to be a "fraud of righteousness," the son of Rohiṇī quickly departed for his own city along with his followers.
When he had departed, Yudhiṣṭhira questioned Vāsudeva: "Is this dharma or is it adharma? To him Keśava replied:
"Those men who are most sinful are not to be slain according to the direct dictates of dharma. (28.83)
