For in the past, the enemies of the gods were slain by the gods only after having been deceived;

therefore, this one too has been slain through unrighteousness, and there is no fault in this. (28.84) And when Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Karṇa were slain by means of a stratagem, [there was likewise no fault].

What fault could there possibly be if the wicked Duryodhana were slain? Even for the sake of fulfilling his vow, Vṛkodara acted as one who would cause division; yet this vow was made by him in accordance with righteousness and propriety.
Even from a worldly perspective, there is no loss of dharma here in any way for those who,
being ignorant of Bhīma’s power, consider him to be acting contrary to dharma (apaddharma),
[despite his] immunity from death due to Śiva’s boon and the strength of his training with the mace. 28.87.
Because the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is so renowned as being like Jarāsaṃdha,
the Lord of the World, speaking thus— that this very true dharma had been practiced by Bhīma— caused even Dharmarāja to fall into doubt. (28.88–28.89)
With the thought that the duty arising from the protection of the earth's burden— which consists essentially of service to me—
would be properly fulfilled by Bhīma alone,
the Supreme Lord [repeatedly] bestowed it upon his own people, namely Balabhadra. (28.90)
Since the son of Dharma did not abandon his doubt even after hearing what was said,
Kṛṣṇa likewise did not cause Yudhiṣṭhira to be free from doubt;
for the Blessed One had taught the primary duty to Balarāma and to the people.

When he says again for the sake of certainty to Arjuna, "The king Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, Suyodhana, was slain by dharma alone," [he refers to] Bhīma saying over and over again that he slew the king strictly according to dharma.

With his lower lip quivering in rage, the most wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to Kṛṣṇa: "The Pārthas have indeed been delivered over to you, O sinner; for you alone are always and pre-eminently the greatest of sinners. To him who had spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa replied: "There has never been anyone equal to you in the commission of sin."
Even the slaughter of Bhīṣma and the others is but your own sin, since they followed you who were resolved upon such extreme wickedness.
Having slain those who were themselves sinful and followed by sin, there is no sin whatsoever for you in any way.
Indeed, not even the slightest sin exists among the Pāṇḍavas, whether by effort or by nature.

Those who take refuge in me possess superior virtues; who indeed would say even the slightest evil of them? (28.95) By nature you are a sinner, having placed others who abide in righteousness upon the path of evil;
being yourself always devoted to sin, you go from evil to an even more evil state. (28.96)
To Kṛṣṇa, who was speaking thus, Duryodhana—the foremost among wrongdoers—spoke again:
"Who indeed is the best of those with a happy end other than myself? What fault, pray, have I committed here?
I have sacrificed with sacrifices, performed works of public utility, and indeed placed my foot upon the heads of my enemies. (28.97)
And death was met by me at the head of the battle while I was still intent on the fight; what more need be said? (28.98) I have enjoyed desired pleasures and attained the supreme goal.
Those sons of Pṛthā, who fight with deceit, shall suffer misery for their misery. (28.99)
"Let this earth, abandoned by heroes who were like the sun and moon— righteous and virtuous— and now devoid of all jewels, be enjoyed solely by the Pāṇḍavas.
As soon as the king had spoken thus, a rain of flowers sent down by the lords of the gods fell.
Having firmly established that very same mindset in the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to cast him further into blinding darkness—
how could he not be intent upon it as he exalts himself and reviles Vāsudeva, especially at the end of his life? (28.101–102)
"When even a single one of these is sufficient for suffering there, how much more so from their combination!
Having said this, the Lord made him do it all in vain, [saying]: "O cruel one, you are ungrateful and always a hater of the virtuous. (28.103)

If the fruit of dharma were darkness, it would be dispelled like the sun; yet the Blessed One, who grants the desires of his own people, repeatedly declared this to the world, saying, "He has been struck down by dharma. (28.104–105)
When Vāsudeva had proclaimed the dharma, it became pleasing to the hearts of all the virtuous;

they recognized that the king had been slain according to dharma, their minds certain that "this man was indeed wicked. Yudhiṣṭhira, who always perceived danger, remained full of apprehension until he was rained upon by flowers from the heavens. (28.106)
Out of affection, the son of Droṇa and Sañjaya said, "It is evil," while the son of Rohiṇī said the same out of loyalty to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by those Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas who were shouting loudly and rejoicing,
departed from the field of battle, smiling as he was honored by Viriñci, the Lord of the Gods, and the foremost of the deities.

Then, having heard this from Sañjaya, Yuyutsu, wishing to awaken his father who was tormented by grief, set out with the consent of Kṛṣṇa and the king; and Janārdana followed right after him, [addressing him] with words endowed with righteousness and truth, which reflected the ways of the world. 28.109.
Having consoled the king with these words, Hari departed for the Pārthas;
Acyuta, together with Pārtha and Śaineya, went to the camp of the Kurus at night, in order to withdraw the celestial weapons according to the proper rites. (28.110–111)
At that very moment, accompanied by Hārdikya and Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa approached Suyodhana as he lay there;
he saw him with his thighs shattered, gasping for breath, and being devoured by creatures that had become jackals.
Struck by grief and sorrow, he censured the sons of Pṛthā, saying, "O King, what is to be done here by me? (28.112).
Thus the king spoke; "Be one who is free from eunuchs," he said, and he appointed him as his consecrated heir.

(28.113) Having cut off the lineage of Paṇḍu and established his own lineage in his own field, he was consecrated with the thought that the earth would be protected by him, and thus he departed. (28.114)

Out of fear of Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Pārtha, that chariot-warrior, accompanied by Kṛpa and the Sātvata, entered the dense forest once again. As he was reflecting upon the slaughter of Droṇa and Duryodhana, [the following occurred].
At midnight, sleep had departed from him as he beheld thousands upon thousands of crows dwelling in the *nyagrodha* tree already slain by a single man of exceeding strength;
then Kausika, having looked at them, spoke to those two, Kṛpa and Sātvata. (28.116–117)
"Indeed, impelled by this supreme Self through this very sign, he said, 'I shall slay the sons of Pāṇḍu,' and mounted his chariot;
though restrained by those two, he rushed toward the camp. (28.118)
The two of them also followed him, and at the gate of the camp he beheld Rudra, who had assumed a fierce form— indeed, his own very body—
surrounded by Vāsudeva in the form of many millions of manifestations.
Upon seeing Vāsudeva, the son of Gautamī (Aśvatthāman) took refuge with him;
and by Vāsudeva’s command,
Sadasiva himself also fought and swiftly seized all the weapons of the son of Droṇa.

The power of Hari is indeed inconceivable, for even those who destroy themselves are seen [to survive]. Therefore, impelled by that very power, even though all his weapons had been swallowed up, the son of Droṇa performed a mental sacrifice.

Having made himself the sacrificial animal, he offered it to Viṣṇu who resides within his own self. Impelled by Hari, who was pleased with the sacrifice, Śaṅkara himself bestowed all his weapons upon the son of Droṇa for his own sake.
And he said: "I was commanded by the sovereign Viṣṇu:
'Protect the camp of the Pārthas for only this much time.
By his very will, I have been directed, and today I shall grant you passage."
"Bring forth all your weapons to slay all these people!
Having thus spoken and swiftly bestowed all his missiles upon them, the bull-bannered god vanished right there; he then addressed Kṛpa and Sātvata.
"Let all those who would depart from the camp be abandoned entirely.
Having spoken thus, the archer, sword in hand, entered [the city] like the God of Death;
then, approaching his own chariot, he struck it with his feet.
Having woken from his sleep, he spoke to him on the chest: "I know you indeed to be the son of my preceptor.

Rise up and strike me with your weapon in hand; for you are a hero, and such is the duty of a hero. May the worlds be mine, purified by the sword"—to him who was speaking thus, he replied in anger: (28.129–130)
Indeed, there are no auspicious worlds for those who slay Brahmins, and especially not for those who betray their teachers.
Nor are there for those like you, O most sinful one, who deserve death even in a righteous war while fleeing in retreat.
Dhrṣṭadyumna, reflecting upon that inevitable death, [advanced].
He remained silent, for even in his dreams he constantly beheld that death;
and the son of Pṛṣata saw in a dream both the son of Droṇa and the Night of Doom, immediately after the fall of Droṇa, as they were slaughtering and tearing him apart. (28.132–133)
The son of Droṇa, standing upon his chest, drew back his bow and fastened its string around his neck;
with great effort he churned him, and having cast off his body, he went to his own abode, as did that Fire-god.
Then, having slain Śikhaṇḍin, [he struck] Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas.
The blazing fire advanced against Janamejaya and the sons of the Pāñcālī princesses;
being struck by the arrows discharged by them as they rose up, he slew them all with his sword,
moving both to the left and to the right, as well as the other sons of the Pāṇḍavas.

Then, at the word of Ṛta, Śarva took that son of Bhīmasena, the grandson of Kṛṣṇarāja, away to Kailāsa in an instant while he was invisible. He became known by the name Śarvatra, and he lived right there.

Formerly, Śaṅkara had been entreated by Khaṇḍikarāja for the immortality of his own grandson; therefore, filled with compassion, he protected him. Having learned Vasudeva’s intention regarding Parīkṣit’s universal sovereignty, [he acted accordingly]. 28.138.
Śiva entreated him, saying, "Do not go to the world of mortals.
(28.139) Although the son of Droṇa had intended it for anyone other than the Pāṇḍavas in general, Rudra, in that very form, thought, "Except for this one [Arjuna]. (28.140)
The Brahmāśiras weapon did not slay him because of the unity between those two;
however, he slew Cekitāna and all the others in every way.
Having struck down the Cedis, Pañcālas, Karūṣakas, Kāṃsyas, and all the others, that hero—

Fierce in his intent to slaughter the children and women, he set that camp ablaze on all sides. Gautama and the Sātvata, stationed at the gate, slaughtered those who sought to live and were fleeing there from every direction; however, by the turn of fate, a single charioteer of Parṣata remained alive.
Seeing himself struck by the sword of Hārdikya, he fell to the ground even before his body touched it, for he was rendered unconscious by that darkness; then,
rising up while still distracted, he fled to where the daughter of Pṛṣata was.
She told him everything; she, being distressed, spoke to Bhīma.
Mounting her chariot, that archer rushed toward the son of Gautamī. In the meantime, the son of Droṇa also advanced, delighted at the prospect of the heads of Kṛṣṇā’s sons.

Having taken Duryodhana, who was about to depart, and being followed by Hārdikya and Kṛpa, [the king] saw him and heard what he said; the wicked man, delighted, cast off his body with the words "Well done!
Then, terrified of Bhīma, Arjuna, and Keśava, the leaders headed by the son of Droṇa departed separately.
There, the car-warrior Māruti pursued the son of Droṇa as he was traveling alone on his chariot.
Seeing him rushing toward him, the son of Droṇa fled in great haste with his horses at full speed.
But seeing Bhīma pursuing him once more, the son of Droṇa, filled with rage—
Turning back and fighting, he was defeated and took up the Brahmāśiras weapon. In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, the son of Dharma, arrived there, rendering that formidable weapon ineffective.
Bhimasena was invulnerable because that weapon was indeed unfailing;
for both were ordained by Viṣṇu himself, and Bhīma was that very weapon.
The Gāyatrī was the mantra there, and Brahmā was the deity of its meditation.
The god Nārāyaṇa himself, the progenitor of the world, was to be meditated upon.
And Kṛṣṇa told the two sons of Pṛthā what had been done previously by the son of Droṇa, who, being powerless to lift them, had uttered a curse against his own weapons. (28.151–152)

When asked, you said, "Having deprived Duryodhana of his cattle, let him give me back my weapons today. When this was said, it occurred to me: "Do not act thus again," as I reflected upon my own situation on the shore of the ocean. (28.153)
Then, seeing that blazing weapon released by the son of Droṇa upon the earth with the desire to deprive him of his non-Pāṇḍava status, Arjuna, urged by Kṛṣṇa, said:
"May it be well with the son of Droṇa, with all beings, and with me as well. (28.154)

Saying this, he released that very weapon for the sake of neutralizing the other weapon; for that weapon, when discharged against those ignorant of weapons, would have slain the one who had loosed it.
Therefore, out of devotion to his preceptor, the son of Vasava said, "May it be well with the son of Drona. (28.155–156)
Then, upon the collision of the two weapons, there would have been the destruction of all beings;
yet even in this situation, the welfare of all beings was desired by the compassionate-souled one.
(28.157) —From the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*.
Nevertheless, those two weapons were certainly destined to destroy all beings without exception.
Therefore, the Supreme Kṛṣṇa, the son of Satyavatī, whose power is limitless, instantly stood between them to ward off their union. (28.158)
Having stationed those two weapons at a distance, Puruṣottama said to them:
"There have indeed been many in the past who were skilled in weapons, yet for the most part this was not done by them.
How could virtuous men ever perform an act that causes affliction to the world? (28.159)

When this was said, Phalguna replied: "O Lord, that which was discharged by me during this great calamity was solely for the sake of pacification; therefore, you must forgive me. Drauni spoke in the same manner, and the Lord of the Vedas then addressed them both.
"Let the weapon be withdrawn," said the son of Śakra, and he did so.
To the son of Droṇa, who was unable to withdraw it, Vāsudeva spoke:
"This Pāṇḍava possesses the splendor of a Kṣatriya and is a celibate student even from his youth. (28.161)
"Even though he is the son of Droṇa, he is not capable of turning back," said Vyāsa when it was stated that this was due to his lack of celibacy; Vyāsa then addressed the son of Droṇa:
"Since you are unable to turn back, give back the jewel that was born with you."
"Already conquered by Bhīma, [this weapon] possesses great power for Bhīma alone;
therefore, by mere word, turn back this weapon from the sons of Pṛthā.
Thus addressed, he [offered] his crest-jewel, which destroys old age and death.

"Having cut off [his head], which dispels hunger, thirst, and fatigue, possesses divine fragrance, removes darkness, and is auspicious, the five Pāṇḍavas released it to Bhīma. Then, from that weapon, the bearer of the Vedas spoke to Vāsavi: 28.164–165.
"Father, you yourself must withdraw this very weapon released by the son of Droṇa.
Being thus addressed, Arjuna bowed to him and quickly withdrew that weapon.
Then, having entered [the body] of Gautamī’s son, who had only one descendant, he spoke to him: 28.166.
"By my word, withdraw your weapon," he was told; and the son of Droṇa replied:
"Out of partiality, you desire the continuation of your sister's son; therefore, I shall hurl that very weapon for the destruction of Uttara’s fetus. (28.167–168)
Vāsudeva spoke again: "If he is indeed to be slain by you, O giver of honor, nevertheless do not discharge this weapon at all upon the embryo;
rather, discharge it upon the body of the deceased Abhimanyu. (28.169)
"In this way, I shall restore to life the fetus slain by your weapon," said the son of Gautamī, "I myself am the fetus for the sake of victory.
Then the Lord Vāsudeva spoke to him, as if slightly provoked: (28.171)
"O evil-minded one, behold my power! Do whatever you are capable of doing.
Even with all my effort and according to my strength, I shall restore your embryo to life, so that there may be a lineage of the Pāṇḍavas on earth for a thousand years. (28.172)
No one anywhere is capable of slaying her while she is protected by me.
I know your wicked intent,
that you desire to destroy the lineage of the Pārthas and wish to extend the thread of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons once more— an exceedingly difficult task.
By my command, that desire for liberation shall become fruitless for Viṣṇu, who has turned his face away from it;

just as by that very act, the ground you must traverse while mounted upon a man shall not be level, but shall be filled with foul odors, its body covered with wounds, and you shall always wander slowly through the forests, O dull-witted one. 28.175.
"As long as the lineage of Pārtha remains here on earth, Vyāsa also said to him, 'So be it,' O Lord.
Thus addressed by Hari in his two forms, Kālī’s son spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
'O All-pervading One, may my union with you take place according to your will, and let there be no obstacle for me in this matter.'"
When this was said, the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa replied, "Om.
Having bowed to him, he too departed, recollecting what he had seen in his dream.
For in the night, he himself had witnessed in a dream the slaughter of the sons of Draupadī.
Arjuna’s vow regarding the slaughter of [Karna] for Draupadī’s sake; his binding [of Karna] and leading him toward the camp; Draupadī’s plea, “Release him!”, and Bhīma’s reply, “No! (28.179).

"Having taken the jewel from Kṛṣṇa's words, I likewise departed from the country"— reflecting thus on how that which he had seen in his dream had mostly come true, the son of Droṇa, the best among weapon-bearers, set out for the forest fire.
Having attained even that which was spoken by Kṛṣṇa, and having obtained the status of being a disciple of Bādarāyaṇa,
he will divide the Vedas in the future Dvāpara age;
thereafter, through the grace of Pārāśarya, he will become one of the Seven Sages.
"Through devotion to Acyuta, he shall attain oneness with his true self.
[End of Chapter 28, titled "The Recovery of the Pāṇḍava Kingdom.
Then Kṛpa, having reached the Pāṇḍavas, was honored by them out of respect.

He became the very teacher of those kings who were to follow in his lineage; furthermore, having attained the status of being Bādarāyaṇa’s disciple, he was to serve him along with his own nephew as one among the seven sages.
Permitted by Kṛṣṇa, Kṛtavarman went to Dvāravatī. Having given that jewel to Kṛṣṇā, Bhīma consoled her;
her anger subsided at Bhīma’s words, and she gave the jewel to the king.
"For if this king-worthy jewel were given to me by Bhīma, people might suspect the King of Wind of partiality toward women. Thus,
Kṛṣṇā, devoted to the welfare and pleasure of her husband, gave the jewel to the king.
Having bound that jewel upon his head, the king shone like a bull with the *ūrṇā* mark on its forehead.

(28.188) Then, joined by Kṛṣṇa—the best of the Yadus and lord of the Vedas—the sons of Pṛthā departed with their wives for their own capital, just as the virtuous, having slain their internal enemies, return to their own kingdom. (28.189)

As Bhīma was bowing at the feet of Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Vicitravīrya, the Supreme Lord drew him aside and fashioned an iron image before the king; that iron figure, which Suyodhana had commissioned for the practice of mace-fighting, possessed a terrifying form. 28.190.

Having embraced him, he crushed him to pieces, vomiting blood and crying out, "Alas, O father Bhīma! as he fell down. (28.191) Kṛṣṇa said to him: "Bhīma has not been killed today; nor can he be slain by you or by others.
Your own intelligence was displayed by you today; for even now, O King, your mind is still wicked. (28.192)

"O Bhīmasena, having increased the evils known as 'sons' through the fault of your own intellect—evils of most wicked character—you have been brought under their control; now, while experiencing the fruit [of those actions], you ought not to be angry.
When this was said, Vṛkodara was addressed by the king with a tranquil mind.
He prostrated at his feet and those of his younger brothers; meanwhile,
Kṛṣṇa had deceived Vṛkodara, whose body was so firm from the *vajra* [exercise] that it remained unchanged, thinking, "Otherwise, no fault would have been revealed in him."

Embracing all his sons with affection, the king joined them in their prayers; for King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the bringer of joy to his lineage, said, "I am indeed worthy of your curse," as Gāndhārī, while he was bowing down, touched the toes of her husband's feet.
Provoked by the hem of the Dharmarāja’s garment, she looked at him;
her nails were scorched by the fire of her wrath, and thus he became one with deformed nails (*kunakha*).
As Bhīma was bowing down again, she, overwhelmed by anger, spoke to him: (28.197)
"O Bhīma, how is it that you have slain my son unrighteously?
When he had spoken thus, Vṛkodara, standing before her, spoke in order to appease her anger:
"In a matter where life itself is at stake, there is no sin in slaying a wicked man."

Having spoken thus, Vṛkodara, knowing that there was no danger to his life and that he would slay his enemies in battle according to his vow, spoke again to her: "There is no doubt for me regarding my life. (28.200) [Until] I have slain my rivals in battle according to my vow.

Wherein lies the unrighteousness of the kṣatriya caste? For there is no life for one who fails in that duty. (28.201) There is a Vedic revelation stating, "The wicked must be slain by means of a non-pure dharma.
And there is a Vedic revelation stating, "One should declare the slaying of the wicked to be like [the slaying of] others."
Therefore, the gods slay the deceitful asuras by means of deceit.
"One should strike deceit with deceit, but one should never strike the righteous with deceit"—this supreme Vedic revelation is always recited by the followers of Paiṅgi. (28.202–203)

Thus addressed, she spoke to him again: "How was it that human blood was drunk by you while you were still a man? Was it not drunk? He replied: "That blood of your son did not reach between my teeth. (28.204)
This was done for the sake of fulfilling his vow and to retaliate;
it was displayed as a terrifying spectacle for his enemies and as something he had drunk.
This dharma, seen in the Vedas, is directed toward those who commit extreme sins. (28.205–28.206)
Having been addressed thus, Vṛkodara said: "O blind couple, by killing these hundred sons, you have left nothing behind but this staff.
Bhīma said to her: "Crush her; she is a criminal deserving of death."
"All have been slain," she said again; "is even that one who committed the offense against you not here? he replied to her. All together, they had resolved to bind Kṛṣṇa. (28.208)
And other very wicked deeds were committed by him here in the past as well— [namely],
speaking [harshly] to Vāsudeva while he was seated in the assembly hall and teaching what is beneficial for dharma.
(A Compendium of All Dharmas)
Reflecting on such things as how everyone followed Duryodhana as he went outside repeatedly with contempt, Vṛkodara thought:
"Not even one among them was innocent; they have themselves taught him [his behavior]. (28.210)

"Being powerless against me, why do you direct your anger fruitlessly? (28.211) When she was addressed thus, she became silent after each of the Pāṇḍavas had paid their respects; then, by the word of Vyāsa, she became somewhat pacified. (28.212)

Having placed Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head, along with all his daughters-in-law, Vidura, and the others, the Pāṇḍavas, together with their wives and Pṛthā, proceeded to the site of the great battle. (28.213)
And the two Kṛṣṇas went there due to the power of Gāndhārī’s asceticism.
Knowing this and wishing to exhaust her penance for the sake of protecting the Pāṇḍavas,
the Lord of the Vedas, the son of Satyavatī, granted him divine vision.

Having seen all those crowded bodies of the departed spirits there, she cursed the Lord of the Yādavas: "Since you have committed the destruction of our lineage, may your own family go to ruin through mutual slaughter! (28.216)

Thus addressed, the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the omnipresent Sovereign, though capable of acting otherwise, said "So be it," confirming that very thing he intended to do. By that act, her ascetic merit was destroyed, and she was consequently deprived of her husband.

"Indeed, Viṣṇu always bestows qualities upon them that exceed their own capacity. (28.218) Then Keśava, having embraced the weeping women, showed them all the bodies of their husbands, Duryodhana and the others.
And she praised that god, who is endowed with perfect virtues;
then the fires of the virtuous consumed their well-known bodies,
while those of others, such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his kin, were consumed only after they had been cast before [the flames].
With their own five charioteers, they cast [the weapons] into the Sarasvatī;
out of affection, the king and the twins did not employ them in that battle.
Due to the great number of corpses, they remained lying here and there in abundance. (28.220–221)
Then, while they were offering water for their kinsmen in the Ganges,
Pṛthā said to Karṇa, "This was given to Karṇa," and she addressed that eldest son of the Pārthas.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter.

Oṃ! At the very moment when the two Kṛṣṇas, having consecrated Yudhiṣṭhira in the sovereignty of the entire realm and Bhīma as the crown prince, were accompanied by brahmins and offered blessings, those two, being appropriately joined, caused them great joy.
At that same time, the one known as Cārvāka, having become a mendicant ascetic bearing a triple staff (tridaṇḍī), [appeared]. 29.1.

He censured Yudhiṣṭhira, saying, "The Brahmins are censuring you as one of very wicked character. (29.2) Upon hearing this, the Brahmins became distressed; seeing the son of Dharma, they, being deeply afflicted, rebuked him:
"O sinful one, since you have today called him—who is never censured by us—censurable!"

As soon as these words were spoken, that most wicked man was reduced to ashes in an instant. When this one wearing the garb of an ascetic had been turned to ashes, the lion of the Vṛṣṇis spoke to the grieving Yudhiṣṭhira:
"This was no ascetic; he was a performer of cruel deeds, a most sinful friend of Suyodhana. (29.3–29.4)
"This lowest of Rākṣasas has been slain today by the brahmins; therefore, O King, do not grieve, for you have accomplished your purpose.
Thus addressed, he became tranquil in mind and gratified the brahmins with wealth and devotion.
He also consoled his kinsmen, the citizens, and those who had sought his protection.
He gave away wealth as much as he desired and protected his subjects like a son.
(29.6) Distressed by the slaughter of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and Duryodhana, and tormented by the loss of his kingdom, he set his mind upon renunciation. (29.7)

Though addressed with instructions on righteousness by his younger brothers, by Kṛṣṇā, and even by the Brahmins, the king, lamenting "Alas! Alas! in extreme distress, cursed all women: "May the secret [of their conduct] not remain hidden in their hearts. (28.223)
"O mother, by your very resolve we have all been utterly ruined;
having slain our eldest brother who was like a father to us, what destiny shall we attain?
To the son of Kuntī who was speaking thus, Vāsudeva, together with Nārada, [replied].
He pacified them with virtuous words and spoke of Karṇa’s merits. Then they all performed the funeral rites in every respect;
and the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas was established in the sovereignty over all.
Having entreated Bhīma, he said to Phalguna, "You do not know [the truth].
When he was thus enraged, the Brahmins said to the king, "He who knows the truth even more than you is Arjuna. Having heard this, Śakra remained in doubt regarding dharma. (29.8–29.9)
"Out of affection for me alone, everyone says, 'This is dharma,'" he thought.
To him who was thus doubting, the brāhmaṇa and the Yādava said:
"Kṛṣṇa is indeed dharma," they told him again and again, supported by scripture and reasoning. (29.10)

Even then, those two imperishable Supreme Persons said to him whose intellect was not yet certain, "Go where Bhīṣma is; he is beyond the reach of such doubt because he has joined the side of the slain. (29.11)
Accompanied by those two brothers as well as the sages,
he went to Bhīṣma while the latter was feeling ashamed; when Keśava said to him,
"Ask," and he was thus addressed by Bhīṣma, he immediately asked everything.
There, Kṛṣṇa, residing within Bhīṣma’s body, spoke all the dharmas.
For Bhīṣma said to Hari: "O Pārtha, you alone must indeed awaken [him].
What power do I have, O Lord of Gods, O Master, to awaken the sons of Pṛthā?"
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said: "For the sake of your fame, and established within you, I shall proclaim all the Dharmas, even the subtle reality.
First among the duties of a king is the protection of the Dharma of the Blessed One.
For that purpose, there is the removal of thorns, as well as duties pertaining to the Bhāgavatas;
and the worship of Viṣṇu through thought, word, and deed must be performed without flaw.
Viṣṇu alone is independent and possesses all perfections and qualities in their entirety. (29.16)
It is the firm conviction that everything else is always under His control. (29.17) The knowledge of the sequence of deities is indeed the non-worship of any other than Hari;
it is the worship of the gods and others in every way through the state of being a Bhāgavata. (29.18)
Your form was always fruitless and entirely devoid of desire for anything anywhere;
yet you were always the very embodiment of opposition to Viṣṇu, the Bhāgavatas, and the devotees.
But when there is mutual conflict, it is the superior one who acts favorably. (29.19)
One should perform everything that is pleasing to Viṣṇu and to His devotees as well;
however, one should never perform even a righteous act if it is displeasing to them.
In cases of equality or conflict, one should indeed follow the majority of Vaiṣṇavas. (29.20)
These are to be known as the common duties of a Bhāgavata (29.21).
However, for a Brahmin specifically, the duty is the communication of reality;
[furthermore,] the abandonment of corporal punishment, except in the case of one's son, wife, and so forth.
Even in that case, there shall be no loss of limb, nor shall there be pain for long.
(29.22) Furthermore, no monetary fine should ever be imposed by Brāhmaṇas or Vaiśyas and others;
regarding corporal punishment, the rule for Vaiśyas and others is the same as for Brāhmaṇas. (29.23)

The best of the twice-born should subsist on whatever is obtained, whether by begging, or by what is received from disciples and patrons, or by the duty of a Kṣatriya in times of distress; and in great distress, a Kṣatriya may live according to the duties of Vaiśyas for the sake of the gods and Brahmins.
Otherwise, he should conduct himself with all-knowingness while protecting these [laws];

and from a hostile Kṣatriya, he should take wealth by force alone. He should apply the methods beginning with conciliation (sāma) according to the principles of dharma, and finally, resort to punishment (daṇḍa).
One who never flees in battle may perform the duties of the virtuous.
Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending constitute the livelihood of a Vaiśya;
service alone is the occupation of a Śūdra, while others follow their respective previous [caste] duties.
The Brāhmaṇas and the others should conduct themselves accordingly; those dear to Hari are to be honored in their respective order.
Even if one is of low caste, if he is a devotee of Hari, he is not to be disregarded; however, one who is high-caste but not a devotee is not to be highly honored.
Yet, even one devoid of caste, if he is dear to Hari, is to be honored with a prostration.
One should apply oneself with diligence to that in which devotion to Hari is supreme.
(29.28) The duty of Kṣatriyas is to give instruction [to others] with the permission of Brāhmaṇas;
in their absence, however, it belongs to Vaiśyas, and in times of extreme distress, to Śūdras. (29.29)
"Among those belonging to the [four] castes, one who is outside the castes (avarṇa) shall by no means be made known.

According to this scriptural injunction, there is no possibility whatsoever of making one outside the castes known. (29.30) All that is to be known, except for the Vedas, may be learned everywhere by women belonging to the three castes.

For women, fidelity to their own husbands is dharma; for men, it is restraint toward their own wives. But for those of the highest virtues, even the mere remembrance [of this dharma] causes one to enter blind darkness. Furthermore, in this world, there is a loss of all one's virtues as one proceeds further and further [away from it].
For women, the fault increases further and further, except for those of middling quality;
even all the Vedas [are mastered] by the most excellent women, such as Kṛṣṇā and others—whether they be goddesses, wives of sages, or born of human lineages and the like. (29.33)
These should be known as the best; even for Śūdras, the name of Hari and one's own duty are to be understood as non-Vedic [in this context].
One who gives away anything other than these goes entirely to blinding darkness, whether it be something inferior or merely equivalent. 29.34.
He who considers Viṣṇu to possess even the slightest thing by way of attributes anywhere;

or he who does not acknowledge even the distinction [of Viṣṇu] from Brahmā, Īśāna, and others; and he who perceives duality even regarding His qualities and so forth, as well as His incarnations—[he is one who sees falsely]. (29.35–29.36)
Or he who considers the natural body, or suffering, ignorance, fatigue, and so forth, as having degrees of excellence among His devotees, or otherwise [regards them]—
or he who, through mind, speech, and body, [acts] toward Him or toward His devotee [in such a manner]. (29.37)
Those who harbor hostility, those who remember anything other than that which is dependent on Viṣṇu,
those who perceive Him as dependent on another, those who lack knowledge of His omnipresence, and those devoid of devotion— all of them undoubtedly go to the blinding darkness. (29.38–29.39)
All those who possess doubt regarding the truth go to hell;
however, when virtues outweigh faults, they do not go to a low state.
When virtues and faults are equal, they always attain human birth again and again. (29.40)
Until the exhaustion of defects, there is upward movement in a gradual sequence;

when all defects are exhausted, liberation occurs according to the fitness of the self. (29.41) And for one of virtuous karma, heaven is attained precisely through the increase of devotion and knowledge.
"By the word of Viṣṇu and his devotees, there is the destruction of sinful action" (29.42).
Thus, the entire essence of dharma was spoken by Viṣṇu himself while standing in the form of Bhīṣma. Having heard that, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) and his younger brothers—
He questioned Vidura regarding the essence of the three goals beginning with dharma.
Vidura replied that dharma alone is the essence, while artha is intermediate;
he stated that kāma is base because it is fruitless. Arjuna, however, declared that artha alone is the essence.
That essence should be known as twofold: divine and human.
The divine is knowledge, while that beginning with gold is proclaimed as the human.
Here, dharma alone is both the means and the end to be accomplished. 29.45.
The object of *dharma* is called knowledge, and by knowledge alone one is liberated.
Even the human goal (*artha*) is a means for knowledge when it is properly employed;
for when the teacher is satisfied with wealth, he is fully capable of bestowing even absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). (29.46–47)
Even without material wealth, the preceptor and the deities may be satisfied by the pursuit of dharma;
yet if dharma is not directed toward its purpose, it merely follows after material gain.
In that case, the status of the preceptor would be reduced to mere material interest, for desire at the lowest level is indeed fruitless. (29.48)
Thereupon the twins, the best among the wise, repeated what Arjuna had said.

Then Bhīma, the foremost of those who perceive the true nature of reality, addressing them all with joy and smiling, said: "There is nothing auspicious whatsoever that exceeds desire; where, then, could one go to attain inferiority? (29.49–29.50)

For the noble ones say that what is desirable is indeed called "kāma"; the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), together with their means, are desirable. That which lacks desirability is not a goal of man at all; for it is called a "goal of man" precisely because it is sought after by man.
Even such things as the worship of Viṣṇu and so forth, though they are excellent means, are excluded from [the category of] *kāma* if they are devoid of desire.

Even the supreme liberation would not be an accomplishment, nor would it attain the status of an object to be achieved, were it not for desire (kāma). Even Hari, the Primordial Person who is higher than the highest, is desired by himself as well as by others. If he were not desired, he would grant only a downward state; therefore, desire is indeed the entirety of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha). 29.52–29.53.
Let desire indeed be nothing other than will; nevertheless, without this [will], consciousness would be like a jar or a wall.

Therefore, that very will is the essence, though it is of the nature of consciousness and its form is ever hidden. O King, if there is a gradation [of states], desire is not something separate and thus not fit to be questioned as such. 29.54.
This threefold object of experience is indeed to be known by you; here, that which is endowed with dharma and artha is considered supreme.
If it does not conflict with one of these two, it is middling; but if it conflicts with both, it is base.
Therefore, being one whose desires are appropriate, you should take your pleasure at will with the young women of your own intellect.
"O King, there is indeed no auspiciousness greater than desire, for Hari alone is the supreme desire by which [it is attained].

Having spoken these words, both concise and detailed, the wise hero Bhīma, smeared with the essence of sandalwood and adorned with various garlands and ornaments, addressed the excellent Rāma. 29.56–57.

Having praised Bhīma and the others, the king then offered praise for his own liberation; however, because of the invincibility of his own yoga, the son of the Wind-god (Hanumān) did not dismiss him. 29.58.
Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
In the *Śrī Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*,
the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Compendium of All Dharmas."
Chapter Thirty (The Completion of the Sacrifice).
Om! Now, having recollected Kṛṣṇa, when Bhīṣma had attained his own state as a Vasu,
Having performed all his duties and having consoled the grieving Gaṅgā,
the son of Dharma, though himself sorrowful, was once again comforted by the two Kṛṣṇas; then he was addressed by Anantāratha, the son of Parāṃśu.
"Because you suspect the sinless of being sinful, sacrifice to Acyuta with horse-sacrifices;
rule the kingdom with righteousness and protect your subjects, who have no other protector.
Thus addressed, he did exactly so, renouncing all enjoyments entirely.
Endowed with vows such as the *govrata* and others, he protected the earth.
He bestowed the primary gifts to be given according to desire and without fail;
never at any time was a worthy supplicant turned away.
There, the son of Dharma alone became the questioner, the giver, the one honored by all kings, the sacrificer,
and the sovereign of kings dwelling in Pāṇḍu’s house, having turned away from women. Bhīma, however, entered the very palace of Duryodhana, which was acquired through his own formidable prowess.
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇā, the crown prince alone enjoyed pleasures worthy of the king of the gods.
And Kṛṣṇā, having left the four sons of Pṛthā, her pure nature clearly manifest through Sarasvatī,
shone eternally with the younger brother of the king through an exclusive union, like the crest of fire.
Conversing with him who was joined by consciousness through love alone, having avoided all other matters as the future time had passed,
she attended upon her very own husband Bhīma with joy.
That younger brother of the king shone with her, who was of two-fold form and born of the Somaka and Kāṃsika lineages.
Just as the lotus-navelled Lord [Viṣṇu], having slain all the sons of Diti, entered the great ocean with Śrī and Bhū;

so too was he known by the name Sarvottuṅga, the pinnacle of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), who at night was struck down by the son of the Guru. His queen, the daughter of Rohiṇī, who had formerly been the beloved Rākā of this very Bhīma, is now dead. (30.10–30.11)
30.12. Furthermore, there were twenty other sons of Vasudeva who were foremost in beauty, as well as the quarters and the waters;
accompanied by them, he—honored by the gods and their followers—enjoyed pleasures unattainable even for the deities.
Having instructed the disciplined brahmins, he protected all the dharmas of Hari, establishing them as repositories.

He maintained five groups of five learned Vaiṣṇavas along with their attendants for each of his own villages; he personally administered punishment to those who fell away from that path and joyfully took up the cause of those who remained therein.
Furthermore, he ensured that all this was carried out by other eminent Brahmins as well, purifying their conduct in accordance with what he had established.

In his kingdom, there was no one who was not a devotee of Nārāyaṇa, nor anyone devoted to another, nor any destroyer of dharma; there was no one who transgressed the injunctions, nor anyone who was miserable, nor anyone whose wealth was incomplete.
As Vasiṣṭha and the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis beheld him, as did Bhīma and the lords of sages, [they were filled with wonder].
In the Kṛta age, the Kali age was superior in merit to the first among those who were well-trained;
for in that age, even a great auspicious act yielded little fruit, whereas in this [Kali] age, the opposite is the case: even a small inauspicious act results in such a fault.
Thus, through his reliance on the Imperishable (Acyuta), Māruti brought about a Kali age that surpassed the Kṛta age in its high merit.
Dhanañjaya, like a raised staff, was ever directed by his elder brother against the wheels of others;
having terrified the kings along with their jewels, he caused them to fall at the feet of the King, the foremost of men.
From the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa, there has always flowed forth the nectar of the definitive determination of reality.
Drinking the pressed soma and other drinks, he took his pleasure in succession, enjoying incessant and excessive delights.
(30.19) Accompanied by Subhadrā and Citrāṅgadā, he dwelt in the palace of Duḥśāsana;
with the splendor of the moon and a full orb, he shone intensely like the moon situated in the sky. (30.20)

He was the foremost giver of wages to all his servants; he dwelt in the residence of Durmukha and lived as the chief consort with the daughter of the Madra king. He remained in the palace of Durmarṣaṇa, engaged in activities concerning peace and discord.
The king’s bodyguard, with sword grasped, stood by his younger brother along with the daughter of Magadha;
Kṛpa was the commander-in-chief, while Yuyutsu, Sañjaya, and Vidura attended upon the son of Ambikā.
Urged by the Pārthas, they all personally waited upon him with devotion as if he were a deity. (30.22–23)
While the Pāṇḍus, dispatched by the two-formed Kṛṣṇa, were ruling the earth, there was no one who was afflicted;
there was no untimely death, nor were women widowed, nor were men separated from their kin.
Sounds and other sensory objects were exceedingly pleasing, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) rained down according to their every desire.
The subjects, untouched by any affliction, worshipped Acyuta with exclusive devotion.
The earth and the cows, together with Sarasvatī, became ever-granting of desires;
and the years, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, the trees, and all mobile beings likewise yielded jewels.
Having brought all this under their control through refuge in Kṛṣṇa and protecting it properly, they always rejoiced like gods in heaven, surrounded by lords of sages, gandharvas, kings, and others;
the radiant lady that is the fame of the Pāṇḍavas, having placed her foot upon the heads of the faction of the asuras. (30.27)
With her two hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, she who was born from Kṛṣṇa enveloped the cosmic egg.
Its feet were the netherworlds (pātāla), its hips the earth, its waist the sky, and its arms extended to the quarters;
its chest was adorned with the planets, constellations, and stars, and its lotus-face was the abode of Brahmā’s world. 30.28–29.

Beholding her named Varabhārata, who respectfully bore upon her head the Lord of Vikuṇṭha with his hand extended in granting fearlessness, all the worlds were purified as if they had entered another sacrificial altar.
While the sons of Pṛthā, together with Kṛṣṇa, were indeed protecting the earth, Kali and Bali truly vanished.
When it was heard that the two Daityas Supārśva and Pāpa had caused a great upheaval in the kingdom,
Bhīma, duly urged by King Yudhiṣṭhira and Kṛṣṇa, then defeated those two along with their hosts;
having routed Bali and bound Kali, he brought them before Kṛṣṇa and the lord of men.
In the presence of Kṛṣṇa, the noble-minded Yudhiṣṭhira asked him:
"O evil-minded one, why do you cause my kingdom to be overwhelmed in this Kali age?
Thus addressed, Time replied: "This is the time for the downfall of Duryodhana."
"Starting from that point, you have remained there having forcibly seized it; therefore, O lord of men, I caused this upheaval in your kingdom.
The king said to him: "For the sovereignty of kings proceeds by means of force."
“Even if your kingdom is overtaken by Time, it will surely be seized by powerful kings like me; how then will you have sovereignty at that time?
Is Time the cause of the king, or is the king the cause of Time? (30.35)
"Thus, let there be no doubt in you: the king is the cause of the Age.
(83/30.36) Kali said to him: "O Kali, how could there be anyone like you in my age? O King, having first entered the king, I shall then enter the Brahmins. (30.37)
"O King, there is no splendor in you who are the allies of Vāsudeva;
where is that king, apart from you, whom I do not overcome? O protector of the earth, this is my own time, which stands in opposition to the Brahmins and the Vedas. (30.38)
"Where are virtues, where are the Vedas, and where are sound arguments when my gaze falls?
the king said, speaking the truth even while intending to speak falsely, as he declared:
"I shall release you from your truthful word only when it concerns someone other than my own lineage."
Do not plunder all properties, and do not pay tax even upon that. 30.40 Regarding boundaries, there shall be much deliberation; regarding weights and measures, there shall be tax for me.
Never, under any circumstances, transgress these rules with your whole being. 30.41
The Blessed Kṛṣṇa said to him: "As long as the lineage of the Pāṇḍavas exists, you shall have no power on this earth, even though you are active;
[only] after the Pāṇḍavas, until Kṣemaka, who will gradually increase [the power]."
"Beyond Kṣemaka, your power will surely reach fulfillment (pūrti).
You must not even look at the surface of the earth, much less touch it. As long as the sons of Pṛthā and I remain here, then set foot upon the ground. (30.43–44)
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva and liberated by the son of Dharma,
he bowed to them and went to the far shore of the ocean, where he took refuge in a cave.
And the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, protected the earth and attained great joy.
(30.45) Having thus established the Pāṇḍavas at Indraprastha, [Kṛṣṇa], along with Arjuna,
spoke divine stories for his amusement in order to dispel the grief for his son.
He spoke again in detail to him that which had been stated in the Gītā but forgotten:
"By these—Vāk, Prāṇa, and Vāsudeva—all is pervaded;
these possess supremacy over all, and this entire world is under their control."
These [beings] are also increasingly superior in qualities, while others are under their control.
Thus, Lord Hari alone is the master, complete with all qualities;
there is no other. Above him is Prāṇa, and below him is Ramā.
He is called *Hutāṇsa* because he consumes all that is offered;
residing eternally between speech and breath, he sustains the entire universe.
He is the Lord (*Īśa*), while Brahmā, Rudra, and others are proclaimed to be merely individual souls (*jīva*). (30.49)
Those who have been devotees of Him from time immemorial are indeed remembered as being fit for liberation;
those who have been hostile toward Him from time immemorial are great sinners fit for darkness (tamas).
Those with mixed dispositions are to be known as middling, revolving within the cycle of saṃsāra. (30.50)
Thus, these living beings are said to be of three kinds, and not otherwise.

(30.51) Furthermore, their relative gradation is to be understood through bodily and mental signs; because they follow the signs of Viṣṇu, that [gradation] is perceived through the degree of such conformity. (30.52)
"The dharma that brings joy to Viṣṇu and his followers has been declared;
any other is adharma. This is the final conclusion; what will mere idle talk accomplish?
(30.53) Having thus instructed him, the Unborn One was duly honored by Arjuna and his kinsmen.
Having somehow restrained those who had followed him from afar,
the Lord set out for the city of Dvārakā by chariot together with Subhadrā. On the road, the Lord was questioned by Udaṅka, who had arisen from his meditative absorption.

He announced that Duryodhana had been slain along with his brothers, sons, and soldiers. As he was preparing to curse himself out of anger at the slaughter of his disciple, Keśava pacified him with words and by revealing his universal form (viśvarūpa).
"This devotee of mine is utterly intent upon my worship;
let him not, by disregarding me, go to a hell from which there is no rising up"—thus enlightened by Vāsudeva out of compassion, his mind became peaceful. (30.57)
With his soul tormented by remorse, he went to him alone for refuge.
Having granted him fearlessness and said, "I shall send the nectar to you so that you may give it to Śakra," the Lord departed for Dvāravatī. (30.58–30.59)
Then Vāsudeva requested the Lord of Gods for the sage’s nectar, saying, "Give it;
I shall deceive [Kamsa]. He too, seeking forgiveness, said, "So be it. Thus addressed by the Blessed One out of affection for him, that husband of Śacī [consented].

Assuming the loathsome guise of a *mātaṅga*, he went to the sage. Placing his water-pot below the stream of urine, the self-controlled Vāsudeva spoke this nectar-like word as if urinating upon him: 30.61.
He sent it for the sake of the great seer, saying, "Drink this.
Thinking it was urine, he said, rejecting it with contempt, "I will not drink this!
Having thus deceived him, Śakra departed delighted to his own abode.

For food is always the exclusive nectar of the gods; therefore, drinking from that [vessel] belonging to others is extremely displeasing to the gods. Furthermore, because he had been shaken by his own transgression, even though he possessed the grace granted by himself... 30.64.
Vāsudeva, however, considered what Udaṅka had said to be entirely proper.
Having reached his own city and been honored by the Yadus,
Keśava related the account to the son of Śūra in the assembly of the Yadus.
Sātvatī, having been informed by the Lord of the Sātvatas that her son’s death had been averted, bowed down and said, "Tell me [the truth]. Then Janārdana spoke.
Thereupon, the sons of Śūra and the others became deeply distressed on account of Abhimanyu.
Accompanied by Keśava, they performed many śrāddha offerings.
While residing here in the presence of Viśveśa, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) sought to perform the supreme sacrifice,
the Aśvamedha, but he did not immediately obtain the necessary wealth.
Compassionate by nature, he did not desire to levy a tax upon the remaining hosts of the warrior class (*kṣatriya*),
nor did his mind turn toward performing a sacrifice according to the middle scale.
Having understood this, Bādarāyaṇa, who is eternally all-knowing, [acted accordingly].
It appeared at the peak of the Himalayas where it joins with the peak of Meru;
there, Viṣṇu, though already liberated from the bonds of karma, sacrificed his own imperishable self for the sake of sustaining the world. (30.71–72)
Where Śaṅkara and other gods, as well as Marutta, worshipped Hari, there the Dānavas and Vṛṣaparvan found inexhaustible wealth.
That supreme Hari, the son of Jamadagni, was residing within the body of Śaṅkara.
"Having performed the sacrifice with his permission, accept [the wealth] and perform the sacrifice with it.
Following these words of Vyāsa, Bhīma also said to the best of kings:
"Viṣṇu, the son of Jamadagni, the lord of all, is the deity of wealth."
Abiding within the body of Śaṅkara, he is the lord of the wealth remaining from the sacrifice.
That supreme weapon was given by Viṣṇu himself to Arjuna;
furthermore, other tasks of ours have been accomplished by this Viṣṇu.
He is the giver of the positions of Brahmā, Rudra, Śakra, and others, the bestower of all things;
he is independent and, by his own will, brings those who are dependent back [to their state]. O King, we are always dear to him, and he is always dear to us.
"Therefore, let us perform the sacrifice with wealth granted by him.
"This very Vyāsa, our grandfather, will bestow it upon us.
Having said this, they set Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana at their head and departed.
Taking wealth from all sides for a distance of a hundred *yojanas*, Kṛṣṇa gave it to them; they, in turn, spoke [of their needs] with elephants, camels, horses, men, and so forth.
With the exception of Yudhiṣṭhira, all of them were led by Bhīmasena.
For the sake of the sacrifice, vast amounts of gold, shining with the luster of the rising sun, were brought forth. At that very time, Vāsudeva also, accompanied by his wife Bhadrā,
arrived at Hastināpura, honored along the way by those traveling northward.
Having granted those clouds— which were raining down whatever was desired— to him who sought water,
and having made his own boon fruitful, he departed for Hastināpura while the Pārthas and Vyāsa, that supreme among men, were still nearby. (30.83)

Then Kṛṣṇa entered the city; at that time Uttarā gave birth to her dead son. Seeing the army slaughtered by the weapon of Droṇa’s son, Kuntī and the other women sought refuge with Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, who is the protector of those seeking shelter.

Keśava brought back to life that which had been visibly protected by himself in the womb but slain at birth, for the sake of Pārtha’s lineage. At that very moment, the Pārthas entered together with Kṛṣṇa and their vast collection of wealth.

Seeing their grandson protected by Keśava, everyone rejoiced. Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, being delighted at the birth of his grandson, gave away gifts in great abundance and bowed down to Vāsudeva.
Hari was praised and bowed to by Kuntī, Kṛṣṇā, Subhadrā, Vairāṭī, and others, as well as by the Pāṇḍavas, other men, and the assembly of sages.
Then, permitted by Kṛṣṇā, those members of the assembly departed.

They commenced the horse sacrifice with sages who were exponents of the Veda. The Lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana himself caused that horse sacrifice, which embodies all sacrifices, to be performed for them by the Lord of the World.
Urged by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the son of Pavamāna prepared all the ritual implements as well as a golden hall. Then,
accompanied by the family priest, he set forth with the sacrificial horse that had been consecrated and released.
The son of Vāsava followed the black-spotted horse.
Having conquered all the kings who obstructed him by the splendor of his sword,
he caused it to roam through all kingdoms, remaining unconquered by his enemies.
By the command of Yudhiṣṭhira, no one was slain by him at that time;
rather, all the kings were invited by him with pleasure for the sake of the sacrifice.
(30.95) Having reached Maṇalūra in due course, Babhruvāhana encountered him there.
Vijaya approached him with offerings of water for honor and for the feet, and said to his son:
"Desiring to fight, I came here today bringing an offering; yet I am not pleased. Shame on your manliness, since you did not restrain my horses as they were being sacrificed! (30.96–97)
Even then, Ulūpikā, out of devotion to her father, spoke to him as he was not yet fighting:
"Fight! For the sake of pleasing your guru, this task is undoubtedly your duty;
fight indeed for his gratification, displaying your prowess before your father. (30.98)

Thus addressed by his father, Arjuna fought, displaying all his strength; yet, out of affection for his son, he fought slowly while smiling. But Dhananjaya remained unperturbed even when all his weapons were hurled at him.
Having seen it, out of childishness he threw a large sacrificial cake, purified by mantras, at his father for the sake of testing him; by that act of fate, delusion took possession of him.
Seeing his teacher thus fainted, he was deeply pained by his devotion to him.
As he sat in the vow of fasting unto death, his mother, overcome with extreme grief, lamented:
"She reviled Ulūpī then, crying, 'Fie upon her who has slain my husband—who was honored by the three worlds—by means of a son of whom she herself was unaware! (30.101–102)

"Having abandoned my husband, the hero of the world, I have no concern for my son; I shall go to the realm of my husband—be satisfied, O you who delight in strife! Having spoken thus, she whose mind was resolved solely upon death—

Seeing her rolling upon the earth, the daughter of the serpent-king took from the world of the Nagas the herb Viśalyakaraṇī and instantly raised up her husband, that great chariot-warrior of the three worlds, by means of it.
And then, laughing, he spoke these words to Śrutasena: "O Bhīṣma, long ago in the world of the gods, I heard what was said by the deities: 'Nowadays, [the world] is not very righteous.
Because of that fault, O son of Pṛthā, those who have been slain by him shall suffer extreme agony."
"I thought that he should go into battle so as not to be overcome by others;
therefore, at the mere word of the gods, I told my son, 'Fight!
Yet, due to the very resolve of the gods, Arjuna became unconscious. (30.107)
Having already experienced the fruit of this transgression, he shall not experience it again from any other source.
(30.108) The fame of this man, which had spread throughout the three worlds, would have perished had he been struck down by another.
It was for the sake of Arjuna’s fame that this was ordained by the gods. (30.109)
Thus addressed, Arjuna, accompanied by his son and wife, attained great joy;
having been invited for the sake of the sacrifice and duly honored, he then departed from there.
Pradyumna and the other sons of Hari [resided] near Dvārakā.

Challenging Arjuna to battle, they forcibly carried off his own property. (30.111) When the horse had been led away by them so that he might recover Subhadrā’s abduction, Dhananjaya [did not intervene] solely out of respect for Vāsudeva and his maternal uncle. (30.112)
Mātula said to the horse, "It has been stolen by your grandsons as if it were no kinsman.
Having rebuked those princes, he released the sacrificial horse.
Then, having bowed to Mātula and invited them for the sake of the sacrifice, [he departed].
While proceeding toward the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura), O King, he sent a messenger ahead;
having heard that Arjuna had arrived along with Kṛṣṇa and his uterine brothers,
he was filled with joy and, his eyes brimming with tears from brotherly affection, spoke.
"Vāsudeva, I do not see any ill omen on Arjuna;
by what ill omen is he so full of sorrow while living in exile?
When asked this, Keśava replied to him, "Your brother has long calves."
Having said, "Therefore, this [world] is full of suffering," Pāñcālī restrained him with a sidelong glance even as he was speaking;
for Kṛṣṇa, Satyā, and Vṛkodara were all experts in the knowledge of all marks.
"Kṛṣṇā is the fifth; there is no science that can be easily mastered [by her]. Yudhiṣṭhira, being of a virtuous nature, would have desired to acquire that science through his engagement [in battle].
Thus, out of concern for him, Pāñcālī restrained Vāsudeva.
Out of respect for him, Vāsudeva did not offer a reply;
instead, by recounting another story, he caused him to forget [the question]. There was a slight enlargement of the belly as well as an enlargement of the testicles.
Likewise, the excessiveness of Arjuna’s left arm was not mentioned by Vāsudeva, even though it was clearly visible;
for these defects are eternal causes of the diminution of knowledge and bliss. (30.121–122)
In the essence of all living beings, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are devoid of those wicked characteristics; they are fit for the fullness of consciousness, bliss, power, and so forth.
Their defining characteristic is the absence of beginningless suffering and the abundance of happiness.
But [the supreme form] belongs to Śrī herself, appearing as Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and others;
it is more principal than even that, due to her absolute independence and so forth.
It is the supreme, eternal mark (liṅga) of the one who exists in the forms of Vyāsa and others, who is the ocean of all qualities.
It belongs to Viṣṇu alone and to no other, for he is the one who possesses all perfect qualities.
When Arjuna had entered the sacrificial enclosure along with his brothers, they,
being honored, joyfully paid honor to him together with Keśava.
Then that sacrifice, protected by the heroes of the Yadu clan, instructed by Vyāsa, and set in motion by the sages, shone brilliantly;
it was attended by all the assembled kings and the most excellent brahmins, and by the pair of Kṛṣṇas—the supreme Person divided threefold, including the descendant of Bhṛgu. 30.127.
Presided over by him, this entire universe shone forth through his universal form;

30.128 / just as in ancient times there was the sacrifice of Viriñca, and just as it was for Śakra in his state as Śatakratu, even so did that [sacrifice] become, exceedingly adorned by the gods headed by Vidhi, Śarva, and Śakra. 30.129 /

There was no one here among the gods, gandharvas, sages, those who follow their own dharma, mortals, and others, who was not present; this abode shone like heaven with its well-adorned, beloved celestial beings. Right there, in debate, he rendered the truths along with their doubts entirely free from doubt.

Established by the three-eyed Hari with his lofty and supreme words arising from their mutual discourse, that king— surrounded by a multitude of gods and monarchs, with the best of Gandharvas singing, the noble Apsarases dancing, and the foremost of Brahmins playing continuous music— shone alone as the sovereign of all holy sacrifices.

All the goddesses, together with the Vāsudevas, well-adorned and with lotus-faces in full bloom, wandered right there along with the Apsarases; they sat as well, delighting in the excellent stories of Acyuta. 30.133.
Indeed, there was no one here seeking liberation, nor anyone wishing for worldly existence, nor anyone desiring to attain [heaven], much less one desiring sense-pleasures.
30.134–135. While that best of wise men, the son of Vāyu, was the donor, their desires were never unfulfilled.

Day after day there appeared great mountains of food, rich in solid nourishment, flavorful, and abundant; there were rivers perpetually filled with milk and ghee, as well as streams of honey and lakes of milk-rice.

There were vast lakes fit for the gods and others, well-provided with *haricandana* and other [fragrant substances], as well as thousands of ponds made of jewels and gold, filled with the finest decorative materials such as collyrium and lac, which were caused to be built by Māruti according to his desire for drink, seats, and enjoyments. (30.136)
There, fragrances, tastes, and all objects of enjoyment were exceedingly heart-pleasing, as if they were in heaven itself.

30.137 "Never before has there been a sacrifice such as this, except for those of Rāma, Viriñca, and the wielder of the thunderbolt," so said all the worlds upon seeing that sacrifice performed by the Supreme Person. 30.138
Thus, that very sacrifice dedicated to Hari, consisting of five horse-sacrifices (aśvamedhas) and of great magnitude,
increased daily in its excellent qualities for three times five years, bringing joy.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, all the Pāṇḍavas and Kṛṣṇā [Draupadī] [gave away] the entire earth along with its wealth.
Having placed merely auspicious items upon the body of their beloved, as well as all the ornaments,
they presented them to the most excellent Aja, Vyāsa, for distribution according to the instructions of the officiating priests.
Since this Viṣṇu was dear to him, they offered these things to him as if for the purpose of distribution itself.
"O Hṛd, everything has been offered by them to Hari; for he, though residing within the twice-born, is the creator of all.
Having surrendered their bodies, senses, vital breaths, and minds along with their consciousnesses to him, they bowed down, saying:
'All this is yours, and we too; O Lord, there is nothing whatsoever that belongs to us.'"
"You are independent and alone; there is no other. You are eternally full in all things"—thus they were delighted.
Then, having divided [the kingdom], the sages said: "We shall hand over the sovereignty among these [princes];
for we are already full with gold, while these [others] are most capable of protecting the earth. (30.142–143)
Having heard these words of the twice-born, the Pārthas, together with their wife, bowed again to Kṛṣṇa and said:
"After we have handed over the kingdom—attained through dharma—to you at the conclusion of the sacrifice, let us perform penance in the forest.
Thus addressed and entreated even by the lords of sages, the Lord Bādarāyaṇa spoke.

"By my command, O sages, enjoy this entire kingdom as your own gold; it has been offered by me and shall bear fruit for you. Furthermore, taking it back will not be a cause of fault. I am your grandfather, and especially your preceptor and lord; therefore, you ought to accept it from me. (30.145–146)
Thus addressed, they accepted the kingdom and gave him all their gold;
having distributed it among the brahmins, he, being pleased, gave his own entire share to Pṛthā.
Having bestowed upon those who had sons, along with their wives, all the excellent jewels and ornaments without exception, [he departed].
Then the Lord, being delighted, bestowed upon them individually the most excellent boons; they bowed down to him.

Having received from them that entire fivefold sacrifice, performed incessantly with triple qualities and accompanied by perfect sacrificial fees, Hari, the Lord of the Rite, performed for each of them one Aśvamedha sacrifice known by the name Bahusuvarṇaka.
Then, while the Pārthas, together with Kṛṣṇa, were fully purified by the final ablution,
shining like five Indras and being praised by the lords of sages,
and while that sacrifice was being celebrated, Wrath took on the form of Nakula.

Having performed the sacrifice with fierce roaring and reviling all those performers of the rite, he spoke thus, accompanied by his wife, son, and daughter-in-law: "A brahmin living by gleaning gave a prastha of barley meal with great devotion. (30.151–152)
When asked by the brahmins for the reason why this sacrifice was not worth even a sixteenth part of that hospitality toward a guest, he replied:
"The golden surface of that guest's feet, wet with the water used for washing them, [surpassed it]. (30.153)

"One was mine, and another [was mine] even among all the various sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like; truly, while bathing in the purificatory rites (*avabhṛtha*) and zealously performing sacrifices, there was no other.
Thus it was said by the preeminent sages who knew that reality. 30.154–155.
When Kṛṣṇa smiled at those who were leading him toward that blinding darkness, he immediately attained invisibility; and by the power of Time, he reached the end of that darkness.
For that very purpose, a golden ploughshare had belonged to him since ancient times. (30.156)
30.157. Proclaiming the many virtues of Kṛṣṇa, the Pāṇḍavas, and the sacrifice, those who knew the mind of the Enemy of Madhu reviled them;
for it was he who previously defiled the milk intended for Jamadagni’s *śrāddha*.
The ancestors cursed that Krodha in the very form of a mongoose:
"Become a mongoose for as long as you shall insult the gods, beginning with Dharma;
furthermore, let this one go again into terrible darkness by means of his sin. (30.158)
Having intended this, he was cursed by them; having acted accordingly, he entered into darkness.
(30.159) Even though wealth given away when one possesses little may yield great fruit, nevertheless, the great virtues of the doer alone bestow infinite fruit. (30.160)
And among the virtuous, there is affection for him; moreover, Hari alone is the most excellent of the virtuous.
For who could be his equal or even superior in virtues, being the creator of all objects? (30.161) Viṣṇu is the foremost among the virtuous, joined by the best of virtuous sages.
What auspicious means is equal to that preeminent sacrifice which he performs visibly with his most beloved sons, the Pārthas?
The followers of Paiṅgi recite these mantras here as being consistent with their literal meaning.
“Every action performed by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is said to be finite;
that which is performed by a Vaiṣṇava is indeed infinite, and among those, it is supreme according to the sequence of the castes (varṇa).
Even among the Vaiṣṇavas, that which is performed by mortals is a hundred times greater than that [of others]. (30.163)
From that [the *gāndharva*], then the *karma*, from that the sages (*munis*), and from those the ancestors (*pitṛs*);
then that which was performed by the gods (*devas*), Śakra, Śiva, and Brahmā, in sequence.
It should be known as "one hundred plus one," and nothing else is equal to that which was performed by Brahmā. (30.164–165)
"Among living beings, the state of being a Vaiṣṇava increases progressively up to the level of Brahmā;
for the superiority of the fruits of actions arises solely from the pleasure of Viṣṇu, and not otherwise.
(30.166) Thus, there is nothing anywhere equal to the action of the sons of Pṛthā.
Therefore, that anger was *tāmasa*, arising from qualities such as ignorance (*jñāna*);
having reviled those established in pure goodness (*sattva*), he entered into the darkness of *tamas*.
Then Vāsudeva was questioned by the assembly of gods, brahmins, and others.
The Lord, being greatly pleased, spoke from his shoulder to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having heard all those duties, they, endowed with supreme devotion,
honored the Lord of the World and attained the highest joy.
Thus ends [the chapter titled] "The Completion of the Sacrifice" in the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Chapter Thirty-four (The Attainment of Heaven by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Others).
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.

Oṃ! While the sons of Pṛthā were ruling the earth with justice, joined by the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñeśvara), an eminent brahmin arrived at night, desiring wealth and wishing to perform a sacrifice. Having heard the king’s words, “I shall give [it] in the morning,” the brahmin, for the sake of the sacrifice, was in haste. 31.1.

Having heard the words spoken by the king, he (Bhīma) requested [the ornament], and the best of brahmins then accepted the priceless jewel from his own hand— an object resembling fire and adorned with various gems. Having achieved his purpose, the son of the Wind-god then caused a joyful proclamation to be made.
Hearing that [news] which was untimely, the King questioned him through messengers; Bhīma said to him:

"Since even the mortal body of the King had its lifespan determined, I have no cause for joy. Being thus addressed, the King, honoring his opinion, thought, "One should hasten for the sake of Dharma."
Then he said, "Excellent! and once more became intent upon righteousness.

(31.5) Then Māruti, perceiving that the son of Ambikā was attached to sense-objects, corrupted by evil company, and a perpetrator of many sins—the very cause of the ruin of the entire kingdom—felt compassion for him. (31.6)

"If he does not perform rigorous austerities, he will never attain the higher worlds; moreover, being excessive in passion, he might not practice asceticism"—thinking thus, [the gods] performed acts intended to produce world-weariness in him.
While he was being highly honored by his siblings and even by the women of the household, they struck at his command.
He groaned even though he was thus highly honored by the others; yet at that time, he felt no detachment.

For all the Pārthas, with the exception of Yudhiṣṭhira, along with their wives, constantly attended upon the son of Vicitravīrya with the utmost respect, together with Draupadī, lest she should suffer the pain of losing her sons. (31.8–31.9)
Although he felt great affection for them all, he did not feel even greater affection for Bhīmasena;
for he remembered that his daughter had been killed by him, and he knew the supreme power of that man.
Bhīmasena, in turn, sought to remove his attachment to sense-objects and likewise his hatred toward himself.
Slapping his arms, he spoke in the presence of the two sons of Mādrī while the king himself was listening:
"These two arms of mine are round, muscular, and smeared with sandalwood paste—having come between them, the sons of this old man were slain. (31.11–12)
The twins rejoiced at that, out of affection for him and also out of respect;
however, it was not known by Kṛṣṇā, nor by Pṛthā and her sons.
Having heard this, Vidura increased the despondency of the eldest brother.
He said: "O King, surely your desire for life is very great;
you accept the morsel of food offered by Bhīma like a domestic dog.
And there is no fault in Bhīma for speaking these words to you. (31.14)
Fire was unleashed against you, poison was administered, and your wife was defiled;
his fields and wealth were seized—what has Bhīma done to you?
Enough of this talk that is being hurled at you today, which only serves to cause you despondency.
Out of a desire to benefit you, Bhīma has harbored this hatred toward you; therefore, abandon it here.
31.16 Freeing yourself from both hatred and desire, frequent the sacred fords in the forest;
propitiate Hari through austerity, and then you shall become purified. 31.17
Having been addressed thus, Bhīma cast off his hatred and, overcome by despondency,
became intent on fasting in order to obtain permission to practice asceticism.
On the fourth day, Yudhiṣṭhira [saw] Dhṛtarāṣṭra not eating.

Having understood this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, overcome with exhaustion, repeatedly requested food; saying, "I shall eat only after obtaining permission from you for my forest exile in every respect, otherwise not," he spoke again and again. (31.19)

Emaciated by fasting, he fainted for a moment and leaned against his wife. Then Dharmaja, gently touching him with a cool hand, slowly restored him to consciousness and spoke, deeply distressed: (31.20–31.21)
"Placing Yuyutsu at the forefront, you should rule the kingdom free from thorns;
we ourselves shall perform all ascetic penance in the forest for your sake.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said to him, "No; for it is our family duty to dwell in the forest."
"The renunciation of the body is at hand; you ought to grant me permission for that.
While the two of them were thus disputing, the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana—the omniscient Lord and creator of all—manifested and spoke to the king.
Grant permission to this king who desires the destruction of all his faults through austerity; do not become an obstacle to his dharma.
Having attained world-weariness in this Kali age, he has burnt away his sins through asceticism.
"He shall attain a bright state; otherwise, by no means could he do so.
Thus addressed, Dharmarāja granted him permission, and being thus authorized, he instructed the wise youth thoroughly in the true Dharma and in statesmanship.
Out of pure affection, he listened to [the advice] for the sake of instructing the king.
When the son of Dharma had returned home after receiving permission, Vidura again sent word to him, desiring wealth for the sake of the ancestral rites (śrāddha). 31.27–28.
Having heard this, Yudhiṣṭhira said to Bhīma: "Today we must immediately give wealth to those who desire the śrāddha for our sons, grandsons, kinsmen, and relatives.
To him, Bhīma spoke regarding the enemies of Madhusūdana who had turned their backs and fled from battle.
One should not provide assistance for the sake of the next world for the benefit of another;
for even with wealth given by him, his son will perform the *śrāddha* ceremony.
Thinking that there would be fault for those who give if they were to know this, [he refrained]. 31.30.
"May all those led by Duryodhana go from misery to even greater misery!
(31.31) What does it matter to us that we are the ones performing the *śrāddha* for Bhīṣma and the others?
For because Karṇa was younger [than us], he indeed lived separately from us."
"Is wealth given to one who is authorized for the *śrāddha* rite?
To him who had spoken thus, the king and Arjuna replied again:
"To one who desires to depart and asks for it, [wealth] acquired by the strength of one's own arms [is given]."
"Give wealth from another source; what does he request from you?
Even when addressed thus, the pure and righteous man replied only, "No. Yudhiṣṭhira, speaking with displeasure, said to him, "Be silent! (31.33–34).
"Whatever wealth outside the treasury— such as the causes for giving and enjoyment—
is currently at my disposal, all of that has today been entrusted by me to my father.
Thus spoke Arjuna, and they both spoke again to Vidura.
"O Bhīma, who delights in the primary dharma, your father ought not to be angry.
Having been told this, the Kṣattṛ took wealth and went; having approached the elder brother, he said:
"Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna have shown you the utmost devotion. (31.36)
"O Bhima, do not be angry with him over this; he is delighted by your command.
