For Vrikodara is entirely devoted to the pure dharma of a Kshatriya, while King Yudhishthira and Arjuna, though devoted to righteousness, are intent on the welfare of the world. (31.37–31.38)
Having heard that, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his anger unaroused and his mind tranquil,
performed funeral rites for all of them; with a pure mind and the intention of being free from debt, he continuously gave great gifts for ten nights.

Having entrusted everything to Govinda and to the sons of Pṛthā as well as to his other kinsmen, the high-minded king, with tears streaming from his eyes, took leave of them and went forth; then he spoke to the citizens and the people of the countryside: 31.40.
"You have been protected by righteousness by our great-souled predecessors;
nor have I ever been told by you—out of supreme affection and your compassionate nature—even in negligence, O virtuous ones, that I am unprotected. (31.41)
Through your protection, I have performed sacrifices and works of public utility;
yet my son is evil-minded, the destroyer of all the kṣatriyas, suspicious of everyone, foolish, and a transgressor of the commands of his elders. (31.42)
Having utterly abandoned his brotherly affection for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
he committed a most great and ignoble deed, the likes of which no one else would ever do;
that evil-minded man performed many acts disagreeable to Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, that dull-witted man did not bring any misfortune upon you;
yet all his brothers, following his own character,
were slain by their own sin along with their sons, ministers, and kinsmen.

Thus, having reached old age and overwhelmed by anxieties for my sons, I am now prepared to wipe away— through ascetic penance— the sin incurred through my connection with them and my own unseemly deeds, upon the Pāṇḍavas together with Kṛṣṇa. (31.46)

In this matter, may you, who are affectionate toward friends, grant me your permission out of compassion. For the sake of my pleasure as well, your love for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas must be maintained and made ever more steadfast. (31.47)
"For they were my little sons, providing happiness both here and in the hereafter"—
with these words, the citizens and countryfolk, deeply distressed, their eyes filled with tears, after a long time and with great difficulty, proclaimed his virtues aloud. 31.48.
Having been granted permission, he departed, followed by the Pārthas for a very great distance.
Sañjaya and Vidura also followed him along with his wife;
Kuntī, having resolved to go to the forest, likewise followed him.
Though she was being restrained by her sons and their wives, who were deeply distressed,
she established them with great difficulty and followed after that king.
The king, shown the way by Kuntī, Vidura, and Sañjaya, [proceeded on].
Accompanied by Gandhārī, he reached in due course the hermitage of the divine Vyāsa, the teacher of the world, which is honored by the gods, at Kurukṣetra. There,
he declared that after three years, he and his wife would attain his own world.
Born from the womb of Brahmā’s lotus, he was highly esteemed by him; instructed by Vyāsa, he practiced supreme austerity.

While the lord Hari was being propitiated through austerities by the King of the Gandhāris along with his brothers-in-law, the Suta, and Sañjaya, the sons of Pṛthā, together with their wives, kinsmen, and servants, arrived there to see the son of Vicitravīrya.
Then, while Vidura was attaining oneness with Yudhiṣṭhira, and while the sons of Pṛthā were sitting near their mother Pṛthā and the son of Vicitravīrya along with Sañjaya and his wife,
there appeared a shower of immeasurable power, splendor, knowledge, wonderful sovereignty, happiness, and other such qualities.
Seeing Vyāsa there, Hari, they all honored him with supreme devotion.

Honored by them, he sat down and said: "Whatever each of you desires, speak it; I shall grant that very thing today. Thus, the sons of Pāṇḍu, together with their wives, displayed an excess of devotion toward him.
There, Kuntī, having been chosen, requested the removal of the defects arising from the birth and death of the son of the Sun (Karṇa).
When their desired wishes had been granted, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his wife,
consulted and requested that Lord for a vision of all those slain in battle without exception.

Then, by the command of that Lord of All, the son of Satyavatī, they all assembled from the heavenly realm in an instant; and divine vision was granted to this king. By his supreme command alone, they all dwelt for the night together with their wives, just as before.

The king, together with his wife, was satisfied, and everyone there beheld that great wonder. Then, by the command of that supreme being, all the women returned to their own homes accompanied by their husbands;
however, having heard that account except for the part concerning Uttarā, the son of Parīkṣit requested the vision of his father.

Then Kṛṣṇa, who possesses inconceivable power, brought him back from the world of Vaikuṇṭha at that very moment. Upon seeing his grandfather restored by the Lord, Parīkṣit attained great satisfaction. Having honored Kṛṣṇa, who is himself worshipped by the Lord, Parīkṣit’s son asked for forgiveness.
And he (Yudhiṣṭhira) placed great trust in Bhārata, and again, joined by the people there,
the Pāṇḍavas returned to their own city and, protecting the earth with righteousness, enjoyed appropriate pleasures without passion, being devoted to Vāsudeva, the sustainer of the world. 31.63–64.

At the end of thirty-four years, those who had abandoned their fires and were consuming the forest heard that Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his wife and Kuntī, had their bodies completely consumed by fire. Hearing that their paternal uncle had ascended to heaven, they stood with faces downcast, absorbed in meditation.
Having met with their husband, they honored Kuntī and performed the funeral rites for her with grief.

(31.66) Those sons of Pṛthā, whose actions were purified by devotion to Viṣṇu and by wisdom, and who at the end remembered Him, attained an inexhaustible and auspicious increase of happiness through their virtuous sons, who had likewise performed meritorious deeds for the sake of their afterlife. (31.67)
Ghaṭotkaca’s son, Ghaṭotkaca, having approached Vyāsa and served him, regained his own former state;
and the sons of Pāṇḍu, awaiting Kṛṣṇa, ruled the earth. Thus, eighteen years passed while those great-souled ones were ruling the entire world.
"Of those whose supreme dharma, purpose, and happiness are unfailing, and whose infinite states and mindfulness are never abandoned.
Thus ends the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Chapter Thirty-One: (The Attainment of Heaven by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Others) (The Ascent to Heaven of the Pāṇḍavas)
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Om! Then, having reached Kurukṣetra, Kṛṣṇa entered upon the initiation for the twelve-year sacrificial session (*sattra*).
He himself—the unborn, immeasurable one, whose soul is the descendant of Vyāsa and Bhṛgu—performed the duties of the assistant priests (*sādasya*) therein. 32.1.
There, the officiating priests, led by Dakṣa and Bhṛgu, together with the foremost of the Pārthas and the Yadus,

and the gods headed by Brahmā, Īśa, and Śakra— all these servants of Ananta— performed the duties of assistants. And all living beings dwelling upon the surface of the earth, as well as those others in the intermediate space, the heavens, and the regions beyond, were present.
All those who dwell there, taking refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa, rejoiced together with the Nāgas.
For those seeking the determination of reality and those devoted to debate on the truth, there arose here a definitive resolution regarding reality;
through mutual discussion among the gods and the Brahmins, by the word of Hari, who has Vyāsa and Bhṛgu as his own manifestations.

Those who desired them obtained from Kṛṣṇa here all their dharma, wealth, and pleasure, as well as liberation; gods, humans, and others wandered about there, clothed in garments and provided with food and drink according to their wish.
That land was equal to the world of Hari, for all virtuous people attained union [with him] by going there.
Consequently, those whose desires were unfulfilled became unable to see Keśava, for he was visible here only with effort.

(32.6) Having thus concluded this twelve-year great sacrifice (*mahāsatra*) of such a nature, Hari performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and after honoring all the people, (32.7) [he departed].
Desiring to withdraw his own family, he granted permission in due order to those who had assembled over the course of a year; thus he brought about the brahmin’s curse.
Having instructed Uddhava, the son of Aṅgiras, in the supreme knowledge, [he departed].
Having brought [the Kali age] to the place called Badarī at one hundred and seven years,
the Lord, awaiting [its end], protected the earth together with the sons of Pṛthā.
When the Kali age had begun, Duryodhana fell.
Furthermore, Kṛṣṇa restored the Kṛta age as it was in the thirty-sixth cycle.
32.10. This is even more distinguished than the original Kṛta age: by Kṛṣṇa’s command, the fruit of merit is greater and the fruit of sin is much smaller than before. 32.11.
Thus, when the world had become exceedingly righteous and devoted to the worship of Hari,
and the marks of the Kali age had vanished, the gods headed by Brahmā and Rudra, desiring to bring about the course of the Yuga, praised the imperishable Keśava.
They requested the attainment of their own worlds, and the Imperishable One said, "Oṃ.
(32.13) "When there is an abundance of virtuous people, the Kali age will not increase easily.
Thinking thus, the Lord led them to Prabhāsa for the sake of the preservation of his own lineage. (32.14)
"Even in a field of merit, death is not as beneficial as it is at one's own home;
yet even a small field, by the very act of going to it, may yield great fruit," said the Unborn One (Brahmā),
desiring to incite them [the gods] to go from Kuśasthalī to Prabhāsa.
Having brought them there, Acyuta caused them to perform the true Dharma, beginning with generosity. Then, deluded by Kṛṣṇa himself through the power of a curse,
they became intoxicated by liquor, struck one another down, and departed for their own bodies [in hell].
Having seen that, Baladeva also departed for his own abode by means of yoga (32.17).
Thereafter, the Supreme Lord, whose majesty is immeasurable, dispatched his charioteer to the presence of the Pāṇḍavas along with Kṛṣṇa,
urging him to hasten back with news of his own departure and of theirs (32.18).
Then, at the root of the Pippala tree, Asat beheld the Lord’s copper-hued sole resting upon his thigh; though he was a devotee, fearing it might be a Rohita fish, he discharged a dart named Jarā.
Even as the dart struck the foot of him whose body is indestructible and indivisible, [the Lord remained unmoved]. (32.19)
The hunter, having approached and seen him, fell to the ground in fear.
Disregarding the words of the brahmin, Hari caused him to pay the fee and led him to heaven as he pleaded, "O God, destroy my sin. (32.20–21)

Janārdana, being well-pleased by the remorse and devotion of Bhṛgu— who had fallen into the state of a hunter due to the fault of striking with his foot— led that embodied soul to heaven by means of a celestial chariot obtained through his own command. 32.22.
A lowly birth was obtained through very base actions resulting from base deeds;
yet, because his mind was not corrupted, there was no loss of devotion. Even though Bhṛgu committed an act here that caused offense, it was done unintentionally. 32.23.
Then Viriñci, Īśa, Purandara, and the others, having bowed down and offered praise once more, departed;
and Kṛṣṇa, illuminating all this universe with his own splendor, went to his own world in an instant.
Bestowing the fruits upon those who worship the Gopāla-mantra, he remained invisible on earth in one form.

With his second [form], he stood upon the solar orb; his third body was that which was worshipped by Śiva. His fourth body was worshipped in the world of Brahmā by the Lotus-born One; then, as he attained his supreme abode, the best of gods followed his fifth body with devotion according to their own power.

Their vision eclipsed by that splendor of him whose radiance was immeasurably vast, Puruhūta and the other gods followed him as far as they were able to go and then stood with eyes closed, their upward movement arrested.
Then Svayambhū, accompanied by Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śeṣa, bowed down to that Unborn One who had entered his own abode.
Though unapproachable even by Indra and the other gods, he embraced his father in private and spoke thus, and likewise praised him.
Having attained oneness with his former form and then divided himself again according to his will,
Hari— whose nature consists of immeasurable, auspicious qualities— delighted while being worshipped by Śrī, Brahmā, and the other liberated ones.

Brahmā, accompanied by Śarva and the other gods, returned to his own world; there he beheld Kṛṣṇa, who had likewise gone there, and rejoiced while honoring him as he stood within the solar orb, as did all the deities. For nowhere, even in his manifestations, was any delusion shown.
By imitating the abandonment of the body, Hari— the Lord who is incapable of falling—
deluded the asuras and brought them into blinding darkness;
for although his sole body is consciousness and bliss, he made it appear as if another body had been cast off.
Having created [the body] resembling his own, he lay upon the earth;
then, having ascended from the earth to heaven, he was struck by Pārtha with a sharp arrow.
At that time, the bodies of Rauhineya and the others were also primarily destroyed.
Dāruka returned to the world of Viṣṇu just as he had come;
likewise, for the sake of deluding the people, he became invisible in the fire.
Having performed such penance, Satyā (Rukmiṇī) went to the side of Hari.

Since those two, though possessing a single body of consciousness and bliss, appear as if they have two forms, therefore, like Kṛṣṇa, you alone shall delude the wicked; while the other great queens, having abandoned their bodies in the sacrificial fire, [shall attain liberation].

Some, having abandoned their bodies through ascetic penance, went to Hari; 32.36 / And all the wives of Rauhiṇeya and the others, being devoted to their husbands, cast their bodies into the mouth of the fire and attained their very lords. 32.37 /
Having heard this from the mouth of Arjuna, Vasudeva, established in yoga,
cast off his body and attained the state of Kaśyapa through his devotion to Kṛṣṇa. Then Arjuna performed the final rites for him in the fire of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
His wife, having abandoned her body, attained that very same state in the fire. Taking the women, the children, and the wealth, Dhanañjaya departed from Dvārāvatī; and the ocean swallowed him up.
While Pārtha was traveling along a path accompanied by women and children, those exceedingly wicked and arrogant Abhīras, driven by a curse, seized the women;
sixteen thousand and a hundred women were carried off. (32.41)
Due to their pride, the Kṛṣṇas fell under the power of the Mlecchas as a result of that curse.
While their wealth and women were being carried away,
the son of Vasava (Arjuna) could only with great difficulty string his Gāṇḍīva bow, even though he was eager for battle.
By fate, his arrows were exhausted and his weapons no longer came to mind;
realizing that this was the work of destiny and remembering Puruṣottama, he continued to strike down his enemies with the Gāṇḍīva bow while protecting the remaining Kurus. 32.44.

Then, beholding that very Hari—the teacher of the world who had gone to Kurukṣetra, possessing the bliss of true existence through the power and perfection of supreme wisdom, and the scion of the Vasiṣṭha lineage—he fell at his feet in grief.
He was awakened by that foremost of men, who was adorned with the splendor of the sun, through various reasoned arguments. 32.45.
Having steadied his mind once again upon that [goal], he abandoned his grief almost entirely through fortitude.
(32.46) The women who had been carried off by the Mlecchas were recovered from Dālbhya, who was sent by Kṛṣṇa;
and having heard of the Govinda-ekādaśī, they performed [the rite] in the waters of the Sarasvatī.

Having immersed themselves at the word of Vāyu, they cast off their bodies and went to heaven. Arjuna, however, consecrated the two sons of Hārdikya and Yuyudhāna in Kurukṣetra, and those of Sārasvata in the region of that name, as kings.

The self-controlled Phalguna made the son of Aniruddha, Vajra—the beloved of Kṛṣṇa and possessor of excellent qualities—king of Śūrasena and Indraprastha; having established there the women, children, and wealth. 32.49.
He went and described to his brothers the entire account of their past;
and they, remembering the time of their separation from the enemy of Mura,
consecrated Parīkṣit, the devotee of the Lord, in the great kingdom.
And they employed him for the slaughter of the Mlecchas who carry off women;
and that deed was performed by him, who bore the ancestral burden, whereas it was not even accomplished by the Pārthas, despite their guarding the agreement. (32.52)
The removal of the thorns from the earth was accomplished by the touch of Vāsudeva’s feet;
indeed, the duty of the Pāṇḍavas was solely to follow him.
By us, who followed the Lord of the Universe, the earth has been abandoned.
"In former times, it was their established agreement that they were to be both fed and protected.
Therein, Kālī, the wife of Bhīma, having resorted to Vaiṣṇava yoga and attained oneness with Kṛṣṇa, cast off her human body.
Then, by the command of the Pārthas, Subhadrā and the other wives, as well as Yuyutsu, dwelt in the city for the sake of training their grandson;
having cast off the insignia of royalty, they established themselves in Vaiṣṇava yoga. (32.56)

All the Pāṇḍavas went along the path of heroes together with Kṛṣṇā. Previously, Arjuna had gone toward the north-eastern direction, but out of greed he did not abandon his bow there; however, the Fire-god approached that ocean.
Having seen him, he entreated the king; thus addressed, the king cast him into the ocean.
But Agni, having fulfilled his guarantee before Varuṇa, became invisible.
They too departed quickly, leaping across the seven seas.
Having ascended their yoga after seven days and performed a circumambulation, they proceeded without lingering anywhere until they reached Mount Gandhamādana.
There, in the sacred field of Nārāyaṇa, their bodies fell down in succession. (32.60)
Because the five— Draupadī, Sahadeva, and the others—
had no desire for their bodies to remain there, that falling of the body occurred;
knowing the reality of their situation as "here," Māruti questioned the son of Dharma.

"By what specific fault did his body fall [into such a state]?"—in this manner, at the time of death, whoever declares the fault that constitutes the "release from debt" (ṛṇamocana), for him there shall be the removal of that declared fault;
for Śruti itself has said that very thing. 32.62.
For the sake of liberating everyone from their debt, Bhīma played the *doṣās*. He,
not knowing that those bodies had fallen by their own will and that their actions were pure,
saw no other cause and said, "The *doṣās* must indeed be the reason."
“O King, mere honor is not to be bestowed without cause.
[The King replied: “By means of yoga, the Pāṇḍavas and Kṛṣṇā, casting off their bodies at will, have attained the supreme state which even the gods do not reach. (32.64)
65. Thus, because of this sacred tradition, those powerful ones did not abandon their bodies due to sin.
Having cleared his debts by speaking of the faults of his own people, Bhīma abandoned his body while meditating on the Supreme, and attained the highest station.
Thus spoke Vyāsa to the sages in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Since Vāsava has partiality for four [of the five] excepting Bhīma, it would not be a fault in any way for Kṛṣṇā [to choose him], as he alone is worthy. (32.66–67)

"Policy, guile, and the great powers of heroism and strength belong to these [elements] respectively; and because they constitute the vital breath (*prāṇa*), their capacity for experience does not lead to fault in the case of Māruta (the Wind).
Just as the knowledge of one's own true nature within the self does not produce fault."

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vyāsa, how could these [three] give rise to the aforementioned defects? (32.69) At times, even excessive pride may arise among these three; nevertheless, that does not bear fruit [in this regard], for the gradation [of merit] pertains to liberation.
For even though the Veda is established as authoritative, it is subject to variation based on the predominance or scarcity of virtues and defects.
Indeed, even for one who is free from sin, the body may fall at the exhaustion of the karma already commenced;
for Yudhiṣṭhira, though he enjoyed heaven, did not do so in that very body.
How indeed could faults such as arrogance exist in the son of the Wind?

From beginningless time, he has been free from all defects and preeminent in virtues. Even those among the multitudes of all living beings who would attain the state of the Wind [would not possess such faults]. 32.72.
The gods known as the Ṛjavas are the deities even of the gods.
Furthermore, Keśava has declared the non-existence of terrible pride and the like:
"O Pāṇḍava, whatever excellence you perceive within yourself... (32.73)
"I consider this [merit] to be a thousandfold even in you.

(32.74) Thus, just as he considered there to be a loss of dharma in battle, so too did the king declare that in this case [death] would result from unrighteousness through the falling of the body. (32.75)
For those who desired the fall of their bodies even before [the arrival of] the venerable ones, the fall of the body occurred through that desire so that they might be liberated from sin;
for in no way does the fall of the body occur upon liberation from the fruit of sin. (32.76)
"But it is certain that in all cases this occurs only through the exhaustion of karma.
(32.77) When they had reached their respective worlds, the son of Dharma, together with his own self, proceeded ahead; then the divine chariot descended for him. (32.78)

When he was told by the charioteer, "Mount the chariot," as Śunaḥ was before him, he said to the driver, "This is not proper. But when the driver replied firmly, "I will not mount it without my master," [Śunaḥ] spoke. 32.79.
For Dharma, having attained his own true form, revealed that very nature;
the Bull (Dharma) proclaimed his own fame through the eloquent words of Dharma, appearing in the form of Kaunteya by means of his supreme compassion. 32.80–81.

Then, having mounted his chariot and passed beyond all the worlds of the kings in ascending order, he who is dear to the Lord of Śrī proceeded to the world of Indra, which is the highest of them all; this very [world] is yours. 32.82.
Having been told by the gods, "This is his place," he gazed upon Duryodhana,
who stood blazing above them all together with his brothers.
Seeing him, he became exceedingly enraged and closed his auspicious eyes.

"Where are my brothers and Kṛṣṇā, along with Karṇa and all my kinsmen? Where are Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the others, the sons of Hiḍimbā and the rest, and the Yādavas? Thus he questioned the gods, and they spoke to him.
"What have they done that they must suffer this here, and not others?"—to this he replied: "This man is a sinner who brings about the destruction of the earth;
he is suspicious of everyone, a betrayer of friends, and one who has turned his back on Nārāyaṇa. (32.85–86)

87. How did Duryodhana—who was deceitful, exceedingly crafty, cruel, and a hater of Viṣṇu and His devotees—attain that most excellent station? And how [did those who attained it] come to be knowers of all dharma and devoted to Nārāyaṇa?
Those dear to me are not seen here among those established in the supreme Dharma; rather,
I must remain wherever those virtuous ones abide—
even in hell, and certainly not here with this sinner.
"This [deed] is worthy of this most heroic son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra," having said this,
the deities dispatched a messenger for the king who desired to see his own people, along the path shown by him.

Having traveled some distance through that place filled with foul stench and oppressive darkness, the king, unable to endure the odor, desired to turn back; there he heard words like those of his own people: (32.91)
"Wait a moment, O Great King; by the power of your presence, our pain is not so great. Hearing this, Yudhiṣṭhira, alarmed by their distressed voices, asked, "Who are you? (32.92)
"I am Bhīma, I am Arjuna, I am Karṇa"—he heard as if these words were being spoken.
Having heard that, overcome with compassion and filled with grief and indignation, he said to the messenger: "Go wherever you wish; I will not go from here."
"I have no need for heaven if I must abandon such kinsmen as these.
Having been addressed thus, the messenger departed, while Yudhiṣṭhira remained right there. Then, out of affection for Yudhiṣṭhira, the gods, led by Indra, arrived at that place.

When they had departed, Yudhiṣṭhira—his mind free from delusion—beheld that supreme region of heaven; there his speech was not dejected, nor did he perceive even the gloom of foul odors. Then Dharma spoke here once more, manifesting his own true glory under the name of the son of Pāṇḍu: 32.96.
"For those who are virtuous, compassion is always seen as superior to righteousness; yet this [compassion] has been observed by me three times more abundantly in you.
Śakra also said to him: "This was shown to you falsely for the sake of Droṇa, O you of false speech.
This was told to you with great difficulty, for you did not place full trust in the words of Kṛṣṇa."
Indeed, by the command of Vāsudeva, no evil whatsoever shall befall even one who violates all laws of dharma;
for even the appearance of Brahman indicates a transgression that serves as the destruction of previously begun sin, just as [the sight of] poison [is destroyed by an antidote].
Look here at those led by Bhīma, established in happiness, well-formed, and being honored by the gods.

How could there be suffering for those lords of the foremost gods, who perceive the Supreme Brahman, whose virtuous deeds are perfectly pure, who are devoted to Kṛṣṇa, and whose bodies have been surrendered through supreme yoga? For these preeminent gods were born upon the earth desiring that the Lord might remove the burden of the world. (32.100)
Having gratified him with their purified thoughts and actions, they ascended again to heaven along with him.
Even today, those kings have not returned to the human state; therefore, they harbor hatred toward Suyodhana and the others.
Having plunged here into the waters of Viṣṇu’s foot and cast off this body, attain the state of a god.
Since these very wicked ones, Suyodhana and the others, having brought about the exhaustion of the karma they initiated,

will inevitably fall into the eternal state devoid of all happiness and filled with constant suffering, from which there is no return; whereas those who belong to the divine lineage, being entirely pure, shall at the appointed time attain their own primordial form.
"They shall attain liberation according to their respective degrees; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
(32.104) Having spoken thus, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, immersed himself right there in the Gaṅgā and cast off his body.
Immediately, having attained a divine form and being freed from all defects such as anger, he shone forth. (32.105)
Beholding all his own kinsmen standing very close to his original form,
he saw Bhīma near the Maruts, blazing in the midst of the host of Maruts;
and he also saw Kṛṣṇā near him, blazing with splendor, surpassing all others.
As he sought to touch her by the power of his past impressions, the king of the gods restrained him and said:
"This is indeed the very life-breath of the one beloved by the worlds, the Lord of the Supreme Life-Soul;
she is known by the name 'The Woman Dear as Life,' for she delights in this [body] which is composed of tranquility. (32.107–108)
The Wind-god’s beloved, likewise created by Puruṣottama for the enjoyment of the wind residing within your four bodies, and for the sake of your own beloveds along with your wives— therefore,
a greater joy arose from her for Bhīma, and subsequently for Pārtha as well. (32.109)

Then, among you yourselves, according to the sequence and in accordance with your qualities, this [earth] was born as the body of Vāyu; she whose form was pure and whose supreme body was freed from the conjunction of the *sattva* and other [guṇas]. And all of you Maruts remained established in your own bodies, devoid of that particular conjunction. (32.110–111)
"Even upon touching this wife of the Purifier, her supreme purity is not fully established now;
nor shall it ever be hereafter, as is the case for those who possess human bodies among the denizens of heaven.
Having spoken thus, he turned back toward him, himself suppressing his own human inclinations.
The Dharma, arising from the breasts of Hari, whose body was pure, embraced him; he became equal to Him in splendor.
Then all the sons of Pṛthā, filled with joy, entered their own abodes together with their original forms.
Thereafter, enjoying no less than before, they dwelt there forever.
There too, Kṛṣṇa met with them as before, for they were exceedingly devoted;
Kṛṣṇa likewise sported together with them, and Arjuna likewise with his chariot.
And all the other gods, including Śambhu, attained oneness with their own original forms.
But the sons of the gods, through the exhaustion of their merit alone, were born upon earth once their merit was spent.
Having experienced divine enjoyments for four thousand three hundred years, even while in human form, I—who am indeed a lord—fell into darkness with the thought that the world is unreal. (32.116–117)
Even among those [who suffer], there is a gradation of suffering here; yet the suffering in the Kali age is greater than all else.
Just as the happiness of Brahmā is supreme, so too is there a distinction for one who hates Hari even in liberation.
Some, having attained the state of Piśācas, Asuras, or Rākṣasas, remain devoted even to Viṣṇu.
Out of hatred, the gods, blinded by darkness, might hastily attain their own appropriate liberation at the proper time. When four thousand three hundred years of the Kali age had passed on earth,
that Bhīma was born again in the body of a Brahmin and declared the hidden reality of Hari to the Daityas.

At that very time, Kṛṣṇā was also born upon the earth to bring joy to Hari; she caused the great asuras to fall into blinding darkness. Viṣṇu, Parā, Arjuna, and the others were born for the sake of what must be done, in order to please Hari.
Furthermore, having all regained their own respective places, they shall attain liberation at the end of the age. (32.121)
Having attained the state of Hanumān, Aṅgada, and Vṛkodara having reached the Brahman-abode,
and Draupadī herself having attained the status of the Goddess of Speech, they all together went to the supreme liberation.
On earth, in the heavenly world, in the state of Brahmā, and in liberation, there is nothing superior to those two.

The Lord of Ramā, whose qualities are complete, is eternally satisfied by that constant and ever-vigorous devotion. (32.123) “Adorning himself among those of tawny hue, he bows down”; “Thus has that beautiful form been established for the sake of the body”;
“O Maghavan, that fame of yours through your greatness”—these and other such hymns (*sūktas*) are the authority for this. (32.124)
Furthermore, other Vedic statements, along with those spoken in the Pañcarātra and the Purāṇas,
were questioned here by Yudhiṣṭhira, and Bhīṣma spoke something on this matter even within the Mokṣadharma section.
(32.125) Thus, when Sukeśava and the others had departed for their own respective worlds, [the narrative continues] among the Yadus and Pāṇḍavas.
Parīkṣit and those born of his lineage, instructed by Vyāsa, protected the earth.

By them—those who were devoted to peace, who heard the *Bhārata* and other scriptures here, and who were knowers of all things—the dharma and knowledge of the *Sūtrānta* did not perish even in the Kali age, owing to the power of Vyāsa. (32.126–127)
When a thousand years had passed and all the [residents of] heaven had arrived,
those who were formerly burned by Rudra as he destroyed Tripura were born upon the surface of the earth;
they remained invisible even to the hosts of the great lords of sages during that great festival of the virtuous.
Even though Vyāsa had departed, the knowledge of the true reality was obtained by them from his tradition;

for, since false traditions had been eradicated and his own tradition had not perished, and because the authentic scriptures had been widely disseminated, even women attained this knowledge. (32.129–130)

The gods could not endure that the Daityas—who were eminently fit for attaining endless suffering—should acquire knowledge, just as one cannot endure a sacrificial cake licked by a dog or the Vedic revelation obtained by outcaste people. (Rigveda 1.140.6, 1.141.1, 10.54.1; Śiśupālavadha 32.131)
There shall be no downward course for those who know well; they will certainly attain eternal happiness.
But the darkness of the blind cannot be reached by the Asuras, nor can liberation ever be attained by them; thus the gods reflected.
These [beings] were created by Viṣṇu for the purpose of bestowing knowledge upon the virtuous and for the destruction of knowledge other than that. 32.132.
Then those gods, led by Viriñca and Śarva, approached Viṣṇu and made their request.
Praised with excellent hymns by those stationed on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, the Lord of Ramā, who is lauded by many,
granted them freedom from fear and in an instant assumed the form of a most beautiful infant.
He who was born here as the first of the three Puruṣas, known as Śuddhodana and called a Jina—Viṣṇu cast his newborn infant far away in the field named Gayā.
Not knowing that their own child had departed, they, upon seeing the infant Hari, believed him to be their own. (32.135)
Seeing their Vedic rituals at that time, Keśava laughed with his very body.
Seeing him laughing as soon as he was born, Viṣṇu was asked by those who were greatly amazed, and he replied:
"I am Buddha," he said to them because of his eternal awakening; thus he revealed the vision of the Buddha. (32.136)
Nevertheless, observing their lack of faith, Janārdana called to mind all the gods;
having understood what was in their minds, they dispatched their own hosts of weapons against him.
As soon as he was born, he swallowed all the weapons, beginning with the trident, belonging to Śiva and the others.
To utterly delude the Daityas, the self-controlled one withdrew his own discus that had been released against them;
having made it his seat, he sat upon it. Then the hosts of gods, having prostrated before him, departed for their own abodes, and the Daityas accepted the words of the Jina as their own. (32.138–139)

Having abandoned those ignoble and evil teachings, all of them, deluded by the best of gods, entered into blinding darkness while firmly remembering that "all knowledge is momentary, and 'I am' is unreal. Nārāyaṇa, too, having approached the host of the lords of the gods and having related their entire conduct, [departed].
Questioned by them, he spoke of his own heart’s conviction regarding the meaning of the Buddhist scriptures: the liberation from the bond of existence.

(32.141) "Since all these particularities, such as moments and so forth, pass away by their very nature, therefore—even though there is stability—I have stated that everything is momentary, because it relies upon those particularities. (32.142)

Since that which possesses [the attribute] and the attribute itself are never distinct, being always endowed with the power that brings about its own manifestation, therefore there is no difference between this entire [universe], which is momentary, and that which is of a stable nature. (32.143) "I am the knower, eternally one and supreme; for all this is always to be led by me, since it is not independent."

Therefore, I have declared that the universe is of the nature of consciousness; how then could it be insentient by nature? Since I am Śaṃśīlaka and am exalted as the one named Śūnya, that which is called "void" (śūnya) must be established by me as being of a form opposed to defects and free from defects, while the other is nameless (anāmā) in every respect.
"By this very [means], that which is non-existent by name alone becomes non-existence itself, because it is so; 32.145.
All of this that has been spoken by me should be understood in this way, and there is nothing in it to be rejected.
Having thus awakened the gods, the divine Buddha dwelt together with them.
Having returned to his own abode, he remained there in another form, both distinct and yet one body, as he desired.
Then the Jina, established in the doctrine proclaimed by the Buddha, formulated yet another system;
and through both the Buddhist and Jain doctrines, all the Daityas and Śakas attained great joy.

The thirty [gods], having obtained the scripture spoken by the Buddha known as *Praśāntavidyā*—which is another name for the essence of the entire Veda—attained satisfaction; for those who abide in this *Yama*, liberation is attained without delay. Other humans as well, having embraced the true tradition of Viṣṇu found in the *Bhārata* and other texts, [attain the same].
The Daityas, performing sacrifices, attained the supreme goal; yet, out of the power of their wrath, they could not endure it.

Having performed extensive asceticism dedicated to Śiva, they obtained from him a world-deluding and mighty power; having acquired this, they were born upon earth and created delusion, propounding distinctions through fallacious reasoning. (32.149–150)
"For their downfall and for the liberation of the virtuous, the birth of Bhīma has been described here;
furthermore, Durgā will descend into a brahmin family and slay the host of asuras.
Then, having reached the end of the Kali age, which is devoid of the primordial auspicious qualities known as Dharma—
In this world, Indra and the other gods, led by Śakra—the destroyer of the three cities—went to the ocean of milk.

Having been entreated with hymns of praise by them for the sake of the world’s welfare, that Nārāyaṇa of inconceivable power appeared in the village called Śambhala in the house of the sage named Viṣṇuyaśas. (32.152–153)
From the sound "kā" of the syllable *kaleḥ*, this Kalkī possesses knowledge (*jñāna*) and the essence (*kala*) of happiness (*ka*);
thus he is called Kalkī. By him, the destruction of all bandits was accomplished from that very day.
Having slain those who lived unrighteously and were averse to Hari, the horseman left no people remaining.
He established a bridge of dharma—namely, knowledge and devotion to himself—among his own subjects.
(32.155) Such are the infinite noble deeds of Hari, as well as his forms and excellent qualities;
he whose name is "Brahman" and "Ananta," and from whom all defects have eternally departed. (32.156)

The sage named Ānandatīrtha, also known as Supūrṇaprajña, composed this work at Badarī, having been commanded by Nārāyaṇa, the sole Lord of the world; he was the disciple of that very Lord, and by His grace, [he mastered] all the Vedas along with the Pañcarātras, including their secret compendiums. (32.157)
The Vedas along with the Itihāsas joined by the Purāṇas, as well as all other sciences,
have been presented here correctly. This work, which provides a definitive determination of the meaning of all the Śāstras and follows specifically the path of the Mahābhārata,
was composed by this very author for the sole purpose of pleasing Hari, the teacher and progenitor of the worlds.

Since there is no definitive resolution for all divergent doctrines without him—just as there is none for all discordant words—Kṛṣṇa composed the Brahma-sūtras; furthermore, he provided their commentary because the supreme nature of the Person, though declared in the Sūtras, had been concealed by other great lords of the Asuras. 32.159.
Having composed the Sūtras while forcefully proclaiming the identity of the individual soul and the Lord, he brought them to light;

32.160. Having composed an excellent commentary at the command of Vyāsa, as well as separate commentaries on the Upaniṣads, and having established that all these declare Hari to be the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama); 32.161.
This third body of Pavana, which illuminates the true meaning of the *Bhārata*,
composed this work— this man of exalted learning in whom those devoted to the feet of Hari take delight.
(32.162) “The young women brought forth Daśapramati for the milking of this bull, his third [offspring].”
"The wise lords, by their power, brought forth from the depths the emergence of the Great One's form;
when Mātariśvan churned Him who was hidden in secret, following the flow of honey from of old"—
all this as stated in such passages, and likewise in the Purāṇas and the Pañcarātra.
All the discourses proclaimed herein have been set forth according to the determinations of the Vedas, Itihāsas, and other scriptures.
Therefore, this excellent work is the cause for attaining all human goals, beginning with dharma and ending with liberation.
What need is there to mention its other virtues? By this alone, Nārāyaṇa attains supreme satisfaction.
He whose three divine forms are proclaimed in the Vedic word—
“That is indeed visible,” thus is established the great splendor (*bharga*) of the God;
the first is the age (*vayas*) consisting of Rāma’s speech, and the second form is the nourishment (*pṛkṣas*).
This book has been composed by me for Keśava, who is the third [manifestation] of Madhu;
may Viṣṇu, who is complete with all virtues and devoid of all defects, my supreme friend, be pleased—indeed, he is already pleased with me. (32.166–167)
Thus ends [the chapter titled] "The Ascent of the Pāṇḍavas to Heaven" in the *Śrīmahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
The thirty-second chapter is completed; this work [ends here].
Oṃ. The Glorious Yamaka-Bhārata (The Essential Meaning of the Mahābhārata), composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya.
One should meditate on that Supreme Bliss which the Mother [attains] when she has attained the Supreme Bliss consisting of her husband;
which is the Supreme Bliss eternally abandoned by the stages of life beginning with that of the householder (dampatya);
and which is indeed the Karālola-cakra, the supreme state beyond all parts (kala). 1.
He whose mace is the purifying wind, who has always been Vyāsa, the ever-purifying one;
2 / Whose mind the goddess Ramā did not grasp, nor did even the Earth, the sustainer of all, enter his mind;
he whose blissful abode the Supreme Person enjoys as his sovereign lord—3 /
When Vāsudeva, the Unborn, displayed his supreme splendor among the supreme ones, he was not one whose mind was fixed on pride; indeed, there was no pride in the mind of the Unborn Vāsudeva.
He was born from Devakī because of her compassionate nature (*kyanta*). 4.
The gods spoke thus to Devakī: "O Goddess, this world indeed always belongs to the gods.
Led by Vasudeva, he was brought to Gokula, which was well-protected by Vasudeva.
There, Yaśodā considered Kṛṣṇa to be her own son, a son of pure character.
Gokula flourished from that God who emerged from the midst of the wondrously agitated universe,
and there he performed the slaying of Pūtanā by means of his own exceedingly pure nature. Now, with the big toe of his lotus-foot, he shook the cart of Vātāpi.

The cowherd girl, whose face was restless with the saliva from her longing for him, spread protection for him who was free from pride; she beheld the world within his mouth, which was filled with fire and extended far.
She understood that this world was the illusory power (*māyā*) of the Lord of the Universe, whose own *māyā* was exceedingly vast. (8–9)
Garga performed auspicious rites for him; he whose deeds were well-spoken performed his duties.
He spoke of himself as the origin of the world, though his name was Vāsudeva.
His friend was named Bala, his elder brother, who was indeed possessed of innate strength.
And whose is this ancient couch upon which Viṣṇu was incessantly worshipping?
By him was the son of Diti named Vātaraya struck down— he who was swift as the wind and possessed a wheel of straw—
and he was brought low while attempting to devour his own most tender self with a throat-obstructing [snare], having become utterly childish.
He, who delights in the earth, delights in the lotus-eyed one;

he, who delights in the form of a child, delights in his own cowherd community. He, who delights in the fresh butter [navanītamadaḥ] among the cowherd women, follows his mother when she has become angry, having been addressed with words of reproach. 13. His mother, overcome with anger, followed him, having been addressed with words of reproach.
She took refuge in that bowing Lord, who is himself bowed down by her very thought;

he who is infinite and who, being without pride, then led her—who was herself free from pride—to the state of Dāmodara, he who delighted the beautiful woman with the fragrance of his own belly. 14–15.

He performed the *arjunana* rite, through which one always attains the name of Arjuna; and those two, being praised by him, went to their own abode, for that very name is one's own liberation. Then the cowherds made their dwelling in Vṛndāvana, a place of refuge for the world upon the earth.
There, Śauri became the slayer of the demon Baka, he who is eternally the destroyer of the Asuras;

he who slew Vatsatanūka and protected the world with his own effort like that of a cow protecting her calf; that immortal one, together with his elder brother, took away the calves—the immortals who were like the calves of the cowherds. (17–18)
That glorious Lord danced in this world; may his fatigue never come to us.
Having led the serpent to the edge of the water, he did not [leave him] at the edge of the water today.
Having slain the foolish Dhenuka by force, and having killed Pralamba along with his wife Kheṭasadhenuka.
Having protected Vraja by drinking the fire from the moving and the stationary, he who protects with immortality;
even by means of the mountain, protection was afforded to Vraja, and by him, protection for his own protection was also performed.
Manifesting his own power to Śakra, he conquered the universe through his very self. 20–21.
There the Lord of the Gopīs sports, he who destroys the pride of beautiful women overcome by love;
his singular body is full bliss, yet though he is the light of the universe and the purifier, his singular body is bliss itself.
22. Now, when the two lords of Galaga had been slain, [the Lord], brought by the son of Śvaphalka, entered the city of the lords of Galaga.

Having broken that most excellent royal bow, he himself struck down the best of kings with it. Crushing a fierce elephant along with its own force, he entered the arena with his army, following a path of formidable power.
Having slain the two powerful wrestlers Kaṃsa and Saṃka, those two strong men were then liberated.

To Sāndīpani, the illuminator of the lamp of knowledge, he gave back his dead son; for the sake of his guru, he shattered the darkness of ignorance and eternally dispelled the thick gloom of nescience. Having conquered the King of Magadha, he forever satisfied that king of yogis who holds the self as his own.
Following his own inclination, he built a beautiful city that served as a dwelling for the son of Subhadrā;

having violently slain Śiśupāla— the best of the Kṣatriyas who possessed great royal power along with his elephant forces— he obtained the daughter of Bhīṣma, the most excellent of women, from Śiśupāla.
By him, the two restless children were protected, the Yavana was slain, and his stainless fame—vast, ceaseless, and purifying the entire world—was spread abroad.
Satyabhāmā and Jāmbavatī were his wives, as were Vindā and others, who possessed the luster of the sun and the moon. 28.

From Modarata, Hari obtained his eldest son Pradyumna; from Modarata [he obtained] the son [of Pradyumna]. Those gods who were the lords of his retinue became, through their human nature, the lords of pleasure (Rati).
That which was filled with poison, serpents, and darkness—neither the wind nor the serpent [could overcome it]. 29–30.
By him who struck down the lords of the Rākṣasas, such as Hiḍimba and Baka,

and by whom immeasurable joy was manifested in Bhīma, may that remnant of his protection reach me. (31) Then, while they were still within the enclosure of the women’s quarters, he heard from the king that they had arrived there.

Then, as they strove to see her, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Balarāma, led that daughter of Pṛthā away from them. Indra made those [enemies] dwell in his own abode, while Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme, made them dwell in his own abode.
With those whose pride was increased by their own strength, yet who were humbled by him, he protected the Dharma.
Out of affection, he established a firm friendship for the sake of conciliating Bali;
indeed, through that very birth as a man, he was especially distinguished by his power, and even more so by his subsequent human incarnation.
(34) His father acted to remove the humiliation [of Bali], while the gods, who were free from humiliation, acted to remove the humiliation of the king.
He who was the enemy of the lords of hell became the enemy of all the lords of hell;
he who had dwelt in heaven with the best of gods took his pleasure in the company of Satyabhāmā, who was not among the best of goddesses.
He sported in a forest containing all seasons with the moon at night, and in a forest devoid of the moon during the day.

From the desire for the welfare of the world, he manifested his own power through the manifestation of his form; among the foremost heroes of the gods, he was the Lord of Life (Jīveśvara) who destroys the enemies of others. Having marched against the city of the enemy, that destroyer of foes bestowed auspiciousness upon the son of Pṛthā.
Having gone to the city of Śakra, he gave the forest to Agni, for he was intent on the welfare of the virtuous.

That man, the foremost among the devotees of Śiva, could not endure the preeminence of the best of Brahmins; he shook him off with his own formidable power, which surpassed even the boon of Indra and the boon of Rudra. 38–39.

Having conquered the earth without exception by force, having subdued the kings who possessed all desired objects, and having taken wealth from all directions by means of his own strength and the essence of his power,
he then caused the sons of Pṛthā to perform the king of sacrifices, which was presided over by the likes of Indra and Rudra.
By him worship was obtained, and the King of Cedi was cut down as if by a boat that had entered its course.
(41) By whom Saubha and Karuṣa were slain, and by whom those two, Bhaka and Rūṣa, were made cool and radiant;
and who conquered Rudra in battle for the sake of Bāṇa, when the moon fell at his feet in prostration. (42)

The most fierce one, the bestower of destruction, effortlessly created a most terrible fever against the excellent [demons]; burning away the universe as a mere sport, he made the entire world his own playground. By the power of whose vast majesty Pārtha slew the asuras through the great strength of the Lord of Creatures.
By the granting of a boon from this very Lord of the World, and by the impelling of Him whose sound follows after [all things],

that Balarāma— possessing strength through His entry— forcibly dragged away the city along with its forces. Indeed, he was called Kurupati (Lord of the Kurus), and because of him, they say the Yamunā became dark and vast, as if it were the Yamunā herself personified.

Because of his strength, Vṛkodara brought the Krodhavaśas under his control; by virtue of his power, he reached a place that was unapproachable for others, and another abode that was inaccessible even to the gods.
Because he bore a weight that could not be moved by mountains, serpents, and the like, due to his capacity to carry a great burden.
Dharma was also a source of fear for Arjuna, by whom even Bhīma—who was licking at his own rashness—was surpassed;

for Dharma was not able to restrain Nahuṣa, nor were the son of Droṇa and the others able to restrain him. Neither King Yudhiṣṭhira nor Karṇa could check him, by whom the best of Brahmins was destroyed; yet he had mastered the supreme Brahma-weapon. (47–48)
By the command of Keśava, Bhīma—who considered himself the sole lord—endured everything with his mind, as if it were his own duty toward his elder brother and for the sake of serving him;
indeed, that Kīcaka was bound within himself by that foremost of devotees. 49.
His proud companions fell together for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
by their devotion, Pārtha and Bhīma were favored, while the two kings of the Gopas were as if captured.
For the sake of liberation from debt and for the sake of a fair exchange, the two heroes gradually released them in turn for a fair exchange.
Through boundless devotion, she entered the service of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī);
because her body was half that of Yamī, she did not suffer from Bhīma, nor did she suffer from Bhīma [the Asura].
She restrained Ajātaśatru (Yudhiṣṭhira), who desired to touch [her], while he himself remained composed and free from enemies.
This Śrī is the one who delights eternally in the form of Śaṃ; this Śrī is the beloved of the gods, born of Aditi.
(53) She who, with a mind that is both with and without mind, follows the Infinite One incessantly;
and he who, dissolving everything, brought all that is inauspicious to its dissolution—(54)
He went as a messenger by the mouth of the Lord, who, for the sake of Pārtha, had previously manifested his own vast form (*bahutanu*) while desiring to diminish his own body (*vahutanutām*);
he was one who, by the power of his vision, destroyed the distress of the people born from the river of heavy ears. 55.

Though dependent on his own infinite power, he did not incite his kinsmen; though independent of others, Arjuna did not regard his enemies as having equal allies because of Sunītha’s excellent counsel. And rushing through the enemy armies, he swiftly brought about a multitude of corpses among those who were not superior.

By whom [was he protected], that Pārtha, the slayer of Jayadratha and the destroyer of enemies on his chariot, who—though even in separation from him—remained forever established in his body; and by whom was he supported, that lord who resembles Bharata, who is filled with water (ambhas), and who overcomes the splendor of the sun? 58.

Bhīma, who by his impetuosity overcomes others, forcibly subdues them with his splendor; he who, through his fullness of grace, is formidable and has no enemies because they are entirely filled [with devotion], burnt those placed in the fire of his wrath by the strength of his own arms. 59–60.
Kṛṣṇa, the most trusted friend of Bhīma, by whom his own heart was shattered, caused the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—who had been established in his mind as "good sons"—to be slain by Bhīma;
he showed his own enemies with their bodies torn apart by Bhīma, their bodies indeed ripped asunder. 61.

He was always a benefactor to Kṛṣṇā, perfectly wise, and dear to her; yet he was always a source of harm to Hari. Then, by means of a great arrow that drank up the power of the son of Droṇa’s weapon—its strength having been swallowed—he brought about the death of Abhimanyu’s son, who had been wearing garments that were like the death of his father. 62–63.

And his protection was well-secured by Janārdana, who is ever devoted to the welfare of others and who, through his devotion to his master, holds no love for his own life; and Bhīṣma, having reached his end, bestowed upon him supreme knowledge that grants final liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
He made the Veda even more excellent in its qualities than it was for the sons of Pāṇḍu, surpassing even his own name.

By him, through his well-born [disciples], the horse-sacrifice of Hari was performed; and by the sons of Pāṇḍu, who were well-born, noble, and self-controlled, as well as by Vyāsa himself, who was noble, self-controlled, and possessed of a pure soul.

Thereafter, that Supreme Lord, the beloved of Śrī, whose nature is incomparable bliss, who is unborn yet born in the form of a horse, and who is the very embodiment of truth, sported with the sons of Pāṇḍu while protecting the earth through those most excellent sons of Pāṇḍu;
he bestowed upon them their final, auspicious state suited to them, and granted them the supreme, stainless knowledge.
There too, he, the supreme and infinite one, rejoiced happily; there too, he, endowed with life and Indirā, and eternally united with the Indirā of great virtues, took delight and was joyful. (68–69)

Thus, all the forms of Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the gods, are full of bliss; they shine forth extensively, without interval, and are devoid of impurity. O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, your Māyā is exceedingly difficult to overcome.
Tell me, who in this world would ever touch your feet?
(O Rāma, you who grant the worlds, you who bestow the Vedas,
you who are the son of Daśaratha, you who are the lord of the earth, you are mine.)
I bow to that divine one, the slayer of the asuras, whom the lords of the gods always recognize as our thought;
O Vāsudeva, supreme nectar, progenitor of all the gods! 72.
O Vāsudeva, O supreme nectar, O embodiment of knowledge, salutations be unto You! 73.
O God of gods, O protector of the world of the gods, O great ocean of perfect bliss, O omniscient Lord, O Consort of Ramā, O God of gods, O protector of the worlds! 74.
He who fashioned the entirety of ancient knowledge; he who fashioned the entirety of ancient knowledge; he who fashioned the entirety of ancient knowledge.

O Lord of infinite and boundless prowess, O Master, you who fashioned her who knows all the Purāṇas; O Infinite One, O Boundless One, O Abode of Lakṣmī, O You of immeasurable being, enriched with great qualities, O Supreme One, enriched with all virtues! 75–76.

(77) There is none higher than this supreme Keśava, nor is there anyone equal to him, the source of happiness and beauty;
this excellent vow of ours has been perpetually maintained as a most noble and auspicious oath. (78)

This narrative of Kṛṣṇa, which restrains the senses and is spoken by the one who has restrained himself at the sacred ford of Suśatī, is always full of devotion toward the Supreme Lord, overflowing with all excellence, and free from sorrow;
thus, the name Nārāyaṇa is worshipped at the sacred ford of Avaka, while the name Surāyaṇa is honored by the gods. 79.
He is full of all virtues, yet He is even more full than those who possess full knowledge, desire, and devotion.
80. Thus ends the *Śrīmadyamakabhārata*, composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within the Supreme Prāṇa, the lover of the Goddess of Speech.
